Title: Comment from Pamela Elders
Comment:
I object to OPM's proposed new rule that would reclassify 50,000 federal workers to "at-will" employees. "At-will" employment will make it easier to fire any employee for political rather than merit-based reasons. Under "at-will" employment, no reason is required for termination. And, there is little recourse for appeal. 

US civil servants are not political appointees and as such are not subject to removal by Presidential authority. The Civil Service was established to create a professional, non-partisan workforce rather than one based on cronyism. Fealty to the President and his agenda should never be a condition of civil service employment and yet, this is exactly what this proposed regulation seeks to establish. The regulation authors say the reclassification will make it easier to fire employees for "intentionally subverting Presidential directives." This is moving our government further in the direction of a dictatorship. This reclassification effort is a huge over-reach by the Executive Branch which will undermine the federal workforce and reduce public trust in government. 

Another reason given for changing civil servants to at-will employees is that the current protections employees enjoy (e.g., a fair workplace) purportedly makes it difficult "to hold employees accountable." If that is the case, improve the evaluation system. 

The drafters of this rule assert that "positions will remain career jobs filled on a non-partisan basis." This is a disingenuous claim. At-will employment undermines career employment. Job security and due process for employees are critical assurances to those who seek a career job in the federal government. These do not rule out a robust training and evaluation program to ensure good job performance. 

In addition, the assertion that one can be fired without due process for "intentionally subverting Presidential directives" undermines the professional, non-partisan character of civil service positions. The message is clear. Obey or be gone. No professional person would choose to work under such conditions. Our government has long upheld model employment regulations. Let's not abandon our commitment to a fair working conditions for a President's political gain.

Comment:
I am a private individual strongly opposing the Office of Personnel Management’s proposed regulation – [Docket ID OPM-2025-0004] RIN 3206-AO80.

The stated reason for the proposed rule is to “allow agencies to quickly remove employees from critical positions who engage in misconduct, perform poorly, or . . .  intentionally [subvert] Presidential directives.”  (Summary 90 FR 17182)  However, this appears to be a thinly disguised effort to impose a “loyalty to President Trump test” for federal employees and fire those employees who are considered not sufficiently loyal to the President.  

The proposed rule may give “lip service” to the E.O. 14171 “directive” that an employee is “not required to pledge personal loyalty to the President or his policies” (Section 213.3501  90 FR 17201), however, if that employee is classified as “at will” and is fired because, for example, he or she is registered to a political party other than the one currently in office, how does that employee fight that wrongful termination?

The Summary states that “[a]gency supervisors report great difficulty removing employees for poor performance or misconduct.” (Summary 90 FR 17182).  There is no cite supporting that assertion.  And while making the process easier for supervisors to take adverse actions for employee misconduct may be a worthwhile objective, reclassifying employees in order to strip them of employees’ appeal rights is not logical and from what I have read may not be lawful. The December 2016 publication “Addressing Misconduct in the Federal Civil Service: Management Perspectives”  states at page 3: 

“Ultimately, what the survey data indicate is that there is some disagreement among supervisors about how many rights the system should provide to employees, including the desired extent of appeal and grievance rights. But, there is little disagreement on one crucial point – supervisors overwhelmingly want a merit-based system where employees are protected from managers who either make mistakes or act in bad faith. “
https://www.mspb.gov/studies/researchbriefs/Addressing_Misconduct_in_the_Federal_Civil_Service_Management_Perspectives_1363799.pdf   

The proposed rule does not address the problem of underperforming employees.  Quoting from the OPM Rule “Upholding Civil Service Protections and Merit System Principles”  [Docket ID: OPM-2023-0013]  RIN 3206-AO56 :

“[T]he characteristics of an employee's job—including whether the employee works on policy—has nothing to do with an employee's performance. Schedule F sought to streamline terminations based on the type of work that an employee performs, not based on how well the employee performs. It is therefore difficult to understand how Schedule F can be reconciled with its purported aim of addressing poor performance.”  89 FR 24995

In my opinion it is not “difficult to understand” how reclassification addresses poor performance, it makes no rational sense whatsoever.  

I am 74 years old and retired.  I receive Social Security based on my 40 years of work and rely on Medicare for health insurance coverage.  It is very important to me that the Social Security Administration employs reliable, knowledgeable employees and that human beings in the office are accessible by telephone, in person and online.

I rely on the Department of Health and Human Resources to be fully staffed with reliable and knowledgeable employees.

I do not trust that the proposed rule will improve the delivery of services by expert and experienced employees.  I believe it will greatly reduce the quality of services (paid for with our taxes) provided by federal agencies.

Title: Comment from Alexander Tsai
Comment:
Comment on Proposed Rule: "Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service" (Docket Number: RIN 3206-AO72)

Introduction

I am submitting this comment as an academic physician-scientist with more than a decade of experience conducting NIH-funded research at Massachusetts General Hospital with appointments at Harvard Medical School and Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. As a researcher with extensive experience in the NIH grant system, I am writing to express significant concerns regarding the section of the proposed rule that designates employees with "substantive participation and discretionary authority in agency grantmaking" as potentially occupying "policymaking positions" that could be reclassified under Schedule Policy/Career.

Specific Concerns with the Proposed Rule

The proposed rule identifies grant-making as "an important form of policymaking" and suggests that employees with "substantive discretionary role in how federal funding gets allocated may occupy policymaking positions." This characterization fundamentally misunderstands the scientific grant review process at agencies like NIH and NSF, which rely on scientific merit and peer review rather than political considerations.

The stated purpose of this rule is to allow agencies to "quickly remove employees from critical positions who engage in misconduct, perform poorly, or undermine the democratic process by intentionally subverting Presidential directives." When applied to scientific grant-making, this creates a dangerous framework that could politicize what should be an independent, merit-based process.

Evidence-Based Arguments

The primacy of American scientific research in the world depends on insulating technical grant review from political influence:

1. NIH and NSF grant review processes are designed to fund the most scientifically promising research through rigorous peer review. The NIH is "arguably the most important institution shaping the rate and direction of scientific research" with significant implications for human well-being. Even small changes to how funding is allocated could have massive effects on social welfare.

2. International examples demonstrate the severe consequences when politics interferes with scientific funding decisions. Soviet biology, which had achieved peak prominence by the mid-1930s, was essentially ruined by Lysenko's politically-backed campaign against genetics (Ptushenko, Genetics, 2021). The damage was so profound that even after Lysenkoism was officially renounced in 1964, it took decades for Russian science to recover from this political interference.

3. Similarly, in countries like China where "personal relationships have affected government decisions, such as the review of scientific grants," scientific integrity issues have damaged progress despite massive investments (Zeng et al. Dev World Bioeth, 2010). Studies indicate that politicization of science funding leads to inefficient allocation of resources, limiting China's ability to achieve global scientific leadership commensurate with its spending (Shu et al. Minerva, 2022; Yu et al. Res Policy, 2022).

4. The existing peer review system, while imperfect, provides important guardrails against bias. These decisions should be made by scientific experts, not political appointees.

Specific Recommendations for Improvement

I propose the following improvements to the rule:

1. Explicitly exclude scientific grant review personnel at NIH, NSF, and similar research agencies from the Schedule Policy/Career designation. Scientific merit review is a technical function, not a political one.

2. Provide a clear, narrow definition of what constitutes "substantive discretionary authority" in grant-making that distinguishes between technical evaluation based on scientific merit (which should remain protected) and truly discretionary policy decisions.

3. Add specific safeguards ensuring the independence of scientific peer review committees from political interference, including explicit protections for review panel members.

4. Require transparency in any actions that would redesignate positions related to scientific grant review, including advance notice and comment periods specific to each affected role.

Conclusion

While improving accountability in government service is a worthwhile goal, applying at-will employment status to scientific grant-making personnel poses significant risks to American scientific leadership. The independence of the scientific grant-making process from political influence has been a cornerstone of American research excellence and must be preserved.

Title: Comment from Rachel F
Comment:
I strongly oppose the implementation or revival of the “Schedule F” classification for federal employees. This proposal threatens the merit-based civil service system that has underpinned a professional, nonpartisan federal workforce for over a century.

First and foremost, the creation of Schedule F directly undermines the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which was enacted to combat the spoils system and establish a merit-based hiring process for federal employees. By allowing a broad swath of career civil servants—particularly those involved in policy-making or analysis—to be reclassified and potentially terminated without cause, Schedule F opens the door to politically motivated hiring and firing. This is antithetical to the principle of an apolitical civil service enshrined in 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8), which mandates that federal employment decisions be based on merit and free from political influence.

Moreover, the vague and sweeping criteria for inclusion in Schedule F violate the due process protections guaranteed by 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which requires cause and procedural safeguards for the removal of career federal employees. Stripping thousands of workers of these protections not only weakens accountability but also risks chilling expert advice and dissent within agencies—undermining the very effectiveness of government operations.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is also bound by 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to support the merit system principles. Implementing Schedule F contradicts this statutory mission and places undue political pressure on career professionals, compromising the integrity and continuity of federal programs across administrations.

In conclusion, the Schedule F proposal poses a grave threat to the foundational principles of good governance, civil service independence, and the rule of law. I urge the administration and OPM to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement or revive this dangerous classification.

Title: Comment from Richard Levy
Comment:
I am writing to express my concerns with this proposed rule change. In short, I think the rule change would open the civil service up to political influence at the expense of carrying out the law and serving the American taxpayers. I am a federal employee yet these views are my own and do not necessarily represent my agency. I am writing as a concerned citizen and a student of good governance, on my own time.

1. The rule conflates issues around performance and conduct with those of allegiance to policy. From my experience, issues with performance revolve around doing work of poor quality, not adequately fulfilling or understanding the assignment, or otherwise acting in ways that do not serve the mission. Conduct issues concern things like consistently showing up to work late, taking excessive breaks, or acting uncooperatively with colleagues. Issues around not following allegiance to policy are another matter, and would concern things like failing to follow the law or a legal Presidential directive.

I'd like to see the evidence of staff not following laws or Presidential directives. From my experience, staff carry out laws and Presidential directives regardless of whether they agree; and if they don't, they switch jobs or quit on their own. For example, some staff at my agency did not agree with the Executive Order (https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/ending-radical-and-wasteful-government-dei-programs-and-preferencing/) which led to the taking down of materials that referenced Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion. Among other factors, we did not see it as a good use of time. But my agency did it. Similarly, prior administrations have made requests of staff that they may have disagreed with, yet they were carried out.

Staff have been trained that if we have concerns, we comply, and then complain. Historically, staff have had the option of contacting the Office of Special Counsel or Inspectors General offices if they were concerned about waste, fraud, and abuse. As such, it has been disturbing these agencies had agency heads fired so early in the administration.

If staff are slow-walking or not carrying out directives now, it would behoove the administration to figure out why there has been a change in behavior. I think it's because this administration has represented a departure from legal or democratic ways of conducting government business. For example, various Executive Orders have directed actions which many consider illegal, such as shutting down federal agencies unilaterally, even though Congress has the legal right to pass laws to create or shut down agencies. It is especially troubling now because the Executive, Legislative, and Judicial branches are all led by the same party, so the administration is acting outside the legal system even when it ostensibly has the support it needs.

2. As for addressing poor performance and conduct, I find that agencies do not use a tool at their disposal which would make their lives much easier: Assigning another manager either to manage a poor performer (from my experience, such performers are rare), or assigning that manager to manage existing staff so the current manager can focus on the poor performer.

3. As it were, the civil service protections are admittedly a double-edged sword. The same protections which protect civil servants from undue political influence -- say, fabricating or withholding data to make an administration look better -- also serve to make it difficult to remove them. However, removing these protections makes any administration vulnerable to having the next administration come in and reverse them, thus catching the protection-removing administration in its own web. It would be short-sighted for any administration to remove these protections.

Thank you for your consideration of my comments.
Rich Levy

Title: Comment from Alexis  Gibson
Comment:
Dear Office of Personnel Management:

I write to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule entitled "Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service", published on April 23, 2025. The proposal seeks to exempt a newly defined category of “Schedule Policy/Career” positions from the statutory protections of 5 U.S.C. Chapters 43 and 75, including the right to appeal adverse personnel actions to the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB). This proposal is inconsistent with governing federal statutes and exceeds the scope of executive authority.

1. Statutory Protections Cannot Be Waived by Regulation

Congress has clearly and intentionally established a legal framework that governs performance-based and adverse actions affecting federal employees. Under 5 U.S.C. §§ 4303 and 7513, covered employees are entitled to procedural protections, including advance notice, an opportunity to respond, and the ability to appeal to the MSPB. These protections were codified by the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (CSRA), which replaced earlier patchwork systems with a unified statutory framework. These rights are not discretionary, nor can they be modified or withdrawn by regulation.

While the statute (5 U.S.C. § 7511(b)(2)) allows for the exclusion of certain positions from Chapter 75, such as political appointees or positions designated as “confidential or policy-determining,” it does not authorize the wholesale transfer of career civil service employees into newly created at-will categories through regulatory action. The authority to exclude positions from Chapter 75 is limited in scope and purpose and must be interpreted narrowly to avoid undermining Congress’s express intent.

2. The Proposal Violates the Separation of Powers

By unilaterally removing procedural protections through the creation of the “Schedule Policy/Career” classification, the Executive Branch is attempting to do through regulation what Congress has expressly prohibited—removing career employees without just cause, due process, or meaningful appeal. This raises significant constitutional concerns under the separation of powers doctrine. The Executive cannot override or nullify Congressional enactments through rulemaking.

The U.S. Supreme Court has recognized that where Congress has created a comprehensive remedial scheme (as with the CSRA), judicial and administrative bodies must follow that framework. The proposed rule contradicts this well-established principle and risks subjecting the Executive Branch to legal challenge on administrative and constitutional grounds.

3. Undermining Merit System Principles

The proposed rule would have a chilling effect on the integrity and independence of the civil service. Career employees in policy-influencing roles—many of whom are technical experts or senior supervisors—would become vulnerable to arbitrary dismissal, political coercion, or reprisal for faithfully executing laws as enacted by Congress. This undermines 5 U.S.C. § 2301, which mandates that employees be retained based on performance and protected from arbitrary action and personal favoritism.

Removing these protections does not enhance accountability—it creates a workforce subject to political influence and fear, contrary to the principles that have guided the civil service for over a century.

Conclusion

For the reasons stated above, I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety. The authority to alter statutory employee protections rests solely with Congress, and any attempt to circumvent that authority via regulation is unlawful and harmful to the public interest. I respectfully request that OPM reconsider this proposed rule in light of its legal and constitutional infirmities.

Title: Comment from Sarah Linden
Comment:
I write in strong opposition to the proposed rule titled *"Restoring Accountability to Policy-Influencing Positions Within the Federal Workforce"* (Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004-0001). Far from promoting accountability, this rule would dangerously politicize the career civil service, subverting the merit principles codified in the **Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (CSRA)** and undermining constitutional protections that guard against arbitrary and politically motivated employment actions.

This proposed rule directly conflicts with the core mandates of the **CSRA (5 U.S.C. §§ 1101 et seq.)**, which enshrines merit system principles as the bedrock of federal employment. Section 2301(b)(8) of the CSRA specifically provides that “employees should be protected against arbitrary action, personal favoritism, or coercion for partisan political purposes.” The Schedule F framework contemplated by this rule would strip due process protections from potentially thousands of career civil servants—precisely the type of arbitrary, political interference the CSRA was enacted to prevent.

Moreover, the rule attempts to redefine and expand the scope of "policy-influencing positions" without statutory authority. Congress has not delegated OPM or the Executive Branch the discretion to bypass civil service protections wholesale by executive fiat. In fact, courts have consistently held that the **nondelegation doctrine** prohibits agencies from arrogating such sweeping powers absent a clear congressional mandate (*Whitman v. American Trucking Ass'ns*, 531 U.S. 457 (2001)).

The proposed rule also implicates serious **Fifth Amendment due process concerns**. Federal employees in the competitive service have a constitutionally protected property interest in their continued employment. Removing their protections without individualized due process hearings violates established procedural safeguards (*Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill*, 470 U.S. 532 (1985)). A mass reclassification of career employees to an at-will status would invite widespread litigation and erode public confidence in the federal government’s commitment to constitutional norms.

Additionally, by consolidating power over hiring and firing into the hands of politically appointed agency heads, this rule raises serious **separation of powers concerns**. It blurs the line between the apolitical implementation of laws by the Executive Branch and partisan control over the machinery of government. A politicized civil service would inhibit Congress's ability to rely on nonpartisan agencies for oversight and undermine the administrative state's legitimacy—an issue the Supreme Court has warned against in cases such as *Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB*, 561 U.S. 477 (2010).

The rule proposed under Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004-0001 is not a restoration of accountability—it is an open invitation to political retaliation, ideological purges, and the dismantling of a merit-based civil service. It contravenes statutory law, violates constitutional protections, and endangers the stability and impartiality of the federal workforce. I urge OPM to reject this rule in its entirety and to stand firm in defense of the apolitical, professional civil service envisioned by the Framers and protected by Congress for over a century.

Removing their protections without individualized due process hearings violates established procedural safeguards (*Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill*, 470 U.S. 532 (1985)). A mass reclassification of career employees to an at-will status would invite widespread litigation and erode public confidence in the federal government’s commitment to constitutional norms.

Additionally, by consolidating power over hiring and firing into the hands of politically appointed agency heads, this rule raises serious **separation of powers concerns**. It blurs the line between the apolitical implementation of laws by the Executive Branch and partisan control over the machinery of government. A politicized civil service would inhibit Congress's ability to rely on nonpartisan agencies for oversight and undermine the administrative state's legitimacy—an issue the Supreme Court has warned against in cases such as *Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB*, 561 U.S. 477 (2010).

The rule proposed under Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004-0001 is not a restoration of accountability—it is an open invitation to political retaliation, ideological purges, and the dismantling of a merit-based civil service. It contravenes statutory law, violates constitutional protections, and endangers the stability and impartiality of the federal workforce. I urge OPM to reject this rule in its entirety and to stand firm in defense of the apolitical, professional civil service envisioned by the Framers and protected by Congress for over a century.

Title: Comment from Jose Espitia

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule aimed at "strengthening employee accountability" by creating Schedule Policy/Career within the excepted service and removing due process protections for employees in policy-influencing positions. While the stated goals of accountability and democratic responsiveness are important, this rule, in its current form, poses significant risks to the integrity of the civil service and the principles of fairness and due process.

The removal of Chapter 43 and 75 protections, including Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) appeals, for a broad category of "policy-influencing" career employees is deeply concerning. This action would essentially create a system of at-will employment for a significant portion of the federal workforce, making them vulnerable to arbitrary or politically motivated removal without adequate recourse. The historical context provided in the proposed rule itself highlights the dangers of a purely patronage-based system, which this rule risks resurrecting in a new guise.

While the proposal claims to maintain nonpartisan hiring for Schedule Policy/Career positions, the lack of meaningful job security and appeal rights inherently politicizes these roles. Employees in these positions would be incentivized to align themselves with the political preferences of the current administration, rather than providing objective and expert advice based on their professional expertise and the best interests of the public. This could lead to a decline in the quality and impartiality of policy recommendations and the erosion of the institutional knowledge that career civil servants provide.

Furthermore, the definition of "policy-influencing" positions appears overly broad and lacks clear, objective criteria. This ambiguity creates the potential for the rule to be applied to a wide range of employees, extending far beyond high-level decision-makers and encompassing individuals whose roles involve technical expertise or the implementation of established policies. Subjecting these dedicated public servants to at-will employment based on such a vague definition is unjust and undermines the principles of a merit-based civil service, where career professionals are selected and retained based on their qualifications and performance, not their political leanings.

The argument that current Chapter 43 and 75 procedures are overly burdensome and impede accountability should be addressed through targeted reforms to those processes, rather than a wholesale removal of fundamental employee protections. Streamlining procedures and ensuring timely resolution of performance issues are legitimate goals, but they should not come at the cost of due process and the creation of a politicized workforce.

In conclusion, I urge OPM to reconsider this proposed rule. Instead of dismantling essential employee protections and risking the politicization of the civil service, efforts should focus on refining existing performance management systems to ensure both accountability and fairness. The creation of Schedule Policy/Career, without adequate safeguards, represents a dangerous step backward that would undermine the professionalism, independence, and effectiveness of the federal workforce.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
With regard to the proposed OPM rule to politicize the civil service via the Schedule Policy/Career reclassification of federal employees, removing their civil service protections, and rendering them at-will workers, subject to illegal terminations based on baseless political preference. As a concerned American and decorated combat Veteran, I argue that the proposed rule is unlawful, procedurally deficient, and contrary to the public interest, particularly for the Veterans Health Administration (VHA). The rule should be withdrawn with prejudice immediately based on the following legal rational:
First, it is a violation of Statutory Civil Service Protections. The proposed rule undermines the merit-based civil service system codified in Title 5 of the U.S. Code, particularly 5 U.S.C. § 2301, which mandates that federal employment be based on merit principles, free from political influence. By reclassifying employees in “policy-influencing” roles as at-will workers, the rule effectively nullifies protections against arbitrary dismissal, violating 5 U.S.C. § 7511, which guarantees adverse action procedures for competitive and excepted service employees. For VHA employees, the rule also conflicts with Title 38 protections (38 U.S.C. § 7401 et seq.), which prioritize stable staffing to ensure quality veteran healthcare. The Department of Veterans Affairs’ planned reduction of 83,000 jobs, tied to this rule, risks destabilizing VHA operations, contravening Congress’s intent to prioritize veterans’ care. 

Second, this rule is a violation of the Arbitrary and Capricious clause under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). Under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A), agency actions must not be arbitrary or capricious. The proposed rule fails to provide a reasoned basis for reclassifying employees, relying on vague criteria for “policy-influencing” positions that lack clear standards, and are subject to the whims of political sycophants. OPM’s estimate of impacting ~50,000 employees, including VHA administrative staff, is unsupported by data demonstrating how these roles undermine agency efficiency or necessitate at-will status. The rule also ignores the chilling effect on employee morale and recruitment, particularly in VHA, where staffing shortages already impair care delivery. OPM’s failure to analyze alternatives, such as targeted performance management reforms, renders the rule arbitrary and capricious.
Third, your insufficient comment period violates is a procedural deficiency in the Rule making process. The APA requires meaningful public participation (5 U.S.C. § 553). The 30-day comment period, ending May 23, 2025, is insufficient for a rule with such far-reaching consequences, especially given OPM’s bypassing of standard regulatory steps (e.g., declaring Biden-era protections inoperative). This curtailed process limits stakeholders, including Veterans, from fully assessing the rule’s impact. Additionally, OPM has not disclosed sufficient data on affected positions or economic impacts, violating APA transparency requirements.
The rule jeopardizes the public interest by politicizing the federal workforce, undermining 5 U.S.C. § 1103’s mandate for OPM to uphold merit principles. For VHA, the rule’s alignment with the VA’s August 2025 RIF threatens healthcare access for veterans, as administrative roles are critical to clinical operations. This conflicts with Congressional directives in the Veterans Access, Choice, and Accountability Act of 2014 to prioritize veteran services. The rule’s reliance on Project 2025’s privatization goals further suggests an intent to weaken public institutions, contrary to Congress’s commitment to a robust VA.
Additionally, the rule raises due process concerns under the Fifth Amendment by depriving employees of protected property interests in their jobs without adequate notice or hearing. Reclassification to at-will status, followed by potential termination without appeal rights, denies procedural protections established in Cleveland Board of Education v. Loudermill (1985). This is particularly egregious for VHA employees with veteran status, who are entitled to hiring and retention preferences under 5 U.S.C. § 2108.
To conclude, your rule is blatantly unlawful, procedurally flawed, and detrimental to the federal workforce and veterans’ care. OPM should withdraw the rule or, at minimum, extend the comment period, provide detailed impact analyses, and revise the rule to comply with Title 5, Title 38, and APA requirements. I urge OPM to prioritize merit-based employment and protect VHA’s ability to serve veterans.

Title: Comment from Madison Young
Comment:
Dear Office of Personnel Management,
I am writing to express serious concerns regarding the proposed rule to create Schedule Policy/Career positions within the excepted service. While I understand the stated goal of enhancing accountability, this rule is fundamentally flawed legally and as a matter of policy. Below, I outline specific issues related to statutory conflicts, constitutional challenges, procedural deficiencies, and broader policy implications.
 
1. Conflict with Statutory Protections
The proposed rule appears to contravene several provisions of the Civil Service Reform Act (CSRA), which established a uniform framework for employee protections. Specifically:
•Adverse Action Rights: By excluding Schedule Policy/Career employees from Chapters 43 and 75 of Title 5, the rule strips them of procedural safeguards, including the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) appeal rights. This exclusion undermines Congress’s intent to provide federal employees with due process and fair treatment, as affirmed in cases like United States v. Fausto (484 U.S. 439 [1988]).
•Merit System Principles: The merit system principles enshrined in Title 5, Section 2301(b), emphasize nonpartisan retention based on performance. Converting these roles into at-will positions risks politicization, directly contravening these principles.
 
2. Constitutional Concerns
•Fifth Amendment – Due Process: The removal of appeal rights infringes upon employees’ constitutional property interests in their jobs, as recognized in Arnett v. Kennedy (416 U.S. 134 [1974]). This lack of due process poses significant constitutional challenges.
•First Amendment – Free Speech: Creating at-will positions could have a chilling effect on employees’ ability to express dissenting or critical views, even outside their professional duties. Such policies risk violating precedents like Pickering v. Board of Education (391 U.S. 563 [1968]), which protect employees’ rights to free expression.
 
3. Violations of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA)
•Lack of Rational Basis: The rule's justification relies on anecdotal evidence rather than a robust analysis of systemic challenges. The cited difficulties in addressing poor performance and misconduct are not substantiated with comprehensive data, falling short of the APA’s requirement for reasoned decision-making (Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 [1983]).
•Arbitrary and Capricious Action: The rule’s sweeping changes ignore less intrusive alternatives for addressing performance issues. This lack of proportionality may render the rule arbitrary under the APA.
•Insufficient Public Engagement: If comments are inadequately addressed or the decision appears predetermined, it could lead to procedural violations, further invalidating the rule.
 
4. Policy Implications
•Undermining Nonpartisanship: Federal employment is merit-based, a cornerstone of public trust in government. This rule risks politicizing critical roles by allowing terminations based on subjective evaluations, which could erode that trust.
•	Impact on Workforce Morale and Recruitment: Moving key positions to at-will status may create a culture of fear and instability, deterring highly qualified professionals from seeking public service roles. This could significantly weaken the federal government’s institutional expertise over time.
•Unintended Consequences: The rule may foster a toxic work environment by discouraging whistleblowing and incentivizing compliance over ethical or professional judgment, potentially diminishing overall efficiency and accountability.

The proposed rule poses substantial legal and policy challenges. It undermines statutory protections, raises constitutional concerns, and conflicts with the core principles of the civil service. Furthermore, it negatively affects workforce morale, public trust, and government efficiency.

I urge the Office of Personnel Management to withdraw this proposed rule and instead explore alternative measures that address performance challenges without compromising legal protections or the integrity of the federal workforce.

Title: Comment from Joan Rogers

For example: if a person wanted to open a business that would distribute food products across the country. They would be subject to Federal FDA rules. NOW they have to put in equipment or process that cost money, perhaps money they don't have. They were caught in an uncertain business climate and now they may have to take out loans to cover the cost or dip into the business's cash, or raise prices, or go out of business. This scenario can be thought through in the opposite direction, as well. Either way, it isn't fair to the business owner, the consumers, or the investors. 
Another scenario: A young person who loves working in the outdoors considers a job at the National Park Service after high school. Due to a learning disability, they do not do well in a school setting and are sure that college is not for them. But they have a service-minded personality and would be thrilled to work in a National Park, cleaning up after disrespectful tourists, manning a booth taking admission fees, maintaining trails and assisting with conservation efforts. People say that this can happen at any job - any company can lay off any worker. But a company is different than a Federal Service. A company is a for-profit entity that needs to do what it has to - to stay in business. Federal Agencies are not for-profit companies. The American government is NOT a for-profit company. The Federal Agencies ALL provide value and increase revenues over the long term. Inefficiencies and unproductive workers should be weeded out, and has been over each political party. I am commenting to express my strong and continued opposition to the proposed rule "Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service" as published in the Federal Register (90 FR 17182), Docket OPM-2025-0004.

The creation of a "Schedule Policy/Career" designation for policy-influencing positions, making them at-will and removing standard adverse action procedures and appeal processes, would fundamentally undermine the principles of a nonpartisan and merit-based civil service. This proposed change appears to inject political considerations into personnel decisions, creating an environment where career employees in critical roles could be removed for reasons other than poor performance or misconduct, specifically for perceived disloyalty to an administration's policy directives. This politicization would erode the professional independence of the civil service and lead to instability and a loss of valuable expertise within government agencies.

The lack of clear and objective criteria for defining "policy-influencing" positions raises concerns that this could be applied too broadly, impacting a significant number of dedicated civil servants who are not in the most senior policymaking roles. The loss of due process protections for these employees would be a significant step backward in ensuring fair treatment and job security within the federal workforce.

Specific aspects of the proposed rule undermine the ability of policy advisors and agency leaders to fulfill their essential duties:

Undermining the Obligation to Highlight Legal Conflicts: This rule could undermine policy advisors' fundamental obligation to thoroughly analyze and highlight potential conflicts between proposed presidential directives and existing laws, regulations, and legal precedents. The fear of being seen as "intentionally undermining" a directive could discourage advisors from providing critical, objective legal assessments, potentially leading to ill-conceived or legally challenged policies.

Jeopardizing Careers for Respecting Legal Authority: The proposed rule jeopardizes the careers of dedicated policy makers who, in upholding their oath and the rule of law, respect congressional veto overrides or comply with court orders that directly oppose presidential directives. An employee should not face the threat of termination for adhering to the legal framework of our government. This rule creates a dangerous precedent where loyalty to a directive could be prioritized over the obligation to respect the balance of powers.

Compromising Congressional oversight and the Independence of Agency Heads: This proposal compromises the intended role and independence of agency heads who are often approved by Congress and mandated to maintain a degree of autonomy to effectively carry out their agencies' missions. The fear of being deemed to be undermining a presidential directive could pressure these leaders to prioritize political alignment over their statutory obligations and professional judgment, ultimately hindering the effective functioning of government.

Moreover, I want to emphasize that processes already exist within our system of governance to prevent federal employees from subverting the intention of laws and regulations. Mechanisms like the Congressional Review Act (CRA) and the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) provide checks to ensure agency actions align with legislative intent and established procedures. The proposed rule appears to disregard these existing robust frameworks designed to ensure accountability and prevent overreach.

Finally, the definition of “policy making or policy influencing” positions in the proposed rule is excessively broad and dangerously open to abuse. Without clear and specific criteria, this designation could be applied arbitrarily to a wide range of career civil servants, including those whose roles have limited direct influence on high-level policy decisions. This lack of precision creates the potential for politically motivated reclassifications and subsequent removals, undermining the merit-based principles of the civil service.

This proposed rule, if implemented, would not only politicize the civil service but also create a chilling effect on objective policy analysis, undermine the rule of law within the executive branch, and compromise the necessary independence of agency leadership. It also disregards existing accountability mechanisms and relies on an overly broad and abusable definition.

I urge the Office of Personnel Management to carefully consider these critical points and abandon this ill-conceived proposal. A robust and effective government relies on a civil service that is both accountable and empowered to provide objective advice and uphold the legal framework of our nation without fear of political reprisal.

Stripping thousands of workers of these protections not only weakens accountability but also risks chilling expert advice and dissent within agencies—undermining the very effectiveness of government operations.

In conclusion, the proposed Schedule Policy/Career rule poses a grave threat to the foundational principles of good governance, civil service independence, and the rule of law. It disregards Title 5 protections, congressional intent, and judicial precedent safeguarding merit-based civil service. Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Office of Personnel Management’s proposed rule (Docket OPM-2025-0004; RIN 3206-AO80) to create a new “Schedule Policy/Career” excepted-service category for policy-influencing positions. I strongly oppose the retroactive application of this rule to current incumbents and instead urge OPM to limit any reclassification to positions as they become vacant and to new hires going forward.

Career employees have accumulated a property interest in their civil-service status, including pre-removal notice, hearing rights, and MSPB appeals under Chapters 43 and 75 of Title 5, U.S. Code. Stripping these protections en masse violates the Fifth Amendment’s guarantee that no person shall be deprived of “life, liberty, or property, without due process of law,” and the Supreme Court has recognized that significant employment-related entitlements constitute such property interests. Retaining protections for incumbents while applying Schedule Policy/Career only prospectively would honor those settled expectations without undermining accountability goals.

Congress narrowly authorized exceptions to civil-service protections for “positions determined to be of a confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating character”—i.e., political appointees—not career incumbents. Section 7511(b)(2) of Title 5 confirms that exclusions from Chapter 75 attach to the position’s nature, not to who occupies it. OPM’s attempt to remove protections from existing incumbents therefore exceeds its regulatory authority under the Civil Service Reform Act.

The Civil Service Reform Act requires that any exception to competitive-service requirements be “necessary” and warranted by “conditions of good administration” (5 U.S.C. § 3302). Retroactively sweeping in current employees en masse cannot satisfy that strict standard, as it neither targets proven instances of serious misconduct nor ensures rigorous, case-by-case determinations by individual agency heads.

Under the APA, rescinding or revising existing regulations requires the same notice-and-comment procedures used to promulgate them (5 U.S.C. § 553). Yet the proposed rule attempts to render inoperative the Biden-era regulations via a brief NPRM rather than full, reasoned analysis of thousands of comments and empirical data. This approach risks arbitrary and capricious decision-making prohibited by APA § 706.

I respectfully oppose the entire concept of creating a Schedule Policy/Career excepted-service category, the proposed rule itself, and the accompanying Executive Order. Title: Comment from Steven Mann
Comment:
To Whom It May Concern:

I strongly oppose the proposed rule that would establish a new Schedule Policy/Career employment category. This rule raises serious legal concerns, including direct conflict with the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (CSRA) and well-established constitutional due process protections for federal employees.

1. Violation of the Civil Service Reform Act (5 U.S.C. §§ 2301–2302)
The CSRA enshrines the merit system principles as the cornerstone of federal employment. Specifically, 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(2) states that "all employees and applicants for employment should receive fair and equitable treatment in all aspects of personnel management… with proper regard for their privacy and constitutional rights."

Furthermore, 5 U.S.C. § 7513 mandates that adverse actions, including removals and suspensions, be carried out only "for such cause as will promote the efficiency of the service," and requires advance notice, representation, and an opportunity to respond. The proposed Schedule Policy/Career classification unlawfully circumvents these statutory protections by permitting at-will removal without these required procedures.

2. Undermining Constitutional Due Process Rights
The U.S. Supreme Court has recognized in Cleveland Board of Education v. Loudermill, 470 U.S. 532 (1985), that public employees with a property interest in their continued employment are entitled to due process before termination. By designating career civil servants as at-will employees and removing their appeal rights, the rule violates this constitutional guarantee.

Even policy-influencing roles do not lose their entitlement to basic procedural protections when filled through competitive, nonpolitical appointments. Attempting to redefine these roles to strip away due process is a de facto repeal of civil service rights without Congressional authorization.

3. Exceeds OPM’s Statutory Authority
The proposed rule attempts to unilaterally reclassify large swaths of the workforce and redefine fundamental aspects of federal employment. This oversteps the regulatory authority granted to the Office of Personnel Management under 5 U.S.C. § 1103, which does not permit wholesale reclassification of employees to evade the merit-based protections mandated by Congress.

Courts have been skeptical of agencies attempting to bypass clear statutory protections through rulemaking. As noted in Util. Air Regulatory Grp. v. EPA, 573 U.S. 302, 324 (2014), "an agency may not rewrite clear statutory terms to suit its own sense of how the statute should operate."

4. Risk of Politicization and Retaliation
The proposed rule’s stated justification includes removing employees who “undermine the democratic process by intentionally subverting Presidential directives.” This vague and subjective standard, when combined with at-will status, invites abuse and may be used to purge qualified employees for ideological reasons, not performance—a direct violation of 5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(10), which prohibits discrimination based on political affiliation.

Conclusion:
The proposed rule is not only bad policy but also likely unlawful. It threatens to erode the apolitical nature of the civil service, bypasses core legal protections enshrined in the CSRA and the Constitution, and grants the Executive Branch undue power over career personnel.

I urge OPM to withdraw this proposal in its entirety.

There is extensive legal precedent, with commentary on the spirit and intent of CSRA from the Supreme Court and Congress itself. Under constitutional and statutory interpretation, ultimately Schedule F is unlawful, if politically convenient. It is my hope that our great Government upholds the rule of law and protects our career civil servants so that federal employment does not become like those seen in adversarial countries, where knowing the right person or currying political favor are the sole keys to success and corruption abounds.

The proposed Schedule F classification raises significant legal concerns as it violates multiple federal statutes and constitutional protections designed to uphold a nonpartisan, merit-based civil service. Below is the detailed analysis of the legal issues associated with Schedule F:

1. Violation of the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (CSRA)
The CSRA establishes a merit-based system for federal employment, providing protections against arbitrary dismissal. Schedule F seeks to reclassify certain policy-influencing positions, effectively removing these protections and allowing for at-will termination. Reclassification undermines the CSRA’s intent and structure. Notably, the CSRA permits exceptions for positions of a “confidential or policy-determining character,” but Schedule F’s broad application exceeds this narrow scope. The Roth v. Brownell decision reinforces that reclassification cannot strip employees of their CSRA protections without due process.
 
2. Contravention of the Lloyd–La Follette Act of 1912
This Act mandates that federal employees cannot be removed without notice and a written explanation. By converting positions to Schedule F, employees lose these procedural safeguards, conflicting with the Act’s requirements. The Roth case further supports that reclassification does not nullify these protections.

3. Potential Violation of the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment
Federal employees have a property interest in their continued employment, protected under the Fifth Amendment. The Supreme Court’s decision in Cleveland Board of Education v. Loudermill affirms that due process is required before terminating such employment. Schedule F’s provision for at-will dismissal without prior notice or hearing raises constitutional concerns.

4. Breach of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA)
The APA requires that significant regulatory changes undergo a notice-and-comment period and that agencies provide a reasoned explanation for such changes. The implementation of Schedule F lacks sufficient justification and fails to adhere to APA procedures.

5. Undermining the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883
The Pendleton Act established the principle of merit-based hiring and protection from political influence. Schedule F’s reclassification could reintroduce a patronage system, allowing for the dismissal of employees based on political considerations, contrary to the Act’s objectives.

6. Erosion of Whistleblower Protections
Whistleblower statutes protect federal employees who report misconduct. By removing civil service protections through Schedule F, employees may be deterred from reporting wrongdoing due to fear of retaliation, thereby weakening these legal safeguards.

7. Application of the Major Questions Doctrine
The Major Questions Doctrine holds that significant policy changes require clear congressional authorization. Given the substantial impact of Schedule F on federal employment, its implementation without explicit legislative approval is considered unlawful under this doctrine.

Conclusion
The proposed Schedule F classification poses several legal challenges by violating established federal laws and constitutional protections. Its implementation could fundamentally alter the structure and integrity of the federal civil service, leading to increased politicization and diminished employee rights.

Title: Comment from Joan Jefferies
Comment:
I am firmly opposed to any effort to create or revive the “Schedule F” classification for federal employees.  This proposal would strike at the heart of the merit‐based civil service system that has ensured a professional, nonpartisan federal workforce since the Pendleton Act was passed in 1883.

Under that landmark reform, hiring and promotion in the federal government became tied to objective measures of competence rather than political allegiance.  By designating large swaths of policy analysts, program managers, inspectors and other career staff as “Schedule F,” the administration could strip them of long-standing due-process protections, reclassify them at will, and terminate them without cause—effectively reinstating the very spoils-system abuses that Pendleton and the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (CSRA) were meant to abolish.  Such a move would conflict directly with 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8), which requires that federal employment decisions rest solely on merit and be insulated from partisan pressure.

Moreover, resurrecting Schedule F would undermine institutional knowledge and discourage top-flight professionals from entering or remaining in public service.  It would chill candid analysis and weaken agencies’ ability to offer neutral, data-driven advice, ultimately eroding public trust in government.  In 2020, an executive order first established Schedule F; it was revoked the following year in recognition of these risks.  Reviving it now would not only reverse that sound judgment but also set a dangerous precedent for politicized personnel management in every corner of the federal establishment.

This proposed rule is not about reform—it is about control. We must not allow a return to a system where public servants are forced to pass political loyalty tests to keep their jobs. Title: Comment from Jon Davies
Comment:
I strongly oppose the implementation or revival of the “Schedule F” classification for federal employees. This proposal threatens the merit-based civil service system that has underpinned a professional, nonpartisan federal workforce for over a century.

As a government supervisor, there are multiple tools and processes at my disposal to reprimand or remove an employee. Further, there are similar tools and process to ensure that all individuals get a fair shake. Getting rid of the something that forces a merit-based system seems counter intuitive to the current administrations policies.

The creation of Schedule F directly undermines the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which was enacted to combat the spoils system and establish a merit-based hiring process for federal employees. By allowing a broad swath of career civil servants—particularly those involved in policy-making or analysis—to be reclassified and potentially terminated without cause, Schedule F opens the door to politically motivated hiring and firing. This is antithetical to the principle of an apolitical civil service enshrined in 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8), which mandates that federal employment decisions be based on merit and free from political influence.

Moreover, the vague and sweeping criteria for inclusion in Schedule F violate the due process protections guaranteed by 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which requires cause and procedural safeguards for the removal of career federal employees. Stripping thousands of workers of these protections not only weakens accountability but also risks chilling expert advice and dissent within agencies—undermining the very effectiveness of government operations.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is also bound by 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to support the merit system principles. Implementing Schedule F contradicts this statutory mission and places undue political pressure on career professionals, compromising the integrity and continuity of federal programs across administrations.

In conclusion, the Schedule F proposal poses a grave threat to the foundational principles of good governance, civil service independence, and the rule of law. I urge the administration and OPM to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement or revive this dangerous classification.

Public Distrust: The perception of an unfair or politicized hiring system can reduce public confidence in government institutions.

We would moving backwards to early 1900s approach with this policy change.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I write this comment to express strong opposition to any proposed rule or executive action that would reintroduce Schedule F or any equivalent classification that would return civil servants to an "at-will" title. Central to my concern is such that this measure poses a major threat to the institutional independence of federal agencies and the long-standing tradition of a nonpartisan, expert-driven civil service. Federal agencies are delegated this power to remain unbiased in regards to political pressures and, should this proposed rule pass, Schedule F would erode the separation between elected leadership and the professional workforce that carries out the law. This is not merely an administrative change, but rather a fundamental shift in how government power is distributed and exercised, and should be strongly considered when voting on this rule. 

The role agencies play is that of an informed and responsible institution that should be distanced from partisan influence and focused directly on the security and wellbeing of both democracy and the government's constituents. Though the NPRM cites that lack of administrative power over federal agencies undermines democracy by "[enabling] government power to be wielded without accountability to the voters or their elected representatives", this is a misleading interpretation of the role agencies play in our government. As discussed in Administrative Procedures as Instruments of Political Control, when any administration gains the ability to easily intervene and control the decisions of bureaucratic agencies, it opens the door for these agencies to be used for political gain (McCubbins et al.). This threatens the safeguards in place to protect against corruption and manipulation, compromising the independence of the bureaucracy and its ability to act impartially in the public interest. Passing this rule would set a precedent that would both diminish the credibility of our federal agencies and threaten our democracy as a whole.

Title: Comment from J B

I am firmly against the introduction or reinstatement of the “Schedule F” employment classification for federal workers. This proposal endangers the merit-based civil service system that has sustained a competent, impartial federal workforce for more than a hundred years.

At its core, Schedule F directly conflicts with the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which was designed to eliminate the patronage system and promote merit-based hiring in the federal government. By allowing a significant number of career civil servants—especially those engaged in policy work—to be reclassified and potentially dismissed without just cause, Schedule F paves the way for politically driven employment decisions. This contradicts the principle of a politically neutral civil service, as outlined in 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8), which requires that hiring and firing decisions be based on merit, not political affiliation.

Additionally, the overly broad and ambiguous standards for placing employees under Schedule F run afoul of the due process protections in 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which guarantees cause and fair procedures before career employees can be removed. Taking away these safeguards from thousands of public servants would not only erode accountability but could also discourage candid advice and dissent, weakening the effectiveness of federal agencies.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM), governed by 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq., has a legal duty to uphold the merit system principles. Instituting Schedule F would undermine this mandate and expose federal employees to excessive political pressure, ultimately jeopardizing the stability and impartiality of government programs from one administration to the next.

In summary, Schedule F represents a serious threat to the core values of good governance, civil service neutrality, and the rule of law. I call on the administration and OPM to reject any move to establish or revive this harmful classification.

Title: Comment from Jo J
Comment:
I am a former Federal Employee and have grave concerns over these suggested changes.

1. Undermines Merit-Based System: Creating such a Schedule Policy/Career for policy-influencing career positions risks politicizing career civil service roles. By prioritizing "accountability to the President" over merit-based principles, it could erode the impartiality and professionalism of the federal workforce, weakening public trust in government institutions.

2. Reduces Employee Protections: Amending 5 CFR parts 752 and 432 to exclude Schedule Policy/Career employees from the procedural protections under chapters 75 and 43 removes critical safeguards against arbitrary adverse actions or performance-based removals. This could lead to unfair treatment, reduced morale, and increased vulnerability to political pressure.

3. Creates Confusion in Service Classification: The amendments to 5 CFR parts 212 and 213 blur the lines between competitive and excepted service by allowing employees to retain competitive status while in excepted positions. This creates administrative complexity, inconsistency in hiring and management practices, and many potential legal disputes over employee rights and status.

4. Reverses Recent Reforms Without Justification: Rescinding the April 2024 rule’s amendments (e.g., clarifying policy-influencing positions as non-career and imposing procedural requirements) without clear evidence of the failure of those amendments undermines regulatory stability. It disregards the rationale behind those reforms, which likely aimed to protect career employees from politicization.

5. Risks Inconsistent Hiring Practices: Allowing positions moved to Schedule Policy/Career to retain their prior hiring procedures (competitive or excepted) creates a patchwork system. This could lead to inequities in recruitment, hinder workforce mobility, and complicate compliance with federal hiring standards.

In total, these changes could destabilize the federal workforce, erode protections, and prioritize political influence over merit, ultimately harming government efficiency and public trust.  Should I ever decide to return to the public service workforce, would I be subject to a test of my Knowledge, Skills and Abilities? Or, instead, would I be subject to a political questionnaire?  Would my job and all of my work be terminated and erased with every new administration (as is currently being done with cancer research via the cancellation of research programs that the US taxpayers have already authorized)?

This series of suggested changes destabilizes my confidence in the effectiveness of the US Government in addition to any confidence in job security in returning to the Federal workforce.

2. Diminishing Job Security and Due Process Rights:
 * Legal Basis: Current federal employees in the competitive service have certain due process rights, including protections against arbitrary dismissal and the right to appeal adverse actions (5 U.S.C. § 7513). These protections are designed to ensure fairness and prevent politically motivated removals.
 * The Issue with Proposed Schedule F: Reclassifying employees under a new Schedule F could significantly weaken or eliminate these job security protections. Employees in these positions might be easier to fire without cause, potentially leading to a chilling effect on their willingness to provide candid advice or challenge political directives. First and foremost, the creation of Schedule F directly undermines the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which was enacted to combat the spoils system and establish a merit-based hiring process for federal employees. By allowing a broad swath of career civil servants—particularly those involved in policy-making or analysis—to be reclassified and potentially terminated without cause, Schedule F opens the door to politically motivated hiring and firing. This is antithetical to the principle of an apolitical civil service enshrined in 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8), which mandates that federal employment decisions be based on merit and free from political influence.

Moreover, the vague and sweeping criteria for inclusion in Schedule F violate the due process protections guaranteed by 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which requires cause and procedural safeguards for the removal of career federal employees. Stripping thousands of workers of these protections not only weakens accountability but also risks chilling expert advice and dissent within agencies—undermining the very effectiveness of government operations.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is also bound by 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to support the merit system principles. Implementing Schedule F contradicts this statutory mission and places undue political pressure on career professionals, compromising the integrity and continuity of federal programs across administrations.

In conclusion, the Schedule F proposal poses a grave threat to the foundational principles of good governance, civil service independence, and the rule of law. I urge the administration and OPM to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement or revive this dangerous classification.

I strongly oppose any effort to implement Schedule F, a proposed federal employment classification that threatens the integrity, impartiality, and effectiveness of the U.S. civil service.

Schedule F, as introduced by the current administration would allow broad reclassification of federal employees involved in "policy-determining, policymaking, or policy-advocating" roles, stripping them of their due process and merit-based civil service protections. This reclassification would open the door to mass politicization of the civil service, undermining a foundational principle of American democracy: that government professionals serve the public interest—not the political interest of any one administration.

Erosion of Merit-Based Employment

The core of the U.S. civil service system is its reliance on merit-based hiring and retention. By creating a new class of federal employees exempt from competitive hiring and procedural protections, Schedule F undermines this foundation. It risks turning experienced, apolitical experts into political appointees subject to loyalty tests and partisan whims. Numerous reports, including those from the Partnership for Public Service and the Government Accountability Office, have documented how politicization of the civil service leads to inefficiency, loss of institutional knowledge, and damage to public trust.

Impacts on Government Functionality and Continuity

Schedule F could destabilize federal agencies by making thousands of career positions vulnerable to sudden dismissal. This would deter qualified individuals from pursuing or remaining in public service, especially in critical policy areas like public health, national security, and environmental protection. These functions depend on continuity, expertise, and institutional memory—not political alignment.

Lack of Transparency and Oversight

The proposed implementation of Schedule F lacks transparency and sufficient safeguards against abuse. There is no clear, objective standard for determining which roles qualify as “policy-determining.” As a result, political appointees could use Schedule F arbitrarily to purge career professionals who provide inconvenient facts or sound legal analysis, silencing dissent and eroding checks and balances.

National Security and Public Safety Concerns

In national security, law enforcement, and public health, policy must be informed by objective data and long-term expertise. Purging career professionals in these areas based on perceived political loyalty could have dire consequences for national preparedness and crisis response. Schedule F would make it easier to dismiss professionals who speak out against unlawful or dangerous policies, weakening the government's ability to protect the public.

Conclusion

In sum, implementing Schedule F would damage the effectiveness, independence, and credibility of the federal workforce. It opens the door to patronage, diminishes the morale of public servants, and threatens the democratic principle of nonpartisan governance. I urge the relevant agencies and the administration to reject any proposal to implement Schedule F and instead protect and strengthen merit-based civil service protections.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I submit this comment in strong opposition to the proposed rule to establish “Schedule Policy/Career” in the excepted service, as published in the Federal Register on April 23, 2025 (90 FR 17182).

The proposed rule constitutes a sweeping reclassification of career civil servants in “policy-influencing” positions into a new category of at-will employees, stripped of long-standing procedural protections under chapters 43 and 75 of Title 5. This raises profound legal, constitutional, and operational concerns.

1. Due Process and Legal Precedent
The rule undermines procedural due process guarantees recognized by the U.S. Supreme Court in Arnett v. Kennedy and its progeny. These protections were codified by Congress in the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 to prevent arbitrary removals and ensure civil servants are not penalized for political or personal reasons. By eliminating appeal rights and adverse action procedures for employees with property interests in their jobs, the rule exposes the government to constitutional challenge.

2. Contravention of Congressional Intent
Congress has repeatedly affirmed the importance of a professional, merit-based civil service. By shifting employees into an at-will status without legislative input, the proposed rule improperly sidelines the statutory framework Congress enacted to protect career employees and maintain government neutrality.

3. Erosion of Merit System Principles
The merit system exists to protect both employees and the public from politicization of the civil service. Removing adverse action protections for “policy-influencing” employees risks creating a chilling effect on internal dissent and encourages self-censorship, undermining the very accountability the rule purports to enhance.

4. Insufficient Justification for Reversal
The rule seeks to overturn the April 2024 final rule with minimal justification. The rationale offered—largely consisting of political preference and unquantified surveys—is insufficient under the Administrative Procedure Act. A mere change in presidential administration does not justify abandonment of established policy without substantial evidence.

5. Unlawful Curtailment of Public Participation
Despite the substantial nature of the rule, OPM has allowed only 30 days for public comment, contravening the 60-day minimum generally required under Executive Order 12866. The rule’s complexity and implications necessitate a full and fair opportunity for public input.

For all of the above reasons, I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety. If not withdrawn, at a minimum, the comment period must be extended to 60 days to allow stakeholders to fully analyze and respond to the significant legal and policy issues raised.

By allowing a broad swath of career civil servants-particularly those involved in policy-making or analysis-to be reclassified and potentially terminated without cause, Schedule F opens the door to politically motivated hiring and firing. This is antithetical to the principle of an apolitical civil service enshrined in 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b) (8), which mandates that federal employment decisions be based on merit and free from political influence.

In conclusion, the Schedule F proposal poses a grave threat to the foundational principles of good governance, civil service independence, and the rule of law. I urge the administration and OPM to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement or revive this dangerous classification.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
As an engaged citizen, I strongly urge OPM to withdraw the proposed Schedule F rule. Its enactment would dismantle long-standing civil service protections, introduce unconstitutional practices, and undermine the core principles of a merit-based, nonpartisan federal workforce.

I. SUMMARY OF POSITION
I respectfully oppose the proposed “Schedule F” classification (5 CFR Parts 210, 212, 213, 302, 432, 451, and 752). By broadly stripping procedural and merit-based protections from thousands of policy-influencing career employees, the rule:
    A. Undermines the competitive, nonpartisan civil service;
    B. Exposes employees to at-will removal without notice or hearing;
    C. Threatens institutional memory, whistleblower reporting, and ethical governance.

II. KEY LEGAL & POLICY CONCERNS
1. Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (CSRA)
The CSRA’s merit-system principles and removal protections cannot be bypassed by a catch-all Schedule F designation and remain eligible only for narrowly defined “confidential or policy-determining” roles.

2. Lloyd–La Follette Act of 1912
Mandates advance notice and written findings before removal. Schedule F would eliminate these statutory safeguards.

3. Fifth Amendment Due Process
Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill confirms a property interest in federal employment; at-will termination without a hearing violates due process.

4. Administrative Procedure Act (APA)
The NPRM provides insufficient analysis of costs, benefits, or less-drastic alternatives, and appears to pre-decide key issues without fully addressing public comments.

5. Pendleton Civil Service Act of 1883
Established merit hiring and protection from patronage; Schedule F risks reintroducing politically motivated dismissals.

6. Whistleblower Protections
By removing tenure safeguards, Schedule F would chill reporting of fraud, waste, and abuse, undermining Congress’s express whistleblower statutes.

7. Major Questions Doctrine
A rule of such sweeping scope requires clear congressional authorization. No explicit statute grants OPM authority to reclassify tens of thousands of careers positions into an at-will service.

III. ALTERNATIVE RECOMMENDATIONS
    A. Rescind the NPRM in favor of targeted reforms that preserve due-process rights.
    B. Limit any new excepted service category to genuinely policy-confidential positions with clear statutory language.
    C. Conduct a GAO cost-benefit and risk analysis, including impacts on recruitment, retention, and whistleblower referrals.

IV. CLARIFYING QUESTIONS
1. Which position descriptions, occupational series, and pay grades are subject to Schedule F reclassification, and what objective criteria will guide those determinations?
2. Under the proposed rule, who—agency HR, OPM, or the White House—has final authority to designate a position as Schedule F, and what documentation must accompany each action?
3. Precisely how will the rule modify existing removal procedures, appeals rights, and grievance mechanisms now found in 5 U.S.C. § 7513 and 5 C.F.R. Part 752?
4. What is the intended timeline for agency review, designation notices to incumbents, and full implementation across all executive departments?
5. On what statutory bases does OPM rely to override or amend CSRA provisions, and how does the rule interact with statutes such as the Lloyd–La Follette and Pendleton Acts?
6. How will OPM address APA requirements—particularly the need for a reasoned explanation of alternatives considered and a detailed response to significant public comments?
7.  What internal or external oversight (e.g., OIG, GAO, Inspector General) will monitor Schedule F designations to prevent abuse or politicization?
8.  How will agencies measure and report on the anticipated benefits, costs, and impacts on workforce morale and institutional knowledge?
9. What training and guidance will be provided to supervisors and HR practitioners to ensure consistent, lawful application of Schedule F criteria?
10. How will Schedule F status affect existing whistleblower channels and protections under 5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(8), and what recourse will employees have if they believe retaliatory removal occurred?
