Title: Comment from Catrina Garcia
Comment:
I. Introduction

On its face, the initiative titled “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service” purports to promote government efficiency. In practice, however, this policy operates as a constitutional wrecking ball—trampling First Amendment rights, undermining due process, violating the separation of powers, and inviting discriminatory enforcement under the Equal Protection Clause.

This memo outlines the legal basis for challenging the initiative’s implementation under multiple constitutional frameworks, with a tone just as unapologetic as the initiative’s overreach.

II. First Amendment Violations – The Silencing of Dissent

The initiative risks weaponizing performance metrics to suppress political expression, whistleblowing, or union activity. Public employees do not surrender their constitutional rights at the government’s doorstep. Under Pickering v. Board of Education, 391 U.S. 563 (1968), the government cannot discipline employees for speaking out on matters of public concern unless it can prove actual disruption.

If this initiative permits or encourages:
	•	Disciplining employees for criticizing agency inefficiency,
	•	Penalizing union members for organizing,
	•	Retaliating against whistleblowers,

…it becomes a government-sanctioned gag order.

III. Due Process Violations – Firing First, Asking Questions Never

The Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments guarantee that no person shall be deprived of “life, liberty, or property” without due process. Long-term federal employees have a protected property interest in their continued employment (Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 470 U.S. 532 (1985)).

The initiative’s streamlined disciplinary procedures lack:
	•	Notice,
	•	A meaningful opportunity to be heard,
	•	A neutral arbiter,

which renders any adverse action unconstitutional. Due process isn’t optional—it’s foundational.

IV. Separation of Powers – The Executive Branch Goes Rogue

This initiative appears to override statutory protections enacted by Congress under Title 5 of the U.S. Code, which governs federal employment. The President cannot unilaterally rewrite these laws by executive fiat without running afoul of INS v. Chadha, 462 U.S. 919 (1983), which reaffirmed that core legislative powers cannot be absorbed by the executive branch.

Any attempt to:
	•	Alter hiring/firing rules,
	•	Bypass Office of Personnel Management procedures,
	•	Reassign authority to political appointees,

is not “efficiency”—it’s a power grab.

V. Equal Protection Violations – Discrimination Hidden in Metrics

If the performance criteria used disproportionately impact employees of a certain race, gender, age, or disability status, the initiative opens the door to Equal Protection claims under the Fourteenth Amendment and Title VII.

Example:
	•	A facially neutral metric that penalizes older workers for “lack of adaptability” may have a disparate impact under the ADEA (Age Discrimination in Employment Act).

The government’s data-driven discrimination may wear a lab coat, but it’s still illegal.

VI. Unconstitutional Delegation – Outsourcing Constitutional Authority

Performance evaluations delegated to private contractors or AI-driven tools? That’s a delegation of government authority without accountability. This violates the nondelegation doctrine, which demands that critical government decisions be made by accountable, constitutionally appointed officials.

No AI algorithm gets to fire a public servant without a human being held responsible.

VII. Vagueness & Overbreadth – Kafka Would Be Proud

Terms like “responsiveness” and “accountability” are so vague they invite arbitrary enforcement. Worse, they chill lawful behavior—an overbreadth problem that courts have historically struck down (Grayned v. City of Rockford, 408 U.S. 104 (1972)).

A law so ambiguous that no one knows what conduct will get them fired isn’t a policy—it’s a trap.

VIII. Conclusion

The “Improving Performance” initiative is not a benign effort at civil service reform. It is a bureaucratic Trojan Horse—a policy riddled with constitutional landmines and authoritarian potential. If challenged, courts will likely find significant portions of the initiative to be in violation of fundamental rights and structural protections enshrined in the U.S. Constitution.

Reform should not come at the cost of liberty. We have the laws. We have the precedent. All that’s left is the fight.

Title: Comment from Roberta VT
Comment:
Please read this entire comment on the proposed rule titled “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service” (RIN: 3206-AO80, Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004).

While I support effective performance management, this rule undermines the core values of a professional, nonpartisan, and merit-based civil service. It removes procedural protections from career federal employees in so-called “policy-influencing” positions and places them in a newly created Schedule Policy/Career—effectively converting them into at-will employees, vulnerable to politically motivated removal without due process.

1. Violation of Merit System Principles and Due Process

Stripping due process protections from career employees—who were hired competitively and serve irrespective of political affiliation—violates the merit system principles established by Congress in 5 U.S.C. § 2301. It also contradicts long-standing bipartisan commitments to protect civil servants from political retaliation and patronage systems. Agencies already have tools to address poor performance and misconduct; this proposal unnecessarily guts essential safeguards. Further, this proposed rule uses ancedotal evidence of a few poor performing/ unprofessional employees to disparage hundreds of thousands of others. The vast majority of civil servants are nonpartisan and successfully implement executive guidance. A few bad apples does not poison the entire civil service

2. Potential Violation of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA)

The proposed rule is vulnerable under the APA. Specifically:

It reverses a recent, well-supported rule (April 2024) without a reasoned explanation or new evidence, violating standards set in FCC v. Fox.

It fails to demonstrate that current accountability mechanisms are inadequate—relying instead on selectively cited surveys and anecdotal evidence,  making the rule arbitrary and capricious (State Farm).

It disregards the reliance interests of long-serving employees whose procedural rights are being stripped without analysis, as prohibited in DHS v. Regents.  

3. Financial Burden on Taxpayers

This rule carries serious fiscal consequences:

Legal costs from inevitable lawsuits filed by employee unions, whistleblowers, and good government groups.

Back pay and damages if removals are reversed by courts or future administrations.

Training and turnover costs due to the loss of experienced personnel.

Declining morale and efficiency, which harm agency performance and public trust.

OPM has not published a cost-benefit analysis, which may violate Executive Order 12866 and further weaken this rule under judicial scrutiny.

4. Inevitable Litigation and Instability

Numerous lawsuits will be filed, and similar efforts (like Schedule F) have been blocked or rescinded before. The uncertainty and fear generated by this proposal will harm recruitment, retention, and continuity in government, particularly in critical policy, regulatory, and scientific roles. Further, it will weaken the faith in the U.S. Government as a trusted employer and partner

Conclusion

This rule will not improve accountability—it will politicize the federal workforce, destabilize agencies, and expose the government to years of litigation and unnecessary taxpayer expense. It is inconsistent with democratic values, statutory merit principles, and established law. I respectfully urge OPM to withdraw this proposal and preserve the integrity of the career civil service.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I write in strong opposition to the proposed rule “Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service” (RIN 3206 AO80), which would create a new “Schedule Policy/Career” excepted service classification. This proposed rule is deeply troubling for several reasons:

1. Undermining Merit System Principles
By reclassifying policy influencing positions as at will roles, this rule eviscerates long standing merit system protections. These positions would no longer be covered by Chapter 75 or 43 of Title 5, eliminating due process rights and appeal protections. Such a change opens the door to politically motivated dismissals, weakening the very fabric of a professional and impartial civil service, which is intended to serve the American people, not transient political agendas.

2. Politicization of the Career Civil Service
The proposed rule dangerously blurs the line between career and political appointees. Even if the rule claims to retain “nonpartisan” hiring practices, stripping removal protections from employees in policy roles invites political loyalty tests and punishes career experts for objective disagreement with an administration’s preferred direction. This undermines the institutional knowledge and independent judgment essential for sound governance.

3. Addressing Performance Does Not Require At Will Employment
The justification that supervisors struggle to remove underperforming employees is not a reason to eliminate due process. The federal government already has mechanisms to address poor performance and misconduct under current law, with structured, reviewable procedures that protect both agency function and employee rights. The notion that accountability necessitates the removal of appeal rights is not supported by the existing body of evidence or practice.

4. Retreading a Harmful and Rejected Path
Schedule F, which this rule effectively reinstates under a new name, was previously revoked for good reason. It was widely opposed by federal employees, unions, and good governance experts. Its reintroduction, regardless of nomenclature, raises the same fundamental concerns: it encourages arbitrary terminations, creates instability, and discourages talented individuals from public service.

In sum, this proposal would fundamentally damage the integrity, independence, and fairness of the US civil service. I respectfully urge OPM to withdraw this rule and preserve the principles of merit based employment and constitutional due process that have long underpinned the effective functioning of the federal workforce.

I am strongly opposed to the implementation or revival of the “Schedule F” classification for federal employees. This proposal threatens the merit-based civil service system that has underpinned a professional, nonpartisan federal workforce for over a century.

First and foremost, the creation of Schedule F directly undermines the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which was enacted to combat the spoils system and establish a merit-based hiring process for federal employees. By allowing a broad swath of career civil servants—particularly those involved in policy-making or analysis—to be reclassified and potentially terminated without cause, Schedule F opens the door to politically motivated hiring and firing. Moreover, the vague and sweeping criteria for inclusion in Schedule F violate the due process protections guaranteed by 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which requires cause and procedural safeguards for the removal of career federal employees. Stripping thousands of workers of these protections not only weakens accountability but also risks chilling expert advice and dissent within agencies—undermining the very effectiveness of government operations.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is also bound by 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to support the merit system principles. Implementing Schedule F contradicts this statutory mission and places undue political pressure on career professionals, compromising the integrity and continuity of federal programs across administrations.

In conclusion, the Schedule F proposal poses a grave threat to the foundational principles of good governance, civil service independence, and the rule of law. I urge the administration and OPM to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement or revive this dangerous classification.

Although the proposed ruling states “Patronage Remains Prohibited”; without due process there is no practical way for employees, the public or oversight bodies to verify that dismissals are not politically motivated. Simply asserting that patronage is prohibited offers little comfort when the system removes the very mechanism that would reveal whether such misconduct has occurred. 

The proposal claims the appointment will remain “nonpartisan” yet it simultaneously strips away the procedural safeguards that shield career employees from politically motivated removals. That contradiction is troubling. This erodes public trust, institutional memory and continuity in government. 

The justification for this rule rests heavily on the claim that it is too difficult to discipline or remove poor performers.  While the removal processes under Chapter 43 and 75 of Title 5 does require time and diligence, it exists to ensure fairness, consistency, and protection for arbitrary actions. The proposed rule manipulates public frustration with government inefficiency by using “poor performance” as a convenient scapegoat-framing the issue in emotionally charged terms to justify sweeping changes. It appeals to a desire for accountability while concealing a far more troubling goal: enabling the dismissal of career professionals who are not politically aligned with the administration. By dismantling due process protections under the guise of performance reform, the rule risks transforming the civil service from a neutral, merit-based institution into one driven by political loyalty.  

This rule is unnecessary, potentially unlawful, and fundamentally misaligned with the principals of a professional, nonpartisan civil service. I respectfully ask OPM to withdraw this proposed rule in full.

Title: Comment from Jane Reid
Comment:
I strongly oppose any implementation or revival of the 'Schedule F' classification for federal employees. This proposal fundamentally endangers the merit-based civil service system that has been the foundation of a professional, nonpartisan federal workforce for more than a century.

The creation of Schedule F directly contradicts the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which was established to eliminate patronage and create merit-based hiring processes. By allowing potentially tens of thousands of career civil servants with policy responsibilities to be reclassified and dismissed without established cause, Schedule F would effectively reintroduce a political spoils system. This contradicts the core principle of an apolitical civil service codified in 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8), which requires federal employment decisions to be based on qualifications and protected from political influence.

The broad and ambiguous criteria for Schedule F designation would circumvent the due process protections guaranteed by 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which ensures career federal employees cannot be removed without proper cause and procedural safeguards. Stripping these protections threatens not only individual livelihoods but also institutional knowledge and continuity of operations. It would create a chilling effect on professional expertise and honest assessment within agencies, as employees fear retribution for providing unbiased analysis.

Additionally, such reclassification conflicts with the Office of Personnel Management's statutory obligation under 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to uphold merit system principles. Implementation would place career professionals under inappropriate political pressure, undermining the consistent, effective delivery of government services across administrations.

The proposed policy would also significantly impact workforce morale, recruitment, and retention. Federal agencies already face challenges attracting top talent; introducing employment instability would further hamper the government's ability to hire and retain qualified professionals committed to public service.

Crucially, Schedule F would deprive the American people of their right to a professional, well-qualified civil service that works for the public interest rather than partisan objectives. Citizens deserve government services administered by experienced professionals selected for their expertise and commitment to public service—not their political loyalty. The merit-based civil service system is a public trust that ensures continuity, expertise, and ethical governance regardless of which party holds power. Dismantling these protections would fundamentally alter the relationship between citizens and their government, replacing professional administration with political favoritism.

In conclusion, the Schedule F proposal represents a serious threat to good governance, civil service independence, continuity of operations, and the rule of law. I strongly urge the administration and OPM to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement or revive this classification that would politicize and destabilize our federal workforce."

I am writing to express strong opposition to the Office of Personnel Management’s (OPM) proposed rule OPM-2025-0004-0001, which seeks to reclassify approximately 50,000 federal employees into a newly designated Schedule Policy/Career (P/C) category. This proposal, a revival of the previously rescinded Schedule F, threatens the foundational principles of a nonpartisan, merit-based civil service and poses significant risks to the integrity, efficiency, and accountability of federal operations.

Erosion of Merit-Based Protections

The cornerstone of the federal civil service is its commitment to merit-based hiring and retention, ensuring that employment decisions are grounded in qualifications and performance rather than political affiliation. By reclassifying positions into Schedule P/C, the proposed rule would strip affected employees of critical protections against arbitrary dismissal, effectively making them at-will employees. This undermines the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978, which was enacted to prevent politicization and ensure a competent and impartial federal workforce.

Increased Risk of Politicization

The reintroduction of Schedule P/C opens the door to replacing experienced, nonpartisan professionals with individuals selected for their political loyalty rather than expertise. Such a shift could compromise the objectivity of policy analysis and implementation, leading to decisions that serve partisan interests over the public good. The National Active and Retired Federal Employees Association (NARFE) has rightly noted that this move "opens the door to replacing nonpartisan, professional civil servants with political loyalists".

Undermining Institutional Knowledge and Continuity

Federal agencies rely on the institutional knowledge and continuity provided by career civil servants. Reclassifying positions and removing job protections could lead to a loss of experienced personnel, disrupting agency operations and diminishing the government's ability to effectively serve the public. The potential for mass dismissals based on political considerations threatens the stability and effectiveness of federal programs.

Legal and Ethical Concerns

The proposed rule raises serious legal and ethical questions. The previous iteration, Schedule F, faced legal challenges and was ultimately rescinded due to concerns about its legality and potential for abuse. Reintroducing a similar framework disregards these concerns and may once again lead to protracted legal battles, diverting resources and attention from the government's primary responsibilities.

Conclusion

The proposed reclassification of federal positions into Schedule Policy/Career represents a significant departure from the principles that have long safeguarded the integrity and effectiveness of the federal workforce. It threatens to politicize the civil service, erode merit-based protections, and disrupt the continuity of government operations. I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule and instead focus on strengthening the existing merit-based system that ensures a competent, impartial, and stable federal workforce.

Title: Comment from Jason Dowd
Comment:
The opening months of the Trump administration represent a historic disruption to America’s scientific agencies. Staff have been fired or reassigned in the name of efficiency, resulting in chaos. Grants have been canceled mid-project for featuring the wrong words. “Pauses” and “reviews” are designed to block spending, in the hope that Congress will make the current impoundment of funds a baseline for permanent disinvestment. While the scientific community waits to see what the new normal will be, the Trump administration has a plan to institutionalize a much more politicized structure of control over government broadly, including both public scientific investments and the use of scientific knowledge in policy actions.

“Schedule F” (now renamed Schedule Policy/Career) is shorthand for an executive order that is a sharp break with civil service merit principles, which assume that career employees should be retained on the basis of performance and protected against political coercion. The US is already unusual in the degree to which it reserves the top layers of organizational leadership for short-term political appointees. Schedule F will vastly expand the number of appointees, adding a proposed 50,000 from the current 4000. It does so by involuntarily reclassifying career civil servants as appointees, removing job protections, the basic constraint against political interference.

The administration says that the purpose of Schedule F is to increase accountability for civil servants involved in policy-making. Set aside the fact that civil servants are accountable in multiple ways, Trump’s own justifications strike a more conspiratorial tone, including “the deep state can and must be brought to heel.” But what better way to actually institutionalize a deep state than by expanding political influence over what constitutes good science?

Studies show that politicization of public services generally worsens public-sector outcomes. Public employees invest less in developing their expertise and become more likely to exit. Instability and lack of experience reduce organizational performance. Politicization increases the influence of more ideologically radical appointees relative to more moderate civil servants. Politicization also reduces accountability. Bureaucrats worried about being fired fail to share uncongenial information with their political bosses and become less likely to respond to congressional oversight. As politicization begets lower transparency and administrative capacity, it increases waste and inefficiency.

What might this mean for scientific agencies? Agencies like the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the National Institutes for Health (NIH) cannot meet their statutorily mandated scientific missions if politics, rather than scientific expertise, drive decision-making. Federally supported science has been so successful, in no small part, because agency staff are typically expert scientists beholden to ensuring that the agencies deliver world-class science. Now, many could be turned into political appointees. The proposed policy defines grantmaking positions as “policy-making,” which includes “drafting of funding opportunity announcements, evaluation of grant applications, or recommending or selecting grant recipients.” This definition, which neatly matches agencies’ own definitions for certain career staff, would include most NIH program officers and NSF program directors.

The past few months at NIH and NSF preview how politicized scientific agencies would operate. Funding choices that reflected the consensus of some of the best scientists in the world were reversed by nonscientists. Program officers have, at points, been told not to communicate with the scientific community or have had their engagement limited. Scientific agencies have been directed to effectively reduce the flow of funds to a trickle by adding new layers of redundant review and red tape and even violating court orders to reinstate cancelled grants.

Other agencies, including regulatory agencies, apply rather than fund basic science, but the risks of politicization are no less. How confident can Americans be that federal employees will not have to choose between their job and scientific values in areas such as climate change, food safety, extreme weather forecasting, or public health?

The purpose of Schedule F is to permanently instill the degree of political control over science fueling the sense of fear that pervades those agencies now.

Vannevar Bush’s 1945 blueprint for America’s scientific infrastructure emphasized the centrality of protecting scientific organizations from politicization. That vision has been extraordinarily successful. Schedule F assumes the opposite: It treats scientific independence as a threat to be minimized.

Title: Comment from Michael Kearns
Comment:
The opening months of the Trump administration represent a historic disruption to America’s scientific agencies. Staff have been fired or reassigned in the name of efficiency, resulting in chaos. Grants have been canceled mid-project for featuring the wrong words. “Pauses” and “reviews” are designed to block spending, in the hope that Congress will make the current impoundment of funds a baseline for permanent disinvestment. While the scientific community waits to see what the new normal will be, the Trump administration has a plan to institutionalize a much more politicized structure of control over government broadly, including both public scientific investments and the use of scientific knowledge in policy actions.

“Schedule F” (now renamed Schedule Policy/Career) is shorthand for an executive order that is a sharp break with civil service merit principles, which assume that career employees should be retained on the basis of performance and protected against political coercion. The US is already unusual in the degree to which it reserves the top layers of organizational leadership for short-term political appointees. Schedule F will vastly expand the number of appointees, adding a proposed 50,000 from the current 4000. It does so by involuntarily reclassifying career civil servants as appointees, removing job protections, the basic constraint against political interference.

The administration says that the purpose of Schedule F is to increase accountability for civil servants involved in policy-making. Set aside the fact that civil servants are accountable in multiple ways, Trump’s own justifications strike a more conspiratorial tone, including “the deep state can and must be brought to heel.” But what better way to actually institutionalize a deep state than by expanding political influence over what constitutes good science?

Studies show that politicization of public services generally worsens public-sector outcomes. Public employees invest less in developing their expertise and become more likely to exit. Instability and lack of experience reduce organizational performance. Politicization increases the influence of more ideologically radical appointees relative to more moderate civil servants. Politicization also reduces accountability. Bureaucrats worried about being fired fail to share uncongenial information with their political bosses and become less likely to respond to congressional oversight. As politicization begets lower transparency and administrative capacity, it increases waste and inefficiency.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
1. I oppose this proposed rule in its entirety, and every section of the proposed rule, as it allows for the reintroduction of a "spoils" system to the federal civil service. The proposed rule allows any given Administration to replace the nation's professional cadre of policy experts who serve the Constitution across Administrations with individuals who subordinate their duty to the Constitution and the law to partisan loyalties. This is major concern regardless of who is in the White House. We need civil servants who have actual expertise and whose loyalty is to the country and the Constitution over any single politician.

2. I oppose the creation of the Schedule Policy/Career as a new category of Excepted Service under 5 CFR Part 213. Moving career civil servants into a category of at-will employment makes those civil service positions vulnerable to political manipulation and influence, including by putting those employees at risk of termination should their efforts to uphold the federal oath of employment to defend the Constitution conflict with a political appointee's belief that the employee has failed to "faithfully implement administration policies to the best of their ability," as required under the proposed amendment to Sec. 213.3501(b).

3. I oppose the amendment of 5 CFR part 752 that removes the right of career civil servants to appeal the transfer of their position into an Excepted Service category, including the proposed Schedule Policy/Career category. The removal of such protection violates the Fifth Amendment due process rights of federal civil servants, specifically by removing the employees' interest in their tenure protections. See Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 70 U.S. 532, 541 (1985). There is a reason we have such protections, and the attempt to remove them is a major red flag.

4. The proposed amendments to 5 CFR Part 213 and 5 CFR part 752 are, additionally, contrary to Congress's intent to create a merit-based civil service free from undue partisan political influence, in accordance with the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 and the Civil Service Due Process Amendments Act of 1990. Congress has determined that an effective and efficient federal civil service must be protected from partisan and improper influences. The current Excepted Services categories are intentionally limited and narrow in scope to properly carry out Congress's intent. OPM may not choose to disregard Congressional mandates in the manner proposed in this rule.

5. The civil service is the backbone to keeping our society running in more ways than one. As a scientist, I am particularly concerned about the impact the proposed rule will have on U.S. science, although this is far from the most important facet. U.S. science has led the world for decades, in part because of the investment in agencies like the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the National Institutes for Health (NIH), but in just as large part due to the expert scientists who make decisions at those agencies. Our science agencies will be unable to adequately support science (and meet their statutorily mandated scientific missions), if they are beholden to the politics of the president. Scientific expertise must drive drive decision-making. All efforts to hobble these agencies, including this one, are doomed to make the U.S. less competitive internationally and will have real-life effects on Americans who rely on these jobs, technological advancements, and medical treatment such as innovative cancer cures. Let scientists do their jobs. Let science agencies fund science, based on science, not politics.

Title: Comment from Nathan Douglas
Comment:
I strongly oppose the implementation or revival of the “Schedule F” classification for federal employees. This proposal threatens the merit-based civil service system that has underpinned a professional, nonpartisan federal workforce for over a century.

First and foremost, the creation of Schedule F directly undermines the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which was enacted to combat the spoils system and establish a merit-based hiring process for federal employees. By allowing a broad swath of career civil servants—particularly those involved in policy-making or analysis—to be reclassified and potentially terminated without cause, Schedule F opens the door to politically motivated hiring and firing. This is antithetical to the principle of an apolitical civil service enshrined in 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8), which mandates that federal employment decisions be based on merit and free from political influence.

Moreover, the vague and sweeping criteria for inclusion in Schedule F violate the due process protections guaranteed by 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which requires cause and procedural safeguards for the removal of career federal employees. Stripping thousands of workers of these protections not only weakens accountability but also risks chilling expert advice and dissent within agencies—undermining the very effectiveness of government operations.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is also bound by 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to support the merit system principles. Implementing Schedule F contradicts this statutory mission and places undue political pressure on career professionals, compromising the integrity and continuity of federal programs across administrations.

In conclusion, the Schedule F proposal poses a grave threat to the foundational principles of good governance, civil service independence, and the rule of law. I urge the administration and OPM to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement or revive this dangerous classification.

Federal statistical agencies are particularly vulnerable to the proposed rule due to the following:

Politicization: Schedule Policy/Career could lead to the politicization of the federal statistical workforce. Official federal statistics clearly influence public policy of all sorts: monetary, fiscal, regulatory, etc. Thus, a President could classify many statistical agency positions as Policy/Career and fire Bureau of Labor Statistics’ leaders for releasing or planning to release jobs or inflation statistics unfavorable to the President’s policy agenda. By making it easier to remove employees whom a President determines are interfering with his or her policies, it increases the potential for passivity or political loyalty to be prioritized over expertise and experience.

Importance of Trust, Impartiality and Objectivity: Statistical agencies, such as the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Census Bureau, and the National Center for Health Statistics, need political autonomy and the ability to act independently from political or other undue external influence regarding their operations, in order to provide impartial, objective, reliable data. Erosion of that autonomy in the agencies' operations, including data collection and analysis, staffing, and publications, would undermine their perceived or actual independence, leading to a loss of public trust in the data they produce.

Erosion of Expertise, Loss of Institutional Memory and Increase of Turnover: These agencies rely on highly specialized professionals, including statisticians, economists, and data scientists, who possess unique technical expertise and long-term institutional memory. Statistical agencies stand to lose experts who see their career paths as less secure and merit-based than before. The loss of these experts or frequent turnover in key positions could disrupt agency operations, hinder long-term planning, undermine the agency's ability to fulfill its mission, and impair the quality and accuracy of the data.

Decreased Employee Morale and Productivity: The uncertainty and fear of arbitrary dismissal could negatively impact employee morale, leading to decreased productivity and difficulty in attracting and retaining top talent.

Importance of Modernization, Research, and Data Continuity: To support their missions, statistical agencies must invest in long-term efforts such as extensive research, critical modernization projects, and efforts to ensure data access and continuity. Schedule Policy/Career could subject to agencies to changing presidential priorities, increasing senior staff turnover and disrupting modernization efforts, measurement of trends, and meaningful research.

On behalf of the American public, I call on you to reject Docket No. OPM–2025–0004 and to protect the trustworthiness of the federal statistics we all rely on.

Title: Comment from E K
Comment:
1. I oppose this proposed rule in its entirety, and every section of the proposed rule, as it allows for the reintroduction of a "spoils" system to the federal civil service. The proposed rule allows any given Administration to replace the nation's professional cadre of policy experts who serve the Constitution across Administrations with individuals who subordinate their duty to the Constitution and the law to partisan loyalties.

    2. I oppose the creation of the Schedule Policy/Career as a new category of Excepted Service under 5 CFR Part 213. Moving career civil servants into a category of at-will employment makes those civil service positions vulnerable to political manipulation and influence, including by putting those employees at risk of termination should their efforts to uphold the federal oath of employment to defend the Constitution conflict with a political appointee's belief that the employee has failed to "faithfully implement administration policies to the best of their ability," as required under the proposed amendment to Sec. 213.3501(b).

    3. I oppose the amendment of 5 CFR part 752 that removes the right of career civil servants to appeal the transfer of their position into an Excepted Service category, including the proposed Schedule Policy/Career category. The removal of such protection violates the Fifth Amendment due process rights of federal civil servants, specifically by removing the employees' interest in their tenure protections. See Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 70 U.S. 532, 541 (1985).

    4. The proposed amendments to 5 CFR Part 213 and 5 CFR part 752 are, additionally, contrary to Congress's intent to create a merit-based civil service free from undue partisan political influence, in accordance with the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 and the Civil Service Due Process Amendments Act of 1990. Congress has determined that an effective and efficient federal civil service must be protected from partisan and improper influences. The current Excepted Services categories are intentionally limited and narrow in scope to properly carry out Congress's intent. OPM may not choose to disregard Congressional mandates in the manner proposed in this rule.

Title: Comment from Jill Ruhnke

Office of Personnel Management

5 CFR Parts 210, 212, 213, 302, 432, 451, and 752

I am writing to oppose in the strongest terms the proposal to amend Schedule F as outlined (Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004, RIN 3206-AO80].  The changes would reduce substantive accountability and facilitate the hiring or firing of federal employees for improper partisan reasons.  It is essential that we have a deep bench of nonpartisan and apolitical subject matter experts, and that we keep employees based on their expertise and performance, and not their willingness to change their views and substantive work based on who won the most recent elections.  For example, during the Iran-Contra War, there were serious charges that intelligence analysts skewed their conclusions to tell DOD and other policymakers what they wanted to hear rather than what they needed to hear to accurately assess the risk to our troops and those of our allies.  The USG has worked hard to de-politicize analysis in intelligence and other fields, and this proposed rule threatens to undo all that.  Besides making our government less effective in its ability to support policymakers, such a rule woud also negatively impact our ability to recruit and retain the best and brightest.  It can already be hard to recruit experts to work in the USG due to generally  lower salaries than in the private sector, and the threat of furlough when Congress can't pass a budget on time.  Adding to this the potential that political pressures will be exerted on their work, and that they could be fired not for cause but simply because our country had an election, and recruitment and retention will be even harder, further eroding the quality of the work of those who strive to protect our national security and promote the common welfare.  In sum, I strongly oppose this rule.

Title: Comment from Edward  Cohen
Comment:
I oppose the proposed changes because they would politicize the civil service, centralize more power in the President, result in unstable government policy and degrade the skill level of individuals who want to devote their careers to serving their government.

The real purpose behind the proposed rule is to make it easier for a sitting President to replace civil servants with whom he may or may not agree and install his own appointees.  For 145 years, our government has been peopled by those dedicated to public service.  They understand that they are hired to implement the law and the policies of the current President.  It is for this reason that there already are 4,000 political appointees in every agency of the government.  There is no need for additional political appointees.  

The ability of the President to effectively remove civil service protections to potentially thousands more will make government service far less desirable.  If an employee can lose his or her job simply by doing as they were instructed by the prior Administration (or for no apparent reason at all) it would remove the security of a government job.  Because many government jobs do not typically pay as well as comparable jobs in the private sector, job security has always been an important consideration for those seeking to make their careers in government, especially for those whose skills would otherwise be in high demand.

Equally important, the government would lose valuable expertise and experience.  If incumbents in so many government positions are subject to removal, newcomers will have to learn new jobs and do so without the benefit of having experience in the agency.  The learning curve is often great.  As a result, the quality of implementation of government functions will suffer, resulting in inefficiency and even ineptness.  Learning on the job is no way to run a government.

Finally, the economy needs stability.  Constant turnover in thousands of positions would undermine consistency of government policies and programs.  Those investing in business will risk less if they are able to reliably anticipate or predict the business and economic environments in which they will function in the future.  The prospect of changing government policies and programs will undermine confidence and retard investment and growth.

Our country has prospered because government, in general, has been both competent and predictable.  It has attracted high levels of talent and public service has always been recognized as a noble profession.  To politicize so many more civil service protected positions will have severe detrimental impacts.  This rulemaking should be withdrawn.

Title: Comment from Kimberly Blair
Comment:
I am submitting these comments in opposition to the Office of Personnel Management’s (OPM) proposed regulation “Schedule Policy/Career.”  The proposed rule undermines more than 140 years of civil service reform following the spoils system. It opens the door to politically motivated firings and tramples on employees’ constitutional and statutory rights.  Moreover, the proposed regulation to dismantle civil service protections destabilizes the career workforce, politicizes the day- to- day work of government, and erodes the very idea of a professional, independent civil service.  Specific concerns are presented below.

·       Performance: This proposal gives lip service to performance management, but rather than providing thoughtful reform, it weaponizes the classification of “policy-influencing” roles to make it easier to purge career staff. It’s the latest attempt from this Administration to replace professionalism with ideological alignment.
·       Massive Expansion of At-Will Employment: The proposed rule would dramatically expand the number of civil servants who serve at the pleasure of the President from approximately 4,000 political appointees to potentially hundreds of thousands of what had been career employees.
·       Ideologically Driven Rulemaking: OPM makes sweeping claims about political “resistance” in the civil service based on cherry-picked anecdotes and selective surveys, using these to justify maximalist removal authority.
·       Undermines Civil Service Integrity: This proposed rule would discourage career civil servants from providing their uncensored opinions and from fully applying their expertise for the benefit of the American people. This would erode public trust in neutral governance.
·       Recruitment and Retention: This proposed rule would undermine the draw of mission-driven work in federal employment and make it harder for the federal government to recruit and retain talent.
·       Undoing Prior Protections: The proposed rule would undo the Biden Administration’s April 2024 civil service rule that was protective of longstanding employee rights and merit system principles.
In short, this rule is not about accountability or performance management—it’s about control. If finalized, it would mark one of the most regressive shifts in Federal workforce policy ever. It would harm the civil service’s ability to deliver services to the American people and, that in turn, would harm the country.

Title: Comment from Catherine Bulka

As a Principal Investigator who has applied for and received NIH funding, I am deeply committed to the NIH’s mission: advancing fundamental knowledge that improves health, extends life, and reduces illness and disability.

Adopting Schedule F would fundamentally undermine this mission. By removing civil service protections for NIH Program Officers, this policy risks politicizing the research funding process and weakening the very foundation of our public health research infrastructure.

NIH Program Officers are highly trained civil servants whose deep institutional knowledge and commitment to scientific integrity ensure that funding decisions are based on peer-reviewed merit. Replacing these professionals with political appointees would have several harmful consequences:

1. It threatens the neutrality and fairness of the peer review system, opening the door to funding decisions based on political agendas rather than scientific merit.
2. It discards critical institutional knowledge, undermining the NIH’s ability to operate efficiently and effectively.
3. It significantly increases the costs of recruitment, training, and turnover, adding unnecessary bureaucracy and reducing responsiveness.

This would not only slow the funding process, but also jeopardize the training pipeline for the next generation of public health professionals. In doing so, Schedule F would severely impair the United States' ability to respond to current and future public health challenges.

For these reasons, I strongly urge that Schedule F not be adopted. Its implementation would raise costs, reduce efficiency, erode the integrity of NIH funding, and politicize a system that has long been a global gold standard for scientific excellence and rigor. The downstream effects on the public health workforce and national research competitiveness would be both immediate and long-lasting.

Title: Comment from Stacy Leff
Comment:
I oppose the further politicization of the civil service.

The Trump Administration is advancing a new rule that would make it easier to fire nonpartisan career civil servants across the federal government without justification, notice, or right to appeal. This would cause particular harm at an agency like the Social Security Administration (SSA), where the Trump Administration and its Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) have already pushed through radical staffing cuts that have jeopardized SSA’s ability to reliably deliver benefits to seniors and workers with severe disabilities. The rule would create a new “Schedule Policy/Career” (Schedule P/C) classification that could be used to get rid of thousands of additional civil servants at SSA, giving the Administration even more power to undermine Social Security.

The Schedule P/C rule would lead to unprecedented politicization of the civil service. On April 23, the Trump Administration published a proposed rule that would let the President unilaterally change the employment status of any civil servant in a position that he deems to be “policy-influencing.” Under the rule — which revives a similar proposal from the first Trump term known then as “Schedule F” — the administration could fire, suspend, demote, or reduce the pay of employees they classify as Schedule P/C without regard for performance or due process. This would strip many current employees of existing protections, effectively converting civil service positions to an “at will” status and treating civil servants like de facto political appointees wholly subject to the whims of politically appointed bosses.

The rule violates the long-standing interpretation of the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 — a post-Watergate reform to protect against abuse of power — among other laws providing civil servants with due process. The law ensures they are “protected against arbitrary action, personal favoritism, or coercion for partisan political purposes.”

Experts have forecast that if the rule were implemented it would lead to “a massive degree of additional politicization, and the most fundamental change to the civil service system since its inception in 1883.” Across government, the proposed rule is likely to:

-undermine the quality of services;
-politicize day-to-day government decision-making;
-negatively impact the performance of core government functions;
-lead to more political favoritism in contracting and grant decisions which also can generate greater cost overruns; and
-cause an exodus of expertise from the federal workforce.

Please do not allow the Trump Administration to further chip away at our democracy by weakening the civil service

Civil servants are intended to be career professionals who serve across multiple administrations, providing continuity, stability, and deep expertise that transcends shifting political agendas. Weakening job protections in the name of "responsiveness" opens the door to purges of seasoned professionals who may offer dissenting or inconvenient expertise. A robust, independent civil service is not an obstacle to democratic governance; it is one of its cornerstones.

I believe the U.S. has a significant state interest in maintaining a professional civil service where job security is tied to one's skill-level and quality of work, not political affiliation. Stacey Iaconelli

Title: Comment from Justine  Moore
Comment:

Title: Comment from Lori Nelson
Comment:
“Schedule F” (now renamed Schedule Policy/Career) is shorthand for an executive order that is a sharp break with civil service merit principles, which assume that career employees should be retained on the basis of performance and protected against political coercion. The US is already unusual in the degree to which it reserves the top layers of organizational leadership for short-term political appointees. Schedule F will vastly expand the number of appointees, adding a proposed 50,000 from the current 4000. It does so by involuntarily reclassifying career civil servants as appointees, removing job protections, the basic constraint against political interference.

The administration says that the purpose of Schedule F is to increase accountability for civil servants involved in policy-making. Set aside the fact that civil servants are accountable in multiple ways, Trump’s own justifications strike a more conspiratorial tone, including “the deep state can and must be brought to heel.” But what better way to actually institutionalize a deep state than by expanding political influence over what constitutes good science?

Studies show that politicization of public services generally worsens public-sector outcomes. Public employees invest less in developing their expertise and become more likely to exit. Instability and lack of experience reduce organizational performance. Politicization increases the influence of more ideologically radical appointees relative to more moderate civil servants. Politicization also reduces accountability. Bureaucrats worried about being fired fail to share uncongenial information with their political bosses and become less likely to respond to congressional oversight. As politicization begets lower transparency and administrative capacity, it increases waste and inefficiency.

Title: Comment from Sheryl Dunton
Comment:
"I strongly oppose the implementation or revival of the “Schedule F” classification for federal employees. This proposal threatens the merit-based civil service system that has underpinned a professional, nonpartisan federal workforce for over a century.

First and foremost, the creation of Schedule F directly undermines the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which was enacted to combat the spoils system and establish a merit-based hiring process for federal employees. By allowing a broad swath of career civil servants—particularly those involved in policy-making or analysis—to be reclassified and potentially terminated without cause, Schedule F opens the door to politically motivated hiring and firing. This is antithetical to the principle of an apolitical civil service enshrined in 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8), which mandates that federal employment decisions be based on merit and free from political influence.

Moreover, the vague and sweeping criteria for inclusion in Schedule F violate the due process protections guaranteed by 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which requires cause and procedural safeguards for the removal of career federal employees. Stripping thousands of workers of these protections not only weakens accountability but also risks chilling expert advice and dissent within agencies—undermining the very effectiveness of government operations.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is also bound by 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to support the merit system principles. Implementing Schedule F contradicts this statutory mission and places undue political pressure on career professionals, compromising the integrity and continuity of federal programs across administrations.

In conclusion, the Schedule F proposal poses a grave threat to the foundational principles of good governance, civil service independence, and the rule of law. I urge the administration and OPM to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement or revive this dangerous classification."

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I am a retired federal employee and oppose this return to the spoils system which was largely eliminated in the 1883 Pendleton Act.  

1. I oppose this proposed rule in its entirety, and every section of the proposed rule, as it allows for the reintroduction of a "spoils" system to the federal civil service. The proposed rule allows any given Administration to replace the nation's professional cadre of policy experts who serve the Constitution across Administrations with individuals who subordinate their duty to the Constitution and the law to partisan loyalties.

2. I oppose the creation of the Schedule Policy/Career as a new category of Excepted Service under 5 CFR Part 213. Moving career civil servants into a category of at-will employment makes those civil service positions vulnerable to political manipulation and influence, including by putting those employees at risk of termination should their efforts to uphold the federal oath of employment to defend the Constitution conflict with a political appointee's belief that the employee has failed to "faithfully implement administration policies to the best of their ability," as required under the proposed amendment to Sec. 213.3501(b).

3. I oppose the amendment of 5 CFR part 752 that removes the right of career civil servants to appeal the transfer of their position into an Excepted Service category, including the proposed Schedule Policy/Career category. The removal of such protection violates the Fifth Amendment due process rights of federal civil servants, specifically by removing the employees' interest in their tenure protections. See Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 70 U.S. 532, 541 (1985).

4. The proposed amendments to 5 CFR Part 213 and 5 CFR part 752 are, additionally, contrary to Congress's intent to create a merit-based civil service free from undue partisan political influence, in accordance with the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 and the Civil Service Due Process Amendments Act of 1990. Congress has determined that an effective and efficient federal civil service must be protected from partisan and improper influences. The current Excepted Services categories are intentionally limited and narrow in scope to properly carry out Congress's intent. OPM may not choose to disregard Congressional mandates in the manner proposed in this rule.

Sincerely,
Melanie Rice Peters

Title: Comment from Jean Greenbaum
Comment:
I am writing in opposition to proposed rule that seeks to reinstate Schedule F, Trump’s never implemented plan to institutionalize political control and loyalty tests for the career bureaucracy by turning 50,000 or more career civil servants into political appointees.

Schedule F” (now renamed Schedule Policy/Career) is shorthand for an executive order that is a sharp break with civil service merit principles, which assume that career employees should be retained on the basis of performance and protected against political coercion. The US is already unusual in the degree to which it reserves the top layers of organizational leadership for short-term political appointees. Schedule F will vastly expand the number of appointees, adding a proposed 50,000 from the current 4000. It does so by involuntarily reclassifying career civil servants as appointees, removing job protections, the basic constraint against political interference.

The administration says that the purpose of Schedule F is to increase accountability for civil servants involved in policy-making. Set aside the fact that civil servants are accountable in multiple ways, Trump’s own justifications strike a more conspiratorial tone, including “the deep state can and must be brought to heel.” But what better way to actually institutionalize a deep state than by expanding political influence over what constitutes good science?

Studies show that politicization of public services generally worsens public-sector outcomes. Public employees invest less in developing their expertise and become more likely to exit. Instability and lack of experience reduce organizational performance. Politicization increases the influence of more ideologically radical appointees relative to more moderate civil servants. Politicization also reduces accountability. Bureaucrats worried about being fired fail to share uncongenial information with their political bosses and become less likely to respond to congressional oversight. As politicization begets lower transparency and administrative capacity, it increases waste and inefficiency.

This measure would further polarize this country with a dictator who is only interested in retaining power, not in governing for the benefit of all Americans.

Title: Comment from Gary Pelton
Comment:
I wrrite to express strong opposition to the proposed regulation seeking to reintroduce a Schedule F–like employment category within the federal civil service system. This change would mark a dangerous step away from the merit-based principles that have underpinned the United States civil service for more than a century.

The core strength of our federal workforce lies in its nonpartisan, expert-driven capacity to serve the American public consistently and fairly across changing administrations. This undermines the Merit System Principles (5 U.S.C. § 2301), which were enacted to ensure fair, competitive, and performance-based hiring and firing decisions. It also directly contradicts the spirit of the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which ended the corrupt patronage system of government employment by establishing a professional civil service grounded in competence and impartiality.

Furthermore, politicizing career roles compromises the continuity, institutional knowledge, and technical expertise that are vital to the functioning of agencies such as the CDC, FEMA, and FAA. The result would be a less effective, more politically vulnerable government—particularly in times of crisis, when independent, science- and law-based decision-making is essential.

I find this proposal runs against the general view that merit should be the main judge for excelence. We see the merit approach being advocated in college admissions and other judgements.

Comment:

·       Recruitment and Retention: This proposed rule would undermine the draw of mission-driven work in federal employment and make it harder for the federal government to recruit and retain talent.
·       Undoing Prior Protections: The proposed rule would undo the Biden Administration’s April 2024 civil service rule that was protective of longstanding employee rights and merit system principles.
In short, this rule is not about accountability or performance management—it’s about control. If finalized, it would mark one of the most regressive shifts in Federal workforce policy ever. It would harm the civil service’s ability to deliver services to the American people and, that in turn, would harm the country."

     Thank you for your consideration.

1. I oppose this proposed rule in its entirety, and every section of the proposed rule, as it allows for the reintroduction of a "spoils" system to the federal civil service. The proposed rule allows any given Administration to replace the nation's professional cadre of policy experts who serve the Constitution across Administrations with individuals who subordinate their duty to the Constitution and the law to partisan loyalties.

2. I oppose the creation of the Schedule Policy/Career as a new category of Excepted Service under 5 CFR Part 213. Moving career civil servants into a category of at-will employment makes those civil service positions vulnerable to political manipulation and influence, including by putting those employees at risk of termination should their efforts to uphold the federal oath of employment to defend the Constitution conflict with a political appointee's belief that the employee has failed to "faithfully implement administration policies to the best of their ability," as required under the proposed amendment to Sec. 213.3501(b).

3. I oppose the amendment of 5 CFR part 752 that removes the right of career civil servants to appeal the transfer of their position into an Excepted Service category, including the proposed Schedule Policy/Career category. The removal of such protection violates the Fifth Amendment due process rights of federal civil servants, specifically by removing the employees' interest in their tenure protections. See Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 70 U.S. 532, 541 (1985).

4. The proposed amendments to 5 CFR Part 213 and 5 CFR part 752 are, additionally, contrary to Congress's intent to create a merit-based civil service free from undue partisan political influence, in accordance with the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 and the Civil Service Due Process Amendments Act of 1990. Congress has determined that an effective and efficient federal civil service must be protected from partisan and improper influences. The current Excepted Services categories are intentionally limited and narrow in scope to properly carry out Congress's intent. OPM may not choose to disregard Congressional mandates in the manner proposed in this rule.

Title: Comment from Molly Hauck
Comment:

Title: Comment from Kirstin Case
Comment:
I strongly oppose the reimplementation of Schedule F as proposed in Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004, "Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service."

Schedule F would politicize the federal workforce by stripping civil service protections from thousands of dedicated public servants, including refuge managers, scientists, and conservation professionals in the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. These roles are essential to the functioning of the National Wildlife Refuge System and are grounded in science, law, and public service—not political ideology.

Since January 2025 alone, the Refuge System has lost more than 20% of its remaining staff, compounding a 30% decline over the past 15 years. Nearly 10% of refuges are already completely unstaffed, and no refuge in the country currently has the resources it needs to operate fully. Implementing Schedule F now would devastate what remains of the conservation workforce.

This rule would allow political appointees to fire experts without cause and replace them with ideologically aligned hires who may lack the experience or qualifications to manage public lands. That’s not accountability—it’s a recipe for instability, inefficiency, and the erosion of public trust.

Our nation’s public lands must be managed by nonpartisan professionals who are free to follow science, serve the public, and uphold conservation laws. I urge the Office of Personnel Management to reject this rule and protect the integrity of the merit-based civil service system.

Sincerely,
Kirstin Case

The proposed rule allows any given Administration to replace the nation's professional cadre of policy experts who serve the Constitution across Administrations with individuals who subordinate their duty to the Constitution and the law to partisan loyalties.

2. I oppose the creation of the Schedule Policy/Career as a new category of Excepted Service under 5 CFR Part 213. Moving career civil servants into a category of at-will employment makes those civil service positions vulnerable to political manipulation and influence, including by putting those employees at risk of termination should their efforts to uphold the federal oath of employment to defend the Constitution conflict with a political appointee's belief that the employee has failed to "faithfully implement administration policies to the best of their ability," as required under the proposed amendment to Sec. 213.3501(b).

3. I oppose the amendment of 5 CFR part 752 that removes the right of career civil servants to appeal the transfer of their position into an Excepted Service category, including the proposed Schedule Policy/Career category. The removal of such protection violates the Fifth Amendment due process rights of federal civil servants, specifically by removing the employees' interest in their tenure protections. See Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 70 U.S. 532, 541 (1985).

4. The proposed amendments to 5 CFR Part 213 and 5 CFR part 752 are, additionally, contrary to Congress's intent to create a merit-based civil service free from undue partisan political influence, in accordance with the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 and the Civil Service Due Process Amendments Act of 1990. Congress has determined that an effective and efficient federal civil service must be protected from partisan and improper influences. The current Excepted Services categories are intentionally limited and narrow in scope to properly carry out Congress's intent. OPM may not choose to disregard Congressional mandates in the manner proposed in this rule.

Comment:
I strongly oppose the reimplementation of Schedule F as proposed in Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004, "Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service."

Schedule F would politicize the federal workforce by stripping civil service protections from thousands of dedicated public servants, including refuge managers, scientists, and conservation professionals in the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. Implementing Schedule F now would devastate what remains of the conservation workforce.

This rule would allow political appointees to fire experts without cause and replace them with ideologically aligned hires who may lack the experience or qualifications to manage public lands. That’s not accountability—it’s a recipe for instability, inefficiency, and the erosion of public trust.

Our nation’s public lands must be managed by nonpartisan professionals who are free to follow science, serve the public, and uphold conservation laws. I urge the Office of Personnel Management to reject this rule and protect the integrity of the merit-based civil service system.

Sincerely,
Crystal Hart

In conclusion, while reform is needed, this proposal risks politicizing the civil service and weakening the very institutions it aims to improve. Title: Comment from Albert  Cornell
Comment:
I strongly oppose any effort to reinstate or expand Schedule F Policy/Career Schedule within the federal workforce. Doing so would reverse nearly a century and a half of progress made to ensure the U.S. civil service operates based on merit, not political allegiance.
The Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883 was enacted in direct response to the corruption of the “spoils system,” in which federal jobs were awarded based on political connections rather than qualifications. That system bred inefficiency, nepotism, and public distrust. The Pendleton Act established that federal employee should be hired and promoted based on competitive examinations and professional qualifications—not loyalty to elected officials or parties. The tipping point came in 1881 when Charles Guiteau, a disgruntled office seeker believed he was owed a patronage position. The public backlash was intense, creating political pressure for reform.
Schedule F Policy/Career Schedule represents a dangerous regression to that earlier era. By designating certain policy-related civil service roles as exempt from standard merit protections, it opens the door to politicized hiring and firing. This would not only reduce the independence and expertise of our federal agencies but would discourage talented individuals from entering public service altogether, knowing their job security could hinge on political tides rather than performance or integrity.
Loss of Institutional Expertise and Continuity: Career civil servants carry forward knowledge that spans administrations and enables consistent policy implementation, especially in complex areas such as health care, veterans’ services, national security, and disaster response. Schedule F  Policy/Career Schedule would enable mass dismissals of such professionals, threatening the operational continuity that the public depends on.
Erosion of Nonpartisan Governance: The American public expects federal decisions to be based on law, data, and professional standards. Replacing seasoned experts with politically aligned appointees reduces confidence that agencies are acting in the public interest rather than for partisan aims.
Historical Precedents Demonstrate the Risks: We have seen the dangers of politicizing the civil service. The DOJ hiring scandal during the 2000s revealed the consequences of using ideology over merit, leading to diminished public trust and legal accountability issues. Similarly, the chaotic response to Hurricane Katrina was widely attributed to leadership appointed based on loyalty rather than experience in emergency management.
Schedule F Policy/Career Schedule does not promote accountability or efficiency—it facilitates control over policy outcomes by allowing administrations to remove those who may disagree on professional grounds. That is not reform; it is structural manipulation of government function.
The Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 reaffirmed merit system principles and created safeguards to protect against exactly this kind of political interference. Those principles—competence, fairness, and impartiality—should remain nonnegotiable.
In sum, Schedule F Policy/Career Schedule poses a long-term risk to the stability, credibility, and fairness of our federal government. I urge the Office of Personnel Management and all relevant agencies to reject any policies that would enable or expand Schedule F Policy/Career Schedule designations. Civil servants must be able to serve the public with professionalism and integrity, not under the threat of politically motivated dismissal.

I write in strong support of the proposed Office of Personnel Management Rule, Upholding Civil Service Protections and Merit System Principles, RIN 3206–AO56, Docket ID: OPM–2023–0013. The proposed rule is excellent, and provides well-considered protections against the dangers posed by politicization. In particular, the previously signed Schedule F Executive Order represents the greatest threat to the system of merit embedded in the American civil service system since its inception.

The bottom line is that Schedule F would represent an unprecedented increase in politicizing the federal workforce, which would predictably undermine performance and accountability in the federal government, as well as democratic values such as transparency and the rule of law. By limiting its scope and specifying how it would work, the proposed rule has provided appropriate protection against the negative effects of Schedule F.

The writers of Schedule F have proposed using it to add 50,000 appointees, an extraordinary increase in politicization. The author of the Schedule F order, James Sherk, offered 50,000 as a likely and low end estimate: "I think there are ways you could broaden the scope of the order. How much is an open question…I think you can expand it beyond 50,000….I think it could be somewhat broadened to sweep in some more of those positions that have an influence on policy.”[1] He also said “All executive authority is vested in the President. Every federal employee should serve at the pleasure of the president."

President Trump has also been clear as to what he sees the purpose of Schedule F. He has said: “Either the deep state destroys America or we destroy the deep state”, vowing "retribution" for his political enemies. Elsewhere, Trump has said: “We will pass critical reforms making every executive branch employee fireable by the president of the United States. The deep state must and will be brought to heel.” Schedule F offers the key means to achieve Trump’s vision. Indeed, Trump loyalists already reportedly have lists of public servants to be purged because of perceived disloyalty to Trump.

The overt purpose of Schedule F is partisan politicization, centered on political loyalty to the President.

While some advocates of Schedule F have presented it as a means of restoring accountability in government, President Trump, who has signed it and made it central to his plans for a second administration has been very explicit about its purpose, which is to impose personal loyalty tests, and to use government as an instrument of his power. This is at odds with the purpose and traditions of the American state.
