Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I write to express my strong opposition to this proposed rule. While the stated goals of enhancing performance and accountability in federal service are important, the proposed changes risk undermining the integrity, stability, and impartiality of the federal workforce.

The proposed rule would significantly weaken long-standing due process protections for federal employees by accelerating procedures for performance-based removals, reducing the opportunity for employees to improve, and limiting their right to challenge unjust actions. These protections are not bureaucratic hurdles—they are essential safeguards that prevent partisan interference and ensure decisions are based on merit, not political loyalty or personal bias.

Moreover, the proposed rule echoes elements of the former “Schedule F” executive order, which threatened to politicize the civil service by allowing for the mass reclassification and removal of policy-influencing employees. This would erode the merit-based principles enshrined in the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 and jeopardize the nonpartisan nature of federal work.

As a career civil service employee, we must be protected from political pressures in order to serve the American public fairly and effectively. Weakening employee protections in the name of responsiveness risks replacing expertise and continuity with instability and politicization.

I respectfully urge the OPM to withdraw this proposed rule and instead pursue reforms that strengthen—not undermine—the impartial, merit-based federal workforce that has long been a pillar of effective governance.

Title: Comment from Colleen Hughes

The proposed rule allows any given Administration to replace the nation's professional cadre of policy experts who serve the Constitution across Administrations with individuals who subordinate their duty to the Constitution and the law to partisan loyalties.

    2. I oppose the creation of the Schedule Policy/Career as a new category of Excepted Service under 5 CFR Part 213. Moving career civil servants into a category of at-will employment makes those civil service positions vulnerable to political manipulation and influence, including by putting those employees at risk of termination should their efforts to uphold the federal oath of employment to defend the Constitution conflict with a political appointee's belief that the employee has failed to "faithfully implement administration policies to the best of their ability," as required under the proposed amendment to Sec. 213.3501(b).

    3. I oppose the amendment of 5 CFR part 752 that removes the right of career civil servants to appeal the transfer of their position into an Excepted Service category, including the proposed Schedule Policy/Career category. The removal of such protection violates the Fifth Amendment due process rights of federal civil servants, specifically by removing the employees' interest in their tenure protections. See Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 70 U.S. 532, 541 (1985).

    4. The proposed amendments to 5 CFR Part 213 and 5 CFR part 752 are, additionally, contrary to Congress's intent to create a merit-based civil service free from undue partisan political influence, in accordance with the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 and the Civil Service Due Process Amendments Act of 1990. Congress has determined that an effective and efficient federal civil service must be protected from partisan and improper influences. The current Excepted Services categories are intentionally limited and narrow in scope to properly carry out Congress's intent. OPM may not choose to disregard Congressional mandates in the manner proposed in this rule.

Our nation’s public lands must be managed by nonpartisan professionals who are free to follow science, serve the public, and uphold conservation laws. I urge the Office of Personnel Management to reject this rule and protect the integrity of the merit-based civil service system.

Sincerely,
Robin Pfeifer

I urge OPM to retract its rule on “Schedule Policy/Career” classification and changing federal employees’ removal protections, as it is unconstitutional and against Congressional intent and established law.
Separation of Powers and Congressional Prerogative
Congress holds exclusive authority to structure the civil service and establish removal protections. The Civil Service Reform Act prescribes merit-based hiring and standards for removal, thus ensuring an impartial public service. The proposed regulation seeks to negate these statutory protections, encroaching upon Congress's legislative prerogative.
Major Questions Doctrine and Non-Delegation

Agencies cannot exercise legislative power without an "intelligible principle" from Congress. Ambiguities should be resolved against expanding agency power, especially following recent Supreme Court decisions.

Merit system safeguards ensure government integrity and public interest. Statutes prevent patronage systems, maintaining nonpartisan civil service.
3.	Statutory Conflict and Ultra Vires Action
Congress has prescribed removal procedures clearly. OPM does not have the authority to contravene these statutes. Agency actions counter to statutory provisions are ultra vires and must be annulled. Ambiguous statutes should be interpreted to avoid constitutional issues.
4.	Legislative History and Reliance Interests
The Civil Service Reform Act ensures strong merit and due process protections. Significant deviations require well-reasoned explanations considering substantial reliance interests. If rules cannot be separated from unlawful components, those components must be vacated.
Anticipated Defenses and Rebuttals
General authority claims may not satisfy major questions tests. Rulemaking must be reasoned, not arbitrary or capricious. Expediency does not justify curtailing rights.
Conclusion and Recommendation
The proposed rule may violate constitutional and legal standards. OPM should seek reforms through explicit Congressional authorization. Withdrawal is recommended.

The removal of such protection violates the Fifth Amendment due process rights of federal civil servants, specifically by removing the employees' interest in their tenure protections. See Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 70 U.S. 532, 541 (1985).

4. The proposed amendments to 5 CFR Part 213 and 5 CFR part 752 are, additionally, contrary to Congress's intent to create a merit-based civil service free from undue partisan political influence, in accordance with the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 and the Civil Service Due Process Amendments Act of 1990. Congress has determined that an effective and efficient federal civil service must be protected from partisan and improper influences. The current Excepted Services categories are intentionally limited and narrow in scope to properly carry out Congress's intent. OPM may not choose to disregard Congressional mandates in the manner proposed in this rule.

Title: Comment from Amanda Schonfeld
Comment:
OFFICIAL COMMENT LETTER
Re: Opposition to Proposed Rule Implementing Executive Order 14171
To: U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM)
Date: May 16, 2025

To Whom It May Concern at the U.S. Office of Personnel Management:

I submit these comments in strong opposition to the proposed amendments to 5 CFR Parts 210, 212, 213, 302, 432, 451, and 752, issued in response to Executive Order 14171. The proposed rule creates a new Schedule Policy/Career category, weakens existing due process protections, and enables the reclassification of competitive service positions into the excepted service. These changes collectively undermine the merit-based, nonpartisan civil service and risk politicizing the federal workforce.

SUBPART 1 – 5 CFR PART 213 (Excepted Service)
The creation of Schedule Policy/Career as a new excepted service schedule enables the reclassification of protected roles into at-will positions based on vague concepts such as “accountability to the President.” This would allow political influence over roles currently held by career professionals and undermines the fundamental protections of the competitive service system.

SUBPART 2 – 5 CFR PART 212 (Competitive Service and Competitive Status)
While the proposed rule allows employees to retain competitive status, it effectively removes them from the competitive service by administrative action. This undercuts core merit system protections and introduces legal ambiguity about rights and appeals, setting a dangerous precedent for bypassing due process through reassignment.

SUBPART 3 – 5 CFR PARTS 752 and 432 (Adverse and Performance-Based Actions)
The proposal to exempt Schedule Policy/Career employees from the procedural protections of 5 U.S.C. Chapters 75 and 43 strips employees of the right to challenge unjust removals or demotions. This action weakens protections specifically designed to guard against retaliation and politicization, particularly for employees in policy-adjacent roles that demand objectivity and professional independence.

SUBPART 4 – 5 CFR PART 210 (Basic Definitions and Conforming Changes)
Removing prior definitions that limited policy-influencing roles to political appointees invites widespread reclassification of career positions without Congressional authorization or oversight. It dilutes the nonpartisan character of career roles and threatens the structural integrity of civil service definitions.

SUBPART 5 – 5 CFR PART 302 (Excepted Service Hiring Procedures)
The proposed elimination of procedural requirements for transferring employees into Schedule Policy/Career positions removes critical transparency and appeal rights. It further allows circumvention of the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB), leaving employees vulnerable to arbitrary or politically motivated personnel actions without recourse.

CONCLUSION

The proposed rule is inconsistent with the merit system principles codified in the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 and opens the door to political influence over previously independent, expert-driven roles. Rather than fostering accountability, the rule enables retaliation, undermines due process, and discourages the apolitical public service ethos foundational to our democracy.

I respectfully urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.

Respectfully submitted,
Amanda Schonfeld
Former GSA employee

Title: Comment from David Wright
Comment:
I am writing to express my unequivocal opposition to the proposed rule to reintroduce a Schedule F-like classification into the federal civil service.

This proposal represents a dangerous and sweeping shift away from the foundational principle that the federal workforce must serve the Constitution and the public—not any single political party or administration. Our nation’s civil service was deliberately designed to ensure continuity, professionalism, and impartiality. Undermining those pillars would jeopardize not just policy effectiveness but also public trust in government itself.

Reclassifying career civil servants into a new at-will employment category, as proposed under changes to 5 CFR Part 213, opens the door to political interference in what must remain neutral, evidence-based decision-making. These are the people who oversee everything from air and water quality to national security and public health. Turning these roles into political spoils risks replacing expertise with ideology, and long-term stewardship with short-term loyalty.

The proposed rule also strips employees of vital due process protections. By eliminating appeal rights under 5 CFR Part 752, it denies career civil servants their constitutional right to contest arbitrary or politically motivated reassignments or terminations. This is not only deeply unjust—it is a direct violation of established due process precedent (e.g., Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill).

Moreover, these changes fly in the face of Congressional intent. The Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 and the Civil Service Due Process Amendments Act of 1990 were enacted specifically to prevent partisan manipulation of federal employment. The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) does not have the authority to override these statutory safeguards by regulatory fiat.

In sum, this proposal would degrade the integrity, stability, and effectiveness of our government institutions. Federal employees are not political operatives; they are public servants, and they deserve legal protections that reflect that vital role. I urge you to withdraw this rule in its entirety and affirm the bipartisan commitment to a professional, merit-based civil service.

Respectfully,

Dave Wright

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Comment Opposing OPM Proposed Rule OPM-2025-0004-0001: Constitutional, Statutory, and Doctrinal Objections

I respectfully urge OPM to withdraw its proposed rule to create a “Schedule Policy/Career” classification and alter removal protections for federal employees. The proposal is unconstitutional, ultra vires, and incompatible with Congressional intent, established statute, and controlling precedent.

Separation of Powers and Congressional Prerogative Congress has exclusive constitutional authority to structure the civil service and establish removal protections. See U.S. Const. art. I, §8; Myers v. United States, 272 U.S. 52, 123 (1926); Humphrey’s Executor v. United States, 295 U.S. 602, 627–29 (1935); Morrison v. Olson, 487 U.S. 654, 685–86 (1988). The Civil Service Reform Act, 5 U.S.C. §§ 1101, 2101 et seq., and related laws mandate merit-based hiring and for-cause removal, ensuring apolitical public service (Arnett v. Kennedy, 416 U.S. 134, 151–52 (1974)). The proposed rule attempts to nullify these statutory safeguards by regulation, usurping Congress’s legislative prerogative (INS v. Chadha, 462 U.S. 919, 954 (1983)).

Major Questions Doctrine and Non-Delegation The Supreme Court has recently reaffirmed that “agencies must point to clear Congressional authorization for the power they claim” over issues of major economic or political significance. West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. ___, slip op. at 19–20 (2022); FDA v. Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp., 529 U.S. 120, 159 (2000); Util. Air Regulatory Grp. v. EPA, 573 U.S. 302, 324 (2014). OPM’s rule would affect thousands of federal positions, triggering the “major questions” doctrine. No clear statutory authorization exists for such sweeping changes. Under the non-delegation doctrine, agencies cannot exercise legislative power absent an “intelligible principle” from Congress (J.W. Hampton, Jr. & Co. v. United States, 276 U.S. 394, 409 (1928); Gundy v. United States, 139 S. Ct. 2116, 2123 (2019)). Any ambiguity must be resolved against expansion of agency power, especially after West Virginia v. EPA and the Supreme Court’s retreat from Chevron U.S.A., Inc. v. NRDC, 467 U.S. 837 (1984).

Merit-Based and Nonpartisan Civil Service The merit system protects government integrity and the public interest (Elrod v. Burns, 427 U.S. 347, 367 (1976)). Congressional statutes were enacted to prevent a return to patronage and the spoils system. See 5 U.S.C. §§ 2301, 7513; Rutan v. Republican Party of Illinois, 497 U.S. 62, 74–76 (1990).

Statutory Conflict, Ultra Vires Action, and Canons of Construction Congress has explicitly defined excepted service categories and removal procedures (5 U.S.C. §§ 2102, 7513). OPM lacks authority to override these statutes (Chevron, 467 U.S. at 843 n.9). Agency action contrary to statute is ultra vires and must be set aside under the APA, 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(C) (City of Arlington v. FCC, 569 U.S. 290, 297 (2013)). Ambiguous statutes must be construed to avoid constitutional issues (NLRB v. Catholic Bishop of Chicago, 440 U.S. 490, 499–501 (1979)), and there is a strong presumption against implied repeal of statutory rights (Morton v. Mancari, 417 U.S. 535, 549–51 (1974)).

Legislative History, Reliance Interests, and Agency Consistency Legislative history of the Civil Service Reform Act and related statutes demonstrates Congressional intent to ensure robust merit and due process protections. Any abrupt change from long-settled OPM practices requires a reasoned explanation that addresses significant reliance interests (Encino Motorcars, LLC v. Navarro, 579 U.S. 211, 222 (2016); FCC v. Fox Television Stations, 556 U.S. 502, 515 (2009)). The Supreme Court has held that if a rule is inseverable from its unlawful aspects, those aspects must be vacated in their entirety (Murphy v. NCAA, 584 U.S. ___, 138 S. Ct. 1461, 1482 (2018)).

Anticipated Defenses and Rebuttals Any OPM reliance on general authority (e.g., 5 U.S.C. § 1103) fails the major questions test (West Virginia v. EPA, slip op. at 19–20). Rulemaking must also be reasoned and not arbitrary or capricious (Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983)). Expediency or administrative efficiency does not justify curtailing statutory or constitutional rights.

Conclusion and Recommendation The proposed rule is plainly unconstitutional and unlawful. OPM should pursue any substantive reforms only through explicit Congressional authorization, not by regulatory fiat. Immediate withdrawal is warranted.

My interest in this proposed rule change is both personal—I would like to be treated fairly as an employee—and civic—I believe the services provided by the federal government are important and I’d like them to be provided effectively. - The overall competency and integrity of the workforce; and
- The overall obedience of the workforce

Specifically, I think these changes will actually punish integrity and, at best, be ineffective in improving competency. I do agree that they will make the workforce more obedient but I question whether that is a desirable goal. If, instead of obedience per se, the President feels that the executive workforce would be more effective with more roles filled by political sympathizers, that’s a goal worth debating, but this new schedule is an inefficient way to accomplish that goal.

I've done my best to justify my objections in my full comment, which is in the attached document.

Title: Comment from Holly Allen
Comment:
OFFICIAL COMMENT LETTER
Re: Opposition to Proposed Rule Implementing Executive Order 14171
To: U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM)
Date: May 16 2025

To Whom It May Concern at the U.S. Office of Personnel Management:

I submit these comments in strong opposition to the proposed amendments to 5 CFR Parts 210, 212, 213, 302, 432, 451, and 752, issued in response to Executive Order 14171. The proposed rule creates a new Schedule Policy/Career category, weakens existing due process protections, and enables the reclassification of competitive service positions into the excepted service. These changes collectively undermine the merit-based, nonpartisan civil service and risk politicizing the federal workforce.

SUBPART 1 – 5 CFR PART 213 (Excepted Service)
The creation of Schedule Policy/Career as a new excepted service schedule enables the reclassification of protected roles into at-will positions based on vague concepts such as “accountability to the President.” This would allow political influence over roles currently held by career professionals and undermines the fundamental protections of the competitive service system.

SUBPART 2 – 5 CFR PART 212 (Competitive Service and Competitive Status)
While the proposed rule allows employees to retain competitive status, it effectively removes them from the competitive service by administrative action. This undercuts core merit system protections and introduces legal ambiguity about rights and appeals, setting a dangerous precedent for bypassing due process through reassignment.

SUBPART 3 – 5 CFR PARTS 752 and 432 (Adverse and Performance-Based Actions)
The proposal to exempt Schedule Policy/Career employees from the procedural protections of 5 U.S.C. Chapters 75 and 43 strips employees of the right to challenge unjust removals or demotions. This action weakens protections specifically designed to guard against retaliation and politicization, particularly for employees in policy-adjacent roles that demand objectivity and professional independence.

SUBPART 4 – 5 CFR PART 210 (Basic Definitions and Conforming Changes)
Removing prior definitions that limited policy-influencing roles to political appointees invites widespread reclassification of career positions without Congressional authorization or oversight. It dilutes the nonpartisan character of career roles and threatens the structural integrity of civil service definitions.

SUBPART 5 – 5 CFR PART 302 (Excepted Service Hiring Procedures)
The proposed elimination of procedural requirements for transferring employees into Schedule Policy/Career positions removes critical transparency and appeal rights. It further allows circumvention of the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB), leaving employees vulnerable to arbitrary or politically motivated personnel actions without recourse.

CONCLUSION
The proposed rule is inconsistent with the merit system principles codified in the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 and opens the door to political influence over previously independent, expert-driven roles. Rather than fostering accountability, the rule enables retaliation, undermines due process, and discourages the apolitical public service ethos foundational to our democracy.

I respectfully urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.

Respectfully submitted,
Holly Allen

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I urge the Office of Personnel Management to withdraw its proposed "Schedule Policy/Career" classification rule. The proposal fundamentally contravenes constitutional principles of separation of powers and due process, exceeds statutory authority, cannot withstand judicial scrutiny, and undermines the merit-based civil service system established by Congress. Fundamental changes to civil service structure require explicit Congressional action—not administrative reinterpretation.

Constitutional Infirmity: Separation of Powers

The Constitution's careful balancing of powers reserves to Congress alone the authority to structure federal employment. Article I, Section 8 vests Congress—not the Executive—with power to "make all Laws which shall be necessary and proper" for executing governmental functions. The Supreme Court has consistently upheld this allocation of power through its canonical decisions in Myers, Humphrey's Executor, and Morrison.
In crafting the Civil Service Reform Act, Congress deliberately established merit-based hiring protocols and for-cause removal protections. This agency cannot, through mere regulatory action, circumvent this comprehensive statutory framework. To do so constitutes a textbook violation of INS v. Chadha's prohibition against executive usurpation of legislative function.

Ultra Vires Action Under Major Questions Doctrine

The Court's recent jurisprudence in West Virginia v. EPA emphatically requires "clear Congressional authorization" for agency actions of significant economic and political consequence. The proposed reclassification of thousands of competitive service positions into a novel "policy-influencing" category plainly constitutes such a major question.

Congress has meticulously delineated the boundaries of excepted service in 5 U.S.C. §§ 2102-2103. Nowhere in this statutory architecture exists authorization for OPM's sweeping recategorization. When Congress intends to permit exceptions to competitive service protections, it does so explicitly—not through silent delegation or statutory penumbras.

Procedural Due Process Violations

Federal employees possess constitutionally protected property interests in their positions, as established in Perry v. Sindermann and Board of Regents v. Roth. The Fifth Amendment demands meaningful procedural safeguards before deprivation of such interests. The proposed rule's nebulous "policy-influencing" standard creates precisely the kind of vague framework that the Court condemned in Connally as inviting arbitrary enforcement.
The inevitable inconsistent application of this vague standard across agencies will produce exactly the sort of capricious governmental action that the APA's § 706(2)(A) prohibits. The rule fails to provide the "ascertainable standard of conduct" required by basic constitutional principles.

Contravention of Merit System Principles

The civil service merit system represents a cornerstone of effective governance, replacing the corrupt patronage system with professional administration. The Supreme Court in Elrod and Rutan has consistently upheld statutory protections against politicization of federal employment. This proposal would effectively nullify the carefully calibrated statutory protections in 5 U.S.C. §§ 2301 and 7513.

Administrative Procedure Deficiencies

OPM has failed to provide the "reasoned explanation" for its abrupt policy reversal that Encino Motorcars and Fox Television Stations demand. The agency has neither acknowledged the substantial reliance interests at stake nor adequately justified its departure from decades of consistent interpretation. Such failure renders the proposed rule arbitrary and capricious under State Farm.

Recommendation

Constitutional principles of separation of powers, due process, and proper statutory construction compel OPM to withdraw this legally infirm proposal. Fundamental changes to the civil service structure require explicit Congressional action—not administrative reinterpretation. The proposed rule cannot withstand judicial scrutiny and should be abandoned.

Title: Comment from John Czajka
Comment:
As a retired statistician whose employment was entirely outside the federal government, I am writing to express my deep concern that the proposed Schedule Policy/Career will adversely affect the quality of data produced and released by the numerous federal agencies that form the backbone of federal statistics. The federal government, industry, academia, and the public rely on the quality and especially the objectivity of federal statistics. Reclassification of non-political, career positions will remove the Civil Service job protections that apply to their occupants. These protections are one of several considerations that move qualified individuals to choose federal employment over better paid positions in academia and industry. I fear that federal employees whose positions are liable to be included in the proposed classification change may become subject to dismissal for simply performing their jobs if their research findings or even statistical estimates based on established methodologies are viewed as inconsistent with the priorities of the current administration. Even low-level political appointees may be able to remove career employees if they become concerned with how such estimates will be viewed by higher-level appointees. I fear as well that employees in the proposed schedule may become subject to dismissal for opinions they express outside of work and which have no bearing on their job performance. In addition, I fear that, because of the uncertainty hanging over their future employment, the most capable researchers and practitioners, who have chosen federal employment over good options in other sectors, will leave the federal government for other, more welcoming opportunities. I also fear that potential recruits who have skills that the federal government sorely needs will see these changes in the Civil Service as one more reason to choose employment in the private sector or academia over the federal government.

From my own observation, there are already too many positions within the federal government that are classified as political and therefore subject to replacement with each successive administration. Many of these positions go unfilled or take so long to fill that their potential contributions to the administration’s policymaking is severely limited. The proposed Schedule Policy/Career will effectively expand this number by making numerous positions that are currently covered under the Civil Service job protections subject to removal on grounds that are purely political, turning them into de facto political positions. While the proposed regulation is presented as enabling the federal government to deal more effectively with misconduct and poor performance, these deficiencies are rare among individuals who have achieved the stature that would make them subject to the proposed new schedule. I can only suppose that the principal purpose of this new schedule is to facilitate the removal of employees when the results of their work (including routine reports) challenges the administration’s assumptions. Recent examples of long-term federal employees being demoted or removed for their efforts to protect confidential data from access by unauthorized individuals (as the law requires) or to prevent the use of such data for purposes other than those allowed by law provide reason to be skeptical that the proposed regulations will make government more effective or efficient.   

Many of the positions that will be reclassified are held by individuals who have developed detailed expertise that cannot easily be replaced by new hires or appointees. This potential loss of expertise is particularly concerning in areas involved with federal data collection, which covers a wide range of disciplines. While positions involved in data collection may not have an obvious role in policy determination or implementation, Schedule Policy/Career would afford the President the ability to reclassify any position within the federal government to the new schedule. Accurate data collection, free from political interference, requires professional autonomy for those charged with compiling and interpreting these statistics. 

Furthermore, public trust in federal data collection, particularly where such data collection requires the public’s cooperation, is critical to both the quality of the data collected and its utility for policymaking. Such trust will be reduced if much of the public comes to view such data collection as motivated by political objectives. This will lead invariably to a declining willingness to participate in government data collection. Response rates to federal surveys have been declining for decades due to many factors; an erosion of public trust in the data being collected could only further these trends, reducing the reliability of the data on which federal policymaking is so dependent.

Title: Comment from Robert Marlay
Comment:
I write to express opposition to the Proposed Rule for the following reasons.

1.	The "problem", as hypothesized, is mischaracterized, over-blown, and not representative of reality. As a Navy Rear Admiral, and later as a career SES, I logged 54 years of distinguished military and civil service, spanning 16 Administrations. I have a long view of federal service. Across different organizational settings, I was blessed by serious work, led by visionary leaders, and supported by extraordinarily skilled and dedicated career professionals without whom important missions would not have been accomplished. We took our orders from those appointed over us. We made many personal sacrifices for the greater good, and worked long hours, professionally and apolitically, to deliver desired outcomes. As they say in the Navy, "If it ain't broke, don't fix it." Putting these teams as risk by subjecting them to potentially arbitrary and capricious “at will” firings, will sap the idea of a high calling, erode morale, constrain critical thinking, and give rise to workplace fear. The rule, if implemented, will change the tenor and attractiveness of career service.

2.	High-risk moments. In my experience, transitions across Administrations are the most challenging time periods for career professionals, mainly because careerists have had no time yet to prove themselves. The incoming appointees, regardless of party, typically arrive as “victorious warriors” full of party idealism and rhetoric. Most know little about the job they are expected to perform but will appreciate with time that they need help. Yet, the initial bias is: (a) “If you were not with us, you must be against us;” or (b) “If you were successful in the last Administration, you must have gone native.” Hence, there is a view that career professionals cannot be trusted. There is a strong press to vacate positions immediately and fill them with loyalists. Such is the rationale for the “spoils” system. It is often the case found in foreign governments. Under an “at will” system there seems to be no brakes on this type of cleansing. I fear that professionals with hard-to-recruit skill sets will be dismissed during this early and awkward transition period for no cause. Worse, the enduring signal that few can survive a transition will quench the flow of talent for the future. This is not how to invest in a technically qualified and skilled workforce of the future. There should be built-in protections from these tendencies, especially during the 1st year of a new Administration.      

3.	Bad eggs. I agree with, and have always supported the need for, a high degree of accountability. I also agree, from my experience of directing hundreds of employees, that there is a small fraction (3 in my career) of truly bad eggs who can poison the will and have no business in public service. I also agree that it is difficult under current rules to effect meaningful discipline or performance improvement. However, rather than wholesale civil service reform that seems to “throw out the baby with the bath water”, the proposed rule should focus more narrowly on streamlining the process for terminating poor performers, and not on reclassifying large swaths of senior career professionals with an undefined label of “policy influencers”.

4.	Pejorative Labeling. Finally, I strongly object to the labeling of large swaths of hard-workin, career professionals as “policy influencers”.  Indirectly, the whole of government, vice the private sector, is about the development, administration, or implementation of public policy. Even the development of atomic weapons is a project directed by national defense policy. Career professionals are repeatedly asked to analyze ideas, assess options, apply critical thinking, and present alternative cases or solutions to political leadership for decision-making, or on how best to carry out their agenda, and at what cost. All such employees would, under most interpretations of this rule, be classified as contributing to or influencing public policy. The label is vastly too broad and, accordingly, dangerous.

For the reasons stated above, I oppose the proposed rule and its broad intent, as presently stated.

Title: Comment from Latricia Powell
Comment:
To Whom It May Concern,

This comment is submitted in response to the Office of Personnel Management’s (OPM) proposed rule, published under Docket Number OPM-2025-0004, concerning the creation of Schedule Policy/Career and the corresponding removal of chapter 43 and 75 procedural protections for certain policy-influencing federal positions.

While the stated goal of increasing employee accountability is valid and necessary, the proposed structural shift toward at-will employment for career civil servants in policy-influencing roles raises substantial concerns related to governance integrity, nonpartisan service, and democratic stability.

 Legal and Governance Implications
	1.	Erosion of Due Process Protections:
The proposed rule circumvents longstanding statutory protections under 5 U.S.C. chapters 43 and 75. These frameworks exist to ensure career federal employees are insulated from arbitrary removal and politically motivated retaliation. Eliminating these protections in the name of efficiency poses a constitutional risk, especially for employees expected to implement, not blindly obey, directives that may raise ethical or legal red flags.
	2.	Chilling Effect on Institutional Dissent and Expertise:
Career professionals bring institutional memory and subject matter expertise critical to government continuity. The threat of at-will removal for non-aligned views—even when those views are technically sound or legally grounded—would foster a culture of compliance over conscience. This impairs the very merit-based service the rule purports to uphold.
	3.	Precedent for Politicization of the Civil Service:
Creating a new “Schedule Policy/Career” classification that strips appeals rights while maintaining career appointment language blurs the line between apolitical public service and political servitude. Historically, protections for policy-implementing roles have been maintained to preserve the integrity of the nonpartisan workforce. Weakening these norms risks turning civil service into a revolving door for ideological alignment, rather than a stable apparatus of governance.

⸻

Accountability Without Arbitrary Power

While there is a legitimate need for agencies to manage poor performance and misconduct efficiently, such outcomes should be pursued within a framework of procedural fairness and administrative transparency. There are already tools available for agencies to address non-performance (including probationary periods and streamlined adverse action procedures). A wholesale removal of due process bypasses reform in favor of disruption.

⸻

 Recommendations
		Narrow the definition of “policy-influencing” positions eligible for this classification and limit it only to those with a clear line of influence on executive-level directives.
	Require independent review panels prior to any dismissal under this schedule to maintain checks and balances.
	Maintain limited appeals rights to the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) for cases involving alleged political or retaliatory terminations.
	Conduct a congressionally monitored impact study prior to full implementation to evaluate potential workforce destabilization or political misuse.
In conclusion, while the goal of performance accountability is important, this rule in its current form introduces significant risk of abuse, institutional destabilization, and politicization of the civil service. Title: Comment from Nancy Allinson
Comment:
Comments on Proposed OPM Rule on “Schedule Policy/Career”

I am submitting these comments in opposition to the Office of Personnel Management’s (OPM) proposed regulation “Schedule Policy/Career.”  The proposed rule undermines more than 140 years of civil service reform following the spoils system. It opens the door to politically motivated firings and tramples on employees’ constitutional and statutory rights.  Moreover, the proposed regulation to dismantle civil service protections destabilizes the career workforce, politicizes the day- to- day work of government, and erodes the very idea of a professional, independent civil service.  Specific concerns are presented below.

Performance: This proposal gives lip service to performance management, but rather than providing thoughtful reform, it weaponizes the classification of “policy-influencing” roles to make it easier to purge career staff. It’s the latest attempt from this Administration to replace professionalism with ideological alignment.  Massive Expansion of At-Will Employment: The proposed rule would dramatically expand the number of civil servants who serve at the pleasure of the President from approximately 4,000 political appointees to potentially hundreds of thousands of what had been career employees.
Ideologically Driven Rulemaking: OPM makes sweeping claims about political “resistance” in the civil service based on cherry-picked anecdotes and selective surveys, using these to justify maximalist removal authority.  Undermines Civil Service Integrity: This proposed rule would discourage career civil servants from providing their uncensored opinions and from fully applying their expertise for the benefit of the American people. This would erode public trust in neutral governance.
Recruitment and Retention: This proposed rule would undermine the draw of mission-driven work in federal employment and make it harder for the federal government to recruit and retain talent.
Undoing Prior Protections: The proposed rule would undo the Biden Administration’s April 2024 civil service rule that was protective of longstanding employee rights and merit system principles.

In short, this rule is not about accountability or performance management—it’s about control. If finalized, it would mark one of the most regressive shifts in Federal workforce policy ever. It would harm the civil service’s ability to deliver services to the American people and, that in turn, would harm the country.

Title: Comment from Anonymous

2. I oppose the creation of the Schedule Policy/Career as a new category of Excepted Service under 5 CFR Part 213. Moving career civil servants into a category of at-will employment makes those civil service positions vulnerable to political manipulation and influence, including by putting those employees at risk of termination should their efforts to uphold the federal oath of employment to defend the Constitution conflict with a political appointee's belief that the employee has failed to "faithfully implement administration policies to the best of their ability," as required under the proposed amendment to Sec. 213.3501(b).

3. I oppose the amendment of 5 CFR part 752 that removes the right of career civil servants to appeal the transfer of their position into an Excepted Service category, including the proposed Schedule Policy/Career category. The removal of such protection violates the Fifth Amendment due process rights of federal civil servants, specifically by removing the employees' interest in their tenure protections. See Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 70 U.S. 532, 541 (1985).

4. The proposed amendments to 5 CFR Part 213 and 5 CFR part 752 are, additionally, contrary to Congress's intent to create a merit-based civil service free from undue partisan political influence, in accordance with the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 and the Civil Service Due Process Amendments Act of 1990. Congress has determined that an effective and efficient federal civil service must be protected from partisan and improper influences. The current Excepted Services categories are intentionally limited and narrow in scope to properly carry out Congress's intent. OPM may not choose to disregard Congressional mandates in the manner proposed in this rule.

To Whom It May Concern, Introduction: OPM-2025-0004 I am writing as a dedicated federal employee who has served our country for 34 years. My position has always been nonpartisan and does not involve the development or influence of public policy. Yet under the proposed schedule policy/career rule, my role is now being considered for reclassification into an excepted service category. I am deeply concerned about the fairness, transparency, and potential harm of this action, both to my family and to thousands of similarly affected public servants. 

Background: This comment is in response to the agency's proposal to implement the schedule policy/career rule, which aims to reclassify certain federal employees into a new employment category outside of traditional civil service protections, based on a vague standard of "policy influence." This rule appears to revive elements of the previously withdrawn Schedule F proposal. 

Analysis: The reclassification process outlined in this rule lacks clear criteria and appears overly broad. My work has been technical and operational in nature, carried out with integrity under multiple administrations without regard to political affiliation, following contracting and purchasing law. To suggest that such roles are "policy-influencing" is incorrect, misleading and unfair. Reclassifying long-serving, nonpartisan employees into a category that allows for removal without due process introduces unnecessary instability into the federal workforce. It undermines trust in public service, affects morale, and puts families like mine at risk of losing hard-earned job security based on politics rather than performance. Additionally, the agency has not sufficiently addressed how this policy will be implemented or reviewed for fairness. There is also no evidence that current civil service protections are inadequate to ensure accountability in the workforce. 

Recommendations: Withdraw the proposed schedule policy/career rule in its current form. Exclude any positions that do not meet a narrow and clearly defined threshold of direct policy development or influence. Publish specific criteria used to identify reclassifications and provide a no fee appeals process for affected employees. Conduct an impact analysis that includes consultation with employee representatives and independent oversight bodies. 

Conclusion: The schedule policy/career rule threatens the foundational principles of a nonpartisan, merit-based civil service. It unfairly targets employees like me, who have dedicated their careers to serving the American people with professionalism, regardless of political changes or affiliations. I urge the agency to reconsider this approach and uphold the values that have sustained effective and ethical government service for generations. 

Sincerely,  Concerned Citizen and Proud Civil Servant

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Comment on Proposed Rule: Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service
Agency: Office of Personnel Management (OPM)
Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004
RIN: 3206-AO80

To Whom It May Concern,

I submit this comment in strong opposition to the proposed rule referenced above. While improving accountability is a valid objective, this rule undermines essential legal protections, due process rights, and the apolitical foundation of the civil service.

Legal and Policy Concerns:

Merit System Principles (5 U.S.C. § 2301): The rule contradicts key principles of fairness, neutrality, and protection from arbitrary action and political coercion.

Prohibited Personnel Practices (5 U.S.C. § 2302): Weakening procedural safeguards may increase risks of retaliation, favoritism, and political influence—especially in policy-sensitive roles.

Due Process Violations (5 U.S.C. § 7513): The rule's proposed shortening of notice and response periods violates established due process expectations. In Loudermill (470 U.S. 532), the Supreme Court reinforced that public employees are entitled to notice and an opportunity to respond before adverse actions.

Schedule F Precedent: Though Schedule F was rescinded by Executive Order 14003, this proposal mirrors its goals by enabling removals based on “responsiveness” or perceived loyalty, risking a politicized workforce.

Impact of the Proposal:

Employee Morale & Retention: These changes will discourage qualified professionals from entering or remaining in public service.

Risk of Political Retaliation: Broad discretion to reclassify or remove employees in sensitive roles weakens the firewall between politics and public administration.

Equity Concerns: The policy may disproportionately affect marginalized employees and contradict government-wide equity commitments.

Recommendations and Alternatives:

Retain the current 30-day notice period and due process safeguards under 5 U.S.C. § 7513.

Expand early intervention tools, including coaching, mediation, and performance improvement plans.

Provide better training and support for managers on handling misconduct and performance concerns.

Require data transparency—no substantial evidence has been provided that current procedures are ineffective.

Pilot reforms in limited settings to study outcomes before nationwide rollout.

Conclusion:

This proposed rule (Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004, RIN: 3206-AO80) risks eroding statutory civil service protections and contradicts key federal laws. It should be withdrawn or significantly revised to align with merit system principles and due process rights.

Respectfully submitted.

Title: Comment from Michelle Edwards
Comment:
As a Veteran, Patriot, Mother, Wife, and full-time employee I strongly oppose the "Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service" rule presented by the Office of Personnel Management (RIN#:2025-06904).  See my bullet points below and please reject this proposal!

•	Changes should be incremental in nature to be fair to both federal employees and the American public. This proposal presents disruptive changes that overturn decades of norms and policy.
•	Exposes public services to increased political instability: Political loyalty would become more important than expertise, which will directly impact the services used by the American public: Social Security, Medicare and Medicaid, housing services, national security, national parks, and much more. 
•	Less experienced federal workforce: By making it easier to fire career civil servants, this proposal would drain the federal government of skilled and experienced workers necessary for the federal government’s complex and necessary work. 
•	Hinders our country’s research and innovation: The proposed rule would allow for political appointees to remove scientists at-will who present scientific findings that are at odds with the administration’s political agenda.
•	Does not adequately justify rescinding and replacing the 2024 OPM rule: The Supreme Court has said agencies are “free to change their existing policies” but must “provide a reasoned explanation for the change,” “display awareness that [it] is changing position,” and “show that there are good reasons for the new policy.” Commenters could argue, for instance, that not enough time has passed between the passage of the 2024 rule and creation of the 2025 rule for OPM to have assessed the effectiveness of the 2024 rule. 
•	Contrary to existing civil service laws’ intentions: The Civil Service Reform Act and The Pendleton Act were meant to end the spoils system and to keep politics out of hiring and firing decisions. The proposed rule, while it purports to preserve merit hiring, is fundamentally opposed to this goal, because it will reclassify career civil servants as at-will employees for the express purpose of making them easier to fire, regardless of merit, if they are perceived as pushing back on Presidential directives.
•	The Costs section of the proposed rule fails to mention other costs, including the decreased ability of Schedule P/C employees to follow lawful statutes or regulations without fear of retaliation if those statutes are deemed inconsistent with the priorities of the governing administration. Stripping over 50,000 federal workers of civil service protections and exposing the American public to increased instability in public service delivery are all concrete harms.
•	Some professionals, like attorneys, have ethical obligations to maintain high standards of honesty, integrity, and fairness to their clients. The proposed rule could force these employees to choose between meeting their ethical obligations or facing retaliation for not giving leadership the advice they want to hear. 
•	The proposed rule is likely to exacerbate the existing loss of experienced, competent employees that is already underway due to the administration’s other extreme actions, including the deferred resignation programs (DRPs), unprecedented layoffs (RIFs), and attempted termination of tens of thousands of probationary and term employees. This policy would provide another avenue for the administration to attempt to illegally dismantle agencies by rendering them inoperable by the removal of their staff.
•	Undermines the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (CSRA), which was enacted to prevent politicization of federal employee work and ensure a competent and impartial federal workforce.
o	The term “partisanship” is not defined anywhere in the proposed rule, giving this and future administrations license to terminate or discipline a reclassified employee simply for being perceived to be pushing back on the policy preferences of the administration.  
•	Congress granted statutory due process rights to federal workers by creating for-cause removal restrictions in the CSRA. OPM’s rulemaking authority is insufficient to revoke a right that Congress created for career federal workers. Revoking such a right would require legislative action from Congress.
•	While the CSRA intended to provide greater presidential control over federal employee removal, this was designed to be channeled through the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB), which the CSRA created. The Trump Administration, however, is attempting to bypass MSPB and, in so doing, deprive civil servants of their due process rights.
•	Removing protections from these workers under 5 U.S.C. Chapter 75 may affect other workers’ protections like union rights.

Title: Comment from Susan Groshen
Comment:
RE: Public Comment in Response to Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service [Docket No. OPM–2025–0004]

I am writing to express my opposition to the effort to reclassify specific federal positions, which would erode necessary protections for those serving within the federal statistical system and could transform positions which rely on specific expertise to political ones. The proposed rule, “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service,” would call into question the objectivity that both sides of the aisle rely on for our economic indicators, public health assessments, energy utilization and many other statistics. The federal statistical system plays an essential role in improving the lives of all Americans as well as informing critical policy decisions with evidence that is timely, relevant, and accurate. Federal statistical agencies are particularly vulnerable to the proposed rule due to the following:
•	Politicization: Schedule Policy/Career could lead to the politicization of the federal statistical workforce. A President could classify many statistical agency positions as Policy/Career. Then, for example, Bureau of Labor Statistics’ leaders could be fired for releasing or planning to release jobs or inflation statistics unfavorable to the President’s policy agenda; they might also face pressure to change methodologies or reveal pre-release information. By making it easier to remove employees if a President determines that they are interfering with his or her policies, it increases the potential for passivity or political loyalty to be prioritized over expertise and experience. Politicization has had dramatic consequences for statistical agencies and their leaders in other countries, notably Argentina and Greece.
•	Importance of Trust, Impartiality and Objectivity: Statistical agencies, such as the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Census Bureau, and the National Center for Health Statistics, need professional autonomy to provide impartial, objective, reliable data. Erosion of professional autonomy in the operations of statistical agencies would undermine their perceived or actual independence, leading to a loss of public trust in the data they produce.
•	Importance of Norms: Schedule Policy/Career would deprioritize and thus weaken the norms that uphold the ethical and professional standards that are critical to the success of statistical agencies. Senior leaders help craft, model and reinforce norms within their agencies and between their agencies and other parts of the government.  Examples include how agencies interact with staff, data users, data subjects, outside experts and host agencies. These norms reflect and go beyond the laws, rules, and policy directives that govern agencies’ operations. Weaker norms threaten trust, efficient operations, and data quality.
•	Erosion of Expertise, Loss of Institutional Memory and Increase of Turnover: These agencies rely on highly specialized professionals, including statisticians, economists, and data scientists, who possess unique technical expertise and long-term institutional memory. Statistical agencies stand to lose experts who see their career paths as less secure and less merit-based than before. The loss of these experts or frequent turnover in key positions could disrupt agency operations, hinder long-term planning, undermine the agency's ability to fulfill its mission, and impair the quality and accuracy of the data.
•	Decreased Employee Morale and Productivity: The uncertainty and fear of arbitrary dismissal could negatively impact employee morale, leading to decreased productivity and difficulty in attracting and retaining top talent.
•	Importance of Modernization, Research, and Data Continuity: To support their missions, statistical agencies must invest in long-term efforts such as extensive research, critical modernization projects, and efforts to ensure data access and continuity. Schedule Policy/Career could subject agencies to changing presidential priorities, increasing senior staff turnover and disrupting modernization efforts, measurement of trends, and meaningful research.

Schedule Policy/Career poses a significant threat to the effectiveness of federal statistical agencies and to the integrity and quality of their products. By undermining the principles of merit-based employment and threatening job security of senior career civil servants, Schedule Policy/Career could lead to politicization, loss of trust and expertise, decreased morale, and disruption of agency operations. On behalf of U.S. businesses, the American public, and policymakers I oppose the proposed rule, “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service,”  and am speaking up to protect the trustworthiness of the federal statistics we all rely on.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
The proposed reclassification of federal employees under “policy making individual” poses a significant threat to the impartiality and effectiveness of the civil service, undermining longstanding legal protections designed to ensure a nonpartisan federal workforce. Such a move would erode the foundational principles of the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which established merit-based employment and sought to eliminate the spoils system. Additionally, it risks violating the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (CSRA), which codified protections against political coercion and prohibited personnel practices, including retaliation for refusing to engage in partisan activities (5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)).

In case OPM does not know, below are some legal and historical safeguards against politicization
Merit System Principles (5 U.S.C. § 2301)- Federal employees must be selected and retained based on ability, fairness, and impartiality—not political loyalty.

The CSRA explicitly prohibits discrimination based on political affiliation (5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(1)(E)).

Prohibited Personnel Practices (5 U.S.C. § 2302(b))- The law bars coercion of political activity, including pressure to pledge loyalty to an administration.

Due Process Protections (5 U.S.C. § 7513)- as inheritors of the great traditions of our ancestors it should be clear that -Career civil servants currently have property rights in their positions, requiring due process before termination and rescheduling them is akin to termination

Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill (470 U.S. 532 (1985)) reinforces that employees with a legitimate expectation of continued employment cannot be removed without cause and a fair hearing.

Dangers of the proposed Reclassification
- Erosion of Neutral Expertise: The federal workforce relies on nonpartisan professionals in agencies like the CDC, EPA, and DoD to provide objective analysis. Politicizing these roles risks regulatory capture and undermines public trust.

- Increased Risk of Retaliation: Without civil service protections, employees could face termination for refusing unethical directives, as seen in past scandals like the Saturday Night Massacre (1973)—where DOJ officials were fired for resisting Nixon’s orders.

-Violation of Anti-Patronage Precedents: Courts have repeatedly struck down patronage systems (Rutan v. Republican Party of Ill., 497 U.S. 62 (1990)), ruling that conditioning employment on political loyalty violates the First Amendment and this rescheduling is a short hop to political patronage.

Conclusion: A Threat to Good Governance

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I strongly oppose any effort to reinstate Schedule F, a proposed federal employment classification that threatens the integrity, impartiality, and effectiveness of the U.S. civil service.

Schedule F would allow broad reclassification of federal employees involved in "policy-determining, policymaking, or policy-advocating" roles, stripping them of their due process and merit-based civil service protections. This reclassification would open the door to mass politicization of the civil service, undermining a foundational principle of American democracy: that government professionals serve the public interest—not the political interest of any one administration.

Erosion of Merit-Based Employment
The core of the U.S. civil service system is its reliance on merit-based hiring and retention. By creating a new class of federal employees exempt from competitive hiring and procedural protections, Schedule F undermines this foundation. It risks turning experienced, apolitical experts into political appointees subject to loyalty tests and partisan whims. Numerous reports, including those from the Partnership for Public Service and the Government Accountability Office, have documented how politicization of the civil service leads to inefficiency, loss of institutional knowledge, and damage to public trust.

Impacts on Government Functionality and Continuity
Schedule F could destabilize federal agencies by making thousands of career positions vulnerable to sudden dismissal. This would deter qualified individuals from pursuing or remaining in public service, especially in critical policy areas like public health, national security, and environmental protection. These functions depend on continuity, expertise, and institutional memory—not political alignment.

Lack of Transparency and Oversight
The proposed implementation of Schedule F lacks transparency and sufficient safeguards against abuse. There is no clear, objective standard for determining which roles qualify as “policy-determining.” As a result, political appointees could use Schedule F arbitrarily to purge career professionals who provide inconvenient facts or sound legal analysis, silencing dissent and eroding checks and balances.

National Security and Public Safety Concerns
In national security, law enforcement, and public health, policy must be informed by objective data and long-term expertise. Purging career professionals in these areas based on perceived political loyalty could have dire consequences for national preparedness and crisis response. Schedule F would make it easier to dismiss professionals who speak out against unlawful or dangerous policies, weakening the government's ability to protect the public.

Conclusion
In sum, reinstating Schedule F would damage the effectiveness, independence, and credibility of the federal workforce. It opens the door to patronage, diminishes the morale of public servants, and threatens the democratic principle of nonpartisan governance. I urge the relevant agencies and the administration to reject any proposal to bring back Schedule F and instead protect and strengthen merit-based civil service protections.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:

I am writing in strong opposition to the Office of Personnel Management’s proposed rule to create a new “Schedule Policy/Career” category of federal employees that would strip longstanding civil servants of procedural protections and job security, effectively making them at-will employees. While I understand the need for accountability in public service, this proposal undermines the very foundation of a professional, apolitical civil service and dangerously revives the corrosive logic of the 19th-century spoils system.

The American merit-based civil service arose in response to widespread patronage and corruption, culminating in the Pendleton Act of 1883. Champions of reform like President Theodore Roosevelt recognized that a government of qualified professionals—insulated from the partisan winds of each new administration—was essential to effective governance, public trust, and democratic stability. This principle has stood for over a century: that while political appointees help carry out an administration’s priorities, career civil servants provide continuity, expertise, and a necessary check on executive overreach.

This proposed rule is a direct attack on that principle. It would allow any administration to terminate civil servants in policy-adjacent roles without cause or due process—undermining the independence of the very experts and stewards of law who have helped sustain this republic through wars, crises, and transitions of power. By enabling the politicization of policy-influencing positions, this rule opens the door to a purge of perceived dissenters and the installation of ideologically aligned but potentially unqualified loyalists. This is not accountability; it is politicization.

The pretext of “subverting Presidential directives” is particularly troubling. Civil servants take an oath to uphold the Constitution and the law—not to any one president. In moments of stress and transition, it is their lawful independence that provides a ballast against abuses of power. Weakening these protections does not defend democracy—it exposes it.

At this moment in our history, we should be strengthening the institutions that preserve the rule of law and the legitimacy of democratic governance. I urge you to withdraw this proposed rule and instead focus on real improvements to agency performance that do not compromise the integrity of the civil service. A strong, nonpartisan federal workforce is not an obstacle to good government—it is its backbone.

Sincerely,
Concerned Citizen
La Crosse, Wisconsin

Government is a complicated thing. In order to run efficiently, there need to be people working at the various agencies who know what these agencies do and how to go about getting things done in order to serve the American people through their particular agency. 
There seems to be this idea that government workers are somehow scamming the American people by their mere presence and that anyone can do their jobs. The following example is about food inspection, but it could very well apply to airplane inspections, highway bridge inspections, or even seaport oversight.
The people who do these jobs are uniquely qualified to do them. They generally start their careers shortly after graduating from college and they begin work at the periphery and are working from or through someone who has way more experience than they do. They will be tasked with a problem that needs to be attended to and working with others in their group, they go about finding answers to this particular problem. Their work is checked by by others who have more experience than they do, and they learn by doing and sometimes by making mistakes. All the while they are learning how this agency works and how to get things done. They were hired in by their merit and abilities,  not by which political party they belong to. And as I understand it, there are currently rules in place that keep political pressure from affecting how they do their jobs. The only thing they have to worry about is that the science is right, not how their solving a problem will affect someone in a particular political office. This is the way it should be. If this agency employee had to worry about how solving a problem was  going to be viewed politically and if a political appointee had the power to fire that employee if he didn’t like how this turned out, it would logically have a chilling effect upon the work that agency was conducting.
As this employee rises through the ranks, he get a better overall picture of how the agency runs. As time goes on, he sees what policies work and which one don’t. After he’s been there for awhile he becomes part of the institutional memory of the agency. People who don’t possess this institutional memory are more apt to repeat a mistake that others have learned from. These longterm employees also know who they can  rely on in other agencies they interact 
with. It just stands to reason that a more seasoned employee will make fewer mistakes than someone with less experience.
Changing how government agencies are run by filling them with sycophants and boot lickers will be a colossal mistake that will have life and death consequences, and I for one, urge you that this idea be rejected completely.

Title: Comment from Anonymous Citizen
Comment:
I oppose the proposed Schedule F classification. As a retired Federal employee I know that a professional, stable, knowledgeable, non-partisan civil service is to a well-functioning government.  Career employees smooth the transitions between administrations.

This new proposal would violate the Civil Service Reform Act protections against arbitrary dismissal. The language and history of the CSRA provides only very narrow exceptions for positions of a “confidential or policy-determining character.” I do not understand how the unprecedentedly broad interpretation of the statutory language could be consistent with the statutory language, legislative history, or caselaw concerning this narrow exception to the CSRA's broad civil service protections. The proposed regulations remove this longstanding and important protection without justification or due process.

The Federal Register notice doesn't provide a reasoned explanation for these wide-ranging changes, doesn't describe how these changes were developed or how lines will be drawn, and doesn't reflect any input from, or consideration of, the current employees who would be affected. It fails to provide sufficient detail on how the changes would be implemented, or by whom.

These new proposals specifically undermine recent properly promulgated regulations meant to assure that the federal civil service would not become a patronage system, sacrificing competence for political fealty. By removing civil service protections through the proposed Schedule F expansion, employees would also be deterred from reporting wrongdoing due to fear of retaliation, thereby weakening whistleblowing safeguards. This would remove a valuable mechanism for identifying and reporting waste, fraud, and abuse.

The proposed Schedule F classification violates established federal laws and constitutional protections, and circumvents the role of Congress. Its implementation could fundamentally alter the structure and integrity of the federal civil service, leading to increased politicization and diminished employee rights and protections.

Please withdraw this proposal.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
OPM’s proposed rule to reintroduce a modernized version of “Schedule F” under the name “Schedule Policy/Career” poses a direct threat to American democracy, the public interest, and the foundational integrity of the federal civil service. By enabling the removal of key civil servants from established due process protections, the rule would create a broad class of at-will government employees in vaguely defined “policy-influencing” roles. This would effectively strip thousands of career professionals of the procedural safeguards that uphold merit-based employment, exposing them to dismissal based on ideological differences or political disfavor. In doing so, it revives the dangerous logic of the spoils system the U.S. overwhelmingly rejected over a century ago.
The justifications for this rule are not only flawed—they are deeply misleading. OPM claims that the rule is necessary to restore merit-based employment, but in reality, it does the opposite. Merit-based employment requires neutral, objective standards for hiring, promotion, and discipline, as protected by civil service laws. By creating a broad class of employees who can be dismissed without cause or appeal, the rule invites arbitrary and politically motivated removals, not meritocracy. Moreover, the rule grossly exaggerates the prevalence of “policy resistance” among civil servants. It relies heavily on a handful of anecdotes, anonymous news reports, and academic speculation to paint a picture of widespread bureaucratic sabotage—claims that are not substantiated by data. The same surveys OPM cites, such as the Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey (FEVS), actually show strong levels of employee engagement, rising job satisfaction, and commitment to public service. The narrative that civil servants are broadly undermining elected leaders is not supported by either empirical evidence or the lived experience of most federal workers.
OPM also misinterprets the purpose and scope of civil service protections. Due process requirements under chapters 43 and 75 were never meant to entrench incompetence; they were created to prevent political retaliation and ensure fair treatment, so that employees can serve with integrity and without fear. Agencies already have tools to discipline or remove employees for poor performance—they simply have to document their reasons and offer a chance to respond.
In short, this rule is a solution in search of a problem. It would politicize the civil service, compromise the independence of expert professionals, and move the federal workforce dangerously close to a loyalty-based system that rewards obedience over competence. 
While the OPM presents this rulemaking as a good-faith effort to strengthen accountability and improve government performance, a closer examination reveals a disconcerting reality: this proposal reflects not a commitment to sound governance, but a politicized effort to dismantle long-standing protections designed to uphold merit, integrity, and democratic accountability in the federal workforce.
It is deeply troubling that the agency charged with safeguarding the principles of the civil service would advance a rule that so clearly undermines them. OPM, whose mission includes ensuring the impartiality and professionalism of the federal workforce, now appears willing to use its regulatory authority to reengineer the civil service into a mechanism of political loyalty rather than public service. The rule's authors attempt to cloak their intentions in the language of merit and performance, but their reasoning is riddled with inconsistencies, mischaracterizations, and ideological assumptions not grounded in evidence.
Their selective use of data, reliance on anecdotal accounts, and inflated narrative of "policy resistance" suggest an intentional effort to manufacture a crisis in order to justify the erosion of due process. This is not honest policy development—it is administrative sleight-of-hand. In redefining “policy-influencing” positions so broadly, and removing vital legal protections under the guise of reform, OPM has positioned itself not as a steward of the civil service, but as a tool for political expediency.
Such rulemaking reflects a disregard for the constitutional balance of power, for the statutory intent of civil service protections, and for the institutional knowledge and dedication of millions of career federal employees. That this effort was undertaken so quickly, with such sweeping implications and such flimsy justification, should raise serious questions—not just about the policy, but about the judgment and motivations of those who wrote it.
If OPM is to retain its credibility as a neutral, professional agency, it must rise above partisan directives and recommit to the values it was created to protect. Otherwise, it risks becoming an enabler of political purges, and a cautionary tale in the degradation of democratic institutions.

OPM should rescind this rule.
