Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I strongly oppose the implementation or revival of the Schedule F classification for federal employees. This proposal threatens the merit-based civil service system that has underpinned a professional, nonpartisan federal workforce for over a century. Schedule F would not offer solutions we deserve, and as a citizen, I would be harmed by this change since the civil service system would become inefficient and no longer be held to a merit-based standard focused on serving the public. 

Schedule F Doesn’t Provide Solutions 

In the fact sheet (attached), the White House outlines how the removal process of an employee is cumbersome and has led to “corruption,” providing examples like,“For example, a recent audit of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) found widespread misconduct by senior leaders, such as male supervisors pressuring female subordinates for sexual favors in exchange for career assistance."

While acts like that are egregious, using these to justify the change to Schedule F is simply confusing. OPM could solve these issues by creating more effective ways to deal with harassment. How would a blanket reclassification of federal employees resolve this? Further, Schedule F would only apply to certain employees, meaning harassment outside of these positions would not be solved.

Civil Service Would Become Inefficient and Politicized

The fact sheet said the proposed rule would address the fact that "some bureaucrats also use the protections the system gives them to oppose presidential policies and impose their own preferences." Federal civilian employees take an oath to the Constitution of the United States, not any leader nor any member of Congress. Federal civilian employees are working to comply with laws. If employees are implementing a law passed by Congress and signed into law that the current president opposes, they are not doing anything wrong, nor does it mean employees are imposing their “own preference.” 
	
	Employees completely changing priorities every time a new president is elected is perhaps the most inefficient way for the government to provide services. Further, under this proposal, employees would likely not last beyond the president they are appointed under, further hampering the civil service functions. These appointees would be beholden to the president, knowing they don’t have tenure to serve long term. In short, they would be at-will political positions more loyal to one person than the American public. 

	Finally, this fact sheet shows the President’s desire to hold “bureaucrats” accountable, implying a focus on “corrupt” employees. OPM further clarifies this by saying that "employees who faithfully perform their jobs to the best of their ability have little to fear from Schedule Policy/Career.” (90 FR 17218). If that's true, I request OPM implement meaningful safeguards beyond those included in its NPRM. Language should prohibit the arbitrary firing or mass firing of Schedule Policy/Career employees. OPM should also provide clear, irrefutable definitions of what would be a fireable offense. No vague statements that allow a president to act at will. All that would do is return us to the “spoils system” that we worked to abolish with numerous laws. 

Citizens Desire a Merit-Based System Outlined by Existing Laws

Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883

This act was enacted to combat the “spoils system” and establish a merit-based hiring process. By allowing a broad swath of career civil servants to be reclassified and potentially terminated without cause, Schedule F opens the door to politically motivated hiring and firing. This is antithetical to the principle of an apolitical civil service enshrined in 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8).

Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (CSRA)

The CSRA reaffirms the merit-based system, providing protections against arbitrary dismissal. Schedule F seeks to reclassify certain policy-influencing positions, effectively removing these protections and allowing for at-will termination. Schedule F’s broad application exceeds this narrow scope of CSRA's exceptions for positions of a “confidential or policy-determining character." The Roth v. Brownell decision reinforces that reclassification cannot strip employees of their CSRA protections without due process. 

Conclusion 

Schedule F proposal poses a grave threat to the foundational principles of good governance, civil service independence, and the rule of law. Stripping thousands of workers of these protections not only weakens accountability but also undermines the very effectiveness of government operations I support as a citizen. I urge the administration and OPM to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement or revive this dangerous classification, as I believe U.S. citizens will be harmed by increased politicization, inefficiency, and loss of government services.

Gutting these protections risks increased turnover between administrations, at great cost to institutional knowledge and taxpayer resources.

Federal agencies are already struggling to recruit and retain talent due to challenges like lower pay and return-to-office mandates. Stripping away job protections will make the civil service even less competitive compared to the private sector, impairing our ability to attract skilled professionals. This will degrade our national capacity in critical areas such as defense, technology, and science—posing long-term strategic risks for the entire country.

While the current merit system may benefit from more targeted reform, this sweeping rule is not the solution. Moreover, I question whether OPM has the authority to override statutory due process rights granted to federal employees by Congress under the CSRA.

I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule to preserve the integrity, stability, and effectiveness of the federal workforce.

Title: Comment from Margaret Champlin
Comment:
This rule is a sharp break with civil service merit principles, which assume that career employees should be retained on the basis of performance and protected against political coercion. The US is already unusual in the degree to which it reserves the top layers of organizational leadership for short-term political appointees. This rule will vastly expand the number of appointees, adding a proposed 50,000 from the current 4000. It does so by involuntarily reclassifying career civil servants as appointees, removing job protections, the basic constraint against political interference.

The administration says that the purpose of this rule is to increase accountability for civil servants involved in policy-making. Set aside the fact that civil servants are accountable in multiple ways, the administration's own justifications strike a more conspiratorial tone, including “the deep state can and must be brought to heel.” But what better way to actually institutionalize a deep state than by expanding political influence over what constitutes good science?

Studies show that politicization of public services generally worsens public-sector outcomes. Public employees invest less in developing their expertise and become more likely to exit. Instability and lack of experience reduce organizational performance. Politicization increases the influence of more ideologically radical appointees relative to more moderate civil servants. Politicization also reduces accountability. Bureaucrats worried about being fired fail to share uncongenial information with their political bosses and become less likely to respond to congressional oversight. As politicization begets lower transparency and administrative capacity, it increases waste and inefficiency.

What might this mean for scientific agencies? Agencies like the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the National Institutes for Health (NIH) cannot meet their statutorily mandated scientific missions if politics, rather than scientific expertise, drive decision-making. Federally supported science has been so successful, in no small part, because agency staff are typically expert scientists beholden to ensuring that the agencies deliver world-class science. Now, many could be turned into political appointees. The proposed policy defines grantmaking positions as “policy-making,” which includes “drafting of funding opportunity announcements, evaluation of grant applications, or recommending or selecting grant recipients.” This definition, which neatly matches agencies’ own definitions for certain career staff, would include most NIH program officers and NSF program directors.

The past few months at NIH and NSF preview how politicized scientific agencies would operate. Funding choices that reflected the consensus of some of the best scientists in the world were reversed by nonscientists. Program officers have, at points, been told not to communicate with the scientific community or have had their engagement limited. Scientific agencies have been directed to effectively reduce the flow of funds to a trickle by adding new layers of redundant review and red tape and even violating court orders to reinstate cancelled grants.

Other agencies, including regulatory agencies, apply rather than fund basic science, but the risks of politicization are no less. How confident can Americans be that federal employees will not have to choose between their job and scientific values in areas such as climate change, food safety, extreme weather forecasting, or public health?

Career officials in scientific agencies are unwilling hostages in the administration’s politicization of science, wondering if they will lose their jobs for trying to defend the congressionally mandated missions of their organizations. Although the current era of layoffs will hopefully soon be over, the purpose of this rule is to permanently instill the degree of political control over science fueling the sense of fear that pervades those agencies now.

Vannevar Bush’s 1945 blueprint for America’s scientific infrastructure emphasized the centrality of protecting scientific organizations from politicization. That vision has been extraordinarily successful. This proposed rule assumes the opposite: It treats scientific independence as a threat to be minimized.

I am strongly opposed to politicizing over 12 times as many executive agency roles as are now politically appointed. I can see no way this will improve Americans' lives. Its only purpose is to make it easier for the leaders of the administration to impose their ideology on the government regardless of the objective facts.

This proposed rule is wrong and bad for America.

Title: Comment from Debra Shore
Comment:
I write in opposition to the rule proposed by the Personnel Management Office on 04/23/25 titled "Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service" (Office of Personnel Management 5 CFR Parts 210, 212, 213, 302, 432, 451, and 752 [Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004] RIN 3206-AO80).

The Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883 established that hiring people to work in the United States federal government would be based on merit, thus replacing a corrupt patronage system.  In other words, the Pendleton Act specified that federal employees should be hired on the basis of what they know rather than who they know.  Advancement and promotions were to be based on actual achievement and meeting performance goals, not based on campaign contributions, votes delivered, or political considerations. 

We have seen nationally and in cities like my own city of Chicago how a "spoils system" or a patronage system is corrosive to the human spirit leading to elevation of incompetence and corruption. It is a system based on fealty not fairness and is contradictory to President Trump's stated goal of efficiency in government.  

It is well known that people perform better in their jobs when their knowledge and expertise are acknowledged, when their progress towards goals is measured through established performance metrics, and when they are trusted and respected.  A system where only loyalty is rewarded and where all employees serve 'at will' is much worse for employees and the country. This is not my opinion but the basis for the Pendleton Act, which remains the law of the land.

Please note OPM’s description of its work on its website: “A strong, merit-based civil service is critical to a functioning democracy. It ensures that our government “of the people, by the people, for the people” continues to serve the American public without interruption, even though our leaders change over time. It also safeguards the public interest in a federal workforce that looks like America and that benefits from the talents, ideas, and skills of people from all our nation’s communities.”

Schedule F seeks to abolish the merit system embedded in the federal civil service since its establishment and convert career civil servants into political appointees. 

According to a recent article in the Journal of Policy Analysis & Management (published February 17, 2025), the politicization of public services and “the frontal attack on the separation between political appointees and civil servants, achieved by weakening civil service protections and purging those deemed disloyal” as is clearly evidenced by the proposed Schedule F rule will result in a less efficient and more corrupt government. 

Don Moynihan, the Ford School’s J. Ira Harris and Nicki Harris Family Professor of Public Policy at the University of Michigan previously wrote that Schedule F “would represent an unprecedented increase in politicizing the federal workforce, which would predictably undermine performance and accountability in the federal government, as well as democratic values such as transparency and the rule of law.”

The summary description of the proposed rule focuses solely on the ability to remove employees at will yet is utterly silent on abundant evidence from our nation's past on how corrosive such systems are to the human spirit and how they undermine foundational American values and ideals, including the rule of law and a government responsive to its people.

If you are going to propose such a drastic change to the way government delivers services to the American people, please present sound evidence that the system you envision will work for the betterment of the American people and the services they depend upon. I am not aware of such evidence.

I urge you to withdraw the proposed rule regarding Schedule F.

Title: Comment from Cory  Churches
Comment:
OFFICIAL COMMENT LETTER
Re: Opposition to Proposed Rule Implementing Executive Order 14171
To: U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM)
Date: may eighteen 

To Whom It May Concern at the U.S. Office of Personnel Management:

I submit these comments in strong opposition to the proposed amendments to 5 CFR Parts 210, 212, 213, 302, 432, 451, and 752, issued in response to Executive Order 14171. The proposed rule creates a new Schedule Policy/Career category, weakens existing due process protections, and enables the reclassification of competitive service positions into the excepted service. These changes collectively undermine the merit-based, nonpartisan civil service and risk politicizing the federal workforce.

SUBPART 1 – 5 CFR PART 213 (Excepted Service)
The creation of Schedule Policy/Career as a new excepted service schedule enables the reclassification of protected roles into at-will positions based on vague concepts such as “accountability to the President.” This would allow political influence over roles currently held by career professionals and undermines the fundamental protections of the competitive service system.

SUBPART 2 – 5 CFR PART 212 (Competitive Service and Competitive Status)
While the proposed rule allows employees to retain competitive status, it effectively removes them from the competitive service by administrative action. This undercuts core merit system protections and introduces legal ambiguity about rights and appeals, setting a dangerous precedent for bypassing due process through reassignment.

SUBPART 3 – 5 CFR PARTS 752 and 432 (Adverse and Performance-Based Actions)
The proposal to exempt Schedule Policy/Career employees from the procedural protections of 5 U.S.C. Chapters 75 and 43 strips employees of the right to challenge unjust removals or demotions. This action weakens protections specifically designed to guard against retaliation and politicization, particularly for employees in policy-adjacent roles that demand objectivity and professional independence.

SUBPART 4 – 5 CFR PART 210 (Basic Definitions and Conforming Changes)
Removing prior definitions that limited policy-influencing roles to political appointees invites widespread reclassification of career positions without Congressional authorization or oversight. It dilutes the nonpartisan character of career roles and threatens the structural integrity of civil service definitions.

SUBPART 5 – 5 CFR PART 302 (Excepted Service Hiring Procedures)
The proposed elimination of procedural requirements for transferring employees into Schedule Policy/Career positions removes critical transparency and appeal rights. It further allows circumvention of the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB), leaving employees vulnerable to arbitrary or politically motivated personnel actions without recourse.

CONCLUSION
The proposed rule is inconsistent with the merit system principles codified in the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 and opens the door to political influence over previously independent, expert-driven roles. Rather than fostering accountability, the rule enables retaliation, undermines due process, and discourages the apolitical public service ethos foundational to our democracy.

I respectfully urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.

Respectfully 
Cory Churches

Title: Comment from Lisa Schneider Fabes
Comment:
I write in opposition to the rule proposed by the Personnel Management Office on 04/23/25 titled "Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service" (Office of Personnel Management 5 CFR Parts 210, 212, 213, 302, 432, 451, and 752 [Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004] RIN 3206-AO80).

The Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883 established that hiring people to work in the United States federal government would be based on merit, thus replacing a corrupt patronage system.  In other words, the Pendleton Act specified that federal employees should be hired on the basis of what they know rather than who they know.  Advancement and promotions were to be based on actual achievement and meeting performance goals, not based on campaign contributions, votes delivered, or political considerations. 

We have seen nationally and in cities like my own city of Chicago how a "spoils system" or a patronage system is corrosive to the human spirit leading to elevation of incompetence and corruption. It is a system based on fealty not fairness and is contradictory to President Trump's stated goal of efficiency in government.  

It is well known that people perform better in their jobs when their knowledge and expertise are acknowledged, when their progress towards goals is measured through established performance metrics, and when they are trusted and respected.  A system where only loyalty is rewarded and where all employees serve 'at will' is much worse for employees and the country. This is not my opinion but the basis for the Pendleton Act, which remains the law of the land.

Please note OPM’s description of its work on its website: “A strong, merit-based civil service is critical to a functioning democracy. It ensures that our government “of the people, by the people, for the people” continues to serve the American public without interruption, even though our leaders change over time. It also safeguards the public interest in a federal workforce that looks like America and that benefits from the talents, ideas, and skills of people from all our nation’s communities.”

Schedule F seeks to abolish the merit system embedded in the federal civil service since its establishment and convert career civil servants into political appointees. 

According to a recent article in the Journal of Policy Analysis & Management (published February 17, 2025), the politicization of public services and “the frontal attack on the separation between political appointees and civil servants, achieved by weakening civil service protections and purging those deemed disloyal” as is clearly evidenced by the proposed Schedule F rule will result in a less efficient and more corrupt government. 

Don Moynihan, the Ford School’s J. Ira Harris and Nicki Harris Family Professor of Public Policy at the University of Michigan previously wrote that Schedule F “would represent an unprecedented increase in politicizing the federal workforce, which would predictably undermine performance and accountability in the federal government, as well as democratic values such as transparency and the rule of law.”

The summary description of the proposed rule focuses solely on the ability to remove employees at will yet is utterly silent on abundant evidence from our nation's past on how corrosive such systems are to the human spirit and how they undermine foundational American values and ideals, including the rule of law and a government responsive to its people.

If you are going to propose such a drastic change to the way government delivers services to the American people, please present sound evidence that the system you envision will work for the betterment of the American people and the services they depend upon. I am not aware of such evidence.

I urge you to withdraw the proposed rule regarding Schedule F.

Title: Comment from Lisa Musgrave
Comment:
https://www.regulations.gov/commenton/OPM-2025-0004-0001


I write in opposition to the rule proposed by the Personnel Management Office on 04/23/25 titled "Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service" (Office of Personnel Management 5 CFR Parts 210, 212, 213, 302, 432, 451, and 752 [Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004] RIN 3206-AO80).

The Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883 established that hiring people to work in the United States federal government would be based on merit, thus replacing a corrupt patronage system.  In other words, the Pendleton Act specified that federal employees should be hired on the basis of what they know rather than who they know.  Advancement and promotions were to be based on actual achievement and meeting performance goals, not based on campaign contributions, votes delivered, or political considerations. 

We have seen nationally and in cities like my own city of Chicago how a "spoils system" or a patronage system is corrosive to the human spirit leading to elevation of incompetence and corruption. It is a system based on fealty not fairness and is contradictory to President Trump's stated goal of efficiency in government.  

It is well known that people perform better in their jobs when their knowledge and expertise are acknowledged, when their progress towards goals is measured through established performance metrics, and when they are trusted and respected.  A system where only loyalty is rewarded and where all employees serve 'at will' is much worse for employees and the country. This is not my opinion but the basis for the Pendleton Act, which remains the law of the land.

Please note OPM’s description of its work on its website: “A strong, merit-based civil service is critical to a functioning democracy. It ensures that our government “of the people, by the people, for the people” continues to serve the American public without interruption, even though our leaders change over time. It also safeguards the public interest in a federal workforce that looks like America and that benefits from the talents, ideas, and skills of people from all our nation’s communities.”

Schedule F seeks to abolish the merit system embedded in the federal civil service since its establishment and convert career civil servants into political appointees. 

According to a recent article in the Journal of Policy Analysis & Management (published February 17, 2025), the politicization of public services and “the frontal attack on the separation between political appointees and civil servants, achieved by weakening civil service protections and purging those deemed disloyal” as is clearly evidenced by the proposed Schedule F rule will result in a less efficient and more corrupt government. 

Don Moynihan, the Ford School’s J. Ira Harris and Nicki Harris Family Professor of Public Policy at the University of Michigan previously wrote that Schedule F “would represent an unprecedented increase in politicizing the federal workforce, which would predictably undermine performance and accountability in the federal government, as well as democratic values such as transparency and the rule of law.”

The summary description of the proposed rule focuses solely on the ability to remove employees at will yet is utterly silent on abundant evidence from our nation's past on how corrosive such systems are to the human spirit and how they undermine foundational American values and ideals, including the rule of law and a government responsive to its people.

If you are going to propose such a drastic change to the way government delivers services to the American people, please present sound evidence that the system you envision will work for the betterment of the American people and the services they depend upon. I am not aware of such evidence.

I urge you to withdraw the proposed rule regarding Schedule F.

Title: Comment from M VP
Comment:
1. I oppose this proposed rule in its entirety, and every section of the proposed rule, as it allows for the reintroduction of a "spoils" system to the federal civil service. The proposed rule allows any given Administration to replace the nation's professional cadre of policy experts who serve the Constitution across Administrations with individuals who subordinate their duty to the Constitution and the law to partisan loyalties.

2. I oppose the creation of the Schedule Policy/Career as a new category of Excepted Service under 5 CFR Part 213. Moving career civil servants into a category of at-will employment makes those civil service positions vulnerable to political manipulation and influence, including by putting those employees at risk of termination should their efforts to uphold the federal oath of employment to defend the Constitution conflict with a political appointee's belief that the employee has failed to "faithfully implement administration policies to the best of their ability," as required under the proposed amendment to Sec. 213.3501(b).

3. I oppose the amendment of 5 CFR part 752 that removes the right of career civil servants to appeal the transfer of their position into an Excepted Service category, including the proposed Schedule Policy/Career category. The removal of such protection violates the Fifth Amendment due process rights of federal civil servants, specifically by removing the employees' interest in their tenure protections. See Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 70 U.S. 532, 541 (1985).

4. The proposed amendments to 5 CFR Part 213 and 5 CFR part 752 are, additionally, contrary to Congress's intent to create a merit-based civil service free from undue partisan political influence, in accordance with the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 and the Civil Service Due Process Amendments Act of 1990. Congress has determined that an effective and efficient federal civil service must be protected from partisan and improper influences. The current Excepted Services categories are intentionally limited and narrow in scope to properly carry out Congress's intent. OPM may not choose to disregard Congressional mandates in the manner proposed in this rule.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I strongly object to introducing or reviving the "Schedule F" classification for federal workers. This plan jeopardizes the civil service system's foundation, which hires and promotes based on merit. Notably, President Trump has supported this merit-based approach in Executive Order 14173. By allowing for the potential dismissal of career employees without cause, Schedule F would undermine the principles established by the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which aimed to end the spoils system and ensure hiring and promotion based on merit.



Implementing Schedule F would lead to politicized employment decisions, contradicting the law's requirement for apolitical civil service. The broad and unclear criteria for Schedule F would also undermine due process rights, violating 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which demands cause and procedural safeguards for removing career employees. Depriving thousands of workers of these protections would harm accountability and might silence experts, ultimately reducing government efficiency.



The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) has a statutory obligation to protect the merit system under federal law (5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq.). Introducing Schedule F would erode this duty by exposing career civil servants to inappropriate political pressure, ultimately weakening the consistency and professionalism of government programs.

The Schedule F initiative endangers fundamental principles of good governance, including an independent civil service and respect for the rule of law. Given these risks, I urge the administration and OPM to reject any efforts to move forward with this proposal.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I strongly oppose this proposed rule. This rule illegally strips federal employees of their appeal rights to the Merit Systems Protection Board (5 U.S.C. § § 7511-7515), runs afoul of 142 years of precedent, and as-applied, will allow agencies to falsely reclassify positions as policy-making.  

The vague criteria in this proposed rule violates federal employees’ statutorily guaranteed process when facing adverse employment action. 5 U.S.C. § §  7511-7515. 

This proposed rule also violates the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which was enacted to combat the spoils system and establish a merit-based hiring process for federal employees. Despite the proposed rule’s language purporting to be nonpartisan with its “[e]mployees in or applicants for Schedule Policy/Career positions are not required to personally or politically support the current President or the policies of the current administration. They are required to faithfully implement administration policies to the best of their ability, consistent with their constitutional oath and the vesting of executive authority solely in the President” language, the requirement to “faithfully implement administration policies to the best of their ability” is clearly a green light to agencies to fire those who are not Trump supporters. 

The proposed regulatory language “Career positions of a confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating character” is problematic. As-applied, agencies will classify positions that are objectively not policy-making as policy-making for the purposes of putting employees into this Schedule F category to more easily fire them. I have seen firsthand documents from within a government agency ready and waiting to reclassify positions, which are decidedly non policy-making, as policy-making for just this purpose. 

The proposed regulatory language “(b) Employees in or applicants for Schedule Policy/Career positions are not required to personally or politically support the current President or the policies of the current administration. They are required to faithfully implement administration policies to the best of their ability, consistent with their constitutional oath and the vesting of executive authority solely in the President. Failure to do so is grounds for dismissal” is similarly problematic. We all know how this is going to be applied. Sham DOGE officials and other political appointees in agencies will use the “faithfully implement administration policies” as a pretense to fire anyone who they disagree with. It is a lie to say that you will not require individuals to support the policies of the current administration. 

This regulation has a chilling effect on the First Amendment, another talking point frequently espoused as of critical importance under this Administration. 

These regulations will hold more individuals to higher standards under the Hatch Act, requiring further agency resources to train those people on what they can and cannot say. This seems like a misuse of taxpayer money this Administration purports to take issue with. 

As a citizen, I am opposed to the government turning over every four years. This runs afoul of the efficiency argument this Administration so often makes. 

I also believe this rule has the potential to violate state laws protecting their citizens from arbitrary firings. 

The provisions in this rule similarly violate collective bargaining agreements across the country. 

Federal government employees make significantly less money than their private industry counterparts. One of the tradeoffs to accepting a lower salary is stability that a position in the federal government gives its employees. This rule strips that stability away from millions of people. It is no surprise that OPM is working to take rights and stability away from federal government workers, as at least one member of this Administration is on record as saying he wants to put federal government workers in trauma. Like so much of what we’ve seen in the last four months, this is a part of Project 2025’s vindictive plot to make life worse for everyday Americans, starting with innocent federal government employees who have dedicated their careers to public service. This is a great shame.

I have had many occasions to deal with government agencies and appreciate the dedication of our federal employees. If anything, I feel their jobs are made harder by a lack of investment, such as software upgrades, in our government agencies over the years. I do not feel this proposed rule is the answer to improving performance, accountability and responsiveness in the Civil Service. Furthermore, the rule appears vague and open to interpretation as to what jobs will fall under its classification.

One need look no further than the recent chaotic firings, and re-hiring in some cases, of federal employees to know that this proposed rule will not serve the American people. I believe in government of the people, by the people and for the people and this includes our federal workforce, not just elected officials. I feel this rule does not take into account why civil service rules/laws were enacted in the first place and does not provide concrete evidence for such a drastic change.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I write to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule (RIN 3206-AO30), which seeks to reestablish a mechanism similar to the defunct “Schedule F” excepted service classification. This proposal poses a direct threat to the integrity, impartiality, and effectiveness of the federal civil service system.

1. Undermines Merit System Principles (5 U.S.C. § 2301)
The proposed rule contravenes the foundational Merit System Principles enshrined in 5 U.S.C. § 2301, which affirm that civil service employment should be based on merit, and free from political influence. Reclassifying policy-adjacent positions to allow at-will employment erodes protections that safeguard against favoritism, coercion, and retaliation. Civil servants must be empowered to uphold the public interest, not beholden to shifting political agendas.

2. Enables Politicization Contrary to the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978
The Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 established clear standards to prevent the politicization of the federal workforce. By creating a class of positions (akin to Schedule F) that may be filled or vacated outside of competitive service norms, the proposed rule undermines the bipartisan intent of Congress to ensure a professional, apolitical civil service. The risk of political loyalty tests being substituted for expertise is not hypothetical; the original Schedule F executive order (E.O. 13957, revoked by E.O. 14003) was widely condemned for doing just that.

3. Weakens Due Process Protections (5 U.S.C. §§ 7512–7513)
By allowing broad reclassification of career positions into at-will roles, the rule would circumvent existing adverse action protections guaranteed under 5 U.S.C. §§ 7512–7513. This not only violates the due process rights of civil servants, but also sets a dangerous precedent that deters qualified individuals from entering or remaining in public service. It creates a culture of fear rather than accountability.

4. Disrupts Continuity and Institutional Knowledge
Government continuity and expertise are fundamental to national resilience, especially during emergencies or political transitions. The proposed rule would invite high turnover in critical policy and operational roles, diminishing institutional memory and the government's ability to deliver consistent, effective public services. The Partnership for Public Service and multiple former federal executives have warned that similar changes would cause long-term damage to the civil service’s effectiveness and morale.

5. Violates Executive Order 14003 and Administrative Procedure Act Concerns
Executive Order 14003, issued on January 22, 2021, explicitly revoked E.O. 13957 and directed agencies to “protect and empower the Federal workforce.” Reintroducing Schedule F-like policies without substantive justification for their necessity could be viewed as arbitrary and capricious, raising serious concerns under the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. § 706).

Conclusion
This rule is neither necessary nor prudent. Real accountability and performance improvement come from strong leadership, clear expectations, and support—not from bypassing merit-based systems in favor of political convenience. I respectfully urge the Office of Personnel Management to withdraw this proposed rule and instead focus on collaborative, lawful reforms that enhance the civil service without undermining its core values.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
To Whom It May Concern,

My writing expresses fierce opposition towards the Office of Personnel Management's OPM proposed rule to create the Schedule Policy/Career classification, which in practice means resurrecting the Schedule F that had been previously removed. This proposal severely damages the intended impact of the civil service merit system and breaches existing laws and constitutional fundamental rights.

1. Violation of Due Process Rights:

The proposed rule aims to carve out a specific set of federal employees who will not be afforded the protective layers of 5 U.S.C. §§ 4303 and 7513, which outlines a performance-based action and an employment adverse action. In stripping these protections, the rule violates the Due Process Clause of the 5th Amendment which states “Nor shall any person be subjected to the shackles of liberty or life or property without a legal process.” The court of supreme judges has ruled that federal workers hold a vested interest in their employment, thus require due process safeguards (Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 470 U.S. 532 (1985)).

2. Violation of Award Criteria Principles:

The 1978 US Civil Service Reform Act allocates merit system principles such as competition that is open and fair, protection from arbitrary action, and upholding the highest integrity ‘standards (5 U.S.C. § 2301). The proposed rule at-will employment model for policy influencing positions jeopardizes these attributes by empowering politicization and arbitrary dismissal that weaken partisanship in the federal workforce.  

3. Similarities to Cancelled Schedule F:

This proposal is almost identical to the spirit and format of Schedule F promulgated by Executive Order 13957 in 2020 then subsequently canceled through Executive Order 14003 in 2021 on the grounds it would undermine protective measures of the civil service. To reintroduce such a framework is to ignore the reasoning behind its cancellation while simultaneously questioning the purpose and legality of the rule.  

4. Risk of Political Manipulation and Abuse:  

By dictating “policy-influencing” as loose and vague, the rule can be abused to make politically charged determinations that incurred redefining position classifications. The results are devastating to the intended neutrality of the civil service and directionally transform career civil service positions to become politically appointed jobs.

Taking into consideration these matters, I strongly encourage OPM to retract the proposed rule and maintain the integrity of the merit-based civil service system.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Office of Personnel Management
5 CFR Parts 210, 212, 213, 302, 432, 451, and 752
[Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004]
RIN 3206-AO80

As a concerned citizen, I am writing to express my strong opposition to the reinstatement of Schedule F. This policy, which would allow for the removal of career civil servants without cause, poses a significant threat to the stability, effectiveness, and impartiality of our federal government.

The implementation of Schedule F would inevitably lead to the loss of invaluable expertise and experience accumulated by dedicated career professionals over many years. These individuals form the backbone of our government agencies, providing the institutional knowledge and technical skills necessary for their smooth operation. Removing them without due cause would create a void that is difficult, if not impossible, to fill quickly, severely hindering the ability of agencies to effectively serve the American people.

Furthermore, reinstating Schedule F carries the grave risk of politicizing government agencies that are meant to operate independently and impartially. Agencies like the Social Security Administration, which millions of Americans rely upon, could become subject to political whims and pressures, undermining the trust and confidence the public has in their essential services. A non-partisan civil service ensures that decisions are based on expertise and the best interests of the public, not political expediency.

The potential for politically motivated firings under Schedule F would also undoubtedly discourage qualified and dedicated individuals from pursuing careers in public service. Why would talented professionals invest their time and energy in a system where their positions could be eliminated arbitrarily, regardless of their performance? This chilling effect would further damage the operational capacity of crucial government agencies, exacerbating existing challenges in recruitment and retention.

Finally, it is imperative to remember that non-partisan government employees deserve protection from political and baseless dismissal. They dedicate their careers to serving the public, often at personal sacrifice, and should not be subjected to the uncertainty and instability that Schedule F would create. A merit-based civil service, with appropriate protections, is essential for maintaining a professional, capable, and accountable government.

For these reasons, I urge you to reject the reinstatement of Schedule F and instead uphold the principles of a stable, expert, and non-partisan civil service that serves all Americans effectively.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I oppose this proposed rule to convert certain federal employees to Schedule Policy/Career for three reasons.

FIRST, the proposed Schedule Policy/Career rule is arbitrary and capricious because the remedy (suddenly converting tens-of-thousands of current career employees to at-will status) has no rational connection to the stated problem (difficulty removing officials for misconduct or poor performance). 

The ostensible objective of the rule is to strengthen employee accountability and the democratic responsiveness of American government, while addressing longstanding performance management challenges in the Federal workforce. Thus, according to the proposal, (a) employees who perform well and faithfully implement the President's agenda to the best of their ability have little reason to fear dismissal based on non-merit factors; (b) [e]mployees who faithfully perform their jobs to the best of their ability have little to fear from Schedule Policy/Career; and (c) [t]he employees at risk of dismissal are those who fail to perform adequately or who engage in serious misconduct such as corruption or injecting their personal politics into the performance of their official duties.

But to achieve that supposed objective, the proposed rule would convert federal employees who influence policy to at-will employees, which means that they may be dismissed for virtually ANY reason (that is, without having to establish just cause for termination), and without warning, as long as the reason is not illegal. For example, under the proposed rule, a federal employee could be terminated not only for misconduct but also because his or her services are no longer required (e.g., for budgetary reasons) or for virtually any other reason. 

But if the rule truly seeks to root out employees who engage in misconduct or attempt to undermine the Administration's agenda, why does it convert them to at-will employment, thereby allowing them to be terminated for virtually any reason and at any time, including for reasons that have nothing to do with misconduct? In other words, there's a fundamental disconnect between the supposed purpose of the rule, on the one hand, and the solution that the rule imposes, on the other. 

If the true purpose of the rule really were to make it easier to terminate employees who engage in misconduct, the rule would offer a solution that fits that problem -- namely, the rule would simply allow agencies to terminate policy-influencing employees for misconduct. Instead, under the proposed rule, covered employees may be terminated for virtually ANY reason, including for budgetary reasons, without going through the normal Reduction-in-Force (RIF) procedures required by law.

Which makes me suspect that the true purpose of the rule is to circumvent regular RIF procedures, so that agencies may save money by terminating any or all policy-influencing employees without going through the RIF process. Indeed, nothing in the proposed rule addresses whether 5 C.F.R. part 351 order-of-retention factors —- tenure group, veterans' preference, length of service, performance -- would still govern separations. Because Schedule Policy/Career employees would serve at will, the rule appears to authorize what is, in substance, a RIF without the procedural guardrails that Congress enacted.

Because there is no logical connection between the problem that the rule says exists and the solution that the rule proposes, the proposed rule is arbitrary, capricious, and not in accordance with the law. The rule therefore should either (a) disclose ALL the true purposes of the rule, so that the public has fair notice of the rule's purposes and intent, or (b) be re-drafted to make it clear that employees who are converted to the new category may be terminated outside the normal RIF process ONLY for misconduct (i.e., for failing to perform adequately or for injecting their personal politics into the performance of their duties).

SECOND, the proposed rule fails to adequately define what factors constitute confidential, policy-determining, policy-making or policy-advocating character. To the extent that the rule attempts to define those factors at all, it implies that any employee who has ANY participation in or involvement with drafting or advising on policy whatsoever would be included in the new category -- even if the employee makes no substantive decisions concerning policy and has no practical ability to undermine policy. 

Any new category should instead be narrowly tailored to include only senior supervisors, who actually make decisions and materially shape, make, and influence policy -- NOT line employees who merely draft, implement and advise on whatever policies have already been decided on by others. 

FINALLY, any rule like this should only apply to those who are hired AFTER a future date, not to those currently in the workforce. It is unlawful to change the status of current employees without due process.

Title: Comment from Bob Zellner
Comment:
1.	The proposed rule claims that Schedule Policy/ Career will remain “nonpartisan” while removing due process protections that prevent politically motivated dismissals. How does OPM intend to ensure that removals are truly based on performance or misconduct – not political affiliation – without independent oversight or appeal rights?

3.	The rule asserts that the President has broad authority under 5 U.S.C. § 3302 to strip employees of adverse action protections. However, the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 established chapter 75 procedures to prevent arbitrary removals. How does OPM reconcile this rule with the CSRA’s intent to safeguard merit system principles, and what legal precedent supports the claim that § 3302 overrides those protections? 

4.	The rule cites poor performance as justification, yet surveys show most federal employees are rated “fully successful” or higher. If the real concern is underperformance, why not strengthen existing chapter 43 and 75 tools- such as streamlining documentation requirements – rather than eliminating due process entirely? How does OPM respond to concerns that this rule will enable dismissals based on policy disagreements rather than genuine performance issues? 

5.	Career employees provide continuity across administrations. By making policy influencing roles “at-will”, how will OPM prevent loss of expertise, institutional memory, and public confidence in the neutrality of civil service? What evidence supports the claim that this rule will improve governance rather than foster instability and politicization?

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I am writing to express strong opposition to the Office of Personnel Management’s (OPM) proposed rule OPM-2025-0004-0001, which seeks to reclassify approximately 50,000 federal employees into a newly designated Schedule Policy/Career (P/C) category. This proposal, a revival of the previously rescinded Schedule F, threatens the foundational principles of a nonpartisan, merit-based civil service and poses significant risks to the integrity, efficiency, and accountability of federal operations.

Erosion of Merit-Based Protections

The cornerstone of the federal civil service is its commitment to merit-based hiring and retention, ensuring that employment decisions are grounded in qualifications and performance rather than political affiliation. By reclassifying positions into Schedule P/C, the proposed rule would strip affected employees of critical protections against arbitrary dismissal, effectively making them at-will employees. This undermines the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978, which was enacted to prevent politicization and ensure a competent and impartial federal workforce.

Increased Risk of Politicization

The reintroduction of Schedule P/C opens the door to replacing experienced, nonpartisan professionals with individuals selected for their political loyalty rather than expertise. Such a shift could compromise the objectivity of policy analysis and implementation, leading to decisions that serve partisan interests over the public good. The National Active and Retired Federal Employees Association (NARFE) has rightly noted that this move "opens the door to replacing nonpartisan, professional civil servants with political loyalists".

Undermining Institutional Knowledge and Continuity

Federal agencies rely on the institutional knowledge and continuity provided by career civil servants. Reclassifying positions and removing job protections could lead to a loss of experienced personnel, disrupting agency operations and diminishing the government's ability to effectively serve the public. The potential for mass dismissals based on political considerations threatens the stability and effectiveness of federal programs.

Legal and Ethical Concerns

The proposed rule raises serious legal and ethical questions. The previous iteration, Schedule F, faced legal challenges and was ultimately rescinded due to concerns about its legality and potential for abuse. Reintroducing a similar framework disregards these concerns and may once again lead to protracted legal battles, diverting resources and attention from the government's primary responsibilities.

Conclusion

The proposed reclassification of federal positions into Schedule Policy/Career represents a significant departure from the principles that have long safeguarded the integrity and effectiveness of the federal workforce. It threatens to politicize the civil service, erode merit-based protections, and disrupt the continuity of government operations. I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule and instead focus on strengthening the existing merit-based system that ensures a competent, impartial, and stable federal workforce.

Comment:
Schedule F (or Schedule Policy/Career) raises serious regulatory and legal concerns that conflict with
 numerous provisions in the United States Code and Code of Federal Regulations (CFR). Below is a synthesis
 of legal objections and concerns, structured as formal comments:
 1. **Violation of 5 U.S.C. § 2301 and § 2302**: The merit system principles, as codified in 5 U.S.C. § 2301,
 emphasize recruitment and advancement based on ability, knowledge, and skills, free from political influence.
 Reclassifying career civil servants to at-will status undercuts these merit principles. Under 5 U.S.C. § 2302,
 converting employees into Schedule F increases the likelihood of prohibited personnel practices, including
 discrimination for political beliefs.
 2. **Undermining 5 U.S.C. § 7513**: This statute provides due process protections for adverse actions
 including removal, suspension, or demotion. Schedule F allows for the circumvention of these rights, enabling
 dismissals without cause, notice, or appeal.
 3. **Noncompliance with 5 C.F.R. Part 302**: Excepted service hiring processes still require structured
 procedures and merit-based considerations. Blanket reclassification violates the structured competitive
 service principles articulated in 5 C.F.R. § 302.101-302.403.
 4. **Conflict with the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. § 553)**: The APA mandates
 notice-and-comment rulemaking for substantive policy changes. The reintroduction of Schedule F was not
 subject to adequate public review, undermining procedural safeguards.
 5. **Violation of Civil Service Reform Act of 1978**: This act aims to protect the federal workforce from undue
 political interference and institutionalizes merit system protections. Schedule F invites political appointees to
 target and remove expert staff whose policy views may differ from the administration's.
 6. **Risk to National Security and Continuity of Government**: By weakening institutional memory and
 depoliticized policy continuity, Schedule F poses risks to national emergency preparedness as governed
 under Homeland Security Presidential Directive-20 (HSPD-20).
 7. **Chilling Effect on Whistleblowing and Public Accountability**: Schedule F deters the exercise of protected
 disclosures under the Whistleblower Protection Act (5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(8)) by eliminating safeguards against
 retaliation.
 8. **Erosion of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Protections**: By removing procedural fairness and increasing
discretion in hiring/firing, Schedule F could reduce workplace diversity in violation of Executive Order 13985
 and EEOC guidelines under 29 C.F.R. § 1604.
 These concerns are not merely hypothetical. Historical abuses of patronage systems illustrate the dangers of
 at-will federal employment. The merit-based civil service system was designed precisely to prevent such
 risks.
 Therefore, Schedule F (Schedule Policy/Career) should be rescinded in favor of preserving the integrity,
 impartiality, and legal structure of the federal workforce.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Comment on OPM Proposed Rule (Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004)
Subject: Objection to Reclassification under "Schedule P/C"

To Whom It May Concern:

This comment is submitted in strong opposition to OPM’s proposed rule published April 23, 2025 (Federal Register Vol. 90, No. 79), which seeks to create a new “Schedule Policy/Career” (Schedule P/C) employment category. The rule authorizes sweeping reclassifications of competitive service positions to at-will status, undermining the statutory merit system.

I. Statutory and Regulatory Violations
Contradiction of the Civil Service Reform Act (CSRA), 5 U.S.C. §§ 1101 et seq.
The CSRA mandates merit-based protections to ensure neutrality and continuity. Reclassifying positions to an at-will Schedule P/C violates 5 U.S.C. §§ 2301 and 7513, removing appeal rights to the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) without Congressional authorization.

Violation of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A)
The proposed rule lacks a reasoned explanation for removing long-standing due process protections. It fails to address reliance interests or provide evidence-based justification, as required by FCC v. Fox Television Stations, 556 U.S. 502 (2009).

II. Legal Precedent Conflicts
Humphrey’s Executor v. U.S., 295 U.S. 602 (1935): Protects independent functions from presidential at-will removal.

Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 470 U.S. 532 (1985): Government employment creates a property interest protected by due process.

Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer, 343 U.S. 579 (1952): Executive action cannot override statutory protections absent Congressional authority.

III. CFR Conflicts
The proposed rule contradicts:

5 CFR § 213.101(c): Excepted service must align with statute-defined categories.

5 CFR § 752.201(a): Adverse action protections are required for covered employees.

5 CFR § 302.101: Excepted appointments do not negate due process rights unless explicitly stated.

IV. Objections to the Rule’s Provisions
Reclassification to Schedule P/C:
No objective, uniform criteria are provided for who qualifies. The proposal enables political misuse and arbitrary removals, which the CSRA was enacted to prevent.

Appeals Elimination:
Stripping MSPB access for these roles undermines 5 U.S.C. § 7513(d), which guarantees employees the right to challenge unjust removals. This change likely violates constitutional due process.

Pretextual Authority:
Citing Executive Order 13957 as the legal basis is insufficient. That EO was previously revoked for its overreach. OPM has not established independent authority to reinstate its framework.

V. Lack of Necessity or Justification
No data supports the assertion that existing protections hinder performance. The APA requires that rulemakings demonstrate a rational connection between problem and solution. OPM fails to cite evidence of inefficiency or abuse justifying a systemic overhaul.

Conclusion
This rule is an unlawful attempt to circumvent Congressionally established protections. It contravenes statutory civil service guarantees, ignores binding judicial precedent, and opens the door to politicization of federal employment.

Requested Action:
Withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety. Any reform must comply with the CSRA, APA, and due process norms, and must be backed by clear legislative authority.

Title: Comment from Adrianne Cohen
Comment:
As a public school teacher and the family member of federal employees, I am writing to express my strong opposition to any attempt to revive or implement Schedule F—or any similar policy that seeks to strip job protections from career civil servants and politicize the federal workforce.

Non-partisan civil servants are the backbone of a functioning, effective government. They serve administrations of both political parties with integrity and professionalism, guided by facts, expertise, and a commitment to the public good—not partisan agendas. I rely on the work of these experts in my own profession. Sound, evidence-based education policy—on everything from student assessments to special education support—is shaped by professionals in the Department of Education and other agencies who understand the real needs of schools, teachers, and students. Politicizing these roles would risk turning education policy into a tool of ideology rather than a means to support learners and educators.

Moreover, I have family members who work for federal agencies. They have dedicated their careers to serving the public in critical areas like environmental protection, public health, and infrastructure. The idea that these professionals could be fired simply for not showing political loyalty to a particular administration is deeply disturbing. It undermines the fairness, stability, and effectiveness of our government institutions and disrespects the dedication of those who have made public service their life’s work.

Policies like Schedule F would weaken our ability to hold powerful interests accountable, enforce labor rights, ensure clean air and water, and deliver essential services like Social Security and healthcare. It would open the door to corruption, cronyism, and a dangerous erosion of democratic norms.

I urge decision-makers to reject any attempts to implement Schedule F or similar efforts to politicize the civil service. We need impartial experts in government now more than ever—to protect the public interest, uphold the law, and ensure that our democracy works for everyone, not just for those in power.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I oppose the proposed measures under "Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service" for the following negative impacts: 

•	Increased bureaucracy or surveillance
•	Reduced job security
•	Biased or unrealistic performance metrics
•	Political misuse of “accountability”
•	Negative impact on public service morale
I oppose the proposed measures under "Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service" due to the risk of overreach and excessive monitoring. While performance improvements are a worthy goal, the implementation of strict metrics and increased surveillance may create a culture of fear and micromanagement rather than fostering innovation and commitment. This could erode trust between civil servants and leadership, ultimately harming productivity rather than enhancing it.
The initiative's focus on accountability raises concerns about the erosion of civil service protections and job security. If not properly safeguarded, these reforms could be weaponized to dismiss employees for political or ideological reasons rather than legitimate performance issues. The neutrality and continuity of the civil service should not be sacrificed in pursuit of arbitrary or shifting performance standards.
Performance-based reforms often rely on rigid metrics that don’t reflect the complexity of public service roles. The one-size-fits-all approach risks penalizing departments that deal with systemic issues outside their control. Real responsiveness comes from investing in capacity, not from punishing workers for challenges beyond their remit.
This policy may have unintended consequences on morale and staff retention. Civil servants are already working under increasing pressure and resource constraints. The imposition of further evaluative frameworks—especially those perceived as punitive—could drive away talented individuals, exacerbating existing workforce shortages and undermining institutional knowledge.
Reforms affecting the civil service should involve meaningful consultation with those who will be impacted. This proposal appears top-down, with little evidence of engagement with civil servants themselves. Sustainable reform must be collaborative, not imposed. I urge reconsideration until all stakeholders, including unions and employees at all levels, are properly consulted.
While accountability is a cornerstone of good governance, I strongly oppose the current framing and implementation of the “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service” initiative due to the high risk of political misuse of accountability mechanisms. Without strict safeguards and transparency, this reform could undermine the civil service’s integrity, neutrality, and independence.

Historically, “accountability” reforms have too often served as a pretext to centralize political control, enabling partisan actors to target civil servants who express dissent, raise concerns, or act in the public interest but contrary to short-term political agendas. By empowering political leadership to evaluate and penalize civil servants under vague or subjective performance standards, this initiative risks becoming a tool for retaliation rather than reform.
Civil servants are meant to serve the public impartially, not cater to the ruling party’s preferences. Introducing performance evaluations and disciplinary processes that lack independent oversight opens the door to ideological purging, patronage, and fear-based compliance. This directly threatens the institutional continuity and objectivity that the civil service is designed to uphold.
Moreover, the vague language often found in such initiatives—terms like “responsiveness” or “agility”—can be interpreted subjectively, allowing political appointees to manipulate them to suit partisan interests. In volatile political environments, such ambiguities invite abuse. The result is a chilling effect: civil servants may self-censor or delay action out of fear that their work could be politically mischaracterized as “non-compliant” or “underperforming.”
If accountability is not enforced by independent, apolitical bodies, it ceases to be a safeguard and becomes a weapon. Accountability without insulation from politics is not reform—it is a pathway to politicization. I urge the government to halt this proposal until clear legal and institutional safeguards are implemented to prevent its abuse for political gain.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule titled “Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service.” While I understand the desire to enhance efficiency and responsiveness within federal agencies, this rule would significantly weaken long-standing protections that ensure fairness, due process, and stability for career federal employees.

The proposed changes would make it substantially easier to discipline or remove employees without providing adequate opportunity to respond or improve. This shift undermines core principles of due process and invites arbitrary or retaliatory decision-making by supervisors. It would create a culture of fear rather than accountability—chilling whistleblowing, discouraging critical thinking, and eroding morale across the federal workforce.

Of particular concern is the risk this rule poses to the nonpartisan integrity of the civil service. By giving more discretion to agency leadership and removing checks on removals, the proposal opens the door to political interference in the career ranks. Federal employees are sworn to serve the public interest, not partisan agendas. Undermining their job security without robust safeguards could lead to the politicization of government functions and damage public trust in agencies that are meant to operate independently of political pressure.

Rather than addressing root causes of performance issues—such as lack of training, poor management, or resource constraints—the rule unfairly places blame on individual employees. True performance improvement requires constructive support, fair evaluation systems, and investment in workforce development, not expedited pathways to termination.

This rule represents a step backward for civil service reform. I urge OPM to withdraw the proposal and engage in a more balanced process that respects the rights of federal workers while pursuing legitimate goals of efficiency and accountability.

As a United States citizen, I strongly oppose the proposed rule "Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service." This rule would dismantle longstanding protections for career civil servants and dangerously politicize the federal workforce.

By creating a new "Schedule P/C" category, the rule would allow any future administration to reclassify nonpartisan employees as “policy-influencing,” making it easier to fire, demote, or reduce their pay without just cause or due process. This would turn thousands of experienced civil servants into at-will employees, stripping away the protections that have guarded our public institutions from political abuse since the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978.

This change opens the door to widespread political favoritism, weakens government accountability, and undermines the delivery of critical services—particularly at agencies like the Social Security Administration, where leaked plans already show that over 10,000 positions could be targeted under this rule. The result would be a loss of expertise, damage to essential programs, and a federal workforce less able to serve the American people with integrity and consistency.

This proposal revives a deeply flawed idea that was previously rejected for good reason. It violates both the spirit and letter of civil service protections, and I urge the Office of Personnel Management to withdraw it in full.

Why Federal Employees Should Not Be Subject to Firing for Their Political Beliefs or Non-Support for the President

1. First Amendment Rights
Federal employees have the right to free speech and political beliefs under the First Amendment. Firing someone for their views would violate those constitutional protections.

2. Merit-Based Civil Service
The federal government operates under a merit-based system, meaning employees are hired and retained based on skill and performance—not political loyalty. This system prevents political favoritism and ensures fairness.

3. Protects Against Corruption and Retaliation
Allowing political-based firings would lead to corruption, where jobs are given based on loyalty rather than competence. It would also discourage employees from speaking up or reporting wrongdoing.

4. Government Stability and Expertise
Federal employees provide continuity and expertise across administrations. Politicizing the workforce would damage long-term projects and make government services less effective.

5. Existing Legal Protections
Laws like the Civil Service Reform Act and the Hatch Act already protect employees from political discrimination, while also setting rules for political activity on the job.

In Summary:

Firing federal workers over their political beliefs or loyalty to a president is unconstitutional, harmful to good governance, and contrary to long-standing laws that protect a fair, nonpartisan civil service. This is why Schedule F should not be permitted to happen.

Title: Comment from Alexis McBrayer
Comment:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule by the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) to increase career employee accountability, as outlined in the Federal Register. I believe this rule, which seeks to reclassify certain policy-influencing positions into a new "Schedule Policy/Career," is fundamentally flawed and would have damaging consequences for the federal workforce and the American people.
My primary concerns are as follows:
•	Undermining Merit-Based Principles: The proposed rule threatens to dismantle the merit-based system that has been the cornerstone of the federal civil service since the Pendleton Act of 1883. By making it easier to remove employees in "policy-influencing" positions, this rule opens the door to political influence and patronage, rather than basing employment decisions on qualifications and performance.
•	Vague and Overbroad Definition of "Policy-Influencing": The rule's definition of "policy-influencing" is dangerously vague and overbroad. It could be interpreted to include a wide range of career employees, including those in technical or analytical roles that support policy development, but do not themselves set policy. This ambiguity creates the potential for abuse and could lead to the removal of dedicated and experienced civil servants for political reasons.
•	Lack of Due Process: Stripping employees in Schedule Policy/Career of their due process rights, including the right to appeal adverse actions, is a direct assault on fundamental fairness. Federal employees, like all Americans, deserve the protection of fair procedures and the opportunity to challenge unwarranted disciplinary actions. This rule would leave them vulnerable to arbitrary and capricious treatment.
•	Negative Impact on Workforce Stability and Expertise: The proposed rule would destabilize the federal workforce and erode the institutional knowledge and expertise that are essential for effective government operations. The threat of summary removal would discourage qualified individuals from pursuing federal careers, leading to a decline in the quality and effectiveness of public services.
•	Weakens Democratic Responsiveness: Ironically, the claim that this rule will strengthen democratic responsiveness is false. A non-partisan, experienced civil service is essential to ensure that policies are implemented effectively and lawfully, regardless of changes in administration. This rule would lead to a politicized civil service, more susceptible to the whims of an administration, and less focused on the long-term public good.
For these reasons, I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule. The rule would damage the ability of the federal government to serve the American people.

Title: Comment from Phillip Bartels
Comment:
Respectfully, switching career civil service employees to an at-will employment system is an idea strongly at odds with continued government effectiveness and U.S. innovation. As a scientist myself, I will focus on the effects to scientific agencies, but the general implications are more broadly applicable.

Scientists generally work on complex projects that take significant time and resources to reach conclusions. Many times, data obtained in the process forces the initial hypotheses to be modified, sometimes significantly. Under these high-pressure conditions, the best science will be done when workers have job security. Accountability DOES NOT mean punishment for finding unexpected or negative results; these are part of the extremely complicated nature of our work and it is not uncommon for a good idea on paper to end up being falsified by harsh reality. Instead, this produces innovation through clever methods developed over the course of research and indicating productive new avenues to get at the heart of a problem. Furthermore, this process reduces waste by indicating which ideas are no longer worth pursuing. Job security enhances the effectiveness by retaining those with the deepest knowledge of a particular project and allows these individuals and groups to move research in a specialized area forward much more effectively than cutting them and relying on others with less experience to fill the void.

Accountability in science is already well-established in the often harsh peer-review process. Far from an insider-based consensus, peer review subjects scientists to intense critique by the very experts best-positioned to do so. Suggestions in this process are anonymous, rejections are frequent, and the ultimate result tends toward a more complete publication with the best possible results; inadequate or (rarely) outright fraudulent work is typically screened out very effectively. 

To summarize, removing job security would be extremely detrimental to U.S. innovation, currently the envy of the world but at risk of falling behind should the below policies be implemented. While my focus is on the area I am most qualified to discuss, the benefits of continuity and retained expertise over insecurity and frequent turnover apply to any agency overseeing complex problems.

Title: Comment from Martha D
Comment:
The recent proposal by the Office of Personnel Management is being done at the behest of the so-called “Department of Government Efficiency” (DOGE) to require civil servants to demonstrate personal loyalty to the President of the United States. This is an affront to the foundational principles of an impartial, professional, and effective federal workforce. This proposal is neither about efficiency, nor accountability—it is a thinly veiled attempt to dismantle a merit-based system in favor of partisan loyalty and political coercion.

The United States civil service was deliberately designed to operate independently of political winds. Civil servants are not political appointees—they are scientists, engineers, analysts, investigators, inspectors, and public safety professionals. These individuals are selected based on expertise, experience, and performance—not ideological allegiance. They serve the Constitution and the American people, not the transient officeholder of the day.

DOGE’s proposal undermines this foundational framework. By introducing a loyalty test, it invites intimidation, rewards sycophancy, and punishes dissent. It does not promote better outcomes; it erodes the integrity and continuity of government. This is not about improving government operations—it is about transforming neutral civil service into a tool of political power.

Performance evaluations, professional standards, and accountability already exist. Civil servants are routinely assessed on their ability to perform, not their willingness to pledge personal fealty to a political figure. Disregarding this process weakens government function and opens the door to corruption, inefficiency, and arbitrary firings.

This proposal is not about loyalty to country—it is about consolidating political control. It must be categorically rejected by anyone who values the stability, impartiality, and effectiveness of the United States government.
