Agency: Office of Personnel Management (OPM)
I submit this comment in my personal capacity as a federal employee and union representative who has directly defended bargaining unit members facing removal from federal service. There are serious risks posed by the proposed Schedule Policy/Career rule, particularly its subpart on removal procedures.

Negative Impact of Proposed Amendments
The recent proposed amendments to 5 CFR Part 432, §432.102(f)(10) and 5 CFR Part 451, §451.302(b)(3)(ii), while appearing to clarify coverage and award eligibility, in fact exacerbate the risks to employee protections and due process in removal actions for Schedule Policy/Career employees.

§432.102(f)(10) Amendment:
This revision explicitly includes employees occupying Schedule Policy/Career positions within the scope of performance-based reduction in grade and removal actions. However, the amendment fails to preserve critical procedural safeguards such as appeal rights to the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) or equivalent protections that currently prevent arbitrary or retaliatory removals. By subjecting Schedule Policy/Career employees to potentially expedited or less transparent removal processes, this amendment enables management to remove employees without adequate opportunity for defense or appeal.

§451.302(b)(3)(ii) Amendment:
While clarifying that excepted service employees remain eligible for Presidential Rank Awards, this amendment does nothing to restore or protect the fundamental merit system principles that safeguard these employees from unjust removal. It risks creating a false sense of security regarding employee status while simultaneously weakening removal protections.

How These Amendments Harm Employees Like Those I Represent
My experience includes representing an employee who, while still within his probationary period after completing a performance improvement plan, was asked by management to perform work that would have improperly benefited a private entity with which his managers sought business relations. This work involved enhancing proprietary materials containing plagiarized content, violating agency integrity policies and federal regulations. When he raised legal and ethical concerns, management chose to initiate his removal rather than address these serious issues.
Under the proposed Schedule Policy/Career rule, this employee would have been removed without the opportunity to defend himself, enabling unethical conduct to persist unchecked and creating a chilling effect on federal employees’ willingness to speak out against abuse. This undermines the merit-based and integrity-driven foundation of the civil service, increasing the risk of corruption at taxpayer expense. After more than a year and multiple appeals, we successfully preserved his job, restored his grade, step, and back pay, and reassigned him. This employee has faithfully served the public for 20 years, contributing significantly to science and technology that benefits public, private, and military sectors. Removing him would have been a tragic loss to the civil service’s mission.
I challenge the underlying premise of this rule that stripping appeal rights and protections will improve accountability. Instead, it risks silencing employees who raise valid concerns and removes critical checks on management abuse. The proposal overlooks the costs to employee morale, public trust, and the loss of experienced talent. I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule and maintain the 2024 protections while focusing on effective alternatives: enhancing first-line supervisors’ management skills, providing mediation tools, and enabling flexible team rotations to better match employees and managers. These measures would better support accountability and responsiveness without sacrificing fairness or integrity.
In conclusion, the proposed rule (Schedule Policy/Career, subpart on removal procedures) threatens to erode essential employee protections, reduce transparency, and weaken the civil service’s ability to serve the public effectively. I respectfully request OPM reconsider this approach and prioritize policies that protect employees’ full appeal rights and procedural safeguards for federal employees under Part 432. This upholds the public interest. Under the proposed amendments:
Conclusion
The amendments to Parts 432 and 451, as currently proposed, threaten to erode essential employee protections, reduce transparency, and weaken the civil service’s ability to serve the public effectively. These changes would have directly harmed the employee I represented and many others who courageously uphold integrity within the federal government.
I respectfully request OPM withdraw these harmful amendments and prioritize policies that protect employees’ rights, uphold merit principles, and safeguard the public interest.

Thank you for consideration.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
As a private citizen, I strongly oppose the implementation of Schedule Career/Policy (a.k.a “Schedule F”) for Federal employees. Others have addressed how the proposed rule change violates government policy; my fundamental concern is the language defining who would be placed on this list and further threats to US Government (USG) STEM mission agencies. 

The language defining “policy-influencing position” is: “authorizes the President or OPM to exclude employees in excepted service positions of a “confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating character” (hereafter “policy-influencing positions”) from chapter 75 procedural requirements and MSPB appeals.” https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/04/23/2025-06904/improving-performance-accountability-and-responsiveness-in-the-civil-service#p-19

The information released on the March 2025 list of proposed Schedule Career/Policy (SCP) workers suggests that the intention is to place people who should not be on the list on SCP status to enact tighter control (i.e., political interference) on the Federal Workforce, including many Federal scientists/engineers and STEM support staff.

Federal career employees in science/STEM mission agencies are required by congressional mandates to carry out science to inform policy—including scientists and administrative workers (IT, finance, HR, etc.). Others do research to develop new understanding of medical, technological, energy, or natural science to fuel development of solutions to societal challenges, from improving disease/treatment options to modernizing energy infrastructure to improving weather forecasts to managing valuable fisheries and beyond. USG research and innovation requires freedom from political interference to maximize productive, beneficial outcomes for U.S. society, including fueling the Nation’s economy.

Federal scientists and support staff implementing congressional mandates are required to respond to requests for information from legislators and many other stakeholders. However, they are NOT allowed to “determine, make, or advocate” (i.e., “influence”) policy. This is strictly enforced, to the extent that they are not allowed to speak about *anything* related to policy in the public sphere (including, for instance, funding levels and decisions). 

Putting Federal scientists—and those whose work is in support of Federal science missions—on a list of people in “policy-influencing positions” opens the door to the erosion of scientific integrity and degradation of US leadership in STEM fields globally due to political interference in science. Much like there are checks and balances among government branches, there are—and should be—effective checks and balances between USG science and policy. Science-relevant policy can and should be informed by sound science, but scientists do not generally have the expertise to shape policy well. However, the information exchange between science and policy experts must remain protected to ensure well-founded, ethical outcomes. The Federal STEM Workforce takes an oath to uphold the U.S. Constitution and receives career protections to ensure that their work can be conducted without political interference.

Putting Federal science workers on Schedule Career/Policy status threatens the integrity of USG science and the future of US STEM innovation, as well as long-standing US status as a well-respected leader in international innovation across STEM disciplines. Further, the proposed rule change threatens to end a long history of exceptionally productive public-private partnerships, fueling American economic growth and dominance. Finally, muzzling U.S. STEM workers and threatening the integrity of USG STEM checks and balances will be harmful to ensuring the access of the American people to clean air, clean water, food and economic security, and medical health.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
In my personal capacity as a U.S. Citizen, I submit comments regarding Office of Personnel Managementʼs (OPM) Proposed Rule “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service,ˮ 90 Fed. Reg. 17182 (April 23, 2025). I write to oppose the Proposed Rule.

While I agree with the overarching goal of enhancing performance and accountability, the mechanism outlined is flawed. As written, this rule could enable sweeping reclassification and dismissal of career staff based on perceived disloyalty, not poor performance. The term “partisanship” is not defined anywhere in the proposed rule, giving this and future administrations license to terminate or discipline a reclassified employee simply for being perceived to be pushing back on the policy preferences of the administration.

Barrier to Meaningful Public Participation: While the proposed rule is open for Public comment, reading through over 100 pages, 43 of which are the rule itself, proves to be a monumental task, taking hours to do. 

While presented as affecting a few Federal positions, the proposed rule, could quite easily affect most positions. if as defined in I.Background, A III. “…the “policy-influencing” terms … have the natural, plain English meaning of describing positions involved in determining, making, or advocating for government policy, or positions of a confidential nature. Such positions include, but are not restricted to, political appointments.” Using Plain English to interpret “policy-influencing” is broad. Using a Plain English definition, the newly proposed classification will include all staff that provide comments on agency policy, enforce policy, or advocate to advance agency policy.  Most federal employees contribute to this in some capacity. 

Lack of Due Process: Removing the procedural protections of Chapters 43 and 75 of Title 5 strips employees of the opportunity to respond to allegations or improve through established mechanisms. The result is not a more efficient government. It is one in which fear of dismissal replaces professional integrity.

Unclear Metrics for Performance Improvement: The rule purports to improve performance, yet provides no tools, support, or measurable outcomes for doing so. It relies solely on the threat of termination, which is ineffective and counterproductive. When Chapters 43 and 75 of Title 5 are removed, an employee has no recourse to either prove wrongful termination or improve performance. As a Federal manager, I have successfully turned around performance/conduct issues using existing tools (coaching, documentation, Letters of Conduct). The employee I coached successfully turned around and is a valuable contributor. The existing tools work when properly applied. While OPM states that surveys say managers have difficulty removing poor performers, there are no details as to the population cited in the survey.  It seems an erroneous, and not a statistically-supported, inference to assume that these poor performers are in fact the same population of policy-making or policy-advocating positions that OPM believes are the poor performers.

Flawed Scope and Impact Estimates: Stating only 50,000 positions will be affected is misleading. The vague definitions in the rule could encompass hundreds of thousands of positions. It is also doubtful that the proposed will produce the transformational benefits claimed.  The Federal workforce is about 2.8 Million. After all the RIFs, resignations, and retirements, there will likely still be 2 Million Federal employees. 50,000 of 2M is 2.5%. The “performance improvement” proposed by this rule that supposedly only affects 2.5% of Federal employees will not result in “Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service.” The rule instead can serve as a loophole to re-classify thousands of positions, allow for dismissal due to undefined “insubordination”, and create fears due to disagreement with superiors. Dismissed staff can be replaced with like-minded individuals of the current political party. 

Recommendation:
Rather than dismantle existing protections, by creating an unnecessary employee classification, OPM should strengthen managerial training and support, enforce existing accountability tools, and reward high performance. Civil service reform should not come at the cost of politicizing the workforce or silencing federal employees who offer dissenting but valuable perspectives. Given political polarization, this will lead to large swaths of Federal employees being fired, or being made to resign, after each administration change. The proposed rule is not a path to better government. It seems a path to instability, politicization, and the erosion of public services and trust.

Title: Comment from Rebecca McCauley Rench
Comment:
Dr. Rebecca McCauley Rench submits these comments regarding Office of Personnel Management’s (OPM) Proposed Rule “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service,” 90 Fed. Reg. 17182 (April 23, 2025). I write to express opposition to the Proposed Rule in its entirety.

I am a Ph.D. scientist and a devoted public servant. My highest desire is to serve humanity and the American people. I am a federal civil servant and have held that role since 2018. As such, I have an innate understanding of how the federal government works and what stymies advancement and efficiency. The proposed rule would change the classification of 1000s of federal civil servants, from their current non-partisan, protected status into one that is at-will to the politicians in Washington. This has the potential to impact me specifically in my federal employment, but definitely would impact me in my workplace and as an American.

I recently learned about the previous Spoils system of federal service and how it changed under Presidents Garfield and Arthur. The American People have no interest in returning to a federal government that is fueled through loyalty to politicians rather than loyalty to the US Constitution. As a non-partisan civil servant, I can attest that amplification of government employees that are akin to political appointees will decrease government progress and create absurdities in the implementation of the will of Congress and the Administration. Federal civil servants need to be able to provide their expertise and guidance without fear of political retribution and the loss of their employment. It is the political appointees at the heads of Agencies that are responsible for ensuring implementation of Administration priorities, not the steady, stable, professional, non-partisan, experts within the civil service.

I can attest personally that the civil service takes its non-partisan status seriously and takes extraordinary measures to prevent violations of the Hatch Act, which prohibits civil servants from participating in political activity in their official capacity. The current classification of these roles is implemented as completely non-partisan government employees that can execute their Oath to the Constitution of the United States without fear of political retribution for providing their expert advice and guidance to faithfully execute the laws of Congress and the policies of the Administration. Changing those positions into ones in which their expert advice is curtailed by the concerns about whether a fact aligns with Administration priority will lead to inaccurate, unsafe, and inefficient use of taxpayer funds to achieve the goals of federal agencies.

In short, I do not support the Proposed Rule in its entirety and there are specific concerns I have with the intentions behind the rule creation and incoherent leaps in logic related to that stated intent. I do not support the movement of career civil servants into positions that would make them de facto political appointees by removing their civil servant protections. Title: Comment from Sarah  Howard
Comment:
I write to express strong opposition to the Office of Personnel Management’s (OPM) proposed rule titled “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service.” While I support efforts to improve government performance and accountability, this rule represents a significant and troubling shift away from the core values and legal protections that underpin the federal civil service.

The proposed rule threatens to undermine the Merit Systems Principles established under 5 U.S.C. § 2301. These principles require that federal employees be selected and advanced based on merit and protected from arbitrary action, personal favoritism, or political coercion. By making it easier to discipline or remove employees without sufficient procedural safeguards, the rule increases the risk of personnel decisions based on non-merit factors, including political considerations.

Our democratic system depends on the integrity of a nonpartisan civil service that serves the American people, not a particular political party or administration. This proposed rule may open the door to increased politicization of the federal workforce by reducing the protections that ensure employees can perform their duties without fear of political retribution. The United States has long rejected a spoils system in favor of professional, career-based public service. Weakening those protections represents a serious threat to good governance.

The proposed rule raises serious constitutional concerns under the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment. Federal employees have a recognized property interest in their employment, and the Supreme Court has held that this interest cannot be taken away without adequate procedural protections (*Cleveland Bd. of Ed. v. Loudermill*, 470 U.S. 532 (1985)). Curtailing the right to respond to allegations or appeal adverse actions would violate employees’ constitutional rights and expose the federal government to legal challenges.

The proposed rule appears to conflict with the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978, which was enacted by Congress to preserve merit principles and establish a fair system for employee discipline and appeals. Any regulatory action that effectively undermines this statutory framework may be challenged as inconsistent with the law and subject to invalidation under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. § 706.

The strength of the federal government lies in the talent, independence, and continuity of its workforce. If civil servants perceive that their jobs can be lost based on political winds rather than performance or misconduct, morale and retention will suffer. In turn, this can degrade the capacity of agencies to deliver on their missions, from public health to national security. The proposed rule risks damaging not only internal agency dynamics but also the public’s trust in the neutrality and professionalism of its government.

For these reasons, I urge OPM to withdraw or substantially revise this proposed rule. The pursuit of government efficiency must not come at the cost of constitutional protections, statutory mandates, or the enduring principle of a nonpartisan civil service. Upholding these values is not only a legal obligation, but also vital to the functioning and legitimacy of our democracy.

Legal Argument Against OPM’s Schedule F NPRM (April 2025)

The Office of Personnel Management’s (OPM) April 23, 2025, NPRM establishing “Schedule Policy/Career” (Schedule F) violates federal law, exceeds executive authority, and undermines the merit-based civil service. Reclassifying employees not hired into Schedule F further violates due process and accrued rights.

Argument 1: Schedule F Violates Statutory Intent and Precedent
Schedule F misinterprets the CSRA’s excepted service exemptions, limited to “confidential, policy-determining” roles (5 U.S.C. § 2103). United States v. Fausto, 484 U.S. 439 (1988), underscores Congress’s intent to protect career employees from arbitrary dismissal. Lovshin v. Department of Navy, 767 F.2d 826 (Fed. Cir. 1985), requires narrow exemptions, yet Schedule F’s broad reclassification lacks statutory basis. Elgin v. Department of Treasury, 567 U.S. 1 (2012), affirms CSRA’s exclusive remedies, including Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) appeals, which Schedule F eliminates, rendering it ultra vires. Under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), OPM’s reversal of the 2024 rule lacks reasoned explanation, violating Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Ass’n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

Argument 2: Reclassifying Non-Schedule F Employees Violates Due Process
Reclassifying existing employees strips accrued protections under 5 U.S.C. § 7513, violating property interests (Perry v. Sindermann, 408 U.S. 593 (1972)) and pre-termination hearing rights (Cleveland Board of Education v. Loudermill, 470 U.S. 532 (1985)). This contravenes Fausto and APA notice requirements (Perez v. Mortgage Bankers Ass’n, 575 U.S. 92 (2015)). Executive Order 14171’s attempt to nullify protections fails under Encino Motorcars, LLC v. Navarro, 579 U.S. 211 (2016).

Conclusion
Schedule F violates the CSRA, APA, and precedent (Fausto, Lovshin, Elgin, State Farm). Reclassifying non-Schedule F employees further breaches due process (Perry, Loudermill, Perez). OPM must withdraw the NPRM to comply with federal law.

Title: Comment from Sh azzam
Comment:
Transforming federal positions into an "at-will" category could significantly erode the due process rights currently afforded to these employees and create an environment where violations of key federal employment laws, particularly the Civil Service Reform Act, the Hatch Act, and the Whistleblower Protection Act, could occur more readily and be more challenging to address. The emphasis on a merit-based, non-partisan civil service, which is foundational to the current federal employment system, would be significantly jeopardized.  See below for more detailed information about these concerns, each of which I'd like addressed:
Potential Due Process Violations:  Currently, federal employees who have completed their probationary period are generally entitled to certain due process rights before adverse actions like removal or demotion can be taken. These rights are rooted in the Fifth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, which protects against the deprivation of life, liberty, or property without due process of law. For federal employees, their employment is considered a property right. Key due process rights that could be jeopardized include:
 * Notice of Reasons: Employees are typically entitled to a clear and specific written notice detailing the reasons for the proposed adverse action. Under an "at-will" system, termination could occur without a stated cause.
 * Opportunity to Respond: Federal employees usually have the right to respond to the charges against them, both in writing and orally, and to present evidence on their behalf before a final decision is made. An "at-will" status could eliminate this opportunity for a meaningful response.
 * Right to Appeal: Current civil service regulations and union agreements often provide avenues for employees to appeal adverse actions to an independent body like the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB). This right to appeal could be significantly curtailed or eliminated under an "at-will" system.
 * Fair and Just Cause: While not strictly a "due process" right in the procedural sense, the CSRA emphasizes that employees should be retained based on the adequacy of their performance. An "at-will" system could allow for terminations without demonstrating just cause related to performance or misconduct.
Increased Risk of Violating Other Relevant Laws:  Changing these positions to an "at-will" status could also make it easier to violate other critical laws and principles governing federal employment:
 * Civil Service Reform Act (CSRA): The CSRA, enacted in 1978, established a merit-based system for federal employment, emphasizing fair treatment, protection against political influence, and accountability. Converting positions to "at-will" could undermine several core principles of the CSRA:
   * Merit System Principles: The CSRA outlines nine merit system principles, including fair and equitable treatment, selection and advancement based on merit, protection against arbitrary action and political coercion, and retention based on performance. "At-will" employment inherently clashes with these principles by allowing for potentially arbitrary dismissals not based on merit or performance.
   * Prohibited Personnel Practices (PPPs): The CSRA lists specific PPPs, such as discrimination based on political affiliation, taking reprisal against whistleblowers, and using official authority to influence elections. Without the due process protections of the current system, it could become easier for managers to engage in these prohibited practices without fear of effective challenge or appeal.
 * Hatch Act: This act restricts federal employees' involvement in partisan political activity to ensure a non-partisan civil service. If "policy influencing" or "policy advocating" roles become "at-will," there's a heightened risk that these employees could face pressure or be incentivized to engage in political activities that align with the administration in power, potentially violating the Hatch Act's provisions against using official authority or influence for political purposes.
 * Whistleblower Protection Act (WPA): This law protects federal employees who report waste, fraud, and abuse. In an "at-will" environment, employees in "policy influencing" roles might be less likely to report wrongdoing for fear of arbitrary termination without recourse, thus weakening whistleblower protections.
 * Anti-Discrimination Laws: Federal employees are protected from discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age, disability, and other factors. While these laws would still technically apply, the lack of due process and the potential for arbitrary dismissal in an "at-will" system could make it more difficult for employees to prove discriminatory intent behind a termination.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
The Case Against Schedule Policy/Career: Why It Is Illegal, Immoral, Impractical, Cruel, and Corrupt

Illegal
Schedule Policy/Career directly undermines civil service protections enshrined in U.S. law. The Pendleton Act of 1883 and the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 were enacted to shield federal employees from political interference and arbitrary dismissal. By reclassifying career positions into Schedule Policy/Career, the government effectively strips employees of due process and merit-based protections. This politicization of the federal workforce violates established statutory principles and could be found unconstitutional for infringing on the legal safeguards that ensure a nonpartisan civil service.

Immoral
The moral foundation of public service lies in impartiality, dedication to the common good, and adherence to the rule of law—not political loyalty. Schedule Policy/Career undermines these principles by turning professional public servants into expendable assets, subject to removal based on political alignment. It penalizes integrity and rewards sycophancy, compromising the ethical fabric of government and violating the public trust.

Impractical
The federal government relies on a knowledgeable and experienced workforce to carry out complex, essential missions in areas like national security, public health, and disaster response. Schedule Policy/Career threatens to purge seasoned professionals and replace them with politically appointed individuals who may lack the necessary expertise or continuity. This not only disrupts agency operations but also leads to inefficiencies, delays, and poor service delivery to the public.

Cruel
Schedule Policy/Career introduces a level of job insecurity that is both unnecessary and inhumane. Public servants, many of whom have devoted decades to their roles, face the risk of termination without cause or recourse. Families are left in financial and emotional turmoil, and morale across the federal workforce plummets. This kind of indiscriminate upheaval punishes loyalty to public service and creates a culture of fear and instability.

Corrupt
Schedule Policy/Career resurrects a spoils system where jobs are handed out based on political loyalty rather than merit. It paves the way for corruption by silencing dissent and discouraging whistleblowing. Civil servants who fear losing their jobs are less likely to challenge unethical behavior or raise concerns about mismanagement. The result is a weakened democracy, where government decisions are driven by politics instead of public interest.

Conclusion
Schedule Policy/Career is not just bad policy—it is a direct threat to the foundations of good governance. It undermines the rule of law, punishes ethical behavior, disrupts the functioning of government, traumatizes loyal empoyees, and opens the door to widespread corruption. Defeating Schedule Policy/Career is essential to preserving a competent, fair, and independent civil service that serves the American people—not political agendas.

Title: Comment from John Lamb
Comment:
I write in strong opposition to the Office of Personnel Management’s proposed rule titled “Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service.” This proposed action fundamentally threatens the integrity, stability, and nonpartisan nature of the federal workforce. By proposing to create a new category—“Schedule Policy/Career”—and stripping essential due process protections from affected employees, OPM is advancing a rule that is inconsistent with long-standing federal statutes, undermines congressional intent, and invites political abuse.

The rule violates the letter and spirit of the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (CSRA), particularly 5 U.S.C. §§ 2301 and 2302, which codify merit system principles and prohibit personnel practices based on political affiliation or retaliation. These protections are the cornerstone of a professional federal workforce. By exempting reclassified positions from the procedural rights found in 5 U.S.C. Chapter 75, including the right to appeal to the Merit Systems Protection Board, the proposed rule effectively turns civil service positions into at-will employment, circumventing statutory due process requirements.

The proposed reclassification echoes the discredited “Schedule F” effort of 2020, which was widely condemned by bipartisan stakeholders, career federal employees, and good governance organizations. Congress responded by proposing legislation specifically designed to block such efforts, recognizing the existential threat they pose to a stable and apolitical civil service. This new rule is an attempt to revive Schedule F under a different name, ignoring not only legal objections but also widespread public concern.

In addition to violating statutory protections, the proposal undermines the original intent of the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which established a merit-based hiring system to replace the corrupt and arbitrary spoils system. The federal civil service was never meant to be an instrument of political loyalty or ideological conformity. Instead, it was designed to ensure continuity, competence, and impartiality in public administration. This proposed rule would dangerously reverse that progress by enabling the removal of qualified professionals based on subjective political assessments.

OPM’s assertion that this rule is necessary for improving performance and accountability is unsupported by evidence. Agencies already have the tools they need to discipline or remove employees for misconduct or poor performance under existing law, and no credible data has been presented to show that these tools are insufficient. Indeed, this rule would do nothing to address real performance problems—it merely provides political appointees a means to remove individuals they disagree with, not those who are underperforming.

The rule is arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. § 706, as it fails to present a rational basis for such a sweeping change. OPM has not adequately considered the reliance interests of existing career employees, many of whom accepted public service positions with the understanding that they would be afforded procedural rights and job protections rooted in law. Nor does the rule contemplate the destabilizing consequences of sudden, politically motivated purges across the federal workforce.

This proposal also creates legal ambiguity in its definition of policy-determining roles. “Policy-adjacent” is a vague and overly broad term that could encompass thousands of roles traditionally occupied by nonpartisan experts. Without a clear, objective framework, this invites uneven application, agency abuse, and litigation. The lack of guidance will likely lead to inconsistent enforcement, with one administration’s interpretation differing dramatically from the next, further eroding public trust and employee morale.

Whistleblower protections under 5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(8) will be rendered meaningless under this rule. If civil servants can be removed without explanation for working in vaguely defined “policy” roles, then speaking out about waste, fraud, or abuse becomes professionally suicidal. This chilling effect not only endangers transparency but increases the risk of corruption and maladministration—outcomes contrary to the public interest.

Moreover, the proposed rule will seriously damage recruitment and retention efforts in the federal workforce. Talented individuals are less likely to join or stay in public service if their employment security can be summarily revoked based on ideological alignment rather than merit. The long-term result will be a less competent, more politicized federal workforce that cannot effectively serve the American people, especially in times of national crisis or transition.

For these reasons, I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.

Title: Comment from Anonymous Anonymous
Comment:
Re: Comment on OPM-2025-0004-0001 (Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service)
To Whom It May Concern:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Office of Personnel Management’s proposed rule “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service” (OPM-2025-0004-0001), which would implement Schedule Policy/Career (formerly Schedule F).
As an American citizen who values effective governance, I believe this proposed rule undermines the foundational principles of our nonpartisan, merit-based civil service system that has served our country effectively for more than a century. The proposed changes would harm government operations in several critical ways:
1. Threatens the Merit-Based Civil Service System
The merit system principles established under the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 were designed to ensure that federal hiring, retention, and advancement decisions are based on qualifications, competence, and performance rather than political loyalty. The proposed rule directly contradicts these principles by making approximately 50,000 career civil servants vulnerable to removal without due process protections.
Such a drastic change would return us to a spoils system where employees are hired and fired based on political loyalty rather than skill, expertise, and dedication to public service. This approach was rejected with the passage of the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883 specifically because it resulted in inefficient and corrupt governance.
2. Will Result in Brain Drain and Loss of Institutional Knowledge
Career civil servants possess specialized expertise and institutional knowledge built over years of service. The proposed reclassification puts these professionals at risk of arbitrary removal, which would significantly harm agencies’ ability to fulfill their missions effectively.
I am particularly concerned that this rule would severely damage employee morale and lead to a mass exodus of talented professionals from government service. Career civil servants would likely leave government rather than accept at-will employment status, taking with them crucial institutional knowledge and skills that have taken decades to build. The resulting brain drain would directly harm government effectiveness and service delivery to American citizens.
3. Undermines Continuity of Government Operations
By making certain career positions vulnerable to mass turnover with each change in administration, the proposed rule threatens the continuity of government operations. Effective governance requires stability and consistency in implementing programs and services that Americans depend upon daily, regardless of which party controls the White House.
4. Compromises Nonpartisan Public Service
The true strength of our civil service lies in employees’ dedication to serving the American people professionally, regardless of which party holds power. Civil servants implement the policies of democratically elected leaders while maintaining ethical standards and professional integrity.
The proposed rule would pressure employees to prioritize political loyalty over their professional expertise and ethical obligations, ultimately undermining the quality of government services provided to all Americans.
5. Conflicts with Congressional Intent
The Civil Service Reform Act’s exemption for “confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating character” positions was intended to apply narrowly to political appointees, not broadly to tens of thousands of career civil servants with policy expertise. The proposed rule represents an unprecedented and expansive reinterpretation of this language that contradicts decades of understanding and practice.
Conclusion
I urge the Office of Personnel Management to withdraw this proposed rule and maintain our effective, merit-based civil service system. The American people deserve a government staffed by professionals selected for their qualifications and expertise, not their political loyalties.
An apolitical civil service that can deliver services efficiently and effectively to all Americans, regardless of party affiliation, is essential to our democracy. This proposed rule undermines that principle and would damage the government’s ability to fulfill its obligations to the American people.
Thank you for considering my comments on this important matter.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
This is a comment on the proposed rule Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service from the Office of Personnel Management, Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004, RIN 3206-AO80. I am submitting my comment in a personal capacity.

“The federal government should be a model employer.” It’s a quote seen repeatedly throughout Agency websites, reports, case cites, and often a phrase codified in statutes related to employment. Merit system principles are not a Goliath-like barrier that needs to be removed. Rather, these protections simply require management to do their job and “show their work” to the American people when firing employees for cause. This work holds management to the standard of a model employer and ensures that managers are not taking adverse actions against employees for bad faith reasoning. 

Before I joined the civil service, I was a Surface Warfare Officer in the Navy. Because “SWOs” are tasked with leading a division of sailors immediately upon stepping aboard their first ship, I received leadership and management training from the beginning of my career. Something that stuck with me and saw me through was the principle of documenting performance–both excellent and unsatisfactory. Even though I was working 80+ hour weeks, taking the time to document my sailors performance was the right thing to do. My top performing sailors received recognition and as a junior-officer, I had the papertrail to support ranking them higher among their peers. Without that paperwork, my sailors would have been bumped down the list on the basis of my rank, but my supporting paperwork made sure that we ranked the sailors on their performance–not extraneous inter-political reasons. This worked for my sailors who needed more guidance as well. I remember a Senior Chief telling me that one of my sailors was going to be ranked first because of the collateral duties he had completed for the Chief’s Mess. The problem was that he was neglecting his primary duties and had a public display of insubordination earlier that quarter. If this sailor was ranked first, morale would tank among the rest of the division and the lesson learned would be “politics and ass-kissing first, mission second.” That did not happen because I documented the incident of insubordination and his performance. He was not ranked first but was still encouraged to grow in his specialty and show maturity and restraint among sailors. I’m so proud to say that he has stayed in the Navy and is now an Officer serving in his same specialty. The other sailors who received positive documentation also stayed in the Navy. Documentation works. Personnel are retained and grow instead of leaving out of frustration.

Why this sea story? It’s simple. Documentation requirements force personnel decisions to be on merit principles. And if a 23 year old junior officer can handle this while learning how to drive a ship and working 80 hour weeks on deployment, it is NOT too much to ask of high level management here to use merit system principles for policy-influencing positions and any other positions contemplated by the NPRM. Indeed, after my time in the Navy, I reviewed potential MSPB cases as a law clerk and found that simple documentation provides more than enough support for adverse actions when the actions are in the best interest of the federal government and American people. 

Furthermore, the April 2024 Rule (Upholding Civil Service Protections and Merit System Principles) has not been found to be procedurally deficient. The evidence and data cited by this NPRM (Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service Proposed Rule) is not concrete fact; it’s survey results, news reports, and academic theory that needs interpretation. In fact, many sources the NPRM relies on are the same as the April 2024 Rule considered and rejected as meritless or unpersuasive. Similarly, the non-political legal questions at the heart of the NPRM were analyzed and settled just a year ago in the April 2024 Rule. With this recent history, it leads to an interpretation that this proposed rule change is not based on sound reasoning. 

Thus, I urge you to reject this rule and uphold merit system principles.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Subject: Public Comment on OPM Proposed Rule: OPM-2025-0004 – Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service
To Whom It May Concern,

I am submitting this comment as a concerned member of the public regarding the Office of Personnel Management’s (OPM) proposed rule, Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service (Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004). While I support efforts to enhance accountability in the federal workforce, I have significant concerns about the rule’s lack of clarity and its potential unintended consequences.

1. Lack of Clear Definition for "Policy Influencing Positions"

The most fundamental issue with this rule is its failure to clearly define what constitutes a "Policy Influencing Position." While  I agree with the rule's assertion that  that these roles extend beyond political appointees, it does not provide a precise definition—only vague descriptions and examples in Section II.B. The guidance issued on January 27 by Charles Ezell, Acting Director of the US OPM further broadens the scope dramatically, stating that positions any position with, "duties that the Director [of the Office of Personnel Management] otherwise indicates may be appropriate for inclusion in Schedule Policy/Career" can be included. This introduces ambiguity and potential inconsistency.

Without a definitive classification, employees cannot determine whether their roles qualify, nor can they challenge misclassification. I am aware that draft lists circulating within agencies include purely technical positions that do not logically belong in this schedule. Additionally, cybersecurity personnel—whom the rule explicitly states should not be categorized as Policy Influencing—have been included in some draft lists. This lack of clarity and oversight must be addressed before implementation.

2. Insufficient Data to Support Performance and Accountability Claims

The rule asserts that performance and "policy resistance" are issues within the federal workforce but relies on anecdotal evidence and partisan sources (e.g., the Napolitan Institute) rather than rigorous analysis. A more objective approach would involve statistical analysis of performance ratings for employees affected by this rule.

While I acknowledge that some supervisors may rate unsuccessful employees as "minimally successful," a comprehensive data-driven review would reveal whether performance issues are widespread among those targeted by this rule. Without such analysis, the justification for these changes remains speculative rather than evidence-based.

3. No Mechanism to Audit or Challenge Agency Misuse

The rule estimates that only 112 employees per year will be removed under this authority and states that "If necessary, OPM can recommend measures to prevent abuse." This is insufficient. There must be a formal mechanism for employees to challenge misclassification and a structured audit process to ensure agencies do not misuse this authority.

4. Misrepresentation of Federal Workforce Accountability

The assertion that the federal workforce is not accountable to the public is misleading. Federal employees serve the public and regularly receive feedback from the public through elected representatives, stakeholder groups, and direct communication with federal programs. Agencies routinely adjust their work based on public input, and in extreme cases, programs are redirected or eliminated through congressional action. The rule should acknowledge these existing accountability mechanisms rather than imply that federal employees operate without oversight.

Conclusion

For this rule to be effective and fair, OPM must:
• Clearly define "Policy Influencing Positions" to prevent misclassification.
• Conduct objective performance analyses to justify its claims.
• Establish formal audit and challenge mechanisms to prevent agency misuse.
• Recognize existing federal workforce accountability rather than mischaracterizing it.

I urge OPM to address these concerns before finalizing the rule. Thank you for considering this comment.

The political staff at any given agency could potentially deem all of its staff as political/career under the guidance provided in this proposed rule.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I am strongly opposed to the proposed rule “Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service” (90 FR 17182). As the summary states, the rule would recategorize a wide range of long-standing career positions from the competitive service into a new excepted service schedule for “policy-influencing” roles. This change would remove long-established due process protections for thousands of civil servants by stripping their rights to adverse action procedures and appeals.

First, I want to acknowledge that I will be personally affected by this rule. I currently serve in a permanent career appointment in the competitive service that would be reclassified into Schedule Policy/Career. This change would immediately render me an at-will employee, vulnerable to dismissal without due process. The fact that I am afraid to sign my name to this comment is itself a powerful reflection of the fear and distrust this administration has instilled in the federal workforce in just its 3.5 months in office.

Although the preamble claims “[t]hese positions will remain career jobs filled on a nonpartisan basis” (90 FR 17182), the true intent is clear. The rule is designed to make it much easier to fire federal employees. The Office of Personnel Management should not move forward with finalizing this rule.
While the administration frames the rule as a response to misconduct and poor performance, its clearest explanation appears in its claim that agencies must be able to “quickly remove employees from critical positions who… undermine the democratic process by intentionally subverting Presidential directives” (90 FR 17182). This vague and subjective language creates an expansive justification for firing career civil servants with no oversight or recourse.
The rule claims to uphold merit-based hiring by stating that “[t]he President has required that agencies appoint and retain employees in Policy/Career positions based on merit, not their personal political affiliation” (90 FR 17208). However, it simultaneously removes the checks and balances designed to protect against politically motivated dismissals. Without the protections of chapter 43 and 75, there is nothing to prevent terminations based on perceived loyalty.
If the real concern is misconduct or poor performance, why remove appeal rights only for “policy-informing” employees? And why now? The proposal gives no clear rationale for why these civil servants, in particular, should be singled out, strongly suggesting that the intent is political, not performance-driven.
The preamble attempts to frame this rule in the context of civil service history, being so audacious as to go all the way back to George Washington and early government reforms. This is a distraction. The rule must be considered in the political environment we are currently in, not as an academic reflection on the history of civil service. 

The proposed reclassification under “Schedule Policy/Career” aligns with Project 2025, a coordinated effort to reshape the federal government. Kevin D. Roberts, president of the Heritage Foundation and a key architect of Project 2025, has publicly stated that the goal is to remove large numbers of civil servants and replace them with politically “aligned personnel.” He told the New York Times that the desired reduction in the federal workforce is “substantial” (Garcia-Navarro, L. (2024, January 21). Inside the Heritage Foundation’s Plans for ‘Institutionalizing Trumpism.’ The New York Times Magazine. https://www.nytimes.com/2024/01/21/magazine/heritage-foundation-kevin-roberts.html).

Against this backdrop, statements like “[c]ontrary to fears of a return to the spoils system, the President expressly forbid [sic] political loyalty tests for Policy/Career employees” (90 FR 17208) are empty. Stripping procedural protections while asserting a commitment to merit-based service is fundamentally inconsistent. There is nothing in the rule that would meaningfully prevent a return to politically motivated hiring and firing. It is part of a broader strategy to destabilize the civil service and concentrate power in the executive branch.

I also reject the administration’s claim that concerns about diminished agency capacity, weakened expertise, and reduced effectiveness are “misplaced” (90 FR 17208). We are already seeing the consequences of this administration’s actions. The Deferred Resignation Program and overly aggressive reduction-in-force plans have already resulted in a loss of institutional knowledge and weakened capacity across federal agencies. Finalizing this rule would only amplify that harm.

For these reasons, I strongly urge the Office of Personnel Management to withdraw this proposed rule.

Title: Comment from Anonymous

Comment:
Argument Against the Proposed Rule: A Federalist Perspective

1. **Undermining the Independence of Civil Service**

The federal civil service system, as designed by the founders and codified over the years, is founded on the principle of an independent, non-partisan, and professional workforce that serves the nation—not the whims of any political administration. While the rule proposed by the OPM purports to enhance accountability in cases of misconduct or poor performance, the mechanism it proposes would dramatically undermine the longstanding tradition of civil service independence.

By allowing agency supervisors to easily dismiss career employees in policy-influencing positions for reasons not constrained by established civil service protections (such as adverse action procedures or appeals), the proposed rule introduces a level of political interference into the daily operations of government agencies. The federal workforce would become susceptible to the shifting tides of political power, rather than maintaining an objective, non-partisan stance that serves the public interest. This not only threatens the integrity of the civil service but also creates the very real potential for arbitrary and politically motivated dismissals. If the civil service is beholden to the executive branch in such a manner, it would no longer serve as a stabilizing force for the nation.

2. **Violation of the Fundamental Right to Due Process**

The proposed rule also bypasses due process protections traditionally afforded to federal employees under the Civil Service Reform Act. While the desire to ensure that employees in key positions are held accountable for misconduct or poor performance is understandable, this rule circumvents established procedures for adverse actions and appeals, which are essential to protecting the rights of employees against unjust termination.

In a republic founded on the principle of liberty and justice, due process is not a mere formality—it is a cornerstone of a just and fair system. The decision to dismiss an individual from a government position must be subject to established procedural safeguards that ensure the individual’s rights are not violated. The lack of such safeguards in the proposed rule could lead to arbitrary dismissals, leaving individuals without recourse to challenge wrongful or politically motivated removals.

3. **Potential for Abuse and Political Patronage**

One of the most troubling aspects of this rule is its potential to foster a system of political patronage, which the founders sought to avoid when they crafted the Constitution. If high-ranking policy-influencing positions are made "at-will" and exempt from procedural safeguards, there exists a significant risk that political motivations could replace merit-based decisions. Rather than advancing individuals based on their qualifications and performance, political appointees could remove career employees based on ideological alignment, partisan loyalty, or perceived disloyalty to the current administration.

The idea that individuals in critical positions could be dismissed without recourse for subverting presidential directives is a dangerously subjective standard that could be used to purge individuals who disagree with the executive's agenda, even when such disagreement is rooted in sound policy analysis or professional duty. Such a regime not only stifles dissent but also threatens the long-term health of democratic governance by undermining the ability of career civil servants to offer objective, independent advice and to act in the best interests of the American people, regardless of the political climate.

4. **Conclusion**

While the intention behind the proposed rule is to enhance the accountability of federal employees, its implementation would violate the core principles of fairness, due process, and stability that underpin our federal system. The independence of the civil service, the protection of employee rights, and the preservation of non-partisan governance are all at risk under this proposal.

If we allow the executive to sidestep due process protections and dismiss federal employees at will, we risk opening the door to greater politicization, eroding the integrity of our institutions, and undermining the trust that the public places in a neutral, professional federal workforce. It is imperative that we maintain the principles of fairness and accountability, not through hasty, broad reforms that strip away protections, but through measured, transparent, and constitutionally sound changes that respect the rights of federal employees and the democratic institutions they serve.

In conclusion, this rule is not a step forward, but a dangerous leap toward undermining the very foundations of our civil service system. It is a proposal that should be reconsidered in light of the enduring need for fairness, due process, and non-partisan government.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Comment on Proposed Rule: “Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service” (RIN 3206-AO26)

I strongly oppose the proposed rule to reestablish a Schedule F classification within the federal civil service. While it is framed as a way to improve accountability and responsiveness, it poses serious legal, constitutional, and policy concerns that threaten the integrity of the merit-based, nonpartisan federal workforce.

Violation of the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978

The Civil Service Reform Act was enacted to ensure that hiring and firing decisions are made based on merit, not political affiliation. This rule would allow broad reclassification and termination of employees without due process protections guaranteed under Title 5. Such actions undermine the very principles Congress intended to preserve and may exceed the executive branch’s legal authority.

Due Process Concerns

Employees gain a property interest in continued employment when protected by statute or regulation. Stripping those protections without individualized review violates the Fifth Amendment’s guarantee of due process. This concern is especially acute for employees reclassified without consent into a category that removes appeal rights and procedural safeguards.

Arbitrary and Capricious Rulemaking

This rule lacks a rational basis for overturning long-standing protections. The Administrative Procedure Act requires agencies to consider reliance interests and provide a sound justification for major policy changes. OPM has not shown that current mechanisms for handling performance and misconduct are insufficient, making this proposed rule arbitrary and capricious.

Encroachment on Congressional Authority

The structure and protections of the civil service are defined by Congress. Executive action that attempts to rewrite those protections through regulation threatens the separation of powers and invites legal challenges on constitutional grounds.

Risk of Politicization

Since the Pendleton Act, the civil service has operated as a professional, politically neutral workforce. This proposal reintroduces the potential for a patronage system by allowing mass removals based on subjective loyalty tests, undermining the effectiveness and credibility of the federal government.

Conclusion

This rule would erode due process, violate federal statutes, undermine congressional authority, and politicize the civil service. For these reasons, I respectfully urge the Office of Personnel Management to withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety.

I strongly oppose this rule for the following reasons:

1. Undermines the Merit System and Nonpartisanship
   The creation of a new “Schedule Policy/Career” category effectively revives the discredited Schedule F scheme by reclassifying career policy positions as at‑will. This shift removes procedural protections under 5 U.S.C. Chapters 43 and 75, inviting political influence into roles that must remain nonpartisan to ensure objective policy implementation.

2. Circumvents Statutory Safeguards
   Congress has consistently protected career civil servants from arbitrary removal to preserve expertise and institutional memory. The Administrative Procedure Act and Civil Service Reform Act establish clear appeals processes; this rule seeks to bypass those safeguards without congressional authorization, risking legal challenges and executive overreach.

3. Chills Whistleblowing and Oversight
   By permitting removal of employees who "subvert Presidential directives," the proposal’s vague language could deter whistleblowers from exposing misconduct at senior levels. Eliminating appeal rights for Schedule P/C employees weakens internal accountability mechanisms essential to public trust.

4. Erodes Morale and Drives Talent Loss
   Career professionals provide continuity and technical expertise. Converting policy roles to at‑will status will damage morale, accelerate retirements, and push top talent to the private or non‑profit sectors. In an era of complex challenges, losing institutional knowledge undermines the responsiveness this rule claims to improve.

5. Politicizes Technical and Front‑Line Roles
   Broadly defined, the rule threatens analysts, scientists, and inspectors whose objective assessments guide policy decisions. Fear of removal for political reasons may pressure experts to tailor findings to leadership preferences, jeopardizing evidence‑based policymaking and public safety.

6. Targeted Alternatives Exist
   Accountability gaps can be addressed through focused improvements: enhanced supervisor training, streamlined removal processes under existing Chapters 43 and 75, and increased resources for timely Merit Systems Protection Board case resolution—without sacrificing due process or the merit principle.

I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule and work with Congress on measured reforms that strengthen performance management while preserving merit‑based hiring, nonpartisanship, and due process.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I respectfully urge OPM to withdraw its proposed “Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service” rule. The proposal conflicts with established statutory protections, violates due process, and undermines the merit-based civil service system enshrined in the Civil Service Reform Act (CSRA) of 1978.

1. Violation of the Civil Service Reform Act (CSRA) of 1978

The CSRA (5 U.S.C. §§ 4301-4305, 7511-7514) ensures that federal employees may only be removed or disciplined for cause, with procedural protections including the right to appeal adverse actions to the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB). The proposed rule creates a new “Schedule Policy/Career” category that exempts employees from Chapters 43 and 75 of Title 5. This directly contradicts the statutory framework of the CSRA. The Supreme Court has upheld the necessity of civil service protections as serving the public interest by safeguarding against political coercion and arbitrary removal (Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 470 U.S. 532 (1985)).

2. Lack of Statutory Authority

OPM lacks the statutory authority under 5 U.S.C. § 3301 to undermine civil service protections explicitly enacted by Congress. The proposal unlawfully circumvents the legislative intent of the CSRA by bypassing essential procedural safeguards without express Congressional approval. This overreach renders the proposed rule ultra vires and likely to be invalidated by the courts (INS v. Chadha, 462 U.S. 919 (1983); FDA v. Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp., 529 U.S. 120 (2000)).

3. Due Process Violations

The Fifth Amendment guarantees that government employees with a property interest in continued employment cannot be deprived of that interest without due process of law (Perry v. Sindermann, 408 U.S. 593 (1972); Goldberg v. Kelly, 397 U.S. 254 (1970)). The proposed rule designates career civil servants as “at-will” employees, stripping them of procedural rights such as notice and a fair opportunity to contest removal. This fundamentally violates due process standards as established in Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319 (1976).

4. Erosion of Nonpartisan Civil Service

The CSRA was designed to maintain a nonpartisan, merit-based civil service by protecting against arbitrary or politically motivated dismissals. The proposed rule contradicts this principle by allowing arbitrary removal of career staff without cause. Such a framework is inconsistent with the prohibition against political coercion within the federal workforce (Elrod v. Burns, 427 U.S. 347 (1976); Branti v. Finkel, 445 U.S. 507 (1980)).

5. Inconsistency with Existing Precedent

The rule mirrors the rescinded Schedule F initiative, which faced broad legal opposition due to its potential to politicize federal positions. Courts have historically rejected attempts to circumvent merit-based protections through administrative action (Humphrey’s Executor v. United States, 295 U.S. 602 (1935); Free Enterprise Fund v. Public Company Accounting Oversight Board, 561 U.S. 477 (2010)). The rule also disregards the Federal Vacancies Reform Act (5 U.S.C. §§ 3345-3349d), which requires Senate confirmation for significant policy-making roles.

6. Lack of Empirical Support

OPM fails to present evidence proving that the new category would enhance accountability or efficiency. Instead, it destabilizes the federal workforce, fostering an environment of fear that undermines public service efficacy. Such arbitrary and capricious changes violate the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) (5 U.S.C. § 706), which prohibits rulemaking without a rational basis (Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29 (1983)).

7. Procedural Flaws

The APA mandates meaningful notice and public participation in rulemaking (5 U.S.C. § 553). OPM’s failure to justify bypassing traditional procedures, given the profound impact on civil service protections, lacks transparency and violates the APA’s standards of fairness and reasoned decision-making.

Conclusion

The proposed rule is legally unsound, procedurally flawed, and contrary to statutory and constitutional principles. It conflicts with the CSRA, violates due process rights, and risks politicizing the federal civil service. OPM should rescind the proposal and strengthen nonpartisan merit-based employment instead.

Title: Comment from Elizabeth Stewart
Comment:
I am submitting this comment in response to the Office of Personnel Management’s proposed rule entitled Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service, published on April 23, 2025.

While I whole-heartedly support efforts to enhance responsiveness and performance accountability across the federal workforce, I urge OPM to consider that the root cause of federal performance and misconduct management challenges lies far upstream from termination authorities. The inability of agencies to remove employees who are underperforming or engaging in misconduct is not primarily due to legal constraints — it is due to the systemic underdevelopment, under-vetting, and under-assessment of federal supervisors.

Specifically:

Supervisors are most often placed in supervisory roles without being vetted for their ability to exercise their legal supervisory authorities under 5 U.S.C. § 7103(a)(10), which include the responsibilities to hire, assign, direct, discipline, evaluate performance, and address labor matters. Many supervisors are selected based on rank, tenure, technical expertise, or as rewards for past performance — not supervisory aptitude or readiness.

Initial and continuing supervisory training is frequently minimal, inconsistent, and not aligned with regulatory requirements under 5 CFR 410 and 412. In some agencies, initial training can be fulfilled by passing a basic quiz. A higher standard of learning, scenario-based training, applied practice, and post-appointment development and assessment are often absent.

Performance assessment of supervisors rarely evaluates how effectively they exercise their supervisory authorities. Supervisors are not held accountable for executing their core duties related to managing employee performance or conduct. This leads to systemic avoidance of difficult personnel discussions and actions that could prevent scenarios from leading to termination. Firing Federal employees who could have been revectored to productivity is wasteful of government resources. 

Supervisors cannot confidently initiate removals or corrective actions because they lack both the procedural knowledge and institutional support. The Leaders and HR personnel supervisors consult may also be unable to advise properly — not because they are unwilling, but because they do not have access to the contextual, day-to-day history of employee behavior that only supervisors possess, and they may not know how, because they were never trained, resourced, or evaluated on these responsibilities either. 

Shifting some career civil servants into a new “at-will” category will not address this larger problem, in fact it will likely make matters worse. OPM should strengthen supervisory development and accountability as the foundation of civil service performance management reform. Otherwise, this policy risks adversely treating a symptom without addressing the cause.

Recommendations:

1) Hold agencies accountable for the outcomes of their supervisor training programs. Conduct a government-wide audit of supervisory training programs for compliance with 5 CFR 410 and 412, and determine whether the training programs meet the standard implied in 5 U.S.C. § 7103(a)(10): supervisors should be able to exercise their authorities independently, in the interest of the agency. 

2) Create a rigorous standardized vetting process for supervisory selection and probationary period that assesses readiness to carry out these responsibilities, and reenforces them during annual performance assessments. 

3) Require agencies to include supervisor competency in exercising 5 U.S.C. § 7103(a)(10) authorities as part of performance appraisals. 

4) Establish supervisory development plans and incentivize long-term mentoring and deliberate development of supervisors to improve talent management decision quality and workforce outcomes over time.

5) Modernize and strengthen the General Schedule Supervisory Guide to align with 5 U.S.C. § 7103(a)(10) and clarify supervisors should spend a preponderance of their time exercising those authorities versus treating supervisor authorities like collateral duties and centralizing supervisory decisions.

The performance and accountability of the federal workforce will not improve until the structure of supervision is modernized and in full alignment with federal regulations. 

I appreciate the opportunity to provide input on this important matter.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Public Comment on FR Doc. 2025–06904

Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004-0001

I. Introduction

I respectfully submit this comment in strong opposition to the proposed rule titled “Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service”. As a long-serving federal employee and citizen deeply invested in the integrity of the merit-based civil service, I believe this rule violates key legal principles, undermines due process, and threatens to politicize what has historically been a neutral and stable federal workforce.

⸻

II. Legal Violations and Overreach

1. Violates the Merit Systems Principles (5 U.S.C. § 2301)

This rule’s creation of “Schedule Policy/Career” at-will positions directly conflicts with the statutory requirement that:

“Employees should be protected against arbitrary action, personal favoritism, or coercion for partisan political purposes…” (5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8)).

2. Evades Procedural Protections in 5 U.S.C. Chapter 75

The proposed rule removes protections under 5 U.S.C. §§ 7501–7513, which provide due process for adverse actions:
	•	Notice
	•	Opportunity to respond
	•	Right to appeal

By reclassifying positions to sidestep these protections, the rule undermines the Administrative Procedure Act and existing precedent (e.g., Vitarelli v. Seaton, 359 U.S. 535 (1959)), where the Court held that the government must follow its own procedures when taking action against employees.

3. Violates OPM’s Statutory Authority (5 U.S.C. § 1103)

OPM does not have congressional authority to create new at-will employment categories. Doing so via regulation is a violation of the nondelegation doctrine, as it seeks to unilaterally restructure the civil service without legislative input.

⸻

III. Precedent and Case Law Supporting Due Process Rights
	•	Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 470 U.S. 532 (1985):
Federal employees with a “property interest” in their jobs are entitled to due process before termination.
The Court rejected attempts to make public employees at-will through regulation.
	•	Service v. Dulles, 354 U.S. 363 (1957):
The government is bound by its own regulations; failure to provide procedural protections is unlawful.
	•	Bush v. Lucas, 462 U.S. 367 (1983):
Reaffirmed that the civil service system provides essential protections for federal employees against abuse.

⸻

IV. Policy Risks and Harm

This rule creates a pathway to purge career professionals in policy roles by stripping them of their appeal rights. It opens the door to:
	•	Political loyalty tests
	•	Retaliatory firings
	•	Suppression of dissenting professional advice

Such risks are exactly what civil service reforms of the Pendleton Act (1883), Civil Service Reform Act (1978), and Whistleblower Protection Act (1989) were designed to prevent.

⸻

V. Conclusion

I urge OPM to withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety. It is both legally vulnerable and deeply corrosive to public trust in a fair, neutral, and competent civil service.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I write to express strong opposition to the proposed rule titled “Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service”, published in the Federal Register on April 23, 2025 (RIN 3206-AO11). While the stated goal of the rule is to enhance accountability in federal employment, its implementation would instead undermine foundational civil service protections, compromise scientific integrity, and threaten the long-term health and effectiveness of our federal institutions.

1. Overbroad and Vague Classification Criteria
The proposed rule allows for the reclassification of civil service positions into an excepted service category based on whether they are involved in “policy determination, policy making, or policy advocacy.” These terms are excessively broad and undefined. They could easily be interpreted to encompass roles that have limited or indirect policy impact—including technical experts, scientific reviewers, and regulatory project managers.

For example, scientists and regulatory professionals at the FDA play essential roles in public health decision-making based on statutory obligations under 21 U.S.C. 355. Their work may inform policy, but they are not policymakers. Reclassifying such professionals strips them of their due process protections based on a mischaracterization of their role.

2. Violation of Merit System Principles and Federal Law
The proposal contravenes the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978, which codifies the merit system principles (5 U.S.C. 2301) and protects employees from arbitrary removal (5 U.S.C. 7511–7513). By establishing a new class of “at-will” employees, this rule undermines the principle that federal employment decisions should be based on merit and free from political influence.

3. Increased Risk of Politicization and Loss of Objectivity
Removing due process protections from civil servants introduces a serious risk of politicization. It opens the door for career professionals to be dismissed for decisions that are not aligned with the current administration’s political views. This is particularly dangerous in regulatory agencies like the FDA, where objective scientific decision-making is essential for drug approval, public health surveillance, and enforcement.

A 2018 report by the Union of Concerned Scientists found that political interference had already eroded morale and hindered federal science. Nearly half of surveyed federal scientists reported that they or their work had been pressured to support a particular political position (UCS, 2018). This rule would exacerbate that environment, deterring employees from providing honest, expert evaluations.

4. Harm to Recruitment, Retention, and Institutional Capacity
Federal agencies already face challenges recruiting and retaining top talent, particularly in high-demand scientific and technical fields. According to the National Academies of Sciences (2022), job security and civil service protections are key factors in attracting and retaining highly qualified personnel in regulatory science roles at the FDA (NAS, 2022).

Allowing mass reclassification of roles into an at-will category will send a chilling message to prospective employees and existing staff: your job security is subject to the whims of political leadership. This is likely to accelerate attrition, damage institutional knowledge, and degrade the government’s ability to protect the public interest.

5. Weakened Whistleblower Protections and Public Accountability
The loss of procedural protections for a large swath of employees will have a profound chilling effect on whistleblowing and internal dissent. Civil service protections act as a safeguard for employees who report misconduct or question unlawful practices. The Office of Special Counsel has long noted that strong whistleblower protections are tied to effective governance and agency performance.

Without these protections, misconduct may go unreported, critical internal checks may disappear, and the public’s trust in government transparency will be undermined.

Conclusion

This proposed rule is a significant and deeply flawed attempt to reverse the merit-based, politically neutral design of the U.S. civil service. If enacted, it would reduce accountability, politicize scientific and regulatory decision-making, undermine whistleblower protections, and impair the government’s ability to attract and retain the talent it needs to serve the American people.

I respectfully urge OPM to withdraw this rule and recommit to the principles of merit, independence, and fairness that have long underpinned public service.

References
Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 – 5 U.S.C. 2301, 7511–7513
21 U.S.C. 355
Union of Concerned Scientists. 2018 Federal Scientist Survey
National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. Evaluating FDA’s Hiring and Retention Needs for Scientific Talent. 2022
U.S. Office of Special Counsel. Annual Reports and Whistleblower
