Title: Comment from Amanda Pease
Comment:
Instituting the proposed Schedule Policy/Career will weaken the very fabric of non-partisan civil service, moving America closer to a spoils system where Americans are not treated equally. I deeply oppose this proposal and urge you to reconsider.
The American system of government is founded on the belief that all Americans are created equal and should be served equally by their federal government. While America has never fully lived up to this promise, the proposed Schedule Policy/Career will move us farther from this goal. The proposal will vastly increase the number of government positions that are at-will under each President, without civil service protections or union representation. These positions are specifically designed to prioritize loyalty to the President rather than to the Constitution of the United States of America.
The current American civil service is made up of public servants who are non-partisan. This is incredibly important as public servants serve under all political parties, bringing expertise with them which is further developed during their federal career, and ensure that the work of government supports all Americans, regardless of their political party. Importantly, civil servants take an oath of loyalty to the Constitution of the United States, not to any President, are required to follow strict rules of ethics and non-partisanship, and are shielded from political retribution for their work by civil service protections and union representation. Stripping over 50,000 federal employees of these protections and judging them not based on expertise or loyalty to the Constitution, but on their loyalty to the current President, will have several debilitating impacts on the federal government's ability to serve the American people. This includes losing the experts and expertise that are invaluable to serve the American people - committed scientists, attorneys, and other professionals that choose to be public servants and deeply value integrity and equality will be pushed out in favor of political loyalists. We have seen this play out in other countries that use a spoils system of government (and, in fact, in America in the past). We know that this will result in the people of America being served not based on need or on the criteria established for each government program, but based on political party of the area where they live.
I agree that the federal government would be improved by an increased ability to deal with poor performers. However, there are many other approaches that can be instituted related to poor performers that does not threaten the expertise and neutrality of the very people who do the work of the federal government.
I have been a proud civil servant for over 12 years, serving communities from rural Nevada to urban California, working with tribes and people in small towns across Arizona, and helping communities from Puerto Rico to Oahu to Tinian recover from disasters. I proudly work to clean up environmental contamination anywhere and everywhere that work is needed, without regard to whether it is a "red" or "blue" area or how citizens voted in the last election. Changing this fundamental paradigm of public service will not make America "great", it will instead deepen the divides that threaten to tear our great country apart.

Title: Comment from karen fontaine
Comment:
I write in opposition to the rule proposed by the Personnel Management Office on 04/23/25 titled "Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service" (Office of Personnel Management 5 CFR Parts 210, 212, 213, 302, 432, 451, and 752 [Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004] RIN 3206-AO80).

The Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883 established that hiring people to work in the United States federal government would be based on merit, thus replacing a corrupt patronage system.  In other words, the Pendleton Act specified that federal employees should be hired on the basis of what they know rather than who they know.  Advancement and promotions were to be based on actual achievement and meeting performance goals, not based on campaign contributions, votes delivered, or political considerations. 

We have seen nationally and in cities like my own city of Chicago how a "spoils system" or a patronage system is corrosive to the human spirit leading to elevation of incompetence and corruption. It is a system based on fealty not fairness and is contradictory to President Trump's stated goal of efficiency in government.  

It is well known that people perform better in their jobs when their knowledge and expertise are acknowledged, when their progress towards goals is measured through established performance metrics, and when they are trusted and respected.  A system where only loyalty is rewarded and where all employees serve 'at will' is much worse for employees and the country. This is not my opinion but the basis for the Pendleton Act, which remains the law of the land.

Please note OPM’s description of its work on its website: “A strong, merit-based civil service is critical to a functioning democracy. It ensures that our government “of the people, by the people, for the people” continues to serve the American public without interruption, even though our leaders change over time. It also safeguards the public interest in a federal workforce that looks like America and that benefits from the talents, ideas, and skills of people from all our nation’s communities.”

Schedule F seeks to abolish the merit system embedded in the federal civil service since its establishment and convert career civil servants into political appointees. 

According to a recent article in the Journal of Policy Analysis & Management (published February 17, 2025), the politicization of public services and “the frontal attack on the separation between political appointees and civil servants, achieved by weakening civil service protections and purging those deemed disloyal” as is clearly evidenced by the proposed Schedule F rule will result in a less efficient and more corrupt government. 

Don Moynihan, the Ford School’s J. Ira Harris and Nicki Harris Family Professor of Public Policy at the University of Michigan previously wrote that Schedule F “would represent an unprecedented increase in politicizing the federal workforce, which would predictably undermine performance and accountability in the federal government, as well as democratic values such as transparency and the rule of law.”

Replacing career civil servants with partisan Schedule F appointees would have a disastrous effect on the competence, performance, impartiality, responsiveness, and professionalism of the federal government -- precisely those areas it purportedly addresses. Career civil servants serving in a nonpartisan capacity are the backbone of the U.S. government, chosen for their qualifications and ethical conduct and serving the American people directly, rather than a political party in power.  

The proposed rule includes language like the following: "Substantive participation and discretionary authority in agency grantmaking, such as the substantive exercise of discretion in the drafting of funding opportunity announcements, evaluation of grant applications, or recommending or selecting grant recipients. Grantmaking is an important form of policymaking, so employees with a substantive discretionary role in how federal funding gets allocated may occupy policymaking positions." The important trust given to those in a grantmaking role is precisely the reason why they should not be selected for personal affiliation or loyalty to any President. Rather, we need career civil servants who are accountable directly to the U.S. public they are sworn to serve in these roles, as opposed to political appointees who frequently lack the necessary educational background and professional experience.  

The U.S. government cannot wholesale alter course with every change in occupation of the White House. Career civil servants enable long-term strategic planning, taking their cues from the will of the American people as embodied by the policies of elected officials but also drawing from evidence-based planning and data-driven execution pertaining to their specific missions and duties. 

If the proposed rule goes forward, the United States of America will lose stability and competitiveness on the world stage. Services for those taxpayers who need them most will become less effective and tailored. The government will spin its wheels in endless cycles of ideologically-driven change for the sake of change.

Title: Comment from Anonymous

This rule threatens to dismantle the nonpartisan, merit-based civil service system that underpins effective governance and public trust in our institutions.
The proposal would enable the reclassification of tens of thousands of career civil servants into a new "Schedule F” category, stripping them of due process protections and making them at-will employees. While the rule currently targets a subset of employees, its vague definition of “policy-influencing” and “partisanship,” as well as OPM’s own guidance available at https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/latest-and-other-highlighted-memos/guidance-on-implementing-president-trump-s-executive-order-titled-restoring-accountability-to-policy-influencing-positions-within-the-federal-workforce.pdf, opens the door for much broader and subjective application across agencies. This reintroduction of political loyalty tests into the civil service is antithetical to democratic principles and the letter and spirit of the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978.
As someone who served in both the excepted and competitive services, I can speak firsthand to the dedication and integrity of public servants. My spouse is also a current federal employee. Though his role is not immediately targeted, the potential chilling effect on ethical and professional conduct across agencies is profound. Civil servants should never be forced to choose between meeting their ethical obligations and preserving their employment.
This rule would not improve performance or accountability—it would suppress dissent, reward loyalty over competence, and undermine psychological safety in the workplace. As a former organizational change consultant, I know this is a recipe for dysfunction, not efficiency.
The ripple effects go far beyond federal workers. Undermining the stability and professionalism of our civil servants endangers the services all Americans depend on—Social Security, healthcare, environmental protection, and national security, to name just a few. A revolving-door federal workforce, beholden to political whims, will weaken these institutions at the very moment they require expertise and continuity.
I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule. Instead:
Maintain the 2024 final rule safeguarding merit-based hiring.
Increase funding to the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) to accelerate appeals.
Streamline performance evaluation policies through existing lawful means—not by stripping rights Congress has enshrined.
The authority to revoke civil service protections lies with Congress—not through executive or agency fiat. The Pendleton Act and CSRA were enacted to prevent exactly this kind of politicization. This rule would be a dangerous step backward.

Title: Comment from Whitney Untiedt
Comment:
RE: Public Comment in Response to Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service [Docket No. OPM–2025–0004]

I am writing to express my deep concern regarding the effort to reclassify specific federal positions, which would erode necessary protections for those serving within the federal statistical system and could transform positions which rely on specific expertise to political ones. The proposed rule, “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service,” would call into question the objectivity that both sides of the aisle rely on for our economic indicators, public health assessments, energy utilization and many other statistics. The federal statistical system plays an essential role in improving the lives of all Americans as well as informing critical policy decisions with evidence that is timely, relevant, and accurate. Federal statistical agencies are particularly vulnerable to the proposed rule due to the following:

Schedule Policy/Career could lead to the politicization of the federal statistical workforce. Official federal statistics clearly influence public policy of all sorts: monetary, fiscal, regulatory, etc. By making it easier to remove employees if a President determines that they are interfering with his or her policies, it increases the potential for passivity or political loyalty to be prioritized over expertise and experience. Politicization has had dramatic consequences for statistical agencies and their leaders in other countries, notably Argentina and Greece.

Importance of Trust, Impartiality and Objectivity: Statistical agencies, such as the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Census Bureau, and the National Center for Health Statistics, need professional autonomy to provide impartial, objective, reliable data. Professional autonomy is the ability to act independently from political or other undue external influence regarding its operations, such as data collection and analysis, staffing, and publications. Erosion of professional autonomy in the operations of statistical agencies would undermine their perceived or actual independence, leading to a loss of public trust in the data they produce.

Schedule Policy/Career would deprioritize and weaken the norms that uphold the ethical and professional standards that are critical to the success of statistical agencies. Senior leaders help craft, model and reinforce norms within their agencies and between their agencies and other parts of the government.  Examples include how agencies interact with staff, data users, data subjects, outside experts and host agencies. See Principles and Practices for a Federal Statistical Agency for examples of these critical norms. These norms reflect and go beyond the laws, rules, and policy directives that govern agencies’ operations. Weaker norms threaten trust, efficient operations, and data quality.

These agencies rely on highly specialized professionals, including statisticians, economists, and data scientists, who possess unique technical expertise and long-term institutional memory. Statistical agencies stand to lose experts who see their career paths as less secure and merit-based than before. The loss of these experts or frequent turnover in key positions could disrupt agency operations, hinder long-term planning, undermine the agency's ability to fulfill its mission, and impair the quality and accuracy of the data.

The uncertainty and fear of arbitrary dismissal could negatively impact employee morale, leading to decreased productivity and difficulty in attracting and retaining top talent.

To support their missions, statistical agencies must invest in long-term efforts such as extensive research, critical modernization projects, and efforts to ensure data access and continuity. Schedule Policy/Career could subject to agencies to changing presidential priorities, increasing senior staff turnover and disrupting modernization efforts, measurement of trends, and meaningful research.

Schedule Policy/Career poses a significant threat to the effectiveness of federal statistical agencies and to the integrity and quality of their products. By undermining the principles of merit-based employment and threatening job security of senior career civil servants, Schedule Policy/Career could lead to politicization, loss of trust and expertise, decreased morale, and disruption of agency operations. On behalf of U.S. businesses, the American public, and policymakers I am speaking up to protect the trustworthiness of the federal statistics we all rely on.

Title: Comment from Jordan  Rose
Comment:
ublic Comment on Proposed Schedule F Rulemaking (Docket No. OPM-2025-0001)

I write to express my strong opposition to the proposed reintroduction of Schedule F, as outlined in the Federal Register notice (Docket No. OPM-2025-0001). This policy threatens to dismantle over a century of civil service reform, undermining the merit-based system established by the Pendleton Act of 1883 and reaffirmed by the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978. Reclassifying federal employees as at-will political appointees would not only degrade the quality of public service but also reintroduce a modern-day spoils system, fostering corruption and eroding public trust in government institutions.

Legal Precedents Against Political Patronage

The United States Supreme Court has consistently upheld the principle that public employment decisions should not be based on political affiliation. In Elrod v. Burns, 427 U.S. 347 (1976), the Court held that dismissing public employees solely for their political beliefs infringes upon First Amendment rights, stating that such patronage dismissals "severely restrict political belief and association, which constitute the core of those activities protected by the First Amendment." Similarly, in Rutan v. Republican Party of Illinois, 497 U.S. 62 (1990), the Court extended this protection to promotions, transfers, and recalls after layoffs, emphasizing that conditioning public employment on political loyalty is unconstitutional.

The proposed Schedule F rule directly contravenes these precedents by enabling the dismissal of federal employees based on political loyalty rather than professional qualifications. This policy would effectively reinstate a patronage system, reminiscent of the "spoils system" that the Pendleton Act sought to eliminate.

Threats to Government Accountability and Public Service

Research indicates that politicizing the civil service leads to decreased government performance and responsiveness. A study by Vanderbilt University professor David E. Lewis found that appointees are associated with lower federal government performance and less responsiveness to the public, suggesting that political loyalty undermines effective governance. Moreover, politicization can impair agencies' ability to serve public interests, as employees may prioritize political directives over their professional duties.

The implementation of Schedule F could result in the mass termination of experienced federal employees, leading to a loss of institutional knowledge and expertise. This disruption would hinder the government's ability to deliver essential services and respond effectively to public needs.

Conclusion

Reintroducing Schedule F would not only violate established legal principles but also undermine the integrity and efficacy of the federal workforce. It is imperative that we uphold the merit-based civil service system to ensure that government employees are selected and retained based on their qualifications and commitment to public service, rather than political allegiance.

I urge the Office of Personnel Management to reconsider this proposal and to prioritize policies that protect the independence and professionalism of the federal workforce.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
To Whom It May Concern:

I write to respectfully oppose the Office of Personnel Management’s proposed rule that would reintroduce a new “Schedule Policy/Career” classification, allowing career federal employees in “policy-influencing” positions to be removed without the procedural protections currently afforded under Chapters 43 and 75 of Title 5.

While I support the goal of fostering accountability and upholding high standards of performance and conduct within the federal workforce, I am deeply concerned that this proposal would significantly undermine long-standing merit system principles, reduce the stability and independence of the civil service, and risk politicizing critical federal positions.

1. Undermining Merit System Protections
The foundational principles of the federal civil service are based on merit, nonpartisanship, and protection from arbitrary removal. The proposed rule would effectively strip procedural due process protections from a broad category of career employees, even though they are hired and classified as nonpartisan. Employees removed from Schedule Policy/Career positions would not have access to the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) or other neutral adjudicative bodies. This lack of recourse opens the door to removals based on subjective or ideological grounds, rather than actual misconduct or poor performance.

This shift threatens the very merit system that has ensured an impartial and expert civil service for decades.

2. Chilling Effect on Professional Integrity
Federal career employees play a vital role in providing continuity, institutional knowledge, and apolitical expertise across administrations. The proposed rule would create a chilling effect on those tasked with giving professional, evidence-based advice—especially when that advice might diverge from the immediate political preferences of agency leadership.

By subjecting these employees to at-will dismissal, the rule disincentivizes honest analysis and dissenting viewpoints. This may lead to poorer policy outcomes, as decisions may no longer be guided by facts or long-term interests, but by political expediency.

3. Vague and Broad Definitions Create Risk of Abuse
The regulation relies on broad and subjective criteria for determining which positions are “policy-influencing.” Without clear, narrow definitions, this could lead to widespread reclassification of positions across agencies, further eroding civil service protections on an unprecedented scale. There is also no mechanism in place to ensure fair and consistent application of these changes, nor safeguards to prevent misuse for political or retaliatory purposes.

4. Historical Precedents and Bipartisan Rejection
Executive Order 13957, which previously attempted to implement similar changes through the creation of Schedule F, was swiftly rescinded by the following administration, recognizing its danger to the independence of the civil service. Bipartisan experts and civil society organizations raised serious alarm about the precedent it would set. Congress also considered legislative action to permanently bar such actions.

This proposal attempts to revive Schedule F under a new name, but with many of the same structural problems.

5. Better Alternatives Exist
If the concern is about improving performance management and accountability, there are more constructive, targeted reforms that can be implemented without dismantling critical due process protections. These might include enhancing supervisor training, reforming the appeals process to reduce delays, and increasing transparency in performance evaluations.

Conclusion
The proposed rule poses a serious threat to the integrity, stability, and nonpartisan character of the federal workforce. It would increase the risk of politicization, reduce accountability to the public, and weaken the safeguards that have historically protected our democracy from undue influence.

I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule and instead pursue reforms that reinforce—not erode—the principles of a professional, merit-based civil service.

I am writing to object to the proposed changes to Schedule F, which would eliminate Civil Service protections for certain categories of federal employees.  This proposal is ill-conceived and is based upon assumptions which, in my opinion, lack factual support.

My background as a federal retiree with more than 30 years of federal service affords me ample experience and knowledge of the federal employment system to opine on this particular rule change.  During my more than three decades as a federal employee, I worked for eight different Presidents - three Democrat and 5 Republican.  For 28 years, I was employed as a federal attorney for two different federal agencies.  For the last 11.5 years of my federal service, I was the director of a large federal law office.  

Although the vast majority of the employees with whom I served were extremely competent and hard-working individuals, given the length of my service there were rare occasions when an adverse action was required to discipline an employee under my supervision.  There was never an occasion in my office for which termination of employment was an appropriate outcome.  However, given my lengthy service, I had significant familiarity with employee disciplinary procedures.  As an attorney, it is my opinion that those procedures are the minimum required to insure that employees facing disciplinary action are afforded due process  Therefore, I strongly disagree with the underlying assumption in this rule change that existing procedures are overly burdensome.

Furthermore, in my more than 30 years of experience under eight Presidents, I can state categorically that there was never an instance when the federal employees with whom I worked, or whom I supervised, undermined the policy directives of the Administration in office.  We all understood that those in elective office in the United States were entitled to direct Executive Branch agencies in accordance with their political preferences.  If a new President set a different course from his predecessor, we were always committed to follow that new course.  To diverge in any way from the Administration's policy directives would have compromised our professionalism and ethics.  That was not an option. 

Finally, let me add that a strictly merit-based Civil Service System is essential to the maintain the workings of the U.S. Government.  There is a place for political appointees in all agencies and departments.  However, the vast majority of government work is performed by career civil servants, many of whom have extended tenure which is essential to the functioning of their agencies.  Partisanship is not a factor.  Professionalism rules.

Therefore, I respectfully urge you to abandon this ill-considered attempt to undermine the Federal Civil Service which has a long and proud history of faithfully serving the people of the United States.

Title: Comment from Cara Anjos Breeden
Comment:
OFFICIAL COMMENT LETTER
Re: Opposition to Proposed Rule Implementing Executive Order 14171
To: U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM)
Date: May 19, 2025

To Whom It May Concern:

I submit these comments in strong opposition to the proposed amendments to 5 CFR Parts 210, 212, 213, 302, 432, 451, and 752, issued in response to Executive Order 14171. The proposed rule creates a new Schedule Policy/Career category, weakens existing due process protections, and enables the reclassification of competitive service positions into the excepted service. These changes collectively undermine the merit-based, nonpartisan civil service and risk politicizing the federal workforce.

SUBPART 1 – 5 CFR PART 213 (Excepted Service)
The creation of Schedule Policy/Career as a new excepted service schedule enables the reclassification of protected roles into at-will positions based on vague concepts such as “accountability to the President.” This would allow political influence over roles currently held by career professionals and undermines the fundamental protections of the competitive service system.

SUBPART 2 – 5 CFR PART 212 (Competitive Service and Competitive Status)
While the proposed rule allows employees to retain competitive status, it effectively removes them from the competitive service by administrative action. This undercuts core merit system protections and introduces legal ambiguity about rights and appeals, setting a dangerous precedent for bypassing due process through reassignment.

SUBPART 3 – 5 CFR PARTS 752 and 432 (Adverse and Performance-Based Actions)
The proposal to exempt Schedule Policy/Career employees from the procedural protections of 5 U.S.C. Chapters 75 and 43 strips employees of the right to challenge unjust removals or demotions. This action weakens protections specifically designed to guard against retaliation and politicization, particularly for employees in policy-adjacent roles that demand objectivity and professional independence.

SUBPART 4 – 5 CFR PART 210 (Basic Definitions and Conforming Changes)
Removing prior definitions that limited policy-influencing roles to political appointees invites widespread reclassification of career positions without Congressional authorization or oversight. It dilutes the nonpartisan character of career roles and threatens the structural integrity of civil service definitions.

SUBPART 5 – 5 CFR PART 302 (Excepted Service Hiring Procedures)
The proposed elimination of procedural requirements for transferring employees into Schedule Policy/Career positions removes critical transparency and appeal rights. It further allows circumvention of the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB), leaving employees vulnerable to arbitrary or politically motivated personnel actions without recourse.

CONCLUSION
The proposed rule is inconsistent with the merit system principles codified in the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 and opens the door to political influence over previously independent, expert-driven roles. Rather than fostering accountability, the rule enables retaliation, undermines due process, and discourages the apolitical public service ethos foundational to our democracy.

I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.

Respectfully submitted,
Cara Anjos Breeden

By allowing a broad swath of career civil servants—particularly those involved in policy-making or analysis—to be reclassified and potentially terminated without cause, Schedule F opens the door to politically motivated hiring and firing. Moreover, the vague and sweeping criteria for inclusion in Schedule F violate the due process protections guaranteed by 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which requires cause and procedural safeguards for the removal of career federal employees. Stripping thousands of workers of these protections not only weakens accountability but also risks chilling expert advice and dissent within agencies—undermining the very effectiveness of government operations.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is also bound by 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to support the merit system principles. Implementing Schedule F contradicts this statutory mission and places undue political pressure on career professionals, compromising the integrity and continuity of federal programs across administrations.

In conclusion, the Schedule F proposal poses a grave threat to the foundational principles of good governance, civil service independence, and the rule of law. I urge the administration and OPM to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement or revive this dangerous classification.

Title: Comment from Ian Hancock
Comment:

1900 E Street, N.W.

RE: Comment on Proposed Rule – “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service”
Docket ID: OPM–2025–0004
90 Fed. Reg. 17182 (April 23, 2025)

To Whom It May Concern:

I write to express strong opposition to the proposed rule titled “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service.” While framed as a reform to enhance government performance, this rule is, in fact, a deeply concerning attempt to erode the bedrock of America’s apolitical, expert-driven civil service.

As a professional working in public policy and strategy with extensive experience engaging with federal agencies on complex environmental and governance issues, I have seen firsthand the importance of a career civil service protected from political interference. This rule, by reviving and repackaging the prior “Schedule F” initiative under the new “Schedule Policy/Career,” would fundamentally undermine the merit-based principles that have guided our civil service for over a century.

The proposed regulation is not grounded in evidence. Instead, it leans on selective anecdotes and unsubstantiated claims about political resistance in the federal workforce. It offers no serious data-driven justification for dismantling the protections that ensure federal employees can provide candid, expert advice—free from fear of politically motivated reprisal. The result would be a chilling effect across agencies, where professionals might be penalized not for poor performance, but for fulfilling their roles with integrity.

Moreover, the rule’s sweeping reclassification power—potentially affecting hundreds of thousands of employees in so-called “policy-influencing” roles—would open the floodgates to politicized purges across departments. This is not a reform for efficiency; it is a tool for control. If enacted, it would not only degrade the quality of governance but also damage recruitment and retention of qualified professionals who are motivated by mission, not political patronage.

The proposal also directly contradicts the merit system principles enshrined in 5 U.S.C. § 2301 and reverses course on the Biden Administration’s April 2024 rule designed to safeguard nonpartisan civil service roles. It destabilizes institutional memory, weakens public trust, and risks turning every policy decision into a partisan one—regardless of the public good.

Recommendation:
I urge OPM to withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety. Instead of adopting a system that prioritizes political loyalty over professional expertise, OPM should reinforce and invest in reforms that support effective performance management within the bounds of merit-based protections. Accountability and responsiveness are critical goals—but they must be pursued without sacrificing the integrity and independence of the civil service.

Conclusion:
This proposal is a regressive and dangerous shift that would weaken the federal workforce’s ability to serve the American public fairly and effectively. I strongly oppose the proposed rule and urge the Office of Personnel Management to abandon this approach in favor of upholding a professional, nonpartisan civil service.

Sincerely,
Ian Hancock

Title: Comment from Z S
Comment:
Employment rules governing the civil service are set out in the Civil Service Reform Act, which has been in place for 50 years, and has, as is written in its introductory text, the goal of providing the "people of the United States with a competent, honest, and productive Federal work force reflective 
of the Nation's diversity." It achieves this goal, as everyone knows, by providing specific protections to members of the civil service, which, besides a miniscule number of high-level, highly influential presidential appointees, is comprised of Americans of all social classes who are dedicated to carrying out often complex tasks in service of the country with little reward, favor, or recognition.

The protections involve simply a requirement for documentation on why an employee has been separated from service, and the chance for a worker to defend their actions for being separated. Anyone who believes that hard work is the foundation of a healthy nation and a happy life, wishes for the American people to have a motivation to do good work and devote themselves to improving the world, and supports due process as a major barrier to the abuse of power (which is antithetical to the founding principles of this country), should recognize that these protections are important for all employees in the entire economy. 

This is not the case for most employees in this country, and it is a shame that it is not the case, as a large number of Americans suffer under instability in employment and precarious finances, with little reason to hope that, when they wake up in the morning, the day will be better than yesterday, and much reason to fear being cast into severe poverty at the whim of a manager. However, it has been the case for the civil service for decades, because congress, following the will of American citizens have recognized and codified in law that the positions in the civil service are too important to be at the mercy of political whims. This fear - that essential services and the protection of the country will be disrupted or used for indecent ends if employees in these positions can be easily fired and replaced not based on merit but rather their friendliness to a current administration, is the basis for the civil service protections outlined in the Civil Service Reform Act. It is directly stated in the act that civil service employees, in fact, "should be (A) protected against arbitrary action, personal favoritism, or coercion for partisan political purposes, and (B) prohibited from using their official authority or influence for the purpose of interfering with or affecting the result of an election or a nomination for election."

The establishment of Schedule F directly contradicts the purpose of the Civil Service Reform Act, as described above and in the actual text of the law. Yes, the Act does mention that certain positions should be excepted from having civil service protections, but it makes a clear distinction between these "excepted" positions and those that are competitively filled - that is, people obtain these positions through a competitive, merit-based process. These categories are represented by actual positions that exist and are occupied by people in the civil service. The positions that are excepted from protections are excepted due to a specific clause in the Civil Service Reform Act that has interpreted identically since the passing of the law - these roles were advertised and filled as excepted service positions. The people in these positions are not boots-on-the-ground workers, because that work is not political and should not change by agency, they are philosophical guides of their departments, wielding great power over their respective agencies.

People in the competitive service, on the other hand, joined their role with all of the protections that the Civil Service Reform Act provides to their position. There is no precedent for, nor reason to think these protections can be taken away. Removing the protections from these positions means that they have now been made politicized against the will of congress, who funded these departments and therefore these positions with the knowledge of the positions being competitive positions acquired based on merit. 

Notably, and most importantly, while the rule change published here alleges that protections are counter to a merit-based civil service, the exception of certain positions and removal of their protections was not done in the Civil Service Reform Act because these positions needed to be more "merit-based," precisely the opposite, it was because these positions should be more attuned to the administration. 

Therefore, simply changing the status of a role to a fabricated "Schedule F" out of the blue runs counter to past and current congressional mandates, removes the due process rights of employees, and puts the expertise and quality of civil service work at risk. None of these are legal, and this publication should be retracted.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
The Schedule Policy/Career (P/C) policy poses a serious threat to the integrity and effectiveness of the federal government. Preserving an apolitical civil service, built on merit, expertise, and a commitment to serving the nation as a whole, is not merely a matter of good governance; it is a cornerstone of a healthy and functioning democracy.

Enacting Schedule P/C will do the following:
1. Politicizes the Civil Service
* Schedule P/C would allow the president or political appointees to hire and fire thousands of career federal employees based on their perceived loyalty or ideology, rather than competence or merit.
* It undermines the long-standing norm that civil servants should serve the public interest, not the political interests of any one administration.
2. Erodes Expertise and Continuity
* Career federal employees often have deep institutional knowledge and technical expertise built over decades. If these employees can be dismissed easily:
    * Continuity across administrations is lost
    * Policy decisions risk being based on short-term political gain rather than the overall public interest.
3. Creates a Chilling Effect
* Fear of retaliation or job loss could discourage civil servants from:
    - Speaking truth to power: discouraging employees from providing feedback when it contradicts political agendas
    - Providing honest, evidence-based advice.
    - Whistleblowing unethical or illegal behavior.
* This stifles innovation and accountability.
4. Reduces Public Trust
* If the public perceives federal agencies as extensions of the ruling political party, confidence in government institutions erodes.
* Trust in impartial administration of law, regulation, and public services diminishes.
5. Increases Risk of Corruption and Cronyism
* Without merit-based protections, hiring and firing decisions could be based on loyalty, favoritism, or political patronage.
* This undermines transparency and fairness in how government operates, leading to decreased public cooperation and compliance.
6. Strips many long-employees of civil servant rights guaranteed under the law.
* When positions are “converted” to Schedule P/C, many long-time high performing civil servants will lose rights and privileges they currently hold for things such as retirement status, veteran’s preference, and due process protection.
* With the ability of OPM and/or the President to make any position under move Schedule P/C, it effectively makes the entire federal workforce essentially “at-will”. This is contrary to statutory limitations currently in effect.

An Apolitical Federal Workforce enables
1. Serves the Nation, Not a Party
* Civil servants swear an oath to the Constitution—not to a president or political party. This fundamental principle ensures their primary allegiance is to the rule of law and the nation's interests.
* Their mission is to implement laws faithfully and fairly, regardless of who is in power.
2. Ensures Professionalism and Competence
* The merit-based civil service system ensures hiring and promotion are based on qualifications, not ideology.
* This supports efficient, effective, and evidence-based governance.
3. Preserves Institutional Memory
* Long-term civil servants carry continuity through transitions of power.
* They help ensure policies are implemented smoothly and legally, even during chaotic political periods.
4. Supports Checks and Balances
* An apolitical workforce can serve as a guardrail against abuses of power.
* They can resist unlawful orders and provide accurate information to Congress, oversight bodies, and the public.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Public Comment Opposing the Establishment of Schedule Policy/Career Authority
Submitted by: Former Federal Employee

To Whom It May Concern:

I respectfully submit this comment in strong opposition to the establishment of the “Schedule Policy/Career” classification under Executive Order 14171. While framed as a tool for accountability, this authority undermines civil service protections, politicizes public administration, and destabilizes constitutional governance.

Though renamed, Schedule Policy/Career mirrors the intent of the rescinded Schedule F and presents even greater risks by suggesting permanence for an inherently anti-merit structure.

I. Civil Servants Owe Loyalty to the Constitution, Not to Political Leadership

Federal employees take an oath under 5 U.S.C. § 3331 to “support and defend the Constitution.” Their allegiance is to law—not to a President, party, or ideology. Reclassifying career roles into at-will appointments opens the door to loyalty tests and political dismissals, not based on performance or law, but on perceived alignment. This violates the spirit of the oath and weakens employee independence.

II. Schedule Policy/Career Conflicts with Civil Service Law

The Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 protects merit-based hiring and due process:
	•	5 U.S.C. § 2301 outlines the merit system principles.
	•	5 U.S.C. § 7513 guarantees due process before adverse actions.

Schedule Policy/Career removes these safeguards by creating a class of employees who can be fired without cause. This bypasses statutory protections and congressional intent.

III. Undermines Constitutional Checks and Balances

Career civil servants implement laws passed by Congress and are subject to judicial and legislative oversight. Redefining these professionals as political appointees collapses the wall between evidence-based administration and partisan direction. This contradicts Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935), which upheld limits on executive removal of certain officials. It threatens agency independence and opens the door to manipulation.

IV. True Accountability Is Legal, Not Political

Proponents argue Schedule Policy/Career increases accountability. But robust systems already exist:
	•	Ethics rules and administrative review;
	•	Oversight by Congress, IGs, and the courts;
	•	Performance-based disciplinary processes under Title 5.

This proposal replaces legal accountability with political compliance—dangerous in a democracy that depends on neutral implementation of law.

V. Threatens Institutional Capacity and Continuity

In 2020, OPM identified over 50,000 positions as eligible for reclassification under similar criteria. These included lawyers, scientists, economists, and program analysts. Replacing career experts with political loyalists during emergencies or transitions would degrade performance, delay services, and jeopardize public trust.

Federal programs require continuity across administrations. Civil servants are not obstacles—they are the backbone of long-term public service.

VI. Independence Is a Safeguard, Not a Flaw

The notion that policy-influencing roles must be politically appointed is overbroad and ahistorical. Agencies depend on career professionals for consistent, lawful, and technically sound operations. Their ability to raise concerns or offer dissenting analysis is essential—not subversive.

The U.S. system relies on this professional independence to ensure implementation serves the law, not the preferences of a temporary political leadership.

VII. Requests for Clarification

Given the scope and implications of this authority, I respectfully request:
	1.	Legal justification for how this aligns with Title 5;
	2.	Criteria for defining “policy-influencing” positions;
	3.	Estimates of how many positions may be reclassified;
	4.	Safeguards to prevent political abuse or retaliation.

VIII. Conclusion

Schedule Policy/Career threatens to undo decades of progress in building a competent, professional, apolitical federal workforce. It weakens due process, undermines agency capacity, and concentrates power in the executive without adequate oversight. Its rebranding does not disguise its effect: politicization of the career civil service.

I urge OPM to reject this proposal and recommit to the foundational principles of a nonpartisan, merit-based civil service that upholds the Constitution and serves the public—not political interests.

It would also have a chilling effect and discourage innovation, suppress informed decision-making, and erode trust in public institutions by causing government employees to fear reprisal for presenting any possibilities or findings or opinions that may be perceived as going against any specific political leader or perspective even when such information is necessary. 

I write to ask OPM not to promulgate this rule and preserve the nonpartisan foundation of our civil service and the principles that have long protected the professionalism, independence, and stability of our federal institutions. Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

Title: Comment from Catherine Chaney
Comment:
I oppose the rule proposed by the Personnel Management Office on 04/23/25 titled "Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service" (Office of Personnel Management 5 CFR Parts 210, 212, 213, 302, 432, 451, and 752 [Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004] RIN 3206-AO80).
A "spoils system" or a patronage system is corrosive to the human spirit leading to elevation of incompetence and corruption. It is a system based on fealty not fairness and would reduce efficiency in government.  

A system where only loyalty is rewarded and where all employees serve 'at will' is much worse for employees and the country. This is not my opinion but the basis for the Pendleton Act, which remains the law of the land.

Please note OPM’s description of its work on its website: “A strong, merit-based civil service is critical to a functioning democracy. It ensures that our government “of the people, by the people, for the people” continues to serve the American public without interruption, even though our leaders change over time. It also safeguards the public interest in a federal workforce that looks like America and that benefits from the talents, ideas, and skills of people from all our nation’s communities.”

Schedule F seeks to abolish the merit system embedded in the federal civil service since its establishment and convert career civil servants into political appointees. 

According to a recent article in the Journal of Policy Analysis & Management (02/17/2025), the politicization of public services and “the frontal attack on the separation between political appointees and civil servants, achieved by weakening civil service protections and purging those deemed disloyal” as is clearly evidenced by the proposed Schedule F rule will result in a less efficient and more corrupt government. 

Don Moynihan, the Ford School’s J. Ira Harris and Nicki Harris Family Professor of Public Policy at the University of Michigan previously wrote that Schedule F “would represent an unprecedented increase in politicizing the federal workforce, which would predictably undermine performance and accountability in the federal government, as well as democratic values such as transparency and the rule of law.”

The summary description of the proposed rule focuses solely on the ability to remove employees at will yet is utterly silent on abundant evidence from our nation's past on how corrosive such systems are to the human spirit and how they undermine foundational American values and ideals, including the rule of law and a government responsive to its people.

I urge you to withdraw the proposed rule regarding Schedule F.

Schedule F would politicize the federal workforce by stripping civil service protections from thousands of dedicated public servants, including refuge managers, scientists, and conservation professionals in the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. These roles are essential to the functioning of the National Wildlife Refuge System and are grounded in science, law, and public service—not political ideology.

Since January 2025 alone, the Refuge System has lost more than 20% of its remaining staff, compounding a 30% decline over the past 15 years. Nearly 10% of refuges are already completely unstaffed, and no refuge in the country currently has the resources it needs to operate fully. Implementing Schedule F now would devastate what remains of the conservation workforce.

This rule would allow political appointees to fire experts without cause and replace them with ideologically aligned hires who may lack the experience or qualifications to manage public lands. That’s not accountability—it’s a recipe for instability, inefficiency, and the erosion of public trust.

Our nation’s public lands must be managed by nonpartisan professionals who are free to follow science, serve the public, and uphold conservation laws. I urge the Office of Personnel Management to reject this rule and protect the integrity of the merit-based civil service system.

My husband and I visit National Wildlife Refuges wherever we travel. Most recently we were in Monte Vista, CO, where thousands come each year to see the sandhill cranes gathering each spring before their long migrations. This refuge, and all others, deserve qualified staff. 

Sincerely,
Lois Johnson

Title: Comment from Danielle  McCaa
Comment:
Potential language: OFFICIAL COMMENT LETTER
Re: Opposition to Proposed Rule Implementing Executive Order 14171
To: U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM)
Date: 19 May 2025

To Whom It May Concern:

I submit these comments in strong opposition to the proposed amendments to 5 CFR Parts 210, 212, 213, 302, 432, 451, and 752, issued in response to Executive Order 14171. The proposed rule creates a new Schedule Policy/Career category, weakens existing due process protections, and enables the reclassification of competitive service positions into the excepted service. These changes collectively undermine the merit-based, nonpartisan civil service and risk politicizing the federal workforce.

SUBPART 1 – 5 CFR PART 213 (Excepted Service)
The creation of Schedule Policy/Career as a new excepted service schedule enables the reclassification of protected roles into at-will positions based on vague concepts such as “accountability to the President.” This would allow political influence over roles currently held by career professionals and undermines the fundamental protections of the competitive service system.

SUBPART 2 – 5 CFR PART 212 (Competitive Service and Competitive Status)
While the proposed rule allows employees to retain competitive status, it effectively removes them from the competitive service by administrative action. This undercuts core merit system protections and introduces legal ambiguity about rights and appeals, setting a dangerous precedent for bypassing due process through reassignment.

SUBPART 3 – 5 CFR PARTS 752 and 432 (Adverse and Performance-Based Actions)
The proposal to exempt Schedule Policy/Career employees from the procedural protections of 5 U.S.C. Chapters 75 and 43 strips employees of the right to challenge unjust removals or demotions. This action weakens protections specifically designed to guard against retaliation and politicization, particularly for employees in policy-adjacent roles that demand objectivity and professional independence.

SUBPART 4 – 5 CFR PART 210 (Basic Definitions and Conforming Changes)
Removing prior definitions that limited policy-influencing roles to political appointees invites widespread reclassification of career positions without Congressional authorization or oversight. It dilutes the nonpartisan character of career roles and threatens the structural integrity of civil service definitions.

SUBPART 5 – 5 CFR PART 302 (Excepted Service Hiring Procedures)
The proposed elimination of procedural requirements for transferring employees into Schedule Policy/Career positions removes critical transparency and appeal rights. It further allows circumvention of the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB), leaving employees vulnerable to arbitrary or politically motivated personnel actions without recourse.

CONCLUSION
The proposed rule is inconsistent with the merit system principles codified in the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 and opens the door to political influence over previously independent, expert-driven roles. Rather than fostering accountability, the rule enables retaliation, undermines due process, and discourages the apolitical public service ethos foundational to our democracy.

I respectfully urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.

Respectfully submitted,
Danielle McCaa 
Frederick, MD

OPM may not choose to disregard Congressional mandates in the manner proposed in this rule.

By allowing a broad swath of career civil servants—particularly those involved in policy-making or analysis—to be reclassified and potentially terminated without cause, Schedule F opens the door to politically motivated hiring and firing. Moreover, the vague and sweeping criteria for inclusion in Schedule F violate the due process protections guaranteed by 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which requires cause and procedural safeguards for the removal of career federal employees. Stripping thousands of workers of these protections not only weakens accountability but also risks chilling expert advice and dissent within agencies—undermining the very effectiveness of government operations.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is also bound by 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to support the merit system principles. Implementing Schedule F contradicts this statutory mission and places undue political pressure on career professionals, compromising the integrity and continuity of federal programs across administrations.

In conclusion, the Schedule F proposal poses a grave threat to the foundational principles of good governance, civil service independence, and the rule of law. I urge the administration and OPM to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement or revive this dangerous classification.

Title: Comment from Michael Pasqua
Comment:
Please consider the following comment vehemently OPPOSED to Proposed Rule ID: OPM-2025-0004-0001, "Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service." There is no rational evidence to support this rule, including the misinterpreted and misrepresented references cited in the proposal. In many cases, the references provided support practices the federal government are already exercising, such as probationary periods and better scrutinized hiring--not firing practices. 

The sources provided, such as the September 2019 article 'U.S. Merit Systems Protection Board, Office of Policy and Evaluation' titled "Issues of Merit" in no way supports a change to Schedule-F employment. In fact, the Director's Perspective section, starting on page three, clearly concludes 1) there should be more focus on communication, 2) agencies should choose appraisal levels that fit their organization (suggesting extra categories for superstars, rather than suggesting more firings), and 3) deploying technology to better administer performance systems. No where in these recommendations or within the article is the removal of employees for merit or poor performance justified. While exceptional circumstances will sometimes warrant exceptional consequences, such as termination, in no way is this an effective tactic for standard "poor performance"-- which we are about to witness as an abuse of power if this rule is promulgated. 

Another example: a quote from reference 101 says that "The 2016 Merit Principles Survey finds that only 41 percent of Federal supervisors are confident that they could remove a subordinate for serious misconduct, and just 26 percent are confident they could remove an employee for poor performance," yet the section in that article, titled 'Removing Unsuccessful Performers from Their Positions' actually states that "...agencies should draw a distinction between removing the employee from the position and removing the employee from the Federal service. When job fit is the source of the problem, transfers and demotions can serve both the public interest and the employee’s interest better than termination." 

In the conclusion of the article, it states "our data show that the most common causes of unsuccessful performance are linked to hiring practices. Agencies may be able to reduce incidences of poor and weak performance by ensuring that they:  (1) hire employees with the right competencies (particularly those that are less trainable such as willingness to perform work and resilience in the face of difficulty); and (2) robustly use the probationary period as a try-out opportunity before the appointment is finalized." 

In short, the very sources of these cherry picked quotes don't even support this rule. It is clear that this rule was not considered with genuine intent to improve the federal workforce. It is clear this rule is not written with the best interest of the public, their public servants, or their country. It is clear that this is another attack by this executive branch to gut the programs, positions, and people that actually make this country great. This is simply another attempt for the current administration to weaken what has taken decades and centuries to build. I implore you to REJECT this rule and maintain what little stability is left for Americans.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
To Whom It May Concern:

I respectfully submit this comment in opposition to the proposed Schedule Policy (reinstatement or rebranding of Schedule F), as outlined in Federal Register Document Number 2025-06904. I believe the rule is legally problematic and inconsistent with foundational civil service statutes and protections.
1. Conflict with the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978

The Civil Service Reform Act (CSRA) of 1978 establishes a merit-based system of employment and protects civil servants from arbitrary dismissal. The proposed Schedule Policy appears to bypass these statutory protections by reclassifying certain positions as "policy-determining" or "confidential" and stripping employees of competitive service protections without due process.

    5 U.S.C. § 2301 outlines the merit system principles, including fair and equitable treatment and protection against arbitrary action or personal favoritism. The Schedule Policy risks undermining these principles.

2. Violation of the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act

The Pendleton Act of 1883 was enacted to prevent the politicization of the federal workforce. By enabling large-scale reclassification of civil servants into positions that can be easily terminated or replaced by political appointees, the Schedule Policy appears to reintroduce a patronage system contrary to the law’s intent.

3. Due Process and Constitutional Concerns

Civil servants are entitled to procedural protections before adverse employment actions under 5 U.S.C. §§ 7511–7513. The reclassification of jobs without individualized review — or offering fewer procedural safeguards to those newly placed in an excepted schedule — raises serious due process concerns under the Fifth Amendment.

4. Arbitrary and Capricious Standard (Administrative Procedure Act)

Under the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. § 706), agency actions must not be arbitrary or capricious. The vague and broad criteria for determining what constitutes a "policy-making" position invite inconsistent application and may result in significant workforce disruption without clear rationale, making the policy vulnerable to legal challenge.

5. Undermining the Career Civil Service

The nonpartisan civil service has been critical to the continuity and integrity of government. The proposed rule could chill internal dissent, discourage whistleblowing, and hinder continuity of government services, especially during transitions of power. These impacts run counter to the intent behind the merit-based civil service protections outlined in 5 U.S.C. Chapter 31 and related statutes.

The proposed Schedule Policy contradicts existing federal statutes protecting civil servants and could have wide-reaching and damaging implications for the independence and continuity of government operations. For these reasons, I urge the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) and the Administration to withdraw this proposed rule.

Respectfully,
Thomas Myers

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I am writing to express strong opposition to the proposed rule titled “Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service” (Docket No. 2025-06904), which includes the repeal of Civil Service Rule 2.4 and lays the groundwork for the possible reimplementation of a Schedule F classification. As a career civil servant who believes deeply in the nonpartisan merit-based principles that undergird the U.S. civil service, I believe this rule poses serious risks to the fairness, integrity, and effectiveness of the federal workforce.

1. Repeal of Civil Service Rule 2.4 and Potential Resurrection of Schedule F
The repeal of Rule 2.4 is deeply troubling because it eliminates a key safeguard that helps protect civil servants from being arbitrarily classified in ways that can circumvent due process and merit protections. This change reopens the door to Schedule F, a proposal originally designed to reclassify thousands of federal employees as “excepted service” with limited or no civil service protections.

Schedule F was widely criticized by bipartisan experts, unions, and good government advocates because it would:

Strip long-standing protections from nonpartisan career employees, effectively undermining the apolitical character of the civil service.

Allow political appointees to remove employees for vague and undefined reasons related to “performance” or “policy alignment,” creating a chilling effect on honest advice and whistleblowing.

Lead to politicization of key policy and legal roles that should be grounded in law, science, and public interest—not political loyalty.

The reintroduction of a Schedule F-style system would also be disruptive, reducing morale and creating a brain drain as experienced personnel exit government service for fear of losing job protections.

2. Changes to Probationary Period Review Timing and Implications for Employees on Administrative Leave
The reference in the April 23 Presidential Action to mandating performance reviews before 60 days from the end of a probationary period raises significant concerns about fairness and implementation. If performance assessments are required at least 60 days prior to the end of probation, this implies that agencies would need to evaluate and finalize decisions earlier than usual—potentially without the benefit of a full year's performance context.

For employees who are currently on administrative leave, this creates a procedural gray area. How will an agency conduct a fair and comprehensive performance review of someone who has been involuntarily removed from the workplace for weeks or months? Will time on administrative leave be excluded from the calculation of the probationary period? Will affected employees be provided with a meaningful opportunity to demonstrate performance once they return?

Absent clear guidance, these changes could have a disproportionately harmful effect on due process rights, especially in cases where administrative leave is triggered by retaliatory or pretextual allegations. This undermines the stated goal of improving “accountability” and instead risks creating procedural traps and unjust outcomes.

3. The Broader Risk: Undermining the Merit System
Civil service reform must aim to enhance trust in government by improving systems of fairness, professionalism, and accountability. However, this proposal does not do that. Instead, it introduces new ambiguity, erodes protections, and creates fertile ground for politicization. The long-standing merit-based system ensures continuity and public trust in government actions, particularly in agencies that regulate health, safety, science, and the rule of law.

Schedule F—and rules that pave the way for its return—are antithetical to that purpose.

4. Request for Action
I strongly urge OPM and the Administration to:

Rescind this proposed rule in its entirety.

Affirm civil service protections that ensure hiring and firing decisions are based on merit, not ideology or political convenience.

Provide clear guidance regarding performance reviews during probation, particularly for employees on extended leave or facing allegations yet to be resolved.

The U.S. civil service is not a partisan workforce—it is a professional, mission-driven body committed to serving the public. We should be reinforcing those values, not undermining them.

Title: Comment from Radon Rosborough
Comment:
Schedule F describes its stated purpose as to "allow agencies to quickly remove employees from critical positions who engage in misconduct, perform poorly, or undermine the democratic process by intentionally subverting Presidential directives". However, it seems unlikely that the proposed rule will have this effect.

A core principle of democracy in the United States is the system of checks and balances. Numerous Presidential directives have been identified as unconstitutional or in opposition to the democratic process by legislators, courts, the general public, or all three. It is not necessarily the case that compliance with all Presidential directives will be the most effective way to ensure the stability of the democratic process. For example, if the President were to issue an Executive Order declaring that federal elections will be suspended and current office-holders will retain their posts indefinitely, then non-compliance with the Presidential directive would be in support of the democratic process, not a subversion of it.

Existing legislation, such as the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978, and decades of experience in routine government function have provided a robust set of processes that serve to effectively manage employee performance in federal agencies in compliance with applicable legislation. Extensive data must be gathered and reported to the public to justify specific amendments that may be proposed to employee classification; it must be shown specifically in what ways the existing evaluation structure is failing to allow employees to be removed who engage in misconduct or perform poorly. Furthermore, it must be explained why the existing adverse action procedures and appeals processes cannot instead be adjusted to remove unnecessary roadblocks to nonpartisan performance evaluation.

Without this information, it seems clear that the proposed rule will undermine the democratic process by allowing nonpartisan functions of government to be manipulated by political figures in ways that do not answer to voters.

This proposal also threatens civil service neutrality, due process, institutional memory, and legal safeguards—all essential to democratic governance. Instead of strengthening accountability, it risks creating a culture of fear and instability.

For these reasons, I urge OPM to reconsider this rule and work instead to improve existing performance management tools without dismantling long-standing civil service protections.

Title: Comment from Anonymous

I respectfully submit this comment in strong opposition to the proposed Office of Personnel Management (OPM) rule that would move policy-influencing career positions into a new “Schedule Policy/Career” category, subjecting these employees to at-will removal and exempting them from standard adverse action procedures and appeals.

While accountability in the federal workforce is important, this proposal fundamentally undermines the principles that define and preserve the integrity of the U.S. civil service. The merit-based, nonpartisan civil service system was designed to protect public administration from political interference, ensuring that government programs serve the American people based on law, science, expertise, and impartiality—not political loyalty.

This proposed rule would introduce serious and lasting harm across multiple dimensions:
	1.	Politicization of the Career Civil Service:
Allowing career federal employees in critical policy-influencing positions to be removed at-will, without the established due process protections, inevitably politicizes the workforce. Career experts would be vulnerable to removal for perceived political reasons, chilling honest advice, professional judgment, and dissent. Instead of a service to the American public, the role of federal civil servants could become a test of political alignment with the administration in power, which is antithetical to the Constitution’s vision of a stable, nonpartisan federal service.
	2.	Erosion of Institutional Knowledge and Program Stability:
Federal programs, particularly those serving vulnerable communities—such as veterans’ health, public health initiatives, disaster response, child welfare, and national security—depend on the deep institutional knowledge and technical expertise of seasoned career employees. By weakening job protections, the proposed rule risks mass turnover, demoralization, and loss of critical expertise, leading to inefficiency, program failures, and diminished public trust in government services.
	3.	Threat to Democracy and Good Governance:
The proposed structure creates dangerous incentives for administrations to purge career staff based on subjective perceptions of loyalty rather than objective measures of performance. A government where civil servants must fear retribution for carrying out the law faithfully—even when doing so may conflict with short-term political agendas—is a government where democratic institutions erode. Democracy depends on the impartial execution of the law, not its politicization.
	4.	Undermining Core Values of Public Service:
Federal employees are bound by core values: commitment to service, stewardship of public resources, integrity, and nonpartisanship. These values are not optional; they are essential to delivering fair and effective governance. Weakening protections and incentivizing at-will removals undercuts these values, discourages qualified individuals from pursuing public service, and ultimately harms every American community that depends on federal programs.

In summary, while improving accountability mechanisms is a valid objective, this proposal would not achieve it without inflicting profound damage to the very foundation of the civil service. Accountability must be pursued through fair, transparent processes that uphold merit system principles—not by opening the door to politicization, fear, and instability.

I urge OPM to withdraw this proposal and to instead invest in strengthening existing performance management systems, improving supervisory training, and reinforcing the nonpartisan, merit-based character of the civil service—hallmarks of a strong democracy and a government worthy of the people it serves.

Title: Comment from Luke Loranger
Comment:
I am writing to express strong opposition to any effort to reinstate Schedule F in the federal workforce. This proposal undermines foundational principles of merit-based civil service, invites undue political interference, and risks violating statutory and constitutional protections.

1. Undermines Merit System Protections

Schedule F represents a sweeping change to the civil service system that bypasses the competitive hiring process and allows for the removal of career professionals without cause. This contravenes the intent of the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act and longstanding statutory protections under Title 5 of the U.S. Code, which are designed to ensure that federal employment decisions are based on merit, not politics.

2. Weakens Due Process and Employee Rights

Federal employees in competitive service positions have a constitutionally recognized expectation of due process before being removed. Reassigning them to Schedule F without cause strips them of these protections, potentially violating the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause. The Supreme Court has affirmed that such employment can create a property interest (see Loudermill, 1985), which cannot be taken away arbitrarily.

3. Politicizes the Career Civil Service

Schedule F blurs the line between career professionals and political appointees. It risks creating a chilling effect in which federal employees may feel pressured to align with political views rather than carry out their duties objectively and in the public interest. This contradicts the spirit of the Hatch Act, which aims to preserve a nonpartisan civil service.

4. Violates the Administrative Procedure Act

The prior attempt to implement Schedule F was done with minimal transparency and justification. Reinstating it without a clear, evidence-based rationale may once again run afoul of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), which requires agencies to avoid arbitrary and capricious decision-making. The APA also requires agencies to consider the reliance interests of employees and the public trust.

5. Threatens Continuity of Government

Schedule F could lead to widespread firings and resignations of experienced public servants, jeopardizing the continuity and institutional knowledge necessary for effective governance—particularly during transitions of power or national emergencies.

Conclusion

The civil service exists to serve the American people, not any political party or administration. Schedule F threatens to erode that foundation. I urge the Administration and the Office of Personnel Management to reject any move to reinstate this classification and to uphold the integrity, independence, and professionalism of the federal workforce.

Conclusion

The proposed reclassification of federal positions into Schedule Policy/Career represents a significant departure from the principles that have long safeguarded the integrity and effectiveness of the federal workforce.
