Title: Comment from Dael Devenport
Comment:
I write in strong opposition to the proposed rule titled *"Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service." This initiative threatens to unravel the very foundation of merit-based governance that has guided our federal workforce for over a century.

To understand the dangers of this rule, we must look to history. In the late 19th century, the federal government was plagued by the *spoils system*, in which public jobs were handed out as political favors. This system culminated in tragedy with the assassination of President James A. Garfield in 1881 by a disgruntled office seeker. His death shocked the nation and galvanized support for reform.

In response, the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883 was enacted, creating a merit-based system designed to ensure that federal employees are hired and retained based on competence, not political loyalty. This act was a cornerstone of good governance, designed to insulate public servants from partisan politics and ensure continuity, professionalism, and accountability in government functions.

This proposed rule effectively seeks to return us to a modern-day spoils system by making it easier to hire and fire career civil servants based on subjective performance measures and, potentially, political considerations. The erosion of protections for career federal employees would not only undermine morale but also compromise the integrity and stability of the civil service.

Recent comments by political figures like Pete Hegseth, who advocates for the "deconstruction" of the administrative state, reveal the underlying motive behind this rule. It is not about improving government performance—it is about gaining control over a nonpartisan workforce that has historically served administrations of both parties with equal dedication.

This politicization could have severe national security consequences. If experienced civil servants feel pressure to conform to political agendas, they may be less likely to speak candidly, even in situations involving military operations. We've already seen the consequences of leaks and politically motivated decision-making on national defense due to placing unqualified individuals in leadership positions. Undermining the apolitical nature of the civil service could increase the risk of politically convenient but strategically disastrous choices being made—potentially putting American lives at risk. 

President Garfield’s legacy reminds us of the dangers of politicized public service. The Pendleton Act was passed not to protect bureaucrats, but to protect the American people from corrupt and incompetent governance. Weakening that legacy now would be a grave mistake.

I urge you to reject this proposed rule and uphold the merit principles that have served our nation for over 140 years.

Respectfully,  
Dael Devenport

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
This rule making has multiple legal and practical issues with moving forward.  The statutory language of the civil service reform act for the exception for policy making employees only applies to those not in the competitive service.  To extend this to employees that have been hired through the competitive service is a clear violation of the statute.  Congress clearly intended the Civil Service Reform Act’s exemption from protections to apply only to policy-making employees hired outside the competitive service.  OPM issued a rule making just last year in 2024 that protected civil service rights to workers and clarified this.  Now, less than a year later, the same agency is interpreting the exact same statute in a completely different way with this updated rule making.  Even if one accepts that there is ambiguity in the statutory language, in light of the Chevron decision, OPM as a federal agency does not have sole authority to determine interpretation of the statute.  Since the civil service reform act of 1978 was approved by congress and signed into law by the president at the time, the government has gone almost 50 years without every interpreting this to apply to employees hired through the competitive process.  There have been no changes to statutory language to justify stripping thousands of employees of their due process rights, and in the event of any sort of ambiguity, the due process rights of the individual must always take priority.  Rule makings such as this one underscore so many problems with the entire rule making process through the federal register - agencies pass rules as they see fit, impacting the public and stakeholders with drastic consequences, with no input or authority from congress.  If the amendments in this rule making are to move forward, congress would need to amend the statute to support it.  Without a change to the underlying statute, there is no legal authority to move forward with this rule making.  

Aside from the legal issues noted above, removing civil service protections of thousands of employees will have a chilling affect on the government's ability to function adequately and implement policy changes.  In the rule making, OPM states that these workers will have nothing to worry about as long as their performance is adequate and they do their jobs.  However, just recently tens of thousands of probationary employees were fired under the lie of "performance", with many having glowing performance reviews, to take advantage of their lack of merit systems protections during their probationary period.  The government has shown that they will have no problem firing employees for any reason they see fit if they do not have civil service protections.  The results therefore will be a lack of qualified individuals even applying for these policy related positions, as why would they jeopardize their careers for a small increase in pay.   The individuals already in these roles will likely seek out other non-policy roles within government, or take a demotion for job security.  Overall, this will lead to these roles being left unfilled, or being filled by employees without proper qualifications.

Title: Comment from Heriberto Leon
Comment: For nearly 150 years, federal law has sought to ensure civil service employees are hired and fired based on merit and are empowered to exercise independent judgment without fear of political retaliation. The proposed Schedule F rule severely undermines democracy and goes against the reforms established in 1871 and in later legislation by the U.S. Congress, which strongly repudiate the spoils system. We should be strengthening the merit system principles so that federal jobs are awarded based on qualifications and performance, rather than political connections. The proposed Schedule F rule does the opposite. The CSRA provides protections for federal employees from discrimination, political coercion, and other unfair personnel practices. Instead of strengthening those protections. The proposed Schedule F rule does away with those protections and makes employees who are upholding the law and the constitution more vulnerable to political retribution by politically-appointed officials. The CSRA includes provisions that protect federal employees who report waste, fraud, or abuse within the government. The proposed Schedule F rule does the opposite of strengthening those protections.The CSRA establishes a framework for federal labor-management relations, allowing employees to organize and bargain collectively through labor organizations. The proposed Schedule F rule undermines that framework by arbitrarily removing vast numbers of the civil service workforce from their agency's bargaining unit. There are legitimate concerns about the effectiveness, capacity, and accountability of civil service employees and many serious plans for reform. Those plans generally focus on how effectively the government serves the American people, including leadership and recruitment practices in the civil service, ethics, streamlining organizational charts, and encouraging innovation. Schedule F advocacy differs by explicitly promoting personal loyalty to the president as opposed to the principles of upholding the laws passed by Congress and the U.S. Constitution. Instead of putting forth this proposed rule, the administration should be focused on strengthening democracy and the constitution and should support the Saving the Civil Service Act, H.R.492/S.134.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I strongly object to introducing or reviving the "Schedule F" classification for federal workers. This plan jeopardizes the civil service system's foundation, which hires and promotes based on merit. Notably, President Trump has supported this merit-based approach in Executive Order 14173. By allowing for the potential dismissal of career employees without cause, Schedule F would undermine the principles established by the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which aimed to end the spoils system and ensure hiring and promotion based on merit.

 

Implementing Schedule F would lead to politicized employment decisions, contradicting the law's requirement for apolitical civil service. The broad and unclear criteria for Schedule F would also undermine due process rights, violating 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which demands cause and procedural safeguards for removing career employees. Depriving thousands of workers of these protections would harm accountability and might silence experts, ultimately reducing government efficiency.

 

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) has a statutory obligation to protect the merit system under federal law (5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq.). Introducing Schedule F would erode this duty by exposing career civil servants to inappropriate political pressure, ultimately weakening the consistency and professionalism of government programs.

The Schedule F initiative endangers fundamental principles of good governance, including an independent civil service and respect for the rule of law. Given these risks, I urge the administration and OPM to reject any efforts to move forward with this proposal.

Title: Comment from Emily Parker
Comment:
Public Comment Opposing OPM’s Proposed Rule to Create Schedule Policy/Career Positions

Docket No.: OPM-2025-0004
Submitted via FederalRegister.gov
Date: 25-April-2025

To Whom It Concerns:

I write to respectfully oppose the Office of Personnel Management’s proposed rule that would reintroduce a new “Schedule Policy/Career” classification, allowing career federal employees in “policy-influencing” positions to be removed without the procedural protections currently afforded under Chapters 43 and 75 of Title 5.

While I support the goal of fostering accountability and upholding high standards of performance and conduct within the federal workforce, I am deeply concerned that this proposal would significantly undermine long-standing merit system principles, reduce the stability and independence of the civil service, and risk politicizing critical federal positions.

1. Undermining Merit System Protections
The foundational principles of the federal civil service are based on merit, nonpartisanship, and protection from arbitrary removal. The proposed rule would effectively strip procedural due process protections from a broad category of career employees, even though they are hired and classified as nonpartisan. Employees removed from Schedule Policy/Career positions would not have access to the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) or other neutral adjudicative bodies. This lack of recourse opens the door to removals based on subjective or ideological grounds, rather than actual misconduct or poor performance.

This shift threatens the very merit system that has ensured an impartial and expert civil service for decades.

2. Chilling Effect on Professional Integrity
Federal career employees play a vital role in providing continuity, institutional knowledge, and apolitical expertise across administrations. The proposed rule would create a chilling effect on those tasked with giving professional, evidence-based advice—especially when that advice might diverge from the immediate political preferences of agency leadership.

By subjecting these employees to at-will dismissal, the rule disincentivizes honest analysis and dissenting viewpoints. This may lead to poorer policy outcomes, as decisions may no longer be guided by facts or long-term interests, but by political expediency.

3. Vague and Broad Definitions Create Risk of Abuse
The regulation relies on broad and subjective criteria for determining which positions are “policy-influencing.” Without clear, narrow definitions, this could lead to widespread reclassification of positions across agencies, further eroding civil service protections on an unprecedented scale. There is also no mechanism in place to ensure fair and consistent application of these changes, nor safeguards to prevent misuse for political or retaliatory purposes.

4. Historical Precedents and Bipartisan Rejection
Executive Order 13957, which previously attempted to implement similar changes through the creation of Schedule F, was swiftly rescinded by the following administration, recognizing its danger to the independence of the civil service. Bipartisan experts and civil society organizations raised serious alarm about the precedent it would set. Congress also considered legislative action to permanently bar such actions.

This proposal attempts to revive Schedule F under a new name, but with many of the same structural problems.

5. Better Alternatives Exist
If the concern is about improving performance management and accountability, there are more constructive, targeted reforms that can be implemented without dismantling critical due process protections. These might include enhancing supervisor training, reforming the appeals process to reduce delays, and increasing transparency in performance evaluations.

Conclusion
The proposed rule poses a serious threat to the integrity, stability, and nonpartisan character of the federal workforce. It would increase the risk of politicization, reduce accountability to the public, and weaken the safeguards that have historically protected our democracy from undue influence.

I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule and instead pursue reforms that reinforce—not erode—the principles of a professional, merit-based civil service.

Respectfully submitted,
Emily Parker
Atlanta, Georgia
ejwest01@yahoo.com

Title: Comment from Christopher Jennison
Comment:
I submit this comment in my personal capacity as a federal employment attorney and supervisor within an agency that operates under an independent personnel system. While not governed by Title 5, we closely follow its merit principles and adverse action framework.

I write in strong opposition to the proposed rule establishing a new “Schedule Policy/Career” category of at-will positions for career federal employees in so-called policy-influencing roles. This is a rebranded resurrection of Schedule F—designed to grant political leadership unchecked power to remove professionals for perceived disloyalty, often meaning anything short of uncritical compliance.

This is not about accountability. It is about control.

And while the current administration may believe it can wield this power selectively, the structural damage would outlast any presidency. Once career positions are stripped of protections, future administrations of either party can use this tool to retaliate or silence. That is not reform. That is sabotage dressed in regulatory language.

1. The Rule Misrepresents the Role of Career Civil Servants.

The rule implies that expressing legal or operational concerns justifies removal. That misrepresents what career employees are obligated to do: implement law ethically and within statutory bounds. Dissenting views and legal caution are not misconduct—they are hallmarks of professionalism. Removing those who offer it erodes both integrity and public trust.

2. The Rule Ignores Effective Accountability Mechanisms.

Federal agencies already have tools—probationary periods, performance improvement plans, and adverse action procedures—to address misconduct or poor performance. The issue is not lack of authority but inconsistent use. Many supervisors either don’t understand their tools or lack support to act. I’ve seen this firsthand.

The solution isn’t eliminating protections. It’s investing in manager training, support, and accountability. Reclassifying roles as at-will won’t fix poor supervision. It will worsen morale and reduce institutional trust.

3. The Rule Politicizes the Career Civil Service.

The “policy-influencing” definition is so broad it may capture professionals—attorneys, analysts, and others—who are expected to provide apolitical, expert advice. Removing their rights creates a loyalty test where alignment with leadership overshadows merit or objectivity.

Career employees are not saboteurs; they are the institutional memory and legal ballast of government. This rule would make them expendable when their expertise is needed most.

4. The Rule Undermines Merit Principles and Due Process.

Merit-based hiring, retention, and discipline are civil service pillars. The rule wrongly suggests at-will status enhances accountability. In fact, accountability requires documentation, clarity, and impartial review—not unchecked discretion.

The change may also raise constitutional due process concerns. Once protections are granted, employees may have a property interest in continued employment under Arnett v. Kennedy, 416 U.S. 134 (1974), and its progeny. Stripping those protections by regulation invites litigation and destabilizes the workforce.

Conclusion

Accountability and fairness are not mutually exclusive. Tools to address performance already exist. The path forward lies in empowering supervisors, not politicizing careers.

This proposal threatens longstanding civil service norms. If modernization were the true aim, we’d see investments in training and management—not a regulatory Trojan horse built to punish expertise.

Accordingly, I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety and refrain from future efforts to reclassify protected career positions inconsistent with merit system principles.

Christopher Jennison
Federal Employment Attorney and Supervisor
[Submitted in personal capacity; views are my own]

While enhancing performance and accountability within the civil service is a commendable goal, this proposed rule raises significant concerns regarding due process, employee rights, and the potential for politicization of the federal workforce.

Erosion of Due Process Protections

The proposed rule appears to streamline procedures for disciplinary actions and removals, potentially at the expense of established due process protections. Civil servants have long been afforded certain rights to ensure fair treatment, including the opportunity to respond to allegations and appeal decisions. Diluting these protections could lead to arbitrary or unjust terminations, undermining the principles of fairness and justice that are foundational to our civil service system.

Risk of Politicization

By making it easier to remove federal employees, the rule could inadvertently open the door to politically motivated dismissals. The merit-based civil service system was designed to insulate federal employment from political pressures, ensuring that decisions are made based on competence and performance rather than political affiliation. Weakening these safeguards threatens the neutrality and effectiveness of our federal agencies.

Impact on Morale and Recruitment

The potential for reduced job security and perceived fairness may adversely affect employee morale and hinder the recruitment and retention of talented individuals. A civil service perceived as unstable or subject to political whims may deter qualified candidates from public service, ultimately diminishing the government's capacity to serve the public effectively.

In conclusion, while the intent to improve civil service performance is laudable, the proposed rule's approach raises serious concerns that could undermine the integrity, neutrality, and effectiveness of our federal workforce. I urge the Office of Personnel Management to reconsider this proposal and engage in a more balanced approach that upholds due process and protects the merit-based principles of our civil service system.

Title: Comment from Anonymous

I am a current Federal employee, with more than three years of Federal service. I just want whoever is reading these comments to know that the discussion about how hard it is to fire poor performers is entirely correct. One of the things you realize when you become a Federal employee is that some employees have "retired in place." They are continuing to collect their full salary but aren't doing much to advance the mission and aren't putting in any noticeable effort. In some cases they just don't work at all. Something that was great about telework was these employees just stayed at home and didn't do anything. Now that everyone has to come into the office full-time you have to work with them directly. Their presence is very demotivating and demoralizing to everyone around them who is actually trying to get the job done. The civil service system had good intentions, but the way it works today it makes it almost impossible to fire someone for poor performance--even when it is obvious to everyone in the work unit that the employee is doing nothing. The supervisors know it. Everyone around them knows it. They know it. 

It is such a horrible waste of money. Agencies are paying the RIPs full salary to make the government LESS effective. If tight budgets mean we need to cut headcount, I wish agencies could selectively remove the RIPs instead of semi-random RIFs that don't really distinguish between high and low performers. A Fed who is trying to serve his country

Title: Comment from Shelby Smith-Janey
Comment:
Docket No.: OPM-2025-0004

Submitted via federalregister.gov

Date: April 25, 2025



To Whom It May Concern:



I write to respectfully oppose the Office of Personnel Management’s proposed rule that would reintroduce a new “Schedule Policy/Career” classification, allowing career federal employees in “policy-influencing” positions to be removed without the procedural protections currently afforded under Chapters 43 and 75 of Title 5.



While I support the goal of fostering accountability and upholding high standards of performance and conduct within the federal workforce, I am deeply concerned that this proposal would significantly undermine long-standing merit system principles, reduce the stability and independence of the civil service, and risk politicizing critical federal positions.



1. Undermining Merit System Protections

The foundational principles of the federal civil service are based on merit, nonpartisanship, and protection from arbitrary removal. The proposed rule would effectively strip procedural due process protections from a broad category of career employees, even though they are hired and classified as nonpartisan. Employees removed from Schedule Policy/Career positions would not have access to the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) or other neutral adjudicative bodies. This lack of recourse opens the door to removals based on subjective or ideological grounds, rather than actual misconduct or poor performance.



This shift threatens the very merit system that has ensured an impartial and expert civil service for decades.



2. Chilling Effect on Professional Integrity

Federal career employees play a vital role in providing continuity, institutional knowledge, and apolitical expertise across administrations. The proposed rule would create a chilling effect on those tasked with giving professional, evidence-based advice—especially when that advice might diverge from the immediate political preferences of agency leadership.



By subjecting these employees to at-will dismissal, the rule disincentivizes honest analysis and dissenting viewpoints. This may lead to poorer policy outcomes, as decisions may no longer be guided by facts or long-term interests, but by political expediency.



3. Vague and Broad Definitions Create Risk of Abuse

The regulation relies on broad and subjective criteria for determining which positions are “policy-influencing.” Without clear, narrow definitions, this could lead to widespread reclassification of positions across agencies, further eroding civil service protections on an unprecedented scale. There is also no mechanism in place to ensure fair and consistent application of these changes, nor safeguards to prevent misuse for political or retaliatory purposes.



4. Historical Precedents and Bipartisan Rejection

Executive Order 13957, which previously attempted to implement similar changes through the creation of Schedule F, was swiftly rescinded by the following administration, recognizing its danger to the independence of the civil service. Bipartisan experts and civil society organizations raised serious alarm about the precedent it would set. Congress also considered legislative action to permanently bar such actions.



This proposal attempts to revive Schedule F under a new name, but with many of the same structural problems.



5. Better Alternatives Exist

If the concern is about improving performance management and accountability, there are more constructive, targeted reforms that can be implemented without dismantling critical due process protections. These might include enhancing supervisor training, reforming the appeals process to reduce delays, and increasing transparency in performance evaluations.



Conclusion

The proposed rule poses a serious threat to the integrity, stability, and nonpartisan character of the federal workforce. It would increase the risk of politicization, reduce accountability to the public, and weaken the safeguards that have historically protected our democracy from undue influence.



I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule and instead pursue reforms that reinforce—not erode—the principles of a professional, merit-based civil service.



Respectfully submitted,

Shelby Smith-Janey

Registered Nurse

Chapel Hill, NC

Title: Comment from Haidee LeClair
Comment:
I am writing to comment on the proposed rule Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service OPM-2025-0004-0001.

This proposed regulation, Schedule F, under Docket ID OPM-2025-0004” and RIN 3206-AO80, raises profound concerns about the future of the Civil Service and its foundational principles. I strongly oppose the proposed move to reclassify all management officials from the competitive service to the excepted service, effectively making them fire-able at will. This shift represents a dangerous step backward towards a spoils system of patronage, undermining the merit-based principles that have long been the bedrock of a nonpartisan and professional public service.

The implications for a functioning democracy are deeply troubling. Replacing a system that prioritizes expertise and neutral competence with one susceptible to political favoritism would erode the stability and effectiveness of government agencies. Subjecting management officials to the constant threat of dismissal based on political allegiance, rather than performance, would inevitably lead to a chilling effect on their ability to provide candid and objective advice, potentially compromising the integrity of policy-making and implementation.

Furthermore, this proposed regulation appears to directly contravene the spirit and potentially the letter of the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (CSRA). The CSRA was enacted to strengthen the merit system principles, protect federal employees from political coercion, and ensure a professional and nonpartisan workforce. Moving an entire class of management officials – a potentially broad and ill-defined category – out of the competitive service circumvents the very protections the CSRA established. The Act outlines specific exceptions to the competitive service based on factors like the confidential or policy-determining nature of the position (5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(1)), but a blanket reclassification of all management officials seems to exceed these narrowly defined exceptions and undermines the fundamental structure of the competitive service as the default for federal employment.

Moreover, the proposed fireable at will status raises significant due process concerns under the Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution. While excepted service employees may have fewer statutory protections than those in the competitive service, the arbitrary removal of individuals from their positions, particularly after they have dedicated years of service and developed a reasonable expectation of continued employment within a merit-based system, could be challenged as a violation of procedural due process. The lack of clear standards for removal, coupled with the potential for politically motivated dismissals, fails to provide the fundamental fairness and protection against arbitrary government action that due process demands. As the Governing for Impact document highlights, the vagueness of the term management official and the lack of clear criteria for Schedule F classification exacerbate these due process concerns, leaving career professionals vulnerable to politically driven purges without adequate recourse.

The transition to a spoils system would obviously have detrimental long-term consequences. It would result in the following negative impacts:

* Replacing experienced managers with politically aligned individuals would disrupt agency operations, lead to a loss of institutional knowledge, and hinder the effective delivery of public services.
 * Agencies would become more susceptible to political pressure, potentially leading to decisions based on partisan agendas rather than evidence and the public interest.
* The instability and politicization of management positions would likely deter talented professionals from pursuing careers in government, leading to a decline in the quality of the civil service. 
* A perception that government jobs are awarded based on political loyalty, rather than merit, would further erode public trust in government institutions.

Ultimately, I strongly believe that the proposed Schedule F regulation represents a dangerous and ill-conceived policy that threatens to dismantle the merit-based principles of the Civil Service and return the nation to a discredited spoils system. It raises serious legal questions regarding compliance with the CSRA and fundamental due process rights (which are cited twice in the Constitution). I urge the Office of Personnel Management to reconsider this proposal and uphold the principles of a professional, nonpartisan, and merit-based public service that is essential for a well-functioning democracy.

Can you provide insight into what you think the economic impacts of this policy will be and clarify in what ways this will or will not improve performance or accountability? Also I would appreciate an in-depth exploration of why you think this change is needed and exactly how it does not violate existing laws.

Title: Comment from Clayton Phipps
Comment:
I strongly oppose the Office of Personnel Management’s (OPM) proposed rule, “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service” (Docket No. OPM-2025-0004), published April 23, 2025. The rule, creating “Schedule Policy/Career” to make career civil servants in policy-influencing roles at-will, is illegal, procedurally flawed, and harmful to the nation. It risks politicizing federal employees, exposing them to retribution for upholding federal laws, and undermining democratic governance. Below are my objections.

Legal Issues

Violation of the CSRA: The rule exceeds OPM’s authority under 5 U.S.C. §§ 3301-3302 by stripping career employees of protections under 5 U.S.C. § 7511. The Civil Service Reform Act (CSRA) guarantees notice and appeal rights, which Congress intended to ensure a merit-based civil service. Reclassifying employees to deny these protections requires legislative action, not agency rulemaking, as executive power is subject to statutory limits (United States v. Nixon, 418 U.S. 683, 1974).

Conflict with 2024 Rule: The Biden administration’s April 2024 rule (89 FR 25046) protects career employees’ CSRA rights even if moved to excepted service. OPM’s reversal fails to address reliance interests, violating APA standards for policy changes (F.C.C. v. Fox, 556 U.S. 502, 2009). Without justification, the rule is arbitrary and capricious.

Due Process: Removing MSPB appeal rights violates Fifth Amendment due process, as career employees have a property interest in their jobs (Cleveland Board of Education v. Loudermill, 470 U.S. 532, 1985). Vague criteria like “subverting presidential directives” risk arbitrary firings for lawful dissent.

Precedent: Schedule F (EO 13957, 2020), a similar policy, faced lawsuits (AFGE v. Trump) and was rescinded before rulings. Ongoing cases (NTEU v. Trump, 2025) suggest reclassification exceeds OPM’s authority. Post-Loper Bright (603 U.S. 369, 2024), courts won’t defer to OPM’s CSRA interpretation, increasing legal risk.

Procedural Flaws

The APA requires reasoned rulemaking (5 U.S.C. § 553(c)). OPM’s claim of supervisor difficulties lacks evidence tying issues to policy-influencing roles. It fails to define “policy-influencing” or consider alternatives like improving existing CSRA processes, violating APA standards (Motor Vehicle Manufacturers v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, 1983).

Adverse Effects

Politicization: Making career employees at-will turns them into political pawns, vulnerable to firing for refusing unlawful directives. The CSRA prevents patronage (Bush v. Lucas, 462 U.S. 367, 1983). Retribution for upholding laws—e.g., whistleblowing—erodes public trust.

Retribution Risk: Employees sworn to the Constitution, not the president, face punishment for lawful objections, as seen in first-term inspector general firings. This weakens accountability and the rule of law.

Loss of Expertise: Reclassifying thousands risks driving out experts, lowering morale, and deterring candid advice. This harms agencies’ ability to address complex issues like public health or national security.

Disrupted Governance: Mass firings disrupt continuity, delaying services like Social Security or disaster response, harming vulnerable Americans.

Democratic Harm: A nonpartisan civil service checks executive overreach. The rule concentrates presidential power, threatening democracy by making employees tools for partisan agendas.

Recommendations

OPM should withdraw the rule and use existing CSRA tools for performance issues. If proceeding, OPM must define roles clearly, preserve protections, and seek congressional approval.

Conclusion

The rule violates the CSRA, APA, and due process, risking a politicized civil service vulnerable to retribution. It undermines expertise, governance, and democracy. OPM must prioritize a merit-based workforce serving the public, not partisan interests. Thank you for considering this comment.

Fifth, the rule does not meet other requirements of Loper Bright. That decision requires agencies (and courts) to honor the best interpretation of statutory language. Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
The federal civil service system was created to ensure that government employees can perform their duties professionally, without fear of political retaliation. Civil service protections are essential for allowing experts to provide nonpartisan advice and uphold the public interest, even when that advice may be politically inconvenient. Removing these protections, particularly for so-called “policy-influencing” positions, would dangerously politicize what should be impartial work and undermine the integrity and effectiveness of government decision-making.

The proposed rule frames its changes as necessary to improve accountability, arguing that existing adverse action procedures make it too difficult to discipline or remove underperforming employees. However, this framing ignores that these procedures — including notice, opportunity to improve, and appeal to an independent body like the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) — serve an essential constitutional and democratic function: they protect against arbitrary or politically motivated firings. If managers find accountability processes burdensome, the answer is not to eliminate protections but to improve management practices, documentation, and use of the probationary period, which already offers agencies significant flexibility to remove unsuitable employees.

The proposal also misrepresents history by suggesting that reducing civil service protections would simply "restore" a baseline from before the 1960s. In reality, the modern civil service evolved because earlier systems led to widespread cronyism, inefficiency, and the infamous “spoils system,” where political loyalty, not competence, determined employment. Key reforms like the Pendleton Act of 1883 and the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 were necessary to professionalize government, promote merit, and ensure the stability and impartiality of public institutions. Rolling back these protections risks a return to politicized, unstable governance that history has already proven harmful.

The reclassification of career employees into a new "Schedule Policy/Career" would allow political appointees to remove technical experts — scientists, economists, attorneys, and others — without cause or independent review. This would have a chilling effect on the ability of civil servants to provide honest, evidence-based advice. Fear of retaliation would discourage candid analysis and critical thinking, promote groupthink, and reduce the overall quality of government decision-making. Over time, the government would lose vital institutional expertise and public trust, as agencies would come to be seen not as stewards of the public good, but as partisan tools.

Claims that civil servants frequently “insert partisan preferences” into their work are not supported by credible evidence. Genuine professional dissent — offering legal, scientific, or technical judgments that differ from political appointees’ preferences — is not partisanship. It is a core feature of professional public service. Civil service laws, the Hatch Act, and existing regulations already prohibit improper political activities and allow for discipline when necessary. Sweeping allegations of misconduct unfairly malign the career workforce and create a dangerous justification for purges based on political considerations rather than actual wrongdoing.

Importantly, the government already possesses substantial tools to manage employee misconduct and poor performance. The probationary period for new hires offers broad discretion for removal. Agencies can and do fire employees under Chapters 43 and 75 when they follow proper procedures. The low removal rate often reflects poor management practices — including failure to document issues — rather than any flaw in the legal framework. Weak or ineffective management should not be a justification for dismantling vital civil service protections that safeguard government neutrality and competence.

Far from undermining democracy, civil service protections strengthen it. They ensure that public institutions are staffed by professionals accountable to the law and the public interest, not to transient political agendas. Career employees provide continuity, institutional memory, and expertise that are critical for effective governance across administrations. Weakening their protections would centralize even more power in political appointees, erode transparency, encourage cronyism, and ultimately harm the quality and credibility of government. True accountability demands a professional civil service capable of independent judgment — not a workforce subject to political loyalty tests.

Title: Comment from Edward Mayes
Comment:
I submit this comment in strong support of the proposed rule titled “Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service.” This rule represents a timely and necessary update to the federal civil service system, better aligning government operations with the expectations of efficiency, accountability, and responsiveness demanded by the American people.

The federal workforce's critical role in administering laws, delivering essential services, and upholding the public interest has been deterred by the current system’s complex and lengthy procedures for addressing underperformance, ineptitude, and misconduct, significantly burdening supervisors and agency leaders. I can personally admit that managers are often disincentivized from taking timely action due to concerns of protracted and complicated processes that ultimately lead to inefficiencies.

The proposed rule balances employee rights with the government’s need to promulgate a high-performing workforce. Streamlining the procedures for removals and adverse actions restore managerial flexibility while preserving core due process protections. Poor performance and misconduct can finally be addressed promptly and fairly, rather than allowing issues to fester to the detriment of agency missions and workforce cohesion. Simplifying processes for performance-based actions and misconduct cases will empower agency leadership to more effectively manage personnel, foster a culture of excellence, and ensure accountability. 

These reforms are consistent with best practices in high-functioning private and public sector organizations, where management accountability and employee performance are closely tied to organizational success. In competitive environments, swift and fair personnel management is a basic expectation and the federal government should be held to the same high standards if our nation is expected to properly compete in the global market. Importantly, the proposed rule does not eliminate due process protections as employees facing adverse actions will continue to receive written notice, a meaningful opportunity to respond, and access to appeal mechanisms. These safeguards ensure that accountability measures remain fair and merit-based. What the rule accomplishes is the modernization of these procedures to make them more timely and effective, ensuring that government agencies can act decisively while maintaining fairness.

In an increasingly dynamic environment—where challenges such as cybersecurity threats, public health emergencies, technological innovation, and complex regulatory changes demand agility—the federal government must not be constrained by outdated or overly rigid personnel procedures. Modernizing performance management and adverse action processes will advance the public interest by promoting a more responsive, efficient, and effective government. These reforms will also help restore public trust by demonstrating that government agencies are committed to maintaining high standards of competence and accountability at every level.

The rule also supports long-term workforce sustainability. By ensuring that management can cultivate high-performing teams and promptly address performance gaps, the federal government will be better positioned to recruit and retain top talent. Skilled professionals are more likely to join and remain in a workforce where performance is valued, excellence is rewarded, and accountability is meaningful. I commend the Office of Personnel Management for advancing these necessary reforms, which reflect a thoughtful balance between maintaining employee protections and enabling effective agency management. The proposed changes recognize that promoting fairness and ensuring accountability are not mutually exclusive goals; rather, they are complementary imperatives that must work together to strengthen public service.

I urge OPM to finalize and implement the rule swiftly. Timely action is crucial to providing agencies with the tools they need to manage their workforces more effectively and deliver better outcomes for the American people. Furthermore, I encourage OPM to provide clear implementation guidance and robust training for agency leadership, human resources staff, and supervisors. Ensuring that the new procedures are applied fairly and consistently across the government will be key to the rule’s success. Special attention should be paid to preserving the merit system principles and safeguarding against any misuse of new authorities. By streamlining disciplinary and performance management processes while maintaining due process rights, it advances the cause of good governance, strengthens the federal workforce, and enhances public confidence in government institutions. I respectfully urge the Office of Personnel Management to adopt the rule as proposed.

Title: Comment from Charles Steindel
Comment:
RE: Public Comment in Response to Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service [Docket No. OPM–2025–0004]

I am writing to express my deep concern regarding the effort to reclassify specific federal positions, which would erode necessary protections for those serving within the federal statistical system and could transform positions which rely on specific expertise to political ones. The proposed rule, “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service,” would call into question the objectivity that both sides of the aisle rely on for our economic indicators, public health assessments, energy utilization and many other statistics. Federal statistical agencies are particularly vulnerable to the proposed rule:

Politicization: Schedule Policy/Career could lead to the politicization of the federal statistical workforce. Official federal statistics clearly influence public policy of all sorts: monetary, fiscal, regulatory, etc. A President could classify many statistical agency positions as Policy/Career. Then, for example, Bureau of Labor Statistics’ leaders could be fired for releasing or planning to release jobs or inflation statistics unfavorable to the President’s policy agenda. They might also face pressure to change methodologies or reveal pre-release information. By making it easier to remove employees if a President determines that they are interfering with his or her policies, it increases the potential for passivity or political loyalty to be prioritized over expertise and experience. Politicization has had dramatic consequences for statistical agencies and their leaders in other countries. 

Importance of Trust, Impartiality and Objectivity: Statistical agencies need professional autonomy to provide impartial, objective, reliable data. Professional autonomy is the ability to act independently from political or other undue external influence regarding its operations, such as data collection and analysis, staffing, and publications. Erosion of professional autonomy in the operations of statistical agencies would undermine their perceived or actual independence. 

Importance of Norms: Schedule Policy/Career would deprioritize and thus weaken the norms that uphold the ethical and professional standards that are critical to the success of statistical agencies. Senior leaders help craft, model and reinforce norms within their agencies and between their agencies and other parts of the government.  Examples include how agencies interact with staff, data users, data subjects, outside experts and host agencies. See Principles and Practices for a Federal Statistical Agency for examples of these critical norms. These norms reflect and go beyond the laws, rules, and policy directives that govern agencies’ operations.  

Erosion of Expertise, Loss of Institutional Memory and Increase of Turnover: These agencies rely on highly specialized professionals who possess unique technical expertise and long-term institutional memory. Statistical agencies stand to lose experts who see their career paths as less secure and merit-based than before. The loss of these experts or frequent turnover in key positions could disrupt agency operations, hinder long-term planning, undermine the agency's ability to fulfill its mission, and impair the quality and accuracy of the data.

Decreased Employee Morale and Productivity: The uncertainty and fear of arbitrary dismissal could negatively impact employee morale, leading to decreased productivity and difficulty in attracting and retaining top talent.

Importance of Modernization, Research, and Data Continuity: To support their missions, statistical agencies must invest in long-term efforts such as extensive research, critical modernization projects, and efforts to ensure data access and continuity. Schedule Policy/Career could subject to agencies to changing presidential priorities, increasing senior staff turnover and disrupting modernization efforts, measurement of trends, and meaningful research.

I am an economist who for roughly 50 years have depended upon the federal statistics.. It has always been of the utmost importance  to know that the staff producing the statistics work without political pressure. They have always been highly responsive to questions that I have had, and I know that their answers have nothing to do with any political allegiance they may have.

Schedule Policy/Career poses a significant threat to the effectiveness of federal statistical agencies. By undermining the principles of merit-based employment, Schedule Policy/Career could lead to politicization, loss of trust and expertise, decreased morale, and disruption of agency operations. On behalf of U.S. businesses, the American public, and policymakers I am speaking up to protect the trustworthiness of the federal statistics we all rely on.

Title: Comment from Vivian Lumbard
Comment:
As a retired federal employee who is currently seeing the effects of this Administration's partisanship and politicizing of the federal workforce, I cannot support Schedule F increasing the damage to our country's services and supports for its citizens. I've experienced first-hand the smaller shifts in management when an Administration changes, as well its negative effects on morale, work priorities, employee performance and accountability when there isn't sufficient oversight of upper management's zeal to prove its adherence to shifting winds. The American people deserve stable, non-partisan civil servants whose first loyalty is to the Constitution and the public--not an individual or party.

Therefore, I write in strong opposition of the proposed Office of Personnel Management Rule, Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service , RIN 3206–AO80, Docket ID: OPM–2025–0004. Providing well-considered protections to career civil servants, the current rules are excellent and limit the potential dangers posed by politicization. We need to consider reliable, trusted performance, accountability and a federal employee's ability to continue to do his/her job as required by statutes, not political favor, for Americans regardless of Administration changes.

The rule of law is the bedrock of our democracy, and our country is best served when that bedrock underlies the civil service--not the favor of the Administration. Transparency and accountability should be to the American people and not subject to the whims of whomever is the caretaker of the White House temporarily. Schedule F would dynamite huge holes into that bedrock, undermining institutional knowledge, experience, performance and accountability, thereby reducing the reliability and trustworthiness of services provided to the public. Retaining competent employees who are not only expected to do their best regardless of politics but who have the expectation of remaining buffeted from changes in Administrations is in the best interests of a merit-based system that serves the American people first, last and always.

Title: Comment from Patrick Murphy
Comment: I'm writing in opposition to the Office of Personnel Management's proposed rule (Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004). As a social worker who previously worked with Social Security (SSA) claimants navigating the application and appeals process, I'm deeply concerned by the OPM's proposal to change administrative law judges (ALJs) into at-will employees. Administrative law judges often need to make very complicated and nuanced decisions for SSA claimants and it's deeply concerning that they could be fired without cause, especially considering the Trump administration's repeated false claims that many SSA claimants are dead or defrauding the government. I have seen the opposite in my work. It is extremely difficult for claimants to get on Social Security and ALJ hearings are one of the only times that claimants are actually able to meet with the a government official who is making a determination about their case. It's concerning to me that Trump political appointees in the SSA could pressure ALJs to deny more claims or fire them because their making decisions based on the letter of the law, rather than political appointees specific ideas of who deserves and does not deserve SSA benefits. I think the independence of ALJs is going to be particularly important now that SSA has laid off of thousands of workers and is now going to likely rely even more heavily on AI to adjudicate disability claims. It's imperative for the fairness of the disability determination process that ALJs and other SSA employees can apply the rules and policies of the US federal government without worrying if their actions are going to cause them to be fired without cause. An effective government requires employees to be able to make decisions based on established law and policies, rather than the whims of Executive Branch.

Title: Comment from Robert Reiland
Comment:
Re: Office of Personnel Management, RIN 3206-AO80

The proposed changes are based on the assumption that there is a problem. I am not convinced the suggested problem exists. In fact the extensive history presented indicates that career civil servants were eventually provided with some reasonable degree of job protection that wasn’t initially there for their predecessors, suggesting that dismissals in the past were often arbitrary and destructive to the expertise of government agencies. But let us consider the possibility that to some degree the suggested problem exists. Then the solution shouldn’t be to remove all protections. That would be to go too far and present the possibility of keeping experts from reporting on peer reviewed studies in their fields out of fear of losing their jobs. 

We’ve already seen in the case of probationary employees that many had been dismissed from their positions only to be asked to return later once it was realized that many of them were essential to the work of their agencies. This was chaotic. Not all of these employees were easily contacted and many didn’t want to return. Making career civil servants into the equivalent of probationary employees could easily repeat this problem.

Telling career civil servants that they have suddenly become “at will” employees sends a strong message that they are not trusted, and this is sure to reduce motivation and the quality of their work. This is counterproductive to the improvement in efficiency of government agencies that we are told is a goal of the current administration.

As can be seen, I find the given rationales for the proposed changes to lack good judgement and I oppose the changes.

On Due Process and Employee Protections

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I write in strong opposition to the proposed rule titled "Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service." While I support the principle of ensuring an efficient and high-performing federal workforce, this proposed rule would undermine the fundamental protections of the merit-based civil service system, politicize federal employment, and threaten the independence and stability critical to the effective operation of our government.

1. Politicization of the Civil Service:
The proposed rule appears to resurrect and expand concepts from the previously rescinded "Schedule F" Executive Order, enabling broad reclassification of career civil servants into categories that would strip them of long-established merit system protections. This shift opens the door to politically motivated hiring and firing, undermining the neutrality of the federal workforce and threatening the continuity and institutional knowledge necessary for good governance.

2. Erosion of Merit Principles and Due Process:
Federal employees are selected and retained based on merit to ensure they serve the public impartially. By making it easier to remove employees outside traditional due process protections, the rule weakens vital safeguards against political retaliation, favoritism, and cronyism. Due process rights are not obstacles but essential components of an accountable and fair government.

3. Harm to Recruitment and Retention:
The prospect of losing civil service protections would make federal employment less attractive to skilled professionals. It would destabilize workforce morale, hinder recruitment of top talent, and exacerbate existing challenges with retention, especially in specialized fields such as cybersecurity, healthcare, and environmental science.

4. No Demonstrated Need for Drastic Changes:
OPM and federal agencies already possess robust mechanisms for managing employee performance and addressing misconduct. The Government Accountability Office (GAO) and other oversight bodies have consistently found that the problems cited to justify sweeping changes like these are anecdotal and not systemic. Instead of improving performance, this rule could introduce chaos, uncertainty, and inefficiency.

5. Threat to Continuity of Government Operations:
If implemented, the rule could lead to mass turnover during presidential transitions or changes in administration, weakening the federal government's ability to provide uninterrupted services to the American people. Stability in federal operations is a national interest that must be preserved.

Conclusion:
Rather than advancing performance and accountability, this proposed rule would inject partisanship into the civil service, erode merit principles, diminish federal workforce expertise, and ultimately harm the American public. I respectfully urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule in favor of strengthening, not weakening, the merit-based foundation of our civil service.

Title: Comment from Stacy White
Comment:
I am a third generation public employee; I followed in the footsteps of my family and have been a public servant for my entire career.  Public employees do not serve the President; by our very title; it cannot be clearer that we are servants of the public. Allowing this to move forward, for starters, is a violation of the Hatch Act.  The entire reason for the Hatch Act was to preserve the impartiality of our service because, as noted, we do not serve a political party-we serve the American public.  Allowing this regulation to move forward sets the stage for rewarding political favoritism, rather than the merit system we have now, which only rewards those who are high performers and do the job they were hired to do impartially and without any political motivations.

Not only for moral and ethical reasons do I completely disagree with this proposal; it would also violate the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978.   

Aside from the legal issues, it is wrong to break contract, which is truly what would be happening with the Schedule F proposal.    Federal employees have worked our entire career under a contract that provisioned certain guarantees, and in return we have made an oath to the public.   It is well-documented that we receive lower salaries working in the public sector over private.  Even health care benefits in federal service cost me three times what I paid working for state agencies.  The most dramatic violation though, here, is that a civil servant may not be stripped of job protections once they are in place-such as at will firings.  This would be a Constitutionally-prohibited act, in violation of the Due Process Clause.  Nobody-including the President-has the authority to strip federal workers from these job protections and fire at will-it would be depriving a person of life, liberty or property without due process.  There is also legal precedent to support my position:  Roth v. Brownell established in the 1950’s that what Schedule F is attempting to do is prohibited.

Are there “bad” public employees?  Of course there are.  But punishing all to detect a select few is wrong.  We are human beings; we have families.  I can think of many better methods of weeding out fraud, waste and abuse than the methods that have been utilized in the past few months.  

It’s so ironic that I sit here writing this.  I actually voted for Donald Trump. This, and other activity that has been taking place is  not only concerning, but it is alarming that an Act that so clearly violates not only a number of Acts, but the very doctrine that our entire country was established on.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Office of Personnel Management
5 CFR Parts 210, 212, 213, 302, 432, 451, and 752
[Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004]
RIN 3206-AO80

Regarding the proposed rule to reclassify policy-influencing career positions to Schedule Policy/Career 'at-will' status, I have significant concerns about the justifications presented:

 * Difficulty Removing Employees: While addressing poor performance and misconduct is important, the current adverse action procedures include mechanisms for removal. The issue may lie in inconsistent application or insufficient training for supervisors, rather than a fundamental flaw requiring the elimination of due process for an entire class of employees. Eliminating appeal rights increases the risk of arbitrary or politically motivated dismissals.
 
 * Undermining Presidential Directives: The claim that 'at-will' status is needed to prevent intentional subversion of Presidential directives overlooks existing accountability measures. Title: Comment from Clint Levee
Comment:
As a career civil servant specializing in water resources management, I feel compelled to express deep concern about the proposed Schedule F rule. While framed as an administrative reform, Schedule F would undermine the integrity, independence, and effectiveness of the federal workforce. Nowhere would the damage be more profound than in critical fields like water management, where scientific expertise, continuity, and nonpartisan service are essential.

Federal employees across agencies like the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), the Bureau of Reclamation, and the Army Corps of Engineers are responsible for safeguarding drinking water, managing infrastructure, responding to droughts and floods, and protecting ecosystems. These missions demand technical excellence, long-term planning, and independence from political pressure.

Schedule F would strip civil servants of due process protections, making them effectively "at-will" employees subject to political loyalty tests. This change would open the door to politicizing vital scientific and technical roles — not only undermining sound decision-making but exposing millions of Americans to increased risks related to water safety, public health, and infrastructure reliability.

We have already seen the dangers when political interference compromises science: delayed responses to PFAS contamination, slow action on lead crises like Flint, and inadequate flood planning in the face of rising climate risks. Career civil servants must be free to provide honest, evidence-based advice, even when inconvenient. Politicizing their roles would lead to worse outcomes, delayed disaster responses, and avoidable harm to communities.

Water management requires institutional memory built over decades. Understanding regional hydrology, dam operations, floodplain management, groundwater systems, and interstate compacts like those governing the Colorado River is not something a politically appointed replacement can acquire quickly. Mass dismissals or politicized hiring would result in the loss of invaluable knowledge just when climate-driven water challenges are escalating.

Moreover, Schedule F would severely hinder recruitment and retention. Talented engineers, scientists, and policy experts — already difficult to recruit into public service — would think twice before entering a workforce where their jobs could hinge on politics rather than professional performance. We risk hollowing out our technical capacity precisely when our nation faces mounting threats: megadroughts, catastrophic flooding, aging water infrastructure, and chemical contamination.

Public trust in government depends on the perception that civil servants act in the public’s interest, guided by law and science, not partisanship. Schedule F would erode that trust, slow transparency, and weaken agency responsiveness to both Congress and the public. In water resources management — where fair, science-based governance is crucial to balancing urban, agricultural, tribal, and environmental needs — this loss of trust could have disastrous consequences.

Protecting America's water future demands expertise, stability, and independence. Federal water managers must be empowered to make decisions based on hydrologic science, environmental law, and engineering best practices, not political pressure. The Clean Water Act, the Safe Drinking Water Act, and major infrastructure initiatives like the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law all depend on an impartial civil service to be effectively implemented.

As someone who has devoted a career to serving the American people, I urge policymakers to recognize the grave risks Schedule F poses — not just to federal workers, but to public health, national security, and environmental stewardship. Political loyalty should never replace technical competence and evidence-based governance, especially when it comes to managing water, our most vital resource.

Our infrastructure, ecosystems, communities, and future generations depend on maintaining a professional, protected, and nonpartisan civil service. I respectfully ask you to withdraw the proposed Schedule F rule and uphold the merit-based system that has served our country well for over a century.

Our future — quite literally — flows from it.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I. Introduction

This memorandum outlines the legal concerns associated with the reinstatement or implementation of "Schedule F," a former federal employment classification created by Executive Order 13957 (October 2020). The proposed classification, which sought to reclassify certain policy-related federal positions as exempt from competitive service protections, raises significant constitutional, statutory, and administrative law issues.

As the agency charged with overseeing the federal civil service system and upholding the merit principles codified in law, the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) has both a legal and institutional obligation to oppose Schedule F on the grounds set forth below.
II. Legal Grounds for Opposition
1. Statutory Violation of the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978

Schedule F contravenes the statutory framework established by the Civil Service Reform Act (5 U.S.C. §§ 2101–2301), which affirms that federal employment must be based on merit and protected from political interference.

    Violation of Merit System Principles: 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(1) requires hiring and advancement decisions to be based solely on ability, knowledge, and skills. Schedule F undermines this by permitting removals based on political or subjective criteria.

    Departure from Congressional Intent: The sweeping reclassification of policy-influencing roles as excepted service positions—without competitive protections—circumvents Congress’s deliberate protections for civil servants.

2. Constitutional Due Process Concerns

Long-serving federal employees often possess a constitutionally protected property interest in their continued employment. By stripping such employees of due process protections, including notice and an opportunity to be heard, Schedule F may violate the Fifth Amendment.

    Precedent: Courts have recognized due process rights for federal employees under existing civil service frameworks (e.g., Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 470 U.S. 532 (1985)).

    Impact: Summary removals enabled under Schedule F would likely prompt constitutional litigation challenging the deprivation of protected interests without appropriate procedural safeguards.

3. Executive Overreach and Lack of Statutory Authority

The President’s authority to manage executive personnel is not unlimited and must operate within statutory constraints established by Congress. Schedule F appears to exceed that authority by altering classification and tenure protections created by law.

    Ultra Vires Action: Executive orders cannot lawfully override statutory employee protections absent congressional authorization.

    Violation of Non-Delegation Principles: Congress did not delegate to the President the power to unilaterally redefine large categories of federal employment outside the competitive service framework.

4. Arbitrary and Capricious Action under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA)

Actions taken to implement or enforce Schedule F could be subject to challenge under the APA (5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A)) as arbitrary, capricious, or not in accordance with law.

    No Factual Basis: The executive order lacked supporting data or agency findings justifying the need for reclassification or the scope of affected positions.

    Failure to Follow Rulemaking Procedures: Any major policy shift affecting federal employment standards would require public notice, opportunity for comment, and a reasoned explanation—none of which Schedule F provided.

5. Politicization of the Civil Service in Contravention of the Hatch Act’s Purpose

Although Schedule F does not amend the Hatch Act directly, it undermines its core purpose—to ensure a politically neutral civil service.

    Increased Risk of Political Interference: Removing protections for policy-related roles opens the door to politically motivated hiring and firing, which Congress has long sought to prevent.

    Conflict with Existing Ethics Frameworks: The reclassification weakens guardrails established by the Hatch Act and federal ethics rules designed to promote impartial governance.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I. Purpose

This memorandum outlines the Office of Personnel Management’s legal, policy, and operational objections to the potential reinstatement of Schedule F, a classification created under Executive Order 13957 (October 2020). This classification would reassign certain policy-related positions to the excepted service, eliminating critical civil service protections and enabling removals based on political considerations.
II. Background

Schedule F was intended to apply to federal employees in “confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating” roles. The order effectively exempted these employees from competitive service protections, including due process rights and appeal mechanisms. Although the executive order was revoked in January 2021, its potential reinstatement poses ongoing legal and operational risks to the integrity of the federal workforce.
III. Legal and Policy Concerns
1. Violation of Civil Service Statutes

Schedule F contradicts the principles codified in the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (5 U.S.C. §§ 2101–2301), which mandates merit-based hiring and protection from political influence. The broad scope of Schedule F would allow partisan dismissals and discourage career public service.
2. Due Process and Constitutional Issues

Federal employees reclassified under Schedule F could be removed without cause or meaningful review, raising significant due process concerns under the Fifth Amendment. Long-serving federal workers have a recognized property interest in their employment, and mass reclassification without individualized process would likely trigger legal challenges.
3. Threat to Nonpartisan Civil Service

Schedule F undermines the foundational principle of a politically neutral civil service. The Hatch Act and related statutes limit partisan activity for good reason. Schedule F would blur these boundaries by exposing career roles to political loyalty tests and undermining trust in impartial governance.
4. Risk of Arbitrary Agency Action

Implementation of Schedule F could be challenged under the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. § 706), as the reclassification of employees and any subsequent terminations would likely be deemed arbitrary, capricious, and lacking evidentiary support.
5. Chilling Effect on Ethics and Whistleblower Protections

Without job security, employees may be deterred from reporting misconduct or pushing back against unethical directives. This directly conflicts with the goals of the Whistleblower Protection Act and OPM’s responsibility to foster a culture of ethical accountability.
IV. Conclusion and Recommendation

Schedule F poses significant legal, constitutional, and institutional risks to the functioning of the federal government. It undermines the merit system, weakens civil service protections, and threatens the nonpartisan character of the workforce. For these reasons, OPM strongly recommends continued opposition to any effort to reinstate Schedule F and supports legislation or administrative action to codify its prohibition.

This document is illegal according to laws and regulations. In addition, OPM has NO authority to implement this. If this illegal document is implemented there are legal consequences.

1. Violation of Due Process Rights Under the Fifth Amendment
The rule would strip federal employees in policy-influencing positions of their statutory and constitutional due process protections, including notice, a hearing, and the right to appeal adverse actions to the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB). The Supreme Court has held that federal employees have a property interest in their employment under the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment. SeeCleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 470 U.S. 532 (1985). The proposed rule unlawfully deprives employees of these protections without adequate justification.
2. Contravention of the Civil Service Reform Act (CSRA) of 1978
The CSRA established a comprehensive framework for federal employee protections, including adverse action procedures under 5 U.S.C. §§ 4303 (performance-based actions) and 7511-7513 (adverse actions). The proposed rule attempts to circumvent these statutory protections by reclassifying career positions into an "excepted service" category without congressional authorization. Congress did not intend for the President or OPM to unilaterally remove these protections for career employees. See United States v. Fausto, 484 U.S. 439 (1988) (emphasizing the CSRA’s exclusive remedial scheme).
3. Exceeds OPM’s Statutory Authority
OPM lacks the authority to categorically exclude employees from chapter 43 and 75 protections. While 5 U.S.C. § 7511(b)(2) allows exemptions for "confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating" positions, this provision was historically applied narrowly to political appointees (e.g., Schedule C). Extending it to career employees contradicts the CSRA’s merit system principles (5 U.S.C. § 2301) and OPM’s own prior interpretations.
4. Undermines Merit System Principles
The rule violates the foundational merit system principles codified in 5 U.S.C. § 2301, including:
• Fair and equitable treatment (§ 2301(b)(2));
• Protection against arbitrary action (§ 2301(b)(8));
• Retention based on performance (§ 2301(b)(6)). By converting career positions into at-will roles, the rule invites politicization and undermines the nonpartisan civil service. 
Allowing removals without cause, contrary to 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(6) (employees should be retained or removed based on performance).
Encouraging political loyalty tests, despite claims to the contrary, which violates 5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(1) (prohibiting political coercion).
5. Unlawful Delegation of Legislative Authority
Congress, not the President or OPM, has the sole authority to determine the scope of federal employee protections. The proposed rule effectively rewrites the CSRA without congressional approval, violating the separation of powers. See INS v. Chadha, 462 U.S. 919 (1983).
6. Unconstitutional Due Process Violations (Fifth Amendment)
The rule eliminates notice, hearing rights, and MSPB appeals for employees moved into Schedule Policy/Career, violating their property interest in continued employment.

Conclusion
The proposed rule is an unlawful overreach that disregards constitutional due process, statutory protections under the CSRA, and merit system principles. OPM should withdraw the rule and preserve the existing civil service framework.

Title: Comment from Justin Novak

Implementing Schedule F runs counter to this mission and subjects career professionals to undue political pressure, jeopardizing the stability and integrity of federal programs across administrations.

Title: Comment from Betty Boldin
Comment:
I oppose the implementation or revival of the “Schedule F” classification for federal employees. This proposal threatens the merit-based civil service system that has underpinned a professional, nonpartisan federal workforce for over a century.

First and foremost, the creation of Schedule F directly undermines the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which was enacted to combat the spoils system and establish a merit-based hiring process for federal employees. By allowing a broad swath of career civil servants—particularly those involved in policy-making or analysis—to be reclassified and potentially terminated without cause, Schedule F opens the door to politically motivated hiring and firing. This is antithetical to the principle of an apolitical civil service enshrined in 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8), which mandates that federal employment decisions be based on merit and free from political influence.

Moreover, the vague and sweeping criteria for inclusion in Schedule F violate the due process protections guaranteed by 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which requires cause and procedural safeguards for the removal of career federal employees. Stripping thousands of workers of these protections not only weakens accountability but also risks chilling expert advice and dissent within agencies—undermining the very effectiveness of government operations.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is also bound by 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to support the merit system principles. Implementing Schedule F contradicts this statutory mission and places undue political pressure on career professionals, compromising the integrity and continuity of federal programs across administrations.

In conclusion, the Schedule F proposal poses a grave threat to the foundational principles of good governance, civil service independence, and the rule of law. I urge the administration and OPM to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement or revive this dangerous classification.
