Title: Comment from Ethan LaPlante
Comment:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed regulation that would reduce job protections for career federal civil servants and move toward an at-will employment model. This proposal undermines the foundational principles of the merit-based civil service system and poses significant risks to the integrity, independence, and effectiveness of the federal workforce.

Career public servants are not political appointees. Their duty is to implement the laws of the United States in accordance with established policy, regulations, and science—not to sway with shifting political winds or serve partisan agendas. The merit system was designed precisely to ensure that government work is conducted by professionals who are hired and retained based on competence, not ideology or loyalty to a particular administration.

Stripping away job protections for civil servants creates an atmosphere of fear and instability. It invites the risk that employees will be disciplined or removed not for poor performance, but for offering expert advice, upholding inconvenient facts, or resisting improper political pressure. This is especially dangerous in fields like public land management, environmental protection, and public health, where the work often involves balancing scientific evidence, public opinion, legal mandates, and long-term stewardship over short-term interests.

I have seen firsthand the extraordinary dedication, professionalism, and resilience of career civil servants who serve across administrations with integrity and commitment. These individuals are not obstacles to efficiency—they are the backbone of effective governance.

If the intent of this rule is to address rare cases of poor performance, that can and should be done within the framework of the current merit-based system, not by dismantling it altogether.

I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed regulation and reaffirm its commitment to a nonpartisan, expert federal workforce. The American people deserve public servants who are empowered to serve the public good—not intimidated into silence or compliance by the threat of arbitrary dismissal.

Title: Comment from Tara Halt
Comment:
I am writing to express concern over several aspects of the proposed rule, which, while presented as a means to enhance performance and accountability, raises significant issues that may undermine the merit-based principles of the civil service and erode employee protections.

First, the rule appears to significantly weaken procedural safeguards for federal employees, particularly regarding adverse actions such as suspensions and removals. By reducing the time employees have to respond to proposed discipline and limiting the ability of agencies to consider mitigating factors, the rule increases the risk of arbitrary or politically motivated terminations. These changes may discourage whistleblowing and chill dissent, ultimately harming the public interest.

Second, the rule seeks to accelerate performance-based removals, but it does so at the cost of due process. The proposed changes to performance improvement plans (PIPs), including shorter durations and fewer requirements for agency support, would make it easier to remove employees without giving them a meaningful opportunity to improve. This undermines the foundational merit system principle that employees should be retained based on their performance, not expediency.

Third, the rule may incentivize a punitive management culture rather than one that supports development and continuous improvement. The civil service functions best when employees are empowered to improve and when management has the tools to address underperformance fairly and constructively—not when discipline is used as a first resort.

Finally, the rule raises constitutional and legal questions related to the scope of executive authority over the career civil service. The cumulative effect of the proposed changes risks politicizing the federal workforce, which is intended to operate independently of partisan influence.

For these reasons, I urge the Office of Personnel Management to reconsider this proposed rule and engage in further consultation with stakeholders, including unions, employee groups, and public administration experts. A transparent, merit-based, and accountable civil service is essential to good governance and public trust.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I respectfully submit this comment in response to the Office of Personnel Management’s (OPM) proposed rule entitled “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service.” While I recognize and support the goal of ensuring a high-performing and accountable federal workforce, I have significant concerns regarding the creation of the new Schedule Policy/Career classification and the accompanying removal of long-standing due process protections.
The proposed rule seeks to reclassify certain career positions—those with influence over policy implementation—into an “at-will” employment category, stripping these roles of adverse action procedures and appeal rights provided under 5 U.S.C. Chapter 75. This raises serious concerns about the legality and constitutionality of the proposed changes. The protections offered by Chapter 75 are not discretionary; they are codified by Congress and cannot be set aside by administrative rulemaking. The reclassification of these roles as “at-will” appears to be a functional end-run around these statutory guarantees.
This change also implicates due process protections under the Fifth Amendment. Career federal employees typically have a property interest in continued employment, and courts have consistently held that such an interest cannot be extinguished without due process of law. Eliminating procedural safeguards such as notice, a meaningful opportunity to respond, and appeal mechanisms not only undermines employee rights but also increases the risk of arbitrary, retaliatory, or politically motivated dismissals. The Constitution does not permit the government to avoid due process by unilaterally reclassifying protected positions into unprotected ones.
Beyond the legal concerns, the rule undermines the merit-based, politically neutral principles foundational to the U.S. civil service. 5 U.S.C. §§ 2301 and 2302 enshrine the core values of impartiality, competence, and protection from political coercion. Allowing policy-influencing employees to be removed without cause risks returning the civil service to a spoils system model, where employment depends on political alignment rather than skill, professionalism, or adherence to the law. This could create a chilling effect on employees’ willingness to provide candid, objective advice to agency leaders, or to act as whistleblowers when they observe legal or ethical violations.
I am also concerned that the proposed rule mirrors the previously rescinded Schedule F Executive Order issued in 2020. That order was widely condemned across the political spectrum and withdrawn due to its potential to destabilize the federal workforce, politicize decision-making, and deter qualified professionals from public service. The present proposal appears to revive many of the same structural features under a new name, without addressing the fundamental risks that led to Schedule F’s rejection.
I agree with OPM’s view that agencies should have tools to address poor performance and misconduct, those tools already exist within the current legal framework. For example, Chapter 75 allows for removal of employees for cause, and streamlined removal processes have been developed in specific contexts (e.g., for VA employees under 38 U.S.C. § 714). Instead of undermining employee rights, OPM should focus on training supervisors in how to effectively use existing accountability mechanisms.
1. Withdraw or substantially revise the proposed rule to ensure compliance with existing statutory due process protections.
2. Clarify and narrow the definition of “policy-influencing” positions to avoid overbroad application and abuse.
3. Provide alternative reforms focused on improving performance management and supervisor accountability within the current legal framework.
4. Engage in further consultation with stakeholders, including federal employee unions, ethics experts, and administrative law scholars.
While  I support efforts to ensure a responsive and high-performing civil service, I believe this proposed rule threatens core principles of democratic governance, legal accountability, and civil service professionalism. I urge OPM to reconsider or revise the rule to preserve the balance between executive responsiveness and employee rights that has long served our nation well.

This proposal is deeply concerning for several key reasons:

Erosion of Nonpartisan Public Service: The merit-based civil service system ensures that federal employees are hired and retained based on their skills, experience, and dedication to public service. This protects the integrity of government operations by ensuring that decisions are informed by expertise and evidence, not political ideology. Weakening civil service protections opens the door to political interference in critical areas such as public health, environmental protection, disaster response, and national security. The public deserves a federal workforce that is independent and committed to serving the nation, not political agendas.

Impact on Agency Performance and Retention: Making it easier to remove federal employees without established due process protections would destabilize the workforce. It would create a culture of fear that discourages open dialogue and constructive feedback within agencies. Talented professionals may choose to leave government service, and others may be discouraged from joining altogether. This loss of experience and institutional knowledge would reduce the effectiveness and responsiveness of federal agencies at a time when strong public institutions are more important than ever.

Lack of Transparency and Oversight: The proposed rule would enable sweeping changes to employee classifications and disciplinary procedures without sufficient congressional or public oversight. Such actions could be used to target employees for political reasons, especially those who speak truthfully about inconvenient or unpopular facts. This lack of transparency contradicts principles of good governance and accountability.

Risk to Public Interest and Trust: Federal employees take an oath to serve the Constitution and the American people. Undermining their job protections for perceived increases in responsiveness or flexibility would erode their ability to offer honest, expert advice. This would ultimately harm the public, particularly in times of crisis when effective and impartial government action is most critical.

In summary, this proposed rule would not improve performance or accountability in a meaningful way. Instead, it threatens to politicize the civil service, weaken federal institutions, and discourage public service. It risks long-term damage to government effectiveness and to the public’s trust in its institutions. I urge OPM to withdraw this proposal and instead focus on policies that strengthen the professionalism, independence, and integrity of the civil service.

Comment:
Comment on Proposed Rule: Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service

Introduction and Position:
I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed rule change titled “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service” (Federal Register, April 2025). I believe this rule threatens the foundational principles of the United States government by politicizing career civil service positions that should remain independent and loyal to the Constitution — not to any political party or leader.

Summary of Objection:
This proposed rule is a transparent attempt to purge experienced, nonpartisan federal employees and replace them with political loyalists. Doing so would fundamentally undermine the stability, neutrality, and expertise of the federal workforce, weaken the system of checks and balances, and erode public trust in government institutions.

Detailed Arguments:

Constitutional and Legal Concerns:
Federal employees swear an oath to uphold the Constitution — not to serve any political leader. Reclassifying career employees into political appointees undermines this principle and risks turning the civil service into a tool of partisan loyalty rather than constitutional governance.

Loss of Experience and Expertise:
Career civil servants provide critical institutional memory, subject matter expertise, and continuity between administrations. Replacing them with short-term political appointees could significantly harm the quality of government services and policymaking.

Threat to Democratic Institutions:
The civil service was intentionally designed to be separate from political influence. Politicizing the workforce weakens independent agency operations and enables executive overreach, concentrating too much power in the hands of a single administration.

Erosion of Public Trust:
The American public depends on agencies to operate fairly and competently, regardless of which political party is in power. If agencies are seen as political arms of an administration, public faith in their legitimacy will collapse.

Conclusion and Requested Action:
For these reasons, I urge the Office of Personnel Management to immediately withdraw this proposed rule. It poses a grave risk to the integrity of the U.S. civil service and to the constitutional system of government designed to serve all Americans, not just political loyalists.

Part 1
Regarding the proposed rule to reclassify policy-influencing career positions to Schedule Policy/Career ‘at-will’ status, I have significant concerns about the justifications presented:
•  Difficulty Removing Employees: While addressing poor performance and misconduct is important, the current adverse action procedures include mechanisms for removal. The issue may lie in inconsistent application or insufficient training for supervisors, rather than a fundamental flaw requiring the elimination of due process for an entire class of employees. Eliminating appeal rights increases the risk of arbitrary or politically motivated dismissals.

•  Undermining Presidential Directives: The claim that ‘at-will’ status is needed to prevent intentional subversion of Presidential directives overlooks existing accountability measures. Presidential appointees are in place to oversee policy implementation and ensure alignment. Furthermore, federal employees take an oath to uphold the Constitution and execute the laws, which provides a framework for accountability that doesn’t necessitate stripping career employees of their due process rights.
•  Impact on Nonpartisan Workforce: While these positions are stated to remain career and filled nonpartisanly, the ‘at-will’ nature inherently introduces the risk of politicization. The lack of appeal rights could make these roles more susceptible to political influence and less attractive to highly qualified, nonpartisan professionals who value job security based on merit and performance.

Title: Comment from Nick Coyle
Comment:
To Whom It May Concern:

I’m writing to strongly oppose the proposed rule OPM-2025-0004-0001, which introduces a new “Schedule F-style” employment category under the name “Schedule Policy/Career.” This rule threatens the foundational integrity of the U.S. civil service by reclassifying tens of thousands of career federal employees into positions that would no longer be protected by merit-based hiring and firing rules.

This matters deeply to me because I believe government policy should be implemented by professionals—scientists, analysts, public health experts, and agency staff—who are qualified and hired based on skill and experience, not political loyalty. When you create a path to fire career employees without cause and fill those roles with people whose main qualification is alignment with the president’s agenda, you open the door to politicized governance. That should concern every American, no matter their politics.

The rule echoes the earlier Schedule F proposal from 2020, which independent oversight bodies and civil service advocates overwhelmingly rejected. Back then, the Office of Management and Budget had already started preparing lists of employees for removal (GAO-21-524). This wasn’t theoretical—it was underway before the rule was revoked. What’s being proposed now is functionally the same mechanism, with a new name and broader reach.

OPM’s estimate that over 50,000 roles could be reclassified under this rule is staggering. That number includes people doing real work—administering Social Security benefits, managing disaster relief logistics, enforcing environmental protections, and more. A recent Reuters report confirmed that SSA has already begun identifying around 10,000 roles for this new classification. This isn’t a plan being shelved for future emergencies—it’s being deployed now.

There is already a process for handling poor performers in the federal workforce. No one is saying civil servants should be untouchable. But this rule isn’t about performance—it’s about ideology. It gives any administration unchecked authority to fire those who may professionally disagree, raise ethical objections, or simply serve the public in ways not politically convenient. That kind of purge is incompatible with a functioning democracy.

To be clear, this isn’t abstract fear. Groups like the Heritage Foundation have laid out this exact plan in their Project 2025 roadmap: reclassify, remove, replace. I urge OPM to reject this proposal and protect the nonpartisan, professional civil service that keeps this country running regardless of who holds office.

Thank you for considering this comment.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Citizen

Subject: Public Comment on OPM-2025-0004-0001 — Opposition to the Reclassification Proposal

To Whom It May Concern:

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule OPM-2025-0004-0001, which would establish a new “Schedule Policy/Career” employment category—effectively a rebranded version of the previously rejected “Schedule F.” This proposal would undermine the foundational principles of the U.S. civil service by removing merit-based protections from tens of thousands of federal employees.

This matters deeply to me because government policies should be implemented by professionals—scientists, analysts, public health experts, and other skilled agency staff—selected for their qualifications, not their political allegiance. The proposed rule would allow mass reclassification of career positions, stripping away job protections and opening the door to political interference in federal operations. That should concern every American, regardless of party affiliation.

The echoes of the 2020 Schedule F proposal are unmistakable. As the GAO reported (GAO-21-524), federal agencies had already begun compiling lists of employees for removal under that rule before it was ultimately rescinded. The Office of Personnel Management’s own estimate—reclassifying over 50,000 roles—is staggering. To be clear, no one is suggesting that civil servants should be immune to accountability. There are existing mechanisms for addressing underperformance. But this rule isn’t about improving performance; it’s about consolidating political control. It enables ideological purges that would silence dissent, discourage ethical resistance, and compromise the effectiveness and impartiality of government service.

This is not speculation. Organizations like the Heritage Foundation have laid out this precise strategy in their Project 2025 roadmap: reclassify, remove, and replace. OPM should not be complicit in a plan to erode the nonpartisan integrity of the civil service.

Title: Comment from Anonymous Civil Servant

I write to strongly oppose the proposed rule that would reintroduce or reconfigure Schedule F, now misleadingly dubbed "Schedule Career/Policy." The very premise of creating a new employment category that strips civil servants of due process protections under the guise of “policy alignment” is a blatant affront to the merit-based system that has underpinned the U.S. government for over a century. It signals a dangerous turn toward political patronage, where loyalty to ideology may eclipse loyalty to law, science, and the public good.

Consider the cybersecurity expert or the climate scientist—will they commit to federal service knowing that a single change in administration could erase their job for merely adhering to evidence rather than party lines?

These vague criteria open the door to arbitrary and politically motivated personnel decisions, with no recourse for those unjustly targeted.

Let us not forget: the original Schedule F executive order was revoked for good reason. It was widely condemned by legal scholars, civil service experts, and even former Republican and Democratic OPM officials. Reviving or repackaging this policy in any form constitutes an authoritarian power grab masquerading as civil service reform.

The proposed rule must be withdrawn in full. A professional, apolitical civil service is not optional in a democracy—it is the last line of defense against corruption, incompetence, and autocracy.

Title: Comment from Concerned Patriot
Comment:
The su8mmary of this rule is brief: "the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is proposing a rule to increase career employee accountability. Agency supervisors report great difficulty removing employees for poor performance or misconduct. The proposed rule lets policy-influencing positions be moved into Schedule Policy/Career. These positions will remain career jobs filled on a nonpartisan basis. Yet they will be at-will positions excepted from adverse action procedures or appeals. This will allow agencies to quickly remove employees from critical positions who engage in misconduct, perform poorly, or undermine the democratic process by intentionally subverting Presidential directives." 

First, I note that the proposed rule is 122 pages in length, making full review extremely difficult for citizens.  Moreover, I find the summary quite misleading based upon my long experience.  As an experienced government scientific manager, I have often been told that it is difficult to discharge govt employees for performance related issues.  What is not stated in the summary is that, in my experience, this has virtually always applied to employees at lower levels, and not to those targeted by this proposed rule making.  I concur that there are challenges in the Merit system and in the Civil Service system.  I do not agree that these issues will be effectively addressed by this proposed rule.  My experience is that upper level employees are much more "manageable," and can be readily moved to positions which do not influence policy.  Such moves happen relatively often, and have the exact impact that is suggested by the rule's summary, of removing persons from positions of influence if they act contrary to agency policy.  These persons are generally highly accomplished individuals whose capacity and performance is not in question.  So in my view, this proposed rule aims (as stated in the summary) to fix a problem that does not exist.  Rather, it appears to operate in the direction of returning important positions to the era of political patronage, and this would be nothing short of an institutional disaster for all of our highly accomplished govt agencies.   This proposed rule would have an extremely negative effect upon the government services.  I have worked for 40 years in the health sector, and have learned that government workers in this domain are skilled and knowledgeable experts in their fields.  They are hired with no regard to political views or affiliations. In fact, by virtue of the Hatch Act, there are severe restrictions on their political activities, to assure that government services are provide in nonpartisan manners, and with the greatest professional expertise.  This rule would render such positions insecure and highly vulnerable to political and partisan management, to the detriment of the services provided., It would clearly subject positions governed by this proposed rule change to partisan influence, and would inject elements of fear and bias into decisions by the position occupants.  The consequence would be less, not more, expression of variety of opinion and viewpoints.  This would be especially harmful in scientific fields, where variety of viewpoints and thoughts are critically important in assuring progress.  There are other means by which government service performance can be monitored and strengthened, but removal of the democratic protection of these position will operate to the detriment of all such services.  Further, by politicizing government employment, this rule would return us to the period when political patronage governed all federal employment.  One especially harmful consequence would be that positions would likely turn over with each new administration; this would greatly impact the retention of the types of long-term expertise which is present in most government agencies, and which (esp in the health fields) has led to the retention of global experts in many fields.  Such experts are only developed thru many years of experience, which would no longer likely be possible in a service with frquent turnover.  There are in place multiple measures and systems which allow for monitoring of performance and for action in cases of notably poor or unacceptable performance.  Moreover, there are many better means to establish or change agency direction; these especially include the Congressional process for resource allocation through budget decisions.  Such influence and power should remain with the Congress and the measures it approves, rather than with any partisan administration.,This is an important part of the system of checks and balances which protects the functioning of this wonderful experiment in democracy which we call the United States of America.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is also bound by 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to support the merit system principles. Title: Comment from Jennifer Riehl

I submit these comments in strong opposition to the proposed rule.
The justification offered for this rule is built on a series of misleading premises. It inaccurately characterizes federal employees as resistant to carrying out lawful directives based on personal preference, ignoring the fundamental legal and ethical obligations that guide civil service behavior. Refusing to execute an order that is unlawful, unconstitutional, or inconsistent with statutory authority is not insubordination — it is adherence to the oath of office and longstanding legal requirements.
The rule also implies that exercising First Amendment rights during personal time is grounds for professional censure, a position that is constitutionally indefensible. Federal employees, like all citizens, retain their rights to free speech and lawful political participation outside of work hours. The Hatch Act already governs appropriate boundaries; this rule seeks to create new, vague standards that would chill lawful expression and invite politically motivated retaliation.
Rather than strengthening accountability, this proposal would expose career civil servants to politicization, destabilize the professional expertise within agencies, and erode the continuity of government operations across administrations. The merit-based civil service system exists precisely to prevent the replacement of expertise with political loyalty. Weakening these protections would harm not only individual employees but the effectiveness and credibility of federal institutions.
Improving performance and accountability within the civil service requires commitment to sound management practices, consistent enforcement of existing performance systems, and robust training for leadership — not dismantling the legal protections that ensure neutrality and professionalism.
This proposed rule represents a dangerous departure from constitutional principles, good governance practices, and the public interest. It should be withdrawn in its entirety.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
This proposal threatens the merit-based civil service system that has underpinned a professional, nonpartisan federal workforce for over a century.

First and foremost, the creation of Schedule F directly undermines the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which was enacted to establish a merit-based hiring process for federal employees. By allowing a broad swath of career civil servants—particularly those involved in policy-making or analysis—to be reclassified and potentially terminated without cause, Schedule F opens the door to politically motivated hiring and firing. This is unetical to the principle in accordance with 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8), which mandates that federal employment decisions be based on merit and free from political influence. 

The vague and sweeping criteria for inclusion in Schedule F violate due process protections guaranteed by 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which requires cause and procedural safeguards for the removal of career federal employees. Stripping thousands of workers of these protections risks loss of expert advice and dissent within agencies - undermining effectiveness of government operations.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is also bound by 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to support the merit system principles. Implementing Schedule F contradicts this statutory mission and places undue political pressure on career professionals, compromising the integrity and continuity of federal programs across administrations.

Specifically as a career civil servant for the intelligence community, the execution of Schedule F and removal of policy and career service federal employees violates: 

1) The Hatch Act: The Hatch Act restricts federal employees from engaging in certain political activities. If Schedule F results in more federal employees being categorized as political appointees, it could blur the lines between partisan political roles and career civil service positions, increasing the risk of Hatch Act violations. It could lead to a politicized workforce where employees are expected to engage in partisan activities, which would undermine the nonpartisan nature of the civil service. 
2) DoD and Intelligence Community Policies: Department of Defense (DoD) policies and intelligence community standards emphasize the need for a professional, nonpartisan workforce, particularly in sensitive areas like national security. Schedule F could potentially allow for political appointees to take over career positions in these areas, where political loyalty could override technical expertise, compromising the integrity of defense and intelligence operations. The intelligence community relies on trust, confidentiality, and professionalism. If Schedule F were implemented broadly in agencies such as the CIA, NSA, or FBI, it could introduce political interference in intelligence gathering, analysis, and operations, which could be seen as a violation of the community’s policy of ensuring independence from political influence.
3) Whistleblower Protection Laws:
Schedule F could undermine whistleblower protection laws that exist to safeguard government employees who report misconduct or violations of law. By politicizing federal positions, employees may feel pressured to either remain silent or risk retaliation. This could undermine laws such as the Whistleblower Protection Act, which guarantees federal employees the right to report wrongdoing without fear of retaliation.
4) Executive Orders and Presidential Directives:
There are various executive orders that guide the relationship between political appointees and career civil servants. By reclassifying large portions of the federal workforce into Schedule F, it could undermine the structure laid out by such directives, potentially violating the spirit, if not the letter, of these orders.

In conclusion, the Schedule F proposal poses a grave threat to the foundational principles of good governance, civil service independence, and the rule of law. I urge the administration and OPM to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement or revive this dangerous classification.

Title: Comment from Peter  Krah
Comment:
Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004
RIN: 3206-AO80
Subject: Comment Opposing Proposed Rule – Schedule Policy/Career (Schedule P/C)
Submitted by: Petra Krah, Program Manager and Analyst
Date: 4/29/2025

To Whom It May Concern:

I respectfully submit this comment in strong opposition to OPM’s proposed rule to establish “Schedule Policy/Career” (Schedule P/C) under 5 CFR Parts 210, 212, 213, 302, 432, 451, and 752. This rule undermines the federal merit system and shifts accountability away from where it belongs—senior leadership—and onto the career workforce.

1. The Rule Dismantles Merit Protections

The proposal removes civil servants’ rights under 5 U.S.C. Chapters 43 and 75, including:

Advance notice of removal,

Opportunity to improve performance,

Appeal rights via MSPB.

These protections prevent retaliation and ensure fairness. Removing them invites political interference and undermines the neutrality of the federal workforce, contrary to 5 U.S.C. § 2301.

2. The Rule Politicizes Career Roles

The term “policy-influencing” is overly broad and undefined. Agencies could misuse it to reclassify nonpolitical roles and remove nonpartisan professionals without cause. This mirrors the rejected Schedule F and endangers continuity and integrity in federal operations.

3. The Rule Targets the Wrong People

In my decade of federal service, I have held multiple roles and consistently delivered results. Yet I’ve seen positions handed to unqualified DEI-backed hires while experienced staff were bypassed. HR certified these applicants despite their lack of experience. The real accountability problem lies with SES and GS-15 leaders who fail to manage, yet are shielded from consequences. One SES in my division has faced numerous complaints for ADA violations, bullying, and ethical breaches—but was promoted instead of disciplined.

4. OPM Should Prioritize Leadership Accountability

OPM must reform how agencies manage leadership by:

Requiring performance action plans with timelines and measurable goals,

Shortening PIPs to 30–45 days,

Holding SES and GS-15 employees accountable based on outcomes.

Agencies should:

Remove ineffective SESs,

Promote capable GS-15s,

Review them within 10 months and replace underperformers,

Promote qualified GS-14s—and repeat the cycle to restore competence.

Limit SESs to one per 2,500 employees to reduce bureaucratic overhead and eliminate non-value-added leadership roles.

5. Reform DEI-Driven HR Practices

DEI has corrupted federal HR processes. I have witnessed qualified employees with 10+ years of experience lose out to individuals with minimal experience—certified purely to satisfy DEI benchmarks. These HR practices erode fairness and workforce quality. OPM must return to merit-based hiring and eliminate identity-based certification and selection schemes.

Conclusion

This rule attacks the wrong tier of the workforce. Instead of stripping due process from career staff, OPM should focus on failed leadership and politicized hiring. True reform means:

Holding SESs and senior managers accountable,

Ending DEI-driven favoritism in HR,

Promoting skilled, experienced professionals based on merit.

I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule and redirect efforts toward restoring effective leadership, fairness, and integrity to the federal civil service.

Respectfully submitted,
Petra Krah
Program Manager and Analyst

Title: Comment from Pam Logan
Comment:
I am writing as a recently retired federal employee who worked at the departments of Energy and Defense. During my 17 years of federal service, I have been affected by poor-performing peers and witnessed the difficulty of removing them, and yet I have also witnessed retaliatory conduct by supervisors toward their staff that was driven by personal animus. As a former member of DoD’s Acquisition Corps, I am particularly concerned about changes that will damage the integrity of the contract award and administration processes. 

Federal contracting officers, by the nature of their warrants, are clearly individuals who have the "Authority to bind an agency to a position, policy, or course of action without higher level review or with only limited higher-level review,” yet the proposed changes do not address the unintended consequences of making them at-will employees. These highly-trained and vetted professionals should not be placed in a position where their jobs are at risk if their decisions are not in accordance with the preferences of agency leadership.

For example, a company that competes unsuccessfully for a federal contract could lobby for the dismissal of the selecting official.  Undue influence of this type will introduce bias in the selection process and politicize and delay the award of contracts, making the government insufficiently responsive to urgent needs such as the outbreak of armed conflict, a natural disaster, or a pandemic. Among agencies, the Department of Defense is particularly vulnerable to these malign impacts because its contracts are so large and the defense industry already employs an army of lobbyists, many of whom are former DoD officials with ties of personal friendship to currently serving DoD leaders.  The size of DOE contracts is smaller, but its leaders, too, are targeted by industry lobbyists who are themselves former DOE officials. 

More broadly, although I believe the goal of making poor performers easier to dismiss is laudable, these proposed changes throw the door wide open to arbitrary and politically motivated dismissals. If adopted, then federal employees who refuse to follow illegal orders can be quickly fired and replaced, weakening the rule of law which is so fundamental to the vision of our nation's Founding Fathers. The changes also will effectively silence whistleblowers who would otherwise report fraud, waste, and abuse in their agencies. 

While the proposed changes will place policy-influencing officials in unreasonable jeopardy, ​​they also do not do enough to ease the process of dismissing poor performing workers in non-policy roles.  One simple fix would be to extend the probationary period for employees whose performance is less than fully successful. 

Because of the grave concerns described above, I think this proposal should not be implemented as written. It needs to be reworked to a more reasonable power balance between career federal employees and officials appointed by the President. Also, reforms to federal employment should be enacted as law by Congress rather than implemented as an EO, lest the federal workforce be subjected to the stress and distraction of a whole new set of changes under each succeeding administration.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
RE: Public Comment in Response to Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service [Docket No. OPM–2025–0004]

I am writing to express my deep concern regarding the effort to reclassify specific federal positions, which would erode necessary protections for those serving within the federal statistical system and could transform positions which rely on specific expertise to political ones. The proposed rule, “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service,” would call into question the objectivity that both sides of the aisle rely on for our economic indicators, public health assessments, energy utilization and many other statistics. The federal statistical system plays an essential role in improving the lives of all Americans as well as informing critical policy decisions with evidence that is timely, relevant, and accurate. Federal statistical agencies are particularly vulnerable to the proposed rule due to the following:

Politicization: Schedule Policy/Career could lead to the politicization of the federal statistical workforce. Official federal statistics influence public policy of all sorts. So, a President could classify many statistical agency positions as Policy/Career. Then, Bureau of Labor Statistics’ leaders could be fired for releasing or planning to release jobs or inflation statistics unfavorable to the President’s policy agenda. They might also face pressure to change methodologies or reveal pre-release information. By making it easier to remove employees if a President determines that they are interfering with his/her policies, it increases the potential for passivity or political loyalty to be prioritized over expertise and experience. Politicization has had dramatic consequences for statistical agencies and their leaders in other countries, notably Argentina & Greece.

Importance of Trust, Impartiality and Objectivity: Statistical agencies need professional autonomy to provide impartial, objective, reliable data. Professional autonomy is the ability to act independently from political or other undue external influence regarding its operations, such as data collection and analysis, staffing, and publications. Erosion of professional autonomy in the operations of statistical agencies would undermine their perceived or actual independence, leading to a loss of public trust in the data they produce.

Importance of Norms: Schedule Policy/Career would deprioritize and weaken the norms that uphold the ethical and professional standards critical to the success of statistical agencies. Senior leaders help craft, model and reinforce norms within their agencies and between their agencies and other parts of the government.  Examples include how agencies interact with staff, data users, data subjects, outside experts and host agencies. See Principles and Practices for a Federal Statistical Agency for examples of these critical norms. These norms reflect and go beyond the laws, rules, and policy directives that govern agencies’ operations. Weaker norms threaten trust, efficient operations, and data quality.

Erosion of Expertise, Loss of Institutional Memory and Increase of Turnover: These agencies rely on highly specialized professionals, including statisticians, economists, and data scientists, who possess unique technical expertise and long-term institutional memory. Statistical agencies stand to lose experts who see their career paths as less secure and merit-based than before. The loss of these experts or frequent turnover in key positions could disrupt agency operations, hinder long-term planning, undermine the agency's ability to fulfill its mission, and impair the quality and accuracy of the data.

Decreased Employee Morale and Productivity: The uncertainty and fear of arbitrary dismissal could lead to decreased productivity and difficulty in attracting and retaining top talent.

Importance of Modernization, Research, and Data Continuity: Statistical agencies must invest in long-term efforts such as extensive research, critical modernization projects, and efforts to ensure data access and continuity. Title: Comment from Shruti Rathnavel

I am writing to express my deep concern regarding the effort to reclassify specific federal positions, which would erode necessary protections for those serving within the federal statistical system and could transform positions which rely on specific expertise to political ones. The proposed rule, “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service,” would call into question the objectivity that both sides of the aisle rely on for our economic indicators, public health assessments, energy utilization and many other statistics. The federal statistical system plays an essential role in improving the lives of all Americans as well as informing critical policy decisions with evidence that is timely, relevant, and accurate. 

Schedule Policy/Career could lead to the politicization of the federal statistical workforce. Official federal statistics influence public policy of all sorts: monetary, fiscal, regulatory, etc. A President could classify many statistical agency positions as Policy/Career. Then, for example, Bureau of Labor Statistics’ leaders could be fired for releasing or planning to release jobs or inflation statistics unfavorable to the President’s policy agenda. They might also face pressure to change methodologies or reveal pre-release information. By making it easier to remove employees if a President determines that they are interfering with his or her policies, it increases the potential for passivity or political loyalty to be prioritized over expertise and experience. Politicization has had dramatic consequences for statistical agencies and their leaders in other countries, notably Argentina and Greece.

Statistical agencies, such as the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Census Bureau, and the National Center for Health Statistics, need to be able to act independently from political or other undue external influence to provide impartial, objective, reliable data. Erosion of this autonomy in the operations of statistical agencies would undermine their perceived or actual independence, leading to a loss of public trust in the data they produce.

Schedule Policy/Career would deprioritize and thus weaken the norms that uphold the ethical and professional standards that are critical to the success of statistical agencies. Senior leaders help craft, model and reinforce norms within their agencies and between their agencies and other parts of the government.  Examples include how agencies interact with staff, data users, data subjects, outside experts and host agencies. See Principles and Practices for a Federal Statistical Agency for examples of these critical norms. These norms reflect and go beyond the laws, rules, and policy directives that govern agencies’ operations. Weaker norms threaten trust, efficient operations, and data quality.

These agencies rely on highly specialized professionals, including statisticians, economists, and data scientists, who possess unique technical expertise and long-term institutional memory. Statistical agencies stand to lose experts who see their career paths as less secure and merit-based than before. The loss of these experts or frequent turnover in key positions could disrupt agency operations, hinder long-term planning, undermine the agency's ability to fulfill its mission, and impair the quality and accuracy of the data.

To support their missions, statistical agencies must invest in long-term efforts such as extensive research, critical modernization projects, and efforts to ensure data access and continuity. Schedule Policy/Career could subject to agencies to changing presidential priorities, increasing senior staff turnover and disrupting modernization efforts, measurement of trends, and meaningful research.

Federal statistical agencies provide data and expertise that are intrinsic to operations in both the public and private sector. Among many other things, data is used to improve public health, monitor employment and inflation, and forecast population trends. Schedule Policy/Career poses a significant threat to the effectiveness of federal statistical agencies and to the integrity and quality of their products. By undermining the principles of merit-based employment and threatening job security of senior career civil servants, Schedule Policy/Career could lead to politicization, loss of trust and expertise, decreased morale, and disruption of agency operations. On behalf of U.S. businesses, the American public, and policymakers I am speaking up to protect the trustworthiness of the federal statistics we all rely on.

A country requires stability and consistency from the government in order for it to function well. Title: Comment from Brady West
Comment:
April 30, 2025

RE: Public Comment in Response to Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service [Docket No. OPM–2025–0004]

I am writing to express my deep concern regarding the effort to reclassify specific federal positions, which would erode necessary protections for those serving within the federal statistical system and could transform positions which rely on specific expertise to political ones. The proposed rule, “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service,” would call into question the objectivity that both sides of the aisle rely on for our economic indicators, public health assessments, energy utilization and many other statistics. The federal statistical system plays an essential role in improving the lives of all Americans as well as informing critical policy decisions with evidence that is timely, relevant, and accurate. Federal statistical agencies are particularly vulnerable to the proposed rule due to the following:

Politicization: Schedule Policy/Career could lead to the politicization of the federal statistical workforce. Official federal statistics clearly influence public policy of all sorts: monetary, fiscal, regulatory, etc. Thus, a President could classify many statistical agency positions as Policy/Career. Then, for example, Bureau of Labor Statistics’ leaders could be fired for releasing or planning to release jobs or inflation statistics unfavorable to the President’s policy agenda. They might also face pressure to change methodologies or reveal pre-release information. By making it easier to remove employees if a President determines that they are interfering with his or her policies, it increases the potential for passivity or political loyalty to be prioritized over expertise and experience. Politicization has had dramatic consequences for statistical agencies and their leaders in other countries, notably Argentina and Greece.

Importance of Trust, Impartiality and Objectivity: Statistical agencies, such as the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Census Bureau, and the National Center for Health Statistics, need professional autonomy to provide impartial, objective, reliable data. Professional autonomy is the ability to act independently from political or other undue external influence regarding its operations, such as data collection and analysis, staffing, and publications. Erosion of professional autonomy in the operations of statistical agencies would undermine their perceived or actual independence, leading to a loss of public trust in the data they produce.

Importance of Norms: Schedule Policy/Career would deprioritize and thus weaken the norms that uphold the ethical and professional standards that are critical to the success of statistical agencies. Senior leaders help craft, model and reinforce norms within their agencies and between their agencies and other parts of the government.  Examples include how agencies interact with staff, data users, data subjects, outside experts and host agencies. See Principles and Practices for a Federal Statistical Agency for examples of these critical norms. These norms reflect and go beyond the laws, rules, and policy directives that govern agencies’ operations. Weaker norms threaten trust, efficient operations, and data quality.

Erosion of Expertise, Loss of Institutional Memory and Increase of Turnover: These agencies rely on highly specialized professionals, including statisticians, economists, and data scientists, who possess unique technical expertise and long-term institutional memory. Statistical agencies stand to lose experts who see their career paths as less secure and merit-based than before. The loss of these experts or frequent turnover in key positions could disrupt agency operations, hinder long-term planning, undermine the agency's ability to fulfill its mission, and impair the quality and accuracy of the data.

Decreased Employee Morale and Productivity: The uncertainty and fear of arbitrary dismissal could negatively impact employee morale, leading to decreased productivity and difficulty in attracting and retaining top talent.

Importance of Modernization, Research, and Data Continuity: To support their missions, statistical agencies must invest in long-term efforts such as extensive research, critical modernization projects, and efforts to ensure data access and continuity. Schedule Policy/Career could subject to agencies to changing presidential priorities, increasing senior staff turnover and disrupting modernization efforts, measurement of trends, and meaningful research.

Schedule Policy/Career poses a significant threat to the effectiveness of federal statistical agencies and to the integrity and quality of their products. On behalf of U.S. businesses, the American public, and policymakers I am speaking up to protect the trustworthiness of the federal statistics we all rely on.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I respectfully submit this comment urging the withdrawal of the proposed rule published on April 23, 2025 (90 FR 17182). The rule unlawfully undermines procedural rights conferred by statute, departs from long-standing legal interpretation, and conflicts with the Office of Personnel Management’s (OPM) own 2024 final rule, “Upholding Civil Service Protections and Merit System Principles” (89 FR 24982). If finalized, this regulation will be vulnerable to legal challenge under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) and the Constitution.

1. Conflict with Statutory Framework
The proposed rule would reclassify “policy-influencing” positions into a new “Schedule Policy/Career,” eliminating coverage under 5 U.S.C. chapters 43 and 75, and removing appeal rights to the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB). This is incompatible with congressional intent and statutory text. Under 5 U.S.C. § 7511, procedural protections apply to most career employees who have completed their probationary periods. The 2024 rule reaffirmed that reclassification does not extinguish these rights unless voluntarily waived by the employee.

The 2025 rule’s interpretation—permitting removal of career protections solely through reclassification—constitutes a de facto repeal of statutory safeguards via regulation, which exceeds OPM’s authority.

2. Violation of Due Process
Under Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 470 U.S. 532 (1985), and related precedent, government employees with a statutory entitlement to continued employment possess a constitutionally protected property interest. Procedural due process requires, at minimum, notice and an opportunity to respond before termination.

The proposed rule would eliminate these safeguards for employees in reclassified positions, enabling termination without cause or process. Courts have consistently held that such deprivation of a vested interest without adequate procedures violates the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause.

3. Major Questions Doctrine
The proposal implicates the major questions doctrine, as reaffirmed in West Virginia v. EPA, 142 S. Ct. 2587 (2022). By removing statutory protections for a large class of federal employees, the rule seeks to effect a policy change of vast economic and political significance—without clear congressional authorization.

There is no express delegation in Title 5 permitting OPM or the President to bypass or nullify the procedural protections of chapters 43 and 75. On this ground alone, the proposed rule is ultra vires and should be withdrawn.

4. Reversal of Legally Sound 2024 Final Rule
The April 2024 final rule clarified that the statutory exception in § 7511(b)(2) for “confidential or policy-determining” positions was never intended to apply to competitively appointed career employees. That rule preserved procedural rights for employees involuntarily moved to the excepted service and provided appeal rights to the MSPB. It was grounded in well-settled legal precedent, including Arnett v. Kennedy, 416 U.S. 134 (1974), and aligned with the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978.

There has been no change in law or compelling justification to reverse this interpretation. The 2025 proposal represents an abrupt and unsupported policy shift, raising concerns under APA arbitrary and capricious review (5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A)).

The proposed rule exceeds OPM’s statutory authority, violates constitutional due process, conflicts with controlling precedent, and undoes a lawful and well-supported regulatory framework finalized in 2024. I urge OPM to withdraw this rule in full and maintain the integrity of the federal merit system.

Title: Comment from The Steady State
Comment:
The Steady State is an organization of over 270 former senior national security professionals, including alumni of the Central Intelligence Agency, Department of State, Department of Defense, Federal Bureau of Investigation, and other agencies within the Intelligence Community. We write to express our strong opposition to the Office of Personnel Management’s proposed rule that would facilitate political reclassification of career civil servants—such as through a revived or expanded Schedule F authority—and thereby erode the core merit-based, nonpartisan character of the federal workforce.
 
Our concern is not academic. This proposed rule strikes at the heart of what makes our national security system work: the integrity, continuity, and political independence of career professionals who serve administrations of both parties, guided by law, fact, and mission—not political loyalty.
 
1. The Rule Would Create a De Facto Spoils System
 
Despite being framed as a matter of administrative efficiency or accountability, this rule would, in practice, enable political appointees to convert large swaths of the civil service into at-will employees, dismissible for any reason or none at all. This mechanism undermines over a century of bipartisan consensus about the importance of an apolitical civil service—particularly in agencies charged with defending the nation.
 
The civil servants who populate our national security agencies—analysts, diplomats, cybersecurity professionals, military strategists, intelligence collectors—would become vulnerable to dismissal based on ideological conformity or perceived disloyalty. The message would be unmistakable: fidelity to political leadership, not expertise or service to the Constitution, determines job security.
 
2. Politicizing National Security Functions Endangers the Country
 
Career professionals in the intelligence and national security fields are often tasked with bringing uncomfortable truths to power. The ability to deliver unvarnished, nonpartisan analysis is essential to effective national defense. Title: Comment from Emperatris Zeiss
Comment:
Subject: Opposition to Proposed Rule on Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service (RIN 3206-AP17 / Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004)

To the Director of the Office of Personnel Management:

I am writing to express my profound opposition to the proposed rule referenced above (OPM-2025-0004-0001), which seeks to establish a new "Schedule Policy/Career" and effectively make career federal employees in policy-influencing roles "at-will" employees, stripping them of essential civil service protections.

This proposal represents a dangerous and misguided attack on the foundations of our professional, nonpartisan civil service. For over a century, the merit system principles enshrined in law have protected the federal workforce from political interference, ensuring that government employees are hired based on qualifications and retained based on performance, not political loyalty. This system is crucial for effective, stable, and impartial governance.

The creation of a new schedule that removes adverse action procedures and appeal rights for career employees in policy roles is nothing short of an attempt to politicize the federal bureaucracy. It closely mirrors the widely condemned "Schedule F" initiative proposed during the previous administration, which was rightly seen as a mechanism to enable political purges of experienced civil servants whose expert advice might conflict with a partisan agenda. Implementing this rule would:

Undermine Merit Principles: It directly contradicts the core concept of a protected civil service, replacing job security based on merit with vulnerability based on political whim.

Enable Political Purges: It would allow administrations to easily remove dedicated public servants for purely political reasons, replacing them with potentially less qualified loyalists. This chills the willingness of experts to provide objective, evidence-based advice.

Degrade Government Effectiveness: Removing experienced personnel leads to a loss of institutional knowledge, disrupts agency operations, and ultimately harms the government's ability to serve the American people effectively and faithfully implement the laws enacted by Congress.

Promote Cronyism and Corruption: Weakening protections opens the door to patronage and makes the civil service more susceptible to corruption and undue influence.

The stated goals of "accountability" and "responsiveness" ring hollow. True accountability is achieved through robust oversight, clear performance standards, and adherence to the rule of law – not by making it easier to fire employees who may disagree with political leadership. This proposal is not about improving performance; it is about consolidating political control over the machinery of government.

An independent, professional civil service is a cornerstone of American democracy. It ensures continuity across administrations and provides the expertise necessary for sound policymaking and implementation. This proposed rule poses a direct threat to that independence and professionalism.

Therefore, I strongly urge the Office of Personnel Management to withdraw this damaging proposed rule in its entirety. We must preserve the integrity and impartiality of our civil service, not dismantle its essential protections under the guise of reform.

Thank you for considering my views.

Sincerely,

Emperatris Zeiss
Munhall, Pennsylvania

Title: Comment from Rory Stierler
Comment:
Docket No. OPM-2025-0001
RE: Comments on Proposed Rule – “Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service”
Dear Office of Personnel Management,

I submit the following comments in response to the proposed rule titled “Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service” (FR Doc. 2025-06904). While the proposal intends to uphold merit principles and prevent politicization of the civil service, it raises serious concerns related to definitional vagueness and potential legal and constitutional implications.
1. Vagueness and Overbreadth in Definitions of “Confidential,” “Policy-Determining,” “Policymaking,” and “Policy-Advocating” Positions
The proposed rule’s definitions for positions such as “confidential,” “policy-determining,” “policymaking,” and “policy-advocating” lack sufficient clarity and objective criteria. These vague standards are problematic under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A), which prohibits agency actions that are “arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law.” Ambiguous classifications could lead to inconsistent application and violate employees’ due process rights under the Fifth Amendment.

Moreover, under 5 U.S.C. §§ 2102 and 2103, statutory definitions of the competitive and excepted services guide classification. The proposed definitions risk overstepping these boundaries by including positions that are advisory or technical but not truly policymaking.

OPM should provide precise, criteria-based definitions, referencing existing occupational series, GS-level thresholds, and the Office of Management and Budget’s guidance on Schedule C and policy-related positions under 5 C.F.R. Part 213.
2. Concern Over Implicit Expectation That Civil Servants Must Implement Unlawful Orders
The proposed rule fails to address the legal obligation of federal employees to refuse unlawful orders. Under 5 C.F.R. § 2635.101(b)(4), employees are required to 'act impartially and not give preferential treatment to any private organization or individual,' and under § 2635.101(b)(5), they must 'put forth honest effort in the performance of their duties.' These principles imply a duty to act lawfully and resist directives that contravene statutory or constitutional obligations.

Additionally, federal employees are protected by the Whistleblower Protection Act (5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(8)) and the Lloyd-La Follette Act (5 U.S.C. § 7211), which affirm the right to disclose illegal or improper government activity and to refuse participation in such activities.

OPM should include a statement affirming that civil servants retain their legal obligations under federal ethics rules, whistleblower protections, and the Constitution, including the right to refuse illegal directives without fear of reclassification or reprisal.
Conclusion
While the proposed rule seeks to uphold merit system principles, its vague classifications and failure to address the lawful duty of civil servants to resist illegal orders raise significant concerns. These issues could result in violations of the APA, the Constitution, and federal employee protection statutes.

I respectfully urge OPM to revise the proposed rule to include more precise definitions and to explicitly reaffirm federal employees’ obligations under existing law to act in accordance with the Constitution and statutes.

Sincerely,


Rory Stierler
Minneapolis, MN

Title: Comment from M G
Comment:
Official Comment on Proposed Rule OPM–2025–0004
Subject: Opposition to the Proposed Changes Regarding "Schedule Policy/Career" Employees

I respectfully submit the following comments opposing the proposed rule, which would significantly weaken essential civil service protections. The rule, if finalized, would inflict serious harm on career civil servants in at least the following ten ways:

I. Elimination of Due Process Rights
The proposed rule exempts Schedule Policy/Career employees from Chapter 75 and Chapter 43 procedural protections (5 U.S.C. §§ 7512, 4303)​. Employees could be removed without prior notice, meaningful explanation, or the opportunity for neutral third-party appeal. This violates fundamental tenets of procedural fairness and significantly deviates from longstanding civil service protections recognized by the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978.

II. Creation of At-Will Employment Without Safeguards
Although Schedule Policy/Career positions are technically designated as "career," they are rendered at-will by excluding them from adverse action protections. This effectively nullifies career tenure for a broad swath of federal employees, resurrecting risks reminiscent of the 19th-century spoils system that Congress sought to abolish through the Pendleton Act​.

III. Exposure to Political Retaliation and Patronage
The rule removes critical barriers to politicized personnel decisions. Without meaningful appeal rights, career employees are vulnerable to removal for perceived disloyalty, policy disagreement, or political nonalignment, regardless of performance. This is antithetical to the merit-based, nonpartisan tradition of federal service (5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8)).

IV. Undermining Merit System Principles
Federal merit system principles guarantee that selections and removals are based on merit, not favoritism or political coercion. By removing Chapter 43 and 75 protections, the proposal enables employment actions inconsistent with 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(1) and (8), inviting partisan abuses.

V. Loss of Institutional Knowledge and Expertise
Schedule Policy/Career employees often occupy highly specialized and policy-intensive roles. Removing such employees at-will endangers the government's ability to maintain subject matter expertise, leading to operational instability and weakening the institutional memory necessary for effective administration​.

VI. Demoralization and Reduced Recruitment
The Federal Employee Viewpoint Surveys (FEVS) demonstrate that employees already have low confidence that poor performance and misconduct are properly addressed​. Creating widespread at-will conditions would further damage morale, discourage high-quality applicants from pursuing federal careers, and increase turnover at a time when experienced professionals are critically needed.

VII. Vague and Overbroad Definitions of "Policy-Influencing" Positions
The proposed rule’s definition of “policy-influencing” roles includes vast categories of employees, including those involved in regulatory drafting, grant administration, and program supervision​. Without clear criteria or limits, this opens the door to overclassification and abuse, impacting far more employees than necessary.

VIII. No Notice or Transparency Requirements
Unlike the April 2024 rule, this proposal contains no requirements for advance notice to employees or opportunity to contest a transfer into Schedule Policy/Career​. Career employees could lose their procedural rights without prior warning or opportunity to be heard, compounding unfairness and sowing confusion within the workforce.

IX. Risk of Retaliation Against Whistleblowers
The lack of meaningful appeal mechanisms under the proposed rule undermines the federal government’s protections for whistleblowers (5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(8)). Employees who expose waste, fraud, or abuse would have no practical defense against retaliatory removal under an at-will regime.

X. Destabilization of Federal Operations and Erosion of Public Trust
Allowing abrupt removal of career experts on tenuous or political grounds would disrupt federal programs and diminish the reliability and objectivity of government services. Public trust in a fair and impartial civil service would erode, undermining the government's ability to function credibly and effectively.

Conclusion
The proposed rule represents a dangerous retreat from over a century of bipartisan civil service reform. It would undermine merit-based hiring, open the door to political patronage, discourage whistleblowing, and destabilize agency operations to the detriment of all Americans. The rule is inconsistent with the statutory framework established in Title 5 and must be withdrawn in full.

Title: Comment from MEGAN BREISETH
Comment:
"I strongly oppose the implementation or revival of the “Schedule F” classification for federal employees. This proposal threatens the merit-based civil service system that has underpinned a professional, nonpartisan federal workforce for over a century.
First and foremost, the creation of Schedule F directly undermines the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which was enacted to combat the spoils system and establish a merit-based hiring process for federal employees. By allowing a broad swath of career civil servants—particularly those involved in policy-making or analysis—to be reclassified and potentially terminated without cause, Schedule F opens the door to politically motivated hiring and firing. This is antithetical to the principle of an apolitical civil service enshrined in 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8), which mandates that federal employment decisions be based on merit and free from political influence.
Moreover, the vague and sweeping criteria for inclusion in Schedule F violate the due process protections guaranteed by 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which requires cause and procedural safeguards for the removal of career federal employees. Stripping thousands of workers of these protections not only weakens accountability but also risks chilling expert advice and dissent within agencies—undermining the very effectiveness of government operations.
The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is also bound by 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to support the merit system principles. Implementing Schedule F contradicts this statutory mission and places undue political pressure on career professionals, compromising the integrity and continuity of federal programs across administrations.
In conclusion, the Schedule F proposal poses a grave threat to the foundational principles of good governance, civil service independence, and the rule of law. I urge the administration and OPM to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement or revive this dangerous classification."

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Subject: Comment Opposing Proposed Rule: “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service” (Federal Register Document Number 2025-06904)

To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule published on April 23, 2025, by the Office of Personnel Management (OPM), which would create a new employment category known as “Schedule Policy/Career” (Schedule P/C). This proposal poses significant legal, ethical, and institutional concerns and threatens to undermine the integrity of the merit-based federal civil service system.

First and foremost, the proposed reclassification of tens of thousands of federal employees into Schedule P/C—effectively stripping them of long-standing due process protections—is a profound breach of trust. Many current employees accepted federal service positions under the promise of fair treatment, procedural rights, and protection from politically motivated or arbitrary termination. To unilaterally alter the terms of their employment, without their consent or any form of individualized assessment, violates this foundational trust and damages morale across the federal workforce.

Moreover, by excluding Schedule P/C positions from the adverse action procedures codified in Chapters 43 and 75 of Title 5 of the U.S. Code, the rule would render affected employees “at-will,” with no effective recourse to challenge improper removals. This change undermines the bedrock principles of fairness, transparency, and accountability that have long governed the federal personnel system.

The proposed rule also poses a threat to the nonpartisan nature of the civil service. Allowing mass reclassification of policy-influencing roles opens the door to politicization, where loyalty or ideology could be favored over competence, experience, and public service ethics. Federal policy development must remain insulated from undue political pressure if it is to serve the public interest effectively and credibly.

Finally, this rule risks deterring highly qualified individuals from entering or remaining in federal service. The prospect of being reclassified into an at-will category with no due process is not conducive to attracting or retaining top talent, especially in mission-critical policy roles.

In conclusion, the proposed rule is an overreach that weakens both the protections of civil servants and the stability of our institutions. It compromises the very values of merit, impartiality, and fairness that the civil service was established to uphold. I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety and to engage in meaningful dialogue with stakeholders to uphold and improve—not undermine—the principles of good governance and public trust. 

If anything, federal employees should be receiving stronger protections and better pay and benefits for being targeted and scapegoated in this current political environment. This country is great in large part due to our public servants that serve to uphold the Constitution. Shame on you!

Sincerely,
Will Anderson
Topeka, KS
