Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Strong Opposition to the Reimplementation of Schedule F
Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004
RIN 3206-AO80

To Whom It May Concern:

I am writing to emphatically oppose the proposed reinstatement of Schedule F. While I am not submitting this comment in an official capacity, I am deeply familiar with the stakes of this policy and the broader implications it has for our democracy, our workforce, and our nation’s long-term stability.

A Short-Sighted and Dangerous Shift
Schedule F is not just a bureaucratic restructuring-it is a deeply concerning attempt to strip federal employees of the nonpartisan protections that have long served as a safeguard against political abuse. It invites the wholesale politicization of the federal workforce by allowing thousands of career employees to be reclassified and dismissed at will, based not on performance, but on perceived loyalty.

This proposal turns back the clock on more than a century of civil service reform. It disregards the very principle that public service should be guided by competence, continuity, and a commitment to serving all Americans-not just those who align with the current administration’s political agenda.

The Stakes Are Higher Than They Appear
The individuals who would be affected by this rule are not shadowy elites or partisan operatives-they are analysts, economists, IT professionals, public health experts, legal advisors, and administrative staff. These are the people who ensure our veterans receive care, our food supply remains safe, our elections are protected, and our laws are faithfully executed.

Stripping protections from these roles doesn’t make government more effective-it makes it weaker, more erratic, and more vulnerable to manipulation. It silences dissent, discourages critical thinking, and undermines the courage to speak truth to power—qualities that are essential in any well-functioning democracy.

We’ve seen how unchecked political loyalty can corrode public institutions. Do we really want a government where facts are filtered through ideology, and truth becomes optional?

A Better Way Forward
If this administration is serious about improving government performance, there are far more constructive solutions: streamline the performance management process, invest in training and leadership development, or create clearer accountability pathways. But destroying the foundation of a merit-based workforce in the name of “flexibility” is not reform-it’s regression.

Recommendation
I urge the agency to abandon this misguided proposal. The cost to institutional integrity, employee morale, and public trust is simply too high. If this rule proceeds, I recommend the agency narrowly define the roles that qualify as “policy-making,” subject any reclassification to congressional oversight, and ensure all impacted employees retain the right to appeal any dismissal.

Closing Thought
This isn’t just a rule change. It’s a test of whether our public institutions are meant to serve everyone, or only those who are politically favored. The answer to that question will shape not only the future of the federal workforce-but the future of democracy itself.

"I strongly oppose the implementation or revival of the “Schedule F” classification for federal employees. This proposal threatens the merit-based civil service system that has underpinned a professional, nonpartisan federal workforce for over a century.

First and foremost, the creation of Schedule F directly undermines the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which was enacted to combat the spoils system and establish a merit-based hiring process for federal employees. By allowing a broad swath of career civil servants—particularly those involved in policy-making or analysis—to be reclassified and potentially terminated without cause, Schedule F opens the door to politically motivated hiring and firing. This is antithetical to the principle of an apolitical civil service enshrined in 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8), which mandates that federal employment decisions be based on merit and free from political influence.

Moreover, the vague and sweeping criteria for inclusion in Schedule F violate the due process protections guaranteed by 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which requires cause and procedural safeguards for the removal of career federal employees. Stripping thousands of workers of these protections not only weakens accountability but also risks chilling expert advice and dissent within agencies—undermining the very effectiveness of government operations.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is also bound by 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to support the merit system principles. Implementing Schedule F contradicts this statutory mission and places undue political pressure on career professionals, compromising the integrity and continuity of federal programs across administrations.

In conclusion, the Schedule F proposal poses a grave threat to the foundational principles of good governance, civil service independence, and the rule of law. I urge the administration and OPM to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement or revive this dangerous classification."

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
To be very clear, I do not support OPM's proposed rule.

The Office of Personnel Management's (OPM) proposed rule to amend civil service regulations under Executive Order 14171 presents significant concerns regarding the erosion of merit-based hiring principles and the potential politicization of the federal workforce. While accountability is vital for effective governance, removing procedural protections for policy-influencing career employees under Chapter 43 and Chapter 75 of Title 5, United States Code, risks undermining the impartiality and professionalism of the federal civil service.
1. The Importance of Merit-Based Protections
Since the passage of the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883 (5 U.S.C. § 2101), the federal government has operated under the principle of merit-based employment, ensuring that hiring and dismissals are based on qualifications rather than political loyalty. The Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (Pub. L. No. 95-454, 92 Stat. 1111) reinforced this by establishing explicit procedural safeguards to protect employees from arbitrary removal. Weakening these protections may lead to undue political interference in career roles, as seen in historical cases like the spoils system before civil service reform (Van Riper, 1958).
2. Risks of Politicization and Loss of Institutional Expertise
Policy-influencing career positions require stability and subject-matter expertise, which are crucial for ensuring continuity in government operations regardless of political transitions. Research from the National Academy of Public Administration (NAPA, 2018) highlights that career employees play a vital role in upholding governance norms. The removal of procedural protections could discourage experienced professionals from remaining in government service, ultimately reducing efficiency and effectiveness in policy implementation (Kettl, 2020).
3. Procedural Safeguards Ensure Fairness and Due Process
Judicial precedents, such as Arnett v. Kennedy, 416 U.S. 134 (1974), reaffirm the necessity of due process in employment dismissals, ensuring that federal workers have the right to appeal adverse actions. The Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB), created under the 1978 Act, plays an essential role in protecting employees from unfair disciplinary measures. The elimination of MSPB appeal rights for Schedule Policy/Career employees could lead to removals driven by political motivations rather than objective performance evaluations, undermining the principles established in Weaver v. U.S. Information Agency, 87 F.3d 1429 (D.C. Cir. 1996).
4. Potential for Corruption and Undue Influence
Studies by the Government Accountability Office (GAO, 2021) emphasize the need for clear accountability structures in personnel decisions to prevent corruption and favoritism in hiring and firing. The proposed rule opens the door to politically motivated dismissals rather than ensuring genuine accountability for poor performance. Removing independent review mechanisms and appeal rights compromises transparency and democratic governance, as outlined in Elrod v. Burns, 427 U.S. 347 (1976), which cautioned against patronage-based employment practices.
Conclusion
Accountability must be balanced with fairness and due process. Rather than dismantling procedural safeguards that protect career employees, OPM should focus on refining existing mechanisms to ensure performance-based assessments remain impartial. The merit-based civil service system has served as a bedrock of American democracy, and removing these protections risks jeopardizing its integrity. A better approach would be strengthening managerial oversight while preserving merit system principles, as advocated by scholars (Lewis, 2021).

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule to implement Schedule Policy/Career (formerly Schedule F), which would move thousands of career federal employees into an excepted service category that strips them of the procedural protections under chapters 43 and 75 of title 5, including the right to appeal adverse actions to the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB).

Legal and Statutory Concerns:
The rule exceeds OPM’s statutory authority by applying 5 U.S.C. § 7511(b)(2) to exclude incumbent employees from chapter 75 procedural protections when they are reclassified or involuntarily transferred. This provision clearly ties exceptions to the position, not to incumbent employees’ accrued rights. The rule’s retroactive denial of fair process contradicts established precedent (Arnett v. Kennedy, 416 U.S. 134 (1974)) recognizing that career employees have a protected property interest in continuation of employment with due process. The NPRM’s dismissal of these protections fundamentally undermines employees’ constitutional rights and the merit system.

Constitutional and Accountability Issues:
Positions covered by Schedule Policy/Career wield significant policymaking authority, thus implicating Article II executive power and separation of powers principles. Supreme Court decisions (Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB, 561 U.S. 477 (2010); Seila Law v. CFPB, 140 S. Ct. 2183 (2020)) make clear that excessive removal protections at multiple levels for officers with policymaking authority are unconstitutional. The proposed rule creates a paradox: it removes protections for many, yet risks destabilizing oversight of key federal officers and undermining presidential accountability.

Merit System and Workforce Stability:
The proposal effectively resurrects the spoils system by making career employees in sensitive policy roles “at-will,” inviting politically motivated removals regardless of merit or performance. Such insecurity will chill dissent and reduce recruitment and retention of experienced professionals vital for effective governance. The merit system principles enshrined in 5 U.S.C. § 2301 demand that employees be retained based on ability and performance, with protections against arbitrary removal.

Insufficient Safeguards:
Removal of MSPB appeal rights removes a critical check against wrongful dismissal. While the rule points to Equal Employment Opportunity complaints as an alternative, EEO processes do not cover wrongful adverse actions broadly, nor do they provide comparable procedural safeguards. The risk of misuse for partisan retaliation or retaliation against whistleblowers is high.

Impact on Democratic Governance:
A politically neutral, merit-based civil service is essential to preserving democratic accountability. This rule threatens to politicize the federal workforce and undermine the principle that career employees should faithfully implement laws regardless of personal or political views. Removing procedural protections risks silencing valuable dissent and critical feedback essential to good governance.

Recommendations:
I urge OPM to withdraw or substantially revise this rule. Procedural protections and appeal rights for incumbent career employees must be preserved. Performance and misconduct issues should be addressed through improved internal management and targeted reforms—not through wholesale elimination of due process. Any exceptions should be prospective, not retroactive, to protect employees’ legitimate rights.

Thank you for considering this important perspective.

Title: Comment from Jenna Ganitano
Comment:
Comment on Proposed Rule: Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service
Agency: Office of Personnel Management (OPM)
Docket Number: OPM-2025-0004
RIN: 3206-AO12

I am writing to submit my formal comment on the proposed rule titled Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service (Docket No. OPM-2025-0004, RIN 3206-AO12).

General Objection (Subpart A; Sections 250.301–250.304):
While the proposed classification of “Schedule Policy/Career” positions under Subpart A claims to improve flexibility and accountability, I oppose this rule because it mirrors the intent and structure of the rescinded Schedule F executive order. These provisions threaten to undermine the merit-based protections that safeguard our federal civil service from politicization.

Concerns Related to Supplementary Information (Federal Register, Page 1):
Under the heading Background, OPM states that this change is meant to “[promote] a high-performing, responsive workforce.” However, creating an at-will category of career federal employees directly contradicts the goal of long-term institutional performance. The lack of due process and appeals for these roles will encourage turnover based on political loyalty rather than objective performance, eroding trust in government institutions and the nonpartisan expertise essential to public service.

Issues of Oversight and Governance (Subpart B; Section 250.305):
Allowing agencies broad discretion to determine which roles fall under the new classification invites inconsistent implementation and misuse. The ambiguity around what qualifies as “policy-determining” could be exploited to replace nonpartisan experts with political appointees, diminishing oversight and weakening democratic safeguards.

(Supplementary Information, Page 3):
The proposal notes that these roles “must serve at the will of the agency head.” This language fosters a climate in which federal employees may fear retaliation for speaking truthfully or independently, compromising the integrity of agencies tasked with enforcing law and providing evidence-based policy recommendations.

I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule and pursue reforms that improve performance and accountability through evidence-based metrics, professional development, and leadership training—not through politicization and erosion of civil service protections.

This rule claims "The proposed rule lets policy-influencing positions be moved into Schedule Policy/Career. These positions will remain career jobs filled on a nonpartisan basis. Yet they will be at-will positions excepted from adverse action procedures or appeals."

The actual effect of this is rule is that the best and brightest career employees will not apply for or take any of these jobs.  The employees of the federal government are notoriously risk-adverse which makes them sound stewards of services for the American public commensurate with their experience and expertise.   Career employees will not risk their benefits and retirements earned over dozens of year to take at-will positions, and as a result the best and brightest employees will not be interested in the policy making positions. Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Comment Opposing the Reinstatement of Schedule F
Docket ID: Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004]
RIN 3206-AO8

To Whom It May Concern:

I am writing to register my strong opposition to the proposed reimplementation of Schedule F. I am not affiliated with any political organization-I’m simply someone who believes in fair governance and the importance of a professional, nonpartisan civil service.

The Problem with Schedule F
The entire premise behind Schedule F-that federal agencies need more control over so-called “policy-making” positions-sounds reasonable on the surface. But dig just a little deeper, and it becomes clear that this proposal isn’t about efficiency. It’s about control. About loyalty. About turning positions that are supposed to be held by qualified experts into revolving doors for political allies.

This is dangerous. The American government is not meant to serve the interests of any one political figure or party-it is meant to serve the people. When you start filling crucial roles based on political allegiance rather than expertise, you erode public trust and put the quality of government services at risk.

Risks That Are Being Ignored
Schedule F could allow an incoming administration to fire tens of thousands of experienced civil servants without cause, removing critical institutional knowledge and silencing independent voices. That’s not reform-that’s a purge. And it would have consequences far beyond Washington.

Think about the public servants who help implement disaster relief, manage public health emergencies, or oversee financial regulations. Do we really want those positions subject to political turnover every election cycle? This kind of instability doesn’t make government stronger-it makes it fragile.

Worse still, it sends a chilling message to current employees: speak up, and you could be out. That kind of fear has no place in a system designed to be transparent and accountable.

A Better Approach
If the goal is better performance, let’s talk about strengthening management tools and supporting employee development. If the concern is about accountability, there are already processes in place to deal with misconduct or poor performance. Gutting civil service protections is not the solution-it’s an overreach.

My Recommendation
I urge you to reject this rule in full. It is a politically motivated maneuver that does not reflect the values of a democratic society. If changes to the federal workforce are truly needed, they should be made with broad input, bipartisan support, and a commitment to protecting the integrity of public service.

Final Thoughts
The people who keep our government running deserve better than to have their careers put on the chopping block for political gain. And the American people deserve a government that runs on competence, not cronyism. Schedule F is a step in the wrong direction-and it must be stopped.

Title: Comment from Miguel Lopez
Comment:
I oppose the addition of this proposed rule in its entirety. The point of the civil service is to be a competitive, merits-based system where the most qualified professionals, scientists, analysts, and workers put forth their best work for the good of the American government and its people. Civil servants play a vital role in placing their priorities upon the American people instead of profit margins. In contrast to the private sector, the stakeholders of civil servants are the American people and are not beholden to private interests. The proposed rule would be a dramatic shift and major regression back to the spoils system of governance that the American people rejected when the the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (CSRA) was passed. The CSRA system prioritized merit system principles which ensured that only the most qualified individuals would enter the Federal Civil Service, “selection and advancement should be determined solely on the basis of relative ability, knowledge, and skills”. The mere existence of Schedule F flies in the face of such values, as it seeks to directly violate and circumvent the CSRA. The purpose of this rule is plain, it is simply to give the Executive branch as much power as possible to seek out individual civil servants, pretend that they are equivalent to political appointees (to which they are not), and unilaterally fire them at will for not being "loyal" to the political tendencies of the current administration. The CSRA explicitly bars expanding the "confidential and policy-making designation" beyond political appointees, yet this rule proposes to do just that. If this rule were to be enacted, then this administration and future presidential administrations would be able to unilaterally classify the majority, if not, the entirety of the federal workforce as Schedule F, fire any dissent based on political reasons/bias, and then fill the entire government workforce by individuals who do not serve the American people and only exist to further the pleasure of the President. Therefore, it could clearly be seen that control over the presidency would effectively mean injecting the entire federal workforce full of political supporters incentivized to capitulate to the political aims of the president instead of highly qualified, merits-based professionals committed to serving the general public regardless of the current political climate. 
Therefore, I must advocate against this rule in its entirety as there is no justification to expand the statutorily narrow interpretation of "confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating character" positions, and the OMB needs to re-emphasize that the federal workforce remains an impartial body committed to the public service of the American people.

Title: Comment from John Smith

I strongly oppose the implementation or revival of the “Schedule F” classification for federal employees. This proposal threatens the merit-based civil service system that has underpinned a professional, nonpartisan federal workforce for over a century.

First and foremost, the creation of Schedule F directly undermines the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which was enacted to combat the spoils system and establish a merit-based hiring process for federal employees. By allowing a broad swath of career civil servants—particularly those involved in policy-making or analysis—to be reclassified and potentially terminated without cause, Schedule F opens the door to politically motivated hiring and firing. Implementing Schedule F contradicts this statutory mission and places undue political pressure on career professionals, compromising the integrity and continuity of federal programs across administrations.

In conclusion, the Schedule F proposal poses a grave threat to the foundational principles of good governance, civil service independence, and the rule of law. I urge the administration and OPM to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement or revive this dangerous classification.

I write anonymously as a senior risk specialist in a federal financial regulatory agency with over a decade of experience overseeing large banks, identifying systemic risk, and advising on emerging threats including AI, crypto, and quantum computing. Comment:
I am writing to express strong opposition to the Office of Personnel Management’s (OPM) proposed rule OPM-2025-0004-0001, which seeks to reclassify approximately 50,000 federal employees into a newly designated Schedule Policy/Career (P/C) category. This proposal, a revival of the previously rescinded Schedule F, threatens the foundational principles of a nonpartisan, merit-based civil service and poses significant risks to the integrity, efficiency, and accountability of federal operations.

Erosion of Merit-Based Protections

The cornerstone of the federal civil service is its commitment to merit-based hiring and retention, ensuring that employment decisions are grounded in qualifications and performance rather than political affiliation. By reclassifying positions into Schedule P/C, the proposed rule would strip affected employees of critical protections against arbitrary dismissal, effectively making them at-will employees. This undermines the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978, which was enacted to prevent politicization and ensure a competent and impartial federal workforce.

Increased Risk of Politicization

The reintroduction of Schedule P/C opens the door to replacing experienced, nonpartisan professionals with individuals selected for their political loyalty rather than expertise. Such a shift could compromise the objectivity of policy analysis and implementation, leading to decisions that serve partisan interests over the public good. The National Active and Retired Federal Employees Association (NARFE) has rightly noted that this move "opens the door to replacing nonpartisan, professional civil servants with political loyalists".

Undermining Institutional Knowledge and Continuity

Federal agencies rely on the institutional knowledge and continuity provided by career civil servants. Reclassifying positions and removing job protections could lead to a loss of experienced personnel, disrupting agency operations and diminishing the government's ability to effectively serve the public. The potential for mass dismissals based on political considerations threatens the stability and effectiveness of federal programs.

Legal and Ethical Concerns

The proposed rule raises serious legal and ethical questions. The previous iteration, Schedule F, faced legal challenges and was ultimately rescinded due to concerns about its legality and potential for abuse. Reintroducing a similar framework disregards these concerns and may once again lead to protracted legal battles, diverting resources and attention from the government's primary responsibilities.

Conclusion

The proposed reclassification of federal positions into Schedule Policy/Career represents a significant departure from the principles that have long safeguarded the integrity and effectiveness of the federal workforce. It threatens to politicize the civil service, erode merit-based protections, and disrupt the continuity of government operations. I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule and instead focus on strengthening the existing merit-based system that ensures a competent, impartial, and stable federal workforce.

⸻

Public Comment on OPM-2025-0004-0001: Why Are We Rebooting the Spoils System

Let me get this straight: OPM wants to bring back a system where federal employees can be fired just for doing their jobs too well—if those jobs involve saying no to a politician. That is not modernization. That is regression. This entire proposal, Schedule Policy/Career, is the bureaucratic version of sticking a fork into a light socket and pretending it is innovative.

Let us break this down.

The idea is to fire policy-influencing employees more easily. Sounds harmless until you remember: nearly every expert in government influences policy. That includes economists, cybersecurity specialists, scientists, bank examiners, engineers, public health analysts, and every person who has ever said Actually, sir, that would violate federal law. Under this rule, those people can be fired for lack of loyalty or subverting presidential direction. Translation: disagreeing with someone politically appointed, even when they are right.

Before 1883, government jobs were handed out as political favors. We called it the spoils system, because every time a new president came in, they fired everyone and replaced them with loyalists—regardless of whether they had any clue what they were doing. This is how we ended up with customs agents who could not do math, postal clerks who could not read, and tax collectors who were too drunk to collect anything.

It got so bad that President James Garfield was shot by an angry office-seeker. That was the last straw. Congress passed the Pendleton Act, creating the modern civil service: a system where you earn your job on merit and cannot be fired for politics. This was not some quaint idea. It was a fix for a completely broken, corrupt, and dangerous way of running government.

We have seen this before. It was called Schedule F, and it was so radioactive that it got shredded almost immediately. OPM’s own documents say this new version is improved, but let us be honest—it is the same monster in a cheaper disguise. Now it is called Schedule Policy/Career, which is like renaming a guillotine the Neck Realignment Device.

The goal is clear: make tens of thousands of career civil servants fireable on a whim, and replace them with hand-picked loyalists. That is not efficiency. That is empire-building.

You know what happens when you fire all your data experts, risk analysts, and IT security leads because they would not rubber-stamp a political narrative?

You get hacked. You miss the next financial crisis. You let snake oil into public health. You destroy morale across the federal government. And no one with a brain wants to work in public service again.

This is not fixing anything. It is lighting the engine on fire and blaming the seatbelts for not doing their job.

But OPM says this is about accountability.

Cool story. Civil servants can already be fired for cause. You just have to follow the rules. You know—due process, documentation, appeals to the Merit Systems Protection Board—the things that stop political abuse. The only reason to get rid of those protections is because you do not want to be held accountable yourself.

Let us be honest: no one is asking for this rule except people who want to fire experts for doing their jobs too well.

You do not improve public service by turning it into a game of musical chairs with political hacks. You improve it by respecting expertise, rewarding truth-telling, and keeping politics out of science, law, and regulatory enforcement.

If OPM has forgotten why the merit system exists, maybe it is time to read a history book—or better yet, the Pendleton Act, the Civil Service Reform Act, and a few of the court rulings that say, shockingly, you cannot just erase constitutional due process because it is politically convenient.

This rule is not new. It is old. It is dangerous. And it is exactly what our ancestors warned us about when they stopped letting presidents treat the federal workforce like their personal chessboard.

Do not bring back a system we buried for good reason. Bury this rule right alongside it.

At school drop-off, your kid’s science teacher has also been replaced. The previous teacher, a PhD who once helped NASA, made the mistake of saying something factual during a unit on climate. Not aligned with the current “direction.” So she’s out. The new teacher is someone’s cousin who once saw an eclipse and described it as humbling. He now runs the class on vibes.

At lunch, you head to your bank. The guy who used to monitor risky lending practices is no longer there. He filed a report that made a powerful person uncomfortable. So now the head of risk management is a guy who owned a few NFTs and once said he has a good gut for numbers. No audits. But strong opinions.

You decide to walk that off by heading to the airport. Your flight is delayed. Surprise. The air traffic controller was replaced with someone who impressed the administration by winning a competitive hot dog eating contest. Experience? No. But when asked if he’d ever disagree with leadership, he said never, not even hypothetically. That’s what we call a team player.

Meanwhile, your bridge inspector is now a former children’s party magician. The cybersecurity lead at the power grid is a retired Instagram influencer who once posted a meme about encryption. The local food safety guy was fired for questioning a mayonnaise-based sushi truck. The new guy is allergic to responsibility but said yes a lot in his interview.

This isn’t satire. This is the logical conclusion of Schedule Policy Career. If your job has any influence on policy and spoiler alert, most real jobs in government do you can be let go for being too good at it. For asking the right questions. For knowing things that make people nervous. Not for incompetence. For competence with a conscience.

This is not reform. You get potholes that explode. You get bridges that bounce. You get regulators who say, “We thought the economy would be fine, based on a feeling.”

And let’s be clear this is not about left or right. It’s about up or down. As in, do you want the plane to go up and then come down in one piece, or not. This rule doesn’t fix government. It removes the people who know how to fix things, and replaces them with whoever claps loudest at the meeting.

Please stop trying to bring back the spoils system. We got rid of it because it did not work. And because we like things like clean water, functioning bridges, and pilots who can land the plane without checking Twitter first.

Respectfully submitted,
A citizen who would like the person inspecting the nuclear reactor to be someone who knows what a nuclear reactor is

Title: Comment from Daniel Schramm
Comment:
The Office of Personnel Management proposes a rule identified as Docket ID# OPM-2025-0004-0001. OPM opened the rule for public comment. I am submitting this comment opposing the proposed rule and requesting that it be withdrawn.

I am submitting this comment as a retired lawyer. I practiced law for a total of 45 years. Earlier in my career, I worked briefly as a staff attorney in the civil service for the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency in Washington, D.C. As part of my law practice, I occasionally represented clients on questions of administrative law and federal government contracts. My deceased father was a career civil servant with the St. Louis office of the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. I present this background information to show my persosal involvement with and basic understanding of the rules of civil service and administrative law.

OPM proposes its new Rule to implement Executive Order 14171 issued by President Donald J. Trump on the first day of his second term in office. The proposed Rule would create a new "Schedule F" to dramatically expand the number of political appointees who would be stripped of civil service protection by including them within the "excepted service."  In my opinion, this controversial tactic probably is unlawful. This is a "major question" of national significance and has not been specifically delegated by Congress to OPM as required by current Supreme Court precedent. (See, West Virginia v. Environmental Protection Agency, 597 U.S. 697 (2022). And OPM will be given no Chevron deference for its interpretation of what constitutes positions of a "confidential, policy-making, policy-advocating character" under existing law. See, Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo and Relentless v. Department of Commerce, Op. No. 22-451 (June 28, 2024.)

I recognize that this particular matter has not yet been tested in the courts. But I believe OPM's proposed new Rule is totally inconsistent with existing civil service law. The Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 provides general safeguards to protect career civil servants from unfair and unwarranted practices. OPM and the Merit Systems Protection Board operate under federal regulations designed to implement those protections. Last April, OPM issued final regulations to provide additional safeguards to protect against anything like Executive Order 14171 and this proposed Rule to create a new "Schedule F."  [See, "OPM Establishes Safeguards Against Schedule F," (NTEU: May 2024).] The proposed new Rule seeks to amend the civil service regulations by removing amendments issued in the final rule adopted in April, 2024. (See, Proposed Rule Summary Items 3, 4, and 5.) I strongly oppose this change. In my opinion, OPM shows no legitimate reason for removing the protections created by the amendments from last year. 

In essence, OPM wants to avoid the protections of the Civil Service Reform Act and its implementing regulations. OPM is doing so by trying to redefine a "confidential and policymaking employee" who may be fired at will. (See, Proposed Rule Summary, Item 1.) This traditional group of political appointees has been narrowly defined by decades of accepted practice. The proposed new Rule purports to be designed to improve "performance, accountability and responsiveness." I consider this to be misleading. The real purpose is clear. OPM wants to create a new spoils system where loyalty is valued over experience and competence. And the new Rule would erode the core merit-based, nonpartisan character of the federal workforce.

I expect the courts ultimately will reject OPM's transparent effort to rewrite the civil service law and its regulations. My hope is that the proposed new Rule will be withdrawn to avoid this kind of judicial confrontation.

Title: Comment from Anonymous

Dear Office of Personnel Management:

I write to respectfully oppose the Office of Personnel Management’s (“OPM”) proposed amendments to 5 CFR Parts 210, 212, 213, 302, 432, and 752, which would establish a new “Schedule Policy/Career” classification, reclassify career employees into this schedule, and strip affected employees of critical civil service protections guaranteed under Title 5, including Chapters 75 and 43. Positions

Summary:
The Office of Personnel Management’s proposed amendments to 5 CFR Parts 210, 212, 213, 302, 432, and 752 — which would reclassify career employees into a new “Schedule Policy/Career” excepted service category and eliminate procedural protections under Title 5 — are unlawful, unconstitutional, and unsupported by evidence.

Key Objections:

No Statutory Authority:
OPM lacks statutory authority to remove civil service protections established by Congress in Chapters 75 and 43 of Title 5. Executive orders and regulations cannot override Congressional mandates.

No Judicial Deference After Loper Bright:
Following the Supreme Court’s decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, courts owe no deference to OPM’s interpretation. The agency must demonstrate clear statutory authorization, which it cannot.

Major Questions Doctrine Applies:
Reclassifying thousands of federal employees and stripping statutory protections presents a major question of political and economic significance that only Congress can authorize.

Constitutional Due Process Violations:
Removing career employees’ rights to notice, hearing, and review violates Fifth Amendment due process principles.

Misuse of Principal-Agent Theory:
OPM wrongly invokes principal-agent theory to claim career employees act against presidential will. Empirical data overwhelmingly shows that federal employees lawfully and faithfully implement policy across administrations. Academic literature and GAO reports confirm that career civil servants support agency missions and lawful directives, not personal political agendas.

Arbitrary and Capricious Action:
The proposed rule ignores decades of settled civil service policy without adequate justification or evidence, rendering it arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act.

Title: Comment from Mark Styczynski
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule. Its scope will have a substantial negative impact on many facets of American life, and will make America worse rather than great. The specific aspect I would like to highlight is the potential for intrusion into the scientific grants process. I have been a professor in chemical engineering for over 15 years, and my work has been supported by federal grants from multiple agencies including NSF, NIH, and DARPA. I have also served on grant review panels in various for capacities for multiple federal agencies. I thus have experience and knowledge related to the scientific grants process. 

The OPM final guidance to agencies for including positions in Schedule Policy/Career indicates that the following role should be included: “substantive participation and discretionary authority in agency grantmaking, such as the substantive exercise of discretion in the drafting of funding opportunity announcements, evaluation of grant applications, or recommending or selecting grant recipients.”  This directly leads to the entirety of the federal scientific grantmaking workforce being able to be dismissed at the whims of the administration regardless of performance.  This is bad for the country and bad for science.

Whatever the funding levels for science may be in the future, the funding of science should be based on merit and not partisan beliefs. However, the Schedule Policy/Career would make it easy to fire any NSF program manager, any NIH program manager, or anyone handling grants reviews, for any perceived slight of executive priorities, regardless of whether those priorities are grounded in scientific fact.  NSF, NIH, and other funding organizations should be compelled to award funds based on scientific merit and not based on favoritism or perceived political views, yet this rule would facilitate patronage of specific political views when science should be the paramount concern.

Schedule Policy/Career could decimate protections for scientific grantmaking, which could in turn potentially decimate scientific investigation in America. There is a reason that basic science and R&D are done with federal support: it is often too far from a potential return on investment for any individual company to justify the research. The days of Bell Labs funding basic scientific research have been gone for decades, and so the only way we can maintain a strategic advantage in science and engineering is through federal support. If that federal support is doled out based on favoritism or political persuasion, it will undermine American excellence and operational readiness. 

Important, the summary in the Federal Register says, “The proposed rule lets policy-influencing positions be moved into Schedule Policy/Career. These positions will remain career jobs filled on a nonpartisan basis. Yet they will be at-will positions excepted from adverse action procedures or appeals.”  Inherently, if these positions are at-will positions with no adverse action procedures or appeals, there are NO guarantees that they will be filled on a non-partisan basis. Any person who is hired into such a position who holds a view that is at odds with the executive branch could be fired, and so ultimately the position could easily be only filled on a de facto partisan basis, returning to the spoils approach that we moved away from so long ago.

The rules and guidance claim that patronage will not be allowed, but those claims ring hollow. Once a single person inclined to reward people of similar political views gets installed at a high enough position, they can then dismiss as many Schedule Policy/Career employees as they like and hire new employees, and can make sure to hire immediate subordinates that will implement their vision of political patronage and spoils through the competitive hiring process. The competitive hiring process does NOT itself avoid patronage; patronage and spoils can only be avoided when people are hired based on merit and cannot be dismissed at will.  They do not work without each other, that is why they both exist. To claim otherwise is an unsupported, illogical argument for the reasons noted above: an infinite cycle of unjustified dismissal until someone with the “right” viewpoint is extremely easy to implement, and soon the competitive hiring process will be shortcircuited even if it is technically followed.

Filling the scientific grant administration ranks with people who have the "correct" political persuasion regardless of their qualifications will lead to a deterioration of the scientific community and of public faith and trust in our government.  The proposed rule will inevitably lead to this result.  It will be a tremendous setback for American science and will make America worse.  I thus strongly oppose this rule.

Title: Comment from Adam Despang
Comment:
I am submitting this comment in opposition to the proposed rule, “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service.” As a former U.S. Army Field Artillery Officer and a Presidential Management Fellow, I took the oath to support and defend the Constitution six times. Service to nation guided my actions during military service and again as a federal civilian employee working across two agencies with exposure to many more. In both roles, I served administrations of different parties—but always with the understanding that my loyalty was to the Constitution and the law, not to any one president. I served knowing there were legal and procedural protections to allow me to act faithfully as I served the American people. 
This rule threatens to upend that tradition. By reviving a version of “Schedule F” and creating a new “Schedule Policy/Career” category, the rule would allow federal employees to be stripped of their civil service protections and reclassified into a category where they can be dismissed without cause. Worse still, it permits existing positions to be involuntarily moved into this category, exposing thousands of public servants to political pressure and retaliation.
Civil servants have long been hired, promoted, and retained based on merit. These protections exist so that professionals can provide their best advice, implement laws, and serve the public without fear of being fired for political reasons. This proposal would undermine that essential principle and create a chilling effect on the workforce. Employees may feel they must choose between doing their jobs with integrity or keeping their jobs altogether.
During my time as a PMF, I saw the immense value of a professional, apolitical civil service. I worked alongside dedicated public servants who brought deep subject-matter expertise and institutional knowledge to their agencies. These are individuals who devoted their careers to making government more efficient, resilient, and accountable. Stripping them of their protections does not reduces performance, and it introduces fear, instability, and partisanship into roles that must remain objective. The fact these long-time civil servants can easily take their experience and relationships to private sector jobs and make double their current salaries but don’t is a testament to the type of people that choose to serve.
The proposed rule fails to provide any real evidence that current civil service rules are inadequate. Agencies already have mechanisms to address underperformance, misconduct, and poor leadership. What this rule would actually do is make it easier for administrations to purge employees for political reasons or ideological disagreements. 

Removing due process protections also increases the risk of abuse. If employees can be demoted or fired without explanation, what is to stop future administrations from targeting individuals who speak out, raise ethical concerns, or resist unlawful orders? That’s not hypothetical, it’s a real risk to institutional integrity and the rule of law.
The proposed rule would also have long-term consequences for recruiting top talent. Why would qualified candidates enter public service if they can be dismissed without cause the moment the political winds shift? Federal agencies already face challenges hiring and retaining specialized professionals; this rule would make that problem worse, not better.
Instead of gutting civil service protections, OPM should focus on constructive reforms. That includes revitalizing institutions like the Federal Executive Institute (FEI), which develop leadership capacity in the federal workforce. Programs like the now defunct Presidential Management Fellows (PMF) and internship programs help bring in the next generation of public servants with diverse backgrounds, new skills, and a commitment to public good. These merit-based hiring pipelines are what strengthen the aging  civil service—not rules that make it more vulnerable to political interference.
OPM should also invest in modernizing performance management systems to ensure fair, efficient, and data-informed evaluations, while preserving employees’ rights to challenge unjust discipline. But reforms should be focused on capacity building, not politicization.
The American civil service has endured because it is professional, independent, and dedicated to implementing the law. It is not meant to shift dramatically with each change in political leadership. This proposed rule would reverse over a century of progress and weaken public institutions and erodes public trust.
In uniform and in government, I served alongside people who prioritized the mission and the Constitution over politics. We need a civil service that can do the same. I urge OPM to withdraw this dangerous and unjustified rule in its entirety and refocus on reforms that build strength, not instability, into the federal workforce.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
To Whom It May Concern:

I write in strong opposition to the proposed rule that would revive or implement any version of Schedule F within the federal civil service. As a career federal employee—and a citizen committed to upholding the values of an impartial, professional, and nonpartisan civil service—I am deeply concerned that this proposal represents an existential threat to the integrity, effectiveness, and continuity of government operations. I urge the Office of Personnel Management to reject this rule in its entirety.

Undermining the Merit System and Nonpartisan Expertise

The foundation of the U.S. civil service is the merit system. The Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 codified principles ensuring that hiring and retention decisions are based on competence, performance, and adherence to the law—not loyalty to political figures or administrations. By enabling the mass reclassification of policy-related positions into Schedule F, the proposed rule subverts these principles and erodes the protection that guards against politicization of the workforce. It invites the dangerous possibility that career professionals may be dismissed or replaced en masse based on ideology or political pressure, rather than merit or performance.

Disruption to Government Continuity and Institutional Knowledge

Federal agencies function efficiently because of the career professionals who bring deep subject-matter expertise, continuity, and institutional knowledge across administrations. Schedule F threatens to strip agencies of this expertise by enabling rapid, large-scale dismissals and replacements. This is not merely a theoretical risk. The short-lived Executive Order 13957 in 2020—rescinded shortly thereafter—made it clear how easily Schedule F could be weaponized for partisan purposes. Even the possibility of such purges will lead to a chilling effect, pushing skilled professionals out of government service and deterring the best and brightest from entering it.

Impairing the Government’s Ability to Serve the Public

The proposed rule would destabilize public trust in federal institutions. Federal employees swear oaths to the Constitution, not to individuals or parties. Allowing political appointees unchecked authority to fire policy-influencing civil servants jeopardizes the ability of agencies to deliver fact-based, consistent, and lawful services to the American public. Moreover, weakening employment protections will lead to increased turnover, decreased morale, and diminished performance—compromising everything from social services to national security.

Lack of Transparency and Oversight

Schedule F lacks sufficient accountability measures. If an agency head can unilaterally reclassify and terminate career employees, this removes key oversight safeguards that are essential in a democratic government. This mechanism could be used to silence dissenting voices, remove whistleblowers, or suppress ethical objections to unlawful actions. Such concentrated power runs contrary to the checks and balances that define our constitutional republic.

Violation of Good Government Principles

This proposed rule stands in direct contradiction to the principles of good governance—namely, transparency, accountability, competency, and impartiality. The civil service was reformed over decades to prevent exactly this type of abuse, after the excesses of the spoils system. Reinstating Schedule F would reverse over a century of progress and make our government less stable, less ethical, and less democratic.

Legal, Operational, and Moral Concerns

This proposal raises significant legal questions regarding the statutory limits of executive power under the Civil Service Reform Act. It also presents massive operational risks by subjecting tens of thousands of roles to sudden reclassification and potential vacancy. The ethical consequences are equally dire: if we teach future generations that government service is contingent upon loyalty to individuals rather than to the rule of law, we dismantle the civic infrastructure of democracy itself.

Conclusion and Request

I urge the Office of Personnel Management and all reviewing bodies to reject this proposed rule and reaffirm their commitment to a merit-based, apolitical civil service. The long-term costs of enacting Schedule F far outweigh any perceived short-term administrative benefits. The American people deserve a government that functions with integrity, competence, and stability—values that Schedule F imperils.

I request that OPM provide a formal response to each of the substantive concerns raised in this comment, in accordance with the requirements of the Administrative Procedure Act.

Title: Comment from Beth Jarosz
Comment:
Comment in Response to Docket No. OPM-2025-0004

I am writing to express my deep concern regarding the effort to reclassify specific federal positions. Reclassification would erode necessary protections for those serving within the federal government and could transform positions which rely on specific expertise into political positions, thus eroding both the quality of work and public trust in the federal government.

My particular expertise is in federal statistics. The proposed rule, “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service,” would call into question the objectivity that both sides of the aisle rely on for key data on the economy, housing, public health, agriculture, transportation, and more. The federal statistical system plays an essential role in improving the lives of all Americans and informs critical policy decisions with evidence that is timely, relevant, and accurate. Federal statistical agencies are particularly vulnerable to the proposed rule for the following reasons:

Politicization: The proposed rule could lead to the politicization of the federal statistical workforce. Official federal statistics clearly influence public policy of all sorts. Thus, a President could classify many statistical agency positions as Policy/Career. Then, leaders could be fired for releasing or planning to release statistics unfavorable to a President’s agenda. They might also face pressure to change methodologies or reveal pre-release information. By making it easier to remove employees if a President determines that they are interfering with his or her policies, it increases the potential for political loyalty to be prioritized over expertise. 

Politicization has had dramatic consequences for statistical agencies and their leaders in other countries, notably Argentina and Greece.

Importance of Trust, Impartiality, Objectivity: Statistical agencies, such as the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Census Bureau, and National Center for Health Statistics, need professional autonomy to provide impartial, objective, reliable data. Professional autonomy is the ability to act independently from political or other undue external influence regarding operations, such as data collection and analysis, staffing, and publications. Erosion of professional autonomy in statistical agencies would undermine their perceived or actual independence, leading to a loss of public trust in the data they produce.

Importance of Norms: The proposed rule would deprioritize and thus weaken the norms that uphold the ethical and professional standards that are critical to the success of statistical agencies. Senior leaders help craft, model, and reinforce norms within their agencies and between their agencies and other parts of the government.  Examples include how agencies interact with staff, data users, data subjects, outside experts, and host agencies. "Principles and Practices for a Federal Statistical Agency" provides examples of these critical norms. Norms reflect and go beyond the laws, rules, and policy directives that govern agencies’ operations. Weaker norms threaten trust, efficient operations, and data quality.

Erosion of Expertise, Loss of Institutional Knowledge, Increased Turnover: Agencies rely on highly specialized professionals, including statisticians, economists, methodologists, and data scientists, who possess unique technical and institutional knowledge and expertise. Statistical agencies would lose experts who see their career paths as less secure and merit-based than before. The loss of experts or frequent turnover in key positions could disrupt agency operations, hinder long-term planning, undermine the agency's ability to fulfill its mission, and impair the quality and accuracy of the data.

Decreased Employee Morale and Productivity: The uncertainty and fear of arbitrary dismissal could negatively impact employee morale, leading to decreased productivity and difficulty in attracting and retaining top talent.

Importance of Modernization, Research, and Data Continuity: To support their missions, statistical agencies must invest in long-term efforts such as extensive research, critical modernization projects, and efforts to ensure data access and continuity. The proposed rule could subject to agencies to changing presidential priorities, which would increase staff turnover and disrupt modernization efforts, measurement of trends, and meaningful research.

In short, the proposed rule poses a significant threat to the effectiveness of all federal agencies--and especially federal statistical agencies. By undermining the principles of merit-based employment and threatening the job security of many career civil servants, the proposed rule could lead to politicization, loss of trust and expertise, decreased morale, and disruption of agency operations--outcomes which would have dire consequences for all Americans, regardless of political affiliation.

The proposed rule to establish the “Schedule Career/Policy” classification is a grave mistake—one that not only threatens the integrity of the federal workforce, but also the foundational principles of American governance. This is not just a personnel matter. It is a constitutional red flag.

Under this rule, broad swaths of civil servants could be reclassified into a vaguely defined category that strips them of their civil service protections. Let’s be clear: this is not about flexibility or modernization. It is about creating a fast-track mechanism for installing political loyalists and removing experts who might speak inconvenient truths.

Such a maneuver is structurally corrosive. It directly undermines the separation of powers by politicizing the very bureaucracy tasked with implementing congressional statutes and overseeing executive accountability. Civil servants are not obstacles—they are safeguards. We have a duty to learn from history. The Pendleton Act of 1883 was enacted to end the spoils system and establish a merit-based civil service. This proposed rule drags us backward toward that era of patronage, cronyism, and institutional instability.

I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety. No responsible government can function if its own employees are afraid to serve with honesty, rigor, and independence.

Title: Comment from Steven Smith
Comment:
I. Introduction

This comment is submitted in strong opposition to any rulemaking or executive policy that would implement or reinstate "Schedule F" as a classification within the federal civil service. Schedule F was first introduced through Executive Order 13957, signed on October 21, 2020, and later revoked by Executive Order 14003 on January 22, 2021. The proposal to reintroduce this classification threatens the apolitical, merit-based principles that are the bedrock of the federal civil service.

II. Legal and Constitutional Concerns

A. Violation of the Merit System Principles

Schedule F contravenes the merit system principles codified in 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b), which require that "employees be selected and advanced solely on the basis of relative ability, knowledge, and skills" and "protected against arbitrary action, personal favoritism, or coercion for partisan political purposes." By placing career civil servants into an at-will employment category based solely on a vague definition of "policy-determining" functions, Schedule F exposes them to politically motivated hiring and firing, contrary to 5 U.S.C. § 2302(b).

B. Erosion of Due Process Rights under the Fifth Amendment

Federal employees in the competitive service possess a constitutionally protected property interest in their continued employment. The Supreme Court has held that due process applies to government employment where individuals have a "legitimate claim of entitlement," rather than a "unilateral expectation" (Board of Regents v. Roth, 408 U.S. 564 (1972); Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 470 U.S. 532, 538 (1985)). By converting employees into an excepted service classification without cause and removing their right to appeal adverse actions to the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB), Schedule F would unlawfully deprive them of these due process protections.

C. Inconsistent with the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978

The Civil Service Reform Act (CSRA), Pub. L. No. 95-454, 92 Stat. 1111 (1978), established a clear framework for federal employment, ensuring a merit-based and politically neutral workforce. The CSRA provides for procedural safeguards and protections against arbitrary removal for career civil servants. Reclassification to Schedule F circumvents this framework and subverts congressional intent, violating the structure and spirit of the Act.

D. Delegation and Separation of Powers Issues

Permitting the Executive Branch to unilaterally redefine broad swaths of civil service roles as Schedule F positions without legislative authorization raises separation of powers concerns. As the D.C. Circuit observed in Humphrey’s Executor v. United States, 295 U.S. 602 (1935), and reaffirmed in Morrison v. Olson, 487 U.S. 654 (1988), Congress may impose limitations on executive control over certain government officials in order to ensure independence and accountability. Schedule F undermines that independence and runs afoul of Congress's constitutional authority under Article I, Section 8 to legislate the structure of the civil service.

III. Policy and Administrative Implications

The federal civil service was designed to serve the public interest, not the political interests of any single administration. The Hatch Act, 5 U.S.C. §§ 7321–7326, further supports this goal by limiting political activity among federal employees. Schedule F encourages politicization by making employment contingent on loyalty to political leadership, thereby eroding public trust in government neutrality.

Reclassifying and potentially removing thousands of employees based on vague policy-related criteria threatens to paralyze agencies, particularly during political transitions. The Government Accountability Office (GAO), in a December 2020 report, warned that Schedule F could lead to "a substantial loss of expertise" and a "chilling effect" on candid advice from civil servants (GAO-21-148R, “Personnel Management: OPM Should Build on Ongoing Oversight Efforts to Ensure Appropriate Use of Special Hiring Authorities,” Dec. 23, 2020).

Schedule F’s implementation would be at odds with Executive Order 12871 (1993) and Executive Order 13781 (2017), which promote performance, accountability, and the strategic use of human capital in the federal workforce. The summary dismissal of experienced personnel without established cause undermines those objectives.

IV. Conclusion

Schedule F threatens the constitutional and statutory foundations of the federal civil service. It would allow for the politicization of career positions, remove due process protections, and violate the Civil Service Reform Act’s merit principles. Congress has long recognized the need for a professional, impartial civil service, and any policy undermining that structure must be rejected. For the reasons cited above, I urge the agency to reject any rulemaking or executive action that would reinstate Schedule F.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I am writing to formally oppose the proposed rule titled Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service (OPM-2025-0004), published in the Federal Register on April 23, 2025. This proposal undermines the constitutional principles of due process and equal protection and revives the discredited spoils system, thereby threatening the stability and integrity of the federal government.

Constitutional Violations

The proposed rule violates the U.S. Constitution in several critical ways:

1. Due Process Concerns: By facilitating the reclassification of career civil servants into the excepted service (Schedule F), the rule removes essential due process protections. This change permits arbitrary dismissal without cause or recourse, infringing upon employees' rights to fair treatment under the Fifth Amendment.


2. Equal Protection Issues: The reclassification disproportionately affects career employees, potentially leading to discriminatory practices based on political affiliation or ideology. Such actions contravene the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, which mandates that no state shall deny any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws.


3. Separation of Powers: The proposed rule grants excessive authority to the executive branch, allowing for unilateral reclassification of positions without legislative oversight. This concentration of power threatens the constitutional balance among the branches of government.



Revival of the Spoils System

The reclassification provisions mirror the historical spoils system, where federal employment was awarded based on political loyalty rather than merit. This system was abolished following the Pendleton Act of 1883 due to its detrimental effects on government efficiency and fairness. The current proposal threatens to undo over a century of progress by:

Political Patronage: Enabling the appointment of individuals based on political connections rather than qualifications, leading to potential incompetence and corruption within federal agencies.

Erosion of Merit-Based Hiring: Undermining the principles established by the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978, which aimed to ensure that federal employment decisions are based on merit and not political considerations.

Instability in Governance: Introducing a cycle of political purges that disrupts continuity and institutional knowledge, essential for effective governance.


Threats to Government Stability

Implementing this rule poses several risks to the stability of the federal government:

Loss of Institutional Knowledge: The arbitrary removal of experienced civil servants disrupts the continuity of government operations and weakens the capacity to respond to crises effectively.

Decreased Public Trust: Perceptions of politicization and unfair treatment diminish public confidence in federal institutions, undermining democratic governance.

Increased Risk of Corruption: Without robust oversight and protections, the reclassification could lead to increased opportunities for unethical conduct and misuse of power.


Conclusion

The proposed rule Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service undermines constitutional protections and revives the outdated and detrimental spoils system. Its implementation would destabilize the federal government and erode public trust. I urge the Office of Personnel Management to withdraw this proposal and uphold the principles of merit-based employment and constitutional integrity.

Thank you for considering this comment.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I strongly oppose the implementation or revival of the “Schedule F” classification for federal employees. This proposal threatens the merit-based civil service system that has underpinned a professional, nonpartisan federal workforce for over a century.

First and foremost, the creation of Schedule F directly undermines the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which was enacted to combat the spoils system and establish a merit-based hiring process for federal employees. By allowing a broad swath of career civil servants—particularly those involved in policy-making or analysis—to be reclassified and potentially terminated without cause, Schedule F opens the door to politically motivated hiring and firing. This is antithetical to the principle of an apolitical civil service enshrined in 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8), which mandates that federal employment decisions be based on merit and free from political influence.

Moreover, the vague and sweeping criteria for inclusion in Schedule F violate the due process protections guaranteed by 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which requires cause and procedural safeguards for the removal of career federal employees. Stripping thousands of workers of these protections not only weakens accountability but also risks chilling expert advice and dissent within agencies—undermining the very effectiveness of government operations.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is also bound by 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to support the merit system principles. Implementing Schedule F contradicts this statutory mission and places undue political pressure on career professionals, compromising the integrity and continuity of federal programs across administrations.

In conclusion, the Schedule F proposal poses a grave threat to the foundational principles of good governance, civil service independence, and the rule of law. I urge the administration and OPM to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement or revive this dangerous classification.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
The proposed rule suffers from fundamental inconsistencies and lacks evidentiary support. While OPM claims the rule will enhance accountability by easing the removal of career employees, citing supervisors’ alleged difficulties addressing underperformance, its practical effect would be to strip due process protections primarily from policy-oriented employees, not the lower-level employees purportedly "hard to fire." Notably, many reclassified positions under this rule are supervisory (e.g., GS-14/15 policy advisors), contradicting its stated goal of targeting non-performing staff. This misalignment raises questions about the rule’s true objectives.

1. Arbitrary Distinction Between Policy and Non-Policy Roles
The rule’s bifurcation of employees into "policy" and "non-policy" categories is legally and logically untenable:

2. No Empirical Basis: OPM provides no evidence that non-policy employees are inherently more responsive to supervisors or that policy roles require weaker protections. This violates basic principles of reasoned rulemaking under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), which prohibits arbitrary agency action (Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 [1983]).

3. Vague and Overbroad Definitions: The term "policy position" is undefined in the rule, creating confusion. For example, would frontline ICE officers implementing border policies be "policy" staff? Would NIH scientists directing research priorities? This ambiguity invites inconsistent application and abuse.

4. Equal Protection Concerns: By creating a two-tiered system where some employees retain appeal rights (e.g., administrative staff) while others lose them (e.g., regulatory analysts), the rule risks violating the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause and merit system principles (5 U.S.C. § 2301(b), which prohibit arbitrary treatment of federal employees.

5. Flawed Alternatives to Genuine Accountability
- OPM’s approach ignores proven solutions to accountability challenges:

6. Managerial Training: The Government Accountability Office (GAO) has repeatedly found that agencies struggle with performance management due to inadequate supervisor training (GAO-21-518). Yet OPM proposes no investment in this area.

7. MSPB Backlog: The Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB)—the adjudicatory body for employee appeals—has been rendered dysfunctional by chronic understaffing. Instead of restoring MSPB’s capacity (per *5 U.S.C. § 1201*), OPM seeks to circumvent due process altogether.

8. Politicization Risk and Legal Vulnerabilities
The rule’s selective targeting of policy staff risks violating the Civil Service Reform Act’s (CSRA) prohibition on personnel actions based on "political affiliation" (5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(1)). By making policy employees at-will, the rule could enable administrations to purge disfavored viewpoints—precisely the harm the CSRA’s merit protections were designed to prevent. Courts have struck down similar attempts to erode civil service safeguards (AFGE v. Trump, 929 F.3d 748 [D.C. Cir. 2019]).

Recommendations
OPM should:
-Withdraw this rule and conduct a rigorous workforce analysis to identify actual barriers to accountability.
-Invest in supervisor training and MSPB staffing to address performance management lawfully.
-Define "policy position" with specificity if retained, ensuring it cannot be applied arbitrarily.
-This proposal undermines the apolitical civil service. OPM must pursue reforms grounded in evidence—not ideology.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I strongly oppose the implementation or revival of the “Schedule F” classification for federal employees. This proposal threatens the merit-based civil service system that has underpinned a professional, nonpartisan federal workforce for over a century.

First and foremost, the creation of Schedule F directly undermines the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which was enacted to combat the spoils system and establish a merit-based hiring process for federal employees. By allowing a broad swath of career civil servants—particularly those involved in policy-making or analysis—to be reclassified and potentially terminated without cause, Schedule F opens the door to politically motivated hiring and firing. This is antithetical to the principle of an apolitical civil service enshrined in 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8), which mandates that federal employment decisions be based on merit and free from political influence.

Moreover, the vague and sweeping criteria for inclusion in Schedule F violate the due process protections guaranteed by 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which requires cause and procedural safeguards for the removal of career federal employees. Stripping thousands of workers of these protections not only weakens accountability but also risks chilling expert advice and dissent within agencies—undermining the very effectiveness of government operations.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is also bound by 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to support the merit system principles. Implementing Schedule F contradicts this statutory mission and places undue political pressure on career professionals, compromising the integrity and continuity of federal programs across administrations.

In conclusion, the Schedule F proposal poses a grave threat to the foundational principles of good governance, civil service independence, and the rule of law. I urge the administration and OPM to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement or revive this dangerous classification.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Contradicts Precedent in National Treasury Employees Union v. MSPB, 743 F.2d 895 (D.C. Cir. 1984)

In NTEU v. MSPB, the D.C. Circuit emphasized that performance-based actions must be based on clearly articulated standards. This rule blurs those standards, enabling removals based on vague or shifting metrics, raising serious legal concerns.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Inconsistent with Veterans’ Preference Rights (5 U.S.C. § 2108 and § 7701)

Veterans’ preference laws require special treatment in hiring and adverse actions. The rule’s fast-track removal process for poor performance may disproportionately affect veterans without appropriate review, violating federal veterans’ protections and triggering heightened scrutiny.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Erodes the Independence of Scientific and Policy Experts

This rule threatens the independence of civil servants in agencies like FDA, EPA, and NIH by facilitating removal for political dissent. The 2009 Scientific Integrity Memorandum and subsequent agency policies require that federal scientific decision-making be protected from political interference—this rule directly contravenes those mandates.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Disregards Legislative Intent Behind Civil Service Reform Act of 1978

The Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 was a bipartisan effort to balance accountability with fair treatment and due process. Congress rejected proposals similar to the current rule, demonstrating that the legislative intent was to retain procedural safeguards—not reduce them.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Opens the Door to Patronage and Cronyism

The proposed rule facilitates removal based on subjective assessments, which revives the spoils system that civil service reform sought to eliminate. The Supreme Court in Elrod v. Burns, 427 U.S. 347 (1976), recognized that patronage dismissals violate First Amendment rights. This rule risks First Amendment violations on a broad scale.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is also bound by 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to support the merit system principles. The proposed rule jeopardizes this foundation by granting political leadership sweeping power to reclassify technical experts into an at-will employment status, stripping them of civil service protections and leaving them vulnerable to political pressure or termination for doing nothing more than reporting objective facts.
