Title: Comment from Sheryl & Brad Hoekstra
Comment:
On the surface, the rule claims it will make removing poor performers easier. But the reality is far more dangerous. This will open the door to political purges of career experts who have served the American people across administrations of both parties.

This would undo more than 140 years of civil service protections that began after the ratification of the Pendleton Act of 1883. Before this act was implemented, American politics operated on the spoils system. This allowed officeholders to give their allies government jobs in return for financial and political support.

History and global experience show us the risks:

A spoils system will result in widespread corruption and inefficiency.
Hungary's governmental takeover of the civil service after 2010 led to democratic backsliding.
Political control over public administration and the judiciary in Poland triggered EU sanctions for rule-of-law violations.
Even in the U.S, watchdog groups have warned that politicizing the bureaucracy harms government performance and erodes public trust. Good governance requires accountability and protections against political retaliation. This proposal forgets the second half of that equation.

Nobody disputes the need for accountability. However, accountability must be balanced with protections against political retaliation. Otherwise, you risk trading professional performance for partisan loyalty. This is precisely what civil service reforms were designed to prevent.

Before the Pendleton Act, the “at-will” system led to massive instability, patronage hiring, inefficiency, and even presidential assassination. History teaches that merit protections were not a luxury but necessary survival reforms.

Hiring procedures matter, but without protections after hire, employees will be judged based on loyalty, not competence. Even the best hires can be fired for politically inconvenient opinions without meaningful job security.

Procedures can be reformed without destroying basic protections. Congress can act to streamline discipline without reverting to a 19th-century spoils system.

This proposal is not “surgical reform,” it is a demolition.

This rule doesn’t fix the civil service, it guts it. It would turn a system built to serve the Constitution into one built to serve the man in power. That is not accountability, that's autocracy.

Senior leaders help craft, model and reinforce norms within their agencies and between their agencies and other parts of the government.  Examples include how agencies interact with staff, data users, data subjects, outside experts and host agencies. See Principles and Practices for a Federal Statistical Agency for examples of these critical norms. These norms reflect and go beyond the laws, rules, and policy directives that govern agencies’ operations. Weaker norms threaten trust, efficient operations, and data quality.

    Erosion of Expertise, Loss of Institutional Memory and Increase of Turnover: These agencies rely on highly specialized professionals, including statisticians, economists, and data scientists, who possess unique technical expertise and long-term institutional memory. Statistical agencies stand to lose experts who see their career paths as less secure and merit-based than before. The loss of these experts or frequent turnover in key positions could disrupt agency operations, hinder long-term planning, undermine the agency's ability to fulfill its mission, and impair the quality and accuracy of the data.

    Decreased Employee Morale and Productivity: The uncertainty and fear of arbitrary dismissal could negatively impact employee morale, leading to decreased productivity and difficulty in attracting and retaining top talent.

    Importance of Modernization, Research, and Data Continuity: To support their missions, statistical agencies must invest in long-term efforts such as extensive research, critical modernization projects, and efforts to ensure data access and continuity. Schedule Policy/Career could subject to agencies to changing presidential priorities, increasing senior staff turnover and disrupting modernization efforts, measurement of trends, and meaningful research.

Schedule Policy/Career poses a significant threat to the effectiveness of federal statistical agencies and to the integrity and quality of their products. By undermining the principles of merit-based employment and threatening job security of senior career civil servants, Schedule Policy/Career could lead to politicization, loss of trust and expertise, decreased morale, and disruption of agency operations. On behalf of U.S. businesses, the American public, and policymakers I am speaking up to protect the trustworthiness of the federal statistics we all rely on.

Title: Comment from Sarah Ferrency
Comment:
Subject: Comments on Proposed OPM Rule: Protection of the Federal Workforce (Docket ID OPM-2025-0004, RIN 3206-AO80)

To the Office of Personnel Management,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule concerning the protection of the federal workforce, identified as Docket ID OPM-2025-0004 and RIN 3206-AO80.

The existing civil service protections are vital for cultivating and maintaining a skilled and experienced federal workforce. These protections are not arbitrary; they serve to ensure stability, encourage dedicated public service careers, and safeguard the institutional knowledge that is critical for effective governance. Federal employees often possess deep expertise and a long-term perspective gained from serving across multiple administrations. This historical context and understanding of how and why policies, regulations, and decisions were made are invaluable assets to their respective agencies and the government as a whole.

I am particularly concerned by recent accounts of abrupt staffing changes and questionable dismissal practices, including the reported use of automated processes leading to the termination of probationary employees without apparent regard for individual performance. Such actions undermine morale, disrupt agency functions, and raise serious doubts about the fairness and transparency of personnel decisions when established procedures are bypassed.

The current framework, including rights under Chapters 43 and 75, already provides mechanisms for addressing poor performance or misconduct. Employees facing accusations should retain their fundamental right to due process and the ability to appeal adverse actions. Removing these protections, as the proposed rule appears to facilitate, risks granting excessive and potentially easily abused power to the executive branch, regardless of the administration in office.

I urge OPM to abandon this proposed rule change and maintain the current civil service protections. Implementing changes akin to a "Schedule F" would be detrimental to the effectiveness, impartiality, and stability of the federal workforce and, by extension, the services provided to the American public.

Sincerely,

Sarah Ferrency

Title: Comment from Gail Kouril
Comment:
I strongly oppose the implementation or revival of the “Schedule F” classification for federal employees. This proposal threatens the merit-based civil service system that has underpinned a professional, nonpartisan federal workforce for over a century.

First and foremost, the creation of Schedule F directly undermines the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which was enacted to combat the spoils system and establish a merit-based hiring process for federal employees. By allowing a broad swath of career civil servants—particularly those involved in policy-making or analysis—to be reclassified and potentially terminated without cause, Schedule F opens the door to politically motivated hiring and firing. This is antithetical to the principle of an apolitical civil service enshrined in 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8), which mandates that federal employment decisions be based on merit and free from political influence.

Moreover, the vague and sweeping criteria for inclusion in Schedule F violate the due process protections guaranteed by 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which requires cause and procedural safeguards for the removal of career federal employees. Stripping thousands of workers of these protections not only weakens accountability but also risks chilling expert advice and dissent within agencies—undermining the very effectiveness of government operations.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is also bound by 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to support the merit system principles. Implementing Schedule F contradicts this statutory mission and places undue political pressure on career professionals, compromising the integrity and continuity of federal programs across administrations.

In conclusion, the Schedule F proposal poses a grave threat to the foundational principles of good governance, civil service independence, and the rule of law. I urge the administration and OPM to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement or revive this dangerous classification.

Please do not implement this.

Thank you.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
OPM presents this proposed rule as necessary for “accountability” and “democratic responsiveness.” It does exactly the opposite. Removing due process protections, making employees at-will, subjects them to being removed for any and all reasons. Error, favoritism, bigotry, retaliation, cronyism, corruption, ignorance of what an employee does, or mere whim on the part of any manager could result in the sudden, unjust and unreviewable termination of civil service careers. This does not just deprive workers of fair treatment; it deprives citizens of receiving the services they deserve from a properly qualified civil service.

Currently, federal employees have some protections for calling out waste, fraud and abuse committed by employees and managers senior to them. In contrast, employees who could be fired for any reason, including by a manager who wishes to cover up his own wrongdoing, become vulnerable to threats, intimidation, and retaliation. Citizens would suffer, because the higher a wasteful or corrupt official is placed in an organization, the more severe the impacts on society that official can inflict. Government services would be increasingly negatively impacted. 

Therefore, this proposed rule does not advance accountability, but destroys accountability. It makes the government less democratically responsive to the needs of citizens by concentrating all power in the hands of a few at the top.

There are already many, many procedures in place to hold employees accountable, including probationary periods; performance reviews; codes of conduct and discipline; and two different sections of the existing US Code (Title 5, Chapters 43 and 75). Any of these tools could be streamlined by the administration if necessary. Considering the huge investment the government makes in interviewing, hiring, onboarding, and training new employees, termination should not be done lightly or quickly; ensuring that terminations occur under due process is simply a wise use of taxpayer dollars.

The idea that the civil service is filled with disloyal operatives eager to resist a Presidential agenda is unfounded. The civil service is politically diverse, despite myths and rumors to the contrary, and most civil servants end up working for presidents of both major parties, ensuring a continuity of basic services. Over the last 50 years, the president’s party has changed eight times (1977, 1981, 1993, 2001, 2009, 2017, 2021, and 2025); the government’s work proceeded nonetheless, without revolt from the federal service. Civil servants take an oath to the country, not to an individual leader; they are bound to follow the laws of the land. Federal workers are not even allowed to strike, under current law. They must follow orders, with only rare and extreme exceptions; otherwise they are subject to disciplinary action for insubordination. Even those employees covered by a union contract are expected to “obey first and grieve later;” in other words, the Presidential agenda is not delayed, and any halts to it come not from the employees, but from disinterested oversight such as the judiciary. In the past few decades, the main cause of delays in government effectiveness have actually come from the chronic underfunding of agencies and long, repeated cycles of hiring freezes.

Due process in the civil service enhances the quality, morale, efficiency and effectiveness of a workforce, the stewardship of government resources, the provision of services, and the accountability of the government.

They are our friends, neighbors and family members, and they do important work in support of communities across this nation. 

There ARE legitimate ways of reducing the ranks of Federal service that are fair and equitable and have been successfully accomplished under previous administrations. And there are other ways to smartly accomplish your objectives; for example, why on earth didn’t you start with termination of people who are known poor-performers and are already on a PIP (performance improvement plan)? In contrast, the way you are going about this is destructive, demeaning, and demoralizing, not to mention counterproductive to the goals of our esteemed nation. In some cases, what you are doing is downright dangerous to the life and wellbeing of Americans. Do you realize this? Do you care?

Treatment of contractors has also been unacceptable, and last week’s no-warning firing of all the Americorps volunteers, who work for a year for almost nothing (~$8,000 for 10 months) to invest in our communities and advance our nation’s goals, is also deplorable. These support staff are especially vital to rural communities, where opportunities are limited, and cost the Federal government almost nothing. The Americorps volunteer program also provides an important entry point for young people to learn and grow their careers. The government should be encouraging this sort of practice if it is concerned about spending, instead of firing everyone without warning.

Please seriously reconsider your thinking, especially this odd paranoia surrounding Federal employees, and do some research about the proper and legal way to accomplish a Federal downsizing process to more effectively and efficiently accomplish your aims. I strongly encourage you to truly prioritize the best interests of the country and the American people, and immediately reverse position concerning these unacceptable proposed changes to Schedule F employees!

Title: Comment from Denise Jackson
Comment:
Office of Personnel Management
1900 E Street N.W.
Washington, DC 20415

Re:  “Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service,” Proposed Rule, 90 Fed. Reg. 17182, Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004

Dear Office of Personnel Management

I write in strong opposition to the proposed rule titled “Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service.” This regulation would dangerously erode the merit-based foundation of the federal civil service by removing critical due process protections and opening the door to politically motivated firings. It lacks sufficient factual justification and poses significant risks to the effectiveness, integrity, and public trust in federal agencies.
As a member of the public who directly relies on the services of agencies like the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), I am deeply concerned about the consequences of this proposal. NOAA plays a critical role in delivering accurate weather forecasts, supporting coastal navigation, monitoring water quality, and ensuring preparedness for extreme weather events. Weakening protections for NOAA’s career staff would reduce the agency’s capacity to deliver reliable, science-based services that communities like mine depend on for safety, infrastructure planning, and economic stability.
If civil servants are no longer hired or retained based primarily on expertise, the impacts will be far-reaching. Permitting processes could become politicized or delayed, local water quality oversight could be compromised, and tourism and recreational activities—so often dependent on accurate environmental data—could suffer. The public expects and deserves knowledgeable professionals guiding these essential processes, not a revolving door of politically aligned appointees.
Furthermore, civil servants must be free to voice professional opinions, particularly in emergency situations like hurricanes, tsunamis, or high tide flooding events. If the proposed rule creates a chilling effect—where scientists and experts fear discipline or termination for delivering inconvenient truths to agency leadership—public safety and preparedness will suffer. The consequences of silencing expert judgment during crises are not hypothetical; they are matters of life and death.
The proposed rule also lacks the evidentiary basis necessary for such sweeping changes. There is no clear or compelling data presented to justify why existing civil service protections hinder accountability or responsiveness. Nor does the rule offer a rigorous impact assessment of how this shift would affect federal performance, public service delivery, or employee morale. In the absence of this information, the rule appears ideologically motivated rather than grounded in evidence or the public interest.
Congress established the merit-based civil service to ensure that federal employees serve the public based on expertise, not political loyalty. The proposed rule undermines this foundational principle and jeopardizes the competence, continuity, and nonpartisan nature of our federal workforce.
For these reasons, I urge you to withdraw the proposed rule and uphold the integrity of the career civil service. The American people deserve a government staffed by experts who are protected in their roles—not punished for their professionalism.

Denise Jackson

Title: Comment from Scott Imberman
Comment:
5/5/2025

RE: Public Comment in Response to Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service [Docket No. OPM–2025–0004]

I am writing to express my deep concern regarding the effort to reclassify specific federal positions, which would erode necessary protections for those serving within the federal statistical system and could transform positions which rely on specific expertise to political ones. The proposed rule, “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service,” would call into question the objectivity that both sides of the aisle rely on for our economic indicators, public health assessments, energy utilization and many other statistics. The federal statistical system plays an essential role in improving the lives of all Americans as well as informing critical policy decisions with evidence that is timely, relevant, and accurate. Federal statistical agencies are particularly vulnerable to the proposed rule due to the following:

Politicization: Schedule Policy/Career could lead to the politicization of the federal statistical workforce. Official federal statistics clearly influence public policy of all sorts: monetary, fiscal, regulatory, etc. Thus, a President could classify many statistical agency positions as Policy/Career. Then, for example, Bureau of Labor Statistics’ leaders could be fired for releasing or planning to release jobs or inflation statistics unfavorable to the President’s policy agenda. They might also face pressure to change methodologies or reveal pre-release information. By making it easier to remove employees if a President determines that they are interfering with his or her policies, it increases the potential for passivity or political loyalty to be prioritized over expertise and experience.

Importance of Trust, Impartiality and Objectivity: Statistical agencies, such as the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Census Bureau, and the National Center for Health Statistics, need professional autonomy to provide impartial, objective, reliable data. Professional autonomy is the ability to act independently from political or other undue external influence regarding its operations, such as data collection and analysis, staffing, and publications. Erosion of professional autonomy in the operations of statistical agencies would undermine their perceived or actual independence, leading to a loss of public trust in the data they produce.

Importance of Norms: Schedule Policy/Career would deprioritize and thus weaken the norms that uphold the ethical and professional standards that are critical to the success of statistical agencies. Senior leaders help craft, model and reinforce norms within their agencies and between their agencies and other parts of the government.  Examples include how agencies interact with staff, data users, data subjects, outside experts and host agencies. See Principles and Practices for a Federal Statistical Agency for examples of these critical norms. These norms reflect and go beyond the laws, rules, and policy directives that govern agencies’ operations. Weaker norms threaten trust, efficient operations, and data quality.

Erosion of Expertise, Loss of Institutional Memory and Increase of Turnover: These agencies rely on highly specialized professionals, including statisticians, economists, and data scientists, who possess unique technical expertise and long-term institutional memory. Statistical agencies stand to lose experts who see their career paths as less secure and merit-based than before. The loss of these experts or frequent turnover in key positions could disrupt agency operations, hinder long-term planning, undermine the agency's ability to fulfill its mission.

Importance of Modernization, Research, and Data Continuity: To support their missions, statistical agencies must invest in long-term efforts such as extensive research, critical modernization projects, and efforts to ensure data access and continuity. Schedule Policy/Career could subject to agencies to changing presidential priorities, increasing senior staff turnover and disrupting modernization efforts, measurement of trends, and meaningful research.

Schedule Policy/Career poses a significant threat to the effectiveness of federal statistical agencies and to the integrity and quality of their products. By undermining the principles of merit-based employment and threatening job security of senior career civil servants, Schedule Policy/Career could lead to politicization, loss of trust and expertise, decreased morale, and disruption of agency operations. On behalf of U.S. businesses, the American public, and policymakers I am speaking up to protect the trustworthiness of the federal statistics we all rely on.

Scott Imberman
Professor of Economics
Michigan State University

Title: Comment from Bill Maurer
Comment:
Public Comment on OPM-2025-0004 (RIN 3206-AO80)
Opposition to Proposed Rule As Undermining Scientific Integrity In Governance and Civil Service Protections

I submit this comment as a United States citizen in my personal capacity, strongly opposing the Office of Personnel Management’s proposed rule (OPM-2025-0004 RIN 3206-AO80), which would open the door to reclassifying tens of thousands of federal civil servants into a new category of political appointees, effectively reviving the previously rejected Schedule F proposal. While framed as a matter of administrative flexibility and accountability, the rule poses a clear threat to the merit-based federal workforce, weakening civil service protections, inviting political interference, and destabilizing the institutional and scientific expertise on which sound governance depends.

I write from the perspective of someone who has worked at the intersection of science and public policy for many years, including service on the Board on Behavioral, Cognitive and Sensory Sciences of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. My work has involved evaluating scientific evidence in service of federal decision-making, including contributing to reports such as Measuring Human Capabilities: An Agenda for Basic Research on the Assessment of Individual and Group Performance Potential for Military Accession (2015). That effort exemplified the importance of unbiased, rigorous science in informing national priorities—particularly when those decisions affect military readiness, resource allocation, and long-term strategic planning. This is just one example from among many, and I am sure there are thousands of scientists with similar stories of the importance of the need for evidence-based science to inform crucial government decisions without regard for political party or ideology.

This proposed rule is deeply troubling. Just focusing on its impact on scientific integrity: It would dilute the definition and enforcement of scientific integrity across agencies, remove key safeguards against political interference, and create an environment in which federal science can be manipulated or suppressed based on ideological pressures rather than empirical evidence. These changes are not administrative clarifications—they are structural erosions of one of the most critical pillars of evidence-based governance.

What this rule effectively does is open the door to politicization of science in government decision-making, pressuring researchers, under the threat of losing their jobs, to go where the politics of the day lead them rather than what the evidence says. But the implications extend further. Reintroducing Schedule F classification for federal employees is fundamentally at odds with the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act. That Act was designed to protect public servants from being hired or fired based on political loyalty, ensuring that government functions are carried out by professionals selected for their qualifications and commitment to public service. Undermining these protections will lead to higher turnover, a shrinking pool of qualified applicants, weakened institutional memory, and ultimately a degradation in the quality of service provided to the American people—not only in science, but across every area where civil servants play a role.

I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule and reaffirm its commitment to a nonpartisan, expert-led federal workforce and to scientific integrity as a cornerstone of evidence-informed policymaking. Americans deserve governance rooted in facts, expertise, and public accountability.

Respectfully submitted,
Bill Maurer
Former Board Member, Board on Behavioral, Cognitive and Sensory Sciences, National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I write to strongly oppose the proposed regulation titled Improving Performance,
Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service (Docket ID: OPM–2025–0004). This
regulation, which seeks to establish a new "Schedule Policy/Career" classification within
the excepted service, is a direct threat to the integrity, independence, and democratic
foundation of the U.S. civil service.
This proposal is not a minor administrative adjustment; it is a sweeping and dangerous
transformation of how federal personnel are hired, retained, and dismissed. Below are five
critical reasons why this rule must be withdrawn.
1. Erosion of Due Process and Merit Protections
This rule would strip thousands of federal employees, those deemed to have “policy-
influencing” responsibilities, of their due process rights and protections under Title 5. Civil
servants who have built their careers on impartiality, subject-matter expertise, and service
to the public would become at-will employees, vulnerable to removal without cause or the
right to appeal. This is antithetical to the merit-based foundation of the modern federal
workforce.
2. Politicization of the Civil Service
By granting the President sweeping authority to reclassify roles into this new category, the
regulation politicizes positions that are meant to remain nonpartisan. From grant managers
to scientists, public affairs officers to regulatory analysts, a broad range of professionals
could be terminated based on political disagreement, not job performance.
This violates key provisions of:
• 5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(1): which prohibits personnel actions based on political
affiliation;
• 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8): which requires that employees be protected against partisan
political coercion.
The rule threatens to dismantle the separation between neutral career service and political
appointees, reverting the government to a pre-Pendleton Act "spoils system." This
concentration of power in the executive branch is incompatible with democratic principles
and opens the door to loyalty tests, purges, and the erosion of public trust in government.
3. Threat to Whistleblowers and Good Governance
Employees in the “Schedule Policy/Career” category may no longer be protected under the
Whistleblower Protection Act if deemed to be in policy-determining roles. This rule could
disqualify thousands of employees from legal recourse after disclosing waste, fraud, or
abuse.
4. Undermining Checks and Balances
The proposed rule not only dismantles protections for civil servants but also alters the
balance of power between the branches of government, weakening core institutions
designed to enforce lawful governance and prevent abuse. By granting the Executive
Branch broad authority to unilaterally reclassify federal roles into “Schedule Policy/Career,”
the regulation effectively bypasses Congress, undermines existing statutory frameworks,
and eliminates essential institutional safeguards. It expands executive power over
personnel in a way that threatens the independence of key administrative bodies, including
the Merit Systems Protection Board and federal adjudicators. This action centralizes power
in the hands of the President in a way that is inconsistent with the constitutional principle
of separation of powers.
These actions contradict the constitutional separation of powers and threaten the impartial
administration of law. A civil service beholden to one branch’s political will is incompatible
with a system designed for checks, accountability, and balance. This not only
compromises individual rights, but also damages the institutional framework that supports
fair and impartial governance.
5. Another Step Toward Authoritarianism
This proposal sets a precedent that is historically associated with autocratic regimes:
eliminating dissent by targeting those who enforce the law and provide independent
analysis. This rule represents a systemic move toward autocracy. A government where civil
servants can be dismissed for political misalignment is a government that no longer
operates under democratic norms. This mirrors the dangerous practices of authoritarian
regimes that replace expertise with loyalty and suppress dissent through fear. It effectively
creates a system where public servants must choose between loyalty to the Constitution
and loyalty to a political leader; a choice no American should ever be forced to make.
What begins as a regulatory change becomes a gateway to an executive branch unbound
by institutional or legal restraint. The Constitution does not grant the President king-like
powers to purge the civil service. It is Congress that has the authority to structure federal

turned into a partisan loyalty game.

Respectfully,

Title: Comment from Allison Eddy
Comment:
I am writing in opposition to OPM’s Proposed Rule: Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service. As a private attorney who has spent my legal career exclusively representing federal employees in employment matters, I cannot help but deduce that the title of this proposed rule is the exact opposite of what the actual results will be if the proposed rule is implemented.

Federal employees are public servants who are subject to the rigorous salary caps imposed by the federal government. They do not work in public service for fame or fortune; rather, the stability and job security traditionally associated with government employment tend to be major draws for hard-working, high-performing individuals to work in civil service. By removing appeal rights and other due process protections from a potentially sizeable segment of federal jobs, those hard-working, high-performing individuals who were willing to trade high-salary private sector jobs for the stability of government service will undoubtedly look elsewhere for work. 

As noted in the Proposed Rule, if the proposed rule is implemented, there will be no need for employees in Schedule Policy/Career jobs to serve a probationary or trial period, because, in essence, the entirety of their government career will be spent in a probationary period, in which they are constantly at risk of being terminated for no reason whatsoever, without any viable recourse. While the operation of government services has benefited greatly from career civil service employees who have become experts in their respective fields based on years of training and experience in their jobs, moving these employees to at-will employment categories will surely lead to a huge amount of turnover of many of the best and brightest civil servants. Employees in these positions will surely be constantly applying for and seeking other jobs that either afford them more job security or that pay higher salaries.  

In addition to the foreseeable problems in recruiting and retaining high-performing individuals to these Schedule Policy/Career jobs, the act of moving jobs into a category in which the incumbents have no appeal or other due process rights will have the effect of removing vital accountability mechanisms that are necessary to ensuring merit-based hiring and firing actions among federal government employees. For instance, if a supervisor of a Schedule Policy/Career employee decides they would like to hire their friend or family member into a subordinate position, that supervisor could simply fire a high-performing incumbent subordinate employee without cause and without any recourse, in order to make a position available for potentially hiring the friend or family member. Because the fired employee would not have an appeal right to challenge their removal, there would be no mechanism to hold the supervisor accountable for firing the employee as a flex of power rather than based on any sort of sound reasoning. Without accountability over supervisors’ actions, there will be no shortage of ill-advised firing decisions within these Schedule Policy/Career positions, as supervisors will be free to ignore merit principles and make such decisions based on personal feelings rather than merit. 

By its very nature, removing employees’ due process rights does not “improve accountability;” rather, it removes accountability. Moving certain positions from the competitive service to excepted service is one thing; entirely removing the appeal and due process rights the employees in such positions would have otherwise had available to them is something completely different. Such an extreme action will do nothing to improve performance and accountability among our federal workforce; in contrast, removing the job security traditionally associated with federal government jobs will remove accountability all together and will deter and drive away high-performing individuals from government service.

Title: Comment from R T
Comment:
I never imagined I’d have to write a public comment asking my own government not to create a political loyalty test for federal employment—but here we are.

The proposed “Schedule Career/Policy” rule is a bureaucratic trapdoor, designed to quietly convert impartial public service into partisan machinery. It’s Schedule F with a fresh coat of paint—and the paint is still wet enough to smear all over the Constitution.

I work in a technical capacity for the federal government. I analyze data, advise on outcomes, and try—like thousands of others—to give elected officials the clearest, most honest picture of what their policies will do. I don’t write policy. I inform it. And now, apparently, that makes me a potential target for reclassification and termination if someone decides I’m “too close to the policy process” or “not aligned with the agenda.”

This isn’t about accountability. This is about control.

Let’s talk about what this rule really says to federal workers: If you're smart, careful, and grounded in facts—but your work challenges a political narrative—you’re disposable. If you flag a legal risk, you're disloyal. If your scientific finding contradicts a talking point, you're a problem. If you express professional judgment, you're out of line.

This isn’t civil service reform. It’s civil service purging, written in HR language.

And let’s also acknowledge the absurdity here: “Schedule Career/Policy” is a category that’s defined so vaguely it might as well include anyone with an opinion and a government email address. It’s like calling every mechanic a “policy influencer” because fixing the brakes affects how fast the car can go.

This rule creates fear. It undermines the value of expertise. It erodes the internal culture of honesty, where professionals can challenge assumptions or raise red flags without wondering if that day’s email will be their last.

No one with a straight face can call this democratic governance.

If this rule takes effect, it will hollow out the federal workforce. Talented people will leave—or never join. Those who remain will be forced to muzzle themselves. The result won’t be a government that works better. It will be a government that lies better.

I urge you in the strongest possible terms: Withdraw this rule. Don’t destroy the civil service to score political points. You won’t just break the system—you’ll lose the people who were holding it together.

Title: Comment from Julia Boonelal
Comment:
This proposed rule's justifications are invalid. There already exist politically-appointed positions within federal agencies, to which the President is given free reign to install an appointee at will. These politically-appointed positions are empowered to oversee the implementation of Presidential priorities for their agencies. Why, in addition to these political appointments, which make up approximately 4,000 positions throughout the government, is there still a need to create a new position type which allows at-will employment and eliminates employee protections? The stated reasons include the need to remove employees within "policy-influencing" positions without the ability to appeal a removal. The merit systems protections allow employees to appeal their removal - it doesn't prevent the removal. Why is it important to remove an employee with "policy-influencing" duties without the merit systems protections? It seems important to this administration to create political appointments at will. Given that we have separate political appointments for a good reason (separation of powers being a huge one), there is no justification for creating what is essentially a political appointment in the federal civil service pool. Also, this rule offers no clear limitation on the President's ability to transform federal positions as they see fit, since you could make an argument that any federal government position has some policy influence of some kind. This needs to be way more specific about what type of employee should qualify for this new position that is stripped of appeal protections; otherwise it's going to expose the entire federal workforce as subject to politicization. We don't live in a monarchy where the President is the sole decision-maker about the federal workforce. 

As to the argument in this rule about supervisors not being able to fire employees, I don't think that's a valid concern. Federal supervisors are perfectly capable of terminating employees who aren't performing their duties adequately or are engaging in malfeasance, etc., so if individual supervisors purport to be having issues with that, they should be addressed case by case, or the root of the trouble with the current standard which creates hardships for supervisors should be addressed, without removing all employee protections. Instead of taking those reasonable steps, this rule proposes throwing it all out in favor of at-will employment, which takes away all employee protections, including Prohibited Personnel Practices such as retaliation against whistleblowing. These are important protections that all civil service employees should have.

To summarize - there's no justification for removing federal civil service positions' employment protections in favor of at-will employment simply for having a "policy-influencing" role. There are already politically-appointed positions throughout the federal government to aid in implementing the President's agenda, while being balanced by statutorily-mandated agencies and their workforce who are at the service of the US Constitution.

Title: Comment from Douglas Lippoldt
Comment:

Office of Personnel Management
1900 E Street, N.W.
Washington, DC 20415

Proposed Rule, 90 Fed. Reg. 17182, Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004

Dear Office of Personnel Management:

I, Douglas Lippoldt, submit these comments regarding Office of Personnel Management’s (OPM) Proposed Rule “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service, ” 90 Fed. Reg. 17182 (April 23, 2025). I write to express opposition to the Proposed Rule.

This proposed rule is relevant to me as a former US Civil Servant myself, as a beneficiary of Federal Services across many agencies (eg, as a user of parks, healthcare, taxpayer services, etc), and as a Federal Pensioner. I am also an economist with decades of service including with respect to labor market issues.

Federal law has long said that civil servants must be hired, promoted, and retained based on merit—basically: expertise, not political loyalty. Civil servants have had certain protections that have ensured they could exercise their best professional judgment without fear of retaliation for saying or doing something simply because it was unpopular with leadership. If those protections are taken away, then the quality of service to users could be negatively affected, loyalty to the US Constitution undermined, and biases could be introduced in the delivery of services. This could harm my interests as well as the national interest.

For example, in my time as an employee of the Labor Department for example, when asked to assess legislation, I was unhindered in my ability to offer my professional opinion without fear of retribution. Under the proposed regulation, I would have to fear dismissal for offering my honest opinion as to what form draft legislation might best have to deliver optimal performance in achieving stated aims of the government.

For example, as a user of Federal services such as Social Security or Parks, if the numbers of civil servants are subject to random and arbitrary alteration based on short term whims of political appointees, then the quality of service may be arbitrarily impaired, e.g., wait times, accuracy of requested actions, or availability of specific services.

If Civil Servants are not hired based on merit, if civil servant jobs are churned based on political motivations, and if honesty in staff opinions is punished, then this will undermine the human capital development of the Civil Service. Outcomes of US Government operations will be diminished. And, there could be economy-wide harms that result.

In light of the foregoing, here are my proposals:

Let us maintain a Civil Service that corresponds in size and quality to the operational requirements of the Federal Government, with operations anchored by loyalty to the US Constitution. 

Sincerely,

Douglas Lippoldt

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I strongly oppose the implementation or revival of the “Schedule F” classification for federal employees. This proposal threatens the merit-based civil service system that has underpinned a professional, nonpartisan federal workforce for over a century, particularly at a time when the civil service is already being threatened with excessive cuts without much forethought.

First and foremost, the creation of Schedule F directly undermines the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which was enacted to combat the spoils system and establish a merit-based hiring process for federal employees. By allowing a broad swath of career civil servants—particularly those involved in policy-making or analysis—to be reclassified and potentially terminated without cause, Schedule F opens the door to politically motivated hiring and firing. This is antithetical to the principle of an apolitical civil service enshrined in 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8), which mandates that federal employment decisions be based on merit and free from political influence.

Moreover, the vague and sweeping criteria for inclusion in Schedule F violate the due process protections guaranteed by 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which requires cause and procedural safeguards for the removal of career federal employees. Stripping thousands of workers of these protections not only weakens accountability but also risks chilling expert advice and dissent within agencies—undermining the very effectiveness of government operations.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is also bound by 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to support the merit system principles. Implementing Schedule F contradicts this statutory mission and places undue political pressure on career professionals, compromising the integrity and continuity of federal programs across administrations.

In conclusion, the Schedule F proposal poses a grave threat to the foundational principles of good governance, civil service independence, and the rule of law. I urge this administration and OPM to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement or revive this dangerous classification. The civil service should remain for the good of the American people and not whatever administration is currently in power.

Title: Comment from Veronica Dave
Comment:
May 5, 2025

RE: Public Comment in Response to Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service [Docket No. OPM–2025–0004]

I am writing to express my deep concern regarding the effort to reclassify specific federal positions. This change will erode necessary protections for those serving within the federal statistical system and could transform positions which rely on specific expertise to political ones. The proposed rule, “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service,” would call into question the objectivity of our economic indicators, public health assessments, energy utilization and many others. The federal statistical system plays an essential role in improving the lives of all Americans as well as informing critical policy decisions with evidence that is timely, relevant, and accurate. I would like to highlight the following major issues with this change:

    Politicization: This change could lead to the politicization of the federal statistical workforce. Official federal statistics clearly influence public policy of all sorts: monetary, fiscal, regulatory, etc. Thus, a President could classify many statistical agency positions as Policy/Career. Then, Bureau of Labor Statistics’ leaders could be fired for releasing or planning to release jobs or inflation statistics unfavorable to the President’s policy agenda. They might also face pressure to change methodologies or reveal pre-release information. By making it easier to remove employees if a President determines that they are interfering with his or her policies, it increases the potential for passivity or political loyalty to be prioritized over expertise and experience. Politicization has had dramatic consequences for statistical agencies and their leaders in other countries, notably Argentina and Greece.

    Importance of Trust, Impartiality and Objectivity: Statistical agencies, such as the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Census Bureau, and the National Center for Health Statistics, need professional autonomy to provide impartial, objective, reliable data. Professional autonomy is the ability to act independently from political or other undue external influence regarding its operations, such as data collection and analysis, staffing, and publications. Erosion of professional autonomy in the operations of statistical agencies would undermine their perceived or actual independence, leading to a loss of public trust in the data they produce.

    Importance of Norms: Schedule Policy/Career would deprioritize and thus weaken the norms that uphold the ethical and professional standards that are critical to the success of statistical agencies. Senior leaders help craft, model and reinforce norms within their agencies and between their agencies and other parts of the government.  Examples include how agencies interact with staff, data users, data subjects, outside experts and host agencies. See Principles and Practices for a Federal Statistical Agency for examples of these critical norms. These norms reflect and go beyond the laws, rules, and policy directives that govern agencies’ operations. Weaker norms threaten trust, efficient operations, and data quality.

    Erosion of Expertise, Loss of Institutional Memory and Increase of Turnover: These agencies rely on highly specialized professionals, including statisticians, economists, and data scientists, who possess unique technical expertise and long-term institutional memory. Statistical agencies stand to lose experts who see their career paths as less secure and merit-based than before. The loss of these experts or frequent turnover in key positions could disrupt agency operations, hinder long-term planning, undermine the agency's ability to fulfill its mission, and impair the quality and accuracy of the data.

    Importance of Modernization, Research, and Data Continuity: To support their missions, statistical agencies must invest in long-term efforts such as extensive research, critical modernization projects, and efforts to ensure data access and continuity.

I am a scientist in the health and biomedical research field. I would like to rely on the accuracy of government statistics. Over my career, my colleagues and I have always placed trust in U.S. government statistics published by statistical agencies. This change would seriously erode that trust, which is already becoming tenuous. 

Schedule Policy/Career poses a significant threat to the effectiveness of federal statistical agencies and to the integrity and quality of their products. By undermining the principles of merit-based employment and threatening job security of senior career civil servants, Schedule Policy/Career could lead to politicization, loss of trust and expertise, decreased morale, and disruption of agency operations.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
As a U.S. citizen and executive leader with 28 years of federal service, I write in strong opposition to OPM’s proposed rule titled “Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service” (Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004-0001).

I’ve already been notified that my position will be reclassified under this rule, despite a long history of outstanding performance, ethical conduct, and service across multiple administrations. I took an oath to support and defend the Constitution — not a political agenda — and this rule would erode that oath by placing nonpartisan civil servants like me under political threat.

The proposed rule revives elements of the discredited Schedule F by reclassifying policy-adjacent positions as at-will. This would remove due process protections for thousands of experienced professionals, subjecting them to dismissal based on perceived political alignment rather than merit. That change undermines the merit system and violates the principles set forth in the Civil Service Reform Act and Pendleton Act, which were explicitly designed to prevent such politicization.

By prioritizing political loyalty over expertise, the rule risks destabilizing critical public services like Social Security, Medicare, national security, housing, and environmental programs. Making long-serving employees fireable at-will introduces instability into the delivery of services that millions depend on — not to mention the chilling effect it will have on scientific research, technical accuracy, and ethical decision-making.

The rule also threatens to degrade institutional capacity by draining federal agencies of experienced personnel. Many federal employees — including myself — could earn more in the private sector, but we choose public service because of the mission and the professional protections that ensure we can do our jobs without fear of retaliation. Removing those protections will drive talent away and deter future public servants from joining.

This proposal claims to improve performance but offers no credible evidence to justify its sweeping changes. It relies on anecdotes and perception surveys rather than hard data. In contrast, the costs are real: loss of institutional knowledge, weakened morale, legal risks, and the likely increase in litigation stemming from due process and First Amendment violations. OPM also fails to fully account for indirect costs such as turnover, EEO complaints, or the long-term consequences of creating a less experienced, less stable workforce.

The rule contradicts the intent of Congress in establishing for-cause protections through Chapter 75 of Title 5. OPM cannot revoke these rights through regulation alone; doing so would violate the legal framework created by Congress and shift employment claims into the courts, contrary to the purpose of the CSRA. Employees affected by reclassification would be left with no practical remedy other than costly litigation.

Additionally, the rule opens the door to retaliatory or politically motivated firings, especially for those who speak up, conduct oversight, or provide honest advice that may not align with the prevailing political narrative. This is a direct threat to the ethical standards many professionals — including attorneys and scientists — are obligated to uphold.

There are better ways to improve performance and accountability without undermining the foundation of a nonpartisan civil service:

Modernize performance evaluation systems and tools;

Provide better training for executive leaders;

Streamline appeals processes while preserving fairness;

Strengthen internal oversight and transparency;

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing in response to the proposed regulation concerning the restructuring of federal civil service protections. As a Human Resources professional with experience in organizational policy and employee relations, I understand the value of accountability in public employment. However, I believe this proposed rule fundamentally threatens the integrity, efficiency, and continuity of our government.

Background and Concerns
The stated intent of the proposal is to "promote a nonpartisan civil service." Ironically, this rule appears designed to do the opposite — to give the executive branch more power to terminate employees who are not politically aligned. This undermines the very foundation of a professional, nonpartisan civil service and risks politicizing a workforce that should operate above political tides.

Impacts and HR Perspective
As someone who works in HR, I am familiar with both the challenges and tools available for addressing employee misconduct. When there is just cause to discipline or terminate an employee, it can and should be done — but through due process, not political influence. The mechanisms already exist; what may be lacking is not authority, but training and proper adherence to procedures.
This proposed rule opens the door for terminations based not on misconduct, but perceived disloyalty — where "insubordination" is used as a label for simply upholding laws or agency procedures that may not align with political whims. This is a dangerous precedent, and it threatens the principle of checks and balances.

Economic Impact of Turnover
There is also a significant economic consequence. Replacing highly specialized federal employees — especially those with deep institutional knowledge — is not simple. Research shows that replacing a tenured employee can cost 100–200% of their annual salary. For example, replacing a civil servant earning $90,000 could cost taxpayers $135,000 or more in recruitment, onboarding, training, and lost productivity.
Multiply that cost by hundreds or thousands of potentially displaced workers, and the financial burden quickly becomes enormous — far outweighing any supposed gains in “efficiency.” Institutional knowledge, once lost, cannot be quickly rebuilt.

Recommendations
Rather than weakening civil service protections, I urge the agency to:
1.	Maintain current protections that shield employees from political retaliation.
2.	Invest in training for management on proper disciplinary procedures.
3.	Promote transparency in accountability while preserving due process.
4.	Consider long-term costs, both financial and institutional, before implementing changes that threaten the continuity and neutrality of our government workforce.

Conclusion
This rule is not about promoting democracy — it risks eroding it. It makes the federal workforce more vulnerable to political manipulation and disregards the decades of public service and expertise that our government relies on. I urge the agency to withdraw or significantly revise the proposal in favor of approaches that truly protect nonpartisan service, government stability, and taxpayer interests.

Submitted anonymously by an HR professional working in the public sector

Title: Comment from Jane Ehrenfeld
Comment:
Jane Ehrenfeld submits these comments regarding Office of Personnel Management’s (OPM) Proposed Rule “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service,” 90 Fed. Reg. 17182 (April 23, 2025). I write to express opposition to the Proposed Rule.

I am an attorney and I have been a federal civil servant in two agencies and the federal judiciary. I am a subject matter expert in civil rights law, and particularly in the areas of employment and education. I am a magna cum laude graduate of Georgetown University Law Center, and in the 16 years I have been practicing law, I have gained significant experience and insight related to matters that deeply affect tens of millions of our nation’s children and adults. I also clerked for a judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, and during my clerkship I worked on an array of matters that depended on expertise from employees of multiple agencies. 

If this Proposed Rule is finalized as written, it will have devastating effects on employees across the federal government. To give an example, I currently supervise a team of policy attorneys who have been instrumental in writing, revising, and explaining multiple federal regulations and other policy guidance. Without their deep expertise and commitment to their subject matter area, the policies they have crafted would not protect the intended audience(s), would be extremely vulnerable to legal challenges, and would make the entire agency (as well as state and local agencies that depend on our guidance) weak and ineffective.

Creation of Schedule P/C will devastate the federal government and destroy its ability to work for the American public. The government works because impartial career employees, who have developed significant subject matter expertise in their fields, drive the work. Political appointees serve an important purpose as well, but cannot adequately do the jobs that tens of thousands of career civil servants have learned to do over careers spent building deep knowledge of their areas of focus.

Further, as the past 100 days have shown, shrinking the federal workforce is an act designed to cause chaos, and doing so means that ordinary, hard-working Americans cannot get the services and protections the government has historically afforded. If employers discriminate against employees, or refuse to accommodate their disabilities or their pregnancies, and if schools discriminate against students, who will help these individuals? Agencies that serve the public and enforce our nation’s civil rights laws were already understaffed and overworked before President Trump and his unelected DOGE squad started indiscriminately and illegally firing thousands of employees. If this Proposed Rule is adopted, things will get even worse. Conservative or liberal, every single American depends on the federal government in a myriad of ways. This rule will hurt them all.

Finally, if career employees lose their job protections and can be fired at will for saying anything that the Trump administration opposes, America is no longer a functioning democracy. It is as simple as that. Dictators and monarchs punish dissent. A nation built on the concepts enshrined in our Constitution – and particularly in the First Amendment – is not afraid of free speech, and does not fire dedicated employees when they dare to speak, especially when their perspective is informed by expertise.

This Proposed Rule is based on the shaky and unproven assertion that too many career civil servants are actually partisan hacks who refuse to implement the agenda of a President they do not agree with. That is a baseless and deeply insulting accusation. In my time in the federal government, I have never encountered – nor heard of – any individual who undermined the President’s agenda based on partisan sentiment. That is simply a lie, designed to do the exact thing that President Trump is falsely accusing civil servants of doing, namely, filling the government with loyalists instead of experts. In this post-Chevron world, where agency expertise is already under attack by the judiciary, moving to a government that is in the grips of deeply partisan individuals who put loyalty to their party over loyalty to the truth will be an act that will destroy the credibility of every agency, perhaps permanently.

Regulations governing this topic were published only one year ago, and there has been zero evidence to support rescinding or revising them. This is a political move, designed to kneecap the federal government (and, ironically, destroy the very careers of the people reading this letter and responding to it). The only right answer here – for democracy and for the American people – is to rescind this Proposed Rule and maintain the Rule that is currently in effect.

Sincerely,
Jane Dimyan Ehrenfeld

Title: Comment from Catherine Meyer
Comment:
I am writing to express my unequivocal opposition to the proposed regulatory change, as outlined in Project 2025, that would reclassify up to 50,000 federal civil service positions as “at-will” roles. This deeply troubling effort would allow mass politicization of expert, career roles across federal agencies—undermining the core values of professionalism, impartiality, and stability that have long defined the U.S. civil service.

I urge you to reject this proposal and take immediate steps to ensure that these essential federal jobs remain protected under the traditional merit-based civil service system.

This proposed rule change is not a minor adjustment—it is a sweeping, dangerous restructuring of government that would:

1. Politicize essential government functions and compromise national integrity.
This change would allow partisan appointees to hire and fire experts based on political loyalty rather than merit or competence. Such a system would open the door to cronyism and ideological conformity, rather than fact-based, public-centered decision-making. In doing so, it threatens to turn professional public service into a revolving door of partisan patronage—weakening our democratic institutions and alienating the very people the government exists to serve.

2. Hurt the American public by degrading the quality of government services.
Federal employees play a crucial role in delivering services that millions of Americans rely on every day—from ensuring clean air and water, to monitoring food safety, to responding to public health emergencies. Turning scientific and policy experts into “at-will” employees will degrade the quality of decisions made in these areas, putting lives, health, and environmental quality at risk. It could mean slower, less effective responses to crises, mismanagement of disasters, and policies shaped more by politics than public welfare.

3. Undermine America’s preparedness and resilience.
In times of crisis—be it a natural disaster, public health emergency, national security threat, or economic upheaval—our country depends on experienced, steady-handed civil servants to respond with urgency, competence, and clarity. This proposal would gut that capability by creating uncertainty, fear, and high turnover in key policy roles. It will also deter future talent from entering federal service, knowing that their employment could be terminated without cause at the whim of changing political leadership.

4. Weaken national decision-making by limiting expertise and silencing independent voices.
The proposed change would discourage or eliminate professionals who are willing to speak truth to power. It would suppress creative thinking, diverse perspectives, and critical feedback—leaving decision-makers with only filtered or sycophantic advice. The absence of honest internal debate leads to poor policy and, ultimately, national harm. When expertise is silenced, consequences are not just bureaucratic—they are human, economic, and lasting.

5. Erode public trust in government.
Trust in our democratic institutions depends on the belief that public servants act in the nation’s interest, not at the direction of partisan leaders. If this rule is implemented, the perception—and likely the reality—will be that policy outcomes are shaped to benefit political agendas rather than the common good. Once that trust is lost, it is incredibly difficult to rebuild.

6. Harm the country’s global standing and competitiveness.
The United States has long been respected for its institutional competence and reliance on scientific and policy expertise. Undermining those institutions from within will not only hurt our citizens—it will also diminish our global leadership, credibility, and ability to engage in evidence-based policymaking at the international level.

In sum, this rule change is not about improving government—it is about replacing professionalism with political control. It would weaken the foundations of our civil service, diminish the quality of government decisions, endanger our ability to respond to crises, and ultimately hurt the American people and our country’s future.

Therefore, I strongly urge you to:

Reject and speak out against the implementation of this harmful rule.

Support legislative and administrative safeguards to maintain civil service protections.

Champion the independence, integrity, and expertise of federal career employees.

Defend the public’s right to receive nonpartisan, scientifically grounded policy and services.

There is still time to prevent this dangerous restructuring of our government. Please act now to preserve the professionalism, effectiveness, and democratic principles that the United States civil service was built to uphold.

Title: Comment from Caitlin Humphreys
Comment:
Re: Proposed Rule by OPM Creating Schedule Policy/Career – Docket ID OPM-2025-0001

To Whom It May Concern:

I submit this comment in strong opposition to the Office of Personnel Management’s (OPM) proposed rule establishing “Schedule Policy/Career,” which would strip procedural protections from career federal employees in policy-influencing roles. This proposal raises grave legal and constitutional concerns, undermines merit system principles, and threatens the integrity and impartiality of the federal civil service.

I. Statutory Conflicts – Violations of Title 5’s Merit System Framework

The proposed rule directly contradicts the merit system principles outlined in 5 U.S.C. § 2301. Specifically:

Section 2301(b)(2) mandates “fair and equitable treatment in all aspects of personnel management,” including respect for constitutional rights.

Section 2301(b)(8) requires that employees be “protected against arbitrary action, personal favoritism, or coercion for partisan political purposes.”

Stripping career employees of chapter 43 and 75 protections—including appeal rights before the Merit Systems Protection Board—violates both the letter and spirit of these protections.

Moreover, OPM’s redefinition of “policy-influencing” career roles oversteps its statutory authority under Title 5. Excepted service provisions were never intended to be used as a mass vehicle for converting politically inconvenient employees into at-will labor.

II. Constitutional Violations – Due Process and Separation of Powers

Under Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 470 U.S. 532 (1985), federal employees possess a protected property interest in continued employment. Eliminating procedural due process rights for employees transferred into Schedule Policy/Career violates the Fifth Amendment. These employees have not been given individualized due process, nor does the proposed rule recognize their existing reliance interests.

Additionally, the proposed rule threatens the Constitution’s separation of powers by subordinating apolitical implementation of Congressional statutes to unchecked Executive discretion. Removing career civil servants based on subjective judgments about “subversion” of Presidential directives invites politicized purges and severely compromises the independence of the administrative state.

III. APA Concerns – Arbitrary, Capricious, and Without Justification

The proposed rule also appears to violate the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A):

It provides no quantitative data demonstrating systemic failure of existing chapter 43 or 75 mechanisms.

It reverses the April 2024 final rule without a reasoned explanation, in conflict with the Supreme Court’s guidance in FCC v. Fox Television Stations, 556 U.S. 502 (2009).

It introduces retroactive elements that diminish vested rights without sufficient legal grounding, contrary to Bowen v. Georgetown Univ. Hospital, 488 U.S. 204 (1988).

IV. Policy-Based Harms – Chilling Effect and Erosion of Public Trust

This rule will chill public servants from engaging in good faith dissent, whistleblowing, or lawful resistance to illegal orders. It risks disproportionate targeting of marginalized and underrepresented federal workers. Rather than fostering accountability, the rule invites instability, political retaliation, and short-term thinking over institutional knowledge and integrity.

Conclusion

For over a century, the merit-based civil service has been a cornerstone of public trust and good governance. This proposed rule threatens to dismantle those foundations in the name of expediency and perceived loyalty. The government functions best when its career workforce can faithfully execute laws without fear of political reprisal. I urge OPM to withdraw this rule in its entirety.

Respectfully submitted,

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Re: Docket ID OPM-2025-0001 – Comment in Opposition to Proposed Rule Establishing Schedule Policy/Career

To the Office of Personnel Management:

The proposed rule to establish “Schedule Policy/Career” is a fundamental departure from the spirit and purpose of the U.S. civil service. It is historically revisionist, legally flawed, and normatively corrosive to democratic accountability.

I. Foundational Mischaracterization of Civil Service Origins

The framing offered in OPM’s background section presents a misleading view of the historical trajectory of the federal workforce. While it is true that early federal employment was politicized, the passage of the Pendleton Act in 1883 represented not a reluctant or temporary compromise, but an intentional pivot toward institutionalized merit, driven by public outrage over abuses.

Rather than reinforcing executive control, the history of civil service reform—from Pendleton to McKinley’s EO 101 and Roosevelt’s EO 173—demonstrates a steady progression away from arbitrary removals and toward transparency, procedural fairness, and professional standards. The emphasis was always on building a capable, impartial, and resilient public workforce, not clearing bureaucratic space for political retaliation.

OPM’s interpretation of these developments as evidence of tolerance for at-will removal lacks support from the actual legislative and executive rationale of the era.

II. Misuse of the Lloyd-La Follette Act and Postwar Precedent

The proposed rule erroneously suggests that early 20th-century reforms favored unchecked removal authority. In fact, the Lloyd-La Follette Act was introduced to limit removals for political and arbitrary reasons—precisely what the proposed rule invites.

The D.C. Circuit’s decision in Roth v. Brownell affirms that procedural safeguards must accompany structural changes such as transfers from the competitive to excepted service. The rule’s assertion that Schedule Policy/Career can be imposed without such process flatly contradicts that precedent.

III. The CSRA and Its Narrow Exceptions Do Not Justify This Rule

The Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 created a comprehensive and balanced framework for managing performance, discipline, and appeals. It introduced streamlined mechanisms (such as Chapter 43) while reinforcing the importance of procedural justice.

Although the CSRA allowed limited exclusions for policy-determining roles, these were never intended as a justification for mass reclassification. The Act’s structure—and the subsequent Due Process Amendments of 1990—make clear that procedural safeguards are central to the legitimacy of personnel actions, even in the excepted service.

IV. Threat to Government Integrity and Constitutional Order

Removing procedural rights from policy-advising career staff based on speculative concerns about political disloyalty is dangerous and destabilizing. It violates the due process rights affirmed in Loudermill and invites a chilling effect across the professional workforce.

The rule’s logic encourages federal employees to substitute loyalty for legality, enabling an executive branch with unchecked purging authority—precisely what the framers sought to avoid in designing a balanced and deliberative government.

V. Institutional Damage Beyond the Law

Beyond its legal infirmities, this rule corrodes the civic foundations of public service. It devalues expertise, undermines morale, and sows distrust in federal institutions. It treats career civil servants not as guardians of continuity, but as political liabilities.

Historically, the U.S. has built a world-class civil service not by making it easy to fire people, but by ensuring that hiring and firing are governed by neutral principles. Any attempt to reverse this logic must be met with moral, legal, and civic resistance.

Final Statement

The proposed Schedule Policy/Career rule is unnecessary, unjustified, and legally indefensible. It risks returning the federal government to the worst excesses of the spoils system under the guise of reform.

This is not accountability—it is vulnerability masquerading as strength. The Office of Personnel Management must preserve its constitutional and statutory role in protecting the integrity of federal employment. I strongly urge full withdrawal of this proposed rule.

With respect,
