Title: Comment from Rebecca Nielsen
Comment:
I strongly oppose creation of a Schedule “Policy/Career” for federal workers. This proposed regulation would decimate the merit-based civil service system that has underpinned a professional, non-partisan federal workforce for nearly 150 years. Merit-based federal employment means a more efficient government for American taxpayers and better public services for the American people. This proposed regulation would make our federal agencies less effective and expose the American public to the type of corruption that civil service laws were enacted to protect against.

The creation of Schedule “Policy/Career” and the broad way in which it is being interpreted by the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) are contrary to Constitutional due process. It has long been recognized that non-probationary government workers are entitled to due process before they can be removed or have other employment actions taken against them. See Gilbert v. Homar, 520 U.S. 924, 935-936 (1997); Cleveland Board of Education v. Loudermill, 470 U.S. 532, 541 (1985). The importance of maintaining due process and having a merit-based apolitical civil service is also enshrined in federal statute. The proposed regulations would deprive a large number of federal workers of their due process rights. 
The sweeping nature of Schedule “Policy/Career” also undermines important federal statutes. The Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883 was enacted to combat the spoils system and establish merit-based employment in federal agencies. The Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 further honed the efficacy of federal service in response to the Watergate scandal and passed Congress with all but 10 Congressmen voting in favor. Contrary to some propaganda currently circulating, these statutes are effective at ensuring the federal workforce is merit-based while allowing workers to be fired, demoted, etc. for poor performance or misconduct. Congress enacted these protections for federal workers, and this proposed regulation would effectively negate Congress’s will for a large swath of federal workers. 

A broadly inclusive Schedule “Policy/Career” will irrevocably damage federal civil service and negatively impact the American public. By allowing a large portion of federal employees to be reclassified and potentially removed without cause, Schedule “Policy/Career” opens the door to baseless or politically motivated hiring and firing. This is antithetical to the principle of an apolitical civil service enshrined in 5 U.S.C. Sec. 2301(b), which mandates federal employment decisions be based on merit and free from political influence. Stripping thousands or tens of thousands of federal employees of protections against non-merit based actions will weaken accountability and have a chilling effect on employees’ sharing of expert advice and dissent within agencies. It undermines the effectiveness of government by allowing employment to be based on political allyship rather than merit and potentially discouraging free and fair exchange of ideas between knowledgeable workers. It places undue political pressure on career professionals, compromising the integrity and continuity of federal programs across administrations. In short, these changes make the government less functional and efficient for the American people.  

The proposed regulations to implement Schedule “Policy/Career” are contrary to law and pose a grave threat to the foundational principles of good governance, civil service independence, and rule of law. I urge the administration and OPM to halt the proposed regulation.  Thank you.

Title: Comment from Daniel Duckwitz
Comment:
Dear Office of Personnel Management,

I write in strong opposition to the proposed rule entitled "Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service" (RIN 3206-AO80), published in the Federal Register on April 23, 2025 (90 Fed. Reg. 17182). Rebranded from the revoked "Schedule F," the proposed "Schedule Policy/Career" undermines statutory merit protections and poses significant risks to the neutrality, stability, and professionalism of the federal workforce.

The proposed rule conflicts with core provisions of Title 5, including:

* **5 U.S.C. §2301(b)**, which mandates protections against arbitrary action and political coercion;
* **5 U.S.C. §7501-7513** and **§4301-4303**, which require procedural safeguards for performance and misconduct-based removals;
* **5 U.S.C. §7701-7703**, which grants appeal rights to the Merit Systems Protection Board;
* And the narrowly defined exemptions in **§7511(b)(2)** and **§4301(2)(G)**, historically limited to Schedule C political appointees, not career civil servants.

The proposed redefinition of "policy-influencing" casts an unreasonably wide net. OPM’s own guidance includes positions involved in grantmaking, supervision, policy drafting, or public communication. These vague criteria could encompass nearly every GS-13 to GS-15 role in budget, procurement, regulatory, research, and program offices. As a result, large segments of the career workforce could be stripped of civil service protections without clear statutory authority or procedural recourse.

This is contrary to the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. §706), which prohibits arbitrary and capricious rulemaking. OPM fails to justify reversing the April 2024 final rule (89 Fed. Reg. 24982) and disregards reliance interests of thousands of federal employees. Additionally, reliance on EO 14171 does not nullify binding statutory protections. Courts have consistently held that presidential orders cannot override congressional mandates.

The rule undermines foundational civil service norms. As established by the Pendleton Act of 1883 (22 Stat. 403), Lloyd-La Follette Act of 1912 (37 Stat. 555), and Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (92 Stat. 1111), career protections exist to insulate federal administration from politicization. Max Weber’s vision of professional, impartial bureaucracy is embedded in this framework. Shifting vast numbers of career roles to at-will status risks recreating a 19th-century spoils system.

Moreover, the rule raises First Amendment concerns by enabling dismissal based on disagreement with administration policies, infringing on the protections upheld in *Pickering v. Board of Education*, 391 U.S. 563 (1968), and *Lane v. Franks*, 573 U.S. 228 (2014).

I urge OPM to withdraw the proposed rule and uphold a nonpartisan, merit-based civil service. At a minimum, OPM should retain narrow definitions, publicly justify reclassifications, and protect employee appeal rights under Chapters 43 and 75.

Respectfully submitted,

Citizen, Virginia Resident

Title: Comment from Sean Williamson
Comment:
Justification: Why Technical and Scientific Experts in the Federal Government Should Not Be Subject to Politicizing and Loyalty Tests

Technical and scientific experts within the federal government play a critical role in informing policy, guiding public health initiatives, supporting national security, and ensuring evidence-based decision-making. These professionals are hired for their expertise, training, and commitment to scientific integrity, not for their political affiliations or loyalty to any administration or ideology. Subjecting them to politicizing or loyalty tests undermines the very foundation of objective governance and endangers the nation’s ability to respond effectively to crises and long-term challenges.

First and foremost, the core principle of science and technical expertise is objectivity. Scientists, engineers, analysts, and other experts rely on empirical evidence, peer-reviewed data, and proven methodologies. Their work is governed by facts, not opinions or political leanings. When loyalty tests or political vetting enter the equation, it creates a chilling effect: experts may feel pressured to alter findings, suppress inconvenient truths, or distort analyses to align with political narratives. This not only diminishes the credibility of governmental research but also erodes public trust in federal institutions. The politicization of expertise during the COVID-19 pandemic, for example, led to widespread misinformation, conflicting messages, and ultimately, avoidable loss of life.

Moreover, technical and scientific work often requires long-term continuity that transcends political cycles. Climate change research, infrastructure planning, space exploration, and pandemic preparedness are multi-decade efforts that cannot afford to be derailed by changing political winds. Subjecting experts to political loyalty tests risks replacing seasoned professionals with less qualified individuals chosen for ideological alignment rather than competence. Such instability hampers institutional memory and reduces the federal government’s ability to maintain consistent progress on key initiatives.

The principle of nonpartisan public service is enshrined in federal law and tradition. The merit-based civil service system was specifically designed to ensure that government functions are carried out by qualified professionals, regardless of the administration in power. Loyalty tests represent a step backward toward the patronage and cronyism that civil service reform sought to eliminate in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Reinstituting such tests undermines the apolitical foundation of government service and threatens democratic norms by encouraging loyalty to individuals over institutions and the Constitution.

Furthermore, requiring political loyalty from technical experts poses national security risks. Intelligence analysts, cybersecurity professionals, and weapons engineers must provide accurate, unbiased assessments. If these individuals are vetted for political alignment, it may discourage dissenting but necessary viewpoints and foster an echo chamber where only politically favorable information is considered. This can lead to poor decision-making at the highest levels of government and increased vulnerability to threats.

In conclusion, politicizing technical and scientific roles in the federal government and subjecting experts to loyalty tests would erode trust, compromise effectiveness, and endanger national well-being. Expertise must be protected as a nonpartisan asset to ensure that government decisions are grounded in facts and guided by the best available knowledge. Upholding scientific integrity and professional independence is essential to the functioning of a competent, trustworthy, and democratic federal government.

Such a move undermines the merit-based principles that have long been the foundation of our federal workforce, replacing them with a system susceptible to political influence and favoritism.

By targeting roles deemed "policy-related," this proposal opens the door to politicizing positions that should remain impartial. Many of these individuals are veterans who have continued their service to the nation through civilian roles. Subjecting them to at-will employment not only disrespects their commitment but also risks disrupting the delivery of critical services that Americans rely on daily.

The proposed reinstatement of Schedule F poses a significant threat to the effectiveness and impartiality of our federal government. I urge the Office of Personnel Management to rescind this proposal and uphold the merit-based, nonpartisan principles that ensure our civil service serves the American people with integrity and professionalism.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I am an Earth scientist who has worked closely with the federal government for my entire career. I have been on the staff of academic institutions, nonprofit organizations, and from last August until February, I was a program director at a federal science agency. Shortly after I was fired I learned that my deputy, who is now acting director, had been designated as Schedule Policy/Career. Had I still been employed as director at that time, I would have been the one designated as Schedule Policy/Career. I am commenting on the proposed rule “Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service” as an independent citizen who has also had experience as a federal employee.

Applying Schedule Policy/Career to a wide swath of federal employees makes no sense. As an example, the work of my former program is inherently nonpolitical. The program funds scientific research at government labs, universities, and independent research organizations. This research is interdisciplinary and includes ongoing monitoring and hypothesis-driven research. It examines how humans and other animals interact with changing Earth systems. The conclusions from the program’s studies are available for anyone, including policymakers, to make the most of Earth system resources today, and to ensure a continued supply of benefits to future generations. Federal science is not policy prescriptive, but it is policy relevant; one of its main aims is to inform decision makers of conditions, risks, and opportunities, now and in the future.

Designating more agency employees, like scientific program directors, as Schedule Policy/Career employees will make them easy to replace and increase the likelihood that science will be designed, selected, and carried out to suit political aims. Assuming that a scientist whose job requires them to carry out legislated scientific activities is carrying out policy-influencing activities – according to the January 20, 2025 Executive Order concerning Schedule Policy/Career– both goes against the professional training scientists have received and misunderstands the role of science. Scientists are trained to be objective, not political loyalists. Replacing experts with political loyalists will hobble science and make the United States the laughingstock of the global science community. Homegrown experts will leave the country in search of intellectual freedom abroad. This will contribute to ongoing erosion of the U.S.’ global scientific leadership, taking away more of the foundation of our robust economy. 

The proposed rule should be withdrawn, keeping the 2024 final rule in place.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I strongly object to introducing or reviving the "Schedule F" classification for federal workers. This plan jeopardizes the civil service system's foundation, which hires and promotes based on merit. Notably, President Trump has supported this merit-based approach in Executive Order 14173. By allowing for the potential dismissal of career employees without cause, Schedule F would undermine the principles established by the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which aimed to end the spoils system and ensure hiring and promotion based on merit.

Implementing Schedule F would lead to politicized employment decisions, contradicting the law's requirement for apolitical civil service. The broad and unclear criteria for Schedule F would also undermine due process rights, violating 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which demands cause and procedural safeguards for removing career employees. Depriving thousands of workers of these protections would harm accountability and might silence experts, ultimately reducing government efficiency.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) has a statutory obligation to protect the merit system under federal law (5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq.). Introducing Schedule F would erode this duty by exposing career civil servants to inappropriate political pressure, ultimately weakening the consistency and professionalism of government programs.

The Schedule F initiative endangers fundamental principles of good governance, including an independent civil service and respect for the rule of law. Given these risks, I urge the administration and OPM to reject any efforts to move forward with this proposal.

Title: Comment from Heidi Markovitz
Comment:
This change will make it harder to recruit new staff. The fact that civil service jobs cannot be terminated except for poor performance or malfeasance makes them appealing to people who want to build a career and keep their eyes on the long term.  It also simplifies planning for new projects. If an agency can count on most of their current staff being available in the future, they can plan their projects with more confidence in what kind of staff is already available and what kind they will need to add. Also, the out-of-pocket costs of hiring and training new staff are high.  Without existing staff in place, the new folks will be slower to start being productive.  Thinking of agencies with public facing functions, such as Social Security, we all know from experience that when large groups of new staff provide services, the service levels decline and more mistakes are made. The blending of tenured and new staff is most effective when adopting new processes to perform ongoing activities.

While hiring and firing processes in government jobs could probably use a update, alienating prospective employees and experienced staff is not the way to do it.

Title: Comment from Rachel Novak
Comment:
This order states Schedule Policy/Career employees:

"are required to faithfully implement administration policies to the best of their ability, consistent with their constitutional oath and the vesting of executive authority solely in the President. Failure to do so is grounds for dismissal."

It also states that:

"the President will make the final decision about which positions go into Schedule Policy/Career."

And "guidance about positions agencies should consider in their Schedule Policy/Career positions" includes those with:

"Substantive participation and discretionary authority in agency grantmaking, such as the substantive exercise of discretion in the drafting of funding opportunity announcements, evaluation of grant applications, or recommending or selecting grant recipients. Grantmaking is an important form of policymaking, so employees with a substantive discretionary role in how federal funding gets allocated may occupy policymaking positions."

This indicates that all involved in all grantmaking are considered policymaking positions and that the President can dictate whether those individuals' actions are aligned with their policies -- no matter who the President is or their party affiliation. Those involved in grantmaking should be nonpartisan career civil servants with appropriate expertise and experience to write funding announcements, evaluate grant applications, and recommend grant funding to achieve the missions of their agencies. They should not have to live in fear that their positions would be at risk if their expert-driven, rigorous decision-making is not consistent with one person's opinions. Adoption of this Proposed Rule will have dire consequences on our country's ability to conduct the best research, educate the best trainees, build the best infrastructure, and provide the best services.

The patronage system was a disaster for good governance in the 19th century. We should not return to it, especially after we have a century worth of global data that show an independent bureaucracy is crucial to success in governance, in war, and in the economy. 

It is important that people make decisions and provide information to leaders and the public on the basis of their best judgment, and not on the basis of what is politically correct or will please the president. 

A president who only hears what the people below him believe he will want to hear will never get the information he needs to make right decisions.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Opposing Proposed Rule: Docket OPM–2025–0001
Re: RIN 3206–AO31 – Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service

I write to respectfully express my strong opposition to the proposed rule, “Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service,” published in the Federal Register on April 23, 2025.

While I agree with the importance of a high-performing and accountable federal workforce, this proposed rule would undermine the fairness, stability, and integrity of the merit-based civil service system. I urge the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) to withdraw or substantially revise the rule for the following reasons:

1. Erosion of Due Process Protections Undermines Merit Principles

The proposed changes would significantly weaken civil service protections by reducing procedural safeguards for employees facing discipline or removal. These protections are not bureaucratic red tape; they are essential to ensuring that employment decisions are based on merit and not subject to political interference, retaliation, or bias. Stripping employees of fair notice, time to respond, and impartial review creates a chilling effect and opens the door to arbitrary or politically motivated actions—contrary to the merit system principles codified in 5 U.S.C. § 2301.

2. Shortened Timelines Will Decrease Agency Effectiveness and Increase Turnover

While the proposed rule aims to expedite performance-based actions, it risks undermining employee morale, trust, and institutional knowledge. Rushed disciplinary processes may result in premature dismissals or costly appeals and litigation. Agencies already struggle with recruitment and retention, particularly in technical and high-skill fields. Weakening job security further will deter qualified candidates from public service, exacerbate talent shortages, and lead to long-term inefficiencies.

3. No Demonstrated Need or Evidence Supporting the Rule’s Efficacy

The rule is based on the assumption that current civil service protections hinder accountability, but no empirical evidence has been provided showing that due process procedures are the primary obstacle to addressing poor performance. In fact, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) and Office of the Inspector General have consistently identified managerial training, documentation practices, and resource constraints—not personnel procedures—as key challenges to managing performance. Reform should address root causes, not eliminate essential safeguards.

This proposed rule represents a significant step toward politicizing the civil service and weakening the foundational merit principles that have supported a nonpartisan, professional federal workforce for over a century. OPM should pursue performance and accountability through investment in training, supervision, and fair evaluation—not by curtailing employee rights. I urge OPM to reconsider this rule and instead pursue reforms that strengthen, rather than destabilize, the federal workforce.

Title: Comment from Elizabeth Kim
Comment:
May 9, 2025

RE: Public Comment in Response to Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service [Docket No. OPM–2025–0004]

I am writing to express my objection to the effort to reclassify specific federal positions, which would erode necessary protections for those serving within the federal statistical system and could transform such positions which rely to political ones. The proposed rule, “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service,” would call into question the objectivity that both sides of the aisle rely on for our economic indicators, public health assessments, energy utilization and many other statistics. The federal statistical system plays an essential role in improving the lives of all Americans as well as informing critical policy decisions with evidence that is timely, relevant, and accurate. Federal statistical agencies are particularly vulnerable to the proposed rule due to the following:

Politicization: Schedule Policy/Career could lead to the politicization of the federal statistical workforce. Official federal statistics clearly influence public policy of all sorts: monetary, fiscal, regulatory, etc. Thus, a President could classify many statistical agency positions as Policy/Career. Then, for example, Bureau of Labor Statistics’ leaders could be fired for releasing or planning to release jobs or inflation statistics unfavorable to the President’s policy agenda. They might also face pressure to change methodologies or reveal pre-release information. By making it easier to remove employees if a President determines that they are interfering with his or her policies, it increases the potential for passivity or political loyalty to be prioritized over expertise and experience. 

Importance of Trust, Impartiality and Objectivity: Statistical agencies, such as the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Census Bureau, and the National Center for Health Statistics, need professional autonomy to provide impartial, objective, reliable data. Professional autonomy is the ability to act independently from political or other undue external influence regarding its operations, such as data collection and analysis, staffing, and publications. Erosion of professional autonomy in the operations of statistical agencies would undermine their perceived or actual independence, leading to a loss of public trust in the data they produce.

Importance of Norms: Schedule Policy/Career would deprioritize and thus weaken the norms that uphold the ethical and professional standards that are critical to the success of statistical agencies. Senior leaders help craft, model and reinforce norms within their agencies and between their agencies and other parts of the government.  Examples include how agencies interact with staff, data users, data subjects, outside experts and host agencies. These norms reflect and go beyond the laws, rules, and policy directives that govern agencies’ operations. Weaker norms threaten trust, efficient operations, and data quality.

Erosion of Expertise, Loss of Institutional Memory and Increase of Turnover: These agencies rely on highly specialized professionals, including statisticians, economists, and data scientists, who possess unique technical expertise and long-term institutional memory. Statistical agencies stand to lose experts who see their career paths as less secure and merit-based than before. The loss of these experts or frequent turnover in key positions could disrupt agency operations, hinder long-term planning, undermine the agency's ability to fulfill its mission, and impair the quality and accuracy of the data.

Decreased Employee Morale and Productivity: The uncertainty and fear of arbitrary dismissal could negatively impact employee morale, leading to decreased productivity and difficulty in attracting and retaining top talent.

Importance of Modernization, Research, and Data Continuity: To support their missions, statistical agencies must invest in long-term efforts such as extensive research, critical modernization projects, and efforts to ensure data access and continuity. Schedule Policy/Career could subject to agencies to changing presidential priorities, increasing senior staff turnover and disrupting modernization efforts, measurement of trends, and meaningful research.

Schedule Policy/Career poses a significant threat to the effectiveness of federal statistical agencies and to the integrity and quality of their products. By undermining the principles of merit-based employment and threatening job security of senior career civil servants, Schedule Policy/Career could lead to politicization, loss of trust and expertise, decreased morale, and disruption of agency operations.

Title: Comment from Sonia Jaffe
Comment:
I am writing to express my deep concern regarding the effort to reclassify specific federal positions, which would erode necessary protections for those serving within the federal statistical system and could transform positions which rely on specific expertise to political ones. The proposed rule, “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service,” would call into question the objectivity that both sides of the aisle rely on for our economic indicators, public health assessments, energy utilization and many other statistics. The federal statistical system plays an essential role in improving the lives of all Americans as well as informing critical policy decisions with evidence that is timely, relevant, and accurate. Federal statistical agencies are particularly vulnerable to the proposed rule due to the following:

Politicization: Schedule Policy/Career could lead to the politicization of the federal statistical workforce. Official federal statistics clearly influence public policy of all sorts: monetary, fiscal, regulatory, etc. Thus, a President could classify many statistical agency positions as Policy/Career. Then, for example, Bureau of Labor Statistics’ leaders could be fired for releasing or planning to release jobs or inflation statistics unfavorable to the President’s policy agenda. They might also face pressure to change methodologies or reveal pre-release information. By making it easier to remove employees if a President determines that they are interfering with his or her policies, it increases the potential for passivity or political loyalty to be prioritized over expertise and experience. Politicization has had dramatic consequences for statistical agencies and their leaders in other countries, notably Argentina and Greece.

Importance of Trust, Impartiality and Objectivity: Statistical agencies, such as the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Census Bureau, and the National Center for Health Statistics, need professional autonomy to provide impartial, objective, reliable data. Professional autonomy is the ability to act independently from political or other undue external influence regarding its operations, such as data collection and analysis, staffing, and publications. Erosion of professional autonomy in the operations of statistical agencies would undermine their perceived or actual independence, leading to a loss of public trust in the data they produce.

Importance of Norms: Schedule Policy/Career would deprioritize and thus weaken the norms that uphold the ethical and professional standards that are critical to the success of statistical agencies. Senior leaders help craft, model and reinforce norms within their agencies and between their agencies and other parts of the government.  Examples include how agencies interact with staff, data users, data subjects, outside experts and host agencies. See Principles and Practices for a Federal Statistical Agency for examples of these critical norms. These norms reflect and go beyond the laws, rules, and policy directives that govern agencies’ operations. Weaker norms threaten trust, efficient operations, and data quality.

Erosion of Expertise and Increase of Turnover: These agencies rely on highly specialized professionals, including statisticians, economists, and data scientists, who possess unique technical expertise and long-term institutional memory. Statistical agencies stand to lose experts who see their career paths as less secure and merit-based than before. The loss of these experts or frequent turnover in key positions could disrupt agency operations, hinder long-term planning, undermine the agency's ability to fulfill its mission, and impair the quality and accuracy of the data.

Importance of Modernization, Research, and Data Continuity: To support their missions, statistical agencies must invest in long-term efforts such as extensive research, critical modernization projects, and efforts to ensure data access and continuity. Schedule Policy/Career could subject to agencies to changing presidential priorities, increasing senior staff turnover and disrupting modernization efforts, measurement of trends, and meaningful research.

Schedule Policy/Career poses a significant threat to the effectiveness of federal statistical agencies and to the integrity and quality of their products. By undermining the principles of merit-based employment and threatening job security of senior career civil servants, Schedule Policy/Career could lead to politicization, loss of trust and expertise, decreased morale, and disruption of agency operations. On behalf of U.S. businesses, the American public, and policymakers I am speaking up to protect the trustworthiness of the federal statistics we all rely on.

Title: Comment from Michael Fairfax
Comment:
RE: Opposition to Proposed Rule on Schedule Policy/Career Positions

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule that would create a new "Schedule Policy/Career" classification for certain federal positions. This rule would fundamentally undermine the merit-based civil service system that has served our nation for over 140 years. I urge you to reconsider this proposal based on the following concerns:

1. Constitutional and Statutory Concerns

The proposed rule appears to circumvent the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978, which explicitly created a balanced system to protect both management prerogatives and employee rights. By removing adverse action procedures and appeals for an undefined class of "policy-influencing positions," this rule contradicts established law protecting career civil servants.

In NTEU v. Reagan (1988), the court affirmed that reclassification schemes designed primarily to facilitate removal of career employees violate the merit system principles established by Congress. This proposed rule appears to replicate problems found in similar past attempts to circumvent civil service protections.

2. Vague and Overly Broad Definitions

The rule's reference to "policy-influencing positions" and employees who "undermine the democratic process by intentionally subverting Presidential directives" lacks clear definition and invites subjective interpretation. Without precise criteria, these standards are susceptible to misuse and political targeting.

The Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) has consistently held that removal standards must be objective and consistently applied. The proposed rule's vague language fails this standard and invites potentially arbitrary enforcement.

3. Existing Processes Are Functional

While the rule claims supervisors face "great difficulty" removing poor performers, existing data suggests otherwise. According to OPM's own FY2020 report, agencies successfully removed thousands of employees for performance and conduct issues using current procedures. The problem is not the existence of due process, but rather management's consistent implementation of performance standards.

The Government Accountability Office (GAO) has found that when managers properly document performance issues and follow established procedures, removal actions are generally sustained. The solution lies in better training and support for supervisors, not in eliminating fundamental employee protections.

4. Threats to Government Effectiveness

Creating a class of at-will employees in policy positions would likely:
- Discourage qualified professionals from pursuing government careers
- Reduce institutional knowledge through increased turnover
- Create a chilling effect on providing objective analysis and honest assessment
- Politicize what should be nonpartisan expert roles

Research by the Partnership for Public Service shows that agencies with stronger due process protections and employee engagement have higher performance ratings and better mission delivery.

5. Alternative Approaches

Rather than eliminating due process rights, OPM should consider:
- Enhancing training for managers on performance management
- Setting clearer, objective performance standards
- Providing better resources for coaching and employee improvement

The long-standing merit system principles that govern our civil service were established to prevent partisan manipulation of government while ensuring accountability. This proposed rule threatens that careful balance without demonstrating that existing systems are fundamentally broken.

I urge OPM to withdraw this proposal and instead engage with stakeholders on targeted improvements to the current system that preserve due process while enhancing accountability.

Respectfully submitted,
Michael Fairfax

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I am writing to express my deep concern regarding the potential reinstatement of Schedule F, a policy that poses significant legal and constitutional challenges to the integrity of the federal civil service.

Legal Concerns:

Schedule F aims to reclassify a broad segment of federal employees into positions that lack the procedural protections established under the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (CSRA). This reclassification undermines the merit-based principles that have been foundational to our federal workforce for over a century. The CSRA ensures that federal employment decisions are based on merit and free from political influence, providing employees with due process rights, including notice, the opportunity to respond to adverse actions, and the right to appeal to the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB).

By circumventing these protections, Schedule F effectively returns the federal employment system to a patronage model reminiscent of the 19th-century “spoils system,” which Congress sought to eliminate due to its propensity for corruption and inefficiency.

Constitutional Implications:

Beyond statutory concerns, Schedule F raises serious constitutional issues. Stripping career civil servants of their due process rights may violate the Fifth Amendment, which guarantees that no person shall be deprived of life, liberty, or property without due process of law. Federal employees often have a property interest in their continued employment, and removing their rights without appropriate legal procedures could be deemed unconstitutional.

Impact on Governance:

Implementing Schedule F could lead to the politicization of the federal workforce, eroding public trust in government institutions. It risks replacing experienced, nonpartisan professionals with individuals selected based on political loyalty rather than competence, potentially compromising the effectiveness and impartiality of federal agencies.

Conclusion:

Given these substantial legal and constitutional concerns, I urge policymakers to reconsider any efforts to reinstate Schedule F. Upholding the principles of merit-based employment and due process is essential to maintaining a fair, effective, and impartial federal government.

Title: Comment from Caroline Crouse
Comment:
I strongly oppose the implementation of the “Schedule F” classification 90 FR 17182 for federal employees.  This rule poses a threat the merit-based civil service system that has been the basis for the United States civil service system and replicated by advanced, stable democracies throughout the world.  The proposed rule is overly-broad, violates the constitutional right of due process, and is unnecessary.  

The phrase “policy-influencing” is overly broad and does not give guidance to agencies or federal employees what would be considered policy-influencing.  Would someone drafting notices of funding opportunities or rules be considered policy-influencing, even though these products go through multiple levels of review, including through political consideration and signature at both the agency and OMB levels?  Would attorneys who are asked simple questions on whether a document is allowed by current law be policy-influencing?  Would implementing staff giving guidance to grant recipients on program implementation be policy-influencing, since this guidance would show how policy can be interpreted? The levels of review and approval above each of these individuals by political and Schedule C staff provide ample protection and facilitation for Administration priorities (5 U.S.C. § 2302(a)(2)(B)(i)).

The preamble states that “Increased accountability would be expected to incentivize employees, where applicable, to improve problematic performance and conduct. This would produce large gains in agency efficiency…Similarly, higher employee performance and greater adherence to nonpartisan norms would be expected to reduce the time it takes agencies to conduct rulemakings.” Logic disagrees with these statements.  Agency staff, with the threat of firing and no recourse for adverse actions by supervisors, would lead to more hesitancy and decreased performance.  The Hatch Act (5 U.S.C. 7323(a) and 5. USC. 7324(a)) prohibits political activity during work for civil servants and, thus, there are already safeguards in place to ensure that civil servants are following the directions of their agency lead.  Further, OMB regulations at 5 CFR Part 752 already outline how a  civil servant can be removed from their position for cause.

While current regulations already allow for the removal of civil servants for cause, the criteria outlined in the proposed rule are overly broad and vague, allowing civil servants to be dismissed without review for disagreeing with a supervisor or presenting alternate opinions, a key part of policy analysis.  Further, these dismissals without review violate the due process of career staff, guaranteed by 5 U.S.C. 7513.  This creates a chilling effect on expert advice and overall will weaken the United States.  

In conclusion, the proposed rule is unnecessary and threatens to send the United States civil service back to the spoils system.  Good governance requires a professional, non-political civil service based on the principles of merit.  The proposed rule is in direct opposition to such a system.

Title: Comment from Timothy Nielsen
Comment:
I strongly oppose creation of a Schedule “Policy/Career” for federal workers. This proposed regulation would decimate the merit-based civil service system that has underpinned a professional, non-partisan federal workforce for nearly 150 years. Merit-based federal employment means a more efficient government for American taxpayers and better public services for the American people. This proposed regulation would make our federal agencies less effective and expose the American public to the type of corruption that civil service laws were enacted to protect against.

The creation of Schedule “Policy/Career” and the broad way in which it is being interpreted by the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) are contrary to Constitutional due process. It has long been recognized that non-probationary government workers are entitled to due process before they can be removed or have other employment actions taken against them. See Gilbert v. Homar, 520 U.S. 924, 935-936 (1997); Cleveland Board of Education v. Loudermill, 470 U.S. 532, 541 (1985). The importance of maintaining due process and having a merit-based apolitical civil service is also enshrined in federal statute. The proposed regulations would deprive a large number of federal workers of their due process rights. 
The sweeping nature of Schedule “Policy/Career” also undermines important federal statutes. The Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883 was enacted to combat the spoils system and establish merit-based employment in federal agencies. The Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 further honed the efficacy of federal service in response to the Watergate scandal and passed Congress with all but 10 Congressmen voting in favor. Contrary to some propaganda currently circulating, these statutes are effective at ensuring the federal workforce is merit-based while allowing workers to be fired, demoted, etc. for poor performance or misconduct. Congress enacted these protections for federal workers, and this proposed regulation would effectively negate Congress’s will for a large swath of federal workers. 

A broadly inclusive Schedule “Policy/Career” will irrevocably damage federal civil service and negatively impact the American public. By allowing a large portion of federal employees to be reclassified and potentially removed without cause, Schedule “Policy/Career” opens the door to baseless or politically motivated hiring and firing. This is antithetical to the principle of an apolitical civil service enshrined in 5 U.S.C. Sec. 2301(b), which mandates federal employment decisions be based on merit and free from political influence. Stripping thousands or tens of thousands of federal employees of protections against non-merit based actions will weaken accountability and have a chilling effect on employees’ sharing of expert advice and dissent within agencies. It undermines the effectiveness of government by allowing employment to be based on political allyship rather than merit and potentially discouraging free and fair exchange of ideas between knowledgeable workers. It places undue political pressure on career professionals, compromising the integrity and continuity of federal programs across administrations. In short, these changes make the government less functional and efficient for the American people.  

The proposed regulations to implement Schedule “Policy/Career” are contrary to law and pose a grave threat to the foundational principles of good governance, civil service independence, and rule of law. I urge the administration and OPM to halt the proposed regulation. If it must go forward, it should be applied only in the narrowest of circumstances to those whose work is directly to make political policies. Thank you.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Executive Summary
OPM's proposal to create "Schedule Policy/Career" (5 CFR § 213.3501) and strip incumbents of Chapter 43/75 protections exceeds OPM's statutory authority, violates Merit System Principles, and fails the APA's requirement for reasoned decision-making. If OPM ignores these comments, the rule will be ripe for vacatur under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A).

⸻

I. Exceeds OPM's Statutory Authority
1. No Statutory Excepted-Service Schedule Exists - Title 5 creates only Schedules A, B, C, D, and SES. Neither CSRA § 3302 nor any statute authorizes a "Policy/Career" schedule.
2. CSRA's Repeal of Lloyd-La Follette Authority - The CSRA eliminated the hybrid-status regime; nothing in Title 5 permits stripping adverse-action protections while retaining "competitive status."

⸻

II. Arbitrary and Capricious Definition of "Policy-Influencing"
1. Failure to Justify Broad Expansion - OPM offers only a "plain English" gloss on "confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating" (§ 213.3501)—reversing its April 2024 rule—without evidence that career roles meet this standard.
2. Inadequate Impact Analysis - While OPM estimates 50,000 affected workers, there's no comprehensive economic impact analysis (EO 12866) or assessment of career employees' reliance interests in established civil service protections.

⸻

III. Violation of Merit System Principles
1. Undermines Fair Treatment - Stripping Chapter 43/75 protections directly conflicts with 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8).
2. One-Year "Acquisition" of Competitive Status Is No Substitute - New appointees must wait one year to regain competitive status under 5 CFR 302.102(d), offering no protection for incumbents removed in the interim.

⸻

IV. Overbroad Definition Creates Legal Conflicts
1. No Meaningful Distinction Between Implementation and Policy - The rule provides no criteria to distinguish between positions that implement versus determine policy. EEOC Field Directors, OSHA Area Directors, and Contracting Officers exercise authority yet primarily implement rather than create policy.
2. Ignores Specialized Statutory Frameworks - Many positions (COs, ALJs, IRS appeals officers) operate under specific statutory regimes with built-in independence requirements. The rule fails to address these conflicts.

⸻

V. Constitutional Concerns
1. Separation-of-Powers Implications - Stripping removal protections from officers exercising significant authority raises Article II removal-power conflicts (Seila Law v. CFPB, 140 S. Ct. 2183 (2020)).

⸻

VI. Inadequate Explanation for Reversal of Prior Policy
1. Failure to Acknowledge Policy Reversal - The proposed rule directly reverses the April 2024 rule that limited "confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating" positions to "noncareer, political appointments."
2. No Reasoned Analysis for Change - Under FCC v. Fox (556 U.S. 502 (2009)), agencies changing positions must display "awareness" and provide "good reasons." OPM offers only vague justifications about "difficulty removing employees" without evidence.
3. Disregarding Reliance Interests - DHS v. Regents (140 S. Ct. 1891 (2020)) requires accounting for "serious reliance interests." OPM makes no attempt to address these, dismissing prior protections as "cumbersome procedures."
4. No Justification for Contradictory Determinations - Under Encino Motorcars (136 S. Ct. 2117 (2016)), policy based on contradictory factual findings requires "more detailed justification." OPM provides none for its contradictory interpretation.

⸻

VII. Requested Action
OPM should withdraw the proposal or revise it to:
• Ground the schedule in explicit statutory authority;
• Provide inventory of affected positions and cost-benefit analysis;
• Limit coverage to political appointees or those with direct policymaking duties;
• Preserve Chapter 43/75 protections for career professionals;
• Comply with APA, EO 12866, and Regulatory Flexibility Act.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

Title: Comment from Anonymous

 Legal Deficiencies  

1. Arbitrary and Capricious Under State Farm  
   - The Supreme Court in State Farm held that agencies must examine relevant data and articulate a satisfactory explanation for their actions, including a "rational connection between the facts found and the choice made."  
   - Here, OPM provides:

      No clear standards for reclassification  
      No analysis of how these changes would impact workforce stability or merit principles

   - By concealing which jobs could be stripped of competitive service protections, OPM denies stakeholders—including federal employees, unions, and oversight bodies—the ability to assess the rule’s real-world impact.  

3. Violation of Merit System Principles (5 U.S.C. § 2301)  
   - Congress mandated that personnel policies be based on fair and open competition.  
   - Secretly reclassifying jobs without transparency undermines public trust in the civil service.  

 Practical Consequences

      Target career civil servants in disfavored agencies  
      Circumvent veterans’ preferences

 Required Actions  

To comply with the law, OPM must:  
1. Withdraw the current proposal immediately;  
2. Publish a new notice with:

Title: Comment from Sally Seiler
Comment:
I oppose the proposed rule that would create a new “Schedule Policy/Career” category.

Civil service protections were first introduced in the late nineteenth century in response to the “spoils” system whereby supporters of government officials were appointed to political offices. The main problem with that system was that it promoted corruption and inefficiency. Several civil service reform acts have been passed over the years to ensure government positions were filled by non-partisan, competent, and qualified civil servants.

America needs a federal workforce that is professional, nonpartisan and can provide honest, evidence-based advice to policymakers without fear of political retaliation. Turning many career roles into at-will positions risks politicizing government operations and threatens the reliability of important public programs.

Additionally, the rule states time and time again that this is not a mechanism by which federal employees can be fired for their political affiliation, but if that were the case, this effort would not only apply to civil servants who serve in “policy positions.” Principles of accountability and democratic responsiveness would apply to all civil servants if this was not a direct attack on those with differing political views from President Trump. In a time and age where the most mundane policies and practices can become politically charged, this risks creating another spoils system whereby federal employees in low-level roles can be fired for inadvertently not carrying out a political agenda.

Finally, widespread insubordination and undermining of presidential authorities simply cannot happen under the current system. First off, there are specific signatory authorities on every official document and decision that is made. Those authorities do not work in career positions and therefore already do not have civil service protections. Second, almost all decisions in the government are made by committee, not by individual workers. Therefore, absent some widespread conspiracy to overthrow the administration (which does not exist), many voices coalesce to provide a recommendation to the signatory authority. The rule as written shows a deep misunderstanding (whether willful or not) of the civil service.  

I urge OPM to maintain due process rights for career employees, protect merit system principles, and ensure that federal programs serve the public interest.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I strongly oppose the implementation or revival of the “Schedule F” classification for federal employees. This proposal threatens the merit-based civil service system that has underpinned a professional, nonpartisan federal workforce for over a century.

First and foremost, the creation of Schedule F directly undermines the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which was enacted to combat the spoils system and establish a merit-based hiring process for federal employees. By allowing a broad swath of career civil servants—particularly those involved in policy-making or analysis—to be reclassified and potentially terminated without cause, Schedule F opens the door to politically motivated hiring and firing. This is antithetical to the principle of an apolitical civil service enshrined in 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8), which mandates that federal employment decisions be based on merit and free from political influence.

Moreover, the vague and sweeping criteria for inclusion in Schedule F violate the due process protections guaranteed by 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which requires cause and procedural safeguards for the removal of career federal employees. Stripping thousands of workers of these protections not only weakens accountability but also risks chilling expert advice and dissent within agencies—undermining the very effectiveness of government operations.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is also bound by 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to support the merit system principles. Implementing Schedule F contradicts this statutory mission and places undue political pressure on career professionals, compromising the integrity and continuity of federal programs across administrations.

In conclusion, the Schedule F proposal poses a grave threat to the foundational principles of good governance, civil service independence, and the rule of law. I urge the administration and OPM to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement or revive this dangerous classification.

Title: Comment from Amy Trost
Comment:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to OPM's proposed amendments to 5 CFR chapter 1 regarding the creation of Schedule Policy/Career and related changes to federal employment classifications.

While I support accountability in government, these proposed changes would dangerously politicize the civil service by:
- Removing vital employment protections from career civil servants in policy-related positions
- Eliminating procedural safeguards for adverse actions against these employees
- Bypassing standard appeals processes through the Merit Systems Protection Board

The proposed changes bear a striking resemblance to the previously rejected "Schedule F" and threaten to return us to a spoils system reminiscent of the 19th century. Such a system would prioritize political loyalty over professional competence and institutional knowledge, ultimately undermining government effectiveness.

Our federal workforce already follows presidential directives through established chains of command. Career civil servants implement administration policies professionally regardless of their personal political views. The existing system contains multiple mechanisms for addressing performance issues without dismantling merit-based protections.

I urge OPM to withdraw these proposed changes and instead focus on strengthening existing accountability measures that maintain the crucial balance between political responsiveness and professional independence in our civil service.

Respectfully submitted,

Amy Trost

Title: Comment from Kade Schemahorn
Comment:
RE: OPM-2025-0004-0001 - Proposed Rule on "Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service"

To the Office of Personnel Management:

I am submitting this comment in strong opposition to the proposed rule that would establish Schedule Policy/Career (formerly Schedule F) and remove vital civil service protections from an estimated 50,000 career federal employees.

As a UX designer who has spent years collaborating with federal employees to improve government technology and build capacity within agencies to deliver better services to the American public, I have witnessed firsthand how the effectiveness of government technology initiatives depends on the stability, expertise, and nonpartisan dedication of the civil service.

The proposed rule would fundamentally undermine the capacity of government to deliver effective digital services for three primary reasons:

First, user-centered design and technology projects require long-term institutional knowledge and continuity that would be severely compromised by converting career positions to at-will employment. The Government Accountability Office has consistently found that successful IT projects depend on stable leadership and institutional memory (GAO-18-655, "Federal Chief Information Officers: Critical Actions Needed to Address Shortcomings and Challenges in Implementing Responsibilities"). By subjecting technical experts to political turnover, this rule would create precisely the conditions that lead to failed government technology projects.

Second, converting digital service professionals to at-will employees would devastate recruitment and retention of technical talent. The most qualified UX designers, developers, and product managers already accept significant salary reductions to serve in government. Removing job security protections would further hinder the government's ability to attract skilled professionals who could easily find more stable employment in the private sector. The Merit Systems Protection Board has explicitly found that "the protections afforded to the career civil service... are essential to recruit and retain a professional workforce" (MSPB, "The Merit System Principles: Guiding the Fair and Effective Management of the Federal Workforce").

Third, the ability to deliver impartial, user-centered government services depends on technical professionals being free from political pressure. When implementing digital services, we routinely make decisions about accessibility, privacy, and security that should be based on empirical research and professional best practices—not political expedience. As scholars have documented (Moynihan, D. P., & Roberts, A. S. (2021), "Dysfunction by Design: Trumpism as Administrative Doctrine"), politicizing the civil service leads to suppression of expertise and prioritization of political goals over public service.

The justifications offered for Schedule Policy/Career mischaracterize the federal workforce. In my years of collaboration with civil servants, I have observed professionals who strive to deliver services effectively to all Americans regardless of administration. They are guided by evidence and user needs, not political ideology. The Merit System Principles already provide sufficient tools to address poor performance while maintaining crucial protections against politicization.

Courts should recognize that this rule represents a fundamental reinterpretation of civil service statutes that contradicts Congress's intent in the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 to prevent a return to a spoils system. The rule also violates procedural requirements by summarily dismissing the previous administration's thorough rulemaking process without adequate justification, as required by the Administrative Procedure Act.

I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule and instead work with Congress on reforms that would preserve merit system principles while addressing legitimate needs for improved performance management in the federal workforce.

Respectfully submitted,
Kade Schemahorn
UX Designer, Civic Tech Professional

Title: Comment from Doug Coulson
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule issued by the Office of Personnel Management on April 23, 2025, that seeks to revive and codify the Schedule F classification. This rule would grant the executive branch the power to convert tens of thousands of career civil servants—estimated at over 50,000—into at-will political appointees, thereby dismantling the professional, nonpartisan civil service on which democratic governance depends.

Schedule F is an unprecedented assault on the merit-based principles of the federal workforce. Its core premise—removing civil service protections from policy-related positions—opens the door to politicized hiring, mass firings of non-loyalists, and loyalty tests that undermine the independence, stability, and institutional memory of our government. In practice, this reclassification would not enhance accountability but erode it by suppressing dissent and enabling ideological conformity at the expense of evidence-based decision-making.

The proposed rule dangerously expands the definition of “policy-determining” and “policy-advocating” roles to include scientists, analysts, and grantmaking staff in agencies like NIH and NSF—professionals whose expertise is essential for upholding statutory mandates. Similar politicization has already had chilling effects on federal science, including the suspension of research grants, silencing of experts, and mismanagement that impedes agency effectiveness.

The justification that this rule would promote efficiency or responsiveness fails in light of well-documented research. Politicized public services correlate with higher turnover, reduced investment in professional development, decreased responsiveness to congressional oversight, and worsened outcomes for the public. By removing employment protections, Schedule F disincentivizes candor, expertise, and transparency—qualities foundational to effective governance.

The proposed rule is not merely a technocratic adjustment; it is a radical restructuring of the administrative state that threatens to institutionalize a “deep state” of political loyalists. That vision is antithetical to the founding ideals of an impartial civil service and dangerous to the long-term health of democratic institutions.

I urge the Office of Personnel Management to withdraw this rule in full.

Title: Comment from Timothy Foreman
Comment:
Office of Personnel Management
RIN 3206-AO80

As a concerned citizen and scientist with interest in effective governance and scientific integrity, I am submitting this comment regarding the proposed Schedule Policy/Career changes (formerly Schedule F).

Summary of Concerns
The proposed reclassification of approximately 50,000 career civil servants as political appointees represents a fundamental shift away from established merit principles in the federal workforce. This change would have particularly detrimental effects on scientific agencies that require independence and expertise to fulfill their missions effectively.

Key Issues

Undermining Scientific Integrity
Converting positions at agencies like NIH and NSF into political appointments threatens the scientific integrity that has made American research preeminent globally. When scientific decisions become politicized, the quality of research funding decisions deteriorates, as expertise is replaced by ideological considerations.

Reducing Agency Effectiveness
Research conclusively demonstrates that politicization of public services correlates with decreased development of expertise among employees, higher turnover of experienced personnel, reduced organizational performance and capacity, diminished transparency and accountability, and increased waste and inefficiency in operations

Specific Impact on Scientific Agencies
The definition of "policy-making" in this proposal would encompass most program officers at NIH and program directors at NSF who are involved in the grant review process. These positions require deep scientific knowledge and commitment to merit-based decision making, not political alignment.

Concerning Precedents
Recent interventions at NIH and NSF demonstrate the potential harm: politically-motivated reversals of expert scientific recommendations, restrictions on communication with the scientific community, introduction of unnecessary bureaucratic processes, and failure to comply with legal requirements regarding grant administration.

Recommendation
I strongly urge reconsideration of this proposal. The current civil service system, while not perfect, provides important protections that ensure federal employees can perform their duties based on expertise rather than political pressure. Particularly in scientific agencies, maintaining this independence is crucial for America's continued leadership in research and innovation.

Rather than expanding political control, I recommend focusing on existing accountability mechanisms that preserve merit principles while addressing legitimate performance concerns.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
This comment is submitted in strong opposition to the proposed Schedule Policy Career rule. The rule fails to justify its necessity, particularly in light of the significant workforce reshaping that has already occurred across federal agencies in recent years.

Since 2020 (and most especially since the begining of the year in 2025), many agencies have undertaken large-scale reductions in force (RIFs), reorganizations, and hiring freezes. These changes have already tested the resilience, adaptability, and integrity of the career workforce. Employees have endured delayed promotions, increased workloads, and shifting priorities with no guarantee of stability. Yet the vast majority of these civil servants remained in their roles, serving administrations of both parties, continuing to uphold the Constitution and implement policies as directed.

If those who remained through the most challenging operational and political climates—amid pandemic upheaval, budget cuts, and uncertainty about agency futures—were not deterred, it is clear they are not clinging to positions for personal benefit. They are demonstrating a commitment to public service and constitutional governance.

It is disingenuous to suggest that additional authority is needed to root out disloyalty when existing tools under Chapters 43 and 75 already allow for the removal of employees for performance or misconduct. What the proposed rule would do is eliminate procedural safeguards and allow removals for subjective or ideological reasons.

Furthermore, if a performance-based separation was warranted, those mechanisms have long existed and have been used. The federal government does not lack tools to address misconduct—it lacks leadership willing to use those tools responsibly and transparently.

The rule also ignores the reality that personnel systems are designed to provide balance—ensuring accountability to elected leadership while protecting against abuse, politicization, and arbitrary removals. Career staff are not above oversight. They are, however, entitled to due process and to the protections that prevent partisan purges and ideological conformity.

In the broader context of government reform, this proposal offers no measurable improvement to outcomes, employee engagement, or public trust. What it does offer is the erosion of neutrality in the professional workforce and the further instability of federal institutions.

This rule is unnecessary, unfounded, and unwise. Federal employees have already shown extraordinary resilience and dedication under immense pressure. To respond to that commitment by removing their basic workplace rights is both unjust and counterproductive. I urge OPM to withdraw this rule in full.

Title: Comment from Teresa Rodriguez

I strongly object to introducing or reviving the "Schedule F" classification for federal workers. This plan jeopardizes the civil service system's foundation, which hires and promotes based on merit. Notably, President Trump has supported this merit-based approach in Executive Order 14173. By allowing for the potential dismissal of career employees without cause, Schedule F would undermine the principles established by the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which aimed to end the spoils system and ensure hiring and promotion based on merit.

Implementing Schedule F would lead to politicized employment decisions, contradicting the law's requirement for apolitical civil service. The broad and unclear criteria for Schedule F would also undermine due process rights, violating 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which demands cause and procedural safeguards for removing career employees. Depriving thousands of workers of these protections would harm accountability and might silence experts, ultimately reducing government efficiency.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) has a statutory obligation to protect the merit system under federal law (5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq.). Introducing Schedule F would erode this duty by exposing career civil servants to inappropriate political pressure, ultimately weakening the consistency and professionalism of government programs.

The Schedule F initiative endangers fundamental principles of good governance, including an independent civil service and respect for the rule of law. Given these risks, I urge the administration and OPM to reject any efforts to move forward with this proposal.

Merit-based retention should be central to government employment. 

The findings of Volcker in 1990 are still applicable today: We need fewer political appointees and more long-term professional civil servants.

Title: Comment from A C Conner
Comment:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed implementation of Schedule F. This policy represents a dangerous step backward for the principles of a nonpartisan civil service and poses a significant threat to the stability and effectiveness of our government.
The creation of Schedule F would strip critical employment protections from a large segment of the federal workforce, potentially reclassifying them in a way that makes them easily removed for political reasons rather than for cause or performance. This undermines the very foundation of a merit-based civil service system, which has historically ensured that qualified professionals carry out the essential functions of our government regardless of political affiliations.

My concerns with Schedule F are numerous:

 * Politicization of the Civil Service: Schedule F would inevitably lead to the increased politicization of government agencies. Replacing experienced civil servants with individuals chosen primarily for their loyalty to a particular administration, rather than their expertise and qualifications, will erode the impartiality and objectivity that are crucial for effective governance.
 * Erosion of Expertise and Experience: The ease with which employees could be dismissed under Schedule F would lead to a loss of valuable institutional knowledge and expertise within federal agencies. This could severely impact the government's ability to implement policies effectively and respond to the needs of the American people.
 * Increased Potential for Corruption and Favoritism: Without the protections afforded by the current civil service system, federal employees would be more vulnerable to political pressure and potential retaliation for decisions that are not in alignment with the administration's agenda. This creates an environment ripe for corruption and the rewarding of political allies rather than qualified professionals.
 * Undermining Accountability and Oversight: Independent agencies that provide crucial oversight and accountability could be weakened if their staff are subject to political whims. This would diminish the checks and balances necessary for a healthy democracy.
 * Negative Impact on Public Trust: A civil service perceived as being driven by political loyalty rather than competence will inevitably lead to a decline in public trust in government.
The current civil service system, while not perfect, provides essential safeguards against political interference in the impartial execution of government functions. Schedule F would dismantle these safeguards, opening the door to widespread politicization and undermining the effectiveness and integrity of our public service.

I urge the Office of Personnel Management to carefully consider the grave consequences of implementing Schedule F and to instead focus on strengthening the existing merit-based civil service system. Preserving the nonpartisan nature of our federal workforce is essential for good governance and the well-being of our nation.

With all due respect and strenuous opposition to an administration not known for listening to the public,

A.C. Conner
Indianapolis, Indiana

Title: Comment from Cynthia Greenleaf
Comment:
I write in strong opposition to the proposed reinstatement of Schedule F. I write as a career-long senior research scientist, a PhD, and a concerned citizen. I am well aware of the civil service merit principles (U.S. Code § 2301 - Merit system principles) which require that career employees should be hired on the basis of their qualifications, retained on the basis of performance, and protected against political coercion. The US already reserves the top layers of organizational leadership for short-term political appointees. Schedule F will vastly expand the number of appointees, adding a proposed 50,000 from the current 4000. It does so by involuntarily reclassifying career civil servants as appointees and emoving job protections, the basic constraint against political interference.
The administration says that the purpose of Schedule F is to increase accountability for civil servants involved in policy-making. 
Agencies like the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the National Institutes for Health (NIH) cannot meet their statutorily mandated scientific missions if politics, rather than scientific expertise, drive decision-making. Federally supported science has been so successful, in no small part, because agency staff are typically expert scientists beholden to ensuring that the agencies deliver world-class science. Now, many could be turned into political appointees. I have looked on the appointments made by the current administration with deepening concern. Few have any of the expected qualifications for the positions they are assuming, and we the American people are witnessing the results in terrible decisions that increase the risk of disease and poor health. 

I relied upon grants for the work I did during my career for the public good. These grants were vetted assiduously and the competition for funds was always stiff. The proposed policy defines grantmaking positions as “policy-making,” which includes “drafting of funding opportunity announcements, evaluation of grant applications, or recommending or selecting grant recipients.” This definition, which neatly matches agencies’ own definitions for certain career staff, would include most NIH program officers and NSF program directors. This is not the definition of science, nor should scientific agencies advance mere policy rather than scientific knowledge to bring the best insight to the policy makers. This shift of power makes the work already done by the scientifically expert community redundant, but more importantly, it instills a degree of political control of science funding that is inappropriate in a democratic society and contrary to the goals of scientific advancement that have resulted in the brilliance and breakthrough work done in this country.
 
Politicized scientific agencies would operate to undercut this extraordinary record, as we have seen in the past few months of chaotic action by the administration. Funding choices that reflected the consensus of some of the best scientists in the world were reversed by nonscientists. Program officers have been told not to communicate with the scientific community. Grantees have had to curtail their studies in mid-stream. Scientific agencies have been directed to effectively reduce the flow of funds by adding new layers of redundant review and red tape and have even violated court orders to reinstate cancelled grants. The purpose of Schedule F is to permanently instill the degree of political control over American science that is now the envy of the world. DO NOT take this move down a troubling path to politicized future for agencies meant to draw on and build expertise to serve the American people, not the whims of any particular political administration.

By allowing for the potential dismissal of career employees without cause, Schedule F would undermine the principles established by the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which aimed to end the spoils system and ensure hiring and promotion based on merit.

Implementing Schedule F would lead to politicized employment decisions, contradicting the law's requirement for apolitical civil service. The broad and unclear criteria for Schedule F would also undermine due process rights, violating 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which demands cause and procedural safeguards for removing career employees. Depriving thousands of workers of these protections would harm accountability and might silence experts, ultimately reducing government efficiency.

Introducing Schedule F would erode this duty by exposing career civil servants to inappropriate political pressure, ultimately weakening the consistency and professionalism of government programs.

The Schedule F initiative endangers fundamental principles of good governance, including an independent civil service and respect for the rule of law. Given these risks, I urge the administration and OPM to reject any efforts to move forward with this proposal.

I strongly oppose the reclassification of civil servants to be political appointees. An underlying bedrock of career, non-partisan civil servants running the day-to-day operations of our Government is the foundation of trust in the American Government. These individuals ensure the smooth functioning of the country and provide continuity and trust even as elected officials come and go. It is essential they remain career employees relatively immune the political winds of the day.
