Title: Comment from Anonymous Anonymous
Comment:
Public Comment on Proposed Rule: OPM-2025-0004 / RIN 3206-AO80
Submitted in My Personal Capacity

To whom it may concern:

I am submitting this comment in my personal capacity as a federal employee with over twenty years of service. I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule that would allow the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) to reclassify a broad range of federal positions into a new “Schedule Policy/Career” (Schedule P/C) category, stripping affected employees of their civil service protections and appeal rights.

Throughout my career, I have faithfully served under multiple administrations, regardless of party affiliation. My job has always been to follow the law, implement policy as written, and provide the best service to the American people. This has often required me to present facts or interpretations that may not align with the political priorities of the moment—but that is what integrity and public service require.

If this rule had been in place during past administrations, I and many of my colleagues would have faced enormous pressure to self-censor, to comply with potentially unlawful directives, or to stay silent rather than speak up when programs or policies were not in compliance with applicable law or evidence. The civil service protections in place today exist precisely to protect the American public from this kind of politicization.

The proposed rule is dangerously vague, allowing any administration to reclassify employees under the undefined concept of “policy influence.” In practice, this could result in mass firings of career experts—scientists, analysts, benefits processors, safety inspectors—whose only offense is offering objective advice or faithfully carrying out their duties. That would damage the delivery of public services, from Social Security to clean air protections, and would erode trust in government.

The rule also ignores well-established legal protections under the Civil Service Reform Act. Removing appeal rights to the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) is not only unfair, but it also places employees in a precarious legal position, with few options for recourse even in cases of clear retaliation or abuse.

If OPM’s intent is to improve accountability and performance, I urge the agency to consider less extreme, more targeted alternatives. These could include additional training for supervisors, streamlined performance management procedures, and increased resources for MSPB to expedite cases. Gutting due process protections for tens of thousands of employees is not the answer.

In summary, I urge OPM to withdraw this rule and preserve the integrity of a professional, nonpartisan civil service. The American public deserves a government staffed by experts who are free to do their jobs without fear of political retaliation. This rule undermines that promise.

Sincerely,
Concerned Citizen

Title: Comment from RISE Stronger
Comment:
Re: RIN 3206-AO80, “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service”

Dear OPM,

On behalf of RISE Stronger, we request an extension of the 30-day comment period provided for OPM’s Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM), “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service.” 90 FR 17182 (April 23, 2025). For context, RISE Stronger is a citizen watchdog organization of nearly 30,000 members that was formed in the wake of the 2016 election. Our mission is to ensure that the government and its leaders are accountable to its citizens, transparent in their actions and policies, and guided solely by the interests and values of the American people.

The Administrative Procedures Act (APA) does not establish a minimum comment period, but courts require agencies to provide a “meaningful opportunity to comment” on proposed rules. Forester v. CPSC, 559 F.2d 774, 787 (D.C. Cir. 1977). Here, for a number of reasons, the 30-day comment period OPM has provided for this rulemaking is unlawfully short.

* INCONSISTENT WITH PRESIDENTIAL DIRECTIVES. Presidential guidance since 1993 has instructed that agencies must afford the public “a meaningful opportunity to comment on any proposed regulation, which in most cases should include a comment period of not less than 60 days.” E.O. 12866 § 6(a), 58 FR 51735, 51740 (1993); see also E.O. 13563 § 2(b), 76 FR 3821-22 (2011) (“[E]ach agency shall afford the public a meaningful opportunity to comment through the Internet on any proposed regulation, with a comment period that should generally be at least 60 days.”). OPM has acknowledged that this rulemaking qualifies as a “significant regulatory action” under Executive Orders 12866 and 13563, 90 FR 17221, so, to comply with those Executive Orders, the comment period for this rulemaking should be extended to at least 60 days. Failing to do so would be hypocritical for a rulemaking purporting to promote the implementation of Presidential directives. 

* INCONSISTENT WITH BEST PRACTICE RECOMMENDATIONS. Consistent with Presidential directives, the American Bar Association (ABA) and the Administrative Conference of the United States (ACUS) have similarly recommended a minimum comment period of 60 days for significant or major proposed rules. See Christopher J. Walker, Modernizing the Administrative Procedure Act, 69 Admin. L. Rev. 629, 641 (2017); ACUS Recommendation 2011-2, 76 FR 48789, 48791 (Aug. 9, 2011).

* INCONSISTENT WITH PAST PRACTICE. The Supreme Court has stated that agencies must “use the same procedures when they amend or repeal a rule as they used to issue the rule in the first instance.” Perez v. Mortgage Bankers Association, 575 U.S. 92, 101 (2015). Here, OPM is proposing to replace a 2024 final rule that was promulgated after OPM published an NPRM with a 60-day comment period. See 88 FR 63862. That 2023 Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) was 24 pages in the Federal Register and proposed to preserve the prior status quo. Now, OPM has published an NPRM which is nearly twice as long (43 pages in the Federal Register) and proposes to strip civil service protections from an estimated 50,000 federal employees, but OPM is providing half of the time to submit comments. This inconsistency is arbitrary and capricious.

· GRATUITOUS LEGAL RISK. OPM will risk a successful legal challenge under the APA if it refuses to extend the comment period, as courts have found comment periods comparable to this 30-day comment period to be unlawfully short. See Centro Legal de la Raza v. Exec. Off. for Immigr. Rev., 524 F. Supp. 3d 919, 954-62 (N.D. Cal. 2021) (holding that plaintiffs were “likely to succeed on their claim that [a 30-day comment period] was deficient under the APA”); see also Pangea Legal Services v. U.S. Dept. of Homeland Security, 501 F.Supp.3d 792 (N.D. Cal. 2020) (holding that “plaintiffs have at minimum shown ‘serious questions going to the merits’ of their claim that [a 30-day comment period] was deficient under the APA”); see also Prometheus Radio Project v. FCC, 652 F.3d 431, 453 (3d Cir. 2011) (holding that a comment period was inadequate where an agency “gave only 28 days for response, not the usual 90 days” it had previously).

RISE Stronger notes that numerous commenters have already requested an extension to the comment period, and more requests are likely. See https://www.regulations.gov/document/OPM-2025-0004-0001/comment?filter=%22comment%20period%22. For all of the reasons discussed above, OPM would be wise to heed those requests.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I oppose OPM's proposed rule, Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service, because it significantly weakens career policy employees' ability to give candid advice and opinions to the political leaders in their agencies. I am a federal employee but, as is obvious by my lack of title or agency identification, I submit this note in my individual capacity. This comment uses interchangeably "career" and "civil servant" to refer to federal employees with polict jobs covered by these proposed rules.

I wanted to focus my comment on two points: 1) the high volume of anonymous comments in this NPRM as opposed to the previous (2023) NPRM relating to Schedule F, and 2) the question of how federal employees with policy jobs can both keep their jobs while retaining their oath to the Constitution.

For the first issue, I anonymously submitted these comments because I am fearful of retribution by the political appointees that run my agency. Note that I have submitted NPRM comments in my personal capacity while a federal employee under previous Democrat and Republican administrations, but not anonymously, because I never worried about my personal opinion outside of work affecting my ability to keep my job. As OPM will note, the percentage of anonymous comments in this NPRM far exceeds those in the prior Schedule F NPRM regarding the same issue. I believe it is because President Trump and his political appointees have already punished people for showing a reasonable difference from his opinion, such as through the investigations, terminations, and suspensions of people who worked on the January 6 insurrection trials. See, for example, news articles found at https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/justice-department/top-fbi-official-forced-criticizing-trump-pursuit-agents-investigated-rcna194610 and https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cj3e70r0dvko and 

For the second issue, I think the proposed rule fails to account for the likely situation where a President's directive requires career policy employee to violate their oath to the Constitution. As explained in new § 213.3501, under the policy employees are "required to faithfully implement administration policies to the best of their ability, consistent with their constitutional oath and the vesting of executive authority solely in the President. Failure to do so is grounds for dismissal.” 

What recourse does a federal policy employee have if the person is fired for upholding their oath to the Constitution? This is not an unlikely hypothetical, since on or about May 4, 2025, President Trump had this exchange with a reporter, Kristen Welker:

"Kristen Welker (KW): Your secretary of state says everyone who’s here, citizens and non-citizens, deserve due process. Do you agree, Mr. President?                                               

President Trump (PT): I don’t know. I’m not, I’m not a lawyer. I don’t know.                                               

KW: Well, the Fifth Amendment says as much.                                               

PT: I don’t know. It seems — it might say that, but if you’re talking about that, then we’d have to have a million or 2 million or 3 million trials. We have thousands of people that are some murderers and some drug dealers and some of the worst people on Earth."

As President, Mr. Trump should know, without a lawyer, that the 5th Amendment of the Constitution grants people inside the US due process via the judicial branch. And while he was correct that there could possibly be millions of trials if every person were afforded due process, that is what the Constitution demands. How then could civil servants creating policies in DHS and DOJ both uphold their own oath to the Constitution if asked to implement a policy to deport immigrants without a trial, if the civil servants believe the directive is unconstitutional but the political employees believe the policies are constitutional? 

Even taking away this specific issue, the question still remains: what do career policy employees do if they believe there is a conflict between their oath to the Constitution and the implementation of an administration's policy, if the administration believes that a directive is constitutional and thus want to fire the career employee? What recourse would the career employee have? Further, what do career employees do if a court believes that an administration's policy is unconstitutional but the administration disagrees with the court and still orders that the career policy employee implements the policy? 

OPM must first identify the solution to that problem, and allow public input on it, before it could reasonably make this type of change to the regulation.

Title: Comment from Patrick King

I write in opposition to the proposed Personnel Management Office rule RIN 3206-AO80, "Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service." I write with over fifteen years' experience as a grant administrator and financial administrator in higher education, as well as five years of work in an instructional capacity at the university level, with extensive experience interacting with the federal bureaucracy's hardworking civil service.

The hallmark of the federal grantmaking and administration infrastructure has been stability and predictability. Incredible biomedical and scientific research has been made possible because researchers and institutions of higher learning understand that regulatory environments and grant-related decision making operate on sound scientific and methodological bases. Governmental incentives are always in flux, and contrary to the rule's claims, changes in administration do frequently impact what kinds of projects receive emphasis in a research environment. What does not change, however, are baseline expectations of research conduct, peer review, project feasibility, budgeting practices, and other ironclad elements that are dictated by statute or longstanding practice. Knowing this allows universities and research institutions to throw their focus where it properly lies: on the acquisition of knowledge and development of new technologies or medicines that have made America a powerful leader in scientific and medical fields.

Making the vast majority of civil servants subject to summary dismissal as political appointees threatens to upend the predictability of this environment and do permanent damage to America's reputation as a place to conduct research and drive innovation. At present, administrators and scientists focus their interactions with the federal government on adhering to universally-applied, well-understood and time-tested processes driven by field-specific best practices. Under the proposed rule, with the vast majority of civil servants transformed into at-will employees easily dismissed for following politically disfavored but methodologically sound outcomes, the focus will necessarily shift to writing proposals and shaping research based on the rhetoric and political agenda of the ruling party - not following the science where the facts lead, but using the buzzwords and seeking the outcomes demanded by a political agenda.

Put bluntly, this would no longer be research but propaganda; no longer administrative oversight but censorship. The rule would be detrimental to the point of the wholesale destruction of America's prosperity in the long run. I urge the rejection of the rule in the strongest possible terms.

Title: Comment from Colin Seftor
Comment:
This is an inherently bad rule and should not be implemented.  

First, it’s violates the Civil Service Reform Act (CSRA) enacted by Congress in 1978.  

The CSRA provides that an agency may only fire, demote, or issue a lengthy suspension to an employee “for cause,” not for arbitrary or improper reasons. And it must first provide notice of its reasons and an opportunity for the employee to respond. The employee may then appeal the action to a neutral federal adjudicator, the Merit Systems Protection Board. If the Board rules against her, she may go to federal court.

The CSRA does carve out employees “whose position[s] ha[ve] been determined to be of a confidential, policy-determining, policy-making or policy-advocating character.”   But this carve out has historically applied only to a small group of employees: political appointees. 

This rule is designed to dramatically reduce the scope of the CSRA by extending the confidential and policymaking designation to thousands more current government employees, thereby stripping them of the protections accorded to them under CSRA.  It’s clear that its implementation, without express further action by Congress, is unlawful.

Second, while the current administraton states that the purpose of the rule is to increase civil servant responsibility, history (and studies) have shown that such a rule would worsen the performance of government employees; concerns about being fired would lead to a failure to share “hard truths” with their political bosses and become less likely to respond to congressional oversight.  This, in turn, leads to lower transparency and administrative capacity, increasing and not decreasing waste and inefficiency.

Federally sponsored science research would be particularly had hit by the implementation of such a rule. The past few months at scientific agencies such as the NIH and NSF show how politicized scientific agencies would operate. Funding choices that reflected the consensus of some of the best scientists in the world were reversed by nonscientists. Program officers have, at points, been told not to communicate with the scientific community or have had their engagement limited. Scientific agencies have been directed to effectively drastically reduce the flow of funds by adding new layers of redundant review and red tape and even violating court orders to reinstate cancelled grants.  

Career officials in scientific agencies are unwilling hostages in Trump’s politicization of science, wondering if they will lose their jobs for trying to defend the congressionally mandated missions of their organizations. The purpose of the proposed rule is to permanently instill the degree of political control over science fueling the sense of fear that pervades those agencies now.

Only the opposite approach will ensure that government agency employees at such agencies will remain expert scientists that are beholden to ensuring the delivery of world-class science.  Only then can we expect the continued hugely success of our current system.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I am writing to express strong opposition to any effort to reinstate Schedule F in the federal workforce. This proposal undermines foundational principles of merit-based civil service, invites undue political interference, and risks violating statutory and constitutional protections. 2. Weakens Due Process and Employee Rights

Federal employees in competitive service positions have a constitutionally recognized expectation of due process before being removed. Reassigning them to Schedule F without cause strips them of these protections, potentially violating the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause. The Supreme Court has affirmed that such employment can create a property interest (see Loudermill, 1985), which cannot be taken away arbitrarily.

3. Politicizes the Career Civil Service

Schedule F blurs the line between career professionals and political appointees. It risks creating a chilling effect in which federal employees may feel pressured to align with political views rather than carry out their duties objectively and in the public interest. This contradicts the spirit of the Hatch Act, which aims to preserve a nonpartisan civil service.

4. Violates the Administrative Procedure Act

The prior attempt to implement Schedule F was done with minimal transparency and justification. Reinstating it without a clear, evidence-based rationale may once again run afoul of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), which requires agencies to avoid arbitrary and capricious decision-making. The APA also requires agencies to consider the reliance interests of employees and the public trust.

5. Threatens Continuity of Government

Schedule F could lead to widespread firings and resignations of experienced public servants, jeopardizing the continuity and institutional knowledge necessary for effective governance—particularly during transitions of power or national emergencies.

Conclusion

The civil service exists to serve the American people, not any political party or administration. Schedule F threatens to erode that foundation. I urge the Administration and the Office of Personnel Management to reject any move to reinstate this classification and to uphold the integrity, independence, and professionalism of the federal workforce.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
he opening months of the Trump administration represent a historic disruption to America’s scientific agencies. Staff have been fired or reassigned in the name of efficiency, resulting in chaos. Grants have been canceled mid-project for featuring the wrong words. “Pauses” and “reviews” are designed to block spending, in the hope that Congress will make the current impoundment of funds a baseline for permanent disinvestment. While the scientific community waits to see what the new normal will be, the Trump administration has a plan to institutionalize a much more politicized structure of control over government broadly, including both public scientific investments and the use of scientific knowledge in policy actions.

“Schedule F” (now renamed Schedule Policy/Career) is shorthand for an executive order that is a sharp break with civil service merit principles, which assume that career employees should be retained on the basis of performance and protected against political coercion. The US is already unusual in the degree to which it reserves the top layers of organizational leadership for short-term political appointees. Schedule F will vastly expand the number of appointees, adding a proposed 50,000 from the current 4000. It does so by involuntarily reclassifying career civil servants as appointees, removing job protections, the basic constraint against political interference.

The administration says that the purpose of Schedule F is to increase accountability for civil servants involved in policy-making. Set aside the fact that civil servants are accountable in multiple ways, Trump’s own justifications strike a more conspiratorial tone, including “the deep state can and must be brought to heel.” But what better way to actually institutionalize a deep state than by expanding political influence over what constitutes good science?

Studies show that politicization of public services generally worsens public-sector outcomes. Public employees invest less in developing their expertise and become more likely to exit. Instability and lack of experience reduce organizational performance. Politicization increases the influence of more ideologically radical appointees relative to more moderate civil servants. Politicization also reduces accountability. Bureaucrats worried about being fired fail to share uncongenial information with their political bosses and become less likely to respond to congressional oversight. As politicization begets lower transparency and administrative capacity, it increases waste and inefficiency.

What might this mean for scientific agencies? Agencies like the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the National Institutes for Health (NIH) cannot meet their statutorily mandated scientific missions if politics, rather than scientific expertise, drive decision-making. Federally supported science has been so successful, in no small part, because agency staff are typically expert scientists beholden to ensuring that the agencies deliver world-class science. Now, many could be turned into political appointees. The proposed policy defines grantmaking positions as “policy-making,” which includes “drafting of funding opportunity announcements, evaluation of grant applications, or recommending or selecting grant recipients.” This definition, which neatly matches agencies’ own definitions for certain career staff, would include most NIH program officers and NSF program directors.

The past few months at NIH and NSF preview how politicized scientific agencies would operate. Funding choices that reflected the consensus of some of the best scientists in the world were reversed by nonscientists. Program officers have, at points, been told not to communicate with the scientific community or have had their engagement limited. Scientific agencies have been directed to effectively reduce the flow of funds to a trickle by adding new layers of redundant review and red tape and even violating court orders to reinstate cancelled grants.

Other agencies, including regulatory agencies, apply rather than fund basic science, but the risks of politicization are no less. How confident can Americans be that federal employees will not have to choose between their job and scientific values in areas such as climate change, food safety, extreme weather forecasting, or public health?

Career officials in scientific agencies are unwilling hostages in Trump’s politicization of science, wondering if they will lose their jobs for trying to defend the congressionally mandated missions of their organizations. Although the current era of layoffs will hopefully soon be over, the purpose of Schedule F is to permanently instill the degree of political control over science fueling the sense of fear that pervades those agencies now.

Title: Comment from Steven Ramsey
Comment:
As a citizen of the United States writing in my personal capacity—and as a former federal employee—I write to strongly oppose the proposed rule to create the “Schedule Policy/Career” classification and to exempt these positions from standard civil service protections under Chapters 43 and 75 of Title 5.

1. Civil Servants Must Remain Nonpartisan and Protected from Political Retaliation
The rule claims that Schedule Policy/Career positions will remain career and “nonpartisan” (Federal Register, p. 17182), yet in the same breath it allows these employees to be fired at-will by political leadership, without the adverse action protections enshrined in law for decades. It is contradictory to claim these roles will remain apolitical while eliminating the very safeguards that insulate them from partisan pressure.

Stripping policy-influencing employees of Chapter 43 and 75 protections (pp. 17182–17183) opens the door to politicizing the civil service. The justification that some civil servants “subvert Presidential directives” (p. 17182) is vague and dangerously subjective. Who decides what counts as “subversion”? This language risks enabling firings based on political disagreement, not misconduct or incompetence.

We need civil servants who serve the public interest, not the agenda of any one administration. Our democracy depends on continuity, competence, and nonpartisanship in federal agencies. This rule undermines those values.

2. The Federal Workforce Has Been Stable Despite Massive Population Growth
According to Congressional Research Service data, the size of the federal civilian workforce has remained relatively flat for over 50 years, even as the U.S. population has grown by more than 68%. The idea that the federal government is “bloated” or overrun by lazy bureaucrats is a political talking point—not a reality backed by facts.

Federal employees today do more with less, serving an increasingly complex and growing society without the commensurate staffing increases. Weakening job protections for those employees sends the wrong message and threatens morale and effectiveness.

3. Probationary Periods Already Exist—and They Work
Every federal employee already serves a probationary period at the start of their service, during which supervisors can terminate employment without appeal rights. This existing framework provides more than enough opportunity to weed out poor performers early on. The solution to long-term underperformance lies in better training, supervision, and resourcing—not in removing legal protections wholesale.

4. Accountability Must Not Come at the Expense of Humanity or Due Process
I agree that improving how we manage performance and remove ineffective employees is a worthy goal. But it must be done strategically, with care and consultation—just as Elaine Kamarck led during the Clinton administration when the government workforce was streamlined without dehumanization or politicization.

This proposed rule represents a reckless, top-down dismantling of institutional protections. It is a blunt instrument being wielded for political gain, not thoughtful reform. If the administration is serious about modernizing the civil service, it should form a bipartisan commission and engage in good-faith dialogue—not impose radical changes through executive fiat.

Stop this "Schedule Policy/Career" madness. Uphold the merit-based, nonpartisan principles that have served our country well for over a century.

Title: Comment from AnonymousFirstName AnonymousLastName
Comment:
Dear OPM Decision-Makers,

I write to express my concerns regarding the proposed reclassification of certain policy-influencing positions under the “Schedule Policy/Career” designation. While I support efforts to improve accountability in the federal workforce, I am troubled by any measures that would diminish the due process protections vital to current federal employees and discourage prospective talent.

Existing Accountability Protections - The federal government already maintains several well-established mechanisms for ensuring accountability. For instance, current performance evaluation procedures, mandated by federal personnel regulations and integrated into annual review systems, offer a structured way of addressing poor performance. In addition, internal oversight mechanisms—including the Inspector General offices and the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB)—provide independent review of adverse employment actions under the existing system. These structures ensure that disciplinary measures are subject to objective review and fair corrective processes while safeguarding employee rights. Strengthening these frameworks, rather than dismantling them, would preserve the integrity of our civil service while addressing performance issues.

A Balanced, Cost-Effective Approach -
Rather than resorting to a system that bypasses established due process in favor of “at‑will” status, I recommend that federal agencies focus on refining and expediting the processes already in place:

1. Enhanced Performance Evaluations: The federal government’s current performance management system can be modernized with more robust evaluation metrics and proactive remediation plans. Refining these processes will not only improve accountability but also leverage an infrastructure that is already in place, thereby avoiding the costs associated with establishing an entirely new system.

2. Optimizing Independent Oversight: Independent review mechanisms, such as the MSPB, already serve as safeguards against arbitrary disciplinary actions. By expediting reviews or reallocating resources to enhance their efficiency, agencies can maintain oversight standards without incurring the administrative and financial costs associated with creating separate, new review panels.

3. Strengthened Internal Oversight: Existing internal oversight measures—including routine audits and performance reviews—should be intensified to ensure adherence to established performance standards. Improving internal procedures will offer a more cost-effective solution compared to the expense of setting up new independent bodies, and can be implemented through careful reallocation of current budgets and resources.

4. Streamlined Administrative Remedies: The present adverse action procedures, though sometimes slow, provide a critical safety net for federal employees. Rather than eliminating these processes, a targeted review to shorten review timelines and remove bureaucratic bottlenecks would serve the dual purpose of enhancing accountability and protecting employee rights, all while staying within existing statutory frameworks.

In conclusion, I urge OPM to reconsider the proposed measure and, instead, focus on enhancing the robust accountability systems already in place. By strengthening performance evaluations, optimizing independent oversight, fortifying internal reviews, and streamlining existing administrative remedies, the federal government can achieve its accountability goals in a manner that both protects employee rights and remains cost-effective. This balanced approach not only secures the current workforce but also sends a positive signal to future prospective federal employees who value fairness, due process, and transparent performance management.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Sincerely,

This very "interesting" regulatory proposal certainly violates the provisions of 5 USC chapters 43, 53 and 75, and the minimum due process requirements of the 5th Amendment of the US Constitution.  The proposed regulations would separate career competitive service and excepted service employees involuntarily from their statutorily and Constitutionally appointed positions and place them into a new, to-be-created created classification system that lacks the procedural and substantive rights of their former positions, without following the above statutory authorities and procedures.  Also, OPM's proposed regulations do not afford Constitutionally required "minimum due process" (i.e., prior notice and an opportunity to be heard by a neutral informed decision maker who has the authority to reach a binding different conclusion than that mandated by the proposed regulations) under the 5th Amendment.  That is the right of all career federal employees by the decisions of the US Courts, before they may be separated involuntarily from their positions.  E.g., Arnett v. Kennedy, 416 U.S. 134 (1974).  Rather, by regulatory fiat, the OPM proposal knowingly violates the substantive and procedural requirements 5 USC and also would knowingly deprive the affected employees Constitutionally required minimum due process before they are separated involuntarily from their current positions. 

Further, the US Supreme Court and lower federal Courts will probably hold that this proposed regulatory framework violates the "Major Questions Doctrine" of judicial analysis that suggests Congress must clearly authorize an agency to act on matters of "vast economic and political significance".  E.g., West Virginia v. EPA, 143 S. Ct. 2587 (2022).  Congress and US Presidents for well over a century have legislated under, e.g., The Pendleton Act of 1883 and the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978, as amended, the structure and substance of the federal personnel system.  OPM's proposed regulations are clearly of national significance.  OPM must demonstrate that Congress has explicitly granted it the authority to address the major question as set forth by the proposed regulations.  The Congress has not granted OPM such explicit authority here.  OPM must obtain prior Congressional authorization for its proposed regulatory action.

Until the above legal requirements are satisfied by OPM, these proposed regulations are not consistent with title 5 USC and the Constitution.  Thus, the proposed OPM regulations should be withdrawn and reconsidered.

By allowing broad categories of career civil servants—especially those involved in policy development or analysis—to be reclassified and dismissed without cause, Schedule F invites the very abuses the Pendleton Act was designed to prevent.

This proposal is directly at odds with the statutory merit system principles laid out in 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b), which guarantee that federal employment should be based on merit and free from political coercion. It also undermines the due process protections in 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which safeguard against arbitrary or retaliatory removals by requiring just cause and fair procedures. Stripping thousands of career officials of these protections not only threatens their job security—it endangers the government’s ability to function based on facts, expertise, and continuity.

Moreover, Schedule F would have a chilling effect on the willingness of civil servants to provide honest, evidence-based advice to political leadership, especially when that advice may be unwelcome. Silencing or punishing dissent weakens the very capacity of agencies to serve the public interest and respond effectively to complex, evolving challenges.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) has a legal and institutional obligation under 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to uphold and defend the merit system. Endorsing or facilitating Schedule F would betray this mission and politicize the federal workforce in ways that would compromise the integrity of government operations across administrations. It would erode public trust in federal agencies and increase the risk of corruption, inefficiency, and incompetence.

In short, Schedule F is a radical and dangerous proposal. It would reverse more than a century of progress in professionalizing the federal workforce and open the door to political purges, cronyism, and abuse of power. I urge the administration and the Office of Personnel Management to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement, revive, or otherwise authorize this deeply misguided classification.

Good governance depends on a career civil service that is expert, stable, and shielded from partisan manipulation. Schedule F must be categorically opposed.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule for several reasons.

First, career federal employees execute their jobs faithfully to the Constitution, in accordance with the oath each took when they began their federal service, without regard to the person or political party who sits in the office of the President. The proposed rule would force those employees, out of fear for their livelihood, to place loyalty to the President and the President’s agenda above faithfulness to the Constitution and the laws passed by Congress. 

Second, OPM’s reasoning fails to rely on any objective data. The surveys and “research” cited in the proposed rule (such as the FedView survey, which asks federal employees to rate their agreement or disagreement, on a scale of 1 through 5, with a series of statements about their experiences in their work environment) consist of a series of opinions and are not data. Moreover, those surveys do not provide any reasoning underlying the respondents’ opinions. Rather, OPM assumes, without basis or fact, that federal managers fail to take action against poor performers because of adverse action procedures. If OPM was truly concerned with the reasons why so many poor performers are not dealt with, it would obtain information regarding the challenges to disciplining federal employees from those who are experts in that field—namely, MSPB administrative law judges, personnel law attorneys (those in the government and in the private sector), human resources personnel, and federal managers themselves. 

Third, OPM states that the only alternative to its proposed rule is to take no rulemaking action and instead train managers. In this regard, OPM fails to consider the many other alternatives that would make the adverse action process more efficient. OPM could propose rulemaking and/or guidance for federal agencies to update and strengthen their charges and tables of penalties. For example, for most offenses, federal agencies currently allow employees to engage in misconduct three times before the penalty is removal. Similarly, many agency tables of penalties provide for too wide of a range in each penalty. OPM could mandate consequences for managers who fail to pursue disciplinary action against employees who engage in misconduct or perform poorly, or for managers who impose penalties that are a ‘slap on the wrist’ compared to the offense. OPM could revise its procedural rules in part 752, consistent with title 5 of the US Code, to make the adverse action process more efficient, for example by shortening timelines and lessening the agency’s burden of proof. There are many, many options for making the process more efficient short of removing appeal rights from employees altogether.    

Lastly, the idea that the proposed rule is needed because of the large number of career federal employees who are imposing policy (and policy contrary to the goals of a particular administration, nonetheless) is a mischaracterization of the federal workforce. Policy decisions are made at the executive level. Most career employees who work in policy simply write and effectuate the policy that their executives have instructed them to execute. Thus, the proposed Schedule Policy/Career would not achieve the agency’s goal of removing appeal rights from the actual employees who influence policy.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
**Statement Opposing the Proposed OPM Rule on Employee Accountability**

We strongly oppose the Office of Personnel Management's (OPM) proposed rule to increase career employee accountability through the introduction of at-will positions within Schedule Policy/Career. While the intention to enhance accountability in federal employment is commendable, the approach outlined in this proposal is fundamentally flawed and poses significant risks to the integrity of our civil service system.

First and foremost, the shift to at-will employment for policy-influencing positions undermines the very principles of fairness and due process that are foundational to our democratic governance. By exempting these positions from adverse action procedures and appeals, the proposal opens the door to arbitrary and capricious dismissals, which can be influenced by political motivations rather than genuine performance issues. This not only jeopardizes the job security of dedicated public servants but also threatens the nonpartisan nature of our federal workforce, which is essential for maintaining public trust in government operations.

Moreover, the assertion that this rule will facilitate the swift removal of employees who engage in misconduct or poor performance is misleading. The existing mechanisms for addressing such issues, while perhaps in need of reform, are designed to ensure that employees are treated fairly and that their rights are protected. The proposed rule, by contrast, risks creating a culture of fear and uncertainty, where employees may be hesitant to voice concerns or dissenting opinions for fear of retribution. This is particularly concerning in positions that require independent judgment and the ability to challenge directives that may not align with the public interest.

Additionally, the vague language surrounding the criteria for removal raises serious concerns about the potential for misuse. The phrase "undermine the democratic process" is alarmingly broad and subjective, leaving room for interpretation that could lead to the dismissal of employees for exercising their rights to free speech or for engaging in legitimate policy debates. Such a chilling effect on discourse within the federal workforce is antithetical to the principles of democracy and accountability that this rule purports to uphold.

In conclusion, while the goal of enhancing accountability in federal employment is important, the proposed rule by OPM is not the solution. It threatens to erode the protections that ensure a fair and impartial civil service, undermining the very values that our democracy stands for. We urge OPM to reconsider this proposal and to engage in a more thoughtful and inclusive process that prioritizes the rights and protections of federal employees while still addressing the legitimate concerns of agency supervisors. The integrity of our government and the trust of the American people depend on it.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
To Whom It May Concern:

I am writing to express my strong and unequivocal opposition to the proposed rule titled “Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service.” This proposal would fundamentally and dangerously alter the landscape of federal employment, eroding long-standing civil service protections, politicizing the workforce, and undermining the foundational principle of a nonpartisan, merit-based civil service.

⸻

I. A False Narrative on Accountability

The central justification for this rule—that current civil service protections prevent accountability—is demonstrably false. Agencies already possess ample authority under Title 5 to address poor performance and misconduct. The challenge lies not in the rules themselves but in inconsistent application, inadequate training, and a lack of managerial follow-through. Rather than strengthening performance systems, this rule bypasses due process entirely.

⸻

II. A Thinly Veiled Resurrection of “Schedule F”

This proposal is, in substance, a repackaged version of the discredited and widely opposed “Schedule F” initiative. The new “Schedule Policy/Career” designation grants agencies the power to classify roles as “policy-influencing,” stripping them of traditional protections and subjecting them to at-will dismissal. This structure invites abuse and undermines the apolitical character of the career civil service. The rule’s language may have changed, but its purpose has not.

⸻

III. An Assault on Constitutional and Institutional Norms

The merit-based civil service has served as a critical check against political interference for more than a century. This proposal would allow federal managers to fire career employees without cause, recourse, or oversight—inviting retaliatory removals based on political, ideological, or personal disagreements. The vague definition of “policy-influencing” roles exacerbates this risk, making nearly any professional vulnerable.

⸻

IV. Harm to Morale, Recruitment, and Retention

Implementing this rule would devastate morale among existing employees and discourage new talent from joining public service. No professional would reasonably enter federal employment knowing their job could be lost at the whim of political appointees. This chilling effect would drive away scientists, lawyers, policy analysts, and countless others whose expertise the public depends on.

⸻

V. A Threat to Whistleblower Protections and Ethical Governance

This proposal would silence whistleblowers and suppress dissent. Civil servants who witness wrongdoing would hesitate to come forward if termination without due process were a looming threat. It is antithetical to transparency, oversight, and lawful government operations. Ethical governance cannot survive under the weight of fear-based management.

⸻

VI. Undermining the Rule of Law

Public service must be governed by laws and regulations—not loyalty tests or political convenience. The very premise of this proposal weakens the safeguards designed to prevent government abuse. The absence of meaningful appeal rights dismantles the structure of impartial enforcement, opening the door to corruption, incompetence, and ideological purges.

⸻

VII. Final Recommendation

This rule is not a refinement of the civil service—it is a repudiation of it. If OPM truly wishes to strengthen performance and responsiveness, it should invest in better training, clearer expectations, and robust supervisory support. It should not abolish due process and codify political vulnerability into the career ranks of government.

I strongly urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule in full and reaffirm its commitment to a professional, apolitical, and accountable civil service.

Title: Comment from Jose Martinez
Comment:
As a proud supporter of a merit-based, nonpartisan civil service, I write in strong opposition to OPM’s proposed rule to create Schedule Policy/Career positions that are “career” in name only, but in practice strip critical job protections from federal employees.

At its core, this rule is a dangerous step backward. It undermines the foundational principles of the merit-based civil service system, fairness, impartiality, and accountability balanced by due process. By allowing career employees in “policy-influencing” roles to be hired and fired at will, this proposal exposes our civil service to politicization and retaliation. It blurs the line between career professionals and political appointees, threatening to turn experts into political pawns.

This is not a hypothetical concern. We have already seen how a similar proposal under the previous administration’s Schedule F sparked widespread alarm among federal workers, civil rights organizations, and good governance advocates. Congress and the public rightly rejected the idea of undermining the apolitical, institutional expertise that keeps our government functioning regardless of who occupies the White House.

The merit system exists to ensure that federal decisions are based on facts, science, law, and public interest, not political loyalty. Removing procedural safeguards for removals invites a chilling effect where civil servants may feel pressured to align with partisan agendas or risk their jobs. That’s not accountability, that’s coercion.

Moreover, OPM’s justification, that current due process protections make it too hard to remove poor performers, is misleading. Agencies already have tools to address misconduct and underperformance, including probationary periods and performance improvement plans. The problem is not the system; it’s the lack of consistent training and managerial follow-through. Gutting due process rights for a whole class of employees is a disproportionate and unnecessary response.

If this rule goes into effect, we risk destabilizing the very institution that helps ensure continuity, stability, and integrity in our federal government. We must not sacrifice long-standing democratic safeguards in the name of expediency or political convenience.

I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule and uphold its duty to protect the impartiality, professionalism, and constitutional integrity of the career civil service.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Comment on OPM-2025-0004: Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service

I am writing as a concerned citizen deeply alarmed by the proposed rule OPM-2025-0004. This rule threatens the foundational principles of a professional, nonpartisan federal workforce by enabling broad reclassification of civil servants into a new “Schedule Policy/Career” category—stripping them of due process, appeal rights, and whistleblower protections.

The stated aim—improving accountability—is misleading. The true impact would be a shift toward political loyalty tests in public employment, bypassing laws that protect merit-based hiring and firing. This proposal revives the worst elements of the defunct Schedule F and contradicts long-standing law and precedent.

1. Background & Legal Context
The Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883 was enacted to end the spoils system, establishing a federal workforce based on merit rather than political loyalty. The proposed rule undermines this legacy by enabling mass reclassification and removal of civil servants in policy-influencing roles, without cause or recourse.

Further, this proposal risks violating 5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(8), which protects employees from adverse action based on political affiliation and safeguards whistleblowers. Reclassifying jobs to evade these protections is regulatory manipulation and an affront to Congress’s intent.

2. Analysis of Harm
This rule would:

Eliminate Due Process - Employees could be fired at will, without the checks and balances that define a lawful and accountable federal workplace.

Enable Political Retaliation - Whistleblowers could be silenced or dismissed under the guise of policy “alignment.”

Erode Public Trust - The civil service exists to serve the Constitution, not the whims of temporary officeholders. Public servants must be free to implement the law objectively.

Open the Door to Partisan Purges - Recent history has shown the dangers of abusing probationary periods for ideological purging. This rule formalizes and expands that threat.

Undermine the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) - By creating a backdoor to bypass its jurisdiction, this rule weakens one of the few remaining structural safeguards of impartiality.

3. Recommendations
Withdraw the Rule  - OPM should immediately retract this proposal and reaffirm its commitment to nonpartisan, merit-based public service.

Reinforce Whistleblower and Due Process Protections - Any reform effort should focus on strengthening, not removing, safeguards for ethical public servants.

Increase Transparency and Oversight - If reform is truly needed, it must be done through Congressional engagement and public input, not administrative fiat.

4. Conclusion
This proposal revives Schedule F in all but name, risking mass politicization of government service and violating over a century of bipartisan civil service tradition. It grants excessive executive power and undermines our democracy by placing loyalty above law.

I urge OPM to reject this dangerous rule and uphold the values that have protected the American people from political interference in government for over 140 years.

Title: Comment from Adam Batkin
Comment:
I strongly oppose this proposed rule. While its stated purpose is to enhance accountability and enable the removal of underperforming or subversive personnel, its structure introduces serious legal and constitutional concerns. Specifically, the rule prioritizes adherence to Presidential directives without providing safeguards for situations in which those directives may conflict with statutory law or Supreme Court precedent.

Federal employees are sworn to uphold the Constitution and the laws of the United States - not to serve at the pleasure of any particular President. Yet this proposed rule frames accountability almost exclusively in terms of alignment with the President's agenda. It uses language such as "subverting Presidential directives," but is silent on the responsibility of employees to follow the law, even when doing so may appear to contradict Executive direction.

A timely and deeply concerning example illustrates this point. On January 20, 2025, President Trump signed an Executive Order titled "Protecting the Meaning and Value of American Citizenship," declaring that "no department or agency of the United States government shall issue documents recognizing United States citizenship..." under certain conditions. This order directly conflicts with longstanding federal law and the Supreme Court’s interpretation of the 14th Amendment in United States v. Wong Kim Ark, which affirms birthright citizenship. Under the proposed rule, a career civil servant who issues a lawful citizenship document in compliance with federal law and binding precedent - despite the Executive Order - could be dismissed without the opportunity for appeal.

This is not hypothetical. It is an active legal conflict, and the proposed rule does not account for such situations. Without clear protections for employees who act in good faith to uphold the law, this rule invites politicized firings and undermines the rule of law. It shifts career civil service from a neutral, legally grounded institution to one defined by loyalty to the political aims of the current President.

At minimum, the rule must be amended to:

- Acknowledge that lawful adherence to statutes and binding legal precedent takes precedence over Executive Orders;

- Provide explicit protections against removal for employees acting in lawful compliance with their duties;

- Ensure access to independent judicial review or appeals in such cases.

Absent these protections, this rule should be withdrawn. It is contrary to the core principles of a professional, nonpartisan civil service and threatens to politicize legal compliance itself.

Our nation’s public lands must be managed by nonpartisan professionals who are free to follow science, serve the public, and uphold conservation laws. I urge the Office of Personnel Management to reject this rule and protect the integrity of the merit-based civil service system.

Joelle Buffa

Title: Comment from Anonymous

I strongly oppose the reinstatement of Schedule F because it undermines the merit-based civil service system that has protected Americans from political favoritism and corruption for over a century.

Schedule F would allow the executive branch to reclassify tens of thousands of career federal employees as “at-will,” stripping them of their statutory job protections under the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978. This would violate 5 U.S.C. § 7511, which reserves such at-will treatment for a narrow class of political appointees—not seasoned, career public servants.

This action also threatens constitutional due process. Courts have long held, including in Loudermill v. Cleveland Board of Education, that tenured public employees have a protected property interest in their positions. They cannot be dismissed without cause, notice, and the opportunity to respond. Reclassifying civil servants retroactively as at-will violates this principle and opens the door to arbitrary and politically motivated firings.

Moreover, the President’s authority under Article II does not override laws passed by Congress. The Supreme Court has confirmed in cases like Humphrey’s Executor and Morrison v. Olson that the President’s removal power is not absolute. Civil servants do not serve at the pleasure of one administration—they serve the American people.

Schedule F also risks violating the Administrative Procedure Act by attempting to implement sweeping changes without formal rulemaking or evidence-based justification. Courts have struck down similar actions as “arbitrary and capricious.”

Ultimately, Schedule F would erode institutional knowledge, politicize government expertise, and make federal agencies less accountable to the public interest. For the sake of good governance, constitutional integrity, and the rule of law, I urge you to reject this proposal.

"I am writing to express strong opposition to the Office of Personnel Management’s (OPM) proposed rule OPM-2025-0004-0001, which seeks to reclassify approximately 50,000 federal employees into a newly designated Schedule Policy/Career (P/C) category. Erosion of Merit-Based Protections

The cornerstone of the federal civil service is its commitment to merit-based hiring and retention, ensuring that employment decisions are grounded in qualifications and performance rather than political affiliation. By reclassifying positions into Schedule P/C, the proposed rule would strip affected employees of critical protections against arbitrary dismissal, effectively making them at-will employees. This undermines the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978, which was enacted to prevent politicization and ensure a competent and impartial federal workforce.

Increased Risk of Politicization

Undermining Institutional Knowledge and Continuity

Reclassifying positions and removing job protections could lead to a loss of experienced personnel, disrupting agency operations and diminishing the government's ability to effectively serve the public. The potential for mass dismissals based on political considerations threatens the stability and effectiveness of federal programs.

Legal and Ethical Concerns

Reintroducing a similar framework disregards these concerns and may once again lead to protracted legal battles, diverting resources and attention from the government's primary responsibilities.

Conclusion

The proposed reclassification of federal positions into Schedule Policy/Career represents a significant departure from the principles that have long safeguarded the integrity and effectiveness of the federal workforce. It threatens to politicize the civil service, erode merit-based protections, and disrupt the continuity of government operations. I urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule and instead focus on strengthening the existing merit-based system that ensures a competent, impartial, and stable federal workforce."

This single sentence risks politicizing the US scientific infrastructure, chilling bold and innovative research, and undermining the United States’ capacity for world-class, evidence-driven science.

Background: What Scientific Program and Grant Staff Actually Do

NIH and NSF program officers implement—they do not set— science policy established by Congress (e.g., 42 U.S.C. §§ 282(b)(4), 284(a)) and by agency leadership.

They are bound by rigorous, statute-based, merit-review processes and conflict-of-interest rules. Any input into funding, NOFO, or initiative development cannot take effect without multiple layers of supervisory and budgetary sign-off. Especially at NIH, scientific and technical staff cannot make funding decisions. Only the Institute Director has this capacity.  

Because program staff apply, rather than set, science policy, they have historically remained in the competitive civil service—a structure that protects scientific integrity and the Merit System Principles (5 U.S.C. § 2301). Recent guidance reinforces this norm:
A Framework for Federal Scientific Integrity Policy and Practice (OSTP/NSTC, Jan 2023) emphasizes that scientific staff must be able to make evidence-based decisions “without fear of reprisal.”  

Legal Considerations 

The problematic language described above could invite legal challenge and legal risk. 

Conflating grant administration with “policy-making” is inconsistent with statutory merit-review mandates and invites APA challenge as “arbitrary and capricious.”

Federal courts have long distinguished between formulating policy and executing it; Humphrey’s Executor v. U.S., 295 U.S. 602 (1935) (independent adjudicatory/technical roles deserve insulation from political removal. 

The Administrative Procedure Act (APA), for instance, governs agency rulemaking and the exercise of discretion, guarding against actions that are "arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law". 

A key distinction within this framework is between administrative discretion and political policymaking. Administrative discretion involves the exercise of expert judgment by civil servants within the confines of established legal and policy directives set by Congress and political leadership. Political policymaking, conversely, typically refers to the setting of broad strategic agendas and priorities, often reflecting the partisan goals of the incumbent administration and carried out by political appointees. 

Scientific and technical grant staff are  implementers of policy and providers of expert, nonpartisan advice, rather than primary political decision-makers.

Furthermore, the rationale that “Grant-making is an important form of policymaking…” is arbitrary. By this logic, almost any federal government function could be considered a form of policymaking, and almost any federal job could be subject to conversion to the Schedule Policy/Career category. This broadness creates legal vulnerability, since the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 was clearly not intended to convert routine grant related positions into policy-making at-will jobs. 

Potential adverse consequences

Deeming large swaths of the scientific and technical staff at grant making agencies as at-will employees could gravely damage US science. It will create the perception of politicizing scientific agencies, will hinder extramural scientists from engaging in frank scientific discussions with agency experts without fear of political considerations, and will create a climate of fear within the agencies that discourages innovative and creative ideas to advance the President’s scientific priorities. 

In addition, the new NIH director, Dr. Bhattacharya, has made academic freedom, innovation, and open exchange of ideas cornerstones of NIH priorities. The policy under consideration will undermine these goals. 

Suggested Revisions

Delete the grant-making bullet or replace it with narrowly tailored language: “Positions whose primary, non-reviewable duties include setting grant-making policy priorities at the agency-wide level…”

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
On April 23, 2025, the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) published a proposed rule titled "Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service," which seeks to establish a new federal employment category akin to the previously rescinded “Schedule F.” This category—referred to as "Schedule Policy/Career"—would classify certain policy-related roles as at-will employment positions, thereby exempting them from statutory adverse action protections and appeal rights under Title 5 of the U.S. Code.

This memo outlines the key legal deficiencies in the proposed rule, including statutory conflicts, constitutional due process concerns, and the lack of statutory authority to effectuate such a significant structural change to the civil service.


---

BACKGROUND ON CURRENT LAW

Career federal employees, once past their probationary period, enjoy substantial protections under Title 5 of the U.S. Code:

5 U.S.C. §§ 4303 & 7513: Require cause, notice, opportunity to respond, and an appeal process for performance- or conduct-based removals.

5 U.S.C. § 2301 and § 2302: Enshrine the merit system principles, prohibiting politically motivated or arbitrary personnel actions.

These protections are further reinforced by case law recognizing a constitutionally protected property interest in continued federal employment.


---

LEGAL ANALYSIS

A. Statutory Conflict with Title 5

The proposed rule seeks to remove procedural protections that Congress has mandated for federal employees. It exempts Schedule Policy/Career employees from Chapters 43 and 75 of Title 5, which explicitly define how and when adverse actions may be taken.

> “An agency cannot by regulation override Congress’s explicit statutory commands.”
— Chevron U.S.A., Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, 467 U.S. 837 (1984)



Courts would likely find that OPM’s action conflicts with binding law and therefore cannot stand under the Chevron framework or post-Chevron-narrowing rulings such as West Virginia v. EPA, 142 S. Ct. 2587 (2022), which reinforce the “major questions doctrine.”

B. Violation of Constitutional Due Process

Career federal employees have a recognized property interest in their employment.

> “The right to due process is not something that can be erased by redefining the terms of employment.”
— Cleveland Board of Education v. Loudermill, 470 U.S. 532 (1985)



Converting these roles to at-will status—without individualized due process or congressional authorization—would almost certainly violate the Fifth Amendment.

C. Ultra Vires Rulemaking

OPM has no express statutory authority to create an entirely new class of federal employment that nullifies statutory protections. Such a significant policy change requires congressional action, not agency discretion.

> “Agencies have no power to ‘tailor’ legislation to bureaucratic policy goals by rewriting unambiguous statutory terms.”
— Utility Air Regulatory Group v. EPA, 573 U.S. 302 (2014)



D. Erosion of the Merit-Based Civil Service

The merit system is fundamental to a nonpartisan, professional federal workforce. By circumventing statutory protections, the proposed rule undermines:

Whistleblower protections

Protections against political coercion

Employee morale and retention in career positions


The rule invites politicization of roles meant to be insulated from partisan influence, a concern explicitly addressed in 5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(8)-(9).


---

CONCLUSION

The proposed rule is legally vulnerable on multiple fronts:

1. It conflicts with statutory rights under Title 5.


2. It potentially violates due process protections under the Constitution.


3. It exceeds OPM’s statutory authority and is ultra vires.


4. It threatens the integrity of the merit-based civil service.



Given these deficiencies, the rule is likely to be challenged and overturned in court if finalized. I strongly urge OPM to withdraw this proposal or, at a minimum, significantly revise it to align with established statutory and constitutional requirements.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
On April 23, 2025, the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) issued a proposed rule titled “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service,” which seeks to establish a new class of “Schedule Policy/Career” federal employees. These positions would be classified as at-will—depriving them of long-standing due process rights, statutory appeal procedures, and civil service protections.

This memorandum outlines how the proposed rule violates federal law and the Constitution. Critically, it examines the rule under the Supreme Court’s post-Chevron legal framework, where agency deference is no longer presumed—especially in cases involving major questions of statutory and constitutional rights.


---

BACKGROUND ON TITLE 5 EMPLOYEE PROTECTIONS

Federal career employees—excluding appointees in political or excepted service—enjoy key protections under Title 5 of the U.S. Code, including:

5 U.S.C. §§ 4303 & 7513: Guarantee adverse action protections, including cause, notice, opportunity to respond, and an appeal right to the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB).

5 U.S.C. § 2301 et seq.: Enshrine merit system principles and prohibit politically motivated removals or reprisals.


These protections have long been recognized as creating a property interest in employment, protected by the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause.


---

LEGAL ANALYSIS

A. The Proposed Rule Conflicts with Statutory Text

OPM’s proposed “Schedule Policy/Career” category exempts employees from Title 5 protections, placing them in an at-will category. This exemption directly conflicts with unambiguous statutory mandates that establish merit-based hiring and removal procedures.

> “An agency cannot override clear statutory text through rulemaking.”
— Utility Air Regulatory Group v. EPA, 573 U.S. 302 (2014)



There is no ambiguity in Title 5 about the conditions under which career employees may be removed. The new rule therefore exceeds OPM’s authority.


---

B. Chevron Deference No Longer Shields Agency Overreach

The Chevron doctrine—previously used to defer to agency interpretations—has been effectively gutted or overruled. As a result:

Courts now conduct de novo review of agency interpretations of statutes.

Ambiguity is no longer a license for agencies to bypass congressional intent.

OPM’s authority must be explicitly grounded in the statute, especially when fundamental rights are involved.


The Supreme Court’s reasoning in West Virginia v. EPA, 142 S. Ct. 2587 (2022) and subsequent rulings establish the “major questions doctrine,” which holds that agencies may not implement rules of vast political and legal significance without clear congressional authorization.

> Creating a new class of at-will federal employees is a major structural change that Congress, not OPM, must enact.




---

C. Due Process Violations Under the Fifth Amendment

The proposed rule violates the Constitution by stripping employees of a constitutionally protected property interest in their employment without due process.

> “The right to due process is not subject to agency redefinition.”
— Cleveland Board of Education v. Loudermill, 470 U.S. 532 (1985)



Even if reclassified, employees who previously held career protections retain their due process interests, and this reclassification scheme could trigger constitutional litigation.


---

D. Ultra Vires Rulemaking and Abuse of Discretion

OPM lacks clear statutory authority to enact such a radical reclassification. This rule is:

Ultra vires (beyond OPM’s authority),

Inconsistent with longstanding interpretation of Title 5,

A threat to the nonpartisan, merit-based federal workforce.


Such sweeping action is exactly what the Supreme Court in West Virginia v. EPA warned against.


---

CONCLUSION

OPM’s proposed rule is likely unlawful for multiple, compounding reasons:

1. It directly conflicts with the plain text of Title 5.


2. It violates constitutional due process by stripping existing property interests without cause.


3. It exceeds OPM’s legal authority—especially under a post-Chevron judiciary now guided by the major questions doctrine.


4. It threatens the independence and integrity of the federal civil service by enabling politicization of roles Congress has shielded.

Title: Comment from W R
Comment:
Public Comment Opposing the “Schedule Career/Policy” Rule
From a Cowboy Who Knows a Rigged Corral When He Sees One

To Whom It May Concern,

I might not be a lawyer or a politician, but I’ve spent enough time under the sun, fixing fences and driving cattle, to know when something smells off. And this rule OPM is pushing—the so-called “Schedule Career/Policy” deal—is about as crooked as a barbed-wire gate in a windstorm.

I’ve always believed a man—or woman—ought to be judged by how well they do the job, not who they butter up to. That’s how I was raised, and that’s how I run my spread. You put in the work, you speak the truth, and you don’t back down when things get tough. That’s what a public servant is supposed to do, too.

But this rule would let political bosses fire folks just for telling the truth or following the law instead of falling in line. It don’t matter how long they’ve served, what they know, or how many times they’ve done the job right. If they get on the wrong side of whoever’s in charge, they’re out. No hearing, no explanation, just gone.

That’s not accountability. That’s a setup.

I've seen this kind of thing before in ranch politics—someone gets to thinking the brand on their vest makes them king of the prairie, and before long, the good hands get run off and the yes-men take over. Things fall apart quick when you fire the ones who actually know what they’re doing just because they won’t lie for you.

The government ain’t supposed to be a one-man show. It’s supposed to serve everybody—fairly, honestly, and by the book. You don’t get that by gutting the civil service and turning it into a team of bootlickers afraid to speak up.

I don’t work in D.C., and I don’t want to. But I care about this country. And I know the difference between leadership and intimidation. One builds trust. The other builds fear. And you don’t get a strong herd out of fear.

OPM needs to scrap this rule. It's not about making government better—it's about clearing the pasture so one side can run it unchecked. That’s not freedom. That’s not America.

Title: Comment from Steven Tyler

Elimination of Due Process Protections for Career Employees Is a Fundamental Breach of the Merit System Compact
As a federal employee with 18 years of service under the competitive civil service system, I built a career on the understanding that tenure, fairness, and merit-based evaluation are not abstract principles, but legally protected rights. The proposed rule, by exempting “policy-influencing” positions from 5 U.S.C. Chapters 43 and 75—destroys that foundation. It would allow my removal without documented performance deficiencies, without an opportunity to respond, and without independent review by the MSPB. These procedural protections exist not to shield misconduct but to prevent arbitrary, retaliatory, or politically motivated removals, precisely the risks this rule invites. OPM cannot credibly argue that it values accountability while removing the mechanisms that ensure it is applied justly. No amount of internal agency oversight or executive guidance can substitute for independent, statutory due process. Codifying this rule signals to every career civil servant that our rights can be revoked not through congressional legislation, but by executive fiat.

It weaponizes proximity to policy against those of us who have remained loyal through multiple administrations, forcing career professionals to either self-censor or risk losing their livelihoods. The federal government has long relied on retirement security as both a recruitment and retention tool; undermining that stability retroactively violates the ethical and practical commitments the government made to its workforce. This rule invites attrition, disincentivizes public service, and will result in the hemorrhaging of institutional knowledge.
