Title: Comment from K Sandler
Comment:
As a longtime, now retired, federal civil servant, I strongly support the stated purpose of this rule, “improving performance, accountability and responsiveness in the civil service” as well as the more specific goal of making it easier to fire poorly performing employees -- after appropriate efforts to remedy the situation, whether through training, discipline or other means have been tried and failed.

However, the proposed rule changes would not in any way actually improve this situation but would likely make it much worse. The reason for this discrepancy is that the rule’s faulty solution is to increase White House political control of the civil service rather than empowering front-line managers to manage the situation with their direct reports more effectively.  

The proposal is pervaded with language making clear that it is based on the fallacy that the sole purpose of the civil service is to serve the whims of the president.  In fact, every public servant is required to take an oath to “support and defend the Constitution of the United States,” not to the president per se.  To be sure, the White House is granted political and administrative control of the Executive Branch, but that power must be executed within the context of laws passed by the Legislative Branch as interpreted by the Judicial Branch.  

Federal workers are rightly trained, instructed and disciplined to strictly follow the law as well as relevant court orders. If the president issues an order to such employees to defy the law or the courts, they cannot carry it out without violating their oath.  If, for example, an employee of the National Weather Service is ordered by the president to make a false claim about the weather for political reasons, they are not “doing their job” by following such an order. Indeed, we have a professional, trained, supervised civil service precisely to ensure that the complicated and important business of the country is carried out in a legal and exemplary manner without undue political interference.  

Yet this proposed rule makes clear that its goals are to ensure that all federal civil servants understand that they must do what the president says or risk losing their jobs.  Hence this proposal makes clear it is targeted at removing employees who “undermine the democratic process by intentionally subverting Presidential directives.” With this strong political focus, this rule risks severely damaging the delicate balance among the commands of the three branches of government that civil servants must balance on a daily basis.

Curiously, the proposal associates politicization of the civil service only with parties other than the president, e.g., “members of Congress and local party machines”. It is a major failing of this proposed rule that it does not even recognize the concept of politicization of the civil service by the White House itself.  

Although the proposal makes nods to the notion of non-partisan hiring and firing, it removes rather than strengthening controls to ensure that end.  During my tenure with the government, I saw several employees successfully terminated, showing that this is not an impossible task as it is so often described.  To be sure, the manager who conducts the firing bears the heavy burden of documenting poor performance and going through the process of attempting to remedy the situation short of firing before being able to carry out such an action, as well as managing the response to any appeals.  

I would welcome a genuine proposal to give such managers new tools, powers and training to conduct their personnel responsibilities effectively. This proposed rule does no such thing, and therefore I recommend that it be replaced with a new proposal to strengthen rather than weaken the powers and professionalism of government managers, and to reduce rather than increase undue politicization of the civil service.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I am commenting on the rule Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service, OPM-2025-0004-0001.

The civil service laws dating back to the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act (1883) and the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 have shaped the modern civil service system.

These are acts of the U.S. Congress, put in place to protect federal workers from the rules like the OPM-2025-0004-0001 is proposing to change.

Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act (1883) aimed to dismantle the "spoils system," where political party members were rewarded with government jobs, regardless of their qualifications.

Additionally, the Pendleton Act established the principle that federal jobs should be awarded based on merit, assessed through competitive examinations.

The act prohibited the firing or demotion of government employees solely for political reasons.

The act prohibited the firing or demotion of government employees solely for political reasons.

The Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 went even further and improved the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act.

The CSRA  replaced the Civil Service Commission with the OPM, MSPB, and FLRA, each with specific roles and responsibilities.

These roles and responsibilities included:

Merit System Principles - The Act reaffirmed the importance of the merit system, emphasizing non-discrimination and non-partisanship in hiring and promotions.

Employee Protections - The CSRA provided legal protections for federal employees from various prohibited personnel practices, such as discrimination, political coercion, and retaliation.

Whistleblower Protections - The Act established the Office of Special Counsel within the MSPB to investigate whistleblower complaints.

Senior Executive Service - The CSRA created the SES, a group of career executives who serve as leaders within federal agencies.

Labor-Management Relations - Title VII of the CSRA, also known as the Federal Service Labor-Management Relations Statute, addressed labor-management relations in the federal sector.

Pay for Performance - The Act introduced a system of pay for performance for SES members, with bonuses and awards for exceptional achievements.

The CSRA is considered one of the most significant overhauls of the federal personnel system since the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883.

It aimed to address concerns about the previous system, which was perceived as being too slow to adapt and inefficient.

The Act has had a lasting impact on how federal agencies are managed, how employees are treated, and how the government operates.

By allowing the President to designate certain positions as at-will, regardless of merit, the rule could lead to the appointment of individuals based on loyalty or political favor rather than expertise.

The removal of adverse action procedures and appeals rights for "Schedule Policy/Career" employees is seen as a violation of due process, as it allows for potential arbitrary firings without adequate safeguards or the ability to contest decisions. This will discourage qualified individuals from seeking these positions, as they would be at risk of losing their jobs and benefits without cause.

This rule could be used to purge civil servants with dissenting opinions or those who don't align with the President's agenda, effectively politicizing the civil service and undermining it.

The  government will lose the benefit of experienced, knowledgeable civil servants who understand the intricacies of their agency and the laws they are tasked with implementing.

The rule could be used to reward political supporters with positions that are not necessarily based on their qualifications, potentially leading to a less effective and accountable government.

The Federal government is not a business that is based on a Profit and Loss Statement. The Federal government serves  the people, not a select few politicians that want to maintain control and power at any cost. OPM-2025-0004-0001 will weaken the country, not strengthen it. Changes to the laws of the United States should be made by the U.S. Congress and not the Executive branch.

Title: Comment from Paul Boyd
Comment:
This comment is for OPM, Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004 and RIN:3206-AO80.

Please withdraw/reject this regulation and sustain the existing laws/regulations governing the US Civil Service.

As a former federal employee I can tell you from experience that if we had to cope with layers of civil service employees who put loyalty above the constitution and so distorted the mission of our agency we would have accomplished very little, and done so at a cost exponentially higher.  

The new regulation proposes to do away with civil service employees' "injecting their personal policy preferences" into the work of the government. But fails to describe how OPM would recognize this injection or what actions would limit or eliminate these. The new regulation, asserts that it would address these "injections" while failing to state how or how such can be measured. 

Certainly statements are made about a lack of confidence among managers regarding their ability to fire or otherwise deal with low performers. Yet as a solution the regulation proposes to fundamentally change who "owns" the civil service. It's like identifying a problem on one's front lawn, and asserting its solution lies somewhere outside the orbit of the moon.

Much as OPM is the chief churning out the rules and regulations governing federal employment, this regulation reveals an inability to target what it appears to believe are poor performers. Section 2.i. cobbles together inapposite sentences in an odd hope that they are not closely read.

The regulation (in 2.i.) asserts that a solution to the problem is best described by taking the Civil Service personnel issues "in totality" and using this totality to describe the much smaller, potential, Schedule F population. At no time does the regulation ever focus its fact-gathering on the population of employees it would classify as Schedule F. This fact makes all else in the regulation suspect, minimally. 

If OPM is intent on solving a problem, it should as a measure of its sincerity, use facts which describe the problem accurately, and not attempt to paper over its lack of effort with a broad brush of obfuscation. OPM simply "concludes this is a widespread phenomenon". 

Well.

The Regulation throws the entire body of supposed "surveys" and non-Schedule F employees actions at the wall, hoping some or all of it will stick. This kind of rule making emanates from lazy strain of oversight. Making assertions, failing to document the facts which support these assertions, then declaring that all intended points have been made, is the work of a weak mind or minds. Section 2.i. and 2.ii, is just such work.

If the assertions made (sections 2.i and 2.ii) are to be believed - that this new regulation will stop an "undermining of democracy and the constitution", no evidence of this is presented, only alleged. This is insufficient to warrant a change in the Civil Service that can have the effect of eliminating Congress' will from Civil Service priorities and behaviors. The Executive is present to "faithfully execute the laws". If the Executive can eliminate Congress' voice and Judicial review, then the Executive can do what it pleases, including making Congress a non-entity. Or said another way, allow the Executive "to undermine democracy and the Constitution".

Finally, the regulation also seems to imply, because without demonstrating how it may avoid, the injection of personal policy preferences can occur under the new rule. How would this new rule be used to eliminate what it asserts in Section 2.i. and 2.ii., this "undermining of democracy and the Constitution"?  The regulation does not say. 

Current law insists, correctly, on an impartial civil service. This effort to redefine the civil service terms of employment lacks any sort of clear, measurable, elements, and as such, should be rejected. 

The regulation instead seems intent on raising the cost of government rather than addressing "accountability". Replacing competent and patriotic civil service members, as this regulation proposes, with 50,000 loyalists, would also raise the cost of government exponentially. History shows that loyalty-based organizations are incredibly expensive and thrive only on oppression. Exponential cost increases alone should guide OPM in rejecting the regulation. Since this regulation does not even openly contemplate costs, it should be rejected on this factor as well.

The regulation seeks, intentionally or not, to undermine the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (CSRA), which was enacted to prevent politicization of federal employee work and ensure a competent and impartial federal workforce. Preventing politicization is to be sought because it reduces friction on the implementation of Congress' will. This regulation seems intent on creating new sources of friction across the government, with each of the 50,000 interpreting the president's will rather than following the law.

Please reject this regulation.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I am submitting a comment on the proposed rule "Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service," proposed by the Office of Personnel Management (OPM), Docket ID (OPM-2025-0004) and RIN (3206-AO80). I strongly oppose the proposed rule. Creating the Schedule Policy/Career designation will severely damage the non-partisan nature of the civil service.

This proposed rule and Executive Order 14171 state that, under Schedule P/C, employees would not be "required to personally or politically support the current President or the policies of the current administration. They are required to faithfully implement administration policies to the best of their ability, consistent with their constitutional oath….” Further, the proposed rule insists that with Schedule P/C, “The civil service will remain professional, non-partisan, and effective” (Page 17218). I fully support the civil service remaining non-partisan and effective. This rule, however, would open the door to politically motivated dismissals. 

The proposed rule states many times that civil servants should be executing the vision of the administration, according to their oath of office. However, the civil service oath of office requires civil servants to support and defend the Constitution of the United States (5 U.S. Code § 3331), not the political party of the president. The current administration has already shown that it is willing to dismiss anyone it believes disagrees with them politically. 

It is in the public’s interest that our federal government makes informed policy decisions, and this often requires gathering information from many sources, weighing potential outcomes, and presenting those to political appointees who then make a decision. Civil servants must be allowed to access and present the facts to political appointees in order to create informed and responsive policies. The proposed rule provides no guardrails to protect an employee who simply presents facts that could be construed as opposing the administration’s stance. Under Schedule P/C, an administration could fire anyone for simply presenting facts that the administration disagrees with. This would do great harm to the American public. This also directly contradicts the Civil Service Reform Act, which was enacted to prevent the federal employee workforce from becoming political “yes men.”

Another stated goal of the proposed rule is to make it easier for the Federal government to dismiss poor performers. However, the administration estimates that Schedule P/C would apply to approximately 50,000 employees, a small fraction of the Federal workforce. If the current administration is concerned about dismissing poor performing employees, they should work with Congress to adjust dismissal processes for all competitive service employees, not just those in "policy influencing" roles. For example, by increasing funding to the Merit System Protections Board to speed up processing and appeals, or by streamlining rules around performance evaluations. Selectively applying “at will” employment to some employees does not solve systemic challenges with managing a large bureaucracy. 

Finally, I believe the comment period for this proposed rule should be extended to at least 60 days so the public can have more time to thoroughly consider the policy change and its potential impact on the services the Federal government provides.

Title: Comment from Jacqueline  A
Comment:
As a veteran and career public servant, I strongly object to any efforts to introduce or reinstate the "Schedule F" classification for federal employees. This proposal poses a serious threat to the foundational principles of the merit-based civil service system—principles I defended in uniform and continue to uphold in federal service.

Schedule F would undermine the safeguards established by the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which ended the spoils system and ensured that hiring and promotion in the federal workforce would be based on merit, not political loyalty. Although Schedule F has been presented as a tool for accountability, in practice it would allow for the dismissal of career professionals without cause, opening the door to politicized employment decisions and weakening the integrity of government service.

Such a move also risks violating due process rights under 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which guarantees that career employees may only be removed for cause and with proper procedural protections. The vague and overly broad criteria proposed under Schedule F would strip thousands of civil servants of these protections, making it easier to remove qualified experts based on political considerations rather than performance.

The Office of Personnel Management has a legal duty under 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to safeguard the merit system. Moving forward with Schedule F would erode that responsibility and subject dedicated federal employees to undue political pressure, ultimately harming the professionalism, consistency, and effectiveness of public programs.

As someone who has sworn an oath to support and defend the Constitution, I am deeply concerned about the consequences this initiative would have on good governance, the rule of law, and the independence of our civil service. I respectfully urge the administration and OPM to reject any revival of Schedule F and instead reaffirm their commitment to a fair, apolitical, and merit-based federal workforce.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I write in strong opposition to the proposed rule creating the “Schedule Policy/Career” (P/C) classification. The legal and policy concerns raised by this proposal—particularly its implications for civil service protections, agency effectiveness, and constitutional norms—warrant discarding the proposed rule.

From a legal standpoint, the rule risks undermining the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (CSRA), which established merit-based employment and procedural safeguards for federal employees. Reclassifying large numbers of positions into an at-will category would erode due process protections and weaken the framework designed to ensure fair and impartial federal employment decisions.

Moreover, while whistleblower protections under federal law technically remain intact, placing employees in at-will positions could chill protected disclosures. Employees may be less likely to report waste, fraud, or abuse if they can be removed without cause, and especially before a complaint can be investigated. This could lead to an increase in legal disputes—such as wrongful termination claims or whistleblower retaliation cases—and reduce the effectiveness of internal accountability systems. Moreover, removing appeal rights would further undermine the checks on fraud, waste, and abuse provided by whistleblowers.  

The proposal also raises concerns under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). Major structural changes to the federal workforce require a reasoned explanation grounded in evidence. Yet the proposed rule offers anecdotal examples and generalized claims about bureaucratic “resistance” without demonstrating that current systems are inadequate to address the concerns raised.

The cited examples—including isolated internal emails, delays in policy implementation, or expressions of professional dissent—are not evidence of systemic failure. In many cases, they reflect employees performing their duties in accordance with legal and ethical obligations: conducting regulatory reviews, complying with court rulings, and raising legitimate policy concerns. These behaviors are not signs of dysfunction; they are safeguards built into the system to ensure lawful and accountable governance.

Absent a clear showing that existing disciplinary and performance management tools are insufficient, this rule risks being deemed arbitrary and capricious under the APA. It proposes a sweeping reclassification of civil service protections based on selective interpretations of routine internal processes, rather than on compelling data or systemic analysis.

In addition, this reclassification could blur constitutional lines regarding the Appointments Clause. If Schedule P/C employees are given substantial policy-making authority—authority traditionally reserved for officers confirmed by the Senate—this approach could functionally bypass the requirement for Senate confirmation. The federal government must be cautious not to use civil service reclassification as a mechanism for consolidating executive control in areas where constitutional accountability mechanisms are required.

On policy grounds, the rule threatens to politicize the civil service. Agencies depend on career professionals with expertise and institutional memory to deliver public services effectively. Allowing wholesale replacement of these individuals based on ideology or perceived loyalty undermines the objectivity, reliability, and stability of government programs.

Finally, this proposal is unnecessary. Agencies already have tools to address misconduct and poor performance, including structured disciplinary processes, probationary periods, and removal authorities. Creating a new at-will classification is not only excessive—it may ultimately hinder government performance by fostering fear and instability.  Moreover, this rule will further discourage a new generation of federal employees from bringing their talents and insights to serve the people of this great country. 

I urge OPM to withdraw this proposal and instead encourage supervisors to use the existing systems that promote both accountability and integrity in public service.

Title: Comment from Lynn Gazis
Comment:
I urge you not to implement this rule change.

Signing the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883 into law was the best action of President Chester Arthur's Presidency. It transformed a civil service that ran on a political patronage spoils system into one that ran on merit and was accountable to all. It would be a great mistake to undo this civil service reform of Chester Arthur by reinstating Schedule F.

Having a large number of non-political civil service employees ensures continuity of knowledge and expertise between presidential administrations. For example, Foreign Service Officers and other State Department employees align themselves with the policies of the new administration but retain their area knowledge. And it provides a barrier against attempts by an administration to weaponize the government - for example, the Department of Justice - against the other party, or critics of the current President.

Please reject this proposed rule change and keep our civil service from returning to 19th century style political patronage.

Title: Comment from Kathryn Bolles
Comment: I strongly oppose this rule change. It's vital that we have civil services performed by experienced, dedicated staff who are not subject to political whimsy. We need to ensure they can continue to perform their jobs and provide consistency in services people rely on for their lives and livelihoods rather than be at risk of at-will firing.

Title: Comment from Katelyn McBride
Comment:
While this proposed rule is described as ensuring that the civil service remains nonpartisan, the ability to move federal jobs into Schedule Policy/Career will in fact increase the number of partisan positions in our civil service. 
The expansion of Schedule F (aka Schedule P/C) was explicitly listed as a strategy to remove and replace current federal employees in the Project 2025 Mandate for Leadership. On page 271, USAID was floated as a potential guinea pig for the implementation of a new Schedule F executive order in combination with an effort to "aggressively recruit and place candidates into term-limited positions under Schedule A of the Excepted Service." In other words, current civil servants would be fired and replaced with appointees. The implication is that the new appointees will be loyal to the administration that appoints them above all else. In the long term, this will cause currently non-partisan positions to become partisan ones which turn over every four to eight years. Such a frequent rate of turnover will result in a disastrous loss of institutional knowledge on an ongoing basis. It also risks changing the priorities of our civil servants from protecting and serving the people of the United States of America to serving whichever administration happens to be in power at the time. This change would be to the detriment of all American citizens.
If the goal truly is to make it easier to remove underperforming or corrupt civil servants, we should pursue reforms to our means of assessing employee performance and responding appropriately to poor performance. An expansion of Policy P/C is not the answer, and implementing this rule will result in serious damage to our civil service system in the long term.

Title: Comment from Julia Mackaronis
Comment: I am very strongly opposed to the proposed rule by OPM (Docket ID OPM-2025-0004 and RIN 3206-AO80) from the Office of Personnel Management (OPM). I am a licensed clinical psychologist. I am proud to have been a federal employee for 7 years in 4 different Veterans Affairs Medical Centers, and currently work in a federally qualified health center. I have been and am currently in charge of personnel decisions for outpatient mental health teams, so I am well-poised to discuss the likely negative impact that this rule will have on the actual performance, accountability, and responsiveness in the civil service. In order to provide the services that are the backbone of a safe and healthy society, our federal government needs to have continuity. Continuity is achieved by hiring experts, especially in specialized fields, who are dedicated to their craft and the people they serve, not political appointees who chance frequently. I have never selected a psychology job based on who was president, and never will. I also do not know of any psychologists in federal service who would. The possibility that they would be surrounded by political appointees potentially hostile to the very nature of their service will make it tremendously difficult to retain and attract responsive and high-performing specialists. I soundly reject the ostensible reasons for this rule.

Title: Comment from Angel Reyes
Comment:
Comment in Opposition to OPM-2025-0004 (RIN 3206-AO80)

Submitted in my personal capacity as a United States citizen.

I write in strong opposition to the Office of Personnel Management’s proposed rule establishing Schedule P/C, which would allow the President to reclassify thousands of federal civil servants as at-will employees. While I submit this comment in my personal capacity, I offer it from the perspective of someone who has spent years enforcing the law on behalf of the public.

I currently serve as an enforcement attorney at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and previously served in a similar capacity at the Federal Trade Commission. At both agencies, my job has been to apply the law as written and protect the public from unlawful and deceptive practices, regardless of who is in political power. That work depends on the ability of civil servants to offer independent legal and policy analysis without fear of political retaliation. This rule would undermine that independence.

There were multiple occasions in the prior administration where, had a rule like this been in place, I may have hesitated to raise legal objections or challenge flawed interpretations of the law. That kind of chilling effect is dangerous—not just for those of us in government, but for the millions of Americans who depend on fair, evenhanded enforcement of the law. When public servants are forced to choose between their careers and their integrity, we all lose.

As an attorney, I am bound by ethical duties that require independent judgment and candor, even when that judgment may be inconvenient to those in charge. This rule would place attorneys and other professionals in untenable positions: caught between their obligations to the public and the political pressures of the moment.

I fully recognize that administrations set enforcement priorities. But the law is not a political tool. It must be applied consistently, regardless of who holds power. To allow it to be warped or silenced to serve political ends is to abandon the core principles of public service.

If OPM is concerned about addressing performance or accountability in the civil service, it should pursue less extreme and more targeted reforms. For example, OPM could work to streamline the rules governing performance evaluations or request changes to the Merit Systems Protection Board’s procedures to increase efficiency and transparency. These steps would address legitimate concerns without dismantling longstanding merit-based protections.

The proposed rule invites instability, undermines due process, and threatens the integrity of the services Americans rely on. I urge OPM to withdraw the proposal and preserve the nonpartisan, expert-driven foundation of our civil service.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

Title: Comment from Sarah Miller

A fundamental principle of effective governance is having a stable core of dedicated, non-partisan civil servants who manage the daily operations of our government. These professionals are vital to maintaining the continuity, stability, and trust in our institutions, regardless of changes in elected leadership. It is essential that they remain career employees, maintaining their independence from the shifting political landscape. Their oath is to us the American people and the Constitution.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I strongly oppose the implementation of proposed rule OPM-2025-0004, “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service.” 

This proposal endangers the merit-based civil service system that has provided a nonpartisan federal workforce for over a century. Career civil service workers should be able to do their job without fear of politically motivated pressure. The protections enacted by the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 are in place for this very reason. This proposed rule would destabilize the civil service and decrease efficiency. It would enable every administration to reclassify and purge employees based on ill-defined “partisanship”, with no recourse for appeal. Having a civil service that is stable across administrations is crucial for creating a predictable regulatory environment, which enables businesses to plan and make long-term investments with confidence. 

The new proposed rule allows a large number of civil servants to be reclassified and potentially terminated due to “political” motivation. This is antithetical to the principle of an apolitical civil service enshrined in 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8), which mandates that federal employment decisions be based on merit and free from political influence.

Moreover, the vague and sweeping criteria for inclusion in Schedule Policy/Career violate the due process protections guaranteed by 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which requires cause and procedural safeguards for the removal of career federal employees. Stripping thousands of workers of these protections not only weakens accountability but also risks expert advice and dissent within agencies—undermining the very effectiveness of government operations.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is also bound by 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to support the merit system principles. Implementing Schedule Policy/Career contradicts this statutory mission and places undue political pressure on career professionals, compromising the integrity and continuity of federal programs across administrations.

In summary, this proposed rulemaking to implement “Schedule Policy/Career” under “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service” (OPM-2025-0004) threatens the very principle of civil service political protections. I urge the administration and OPM to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement or revive this dangerous classification.

Comment: As a retired HR director, I am concerned about any effort to reclassify federal employees just so it is easier to fire them. Comment: I am submitting this comment regarding Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004 for the Office of Personnel Management. Comment:
am writing in regards to the Office of Personnel Management, Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004, RIN 3206-AO80.  

This is a terrible proposed rule change. This rule change seems like an attempt to permanently cripple the American government and oust hard-working citizens from their careers and harm American families. Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:

Introducing schedule F would significantly erode this obligation by exposing career civil servants to political pressure. In this way, the consistency and professionalism of our governmental system would be significantly weakened.

In his Executive Order 14173, President Trump has also shown his support for a merit-based approach. As well, the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883 would be undermined if Schedule F were to be implemented.

Taking all of this into consideration, and adding that since an independent, apolitical civil service is both a bedrock principle of good governance and a legal requirement, I urge both the OPM and the administration not to move forward with implementation of Schedule F.

Title: Comment from Deirdre  Clarkin
Comment:
I am writing to oppose the proposed rule, [Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004], RIN 3206-AO80, entitled:  “Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service.  While our country's leadership can change election-to-election, we rely on federal civil servants to retain valuable institutional knowledge and provide nonpartisan expertise to ensure the efficient running of the government.

Reclassifying federal workers to enable firing for political reasons undermines the entire purpose of the civil service. Our country is meant to change slowly on purpose, to keep from whipsawing between extremes (both liberal and conservative) as the administration changes.

This rule would give more power to an already bloated executive branch, moving our country one step closer to authoritarianism. This is not merely a critique of the current administration, but of the presidency as a whole, which--over the last two centuries--has slowly expanded its authority to encompass powers that should rightfully belong to Congress and the Judiciary.

The proposed rule will apply to positions that have been traditionally nonpartisan and as a result may encourage cronyism due to fear of firing. It may also increase turnover with each administration, resulting in loss of knowledge, the ability to perform succession planning, and wasted resources on hiring and training as a result of the higher attrition we can expect with each new president.


Policies already shift with each new administration, resulting in the expenditure of resources to undo current policies or revive prior policy initiatives based on the politics and priority of the sitting president. 


I fear that this proposed rule will worsen this issue and that we will have fewer long term, successful projects that span multiple administrations. The current civil service employs many nonpartisan experts whose job is to advise political appointees based on objective data. What happens when these are replaced by political appointees who base advice on what their president wants to hear?


This proposed rule will also discourage federal whistleblowers from reporting waste, fraud and abuse.

I ask you to please consider the effect of this proposed rule in the current, highly-partisan, political climate. By making civil servants easier to fire for political reasons, we let the country slip toward extremism, instead of trying to ensure it retains an even keel for decades to come.

I strongly oppose the proposed rule.

Title: Comment from Judith Yarrow
Comment:
I oppose the Office of Personnel Management's proposed rule reclassifying federal workers (Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004 or RIN 3206-AO80).
 Our civil service was designed to be as free as possible from political extortion and coercion. This rule will effectively erode our nonpartisan civil service, and place thousands of civil servants at risk of partisan revenge firings.

Judith Yarrow

Title: Comment from Gabrielle Aines
Comment:
Part of the duty of policymaking positions is to protect agencies and serve the best interests of the public by considering the history of the issue at hand and determining a solution that is practicable in light of the agency's resources and abilities, within the agency's proper authority. The stated goal of this proposed rule is to increase "accountability", but nothing in the rule or supplementary materials explains how making policymaking employees at-will would actually better ensure that such employees are able to complete the duty as I've described it. Instead, the circumstances that this rule anticipates are one in which an administration directs career federal employees to enact a specific policy and, if the employee does not comply, that employee is deemed "partisan" and at risk of being summarily fired. What if that career employee, when researching the a specific policy, determines that a specific policy cannot be implemented because it does not conform to existing law, because the proposed policy exceeds the agency's authority, because the agency simply does not have the staff or technical resources to implement or enforce the policy, or the policy would in some way harm the public in an unacceptable way, say by impeding on their civil rights or creating undue hardship? All of these would be valid, non-political reasons not to implement a specific policy, but under this rule, such an employee, acting well-within their authority and with a sense of responsibility to the public and to the quality of their work, could be punished or retaliated against. There is nothing "partisan" about the policymaking process, and policy decisions that are made with due consideration and well-documented cannot properly be called partisan under any fair use of the term. This rule would not improve public policy or benefit the American people. Instead, it lead to a cowed, non-independent federal workforce that no longer feels empowered to give honest, high-quality advice and analysis to their agencies without their jobs being placed at risk. This would clearly lead to worse policy, a more dysfunctional workforce and policymaking process, and worse outcomes for the public. 

Additionally, public reporting indicates some agencies are considering a very broad application of this staffing category beyond individuals who clearly create policy as part of their job. It is apparent that this categorization is viewed as a tool for shaping the workforce, not for ensuring the public's best interest, and it is ripe for abuse.

Title: Comment from John Haresch
Comment: I have worked in the U.S. government, in the Senior Foreign Service. The current hiring system allows for maintaining important institutional knowledge and functionality while allowing new administrations to implement their policy priorities. All the management I worked with understood that priorities would change, and directions would need to be adjusted, with each administration. They also understood that the government's important functions needed to continue uninterrupted. Firing that important level of management with each administration would be disastrous. Swinging the basic functions of government from pole to pole every four years is a terrible idea. Altering this essential stability because one administration wants to undermine basic functionality would be the height of foolishness.

Title: Comment from Mark Goodman
Comment:
I am writing in opposition to the proposed rule to establish a “Schedule Policy/Career” (formerly Schedule F) classification for the career Civil Service. This proposal is based on the false pretext of rampant corruption and underperformance in the senior ranks of the Civil Service and, if adopted, would engender the very problems it purports to correct. It misrepresents the essential precepts of sound policy making as “insubordination” and, by undermining those precepts, would result in worse decision making and worse outcomes for the American people.

The rule cites no evidence that the poor performance is a problem at the senior levels to which the proposed rule would apply. In my experience, those in policy positions are among the top performers in the Civil Service, and have been promoted to their positions for their high performance. The proposed rule would enable political appointees to fire them at will. Their replacements are likely to be less qualified, have less experience and, at least until they learn the job, perform less effectively.

Senior Civil Servants are also among the most committed to high ethical standards. They are both unlikely to engage in corrupt acts and likely to report corrupt acts on the part of others. The proposed rule would place them under pressure to turn a blind eye to corruption by political appointees.  And if they are fired, their replacements are even more likely to turn a blind eye to such corruption. I have never witnessed corruption within the Civil Service, but I cannot say the same for political appointees.

The proposed rule presents “insubordination” as a significant problem in the Civil Service. This is not something I have witnessed. I have seen political appointees express frustration with a decision-making process, but a disciplined process takes into account the relevant facts and constraints and considers a range of perspectives and policy options is the essence of sound policy making, not “insubordination.” Sometimes the options preferred by political officials are impractical, dangerous, or even unlawful. Experienced professional Civil Servants can identify feasible, safe, and legal alternatives. Suppressing or firing those who offer such critiques and alternatives would not improve policy making. It would impose blinders that lead to ill-considered decisions and to worse outcomes.

Finally, the Federal Government should want to attract and retain the best talent, but the proposed rule would make it harder to recruit and retain talented people for careers in public service. Most people who join the Civil Service do so to make a positive difference in the world. They look forward to being able to learn and grow and advance into more senior position where they can develop new skills and expertise and exercise greater responsibility. They are much less likely to pursue a career in public service if they know their careers could be cut short by arbitrary or capricious decisions by political appointees. One benefit of the Civil Service is the opportunity to work with and learn from those who came before and have experience and wisdom to impart. The proposed rule would have the effect of purging those best positioned to serve as mentors to help junior staff develop and advance their careers.

For all these reasons, I believe proposed rule is misguided and should be withdrawn.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Agencies like the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the National Institutes for Health (NIH) cannot meet their statutorily mandated scientific missions if politics, rather than scientific expertise, drive decision-making. Federally supported science has been so successful, in no small part, because agency staff are typically expert scientists beholden to ensuring that the agencies deliver world-class science. Now, many could be turned into political appointees. The proposed policy defines grantmaking positions as “policy-making,” which includes “drafting of funding opportunity announcements, evaluation of grant applications, or recommending or selecting grant recipients.” This definition, which neatly matches agencies’ own definitions for certain career staff, would include most NIH program officers and NSF program directors.

The past few months at NIH and NSF preview how politicized scientific agencies would operate. Funding choices that reflected the consensus of some of the best scientists in the world were reversed by nonscientists. Program officers have, at points, been told not to communicate with the scientific community or have had their engagement limited. Scientific agencies have been directed to effectively reduce the flow of funds to a trickle by adding new layers of redundant review and red tape and even violating court orders to reinstate cancelled grants.

Other agencies, including regulatory agencies, apply rather than fund basic science, but the risks of politicization are no less. How confident can Americans be that federal employees will not have to choose between their job and scientific values in areas such as climate change, food safety, extreme weather forecasting, or public health?

Office of Personnel Management, OPM-2025-0004, RIN (3206-AO80)

On page 17187 under the heading 2. Executive Order 14171 - "Substantive participation and discretionary authority in agency grantmaking…" If political appointees are responsible for grantmaking decisions, it will be extremely harmful to scientific progress in this country. Policy should always be informed by science, but science should never be informed by policy. The president and their politics should have no influence over what science gets funded. We are already seeing effects of politics disrupting science through the cancellation of highly successful study grants simply because they concern vulnerable populations our current administration is hellbent on destroying.

Title: Comment from Robert  Riley
Comment:
The professional Civil Service was created in 1883 because the problems of patronage in government service had become extreme, and even resulted in the assassination of President Garfield. The idea of Schedule F is not new - it's what we had in the United States from its founding until the Civil Service Act was passed in 1883. It did not work well. Corruption was rife, and political considerations trumped the professional execution of the duties of the federal workforce. Since 1883, the Civil Service continued on the path of professionalism, and it remains a neutral and professional force within the government, dedicated to the American people and the best interests of the United States. Civil servants are expected to carry out the policies of the President of the United States, while also ensuring that governmental actions are carried out in accordance with the relevant laws.

The idea that a Schedule F cadre will improve the quality of the workforce is folly. When the Civil Service is politicized, patronage and corruption will follow. Professionals and experts will cease to apply for government positions . The quality of government service will decline, and our very sophisticated American system that depends on qualified professionals in the Civil Service will decline with it. There is a virtuous symbiosis that exists between the federal government and business, civil society, and educational institutions that will decay, and we will all be poorer for it, both figuratively and literally.

Title: Comment from Christian Thomas
Comment:
Rescheduling federal employees to Schedule F undermines the merit-based civil service system established to ensure government positions are filled based on qualifications rather than political loyalty. The United States Code, particularly Title 5, outlines protections for federal employees, ensuring due process and fair treatment in hiring and firing decisions. By shifting employees into Schedule F, these protections are significantly weakened, allowing for arbitrary dismissals that could lead to a politicized workforce. This change threatens the stability and expertise of the federal workforce, as career professionals who have dedicated years to public service could be replaced based on political considerations rather than competence.

Additionally, the move contradicts the principles of the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act, which was designed to prevent patronage and ensure a nonpartisan government workforce. Federal employees in policy-related roles play a crucial role in implementing laws and regulations, and their ability to provide objective, expert advice should not be compromised by political pressures. The National Treasury Employees Union has raised concerns that Schedule F would strip employees of their rights, making them easier to fire without cause. This could lead to inefficiencies in government operations, as experienced professionals may be replaced by individuals with less expertise, ultimately harming the effectiveness of federal agencies.

If this proposed rule is enacted, federal employees will be beholden only to Presidential authority and will no longer be able to make informed decisions free of political interference in their areas of expertise that are in the best interests of Americans.

Title: Comment from Matthew Bolanos-Wood
Comment: I am leaving this comment for the OPM in reference to Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004 or RIN 3206-AO80. I oppose this change that will make it easier to fire critical federal employees. Title: Comment from Nora Underwood
Comment:
This proposed rule is a terrible mistake that will degrade the quality of US government and do the opposite of what it is intended to do.  It will lower performance, and decrease accountability and responsiveness to the needs of the people of the USA. Increasing the number and power of political appointees essentially extends the power of the executive branch - a major change in the constitutional balance of power that has made our country so successful.  

People who have studied how government functions have found that political appointees are less likely to be willing to contradict their bosses, but we need people in government who can provide honest information about national safety, economy, health and any other topic that matters.  Political appointees are short-term, but we need people in government with experience and a long-view of how things work.  We have elected leadership and other mechanisms (like this comment opportunity) for the public to express its opinion. For stability and function, we also need staff who don't get fired every 4-8 years.

My closest personal experience with this is through the National Science Foundation.  I am a scientist, and have received NSF funding and have served on NSF panels where funding decisions are made.  NSF's decision-making process is considered the gold standard around the world, and I have always been hugely impressed by how well the system works to bring the best science for the USA, even when my own proposals are rejected.  NSF has had the stable leadership of excellent scientists who work there long-term, combined with rotating short-term scientists on leave from their regular jobs, to ensure that the NSF community is always up-to-date. NSF funding decisions are driven by choosing the best work, by fairness, and by helping to develop science into the best work it can be.  Stable long-term NSF leaders ensure great science by having the long-view and their sights focused only on providing the best information to the people of the US.  They also mentor young scientists in how to improve their work.  They never tell people what to study, or direct the science themselves. But they provide critical insight into how the scientific community functions, how to give and respond to feedback from others, and generally how to be the best scientist you can be, so that our nation can continue to benefit from the economic and health advantages science gives us.

Right now, political appointees are destroying the NSF.  They are reversing decisions made by scientists, they are freezing some funding and reducing funding overall. They are picking which areas to fund or not fund.  Even if one agrees with any particular decision these appointees are making, imagine how it will feel if/when the executive branch is run by someone you do not agree with, and suddenly the decisions are all about things you do not agree with?

This rule is the executive branch increasing its power. This is a constitutional issue and should not be changed through rule making, but rather debated and decided by congress.  This rule is bad for the US.

Title: Comment from Bobbie Z.
Comment:
The proposed rule claims that Schedule Policy/ Career will remain “nonpartisan” while removing due process protections that prevent politically motivated dismissals. How does OPM intend to ensure that removals are truly based on performance or misconduct – not political affiliation – without independent oversight or appeal rights?

2.Given the elimination of MSPB appeals, what concrete mechanisms will remain in place to protect whistleblowers from retaliation if they report waste, fraud, abuse or unlawful directives? How will OPM ensure compliance with the Whistleblower Protection Act when employees lack recourse to challenge adverse actions?

3.The rule asserts that the President has broad authority under 5 U.S.C. § 3302 to strip employees of adverse action protections. However, the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 established chapter 75 procedures to prevent arbitrary removals. How does OPM reconcile this rule with the CSRA’s intent to safeguard merit system principles, and what legal precedent supports the claim that § 3302 overrides those protections?

4.The rule cites poor performance as justification, yet surveys show most federal employees are rated “fully successful” or higher. If the real concern is underperformance, why not strengthen existing chapter 43 and 75 tools- such as streamlining documentation requirements – rather than eliminating due process entirely? How does OPM respond to concerns that this rule will enable dismissals based on policy disagreements rather than genuine performance issues?

5.Career employees provide continuity across administrations. By making policy influencing roles “at-will”, how will OPM prevent loss of expertise, institutional memory, and public confidence in the neutrality of civil service? What evidence supports the claim that this rule will improve governance rather than foster instability and politicization?

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I am submitting this comment to oppose the proposed rule change by OPM Docket ID OPM-2025-0004, RIN 3206-AO80. I am a federal employee who has extensive experience working in the nonprofit, private, and public sectors in technical leadership and individual contributor roles. I am submitting this comment in my personal capacity. 

Even if well-intended, the theory of change underpinning this proposed rule change is illogical. The intended outcome of ”strengthen[ing] employee accountability and the democratic responsiveness of American government” and “Promot[ing] a Nonpartisan Civil Service” will not be achieved through the proposed removal of protections from civil servants in “policy-influencing” roles. Rather, the proposed rule change would shift the nature of estimated 50,000 career civil servants into roles that are more similar to political appointees. This shift would exacerbate the instability of the American federal government between administrations. As demonstrated by the University of Chicago’s Center for Effective Government: (https://effectivegov.uchicago.edu/primers/political-appointees-to-the-federal-bureaucracy):

- The U.S. has an unusually large number of leadership positions filled by political appointees.
- Presidents and their parties have few incentives to reduce the number of political appointees and in many cases have incentives to increase the number.
- Programs run by political appointees and agencies with large numbers of appointees perform worse than other agencies on a diverse set of metrics.
- Performance problems stem from regular vacancies in appointed positions and less qualified leaders in positions filled by political appointees.

Today, career civil servants fill the non-partisan professional role in the Executive branch. They bring the experience and technical subject matter expertise of knowing how to implement policies, what will likely be effective, and what has historically failed for what reasons. When engaged as partners, these career civil servants can strengthen delivery of policies by providing important constructive feedback to administration leadership on proposed actions. However, by removing protections from career civil servants, this regulation change would have a chilling effect that is likely to result in less effective and more costly government. Rather than engaging in constructive feedback, civil servants who would otherwise raise concerns and alternative approaches that would serve the same objectives may keep silent for fear of retaliatory action by an administration. The scope of roles that would be reclassified as Schedule P/C are disproportionately senior GS-level employees. Chilling this level of career civil servant will ultimately have a domino effect on the entire civil service.

Rather than removing protections from the civil service, OPM could streamline rules concerning performance evaluations. This approach would directly address the identified challenge of strengthening employee accountability.

Title: Comment from Anonymous

To Whom It May Concern:

I am writing to express strong concern about the proposed rule titled "Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service" (RIN 3206–AO80), specifically as it relates to its implementation within the Internal Revenue Service (IRS).

The IRS is the foundation of the United States’ system of voluntary tax compliance—a system that depends not merely on enforcement but on public trust, perceived fairness, and the consistent application of law and policy. The proposed Schedule Policy/Career reclassification threatens to undermine these principles by introducing the possibility of politically influenced or arbitrary personnel actions within one of the most sensitive and consequential federal agencies.

Key Concerns:

    Threat to Perceived Independence and Neutrality:
    Reclassifying policy-influencing IRS positions as at-will risks creating the perception—or reality—of political interference in tax administration. IRS personnel responsible for drafting regulations, providing technical guidance, or interpreting statutes must operate without fear that carrying out politically inconvenient interpretations will lead to termination.

    Chilling Effect on Professional Judgment:
    IRS employees in roles such as senior revenue agents, Office of Chief Counsel attorneys, and subject matter experts may be deterred from offering candid, legally grounded analysis if doing so could result in dismissal without appeal. This erodes the agency’s ability to maintain consistent and principled enforcement of the tax code.

    Undermining Public Confidence in Voluntary Compliance:
    The tax system functions largely because the public believes IRS decisions are grounded in law, not political whim. Reclassifying positions to permit at-will removal without MSPB oversight creates a system where taxpayers may question the legitimacy of audits, legal interpretations, and enforcement priorities—especially in politically sensitive cases.

    Contradiction with Treasury and Congressional Intent:
    The Internal Revenue Code explicitly insulates tax administration from political influence (see 26 U.S.C. § 7804(e), which prohibits certain IRS employees from acting with respect to taxpayers based on political considerations). Implementing Schedule Policy/Career in the IRS appears inconsistent with this statutory intent.

Conclusion:

While I support effective performance management, the proposed rule is a blunt instrument that sacrifices vital safeguards. The IRS cannot fulfill its mission if its career staff are exposed to dismissal without due process. Doing so jeopardizes the integrity of the voluntary tax system and risks long-term damage to taxpayer trust.

I respectfully urge OPM to exempt the IRS from Schedule Policy/Career implementation.

Thank you for considering this comment.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Citizen

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Public Comment on Proposed Rule (RIN 3206–AO80)

To Whom It May Concern:

I am submitting this comment in strong opposition to the proposed rule titled "Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service" (RIN 3206–AO80), specifically regarding its potential implementation at the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). The IRS is fundamental to the U.S. system of voluntary tax compliance, and public trust in its impartiality, professionalism, and non-political nature is paramount.

The proposed Schedule Policy/Career reclassification undermines this vital trust and raises significant statutory, constitutional, and practical concerns:

1. Statutory Conflicts

Internal Revenue Code (26 U.S.C. § 7804(e)) explicitly bars IRS personnel from being influenced by political considerations in their official duties. Implementing Schedule Policy/Career risks exposing IRS employees to politically motivated dismissals, violating explicit statutory prohibitions.

Merit System Principles (5 U.S.C. § 2301) mandate retaining and managing federal employees based solely on merit, protecting against arbitrary or politically motivated actions. The proposed rule undermines these protections by stripping procedural and appellate rights, directly conflicting with the clear statutory intent.

Prohibited Personnel Practices (5 U.S.C. § 2302) forbid political discrimination, retaliation, or actions violating merit principles. Removing procedural safeguards renders these protections effectively unenforceable, contradicting the statute’s intent.

Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (CSRA) established comprehensive adverse action procedures to prevent politically influenced or arbitrary personnel actions. Eliminating these statutory protections for Schedule Policy/Career employees directly contravenes congressional intent behind CSRA.

Whistleblower Protection Act (5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(8)) protects federal whistleblowers. Removing appeals and procedural rights significantly chills disclosures of waste, fraud, abuse, or political interference within IRS operations, undermining the integrity Congress sought to preserve.

Civil Service Due Process Amendments Act of 1990 and historical practice narrowly limited exclusions from civil service protections. The broad reclassification under Schedule Policy/Career greatly exceeds Congressional intent, weakening statutory safeguards.

2. Constitutional Concerns

Due Process (Fifth Amendment): Federal employment creates recognized property interests requiring procedural due process. The proposed reclassification eliminates established due process protections (adverse action procedures and MSPB appeals), raising serious constitutional questions.

Separation of Powers: Congress explicitly set conditions and protections for federal employees under Article I authority. The expansive executive reclassification under Schedule Policy/Career encroaches on Congressional authority, raising profound separation-of-powers concerns.

Canon of Constitutional Avoidance: OPM's use of constitutional avoidance to broadly interpret statutory exemptions undermines explicit congressional protections. Such interpretations are inappropriate without clear congressional authority, representing a misuse of constitutional doctrines.

3. Historical and Legislative Context

Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act (1883) explicitly established merit-based protections against political influence in federal employment. The proposed reclassification undermines this foundational civil service reform, directly contradicting its historical legislative intent.

Lloyd-La Follette Act and subsequent Supreme Court interpretations have recognized legitimate property interests in federal employment. Schedule Policy/Career would infringe these historically recognized protections.

4. Practical and Administrative Risks

The IRS uniquely relies on voluntary compliance rooted in public trust that the agency acts impartially and apolitically. Schedule Policy/Career creates significant public perception risks, severely damaging taxpayer trust and compliance.

Eliminating established procedural protections and appeal rights introduces significant administrative instability and litigation risk, directly countering OPM’s stated objectives of improved accountability and efficiency.

The proposal itself acknowledges the high likelihood of protracted litigation and confusion, undermining agency effectiveness and potentially creating administrative chaos.

Conclusion and Recommendations

Given these extensive legal, constitutional, historical, and practical concerns, I strongly urge OPM to explicitly exempt the IRS from the Schedule Policy/Career reclassification. Preserving the IRS's impartiality, independence, and public trust is paramount to maintaining the integrity of the U.S. voluntary compliance system.

Thank you for carefully considering these serious concerns.

Title: Comment from Kathy Camp
Comment:
I strongly object to introducing or reviving the "Schedule F" classification for federal workers. This plan jeopardizes the civil service system's foundation, which hires and promotes based on merit. Notably, President Trump has supported this merit-based approach in Executive Order 14173. By allowing for the potential dismissal of career employees without cause, Schedule F would undermine the principles established by the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which aimed to end the spoils system and ensure hiring and promotion based on merit.

Implementing Schedule F would lead to politicized employment decisions, contradicting the law's requirement for apolitical civil service. The broad and unclear criteria for Schedule F would also undermine due process rights, violating 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which demands cause and procedural safeguards for removing career employees. Depriving thousands of workers of these protections would harm accountability and might silence experts, ultimately reducing government efficiency.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) has a statutory obligation to protect the merit system under federal law (5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq.). Introducing Schedule F would erode this duty by exposing career civil servants to inappropriate political pressure, ultimately weakening the consistency and professionalism of government programs.

The Schedule F initiative endangers fundamental principles of good governance, including an independent civil service and respect for the rule of law. Given these risks, I urge the administration and OPM to reject any efforts to move forward with this proposal.

This proposal is directly at odds with the statutory merit system principles laid out in 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b), which guarantee that federal employment should be based on merit and free from political coercion. It also undermines the due process protections in 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which safeguard against arbitrary or retaliatory removals by requiring just cause and fair procedures. Stripping thousands of career officials of these protections not only threatens their job security—it endangers the government’s ability to function based on facts, expertise, and continuity.

Moreover, Schedule F would have a chilling effect on the willingness of civil servants to provide honest, evidence-based advice to political leadership, especially when that advice may be unwelcome. Silencing or punishing dissent weakens the very capacity of agencies to serve the public interest and respond effectively to complex, evolving challenges.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) has a legal and institutional obligation under 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to uphold and defend the merit system. Endorsing or facilitating Schedule F would betray this mission and politicize the federal workforce in ways that would compromise the integrity of government operations across administrations. It would erode public trust in federal agencies and increase the risk of corruption, inefficiency, and incompetence.

In short, Schedule F is a radical and dangerous proposal. It would reverse more than a century of progress in professionalizing the federal workforce and open the door to political purges, cronyism, and abuse of power. I urge the administration and the Office of Personnel Management to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement, revive, or otherwise authorize this deeply misguided classification.

Good governance depends on a career civil service that is expert, stable, and shielded from partisan manipulation. Schedule F must be categorically opposed.

I am an assistant professor on the tenure track in the College of Engineering at a U.S. R1 university. My research group depends on federal partnerships and grants from the National Science Foundation, the Department of Energy, and other mission agencies to develop advanced materials and resilient infrastructure. I write in my personal capacity—drawing on a decade of experience working with federal scientists and civil-service program officers—to oppose the proposed rule.

Modern engineering breakthroughs—from low-carbon cement to AI-enabled grid controls—emerge only when long-term federal investments are stewarded by career experts who are insulated from partisan pressure. The proposal would place tens of thousands of “policy-influencing” technical positions into an at-will category (the new “Schedule Policy/Career,” reviving many features of the rescinded Schedule F), eliminating chapter 43 and chapter 75 due-process protections. Engineering program managers and staff scientists would become vulnerable to removal for political—not performance—reasons.

Such vulnerability is not hypothetical. Since January, agencies have already cancelled active research grants for including “the wrong words,” frozen spending via ad-hoc “reviews,” and reassigned subject-matter experts in the name of “efficiency,” creating chaos and wasting taxpayer dollars. Expanding that approach government-wide would institutionalize the very politicization that has disrupted U.S. science this year. 

Anticipated harms to engineering research, innovation, and national competitiveness:
1. Erosion of technical capacity: Federal engineers at DOE, DoD, NASA, and FHWA translate fundamental discoveries into standards, test protocols, and safety regulations. An at-will regime will accelerate retirements and deter early-career talent—already in short supply—from federal service.
2. Project volatility and sunk costs: Engineering R&D lifecycles regularly exceed a presidential term (e.g., fusion pilot plants, next-generation semiconductors). When program officers can be dismissed overnight, academic and industry partners face unpredictable funding gaps, driving projects offshore.
3. Loss of scientific integrity in rulemaking: Engineering standards in areas such as pipeline safety, autonomous vehicles, and carbon sequestration rely on impartial risk assessment. Allowing political appointees to terminate the very analysts who supply inconvenient evidence undermines evidence-based regulation and public safety.
4. Competitive disadvantage: Nations including China, Germany, and South Korea are doubling down on stable public R&D institutions. Weakening ours invites a talent exodus and jeopardizes U.S. leadership in emerging technologies.

Recommended actions:
1. Withdraw the rule in its entirety: Merit-based civil-service protections are not the source of bureaucratic lag; chronic under-resourcing and ever-shifting political directives are.
2. If the rule proceeds, explicitly exempt positions that: Require a professional engineering license and an advanced STEM degree; Manage external research portfolios; or Produce scientific analyses used in regulatory decisions.
3. Strengthen whistle-blower and scientific-integrity safeguards: Codify that any adverse action against a technical employee must clear an independent scientific-integrity review board before taking effect.
4. Commission an Office of Management and Budget cost–benefit analysis focused on talent retention in STEM jobs. OMB’s own Circular A-4 requires evidence that benefits exceed costs; no such evidence has been provided.

As an engineering faculty member mentoring the next generation of innovators, I urge OPM to abandon this proposal. America’s prosperity and security rest on a career civil service able to follow the evidence wherever it leads—regardless of which party controls the White House. The proposed rule would instead codify politicization, diminish technical excellence, and jeopardize the return on every federal research dollar.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:

Re: Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service,”
Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004-0001

President Theodore Roosevelt is considered by some scholars as the first president to
expand presidential powers in questionable ways. Yet in 1895, in “The Present Status of
Civil Service Reform,” an article he published in The Atlantic, he said:
“The minute that we make men’s bread and butter depend upon their political
action, that action ceases to be influenced by considerations of the public weal,
and is taken from considerations of private benefit.” (1)
That is why I oppose the proposed rule in its entirety. It would give too much power to
the President and would politicize the Civil Service again. Returning to the patronage
system would undermine public confidence in the Service and erode the morale of
current federal employees, as well as their effectiveness.

expertise, not political affiliation, to govern the hiring, promoting, and firing of federal
employees. Of course it’s not perfect. Nothing is.
My friend is a former Land Steward, she interacted with wildlife biologists who worked for state and
federal agencies as well as private organizations, often addressing controversial issues.
While all of us wanted policy that was rooted in sound science, the federal biologists
were able to speak more freely than their state agency colleagues, many of whom
feared the loss of their jobs if they championed the approach they considered most
credible.
In addition, my mother had dementia, and my family relied on Social Security
and Medicare to help care for them through that exceedingly difficult decade. As any
caretaker can tell you, things go wrong. I can imagine how much worse it would’ve been
if these agencies had not been properly staffed, or if the staff had lacked the skills or
expertise needed to help us.
I’ve only known a few federal civil servants personally. They were all extremely
dedicated to the public good, committed to their oath of service, hard-working and
talented people. We need and deserve such competent staff. The way to hire and retain
them is through a merit-based system, not a loyalty test.

1: The Present Status of Civil Service Reform, The Atlantic (Feb. 1895):
https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/1895/02/the-present-status-of-civil-
service-reform/519723/

Title: Comment from Kimball Jonas

I was a Federal employee for 25 years, retiring from the Census Bureau at the end of 2023, so I served there under presidents Clinton, W.Bush, Obama, Trump, and Biden.

On January 21 of each new Administration, I wasn't starting from zero in my knowledge of my job. I carried forward the benefit of my previous years of experience and accumulated knowledge and skill. The same obviously could not have been said for a political appointee, if one had replaced me at any of these changes of Administration.  They would have had to learn their job from the very basics on up.  And they would have had no assistance from their superiors in this, since presumably everyone above them would also be political appointees starting from the same level of inexperience.  They would have to start from the very basic level of finding out what work the laws passed by Congress require them to do, let alone how one goes about doing it.

If certain civil service employees at those agencies were replaced, would there even be anyone left there who knew that the work for those surveys had been outsourced to the Census Bureau, or would they start off with a mad scramble to figure out how to conduct them from scratch, once they realized the law required them to conduct these surveys and regularly publish the results - monthly, in the case of the CPS?  And would there still be staff at the Census Bureau that knew how to conduct those surveys?

Politicizing tens of thousands of civil service positions would put all of this in doubt, and throw a huge monkeywrench in the ability of the Federal government to continue to do the work that Congress has charged it with.  Therefore this rule should be rejected; it must be prevented from taking effect.
