Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I submit this comment anonymously as a long-time career public servant who spent more than a decade in a major operating division of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). For roughly fifteen months I endured sustained bullying, harassment, and retaliation from a GS-15 director who already carried a documented record of similar misconduct. Two Senior Executive Service (SES) officials were fully aware of these behaviors—through my e-mails, in-person briefings, and independent corroboration from my immediate supervisor—yet meaningful action never materialized. The eventual “remedy” was to detail me, the high-performing victim, to another office, while the offending manager ultimately left federal service with yet another unresolved EEO complaint. A promised report on corrective steps was never provided.

This episode illustrates a systemic accountability gap. Government Accountability Office studies show that formally removing a poor performer can take six months to a year—or longer—once chapters 43 or 75 procedures begin. Faced with such delays and multiple layers of appeal, supervisors often choose work-arounds: detailing employees or negotiating quiet exits instead of confronting the source of toxicity. The operational costs—lost productivity, diminished morale, and talent flight—never appear in budget lines but are real and substantial.

OPM’s proposal to establish Schedule Policy/Career would help close this gap. By keeping competitive, non-partisan hiring in place while making these policy-influencing roles at-will, agencies gain a calibrated tool to remove actors whose conduct undermines mission delivery or subverts duly elected priorities. Because the authority is limited—estimated to cover only about two percent of the civil service—it preserves the merit-system backbone while restoring timely accountability where it matters most.

Recommendations for refinement

Transparency – Require agencies to publish anonymized annual statistics on Schedule Policy/Career separations and their stated bases (misconduct, performance, etc.) to guard against misuse.
Whistle-blower and EEO safe harbors – Explicitly prohibit removals under this schedule when an employee is engaged in protected disclosures or equal-employment activity.
Inspector-General oversight – Mandate automatic IG review of any separation occurring within 120 days of a protected disclosure or EEO filing.
Supervisor training – Pair the new authority with robust training on evidence standards and documentation to ensure decisions remain fact-driven and defensible.
Had such a mechanism existed during my tenure, SES leadership could have resolved my case in weeks, sparing resources and reinforcing trust in agency governance. I therefore urge OPM to finalize the rule, incorporating the safeguards above, so the federal workforce can uphold both merit-system principles and the public’s expectation of responsive, accountable government.

Title: Comment from Anonymous

It will cause short and long term havoc for any American who depends on the federal government, even to the smallest degree. Dear Office of Personnel Management,

As a current federal employee, I am writing to express deep concern regarding the proposed policy changes outlined in OPM-2025-0004-0001. These changes threaten to undermine both the integrity of the civil service and the foundational principles that protect and support federal workers.

1. Erosion of Title VII Protections and Workplace Safety

The removal of explicit prohibitions against discrimination based on gender identity—specifically through the elimination of the "Prohibition of Segregated Facilities" clause (FAR 52.222-21)—is deeply troubling. While the proposal suggests reliance on existing civil rights laws such as Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the absence of these specific contractual protections weakens our ability to ensure safe, inclusive workplaces. As a federal worker, this change leaves me and my colleagues more vulnerable to discrimination and erodes confidence in our agency's commitment to equity and equal treatment.

2. Threat to Merit-Based Civil Service

The reintroduction of policies similar to the former Schedule F—rebranded here as “Schedule Policy/Career”—presents a serious risk of politicizing the federal workforce. These changes would allow for the reclassification of career civil service roles into an excepted service status, stripping away vital due process protections and creating uncertainty about job security for thousands of dedicated employees. This undermines the core merit system principles established by the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978. As a career public servant, I rely on these principles to ensure fairness, consistency, and protection from arbitrary dismissal.

3. Deferred Resignation Program and Budgetary Irregularities

The introduction of a deferred resignation program—promising continued salary and benefits to those who voluntarily resign by a certain date—raises potential legal and ethical concerns. This program may violate the Anti-Deficiency Act (31 U.S.C. § 1341) if compensation is promised without appropriated funds. It also sets a dangerous precedent that may incentivize the quiet exit of experienced personnel, leading to knowledge gaps, reduced institutional capacity, and morale decline among those who remain.

4. Harm to Workforce Stability and Morale

The cumulative effect of these changes would create a chilling environment for federal workers. The fear of reclassification, weakened anti-discrimination protections, and subtle pressures to resign could lead to widespread attrition, decreased morale, and an erosion of institutional trust. These impacts will not only be felt by workers like me but also by the public we serve, who depend on a stable, competent, and apolitical civil service.

5. Lack of Transparency and Due Process

Finally, the sweeping nature of these changes—implemented with minimal public input or clear justification—raises red flags about transparency and governance. Federal employees, stakeholders, and the general public deserve an open dialogue on matters that so directly affect the functioning of our government.

I strongly urge the Office of Personnel Management to withdraw or substantially revise the proposed policy. Reforms of this magnitude require not only legal scrutiny but also meaningful engagement with the very workforce they are intended to govern.

Respectfully,

A Federal Employee

When employees accept a job, they are accepting a bundle of goods including: monetary compensation, work life balance, the commute, and the level of job security that comes with that position. Title: Comment from Myriam Ramsey
Comment:
I am writing as a private citizen who strongly opposes the proposed rule to create a new “Schedule Policy/Career” classification in the federal civil service.

As someone who knows and has worked alongside many federal employees—people I deeply respect—I find this proposal misguided and damaging to the fabric of our government. I personally know civil servants who have dedicated their lives to the public good: veterans who served this country in uniform and now work for the VA, researchers leading groundbreaking studies on Alzheimer’s disease, and agency professionals who work long hours in service of missions that affect millions of Americans. These are not faceless bureaucrats. They are deeply committed, hardworking individuals who embody integrity and excellence.

The proposed rule would strip these employees of long-standing protections, allowing them to be fired without due process (Federal Register p. 17183). It targets so-called “policy-influencing” roles, claiming that some federal workers “undermine the democratic process” by “subverting Presidential directives.” That language is deeply troubling. It politicizes civil service and creates a chilling effect, implying that any disagreement or hesitation—even from subject-matter experts—could lead to dismissal.

While the rule claims these roles will remain “nonpartisan” and “career,” it simultaneously eliminates procedural safeguards from Chapters 43 and 75 (p. 17186). That contradiction is hard to ignore. We’ve spent decades building a federal workforce that serves the nation, not a political party. The idea that these employees can be hired through merit-based procedures but fired at-will by politically appointed leadership is dangerous and destabilizing.

I’m also concerned that the rule removes Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) appeal rights for employees whose positions are reclassified into this new schedule (p. 17184). It’s hard to square this with the idea of accountability or fairness. There is already a probationary period for new federal employees, and existing tools exist to address poor performance. If anything, agencies need better resources and training to use those tools—not new authorities that encourage fear and politicization.

What this rule calls “reform” reads more like retaliation. It reopens the door to a spoils system we deliberately moved away from after the Pendleton Act of 1883. It creates an unstable environment where employees may be dismissed not because they’ve failed in their duties, but because they failed to toe a political line.

If the administration truly cares about performance and responsiveness, it should look to past efforts that took a strategic, human-centered approach—such as the Clinton-era reforms led by Elaine Kamarck. That process eliminated hundreds of thousands of government jobs but did so with dignity and deliberation, not punishment and fear. The expertise to do this right still exists. Reach out to the people who’ve led real reform. Don’t rush into changes that risk losing our country’s best public servants.

I urge OPM to withdraw this rule and instead convene a bipartisan, evidence-based process to explore how to improve performance while preserving the merit principles that have protected our democracy for generations.

Title: Comment from Susan Offutt
Comment:
I oppose the establishment of "Schedule F" based on my experience as a member of the career Senior Executive Service and because of my belief as a citizen in the value of a non-partisan Federal civil service.  

I served in senior roles under Presidents Ronald Reagan, George H.W. Bush, Bill Clinton, and George W. Bush.  I entered the Senior Executive Service (SES) at the Office of Management and Budget in 1989 and later served at the Department of Agriculture from 1996 to 2007.  The positions I held (OMB branch chief, USDA agency head) would be considered "policy-influencing."  Whatever my personal views, I understood and acted on my obligation to execute faithfully the policies of the Administration in which I served.  My SES colleagues did likewise.  At times I provided perspectives on policies and programs that might have run counter to the preferences of my political superiors, but such objective, non-partisan analysis is necessary to good decision making.  My experience was that political appointees understood the value of being fully informed even if it might have been discomfiting.  Once a decision was made, it was my job to execute.  
My view on this rule is that it is not about solving the problem it identifies (poor performance and misconduct) but is aimed at ensuring that policy decisions are made without fully considering the effects.  Policymakers usually know what it is they want to achieve, but the means contemplated may not be suited to the ends and often there are unantcipated consequences.  Career civil servants can provide analysis and draw on experience to fill out a full picture, and a wise political official will consider - if not heed - this advice carefully.  Under Schedule F, any such offering perceived as adverse to contemplated policy could apparently be considered grounds for dismissal.  But the criteria for dismissal are not clearly established.  This is in contrast to existing requirements for evaluating performance, which though often viewed as unduly cumbersome do require specific allegations with evidence to back them up. Moreover, the evidence for the existence of policy insubordination is weak; anecdotes from media reporting are not sufficient to establish a significant problem.  

Ultimately, the value of a non-partisan civil service arises from its accumulated expertise and its competence.  It is the case that talented people choose to work in government because they are dedicated to improving public welfare (and certainly not because they expect large financial reward).  The loss of such employees under flimsy pretenses can only weaken the ability of government to deliver the services that citizens expect and are owed.  The credibility of government decisions is badly tarnished when those in charge are suspected of partisan political motives.  

Once trust in the neutrality and competence of the career civil service is broken, it cannot be easily re-established.  The adoption of an ill-conceived and ill-advised "Schedule F" would precipitate this loss of confidence.  The US turned away from the "spoils" system because it did not deliver results that voters demanded.  Going back would only weaken this country's standing and the well-being of its citizens.

Title: Comment from Marjorie Otto
Comment:
As a parent and patriot, I am writing to express my deep concerns about the proposed Schedule Policy/Career rule. While I understand the intent to improve federal workforce accountability, I believe this proposed rule poses significant risks to the independence, effectiveness, and democratic principles of our civil service.

The proposed rule fundamentally undermines the core principles of a merit-based civil service that has been carefully developed since the Pendleton Act of 1883. By making policy-influencing career positions more vulnerable to removal, we risk transforming professional civil servants into political pawns. Our federal workforce should be composed of dedicated professionals who serve the American people, not those who can be easily dismissed for failing to align with a particular administration's political preferences.

The merit system was designed to ensure that federal employees are hired and retained based on their competence, expertise, and ability to serve the public effectively, not their political allegiance. The proposed rule threatens to erode this fundamental principle, potentially replacing expertise with political loyalty.

The expansion of executive power proposed in this rule raises serious constitutional questions. While the President has significant authority in managing the federal workforce, there must be checks and balances to prevent the wholesale politicization of career civil service positions. The proposed rule appears to grant unprecedented discretion to remove employees in policy-influencing positions, which could undermine the stability and continuity of government operations.

Our federal agencies rely on institutional knowledge and expertise that transcends any single administration. By making these critical positions more vulnerable to political whims, we risk destabilizing the very institutions designed to serve the American people consistently and effectively.

A strong, nonpartisan civil service is essential to a functioning democracy. The proposed rule could create a chilling effect, discouraging talented professionals from pursuing public service out of fear of arbitrary removal.

The examples cited in the proposed rule of "policy resistance" should not be addressed by making it easier to remove career employees. Instead, we should focus on fostering a culture of professional integrity, open communication, and mutual respect between political leadership and career professionals.

Ultimately, this proposed rule threatens to reduce the effectiveness of our federal government. Experienced, dedicated civil servants are the backbone of public service. By making these positions more precarious, we risk:
- Losing institutional knowledge and expertise
- Discouraging talented professionals from pursuing public service
- Creating a culture of fear and political compliance
- Undermining the ability of federal agencies to serve the American people consistently

As a parent, I want my children to inherit a government that values expertise, integrity, and public service over political expediency. As a patriot, I believe in the principles of a professional, nonpartisan civil service that serves all Americans.

I urge the Office of Personnel Management to withdraw this proposed rule and instead focus on:
- Strengthening merit-based hiring and retention
- Improving performance management within existing frameworks
- Protecting the independence of career civil servants
- Maintaining the high standards of public service that have made our federal government effective

Respectfully submitted,
Concerned Citizen and Patriot

Title: Comment from Dakota Krist
Comment:
As a federal employee, I strongly oppose the proposed rule to allow the president to appoint Schedule F employees. This move represents a direct threat to the principles of an apolitical, professional civil service, undermining the long-standing norms of merit-based federal employment that are critical to the effective functioning of our government. I urge you to reconsider this proposal for the following reasons:

1.	Erosion of Nonpartisan Expertise: The federal civil service was designed to be apolitical, ensuring that government decisions are guided by long-term public interest rather than short-term political gain. Introducing a new category of Schedule F employees, who could be hired and fired based on political loyalty rather than expertise, risks transforming the civil service into a partisan workforce. This shift would severely undermine the credibility and effectiveness of government agencies, which depend on nonpartisan professionals to deliver public services consistently and impartially (OPM, “Merit System Principles,” 2024).

2.	Destabilization of Agency Operations:
In my experience as an engineer with the U.S. Forest Service, I have seen firsthand how critical long-term planning is for managing complex, interdependent interests across multiple user groups, including private and commercial stakeholders. For example, wildfire logistics and infrastructure projects require years of coordinated planning to balance competing demands for public safety, economic development, recreation, and conservation. This delicate balance is already strained by inconsistent funding and shifting political priorities. Adding politically appointed personnel to this process risks introducing short-term political pressures that would further degrade this challenging but essential work, ultimately reducing the long-term benefit to the American public. Such instability would disrupt the efficient and effective delivery of services that are critical to managing our nation’s public lands (GAO, “High-Risk Series,” 2023).

3.	Chilling Effect on Policy Integrity: If civil servants face the risk of dismissal for making decisions that are politically inconvenient, this will inevitably lead to self-censorship, undermining the quality and integrity of policymaking. A politicized workforce is less likely to challenge flawed policies or offer honest assessments, ultimately eroding public trust in government (National Academy of Public Administration, “Building a 21st Century Federal Civil Service,” 2022). In technical fields like engineering, where decisions must be based on data, safety, and long-term sustainability, this pressure could lead to significant long-term costs and increased risk to public safety.

4.	Threat to Accountability and Transparency:
Politically appointed employees often lack the protections afforded to career civil servants, making it more difficult to hold them accountable for their actions. Without the safeguards of the merit system, these employees may be more susceptible to political pressure, further compromising transparency and good governance (CRS, “Congressional Oversight Manual,” 2023).

5.	Impact on Workforce Morale, Retention, and Cost to Taxpayers: The U.S. Forest Service, like many federal agencies, already faces significant challenges in recruiting and retaining specialized professionals, such as engineers, due to substantial pay disparities compared to the private sector. Adding the risk of political interference to this equation would likely worsen already high turnover rates and reduce the pool of skilled professionals willing to serve. Contrary to popular belief, contracting out these specialized roles—many of which, like contracting officers and contracting officer representatives, are legally restricted to federal employees—does not offer a cost-effective alternative. Contracting often introduces additional layers of cost, reduced oversight, and potential conflicts of interest, ultimately costing the American taxpayer far more than a stable, professional civil service (GAO, “Contract Management: DOD’s Use of Contractors,” 2023).

In summary, this proposal risks undermining the apolitical nature of our federal workforce, destabilizing agency operations, and compromising the integrity of public policy. I strongly urge you to reject this rule in favor of preserving a professional, merit-based civil service that can effectively serve the American public without fear of political retaliation.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,

A US Forest Service Engineer, veteran, citizen

Title: Comment from Lauren Gase
Comment:
May 12, 2025 

Office of Personnel Management 
1900 E Street, N.W. 
Washington, DC 20415 

Re: “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service,” Proposed Rule, 90 Fed. Reg. 17182, Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004 

Dear Office of Personnel Management: 

Lauren Gase submits these comments regarding Office of Personnel Management’s (OPM) Proposed Rule “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service,” 90 Fed. Reg. 17182 (April 23, 2025). 

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Office of Personnel Management's proposed rule changes that would establish Schedule Policy/Career as a new excepted service schedule and eliminate critical employment protections for federal civil servants.
The proposal would fundamentally undermine the merit-based civil service system that has served our nation well for over a century. By allowing federal employees in positions deemed "policy-influencing" to be removed without due process protections, the rule creates a mechanism to replace career civil servants with individuals chosen for their political loyalty rather than their expertise and competence.

Concerns with the Proposed Rule
Dismantling Merit-Based Civil Service
This rule would effectively dismantle the longstanding protections that ensure federal employees are hired, retained, and promoted based on their qualifications and performance rather than political allegiance. The proposal characterizes these protections as impediments to accountability, but they are in fact essential safeguards against politically-motivated personnel decisions that would corrupt government function.

Weakening Government Expertise and Institutional Knowledge
By removing employment protections for those in "policy-influencing" positions, the rule would create a chilling effect across agencies, driving out experienced civil servants with invaluable institutional knowledge. The proposed rule uses vague and overly broad terminology to define which positions would fall under Schedule Policy/Career, potentially encompassing thousands of positions that require specialized expertise and experience.

Undermining Government Services That Protect Americans
This rule would make it easier to purge the government of people who enforce regulations that protect everyday Americans. Agencies that hold corporations accountable, protect labor rights, ensure clean air and water, provide healthcare and Social Security benefits, and enforce safety regulations could be systematically weakened by removing experienced staff and replacing them with politically-aligned individuals who may prioritize special interests over the public good.

Threatening Democratic Accountability
Contrary to the rule's stated intent to "strengthen democracy," it would actually undermine democratic accountability by making it easier to remove career officials who provide factual information or professional analysis that contradicts political messaging. The integrity of government data, analysis, and implementation depends on civil servants being able to provide honest assessments without fear of political retribution.

Creating a Politicized Federal Workforce
The removal of chapter 43 and 75 protections for employees in Schedule Policy/Career positions would create a workforce vulnerable to political purges with each administration change. Rather than ensuring nonpartisanship, as claimed, this would lead to increased partisanship as employees would be incentivized to demonstrate loyalty to the current administration's political priorities rather than focus on faithful execution of the law.

Historical Context
The proposed rule would effectively return us to a spoils system reminiscent of the 19th century, before the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883 established a merit-based civil service. That reform was necessary precisely because the spoils system led to corruption, incompetence, and inefficiency in government. The current proposal would reverse over a century of progress in professional government administration.

Request for Withdrawal
I strongly urge OPM to withdraw this proposed rule. Instead of weakening civil service protections, OPM should focus on strengthening existing performance management tools within the current merit-based system. Enhanced training for supervisors on effectively managing performance, along with clearer performance standards and streamlined processes, would address legitimate concerns about accountability without undermining the fundamental principles of the merit system.

The American people deserve a federal workforce that serves the public interest with professionalism, expertise, and integrity—not one that shifts with political winds. This proposal sacrifices long-term government effectiveness for short-term political expediency and should be rejected.

Respectfully submitted,
Lauren Gase

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I respectfully submit this comment in strong opposition to the proposed rule to expand the use of Schedule F within the federal civil service. This proposal undermines the foundational principles established under the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which created a merit-based system to ensure that government employees are selected for their qualifications rather than their political affiliations. Expanding Schedule F would mark a serious regression, reintroducing the very conditions of patronage and political interference that civil service reform sought to eliminate.

The merit system is further enshrined in 5 U.S.C. § 2301, which outlines merit system principles that protect against arbitrary action, personal favoritism, and political coercion. These protections ensure a professional and impartial civil service capable of executing the law effectively and consistently across administrations. The proposed rule would enable the reclassification of potentially thousands of career positions into excepted service roles under Schedule F, stripping them of due process rights and opening the door to removals based solely on ideological or political considerations.

This approach contradicts the longstanding bipartisan consensus that the civil service should remain insulated from political influence. Executive Order 13957—initially issued in October 2020 to establish Schedule F—was rescinded by President Biden through Executive Order 14003 in January 2021, which recognized that such measures “undermine the foundations of the federal career civil service.” The administration's rationale was sound: ensuring that civil servants are protected from political retaliation is not just a matter of fairness; it is essential for government efficiency, continuity, and accountability.

Politicizing civil service roles poses a direct risk to institutional knowledge, operational readiness, and public trust. Agencies depend on seasoned professionals who can carry out complex policy implementation, manage budgets, and uphold statutory obligations. Removing or deterring this expertise, especially during transitions in leadership, would significantly impair the government’s ability to deliver services efficiently and responsibly.

Moreover, expanding Schedule F would discourage highly qualified individuals from pursuing federal careers, further weakening the talent pipeline into public service. It sends the wrong message to career professionals: that their positions are conditional not on their performance or public service commitment, but on their alignment with the prevailing political ideology.

In sum, this proposal endangers the impartiality, efficiency, and credibility of the federal government. I urge the Office of Personnel Management and all relevant decision-makers to uphold the merit principles codified in federal law and reject this rule. Preserving a professional, apolitical civil service is not merely a procedural matter—it is essential to good governance and the effective functioning of democracy.

Title: Comment from Darla Hugaboom
Comment:
Public Comment Opposing Schedule F – Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004 / RIN: 3206-AO80

I am writing to oppose the proposed regulation establishing “Schedule F” in the excepted service. This proposal creates a solution where there is no demonstrated problem and risks undermining the merit-based federal civil service system that has served the public well for decades.

Career federal employees are essential for maintaining consistent, effective government operations—especially during transitions between administrations. In every agency, political appointees already work closely with experienced career staff to implement laws and policies. However, these programs and operations are often highly complex, requiring years of institutional knowledge and specialized expertise. It is common for political appointees to be new to the agency’s mission and the intricacies of its work; without the continuity provided by career staff, critical public services would be at risk.

The current system already allows for the removal of employees who do not perform or violate standards. Creating a new class of “at-will” employees among management officials not only disregards this reality, but threatens to discourage talented individuals from joining or remaining in public service. The result would be a loss of expertise and a decline in the effectiveness and reliability of government programs.

Instead of improving accountability, this proposal would politicize positions that are best served by impartial, experienced professionals. The merit system was put in place to prevent exactly this kind of political interference, and there is no evidence that the current framework is failing to achieve its purpose.

For these reasons, I urge OPM to withdraw this proposal and maintain the protections that have ensured a professional, effective, and nonpartisan civil service.

Thank you for considering this comment.

Title: Comment from Amelia Frelier
Comment:
I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed rule titled Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service. In reality, this proposal threatens to undermine the integrity and independence of the federal civil service by stripping critical job protections from career public servants — including government attorneys.

Civil servants, and especially public lawyers, are not supposed to be political operatives or yes-men. Their role is not to rubber-stamp decisions, but to offer honest, legally sound advice — even when that advice is inconvenient. Government attorneys have a professional and ethical duty to assess legal risks, uphold the rule of law, and speak truth to power. These are not optional guidelines — they are core obligations, enshrined in professional standards and essential to the functioning of a healthy democracy.

This proposed rule would effectively replace those ethical obligations with a single, dangerous mandate: loyalty to political leadership. That shift would open the door to politicized decision-making, weakened accountability, and legal advice tailored to serve political ends rather than the public interest.

Our government works best when it is staffed by professionals who are allowed — and encouraged — to act in the interest of the law and the public, not the political whims of the moment. Gutting civil service protections compromises that foundation. I urge you to withdraw this rule and preserve the independence, integrity, and professionalism of our civil service.

Title: Comment from M. Blake Emidy
Comment:
The proposed rule to move policy-influencing positions be moved into Schedule Policy/Career will have disastrous consequences for the US federal service, the rule of law, and American society. I am a researcher of public administration with a specialization in human resource management in the federal service -- the broad conclusion in the research is that the politicization of the federal workforce reduces organizational performance (https://doi.org/10.1111/padm.12945). Even if the appointments made following this regulatory change are filled on a "nonpartisan basis" (which I doubt is actionable, given the lack of details that specify its ability to be implemented and monitored), the "at-will" status of both current and future public servants in this classification will certainly undermine the neutral competence necessary for effective and efficient governance.

The current administration outwardly claims that the federal government has been "weaponized" to persecute political opponents with no basis in the rule of law or neutrality. Even if this were true (and it is misleading, at best), this regulatory change makes such problems incalculably worse. We have already seen over the past few months -- particularly in the new administration's Department of Justice -- how at-will political appointments undermine the rule of law, rather than upholding it. Public servants require insulation from extraneous political influence to ensure that neutral, mission-driven work can occur in agencies across administrations. This rule would return the US back to the spoils system that preceded the Pendleton Civil Service Act, when government was ineffective, inefficient, and beholden to political interests above those of the state.

Government accountability is crucial for a healthy, functioning nation. This rule does not contribute to the cause of accountability, though. A more prudent way to achieve government accountability would be to reinstate neutral inspectors general across the federal government, and strengthen their ability to investigate waste, fraud, and abuse where it occurs. Unfortunately, as we have destroyed many of the avenues to monitor and punish these abuses, the proposed rule will likely persuade bad actors to infiltrate the civil service with the knowledge that there are no consequences, so long as they act in the interests of a presidential administration.

Title: Comment from Stephanie Goodwin
Comment:
As a scientist who has been funded by and served to review funding proposals for scientific agencies, including the National Science Foundation, I am writing to express strong opposition to the proposed rule reintroducing the "Schedule Policy/Career" classification, formerly known as Schedule F. This rule would allow for the reclassification of tens of thousands of federal employees into positions that lack traditional civil service protections, particularly those with roles in developing or implementing public policy. Should this proposed rule be adopted, it poses a threat to scientific integrity, a risk to research funding integrity, and undermines equity and excellence in STEM as well as the public trust and institutional knowledge. 

Threat to Scientific Integrity: The proposed rule is especially concerning because it opens the door to politicization of federal science. Researchers, analysts, and program managers in agencies such as the EPA, NSF, NOAA, NASA, NIH, CDC, and USDA play critical roles in producing objective, evidence-based guidance that informs public health, environmental protections, and national innovation. By removing job protections from these employees, the rule makes it possible to dismiss experts for political reasons rather than for cause or performance.

Science should inform policy—not be shaped to fit partisan agendas. This rule increases the likelihood that scientific findings may be suppressed or altered when inconvenient to the administration in power. The chilling effect alone could deter experts from working in federal service, degrade morale, and damage the quality of research and oversight for years to come.

Risk to Research Funding Integrity: Schedule F-style reclassification risks redirecting federal research funding based on ideology rather than merit or societal need. When those who oversee grant programs or review scientific proposals can be removed without cause, it sends a dangerous signal: only politically favorable science is welcome. This undermines the very foundation of peer-reviewed, objective research and jeopardizes the public’s trust in federal institutions. We have seen this risk in the past when scientists have been pressured to alter climate data, public health guidelines, and environmental assessments. 

Undermining Equity and Excellence in STEM: This rule also poses a serious threat to the federal government's ongoing efforts--including congressionally mandated programs at NSF--to promote diversity, equity, and excellence in STEM. Programs aimed at expanding opportunities for historically underrepresented groups in science and engineering—such as federal STEM education initiatives, inclusive grantmaking, and equitable data policies—are often championed by career officials with deep expertise and a long-term vision. By allowing politically appointed leadership to dismiss these professionals without cause, the rule creates a pathway to dismantle progress toward a more inclusive scientific workforce. It sends a dangerous message: that advancing equity in science can be reversed with a change in administration, rather than treated as a core public value. This undermines the merit-based principles on which scientific advancement relies and weakens our national competitiveness.

Undermining Public Trust and Institutional Knowledge: Stable, nonpartisan civil service protections are essential to maintaining public confidence in government. Eroding these protections will encourage turnover, loss of institutional memory, and reduced transparency. Over time, this weakens the resilience and credibility of our federal agencies—especially during times of crisis when scientific clarity and honesty are most needed.


I therefore urge the Office of Personnel Management to withdraw this proposed rule. It poses a serious threat to the independence of scientific and policy-based decision-making in government, and it erodes the fundamental principle that civil service should serve the public interest—not the interests of any single administration.

Comment:
I oppose the proposed regulation Docket ID: OPM–2025–0004. This regulation is a direct threat to the integrity, independence, and democratic foundation of the U.S. civil service. Below are five critical reasons why this rule must be withdrawn.
1. Erosion of Due Process and Merit Protections
This rule would strip thousands of federal employees, those deemed to have “policy- influencing” responsibilities, of their due process rights and protections under Title 5. Civil servants who have built their careers on impartiality, subject-matter expertise, and service to the public would become at-will employees, vulnerable to removal without cause or the right to appeal. This is antithetical to the merit-based foundation of the modern federal workforce.
Federal law (5 U.S.C. § 2301) enshrines merit system principles that include selection and advancement based solely on "ability, knowledge, and skills," and protection against "arbitrary action, personal favoritism, or coercion for partisan political purposes."
Further, this regulation stands in sharp contrast to the administration's own Executive Order on Restoring Equality of Opportunity and Meritocracy (April 2025), which affirms:
"It encourages meritocracy and a colorblind society, not race- or sex-based favoritism... [and] encourages achievement, and sustains the American Dream."
Yet this rule enables removals based not on merit or performance, but on vague and subjective classifications of influence. That is not meritocracy; it is political vulnerability.
2. Politicization of the Civil Service
By granting the President sweeping authority to reclassify roles into this new category, the regulation politicizes positions that are meant to remain nonpartisan. From grant managers to scientists, public affairs officers to regulatory analysts, a broad range of professionals could be terminated based on political disagreement, not job performance.
This violates key provisions of:
• 5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(1): which prohibits personnel actions based on political affiliation;
• 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8): which requires that employees be protected against partisan political coercion.
The rule threatens to dismantle the separation between neutral career service and political appointees, reverting the government to a pre-Pendleton Act "spoils system." This concentration of power in the executive branch is incompatible with democratic principles and opens the door to loyalty tests, purges, and the erosion of public trust in government.
3. Threat to Whistleblowers and Good Governance
Employees in the “Schedule Policy/Career” category may no longer be protected under the Whistleblower Protection Act if deemed to be in policy-determining roles. This rule could disqualify thousands of employees from legal recourse after disclosing waste, fraud, or abuse.
This conflicts with the:
• Inspector General Act of 1978, which depends on protected disclosures;
• Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB), which provides recourse for retaliation victims.
If enacted, this rule would silence the very people we rely on to expose corruption. It would discourage good-faith reporting and enable a culture of impunity inside federal agencies. This could have a chilling effect on ethical oversight and weaken safeguards against corruption, fraud, and abuse. It would discourage courageous public servants from speaking out, further insulating the executive from accountability.
4. Undermining Checks and Balances
The proposed rule not only dismantles protections for civil servants but also alters the balance of power between the branches of government, weakening core institutions designed to enforce lawful governance and prevent abuse. By granting the Executive Branch broad authority to unilaterally reclassify federal roles into “Schedule Policy/Career,” the regulation effectively bypasses Congress, undermines existing statutory frameworks, and eliminates essential institutional safeguards. It expands executive power over personnel in a way that threatens the independence of key administrative bodies, including the Merit Systems Protection Board and federal adjudicators. This action centralizes power in the hands of the President in a way that is inconsistent with the constitutional principle of separation of powers.
These actions contradict the constitutional separation of powers and threaten the impartial administration of law. A civil service beholden to one branch’s political will is incompatible with a system designed for checks, accountability, and balance. This not only compromises individual rights, but also damages the institutional framework that supports fair and impartial governance.

Title: Comment from Jim Carlucci

I am submitting this comment in opposition to the proposed rule that would allow policy-influencing positions into “Schedule Policy/Career (aka Schedule F). Removing civil service protections for federal employees through something like Schedule Policy/Career is a risky proposition with potentially damaging consequences for the efficiency and integrity of our government.

One of the core strengths of the current civil service system is its insulation of the public workforce from partisan political pressures. These protections ensure that federal employees are hired and retained based on merit and expertise, rather than political affiliation or loyalty. Eliminating these safeguards opens the door to a "spoils system" where political appointees could prioritize personal connections and agendas over the public interest and professional competence. This could lead to a less qualified and less effective federal workforce, hindering the government's ability to deliver essential services to the American people.

Furthermore, the erosion of job security could significantly impact the morale and retention of experienced and dedicated public servants. Knowing their careers are subject to the whims of changing administrations could discourage talented individuals from entering or remaining in public service. The loss of institutional knowledge and expertise that would inevitably follow would further weaken the government's capacity to function effectively.

Proponents might argue that Schedule Policy Career/Schedule F would increase accountability and make it easier to remove underperforming employees. However, the current system already provides mechanisms for addressing poor performance, albeit sometimes cumbersome. Wholesale removal of protections risks throwing the baby out with the bathwater, potentially leading to politically motivated dismissals rather than genuine efforts to improve employee performance. Streamlining existing disciplinary processes would be a more targeted and less disruptive approach to addressing legitimate concerns about accountability.

In conclusion, while the desire for government efficiency and accountability is understandable, dismantling the foundational protections of the civil service through this new edict carries significant risks. It threatens to politicize the public workforce, undermine its expertise, and ultimately diminish the government's ability to serve the American people effectively. A more measured approach focused on improving existing systems, rather than wholesale dismantling, is the more prudent path forward.

Title: Comment from Stephanie Compton
Comment:
Schedule F Is a Path to Politicized Mismanagement and Institutional Collapse
President Donald Trump’s proposal to revive and expand Schedule F deserves urgent scrutiny. Originally introduced by executive order in October 2020 during the final months of Trump’s presidency, Schedule F would reclassify tens of thousands of federal civil service positions—particularly policy-related roles—as “excepted service.” In plain terms, this would strip career civil servants of job protections and make them subject to at-will removal, allowing an administration to purge and replace experts with political loyalists. The order was rescinded by President Biden, but Trump and his allies are working to reinstate and expand it. 
The implications are chilling. At its core, Schedule F threatens the apolitical foundation of the federal workforce—an essential safeguard against authoritarianism and incompetence. Federal agencies are not meant to function like private companies; their missions span national security, public health, infrastructure, education, environmental protection, and economic regulation. These are complex, often high-stakes domains that depend on institutional memory, scientific expertise, and continuity—not fealty to a political agenda.
Consider the potential impact on public health. Under Schedule F, a future administration could fire infectious disease specialists at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) who issue science-based guidance that conflicts with political messaging. During the COVID-19 pandemic, career professionals pushed back against misinformation and politicized interventions; under Schedule F, they could be swiftly replaced by less-qualified ideologues.
In environmental policy, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) depends on decades of accumulated scientific knowledge to enforce clean air and water regulations. If these roles are politicized, regulatory decisions could be bent to favor corporate interests over environmental protection, undermining climate action and public health.
In national security, imagine intelligence analysts at the CIA or Department of Homeland Security being removed not for misconduct or incompetence but for refusing to tailor reports to flatter the president’s worldview. The consequences could be disastrous, leading to blind spots in foreign policy and internal threats.
Moreover, removing protections from thousands of policy analysts, economists, and legal experts would corrode the integrity of federal economic and legal governance. Independent assessments of budgetary impacts, regulatory reviews, or antitrust enforcement could be rewritten to serve partisan narratives.
Schedule F is not just a bureaucratic reshuffling—it is an attempt to dismantle the professional civil service and consolidate unprecedented executive power. It opens the door to corruption, cronyism, and catastrophic mismanagement. While every administration rightly seeks to implement its policy vision, the long-standing guardrails of a merit-based civil service ensure that government continues to function competently and in the public interest, even during turbulent political transitions.
Handing Trump—or any future president—unchecked authority over the machinery of government would be a grave mistake. The revival of Schedule F must be recognized for what it is: an assault on democratic institutions and the professional standards that underpin effective governance.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I strongly oppose the implementation of proposed rule OPM-2025-0004, “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service.”

This proposal endangers the merit-based civil service system that has provided a nonpartisan federal workforce for over a century. Career civil service workers should be able to do their job without fear of politically motivated pressure.  The protections enacted by the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 are in place for this very reason. This proposed rule would destabilize the civil service and decrease efficiency. It would enable every administration to reclassify and purge employees based on ill-defined “partisanship”, with no recourse for appeal. Having a civil service that is stable across administrations is crucial for creating a predictable regulatory environment, one which enables businesses to plan and make long-term investments with confidence.

The new proposed rule allows a large number of civil servants to be reclassified and potentially terminated due to “political” motivation. This is antithetical to the principle of an apolitical civil service enshrined in 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8), which mandates that federal employment decisions be based on merit and free from political influence.

Moreover, the vague and sweeping criteria for inclusion in Schedule Policy/Career violate the due process protections guaranteed by 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which requires cause and procedural safeguards for the removal of career federal employees. Stripping thousands of workers of these protections not only weakens accountability but also risks expert advice and dissent within agencies, undermining the very effectiveness of government operations.  

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is also bound by 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq. to support the merit system principles. Implementing Schedule Policy/Career contradicts this statutory mission and places undue political pressure on career professionals, compromising the integrity and continuity of federal programs across administrations.  

In summary, this proposed rule-making to implement “Schedule Policy/Career” under “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service” (OPM-2025-0004) threatens the very principle of civil service political protections. I urge the administration and OPM to reject any regulatory framework that seeks to implement or revive this dangerous classification.

Title: Comment from Nicolle Hill
Comment:
To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Office of Personnel Management’s (OPM) proposed rule titled “Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service.” The proposal to reclassify policy-influencing positions as Schedule F (Policy/Career), making them at-will and exempt from standard adverse action procedures and appeals, is deeply concerning. While the administration asserts that this change will allow for the swift removal of employees who engage in misconduct, perform poorly, or intentionally subvert Presidential directives, the broad scope and potential for misuse of this authority outweigh the purported benefits.

My own experience highlights the overreach of this proposed regulation. I previously held a federal position identified as potentially subject to this reclassification. I led scientists and oversaw the planning and execution of operations. Similarly, positions in my organization marked for reclassification included budget, science, administrative, and communication managers. My responsibilities did not involve influencing policy decisions in any significant manner, nor did those of the other identified positions in my organization. The prospect of career civil servants in non-policy roles being stripped of fundamental due process rights based on a broad and potentially inaccurate categorization is alarming.

My specific concerns with this proposed regulation are as follows:
	•	Erosion of Due Process: Eliminating adverse action procedures and appeal rights for a significant number of career employees undermines fundamental principles of fairness and due process. This lack of recourse could lead to arbitrary or politically motivated removals, chilling dissent and potentially discouraging qualified individuals from entering or remaining in public service.
	•	Risk of Politicization: While the regulation states these positions will remain career jobs filled on a nonpartisan basis, the ability to remove employees without cause or meaningful appeal creates a significant risk of political influence in personnel decisions. This could lead to the replacement of experienced professionals with individuals chosen for loyalty rather than expertise, ultimately undermining the effectiveness and impartiality of government agencies.
	•	Broad and Potentially Inaccurate Categorization: The proposal to convert 50,000 existing positions raises serious questions about the criteria used to identify “policy-influencing” roles. As my own experience demonstrates, this categorization may be overly broad and encompass positions with little to no direct impact on policy formulation or implementation. The term “policy-influencing” is not clearly defined, leaving room for subjective interpretation and potential misapplication.
	•	Disincentive for Public Service: The creation of a large class of at-will career employees without standard protections could discourage talented individuals from pursuing or continuing careers in public service. The uncertainty and lack of job security may outweigh the benefits of public sector employment.
	•	Potential for Abuse: The lack of clear and objective standards for determining “poor performance” or “undermining the democratic process” in this context leaves significant room for subjective interpretation and potential abuse of power.

While addressing poor performance and misconduct within the civil service is a legitimate concern, the proposed regulation is a drastic and overly broad measure that risks undermining the foundations of a professional, nonpartisan civil service. Less disruptive and more targeted approaches should be explored to enhance accountability without sacrificing due process and the principles of a merit-based system.

I urge the administration to reconsider this proposed regulation and to engage in a more thoughtful and collaborative process to address concerns about employee performance and accountability in a way that respects the rights of civil servants and safeguards the integrity of our government.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I strongly object to introducing or reviving the "Schedule F" classification for federal workers. This plan jeopardizes the civil service system's foundation, which hires and promotes based on merit. Notably, President Trump has supported this merit-based approach in Executive Order 14173. By allowing for the potential dismissal of career employees without cause, Schedule F would undermine the principles established by the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883, which aimed to end the spoils system and ensure hiring and promotion based on merit.

Implementing Schedule F would lead to politicized employment decisions, contradicting the law's requirement for apolitical civil service. The broad and unclear criteria for Schedule F would also undermine due process rights, violating 5 U.S.C. § 7513, which demands cause and procedural safeguards for removing career employees. Depriving thousands of workers of these protections would harm accountability and might silence experts, ultimately reducing government efficiency.

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) has a statutory obligation to protect the merit system under federal law (5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq.). Introducing Schedule F would erode this duty by exposing career civil servants to inappropriate political pressure, ultimately weakening the consistency and professionalism of government programs.

The Schedule F initiative endangers fundamental principles of good governance, including an independent civil service and respect for the rule of law. Given these risks, I urge the administration and OPM to reject any efforts to move forward with this proposal.

Title: Comment from Dino Di Carlo

As a biotech entrepreneur who has successfully partnered with multiple federal agencies to bring new biomedical technologies from the lab to market, I write in strong opposition to the proposed creation of the “Schedule Policy/Career” service category (OPM-2025-0004). This change would severely undermine the merit-based foundations and institutional stability that are essential to America’s leadership in science and innovation.

The process of scientific discovery, development, and commercialization is inherently long-term. It often spans decades, requiring persistent effort, rigorous evaluation, and substantial investment. Federal agencies like the NIH, NSF, and FDA play critical roles not only in funding the early, high-risk stages of research but also in ensuring regulatory and programmatic continuity. These functions depend on career civil servants who possess deep technical knowledge and are insulated from political turnover.

Introducing broad at-will authority over scientific and policy-making positions injects a new level of uncertainty—not market uncertainty, which we can model and manage, but political uncertainty, which is inherently volatile and incalculable. If the character of our scientific institutions can shift dramatically with each administration, it becomes nearly impossible to make responsible long-term investments. Why would a startup pursue regulatory approval for a technology if agency priorities might reverse next year? Why would an academic group launch a multi-year research collaboration if funding could be revoked by political fiat?

Merit-based, stable governance is not a bureaucratic luxury; it is the bedrock upon which public-private partnerships in science are built. I have seen firsthand how dedicated, apolitical program officers enable innovations to move from concept to clinic—objectively, transparently, and based on evidence. Undermining their security and independence in favor of political loyalty will degrade the very system that has made the U.S. the global leader in science and technology.

I urge OPM to withdraw this proposal. The long arc of scientific progress cannot be bent to short-term political agendas without sacrificing public trust, economic potential, and societal benefit.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004
RIN 3206-AO80
To Whom it may concern:
The Office of Personnel Management’s (OPM) proposed rule seeks to implement Executive Order 14171 by reclassifying certain career federal positions into a new “Schedule Policy/Career” in the excepted service. This reclassification would render these positions “at-will,” stripping employees of adverse action protections under 5 U.S.C. Chapters 43 and 75. 
Here are Legal Arguments Against the Proposed Rule:
1. Lack of Statutory Authority
The proposed rule and Executive Order 14171 claim authority to reclassify career positions into at-will roles, but this action exceeds the scope of OPM’s statutory powers under 5 U.S.C. 1104 and related provisions. The Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 and the Pendleton Act of 1883 establish a merit-based system that guarantees job security for career employees, subject to procedural protections for adverse actions. The creation of Schedule Policy/Career, which removes these protections for policy-influencing positions, appears to contravene Congress’s intent to protect career employees from arbitrary dismissal. The document cites historical practices before the 1960s (p. 17183), but fails to demonstrate how modern statutory frameworks permit reverting to such practices without explicit legislative approval. Without clear congressional authorization, OPM’s action risks being ultra vires and subject to invalidation under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 U.S.C.  706(2)(C).

2. Violation of Due Process

The removal of adverse action protections for employees transferred to Schedule Policy/Career raises serious constitutional concerns under the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause. Career federal employees have a property interest in their continued employment, as recognized in cases like Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 470 U.S. 532 (1985). Stripping these employees of notice, opportunity to respond, and appeal rights (as proposed in amendments to 5 CFR part 752, p. 17183) deprives them of due process. The document’s assertion that at-will status enhances accountability (p. 17182) does not justify bypassing constitutional safeguards. Courts have consistently upheld procedural protections for public employees, and this rule’s blanket exemption for Schedule Policy/Career positions is likely to be struck down as unconstitutional.

3. Undermining the Pendleton Act and Merit System Principles

The Pendleton Act of 1883, referenced in the document (p. 17184), was enacted to eliminate patronage and ensure a merit-based civil service. By reclassifying career positions as at-will, the proposed rule risks reintroducing patronage-like vulnerabilities, where employees could face dismissal based on political or personal considerations rather than performance or conduct. The document acknowledges the historical inefficiencies of the spoils system (p. 17184), yet proposes a framework that could replicate those flaws by reducing job security for policy-influencing roles. This contradicts 5 U.S.C.  2301, which mandates fair treatment and protection from arbitrary action. The rule’s failure to balance accountability with merit system principles undermines the foundational goals of federal civil service law.

4. Arbitrary and Capricious Action Under the APA

Under the APA, agency actions must not be “arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law” (5 U.S.C.  706(2)(A)). The proposed rule lacks a reasoned explanation for why removing protections for career employees is necessary or beneficial. The document’s repeated reference to “public health” (p. 17182) is vague and unsupported, failing to articulate a nexus between the rule and specific public health outcomes. Additionally, OPM does not adequately address the potential negative impacts on employee morale, recruitment, retention, or agency efficiency, which are critical to effective governance. The absence of empirical data or stakeholder input (beyond a cursory request for comments, p. 17221) suggests a rushed and inadequately considered policy, vulnerable to judicial review under Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).

5. Severability Concerns

The proposed rule includes a severability clause (p. 17221), asserting that invalid provisions can be separated without affecting the remainder. However, the rule’s components—amendments to 5 CFR parts 213, 212, 752, and others—are deeply interconnected. For example, the creation of Schedule Policy/Career (5 CFR part 213) relies on the removal of adverse action protections (5 CFR part 752). If one provision is invalidated (e.g., due to due process violations), the entire framework may become unworkable, as agencies would lack clear guidance on managing these positions. Courts may find severability impractical, necessitating the rule’s complete withdrawal.

In reality, there are systems and procedures in place to address behavioral and performance problems in the federal government. While these policies and processes are differentially used, this does not serve as proof that they are not effectual overall when employed correctly. 

This administration offers no credible data or legal/historical argument that warrants or justifies the creation of the so-called Schedule F classification. The only function this action will serve is to make it easier for the administration to terminate individuals who voice concerns about administration behavior, or individuals who seek to thwart illegal or unethical activities by the same. This, of course, is obviously the true purpose of this proposed policy. Placed in a Scheduled F position, federal employees would have no protection from the type of targeting and retaliatory behavior that has become a hallmark of this administration. 

Another concern is the application of this new career status across the federal employment sector. My understanding is that, while “policy-influencing” positions are targeted, the interpretation of what types of positions are included is less clear. There is the concern that this administration will target particular people or groups, unilaterally change them to this unprotected status, and terminate them without cause or recourse. Not surprising given the way federal probationary employees were terminated, but still an embarrassment to our democracy.

Finally, I would like to point out that the Schedule F approach is a policy imagined and perused by individuals who are clearly unskilled at workforce management and, importantly, are dismal leaders. If the only way to gain the cooperation and loyalty of your staff is to threaten them with termination, you have failed before you have begun. You will not retain the talent currently in federal service, and you will certainly no longer recruit those actually worth recruiting. Given the state of affairs in the executive agencies currently, this obviously is not of concern of this administration. However, at some point, it will become a concern of the American people. 

I urge this administration not to pursue this policy, although I suspect gathering public comments is a mere formality. I write to express my opposition to the proposed "Schedule F" changes reclassifying many civil service positions so they might be held by political appointees as opposed to career civil servants.  This is a terrible idea that will lead to the loss of substantial amounts of institutional memory, increased inefficiency, and chaos throughout countless federal agencies. Although this is a generalized problem across all branches of the federal service, I would like to specifically comment on the damage that these proposed changes will do to federally-funded research conducted through the National Institutes of Health, the National Science Foundation, and numerous other agencies. 

I am a Professor of Biomedical Informatics at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine. I provide these comments based on more than 15 years of experience as a federally-funded reseracher, but I do not in any way speak for my employer. The opinions provided in these comments are mine alone.

As a federally-funded scientists,  I have written or reviewed research funding proposals for the NIH, NSF, the Veterans Association, and the Centers for Disease Control. Although details differ across agencies, these organizations all employ expert scientists to manage the process of setting research priorities, develop announcements of funding opportunities, administer the grant submission and review process so as to ensure scientific integrity, and oversee funded research efforts to ensure compliance with funding rules, legal requirements, and organizational priorities. 

This work requires substantial expertise on many levels. The staff members who write funding announcements, oversee proposal reviews, and manage funded projects are all experienced scientists, many of whom who worked as funded academic researchers before joining federal agencies. Their detailed knowledge of agency procedures is invaluable for the appropriate handling of the funding process. More importantly, their deep understanding of the science underlying the proposals is vitally important for understanding the broad scientific landscape, identifying research needs, setting priorities, and selecting the most promising projects for funding.  

The results of these processes have been undeniable successes. Years of funding from the Defense Department and the NSF led to the creation of the Internet. NIH efforts have led to huge health advances, with virtually every new medication developed in recent years originating in NIH-funded projects. Research funding is also a huge economic driver, with every dollar in NIH grants leading to more than $2.50 in economic activity. 

The contributions of countless staff experts over the years have played a huge part in these successes.   Replacing experienced, knowledgable, and dedicated staff with political appointees will cripple the ability of agencies to provide appropriate guidance.  Our health and scientific research will suffer. 

Schedule F would be a death blow to the scientific research that has made the US a world leader in education, research, science, and health, driving revolutionary advances that drive our modern economy.  These changes must not be implemented.

Title: Comment from Katherine Smith
Comment:
I am submitting this comment in strong opposition to the proposed rule that seeks to establish a new category of employees, "Schedule Policy/Career," which would allow federal agencies to place employees in this new category, exempting them from the protections afforded to competitive service employees. This proposed rule threatens to undermine the principles of a professional, nonpartisan, and merit-based federal workforce, and I have several concerns that I urge you to address.

1. The Scope of the Proposed Rule
While the rule is presented as a mechanism to provide more flexibility in managing senior policymakers, there is a clear and concerning lack of specificity regarding which employees will be affected. How exactly will the scope of this rule be limited? Could this rule be applied to roles well beyond senior leadership, including highly skilled subject matter experts, analysts, and other nonpartisan professionals? If so, how will you ensure that only positions truly engaged in policy decisions are affected, and not civil servants performing essential, apolitical work?

2. Impact on Nonpartisan Professionalism
One of the core values of the federal civil service is that it is supposed to be nonpartisan and focused on public service rather than political loyalty. This proposed rule seems to undermine this fundamental principle by allowing political loyalty to influence staffing decisions. What specific safeguards will be put in place to ensure that political bias does not determine employment decisions for those reclassified under this rule? How will the OPM ensure that professional expertise and public service values are preserved and protected?

3. Accountability and Transparency in Reclassification
Reclassifying employees under this new category could open the door to arbitrary and politically motivated firings. How will OPM ensure that the reclassification process is transparent and accountable? Will affected employees be given an opportunity to appeal or challenge their reclassification, and if so, through what process?

4. Long-Term Consequences for Federal Workforce Stability
This rule has the potential to create significant instability within the federal workforce by encouraging the politicization of civil service roles. Have you conducted a thorough analysis of the long-term consequences of this rule on the morale and retention of federal employees, particularly those in technical and policy roles? What specific measures will be taken to ensure that the talent pool within the federal workforce does not diminish as a result of this rule?

5. Potential Impact on Federal Service Integrity
The rule could pave the way for hiring and firing decisions based on political affiliation rather than professional qualifications. How will OPM ensure that qualified individuals, regardless of their political views, are not excluded from federal service as a result of this rule? What steps will be taken to prevent this rule from being used to create a “political patronage” system, rather than a fair and merit-based hiring process?

6. Consideration of Alternative Approaches
Rather than creating a separate and less protected category of employees, what alternatives to this rule has OPM considered that could achieve the goal of more flexible management of senior employees without undermining the integrity of the civil service? Could existing rules and processes be adapted or improved without politicizing the federal workforce?

7. The Rule’s Alignment with Executive Orders and Constitutional Principles
The proposed rule seems to run counter to long-standing Executive Orders that ensure that the federal workforce remains politically neutral and focused on serving the public. Has OPM conducted a review of how this proposed rule aligns with existing Executive Orders regarding civil service protections and the principles outlined in the Constitution regarding federal employment?

In conclusion, I strongly urge OPM to reconsider the implementation of this rule. The proposed changes risk politicizing a workforce that is meant to remain nonpartisan and merit-based, which is crucial to the effective functioning of our government. These changes would undermine the professionalism and integrity of our federal workforce and damage the public’s trust in the impartiality of government services.

I appreciate the opportunity to provide input on this proposed rule and ask that these questions and concerns be addressed in the final rule.

Title: Comment from Ahmed Kablan
Comment:
Comment on OPM : Docket ID (OPM-2025-0004) and RIN (3206-AO80). 
The use of Schedule F undermines the foundational principles of the U.S. civil service system—merit-based hiring, nonpartisan professionalism, and the continuity of government expertise. Reinstating Schedule F, which allows for the reclassification of career civil servants into a category that strips them of employment protections, poses significant risks to the functionality, integrity, and public trust in the federal government.

1. It Politicizes the Civil Service

The merit-based civil service was designed to insulate federal employees from partisan political influence. Schedule F threatens this by enabling political appointees to replace experienced, nonpartisan professionals with ideologically aligned staff. This would erode the capacity of federal agencies to deliver services impartially, creating a workforce that may feel pressured to support the political priorities of the administration in power, regardless of legality, science, or evidence.

2. It Undermines Institutional Knowledge and Expertise

Federal agencies depend on career civil servants with deep institutional knowledge to implement laws, design policies, and ensure continuity across administrations. Schedule F allows for the dismissal of these professionals without cause, risking the loss of decades of expertise and making government operations more vulnerable to instability and inefficiency.

3. It Weakens Government Accountability and Transparency

A politicized civil service is less likely to speak truth to power. Federal employees must feel protected when raising concerns about waste, fraud, abuse, or policy decisions that deviate from science, law, or ethics. Schedule F weakens whistleblower protections and deters civil servants from offering honest, evidence-based advice—ultimately harming public policy outcomes and accountability.

4. It Damages Morale and Recruitment

Top talent—especially those motivated by public service—seek stability, fairness, and a mission-driven workplace. The threat of arbitrary dismissal under Schedule F diminishes the appeal of federal employment, complicating efforts to recruit and retain skilled professionals in an already competitive job market. It also lowers morale among current staff, many of whom may feel their careers are subject to political whims.

5. It Risks Government Performance and Service Delivery

Public services—such as health, safety, national security, and emergency response—rely on objective expertise and long-term planning. The instability and turnover that Schedule F invites could delay programs, disrupt implementation, and compromise the government’s ability to respond effectively to crises, from pandemics to natural disasters.

In conclusion: Schedule F is a solution in search of a problem. The existing civil service system already provides mechanisms for accountability and removal of underperforming employees. What Schedule F does is open the door to political loyalty tests, the loss of nonpartisan expertise, and the erosion of trust in government institutions. Protecting the integrity of the federal workforce is not just a bureaucratic issue—it is essential to upholding democratic governance and the public interest.
