Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Public Comment on “Improving Performance, Accountability, and Responsiveness in the Civil Service” (RIN 3206-AO55)
Docket No. OPM–2023–0013
Submitted May 13, 2025

I write in strong opposition to provisions in the proposed rule that would allow the reintroduction of “Schedule F” or similar classifications. This measure would upend the merit-based foundations of the U.S. civil service, erode essential safeguards against political interference, and run counter to more than a century of legal precedent and public policy.

1. Undermining the Merit System and Legal Protections
The proposed rule contradicts the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (CSRA), which codifies a merit-based personnel system and specifically prohibits adverse personnel actions motivated by political affiliation or personal loyalty. The CSRA established that hiring and firing in the federal workforce must be based on merit and fitness, not political expediency.

By enabling broad reclassification of career civil servants into a new at-will employment category, the rule would strip critical due process rights, exposing career officials to politically motivated removals. This fundamentally violates 5 U.S.C. § 2301, which mandates that employees be protected “against arbitrary action, personal favoritism, or coercion for partisan political purposes.”

2. Historical Lessons: The Pendleton Act and the Danger of Spoils
The effort to revive Schedule F betrays the hard-earned lessons of the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883. That legislation was a direct response to the abuses of the “spoils system,” which fostered corruption, inefficiency, and patronage. The modern career civil service arose precisely to prevent executive overreach and to preserve continuity, competence, and impartiality in public administration.

Resurrecting a Schedule F-like system effectively reinstates the spoils model. It invites future administrations—of any political stripe—to purge experts for ideological reasons, thereby threatening the institutional memory and integrity of government functions.

3. Schedule F as an Unconstitutional End-Run
While framed as an accountability measure, Schedule F circumvents established law and judicial precedent. In Humphrey’s Executor v. United States, 295 U.S. 602 (1935), the Supreme Court held that Congress has authority to limit the President’s removal power over officials performing quasi-legislative or quasi-judicial functions. Most career civil servants fit this category—they serve the law, not the administration.

Additionally, in Myers v. United States (1926), although the Court acknowledged the President’s removal power for purely executive officers, subsequent rulings emphasized the constitutionality of statutory tenure protections for civil servants. The Schedule F proposal risks violating the Appointments Clause and the separation of powers.

4. Erosion of Institutional Competence and Public Trust
The proposal would cause an exodus of experienced, nonpartisan experts. This “chilling effect” would undermine agencies’ ability to fulfill statutory missions and threaten democratic accountability. Instead of promoting responsiveness, it would incentivize sycophancy, suppress whistleblowers, and weaken the government’s capacity to act on evidence and professional expertise.

At a time when public trust in institutions is fragile, the United States needs an impartial and competent civil service—not one subservient to shifting political winds.

5. Conclusion and Recommendation
This rule is neither neutral nor technocratic. It represents a political attempt to centralize control over the civil service in a manner inconsistent with the U.S. Constitution, administrative law, and democratic norms.

I urge the Office of Personnel Management to withdraw any provision that would revive Schedule F or create any similar employment classification. Instead, reforms should reinforce due process, strengthen performance management under existing authorities, and preserve the nonpartisan, professional civil service envisioned by both the Pendleton Act and the CSRA.

This rule would give more power to an already bloated executive branch, moving our country one step closer to authoritarianism. This is not merely a critique of the current administration, but of the presidency as a whole, which--over the last two centuries--has slowly expanded its authority to encompass powers that should rightfully belong to Congress and the Judiciary.

The proposed rule will apply to positions that have been traditionally nonpartisan and as a result may encourage cronyism due to fear of firing. It may also increase turnover with each administration, resulting in loss of knowledge, the ability to perform succession planning, and wasted resources on hiring and training as a result of the higher attrition we can expect with each new president.


Policies already shift with each new administration, resulting in the expenditure of resources to undo current policies or revive prior policy initiatives based on the politics and priority of the sitting president. 


I fear that this proposed rule will worsen this issue and that we will have fewer long term, successful projects that span multiple administrations. The current civil service employs many nonpartisan experts whose job is to advise political appointees based on objective data. This proposed rule will also discourage federal whistleblowers from reporting waste, fraud and abuse.

I ask you to please consider the effect of this proposed rule in the current, highly-partisan, political climate. By making civil servants easier to fire for political reasons, we let the country slip toward extremism, instead of trying to ensure it retains an even keel for decades to come.

I strongly oppose the proposed rule.

Title: Comment from Anonymous

This policy also misrepresents the nature of "policy" work at the agency level.  I have worked on policy and partnerships teams for over a decade, and we DO NOT determine the direction of a program or make decisions regarding the execution of programs.  Our job is to advise, warn, and explain.  The advising and warning are for internal leadership.  As experts in our fields, we know what has been tried in the past and what issues resulted or may result in trying it again.  Our job is to know what's going on in the environment that affects our program.  We follow political developments, interest groups active in our programmatic issues, and outside organizations that participate in our work; this is called "environmental scanning" and it is non-partisan.  Our duty to warn leadership is part of our portfolio of looking out for the reputation of our agencies - keeping in mind our duties to the public under law.  We take seriously our obligation to be stewards of taxpayer funds entrusted to us by Congress, and in program policy offices, we spend a great deal of time promoting transparency in the work our colleagues.  We take often complex scientific activities and communicate them in ways that people not steeped in our work can understand what we are doing and why.  Our job is NOT to make decisions.  We do provide arguments in pre-decisional spaces to ensure that all sides of an issue have been considered and any potential problems we foresee are explained to our leadership - the people who make the decisions.   Often, leadership will hear our arguments, disagree, and make a decision that we might not have made if we were the decision maker.  However, once the decision is made, we always execute it to the best of our ability.  In my 23 years of federal service in public health, I have not seen a single instance of defiance of a clear decision by leadership by those of us who work in policy offices to carry it out.  The proposed rule preliminarily estimates that 50,000 federal employees could be reclassified as Schedule P/C (https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2025-06904/p-698), but it is clear by the recent actions of the Administration  (https://www.govexec.com/workforce/2025/04/dudek-calls-entire-ssa-offices-be-converted-new-schedule-f/404755/) that hundreds of thousands could be reclassified based and OPM guidance (https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/latest-and-other-highlighted-memos/guidance-on-implementing-president-trump-s-executive-order-titled-restoring-accountability-to-policy-influencing-positions-within-the-federal-workforce.pdf) shows that agencies will likely attempt to apply this more broadly.  OPM estimates that separating reclassified employees under Schedule P/C procedures will save the government money (https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2025-06904/p-702), but fails to quantify costs from increased EEO complaints (https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2025-06904/p-706) and potentially thousands of federal court complaints alleging constitutional due process and First Amendment violations. If Schedule P/C leads to large scale firings, this is likely to lead to a flood of federal court litigation.  In fact, we are already seeing this play out with the mass firings that have ensnared the government in expensive court proceedings (https://thehill.com/regulation/court-battles/5238128-supreme-court-trump-probationary-worker-firings/) (https://www.govexec.com/workforce/2025/05/most-major-agencies-must-pause-rifs-least-two-weeks-judge-orders/405232/).  This rule is an ex-post-facto attempt to justify the actions already taken to decimate the federal civil service.  OPM claims that the policy will not cause recruitment and retention problems (https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2025-06904/p-645). However, it does not consider how strong an incentive for-cause removal protections are for federal employees.  The stability of federal employment and knowing that only my poor performance would result in my removal was a strong benefit when I considered a federal career as a Presidential Management Fellow.  Based on my observations, I expect this policy will increase politically motivated and retaliatory firings, which will in turn hinder recruitment of the highest-quality candidates. An increase in firings and subsequent hirings will unnecessarily cost the federal government more money over the long run.   OPM claims that “Employees who faithfully perform their jobs to the best of their ability have little to fear” (https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2025-06904/p-674). However, this policy puts threatens employees to be fired at-will if doing work to the best of their ability, such as providing balanced considerations, is inconvenient to those in charge.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I respectfully submit this comment to raise several material concerns regarding OPM's proposed rule establishing Schedule Policy/Career, which would exempt certain career federal positions from Chapter 43 and 75 protections. These concerns are grounded in federal law, administrative precedent, and government-wide operational policy and such, warrant detailed consideration and formal response under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), 5 USC 553(c).

1. Lack of impact analysis on DEIA (Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Accessibility) - The proposed rule includes no assessment of how removing adverse action protections might disproportionately impact underrepresented groups. EO 14035, which mandates agency support for DEIA, and Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, obligate OPM to evaluate the potential for disparate impact across protected classes. Reclassifying positions without analyzing whether women, racial minorities, veterans, individuals with disabilities, or LGBTQ+ employees are more likely to be affected may violate equal employment obligations and procedural due process under federal law. A recommendation here is to include a DEIA focused disparate impact assessment prior to finalizing the rule. 

2. There is inconsistency with OPM's 2024 final rule and regulatory history. In April 2024, OPM finalized regulations interpreting "policy-influencing" roles as exclusive to political appointees. The current proposal reverses that rule without a detailed legal or factual justification. Under FCC vs. Fox Television Stations, 556 US 502 (2009), agencies must provide a "reasoned explanation" when changing course, especially where past policies created reliance interests or had been in place only recently. The proposed rule does not meet that threshold and fails to account for the reasoning underlying the prior regulatory interpretation. A recommendation is OPM must provide a clear legal rationale for overturning its 2024 interpretation of policy-influencing roles. 

3. There is a lack of cost-benefit or workforce impact analysis. There is no quantitative estimate of how many positions will be reclassified, nor any analysis of the operational and financial costs of turnover, morale decline, legal challenges, or productivity loss. EO 12866 and 13563 require cost-benefit analysis for significant rules, and the Regulatory Flexibility Act (5 USC 601-612) mandate consideration of effects on workforce size and efficiency. The absence of such analysis undermines transparency and may render the rule arbitrary and capricious under the APA. A recommendation is to include a cost-benefit and workforce impact analysis in the final rule. Use data to make these decisions.

4. There is conflict with constitutional due process principles. Removing procedural protections while retaining employees' "career" status creates tension with due process precedents. Under Arnett vs. Kennedy, 416 US 134(1974) and Cleveland Bd. of Education vs Loudermill, 470 US 532 (1985), civil service employments, particularly that based on competitive merit selection, confers a constitutionally protected property interest in continued employment. The proposed rule eliminates access to Chapter 43 and 75 procedures without offering alternative due process safeguards, raising serious constitutional questions. A recommendation is to incorporate notice, justification and appeal procedures or clarify legal standing for career protections.

5. There is a lack of clear guidance to prevent misclassification. This rule does not require agencies to follow a standardized rubric or checklist to determine whether a position is genuinely "policy-influencing." This will likely lead to inconsistent and unfair implementation, misclassification, morale issues, and legal exposure. OPM has previously issued interpretive guidance for other excepted service categories such as Pathways and Schedule A hiring. The absence of such guidance here is marked deviation from established practice and increases the likelihood of arbitrary outcomes. The recommendation here is to develop a published, standardized classification guide and require independent OPM review before designations become final.

These concerns are not theoretical. They are grounded in binding legal precedent, agency policy obligations, and the operational realities of public administrations. Without careful revision, this rule risks undermining constitutional rights, policy consistency, and effective governance. I respectfully request OPM revised the proposed rule to address these deficiencies before proceeding to finalization. Thank you for the opportunity to provide comment on this matter.

Comment:
I respectfully submit this comment to raise concerns over the lack of procedural safeguards and classification clarity in the proposed Schedule Policy/Career rule. 

1. There are no appeals or redress mechanism. The rule provides no way for employees to challenge a reclassification, even if it is incorrect or inconsistent with their actual duties. This violates principles of procedural fairness and may run afoul of Loudermill, 470 US 532 (1985), which recognizes due process protections for career employees. Many supervisors manage operational staff and execute and not shape policy. OPM must provide clear, functional guidance and prevent misuse based on position titles alone.

3. There is no notice or explanation requirement. The rule allows agencies to reclassify employees without providing written notice or justification. This creates opacity, undermines morale, and violates good administrative practice. Employees should receive advance notice with an opportunity to respond. 

4. There is risk of misclassification without oversight. Agencies could target staff based on office proximity or organizational politics. Withouth review or oversight, reclassifications may be used inconsistently or as a tool for removing disfavored employees. This risk requires a formalized internal review process and transparency measures. 

Here are some requested actions: 

1. Add a right for employees to be notified and respond prior to reclassification (and make this process fair)
2. Create a neutral review or appeal process for contested classifications
3. Require OPM to publish clear, position-based criteria, not just general references to "policy"
4. Exclude positions that execute but do not shape policy, even if they involve supervision or analysis (even provide data to policy analysts)

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
At the beginning of Trump’s presidency, there were major disruptions to the government’s science agencies. Many employees were fired or moved to new roles under the excuse of improving efficiency, but this caused confusion and chaos. Some research projects lost funding halfway through just for using certain terms. Spending was delayed or blocked on purpose, with the goal of making these cuts permanent.

While scientists were still trying to figure out how things would work under this new leadership, the Trump administration had a plan to bring more political control over government science—both in how science is funded and how it’s used in policymaking.

A big part of that plan is something called “Schedule F” (now “Schedule Policy/Career”). It’s an executive order that would change how thousands of government workers are classified. Right now, most career civil servants are hired based on skill and protected from political pressure. But Schedule F would remove those protections, reclassifying as many as 50,000 workers as political appointees who could be fired more easily. That’s a huge jump from the current number of about 4,000.

The stated goal is to hold government workers more accountable. But in practice, Trump has argued this change is needed to control the so-called “deep state”—a term that suggests career civil servants are secretly working against the president. Ironically, this move would create exactly the kind of political interference he claims to oppose.

Research shows that when governments become too politicized, performance suffers. Workers are less motivated to become experts, more likely to quit, and agencies lose both stability and experience. Radical appointees often gain more influence, while experienced professionals lose their voice. People become afraid to speak up or share honest information, which means less oversight and more mistakes.

So what does this mean for science agencies? Places like the National Science Foundation (NSF) and National Institutes of Health (NIH) are supposed to focus on science—not politics. Their success has come from having experienced scientists decide how to fund research. But under Schedule F, many of these expert positions could be turned into political roles. The policy redefines jobs like grant reviewers and program directors as “policy-making” positions, making them easier to politicize.

We’ve already seen what that might look like: non-scientists overruling expert decisions, scientists told not to talk to the public, and agencies buried in red tape to slow down or block funding—even in defiance of court orders.

It’s not just science funding that’s at risk. Agencies that use science to protect the public—like those overseeing climate change, food safety, or public health—could also be pressured to prioritize politics over facts. Scientists might face a tough choice: do their jobs honestly, or risk being fired.

Schedule F is designed to make this kind of political control over science permanent. While recent job cuts may eventually stop, the fear and uncertainty will remain if this policy takes hold.

Back in 1945, Vannevar Bush laid out a plan for keeping science free from politics, and that system has helped America thrive. Schedule F flips that idea on its head. It treats independent science as a problem, not a strength.

Erosion of Merit-Based Protections

The cornerstone of the federal civil service is its commitment to merit-based hiring and retention, ensuring that employment decisions are grounded in qualifications and performance rather than political affiliation. Title: Comment from Bonnie Janowiak
Comment:
Do not politicize government civil service work.

“Schedule F” (now renamed Schedule Policy/Career) is shorthand for an executive order that is a sharp break with civil service merit principles, which assume that career employees should be retained on the basis of performance and protected against political coercion. The US is already unusual in the degree to which it reserves the top layers of organizational leadership for short-term political appointees. Schedule F will vastly expand the number of appointees, adding a proposed 50,000 from the current 4000. It does so by involuntarily reclassifying career civil servants as appointees, removing job protections, the basic constraint against political interference.

Studies show that politicization of public services generally worsens public-sector outcomes. Public employees invest less in developing their expertise and become more likely to exit. Instability and lack of experience reduce organizational performance. Politicization increases the influence of more ideologically radical appointees relative to more moderate civil servants. Politicization also reduces accountability. Bureaucrats worried about being fired fail to share uncongenial information with their political bosses and become less likely to respond to congressional oversight. As politicization begets lower transparency and administrative capacity, it increases waste and inefficiency.
What might this mean for scientific agencies? Agencies like the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the National Institutes for Health (NIH) cannot meet their statutorily mandated scientific missions if politics, rather than scientific expertise, drive decision-making. Federally supported science has been so successful, in no small part, because agency staff are typically expert scientists beholden to ensuring that the agencies deliver world-class science. Now, many could be turned into political appointees. The proposed policy defines grantmaking positions as “policy-making,” which includes “drafting of funding opportunity announcements, evaluation of grant applications, or recommending or selecting grant recipients.” This definition, which neatly matches agencies’ own definitions for certain career staff, would include most NIH program officers and NSF program directors.
The past few months at NIH and NSF preview how politicized scientific agencies would operate. Funding choices that reflected the consensus of some of the best scientists in the world were reversed by nonscientists. Program officers have, at points, been told not to communicate with the scientific community or have had their engagement limited. Scientific agencies have been directed to effectively reduce the flow of funds to a trickle by adding new layers of redundant review and red tape and even violating court orders to reinstate cancelled grants.
Other agencies, including regulatory agencies, apply rather than fund basic science, but the risks of politicization are no less. How confident can Americans be that federal employees will not have to choose between their job and scientific values in areas such as climate change, food safety, extreme weather forecasting, or public health?
Career officials in scientific agencies are unwilling hostages in Trump’s politicization of science, wondering if they will lose their jobs for trying to defend the congressionally mandated missions of their organizations. Although the current era of layoffs will hopefully soon be over, the purpose of Schedule F is to permanently instill the degree of political control over science fueling the sense of fear that pervades those agencies now.
Science is bipartisan - simply a description of observable facts. That description is rendered biased when fear for the job is added to the mix.
job protection allows honesty and transparency - politicizing requires bias and corrupts the process.

This is a bad idea.

We have already seen the current administration embroiled in legal fights over their attempts to compromise the effectiveness of the Federal workforce by terminating thousands of Federal workers illegally. Judges have ordered that some workers be allowed to resume their jobs, but other firings have taken place, and other court proceedings are underway. Using questionable methods, the Executive branch as withheld funds obligated by Congress for research and grants, causing a chilling effect on entire industries and a ripple effect of layoffs. The current administration will have removed the bulwark of non-partisanship that has kept the Federal service trustworthy through so many administrations before it.

We have already seen the cost of lost institutional knowledge and reduced staffing with cuts to the HHS and the FAA in our own country. A president is not a dictator. This is the United States of America. It's about time we act like we care about enforcing the Constitution and the laws, even to protect private individuals from the president himself. I think we've reasonably demonstrated through the analyses of the aftermath of "DOGE" firings that the Federal government is actually accomplishing something, and the level of waste is incredibly lower than the amount of money these cut programs are contributing in savings and accomplishments.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
The OPMs proposed rule is fundamentally flawed and threatens the integrity and effectiveness of the federal workforce. This initiative is unnecessary and harmful, risking long-standing protections that ensure fair, merit-based employment. I request OPM respond with a detailed explanation of evidence, research, and reasoning behind the conclusion that this rule is necessary or beneficial. Given the extensive employee performance reviews and HR processes already in place; what specific problem does this rule aim to address?

Federal agencies already have strong procedures, performance evaluations, improvement plans, disciplinary measures, and legal pathways that effectively address poor performance and misconduct. I ask OPM to provide empirical evidence that these mechanisms are so inadequate as to require this rule and provide any research suggesting current processes fail to ensure accountability.

Removing due process protections from federal employees raises legal and constitutional concerns. The rule must address the loss of importance of protections like tenure and due process, which serve as safeguards against politicization and abuse. I urge OPM to clarify what evidence, legal authorities, or court decisions support the idea that stripping these protections is lawful or necessary. Additionally, I request details on how the agency evaluated the constitutionality of such a sweeping change.

The assertion that removing merit-based promotion and retention requirements and due process will improve government responsiveness and performance is troubling. This approach effectively creates at-will employment for certain roles, undermining transparency and accountability. I ask OPM to explain how eliminating these protections will lead to better outcomes, and to cite any research or case studies that support this claim.

The focus on policy-influencing positions as an exception seems arbitrary and overly broad. The way the rule defines policy-determining or policy-making responsibilities could include many positions vital to agency operations that require independence and stability. Explain how OPM identified which roles fall into this category, what criteria were used, and whether they considered potential negative impacts on expertise and continuity.

The claim that federal employees inject personal politics into their work is not supported by evidence. Studies show many career employees act impartially and ethically, often at great personal sacrifice. Reports cited by critics suggest concerns about bureaucratic bias are exaggerated or based on misunderstanding. I request OPM disclose the research or data that led to the conclusion that widespread politicization exists among federal workers, and how this justifies removing due process protections.

The underlying intent behind this rule appears to be controlling and intimidating federal employees, especially those who might speak out about misconduct or poor leadership. The timing and language of the proposal suggest political motives rather than genuine management reform. I urge OPM to share the rule development process, including consultations and evidence considered, and clarify whether political motives influenced the decision.

The claim that removing protections will strengthen democracy ignores a fundamental point, that federal employees are ultimately accountable to the Constitution and the law, not to any political figure. This prevents politicization, favoritism, and abuse of power. I ask OPM to provide evidence supporting the claim that fire-at-will without due process enhances democratic accountability, and how this aligns with principles of a fair, impartial civil service.

The broad interpretation of policy-influencing roles blurs the line between career civil servants and political appointees. This politicizes the federal workforce, undermines the merit system, and discourages talented individuals from entering public service. Explain how OPM determined which positions qualify as policy-influencing, the criteria used, and whether the agency considered long-term impacts on professionalism and stability.

The rule politicizes critical government functions such as scientific research, safety, and health. It enables political appointees to dismiss dissenters or silence critics, threatening independence and scientific integrity. I request OPM provide evidence that demonstrate this rule will not lead to increased politicization or harm public service delivery, especially science-based work.

The rule misinterprets and ignores existing statutes and constitutional limits. I request a detailed legal analysis from OPM, including citations, that support this expansive interpretation. OPM must explain how protections will be maintained to prevent further erosion of the separation of powers, specifically, how federal employees will be able to implement programs and follow congressional appropriations if threatened with termination.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
The proposed rule Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service, while intended to streamline federal employment practices, presents substantial concerns and I oppose the rule, as proposed. One of the core provisions of the rule is to make it easier to remove underperforming federal employees. However, data from the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) consistently shows that the rate of removal for poor performance in the federal workforce is already low not due to inefficiency, but because of structured performance improvement plans and review mechanisms that prioritize fairness and due process. Accelerating removals risks undermining these mechanisms without data-backed evidence of improved outcomes.

Secondly, the proposed changes could have a chilling effect on workforce morale and retention. Surveys such as the Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey (FEVS) highlight that trust in leadership and job security are key predictors of employee engagement and productivity. If employees perceive that their positions are subject to arbitrary dismissal, overall organizational effectiveness may decline. Stripping away procedural protections without adequate data showing that such changes improve performance metrics could lead to a deterioration of the very performance the rule seeks to enhance.

Another concern is the absence of a robust economic analysis. Historical data from prior attempts at civil service reform indicate that faster removals did not necessarily lead to better hiring outcomes or reduced litigation costs. In fact, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that legal challenges and appeals often offset any time savings in the termination process. Without longitudinal data demonstrating that this rule will yield net efficiency gains, its implementation will lead to unintended and costly administrative burdens.

Moreover, the rule fails to address systemic issues that data show have a far greater impact on performance, such as poor training, inadequate managerial support, and outdated technology infrastructure. GAO reports and internal audits have repeatedly shown that these structural issues—not the existence of due process protections—are the more significant barriers to responsiveness in federal agencies.

Finally, the proposed rule may exacerbate disparities in employment outcomes across demographic groups. OPM data reveal that women, minorities, and older employees are disproportionately affected by subjective performance evaluations. By reducing the safeguards that allow for appeals and third-party review, the rule may unintentionally increase the risk of discriminatory practices. The data suggest that preserving these protections is not merely a bureaucratic formality but a necessary check against bias in performance management. As written, its implementation could lead to legal challenges and further erode public trust in civil service institutions.

Civil servants are the backbone of the federal government —they are the gears that make the government “work.” Evidence shows that the establishment of a professional, stable civil service has made the U.S. government more effective. This rule will be detrimental to the core continuity functions of the government that all Americans rely on.

Title: Comment from Eileen Scheff
Comment:
RE: Public Comment in Response to Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service [Docket No. OPM–2025–0004]

May 13, 2025

I am writing to urge you to reject the effort to reclassify specific federal positions, which would  transform positions that rely on specific expertise into political ones. The proposed rule, “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service,” would call into question the objectivity that our elected officials rely on for our economic indicators, public health assessments, energy utilization and many other statistics. The federal statistical system plays an essential role in improving the lives of all Americans as well as informing critical policy decisions with evidence that is timely, relevant, and accurate.

Schedule Policy/Career poses a significant threat to the effectiveness of federal statistical agencies and to the integrity and quality of their products. By undermining the principles of merit-based employment and threatening job security of senior career civil servants, Schedule Policy/Career could lead to politicization, loss of trust and expertise, decreased morale, disruption of agency operations, and further promote the grift and cronyism that already is permeating the federal government under the Trump Administration. 

Federal statistical agencies are particularly vulnerable to the proposed rule due to the following:

    Politicization:  Schedule Policy/Career could lead to the politicization of the federal statistical workforce. Official federal statistics clearly influence public policy of all sorts: monetary, fiscal, regulatory, etc. Thus, a President could classify many statistical agency positions as Policy/Career and fire Bureau of Labor Statistics’ leaders for releasing or planning to release jobs or inflation statistics unfavorable to the President’s policy agenda. By making it easier to remove employees whom a President determines are interfering with his or her policies, it increases the potential for passivity or political loyalty to be prioritized over expertise and experience.  

    Importance of Trust, Impartiality and Objectivity:  Statistical agencies, such as the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Census Bureau, and the National Center for Health Statistics, need political autonomy and the ability to act independently from political or other undue external influence regarding their operations, in order to provide impartial, objective, reliable data. Erosion of that autonomy in the agencies' operations, including data collection and analysis, staffing, and publications, would undermine their perceived or actual independence, leading to a loss of public trust in the data they produce.

    Erosion of Expertise, Loss of Institutional Memory and Increase of Turnover:  These agencies rely on highly specialized professionals, including statisticians, economists, and data scientists, who possess unique technical expertise and long-term institutional memory. Statistical agencies stand to lose experts who see their career paths as less secure and merit-based than before. The loss of these experts or frequent turnover in key positions could disrupt agency operations, hinder long-term planning, undermine the agency's ability to fulfill its mission, and impair the quality and accuracy of the data.

    Decreased Employee Morale and Productivity:  The uncertainty and fear of arbitrary dismissal could negatively impact employee morale, leading to decreased productivity and difficulty in attracting and retaining top talent.

    Importance of Modernization, Research, and Data Continuity: To support their missions, statistical agencies must invest in long-term efforts such as extensive research, critical modernization projects, and efforts to ensure data access and continuity. Schedule Policy/Career could subject to agencies to changing presidential priorities, increasing senior staff turnover and disrupting modernization efforts, measurement of trends, and meaningful research.

On behalf of the American public, I urge you to reject Docket No. OPM–2025–0004 and to protect the trustworthiness of the federal statistics we all rely on. 

Eileen R. Scheff
Detroit, MI

Title: Comment from Chanda Prescod-Weinstein
Comment:
1. I oppose this proposed rule in its entirety, and every section of the proposed rule, as it allows for the reintroduction of a "spoils" system to the federal civil service. The proposed rule allows any given Administration to replace the nation's professional cadre of policy experts who serve the Constitution across Administrations with individuals who subordinate their duty to the Constitution and the law to partisan loyalties.

2. I oppose the creation of the Schedule Policy/Career as a new category of Excepted Service under 5 CFR Part 213. Moving career civil servants into a category of at-will employment makes those civil service positions vulnerable to political manipulation and influence, including by putting those employees at risk of termination should their efforts to uphold the federal oath of employment to defend the Constitution conflict with a political appointee's belief that the employee has failed to "faithfully implement administration policies to the best of their ability," as required under the proposed amendment to Sec. 213.3501(b).

3. I oppose the amendment of 5 CFR part 752 that removes the right of career civil servants to appeal the transfer of their position into an Excepted Service category, including the proposed Schedule Policy/Career category. The removal of such protection violates the Fifth Amendment due process rights of federal civil servants, specifically by removing the employees' interest in their tenure protections. See Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 70 U.S. 532, 541 (1985).

4. The proposed amendments to 5 CFR Part 213 and 5 CFR part 752 are, additionally, contrary to Congress's intent to create a merit-based civil service free from undue partisan political influence, in accordance with the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 and the Civil Service Due Process Amendments Act of 1990. Congress has determined that an effective and efficient federal civil service must be protected from partisan and improper influences. The current Excepted Services categories are intentionally limited and narrow in scope to properly carry out Congress's intent. OPM may not choose to disregard Congressional mandates in the manner proposed in this rule.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Based on more than two decades in the Senior Foreign Service (now retired) and of working with civil servants of all ranks across the U.S. interagency, I believe the reinstatement of Executive Order 13957 of October 21, 2020 (“Creating Schedule F in the Excepted Service”) with the amendments outlined in the January 20, 2025 Executive Order on the same subject would gravely damage the integrity and future of the U.S. federal civil service and poorly serve this Administration, future administrations, the United States, and the American people.

I agree with the many observers of the U.S. federal civil service argue that while our civil service cadre is generally hard-working and high-performing, the service would benefit from thoughtful reforms.  Hiring preferences for veterans and other restricted categories have in some cases limited the ability of federal civil service supervisors to hire the candidates best suited to fill vacant positions.  In federal departments and agencies without significant opportunities for vertical career development, either through promotion or through internal application for new positions of increased responsibility, fixed pay schedules and the absence of meaningful financial bonus programs limit the tools civil service managers have to incentivize performance and productivity.  I would support a structured conversation among the political leadership of the current Administration, Members and relevant Committees of Congress, groups representing federal workers, and federal workers themselves — who have many useful suggestions to offer — about how these challenges could best be addressed through existing or new legislation, regulations, and practices.  This could and should include steps to ensure federal civil service managers and supervisors who believe subordinates are underperforming or engaged in misconduct can be held accountable and, if appropriate, separated from federal service in a timely manner through transparent, fair, and non-partisan procedures.

However the changes proposed in the October 2020 and January 2025 Executive Orders will not achieve these objectives.   They are based on the assumption that senior members of the federal civil service — in positions of a confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating character — have demonstrated a widespread inability or unwillingness to implement administration policies faithfully and to the best of their abilities, and that the solution is to render them subject to dismissal without reference to long-standing procedures instituted to ensure the political neutrality of the civl service.  No credible, detailed, non-anecdotal evidence is offered of the widespread inability or unwillingness of senior U.S. civil servants to implement the policies of this or any other Administration.  In my 22-year career of service, which ended in the senior ranks, I did not observe any such evidence myself.  That includes times — such as the invasion of Iraq — at which many of my federal worker peers shared grave concerns about the wisdom and benefit for the United States of the tasks we were instructed to undertake.  Nevertheless, we faithfully executed those tasks, often at risk to our own lives and limbs.  The ranks of today’s senior U.S. federal civil service are composed, by necessity, of civil servants who were steadily promoted over several decades based on their success in furthering the policies and priorities of Presidents Bush and Obama as well as President Trump himself in his first term in office, not just those of President Biden.  Their objective professionalism is documented.

The potential replacement of these highly experienced career civil servants, whose subject-matter expertise has been developed over many years of specialized government service, with individuals who would not normally be considered qualified to assume these roles or undertake these responsibilities under existing civil service procedures would pose grave risk to the functioning of the U.S. government.  Political appointees have an important role to play in federal departments and agencies in providing essential connectivity to elected leaders, articulating the Administration’s vision, and ensuring that resources and efforts are properly aligned to promote Administration priorities.  However they are effective only when supported by a non-partisan bench of career experts familiar with the workflow of the U.S. government as well as the specialist issues at hand, who are capable of translating that vision into meaningful action.  As noted above, the U.S. federal civil service is not perfect, and would benefit in some areas from careful reform carried out through a consultative and deliberative process.  This, however, is not that.  This is naked political animus towards a class of citizens who are working hard for America.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I strongly oppose this proposed rule.  As our country's leadership changes with each election, we rely on federal civil servants to retain valuable institutional knowledge and provide nonpartisan expertise to ensure the efficient, even-keeled running of the government. I see the following specific dangers in this proposed rule:

* Swinging from extreme to extreme: A stable civil service keeps our country from swinging from one extreme to the other when we elect a new president, whether the new president is a liberal or a conservative. Reclassifying federal workers to allow them to be fired for political reasons undermines this important purpose.

* One step closer to authoritarianism: Quite apart from the current administration, the presidency as a whole has slowly expanded its authority over the past 200 years to encompass powers that rightfully belong to Congress and the Judiciary. This rule would further expand those already bloated Executive powers. It would make traditionally nonpartisan positions weaponizable and would encourage cronyism due to fear of firing. In other words, it would move our country closer to authoritarianism.

* Less long-term, successful work based on objective data: The current civil service employs many nonpartisan experts whose job is to advise political appointees based on objective data. When these people are replaced by political appointees who base their advice on what their president wants to hear, the result could very well be that we will have fewer long term, successful projects that span multiple administrations. Our country stands to lose ground in the fields of medicine and health, technology, climate, education, and commerce, just to name a few.

* Discourage whistleblowing: This proposed rule will discourage federal whistleblowers from reporting waste, fraud, and abuse because they fear retribution.

* Government inefficiency and waste: It's not just political dangers. The proposed rule is likely to simply cause inefficiency and waste. Each change of administration already brings significant turnover in the federal government. The proposed rule would increase this turnover. The result: loss of institutional knowledge, interrupted succession planning, and resources spent on hiring and training that could have gone to other pressing needs.

In summary, please consider the effect of this proposed rule in the current, highly-partisan, political climate. By making civil servants easier to fire for political reasons, we let the country slip toward extremism, instead of trying to ensure it retains an even keel for decades to come. This proposed rule should not be allowed to take effect.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
As an attorney who works in the federal government commenting in my personal capacity, I strongly oppose the proposed rule. The proposed rule states that one of its goals is to prevent the insertion of partisan or personal preferences into official duties. Unfortunately, however, the proposed rule, in fact, accomplishes exactly the opposite: far deeper penetration of partisan or personal preferences into what should be nonpartisan federal government work. 

OPM argues that under this proposed rule, the newly defined “Schedule Policy/Career” jobs will be “open to employees of any political persuasion so long as they perform well and faithfully implement the President's agenda to the best of their abilities.” But the vague phrases “perform well” and “faithfully implement” are obviously subject to numerous possible definitions and, under the text of the proposed rule, subject to the President’s own interpretation. As a result, the proposed rule allows the President or executive branch officials to fire rank and file employees who they determine, based on their own partisan or personal preferences, are not “performing well” or “faithfully implementing” the President’s agenda. 

In my personal experience working in the federal government as an attorney, existing civil service protections, as maintained by Congress in the Civil Service Reform Act, allow employees whom this rule would newly define as “Schedule Policy/Career” to make nonpartisan decisions to faithfully carry out the law and insulate them from the political pressure of fulfilling Presidential priorities or political agendas. This proposed rule would eliminate that insulation, and replace it with a system that could require rank and file employees to follow political orders or else face termination. As a result, in my view, the proposed rule should be withdrawn, and the 2024 rule should be kept in place.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
This comment is in regards to the Office of Personnel Management’s proposed rule identified by Docket ID OPM-2025-0004, RIN 3206-AO80, which would establish a new “Schedule Policy/Career” classification. This proposal represents an arbitrary and capricious departure from established civil service protections and poses a significant threat to the integrity, fairness, and effectiveness of the federal workforce. By enabling political appointees to dismiss career civil servants without due process, the rule undermines the foundational principle of a nonpartisan civil service dedicated to serving the American public and upholding the Constitution, rather than advancing the interests of any particular administration or political ideology.

The proposed rule also raises serious constitutional concerns. The structure and protections of the civil service were clearly established by Congress through its Article I authority, most notably in the Civil Service Reform Act. Attempting to alter these statutory protections through executive action circumvents the legislative process and violates the separation of powers enshrined in the Constitution. Such action sets a troubling precedent by allowing the executive branch to erode civil service safeguards without Congressional approval.

From a practical standpoint, politicizing civil service appointments would severely impair the federal government’s capacity to operate effectively and efficiently. Experienced and qualified public servants would be replaced by individuals chosen for their political allegiance rather than competence, increasing the risk of waste, fraud, and abuse. Frequent turnover, loss of institutional knowledge, and weakened oversight mechanisms would compromise the government’s ability to safeguard taxpayer resources and implement internal controls critical to sound financial management and ethical governance.

Furthermore, the proposed rule could have a chilling effect on whistleblowers and public servants who act in the public interest, as political loyalty may become a condition of employment. This threatens accountability and transparency at all levels of government.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge the Office of Personnel Management to withdraw this proposed rule. Preserving a merit-based, apolitical civil service is essential to ensuring that the federal government functions in accordance with democratic principles and serves the interests of all Americans—not just those in power.

Title: Comment from Sam Garvey
Comment:
The concept of a "Schedule F" job designation within the federal government warrants my firm disapproval. This proposition jeopardizes the foundational structure of a skilled and impartial public sector workforce, a system cultivated over generations based on competence.
At its core, establishing Schedule F directly challenges the spirit and intent of the Pendleton Act of 1883, legislation born from a need to eradicate patronage and establish a system of hiring based on demonstrated abilities. By creating a pathway to reassign and potentially dismiss a significant number of career civil servants—especially those engaged in formulating and evaluating policy—without demonstrating just cause, Schedule F invites the very political favoritism the Pendleton Act sought to eliminate. This runs counter to the established legal framework outlined in 5 U.S.C. § 2301(b)(8), which explicitly demands that federal employment decisions be rooted in merit and shielded from partisan pressures.
Furthermore, the imprecise and expansive scope for classifying positions under Schedule F disregards the essential protections of due process afforded by 5 U.S.C. § 7513. This statute mandates justifiable reasons and established procedures for removing tenured federal employees. Eliminating these safeguards for a large segment of the workforce not only erodes accountability but also creates a substantial risk of stifling independent expert counsel and discouraging critical internal feedback within government agencies, ultimately impairing their operational effectiveness.
The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) also operates under a statutory obligation, as defined in 5 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq., to uphold the principles of a merit-based civil service. Implementing Schedule F would be a direct contradiction of this mandated mission, subjecting career professionals to inappropriate political influence and thereby undermining the reliability and consistency of federal programs across different administrations.
In summary, the Schedule F proposal represents a serious danger to the fundamental tenets of sound government, the autonomy of the civil service, and the principles of legal order. I strongly urge the administration and the OPM to reject any regulatory measures aimed at enacting or reinstating this detrimental job classification.

Thank you for your time.

The existing federal human resources framework already provides mechanisms—such as performance reviews, performance improvement plans, and lawful grounds for removal—that are sufficient to address poor performance or misconduct. OPM should disclose the specific data and research that justify stripping protections from the vast majority of federal employees who are hardworking, honest, and committed to public service. This is a direct rollback of the core merit principles established by the Pendleton Act of 1883 and subsequent reforms, which sought to insulate federal employees from political retaliation and ensure appointments based on merit, not loyalty. How does the agency justify this departure from long-standing legal protections?

This is not a neutral or evidence-based reform but a partisan power grab designed to intimidate federal employees from speaking out against corruption, misconduct, or poor management. The fact that the rule was written specifically to strip protections from low and mid-level employees and to facilitate mass layoffs suggests an intent to weaken the civil service’s independence and accountability. I am requesting a response to this comment and specifically asking OPM to provide a detailed explanation: what evidence or expert consultations did the agency rely on to conclude that weakening due process protections will improve government responsiveness?

Title: Comment from Jordan Hirsch
Comment:
1. I oppose this proposed rule in its entirety, and every section of the proposed rule, as it allows for the reintroduction of a "spoils" system to the federal civil service. The proposed rule allows any given Administration to replace the nation's professional cadre of policy experts who serve the Constitution across Administrations with individuals who subordinate their duty to the Constitution and the law to partisan loyalties.

2. I oppose the creation of the Schedule Policy/Career as a new category of Excepted Service under 5 CFR Part 213. Moving career civil servants into a category of at-will employment makes those civil service positions vulnerable to political manipulation and influence, including by putting those employees at risk of termination should their efforts to uphold the federal oath of employment to defend the Constitution conflict with a political appointee's belief that the employee has failed to "faithfully implement administration policies to the best of their ability," as required under the proposed amendment to Sec. 213.3501(b).

3. I oppose the amendment of 5 CFR part 752 that removes the right of career civil servants to appeal the transfer of their position into an Excepted Service category, including the proposed Schedule Policy/Career category. The removal of such protection violates the Fifth Amendment due process rights of federal civil servants, specifically by removing the employees' interest in their tenure protections. See Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 70 U.S. 532, 541 (1985).

4. The proposed amendments to 5 CFR Part 213 and 5 CFR part 752 are, additionally, contrary to Congress's intent to create a merit-based civil service free from undue partisan political influence, in accordance with the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 and the Civil Service Due Process Amendments Act of 1990. Congress has determined that an effective and efficient federal civil service must be protected from partisan and improper influences. The current Excepted Services categories are intentionally limited and narrow in scope to properly carry out Congress's intent. OPM may not choose to disregard Congressional mandates in the manner proposed in this rule.

Title: Comment from Christine Robinson Coon
Comment:
I absolutely oppose the proposed rule, “Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service,” because it involves politicizing civil servants.  In fact, I oppose any plan “to institutionalize a much more politicized structure of control over government broadly,” especially when it comes to “public scientific investments and the use of scientific knowledge in policy actions” (Don Moynihan and Pamela Herd, U of MI).

The last line of the rule’s summary is particularly troubling. It contradicts the two lines before it which try to suggest that the plan is “nonpartisan” in nature: “These positions will remain career jobs filled on a nonpartisan basis. Yet they will be at-will positions excepted from adverse action procedures or appeal.” This is immediately followed by: “This will allow agencies to quickly remove employees from critical positions who […] undermine the democratic process by intentionally subverting Presidential directives.” 

Based on these lines in the summary, it is clear to me that any employee who is seen as disagreeing with the current President will be removed for their positions without any due process. This is not a democratic process. It is an authoritarian one.

I am especially concerned about the potential effects of such a rule on scientific agencies. According to Don Moynihan and Pamela Herd, both Professors of Public Policy at the University of Michigan, “[t]he past few months at NIH and NSF preview how politicized scientific agencies would operate. Funding choices that reflected the consensus of some of the best scientists in the world were reversed by nonscientists.” They add that “[p]rogram officers have, at points, been told not to communicate with the scientific community or have had their engagement limited. Scientific agencies have been directed to effectively reduce the flow of funds to a trickle by adding new layers of redundant review and red tape and even violating court orders to reinstate cancelled grants” (Moynihan and Herd). This is all very troubling to me.

Two of our country’s greatest strengths (in other words, what makes America great already) include our investment in the democratic process and scientific innovations. This rule would negate these strengths. We should not exert political control over scientific agencies. Let highly skilled scientists engage in the scientific process and reveal their findings without fear of political sabotage. 

They should not be forced “to choose between their job and scientific values” (Moynihan and Herd). They deserve better. And all Americans deserve to benefit from their research.

There are already processes in place to address the concerns behind this proposed rule. In sum, this rule is unnecessary and authoritarian. It is unAmerican.

Title: Comment from Anonymous

The first four+ months of the Administration have witnessed strong performers labeled as either poor performers or simply unwanted to expedite mass terminations--inviting the kinds of process the proposal complains about.  The proposal focuses on support for the incumbent president--that is clearly important when policy is at issue.  But such support is not the only factor in crafting good policy.  In particular, the proposal doesn't indicate how something eventually mentioned--respectful and professional substantive disagreement--will be possible under the proposed system, which instead seems designed to chill the kind of constructive discussion that is core to true deliberation and the best analysis and decision-making.  We are at a moment in time when quick, mass terminations and related send a strong signal that federal employment is unattractive.  What kind of system will attract talent and maintain accountability at all levels?  This isn't it.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
I am a civil servant with 19 years of federal experience, and I have served across six changes in administration. Most of this time has been working on foreign policy topics. I also have a Master’s degree in public policy and many years studying and working on topics of governance and how to craft effective public policy.  I believe that a nonpartisan civil service is important to American democracy, but I do NOT think that this rule will effectively support that goal. 

I believe it is important that civil servants continue to be hired, promoted, and retained based on merit, not political loyalty. Civil service protections should remain in place so employees can continue to exercise their best professional judgment without fear of retaliation for saying or doing something simply because it was unpopular with
leadership. As a wise civil servant once told me, my job is to advise political appointees on their proposed policies, pointing out potential pitfalls and problems, in order to help them achieve their ultimate goals. To help them avoid ‘stepping in it’. Making policy-influencing civil servants at will employees, removing their civil service protections, and taking away their right to contest terminations will make civil servants reluctant to share their advice if they think it will be unpopular with their leadership.

Bad policy proposals are common across administrations and political parties, and with the civil service protections that I enjoyed in the past, I have felt comfortable pointing out potential problems of policies proposed by appointees across the political spectrum. I have regularly highlighted adverse consequences of proposed policies on our bilateral relations with ally and adversary countries based on my expertise and experience. I have also helped advise on alternatives to achieve the stated goal. I would not have felt comfortable offering such constructive criticism if I had been an at-will employee without civil service protections.  

The proposed rule goes on at length about how difficult it is to address poor performance and misconduct among the civil service. And I agree that this is a problem. However, this rule is not designed to address that problem. Poor performance and misconduct is not committed only by people in policy-influencing roles, it takes place across all levels and types of roles in the government. Thus making policy-influencing employees easier to terminate and taking away their protections will not resolve the problems of poor performance and misconduct. In fact, by removing safeguards for those who refuse to break the law in pursuit of partisan outcomes, or presenting balanced considerations, it will politicize government functions, weaken delivery of public services, and lead to bad policies that hurt Americans.

Title: Comment from Anonymous
Comment:
Agency name (OPM), Docket ID (OPM-2025-0004) RIN (3206-AO80).
I am a civil servant with 19 years of federal experience, and I have served across six changes in administration. Most of this time has been working on foreign policy topics. I also have a Master’s degree in public policy and many years studying and working on topics of governance and how to craft effective public policy.  I believe that a nonpartisan civil service is important to American democracy, but I do NOT think that this rule will effectively support that goal. 

I believe it is important that civil servants continue to be hired, promoted, and retained based on merit, not political loyalty. Civil service protections should remain in place so employees can continue to exercise their best professional judgment without fear of retaliation for saying or doing something simply because it was unpopular with
leadership. As a wise civil servant once told me, my job is to advise political appointees on their proposed policies, pointing out potential pitfalls and problems, in order to help them achieve their ultimate goals. To help them avoid ‘stepping in it’. Making policy-influencing civil servants at will employees, removing their civil service protections, and taking away their right to contest terminations will make civil servants reluctant to share their advice if they think it will be unpopular with their leadership.

Bad policy proposals are common across administrations and political parties, and with the civil service protections that I enjoyed in the past, I have felt comfortable pointing out potential problems of policies proposed by appointees across the political spectrum. I have regularly highlighted adverse consequences of proposed policies on our bilateral relations with ally and adversary countries based on my expertise and experience. I have also helped advise on alternatives to achieve the stated goal. I would not have felt comfortable offering such constructive criticism if I had been an at-will employee without civil service protections.  

The proposed rule goes on at length about how difficult it is to address poor performance and misconduct among the civil service. And I agree that this is a problem. However, this rule is not designed to address that problem. Poor performance and misconduct is not committed only by people in policy-influencing roles, it takes place across all levels and types of roles in the government. Thus making policy-influencing employees easier to terminate and taking away their protections will not resolve the problems of poor performance and misconduct. In fact, by removing safeguards for those who refuse to break the law in pursuit of partisan outcomes, or presenting balanced considerations, it will politicize government functions, weaken delivery of public services, and lead to bad policies that hurt Americans.

Title: Comment from Geoffrey Chalmers
Comment:
I am very strongly against the Schedule Policy order because it risks gutting the expertise-based civil service and replacing this with loyalists to one administration. This is highly inefficient, as new administrations will consistently bring in their own loyalists. Every four years, removing all expertise based consistency and long-term planning. A new Schedule F policy poses a significant threat to the integrity and effectiveness of our government by undermining the professional civil service. For over a century, a merit-based system has been the cornerstone of a stable and capable public sector, ensuring that individuals are hired and retained based on their skills, qualifications, and expertise, rather than political affiliation. This nonpartisan approach fosters a culture of professionalism, continuity, and institutional knowledge that is essential for the government to function efficiently and serve the public interest effectively. Politicizing the civil service through a broad expansion of Schedule F would erode this foundation, replacing experienced professionals with potentially less qualified individuals whose primary allegiance lies with the administration in power.
The danger of injecting political loyalty into critical government positions, particularly within scientific agencies and those requiring specialized sector expertise, cannot be overstated. Agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency, the Food and Drug Administration, and the National Institutes of Health rely on the deep knowledge and impartial judgment of scientists, researchers, and other experts to make informed decisions that impact public health, safety, and the environment. Replacing these professionals with political loyalists lacking the necessary technical understanding could lead to misguided policies, compromised scientific integrity, and ultimately, harm to the American people. The same holds true for other agencies requiring specific expertise in fields such as economics, foreign policy, and law enforcement; a government staffed by unqualified loyalists is a government ill-equipped to address complex challenges.
Furthermore, the implementation of a broad Schedule F policy risks creating a system of instability and brain drain within the civil service. As administrations change, so too could the ranks of key government positions, leading to a constant turnover of personnel and a loss of valuable institutional memory. Experienced civil servants, facing the prospect of being replaced by political appointees, may choose to leave public service altogether, further weakening the government's capacity to perform its essential functions. This instability would not only hinder the development and implementation of effective long-term policies but also create an environment of uncertainty and disengagement among remaining career staff.
In conclusion, the proposed expansion of Schedule F represents a dangerous step towards the politicization of the civil service. By prioritizing loyalty over expertise, this policy threatens to undermine the professionalism, effectiveness, and stability of our government. Protecting a merit-based civil service, where qualified professionals can serve the public without fear of political reprisal, is crucial for ensuring sound governance, maintaining scientific integrity, and safeguarding the well-being of all citizens. Abandoning this principle in favor of political patronage would be a disservice to the nation and a significant setback for effective public administration.

Title: Comment from Deirdre Beck
Comment:
1. I oppose this proposed rule in its entirety, and every section of the proposed rule, as it allows for the reintroduction of a "spoils" system to the federal civil service. The proposed rule allows any given Administration to replace the nation's professional cadre of policy experts who serve the Constitution across Administrations with individuals who subordinate their duty to the Constitution and the law to partisan loyalties.

2. I oppose the creation of the Schedule Policy/Career as a new category of Excepted Service under 5 CFR Part 213. Moving career civil servants into a category of at-will employment makes those civil service positions vulnerable to political manipulation and influence, including by putting those employees at risk of termination should their efforts to uphold the federal oath of employment to defend the Constitution conflict with a political appointee's belief that the employee has failed to "faithfully implement administration policies to the best of their ability," as required under the proposed amendment to Sec. 213.3501(b).

3. I oppose the amendment of 5 CFR part 752 that removes the right of career civil servants to appeal the transfer of their position into an Excepted Service category, including the proposed Schedule Policy/Career category. The removal of such protection violates the Fifth Amendment due process rights of federal civil servants, specifically by removing the employees' interest in their tenure protections. See Cleveland Bd. of Educ. v. Loudermill, 70 U.S. 532, 541 (1985).

4. The proposed amendments to 5 CFR Part 213 and 5 CFR part 752 are, additionally, contrary to Congress's intent to create a merit-based civil service free from undue partisan political influence, in accordance with the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 and the Civil Service Due Process Amendments Act of 1990. Congress has determined that an effective and efficient federal civil service must be protected from partisan and improper influences. The current Excepted Services categories are intentionally limited and narrow in scope to properly carry out Congress's intent. OPM may not choose to disregard Congressional mandates in the manner proposed in this rule

Title: Comment from Susan Krivacic
Comment:
I strongly oppose the reimplementation of Schedule F as proposed in Docket ID: OPM-2025-0004, "Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service."

Schedule F would politicize the federal workforce by stripping civil service protections from thousands of dedicated public servants, including refuge managers, scientists, and conservation professionals in the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. These roles are essential to the functioning of the National Wildlife Refuge System and are grounded in science, law, and public service—not political ideology.

Since January 2025 alone, the Refuge System has lost more than 20% of its remaining staff, compounding a 30% decline over the past 15 years. Nearly 10% of refuges are already completely unstaffed, and no refuge in the country currently has the resources it needs to operate fully. Implementing Schedule F now would devastate what remains of the conservation workforce.

This rule would allow political appointees to fire experts without cause and replace them with ideologically aligned hires who may lack the experience or qualifications to manage public lands. That’s not accountability—it’s a recipe for instability, inefficiency, and the erosion of public trust.

Our nation’s public lands must be managed by nonpartisan professionals who are free to follow science, serve the public, and uphold conservation laws. I urge the Office of Personnel Management to reject this rule and protect the integrity of the merit-based civil service system.

Our public lands need to remain public lands for and by the people not administrations and need to be maintained and managed by their stewards and not rid them of these incredible civil servants.  Have we lost our way?  I hope not. Please do the right thing and remove the implementation of Schedule F.

Sincerely,
Susan Krivacic

Title: Comment from Bram Boroson
Comment:
I am very concerned that this rule, while ostensibly motivated by a desire to improve performance, and one could argue also to remote outdated "deep state" practices, will lead to results that are disastrous, anti-democratic, and contrary to the rights of Americans. 

Non-partisan expertise really matters. Civil servants have been appointed by disparate administrations with differing philosophies, and employees are themselves representatives given limited power where they have been trusted by the elected officials who appointed them.

Comment:
This proposed rule is simply an attempt at the politicization of the civil service in order to broadly expand executive power. Crippling the civil service will only further increase the whipsawing and dysfunction that the country faces as new administrations take over and seek to unmake their predecessor's policies while building their own edifice of executive orders and political appointments. By vastly expanding the pool of positions that can be controlled in this way and extending them further down into functional roles at a wide array of agencies will only amplify the uncertainty and chaos every 4-8 years and will cripple the USA's ability to make methodical progress on strategic goals--leaving other countries without such short-term views to supersede us. 

The impact on the scientific funding environment will be particularly stark and will only lead to further destruction of the once great US science ecosystem. Researchers and institutions will be required to remake their programs to align with the interests of each incoming administration rather than with the long-term direction of progress in their field or recommendations of bodies like the National Academy of Sciences. Waste and inefficiency will increase as work is abandoned after significant investment, and scientists will simply leave and seek employment in less dysfunctional funding environments.
